docs.title: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Architecture Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Put the application's core (domain + use cases) in the middle and let everything else plug in through ports (interfaces the core owns) and adapters (implementations for HTTP, databases, message brokers, external APIs). Driving adapters call the core; driven adapters are called by it. The core depends on nothing technical, so it can be tested without infrastructure and adapters can be swapped freely.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: checkout logic is tangled with Spring MVC, JPA and the payment provider's SDK. Switching payment providers means editing business code; testing a checkout rule requires a database and a sandbox account; a nightly batch import can't reuse the logic because it's buried in a controller.

Definition (Alistair Cockburn, 2005):

Allow an application to equally be driven by users, programs, automated test or batch scripts, and to be developed and tested in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and databases.

Term Meaning Example Core Domain model + application logic CheckoutService Driving (primary) port What the app offers PlaceOrderUseCase Driven (secondary) port What the app needs, in its own terms PaymentPort, OrderRepositoryPort Driving adapter Calls a driving port REST controller, CLI, message listener, test Driven adapter Implements a driven port JPA repository, PayFast HTTP client, SMS sender, fake

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A laptop's ports

The laptop (core) defines USB-C and HDMI ports. You can plug in any monitor, charger or keyboard that fits, from any brand, and swap them anytime. The laptop's design doesn't change when you buy a new monitor; you just need the right adapter.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph Driving["Driving adapters"] REST[REST controller] CLI[CLI] MSG[Message listener] TEST[Unit test] end subgraph Core["Application core (hexagon)"] IN((PlaceOrderUseCase)) --> SVC[CheckoutService] SVC --> OUT1((PaymentPort)) SVC --> OUT2((OrderRepositoryPort)) SVC --> OUT3((NotificationPort)) end subgraph Driven["Driven adapters"] PAY[PayFast adapter] DB[JPA / in-memory repo] SMS[SMS adapter] end REST --> IN CLI --> IN MSG --> IN TEST --> IN OUT1 -.implemented by.- PAY OUT2 -.implemented by.- DB OUT3 -.implemented by.- SMS

The dependency rule: source-code dependencies always point into the hexagon. Adapters depend on ports; the core never imports an adapter.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@RestController
class CheckoutController {
    @Autowired PayFastClient payFast;         // vendor SDK inside business flow
    @Autowired OrderJpaRepository repo;       // JPA types in the use case
    @PostMapping("/checkout") ResponseEntity<?> checkout(@RequestBody CheckoutJson json) {
        var r = payFast.charge(new PayFastRequest(json.amount().toString(), "MK-GROCERY"));
        if (!"CAPTURED".equals(r.status())) ...   // vendor status codes in business logic
    }
}

docs.title: Example 1: Checkout with Two Driving and Three Driven Adapters (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The same CheckoutService is driven by a REST adapter (JSON with rupee amounts) and a CLI used by phone-order staff (amounts in paise). It needs a payment provider, a repository and a notifier, defined as ports in its own terms. The PayFast adapter translates to PayFast's language (rupee strings, merchant key, CAPTURED/DECLINED_LIMIT).

Full Code:

CheckoutService.java (core)PortsPayFastPaymentAdapter.javaDriving adaptersOther driven adaptersHexagonalCheckoutDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out.NotificationPort;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out.OrderRepositoryPort;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out.PaymentPort;

/**
 * The hexagon's core: implements the driving port, depends only on driven PORTS (interfaces it
 * owns), never on adapters. It can run in a unit test, a web app or a CLI unchanged.
 */
public class CheckoutService implements PlaceOrderUseCase {

    private final PaymentPort payments;
    private final OrderRepositoryPort orders;
    private final NotificationPort notifications;
    private int nextId = 1;

    public CheckoutService(PaymentPort payments, OrderRepositoryPort orders, NotificationPort notifications) {
        this.payments = payments; // (1)!
        this.orders = orders;
        this.notifications = notifications;
    }

    @Override
    public Order placeOrder(PlaceOrderCommand cmd) {
        String id = "ORD-" + nextId++;
        boolean paid = payments.charge(cmd.customerId(), cmd.totalPaise(), id);
        Order order = new Order(id, cmd.customerId(), cmd.totalPaise(),
                paid ? Order.Status.PAID : Order.Status.PAYMENT_DECLINED);
        orders.save(order);
        notifications.notify(cmd.phone(), paid ? "Order " + id + " confirmed" : "Payment for " + id + " declined");
        return order;
    }
}
  1. Constructor injection of ports. The core has no idea whether payments go to PayFast, a fake, or a test double.
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.Order;

/** Driving (primary) port: what the application offers to the outside world. */
public interface PlaceOrderUseCase {

    record PlaceOrderCommand(String customerId, String phone, long totalPaise) {
        public PlaceOrderCommand {
            if (totalPaise <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("total must be positive");
            }
        }
    }

    Order placeOrder(PlaceOrderCommand command);
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out;

/** Driven (secondary) port: what the core needs from a payment provider, in the core's terms. */
public interface PaymentPort {
    boolean charge(String customerId, long amountPaise, String reference);
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.Order;

/** Driven port for persistence. */
public interface OrderRepositoryPort {
    void save(Order order);

    int count();
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out;

/** Driven port for telling the customer something. SMS, push or e-mail is an adapter decision. */
public interface NotificationPort {
    void notify(String phone, String message);
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out.PaymentPort;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Driven adapter for a (fictional) payment provider "PayFast". It speaks PayFast's language:
 * rupee strings, a merchant key, and status codes, and translates back to the port's boolean.
 */
public class PayFastPaymentAdapter implements PaymentPort {

    private final Function<Map<String, String>, Map<String, String>> payFastApi; // the HTTP client

    public PayFastPaymentAdapter(Function<Map<String, String>, Map<String, String>> payFastApi) {
        this.payFastApi = payFastApi;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean charge(String customerId, long amountPaise, String reference) {
        Map<String, String> response = payFastApi.apply(Map.of(
                "merchant_key", "MK-GROCERY", // (1)!
                "amount", String.format("%d.%02d", amountPaise / 100, amountPaise % 100),
                "customer_ref", customerId,
                "txn_ref", reference));
        return "CAPTURED".equals(response.get("status")); // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Vendor-specific details (merchant key, rupee strings) live only in the adapter.
  2. The vendor's status codes are translated into the port's simple contract.
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.in;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.Order;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase.PlaceOrderCommand;

import java.util.Map;

/** Driving adapter: HTTP/JSON → command → use case → HTTP response. (A @RestController in Spring.) */
public class RestCheckoutAdapter {

    private final PlaceOrderUseCase useCase;

    public RestCheckoutAdapter(PlaceOrderUseCase useCase) {
        this.useCase = useCase;
    }

    public String post(Map<String, String> json) {
        try {
            Order o = useCase.placeOrder(new PlaceOrderCommand(json.get("customerId"), json.get("phone"),
                    Math.round(Double.parseDouble(json.get("totalRupees")) * 100)));
            return (o.status() == Order.Status.PAID ? "201 " : "402 ") + o;
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            return "400 " + e.getMessage();
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.in;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase.PlaceOrderCommand;

/** Another driving adapter: support staff place phone orders from a terminal. Same use case. */
public class CliCheckoutAdapter {

    private final PlaceOrderUseCase useCase;

    public CliCheckoutAdapter(PlaceOrderUseCase useCase) {
        this.useCase = useCase;
    }

    /** Input like: {@code order CUST-77 +91-98450-22222 64900} (amount in paise). */
    public String run(String commandLine) {
        String[] p = commandLine.split(" ");
        return "cli> " + useCase.placeOrder(new PlaceOrderCommand(p[1], p[2], Long.parseLong(p[3]))).status();
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.Order;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out.OrderRepositoryPort;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Driven adapter for persistence. A JPA or JDBC adapter would implement the same port. */
public class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepositoryPort {

    private final List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public void save(Order order) {
        orders.add(order);
    }

    @Override
    public int count() {
        return orders.size();
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.out.NotificationPort;

/** Driven adapter: sends an SMS (printed here instead of calling an SMS gateway). */
public class SmsNotificationAdapter implements NotificationPort {

    @Override
    public void notify(String phone, String message) {
        System.out.println("    sms to " + phone + ": " + message);
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.in.CliCheckoutAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.in.RestCheckoutAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out.InMemoryOrderRepository;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out.PayFastPaymentAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out.SmsNotificationAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.CheckoutService;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class HexagonalCheckoutDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Fake PayFast HTTP API: declines amounts over ₹5,000.
        var payFast = new PayFastPaymentAdapter(request -> {
            System.out.println("    PayFast API <- " + new TreeMap<>(request));
            boolean ok = Double.parseDouble(request.get("amount")) <= 5_000;
            return Map.of("status", ok ? "CAPTURED" : "DECLINED_LIMIT");
        });
        var repository = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
        var core = new CheckoutService(payFast, repository, new SmsNotificationAdapter()); // composition root

        var rest = new RestCheckoutAdapter(core);
        var cli = new CliCheckoutAdapter(core);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: one core, two driving adapters, three driven adapters ===");
        System.out.println(rest.post(Map.of("customerId", "CUST-42", "phone", "+91-98450-11111", "totalRupees", "1447.00")));
        System.out.println(cli.run("order CUST-77 +91-98450-22222 899000"));
        System.out.println(rest.post(Map.of("customerId", "CUST-42", "phone", "+91-98450-11111", "totalRupees", "-5")));
        System.out.println("Orders saved: " + repository.count());
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: one core, two driving adapters, three driven adapters ===
    PayFast API <- {amount=1447.00, customer_ref=CUST-42, merchant_key=MK-GROCERY, txn_ref=ORD-1}
    sms to +91-98450-11111: Order ORD-1 confirmed
201 Order[id=ORD-1, customerId=CUST-42, totalPaise=144700, status=PAID]
    PayFast API <- {amount=8990.00, customer_ref=CUST-77, merchant_key=MK-GROCERY, txn_ref=ORD-2}
    sms to +91-98450-22222: Payment for ORD-2 declined
cli> PAYMENT_DECLINED
400 total must be positive
Orders saved: 2

Why hexagonal here:

  • Switching payment providers = writing one new adapter.
  • The core is unit-tested with lambdas as adapters (see the tests); no Spring context, no database.
  • New channels (CLI, batch, events) reuse the exact same use case.

docs.title: Example 2: Swappable Routing for Fares (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: The fare core needs a route (km, minutes). The GeoMaps adapter calls an online API that returns meters and seconds; an offline adapter estimates from straight-line distance. A composite fallback adapter tries GeoMaps and falls back offline when it's down. The fare rules never change.

Full Code:

FareHexagon.javaFareDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** The fare core and its driven port for routing, with three interchangeable adapters. */
public final class FareHexagon {

    private FareHexagon() {
    }

    public record Point(double lat, double lon) {
    }

    public record Route(double km, int minutes, String source) {
    }

    /** Driven port, owned by the core and expressed in its units (km, minutes). */
    public interface RoutePort {
        Route route(Point from, Point to);
    }

    /** The core: fare rules only. */
    public static final class FareCalculator {
        private final RoutePort routes;

        public FareCalculator(RoutePort routes) {
            this.routes = routes;
        }

        public String quote(Point from, Point to) {
            Route r = routes.route(from, to);
            long paise = 5_000 + Math.round(r.km() * 1_200) + r.minutes() * 150L; // base + per km + per minute
            return String.format("₹%d.%02d for %.1f km / %d min (route from %s)",
                    paise / 100, paise % 100, r.km(), r.minutes(), r.source());
        }
    }

    /** Adapter for a (fictional) online maps API returning meters and seconds as JSON-ish maps. */
    public static final class GeoMapsAdapter implements RoutePort {
        private final Function<String, Map<String, Long>> api;

        public GeoMapsAdapter(Function<String, Map<String, Long>> api) {
            this.api = api;
        }

        @Override
        public Route route(Point from, Point to) {
            Map<String, Long> json = api.apply(from.lat() + "," + from.lon() + ";" + to.lat() + "," + to.lon());
            return new Route(json.get("distance_m") / 1000.0, (int) (json.get("duration_s") / 60), "GeoMaps traffic"); // (1)!
        }
    }

    /** Adapter that needs no network: straight-line distance × detour factor, average city speed. */
    public static final class OfflineEstimateAdapter implements RoutePort {
        @Override
        public Route route(Point from, Point to) {
            double dLat = StrictMath.toRadians(to.lat() - from.lat());
            double dLon = StrictMath.toRadians(to.lon() - from.lon());
            double a = StrictMath.pow(StrictMath.sin(dLat / 2), 2) + StrictMath.cos(StrictMath.toRadians(from.lat()))
                    * StrictMath.cos(StrictMath.toRadians(to.lat())) * StrictMath.pow(StrictMath.sin(dLon / 2), 2);
            double km = 6371 * 2 * StrictMath.atan2(StrictMath.sqrt(a), StrictMath.sqrt(1 - a)) * 1.3; // (2)!
            return new Route(km, (int) Math.ceil(km / 22 * 60), "offline estimate");
        }
    }

    /** Adapters compose: try the primary, fall back to the secondary. The core never knows. */
    public static final class FallbackRouteAdapter implements RoutePort {
        private final RoutePort primary;
        private final RoutePort fallback;

        public FallbackRouteAdapter(RoutePort primary, RoutePort fallback) {
            this.primary = primary;
            this.fallback = fallback;
        }

        @Override
        public Route route(Point from, Point to) {
            try {
                return primary.route(from, to);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                return fallback.route(from, to); // (3)!
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. The adapter converts the API's units (meters, seconds) into the port's units (km, minutes).
  2. Haversine distance × 1.3 detour factor. StrictMath keeps results identical on every platform.
  3. Adapters can be composed (a Decorator/Composite of ports) for resilience, invisible to the core.
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare.FareHexagon.FallbackRouteAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare.FareHexagon.FareCalculator;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare.FareHexagon.GeoMapsAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare.FareHexagon.OfflineEstimateAdapter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.fare.FareHexagon.Point;

import java.util.Map;

public class FareDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Point koramangala = new Point(12.9352, 77.6245);
        Point airport = new Point(13.1986, 77.7066);
        boolean[] mapsUp = {true};
        var geoMaps = new GeoMapsAdapter(query -> {
            if (!mapsUp[0]) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("GeoMaps 503");
            }
            return Map.of("distance_m", 38_400L, "duration_s", 4_020L);
        });

        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: same fare core, swappable routing adapters ===");
        System.out.println("GeoMaps adapter  : " + new FareCalculator(geoMaps).quote(koramangala, airport));
        System.out.println("Offline adapter  : " + new FareCalculator(new OfflineEstimateAdapter()).quote(koramangala, airport));

        var resilient = new FareCalculator(new FallbackRouteAdapter(geoMaps, new OfflineEstimateAdapter()));
        mapsUp[0] = false;
        System.out.println("GeoMaps down     : " + resilient.quote(koramangala, airport));
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: same fare core, swappable routing adapters ===
GeoMaps adapter  : ₹611.30 for 38.4 km / 67 min (route from GeoMaps traffic)
Offline adapter  : ₹691.00 for 39.8 km / 109 min (route from offline estimate)
GeoMaps down     : ₹691.00 for 39.8 km / 109 min (route from offline estimate)

Why hexagonal here:

  • External dependencies are replaceable and composable.
  • Each adapter can be tested against recorded API responses; the core against a trivial fake.

docs.title: Example 3: One Use Case, Event and Batch Channels (Insurance)
docs.text:
Scenario: Claims come from the mobile app (as events on a topic) and from a partner garage network (as a nightly CSV). Two driving adapters parse their formats and call the same SubmitClaim port, so validation and triage rules are identical for every channel.

Full Code:

ClaimsHexagon.javaClaimsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.claims;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** The claims core with ONE driving port used by two very different driving adapters. */
public final class ClaimsHexagon {

    private ClaimsHexagon() {
    }

    public record Claim(String policy, String type, long amountPaise) {
    }

    /** Driving port. */
    public interface SubmitClaim {
        String submit(Claim claim);
    }

    /** The core: validation and a simple triage rule. */
    public static final class ClaimsCore implements SubmitClaim {
        private final List<Claim> accepted = new ArrayList<>();

        @Override
        public String submit(Claim c) {
            if (!c.policy().matches("POL-\\d{4}")) {
                return "REJECTED " + c.policy() + ": invalid policy number";
            }
            if (c.amountPaise() <= 0) {
                return "REJECTED " + c.policy() + ": amount must be positive";
            }
            accepted.add(c);
            String route = c.amountPaise() > 5_000_000 ? "manual review" : "fast track"; // (1)!
            return "ACCEPTED " + c.policy() + " " + c.type() + " -> " + route;
        }

        public int acceptedCount() {
            return accepted.size();
        }
    }

    /** Driving adapter 1: an event from the mobile app arrives on a message topic. */
    public static final class MobileClaimListener {
        private final SubmitClaim port;

        public MobileClaimListener(SubmitClaim port) {
            this.port = port;
        }

        public String onMessage(String json) { // {"policy":"POL-1234","type":"MOTOR","amount":"12500.00"}
            String body = json.replaceAll("[{}\"]", "");
            String policy = null;
            String type = null;
            long paise = 0;
            for (String field : body.split(",")) {
                String[] kv = field.split(":");
                switch (kv[0]) {
                    case "policy" -> policy = kv[1];
                    case "type" -> type = kv[1];
                    case "amount" -> paise = Math.round(Double.parseDouble(kv[1]) * 100);
                    default -> { }
                }
            }
            return "[topic] " + port.submit(new Claim(policy, type, paise));
        }
    }

    /** Driving adapter 2: a nightly CSV file from a partner garage network. */
    public static final class GarageCsvImporter {
        private final SubmitClaim port;

        public GarageCsvImporter(SubmitClaim port) {
            this.port = port;
        }

        public List<String> importFile(List<String> lines) {
            return lines.stream().skip(1) // header
                    .map(l -> l.split(";"))
                    .map(f -> "[csv]   " + port.submit(new Claim(f[0].trim(), "MOTOR", Long.parseLong(f[1].trim()))))
                    .toList();
        }
    }
}
  1. Triage is a core decision; neither adapter knows the ₹50,000 threshold.
package com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.claims;

import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.claims.ClaimsHexagon.ClaimsCore;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.claims.ClaimsHexagon.GarageCsvImporter;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.claims.ClaimsHexagon.MobileClaimListener;

import java.util.List;

public class ClaimsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ClaimsCore core = new ClaimsCore();
        var listener = new MobileClaimListener(core);
        var importer = new GarageCsvImporter(core);

        System.out.println("=== Insurance: claims arrive by event and by nightly file, one core ===");
        System.out.println(listener.onMessage("{\"policy\":\"POL-1234\",\"type\":\"MOTOR\",\"amount\":\"12500.00\"}"));
        System.out.println(listener.onMessage("{\"policy\":\"PX-99\",\"type\":\"HEALTH\",\"amount\":\"800.00\"}"));
        importer.importFile(List.of(
                "policy;amount_paise",
                "POL-5678; 7500000",
                "POL-9012; 0")).forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("Accepted claims: " + core.acceptedCount() + " (same rules for every channel)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Insurance: claims arrive by event and by nightly file, one core ===
[topic] ACCEPTED POL-1234 MOTOR -> fast track
[topic] REJECTED PX-99: invalid policy number
[csv]   ACCEPTED POL-5678 MOTOR -> manual review
[csv]   REJECTED POL-9012: amount must be positive
Accepted claims: 2 (same rules for every channel)

Why hexagonal here:

  • Driving adapters are as replaceable as driven ones: an API, a topic, a file, or a test.
  • No more "the batch import has slightly different rules".
Tests (ArchUnit enforces that the core never depends on adapters) 
package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.domain.JavaClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ClassFileImporter;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures.layeredArchitecture;

/** The architecture of the examples, enforced by ArchUnit on every build. */
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    private final JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter()
            .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
            .importPackages("com.handbook.architecture");

    @Test
    void groceryLayersOnlyCallDownwards() {
        layeredArchitecture().consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
                .layer("Web").definedBy("..layered.grocery.web..")
                .layer("Service").definedBy("..layered.grocery.service..")
                .layer("Repository").definedBy("..layered.grocery.repository..")
                .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
                .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
                .whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreNeverDependsOnAdapters() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.domain..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.port..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void cleanArchitectureDependencyRulePointsInwards() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.entities..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..", "..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void billingModuleDoesNotDependOnOrdering() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.billing..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.ordering..")
                .check(classes);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
checkout/
├── domain/            Order, CheckoutService          ← no framework imports
├── port/in/           PlaceOrderUseCase
├── port/out/          PaymentPort, OrderRepositoryPort, NotificationPort
├── adapter/in/web/    CheckoutController (@RestController)
├── adapter/in/cli/    CliCheckoutAdapter
├── adapter/out/jpa/   OrderJpaAdapter (@Repository, JPA entities live here)
├── adapter/out/payfast/ PayFastPaymentAdapter
└── config/            @Configuration wiring adapters to ports
  • Spring wiring: the core classes stay annotation-free; a @Configuration class creates them as beans with adapters injected.
  • JPA entities live in the adapter, mapped to domain objects, so the domain isn't shaped by ORM needs. (A pragmatic variant allows JPA annotations in the domain; decide consciously.)
  • Testing pyramid: core unit tests with fakes; adapter integration tests (Testcontainers for DB, WireMock for HTTP); a few end-to-end tests.
  • Contract tests for ports keep fakes honest (see the coding challenge).

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Ports & adapters Spring Boot apps structured as hexagons Core + @Configuration wiring; ArchUnit's onionArchitecture() checks it jMolecules Annotations (@Port, @Adapter) and ArchUnit rules for architecture concepts Micronaut / Quarkus apps Same structure; frameworks only in adapters Testcontainers / WireMock Test driven adapters against real dependencies

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Core testable without infrastructure More interfaces and mapping code Adapters swappable (vendor, DB, channel) Overkill for simple CRUD Multiple channels share one use case Team discipline needed to keep frameworks out of the core Postpone technology decisions Mapping between domain and persistence models takes effort

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Ports shaped like the vendor's API

A PaymentPort with merchantKey and PayFastStatus defeats the purpose. Define ports in the core's language.

Framework annotations creeping into the core

@Transactional, @Entity and @JsonProperty in domain classes bind the core to frameworks. Keep them in adapters or configuration.

One port per method, interfaces everywhere

Ports should be cohesive, per capability (payments, orders), not one interface per method or per class "just in case".

Fakes that lie

A fake adapter that behaves differently from the real one makes core tests pass while production fails. Run the same contract tests against both.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Hexagonal vs. Clean vs. Onion. All three apply the dependency rule (dependencies point inward to the domain). Hexagonal emphasizes ports and adapters, symmetric for driving and driven sides; Onion emphasizes concentric layers (domain model, domain services, application services); Clean adds named circles (entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks) and presenters. In practice, teams mix their vocabulary.

Transactions and cross-cutting concerns. Use-case boundaries are natural transaction boundaries; apply them with decorators or Spring AOP around port implementations, keeping the core annotation-free if you want strict purity.

When the hexagon pays off. Several integrations, long lifespan, changing vendors, or heavy testing needs. For a two-table CRUD admin app, a layered design is cheaper.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design / architecture round)
docs.text:
"I'd structure the checkout service as a hexagon. The core holds the domain model and use cases, with driving ports like PlaceOrderUseCase and driven ports like PaymentPort and OrderRepositoryPort, all in business terms. Adapters on the outside: a REST controller and a Kafka listener drive it; a JPA adapter, a payment-provider client and an SMS client implement the driven ports. Spring wiring lives in configuration. Core tests run in milliseconds with fakes, contract tests keep fakes honest, and ArchUnit fails the build if the core imports an adapter. Changing payment provider is one new adapter."

War story: the payment provider migration

A food-delivery company had to switch payment providers within 8 weeks after a pricing dispute. The old provider's SDK types appeared in 140 classes, including discount and refund logic. The migration took 5 months and caused two incidents where refunds were issued in the wrong currency unit. Fix (for the next migration): a PaymentPort in business terms; all provider specifics in one adapter per provider; contract tests run against both adapters; a feature flag to route by merchant. Lesson: vendor types inside the core turn a vendor change into a rewrite.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Core in the middle; ports (owned by the core) at the edge; adapters outside.
  • Driving adapters call in; driven adapters are called out.
  • Dependencies point inward; frameworks and vendors only in adapters.
  • Test the core with fakes; keep fakes honest with contract tests.
  • Swap vendors and add channels by writing adapters.

docs.title: Layered Architecture
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Architecture Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Organize code into horizontal layers (presentation → business/service → persistence), where each layer has one kind of responsibility and depends only on the layers below it. It's the default architecture of most Spring Boot applications (@Controller → @Service → @Repository): easy to learn and to staff, but it can turn into "pass-through" layers and database-centric designs if you're not careful.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: without structure, a grocery app's HTTP handler parses JSON, checks stock, calculates discounts, writes SQL and formats the response, all in one 400-line method. Changing the database means touching UI code; testing a discount rule needs a web server and a database.

Definition (Mark Richards, Software Architecture Patterns):

Components within the layered architecture pattern are organized into horizontal layers, each layer performing a specific role within the application.

Layer Responsibility Spring stereotype Presentation HTTP/UI: parse input, call the service, format output @RestController Business / Service Use cases, validation, rules, transaction boundaries @Service + @Transactional Persistence Load/save data @Repository (JPA/JDBC) Database Storage PostgreSQL, etc.

Closed vs. open layers: a closed layer must be passed through (presentation can't skip the service layer); an open layer may be skipped. Relaxed layering allows calling any lower layer; strict allows only the one directly below.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant: waiter, kitchen, pantry

The waiter (presentation) takes orders and serves plates, but never cooks. The kitchen (business) decides how dishes are made and refuses impossible orders. The pantry (persistence) stores and hands out ingredients. Customers never walk into the pantry, and the pantry never talks to customers.

docs.title: Example 1: Placing an Order Through Three Layers (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: POST /orders flows through the controller (parses the form, maps errors to 400/422), the service (validates the 20-item limit, prices items, creates the order; this is the transaction boundary), and the repository (stores it). Each layer logs when it's involved, so you can see that invalid input never reaches the service, and invalid orders never reach the repository.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant W as OrderController participant S as OrderService participant R as OrderRepository W->>W: parse form (400 if not numbers) W->>S: placeOrder(customer, quantities) S->>R: priceOf(sku) S->>S: rules (422 if violated) S->>R: save(order) W-->>W: 201 + response DTO

Full Code:

OrderController.javaOrderService.javaOrderRepository.javaOrder.javaLayeredOrderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.web;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.domain.Order;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.service.OrderService;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Presentation layer: translates HTTP input into a service call and the result into a response.
 * No business rules here, and no direct access to the repository.
 */
public class OrderController {

    /** The response DTO: what the API exposes, decoupled from the domain object. */
    public record OrderResponse(int status, String body) {
    }

    private final OrderService service;

    public OrderController(OrderService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    /** POST /orders with form fields like {@code customer=CUST-42&MANGO-1KG=2}. */
    public OrderResponse post(Map<String, String> form) {
        System.out.println("    [web] POST /orders " + form);
        Map<String, Integer> quantities = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        try {
            form.forEach((k, v) -> {
                if (!k.equals("customer")) {
                    quantities.put(k, Integer.parseInt(v)); // (1)!
                }
            });
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return new OrderResponse(400, "quantities must be numbers");
        }
        try {
            Order order = service.placeOrder(form.get("customer"), quantities);
            return new OrderResponse(201, order.id() + " total ₹" + order.totalPaise() / 100); // (2)!
        } catch (OrderService.InvalidOrderException e) {
            return new OrderResponse(422, e.getMessage()); // (3)!
        }
    }
}
  1. Input translation is the presentation layer's job: strings to numbers.
  2. A response DTO: the API's shape is decoupled from the domain object.
  3. Business errors map to HTTP status codes here, not in the service.
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.service;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.domain.Order;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.repository.OrderRepository;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Business layer: use cases, validation and transaction boundaries. Calls only the layer below. */
public class OrderService {

    public static final class InvalidOrderException extends RuntimeException {
        InvalidOrderException(String message) {
            super(message);
        }
    }

    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private int nextId = 1;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    /** In Spring this method would be @Transactional: the use case is one unit of work. */
    public Order placeOrder(String customerId, Map<String, Integer> quantities) { // (1)!
        System.out.println("    [service] validating and pricing " + quantities.keySet());
        if (quantities.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum() > 20) {
            throw new InvalidOrderException("max 20 items per order");
        }
        List<Order.Line> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        quantities.forEach((sku, qty) -> lines.add(new Order.Line(sku, qty,
                repository.priceOf(sku).orElseThrow(() -> new InvalidOrderException("unknown product " + sku)))));
        Order order = new Order("ORD-" + nextId++, customerId, List.copyOf(lines));
        repository.save(order);
        return order;
    }
}
  1. The use case: validation, pricing, creation, persistence, as one unit of work (@Transactional in Spring).
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.repository;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.domain.Order;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Persistence layer: stores and loads domain objects. A JPA/JdbcTemplate repository in a real app. */
public class OrderRepository {

    private final Map<String, Order> orders = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Long> prices = Map.of("MANGO-1KG", 39_900L, "RICE-5KG", 64_900L);

    public Optional<Long> priceOf(String sku) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(prices.get(sku));
    }

    public void save(Order order) {
        System.out.println("    [repository] INSERT order " + order.id());
        orders.put(order.id(), order);
    }

    public int count() {
        return orders.size();
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.domain;

import java.util.List;

/** Domain layer: plain data and rules about orders. Knows nothing about HTTP or storage. */
public record Order(String id, String customerId, List<Line> lines) {

    public record Line(String sku, int qty, long unitPaise) {
        public long totalPaise() {
            return qty * unitPaise;
        }
    }

    public long totalPaise() {
        return lines.stream().mapToLong(Line::totalPaise).sum();
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.repository.OrderRepository;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.service.OrderService;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.grocery.web.OrderController;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class LayeredOrderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderRepository repository = new OrderRepository();
        OrderController controller = new OrderController(new OrderService(repository)); // wiring = Spring's job

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: one request through three layers ===");
        System.out.println("-> " + controller.post(form("customer", "CUST-42", "MANGO-1KG", "2", "RICE-5KG", "1")));
        System.out.println("-> " + controller.post(form("customer", "CUST-42", "MANGO-1KG", "two")));
        System.out.println("-> " + controller.post(form("customer", "CUST-42", "SAFFRON-1G", "1")));
        System.out.println("-> " + controller.post(form("customer", "CUST-42", "RICE-5KG", "25")));
        System.out.println("Orders stored: " + repository.count());
    }

    private static Map<String, String> form(String... kv) {
        Map<String, String> m = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < kv.length; i += 2) {
            m.put(kv[i], kv[i + 1]);
        }
        return m;
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: one request through three layers ===
    [web] POST /orders {customer=CUST-42, MANGO-1KG=2, RICE-5KG=1}
    [service] validating and pricing [MANGO-1KG, RICE-5KG]
    [repository] INSERT order ORD-1
-> OrderResponse[status=201, body=ORD-1 total ₹1447]
    [web] POST /orders {customer=CUST-42, MANGO-1KG=two}
-> OrderResponse[status=400, body=quantities must be numbers]
    [web] POST /orders {customer=CUST-42, SAFFRON-1G=1}
    [service] validating and pricing [SAFFRON-1G]
-> OrderResponse[status=422, body=unknown product SAFFRON-1G]
    [web] POST /orders {customer=CUST-42, RICE-5KG=25}
    [service] validating and pricing [RICE-5KG]
-> OrderResponse[status=422, body=max 20 items per order]
Orders stored: 1

Why layers here:

  • Each concern has an obvious home; new developers know where to look.
  • The service can be unit-tested without HTTP; the controller with a mocked service.

docs.title: Example 2: One Service, Two Front Ends (Clinic booking)
docs.text:
Scenario: Patients book online; receptionists use a kiosk that accepts "10:30" for today. Both front ends call the same BookingService, which owns the rules: clinic hours, no double-booking a doctor, at most 2 appointments per patient per day. Because the rules live in the service layer, the kiosk can't accidentally allow what the website forbids.

Full Code:

BookingService.javaWebBookingPage.javaReceptionKiosk.javaAppointmentDao.javaClinicBookingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.service;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.data.AppointmentDao;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.data.AppointmentDao.AppointmentRow;

import java.time.LocalDateTime;

/**
 * The booking rules live here, ONCE. Every front end (web, reception desk, kiosk, phone bot)
 * calls this service, so the rules can't diverge between channels.
 */
public class BookingService {

    private final AppointmentDao dao;

    public BookingService(AppointmentDao dao) {
        this.dao = dao;
    }

    public String book(String patient, String doctor, LocalDateTime slot) {
        if (slot.getHour() < 9 || slot.getHour() >= 17) { // (1)!
            return "REJECTED: outside clinic hours";
        }
        if (dao.slotTaken(doctor, slot)) {
            return "REJECTED: " + doctor + " is already booked at " + slot.toLocalTime();
        }
        if (dao.countForPatientOn(patient, slot.toLocalDate()) >= 2) {
            return "REJECTED: max 2 appointments per patient per day";
        }
        dao.insert(new AppointmentRow(patient, doctor, slot));
        return "CONFIRMED: " + patient + " with " + doctor + " at " + slot.toLocalTime();
    }
}
  1. Rules in one place. If they lived in the web controller, the kiosk would need a copy, and the copies would drift.
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.presentation;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.service.BookingService;

import java.time.LocalDateTime;

/** Web front end: parses the ISO date-time from the form and shows a green or red banner. */
public class WebBookingPage {

    private final BookingService service;

    public WebBookingPage(BookingService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    public String submit(String patient, String doctor, String isoSlot) {
        String result = service.book(patient, doctor, LocalDateTime.parse(isoSlot));
        return (result.startsWith("CONFIRMED") ? "[green] " : "[red] ") + result;
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.presentation;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.service.BookingService;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import java.time.LocalTime;

/** Reception kiosk: staff type "10:30" for today's date. Different input, same rules. */
public class ReceptionKiosk {

    private final BookingService service;
    private final LocalDate today;

    public ReceptionKiosk(BookingService service, LocalDate today) {
        this.service = service;
        this.today = today;
    }

    public String enter(String patient, String doctor, String hhmm) {
        return "KIOSK> " + service.book(patient, doctor, LocalDateTime.of(today, LocalTime.parse(hhmm)));
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.data;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Data layer: simple queries over stored appointments. */
public class AppointmentDao {

    public record AppointmentRow(String patient, String doctor, LocalDateTime slot) {
    }

    private final List<AppointmentRow> rows = new ArrayList<>();

    public boolean slotTaken(String doctor, LocalDateTime slot) {
        return rows.stream().anyMatch(r -> r.doctor().equals(doctor) && r.slot().equals(slot));
    }

    public long countForPatientOn(String patient, LocalDate day) {
        return rows.stream().filter(r -> r.patient().equals(patient) && r.slot().toLocalDate().equals(day)).count();
    }

    public void insert(AppointmentRow row) {
        rows.add(row);
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.data.AppointmentDao;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.presentation.ReceptionKiosk;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.presentation.WebBookingPage;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.clinic.service.BookingService;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public class ClinicBookingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BookingService service = new BookingService(new AppointmentDao());
        WebBookingPage web = new WebBookingPage(service);
        ReceptionKiosk kiosk = new ReceptionKiosk(service, LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14));

        System.out.println("=== Clinic: two front ends, one service layer with the rules ===");
        System.out.println(web.submit("PAT-1", "Dr. Iyer", "2026-10-14T10:30"));
        System.out.println(kiosk.enter("PAT-2", "Dr. Iyer", "10:30"));
        System.out.println(kiosk.enter("PAT-2", "Dr. Iyer", "11:00"));
        System.out.println(web.submit("PAT-2", "Dr. Rao", "2026-10-14T12:00"));
        System.out.println(web.submit("PAT-2", "Dr. Rao", "2026-10-14T15:00"));
        System.out.println(kiosk.enter("PAT-3", "Dr. Rao", "18:15"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Clinic: two front ends, one service layer with the rules ===
[green] CONFIRMED: PAT-1 with Dr. Iyer at 10:30
KIOSK> REJECTED: Dr. Iyer is already booked at 10:30
KIOSK> CONFIRMED: PAT-2 with Dr. Iyer at 11:00
[green] CONFIRMED: PAT-2 with Dr. Rao at 12:00
[red] REJECTED: max 2 appointments per patient per day
KIOSK> REJECTED: outside clinic hours

Why layers here:

  • Multiple channels, one set of rules.
  • Adding a phone bot later is a new presentation class, not a rewrite.

docs.title: Example 3: Closed vs. Open Layers for Reports (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A statement report is a pure read. With strictly closed layers, the presentation calls a service method that just forwards to the query: the architecture sinkhole anti-pattern. Marking the read-only query layer as open lets presentation read it directly, while writes (transfers) still must go through the service layer and its rules.

Full Code:

StatementLayers.javaOpenLayerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Closed vs. open layers for a read-only report. In strict (closed) layering every call passes
 * through the service layer, even when it adds nothing: the "architecture sinkhole".
 * Marking a query layer as OPEN lets the presentation layer read it directly.
 */
public final class StatementLayers {

    public record Txn(String date, String description, long paise) {
    }

    /** Data layer: a read-optimized query (in a real app, a SQL view or a reporting replica). */
    public static final class StatementQueries {
        private final Map<String, List<Txn>> data = Map.of("ACC-1", List.of(
                new Txn("2026-10-01", "Salary", 5_000_000),
                new Txn("2026-10-03", "Rent", -1_250_000),
                new Txn("2026-10-07", "Groceries", -89_900)));

        public List<Txn> forAccount(String account) {
            return data.getOrDefault(account, List.of());
        }
    }

    /** Service layer method that only forwards: no rules, no transaction, no transformation. */
    public static final class StatementService {
        private final StatementQueries queries;
        int passThroughCalls;

        public StatementService(StatementQueries queries) {
            this.queries = queries;
        }

        public List<Txn> statement(String account) {
            passThroughCalls++; // (1)!
            return queries.forAccount(account);
        }
    }

    public static String render(Supplier<List<Txn>> source) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Txn t : source.get()) {
            sb.append(String.format("  %s %-10s %,12.2f%n", t.date(), t.description(), t.paise() / 100.0));
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    private StatementLayers() {
    }
}
  1. A layer that only forwards adds code, tests and indirection with no value. If most requests look like this, the layering is too strict.
package com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting;

import com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting.StatementLayers.StatementQueries;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.reporting.StatementLayers.StatementService;

public class OpenLayerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StatementQueries queries = new StatementQueries();
        StatementService service = new StatementService(queries);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: statement report through closed vs. open layers ===");
        System.out.println("Closed layering (presentation -> service -> queries):");
        System.out.print(StatementLayers.render(() -> service.statement("ACC-1")));
        System.out.println("service methods that only forwarded: " + service.passThroughCalls);

        System.out.println("Open query layer (presentation -> queries, read-only):");
        System.out.print(StatementLayers.render(() -> queries.forAccount("ACC-1")));
        System.out.println("Same output, one less layer to maintain for a pure read.");
        System.out.println("Writes (transfers, payments) still go through the service layer and its rules.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: statement report through closed vs. open layers ===
Closed layering (presentation -> service -> queries):
  2026-10-01 Salary        50,000.00
  2026-10-03 Rent         -12,500.00
  2026-10-07 Groceries       -899.00
service methods that only forwarded: 1
Open query layer (presentation -> queries, read-only):
  2026-10-01 Salary        50,000.00
  2026-10-03 Rent         -12,500.00
  2026-10-07 Groceries       -899.00
Same output, one less layer to maintain for a pure read.
Writes (transfers, payments) still go through the service layer and its rules.

Why it matters:

  • Mark Richards' rule of thumb: if more than about 20% of requests are simple pass-throughs, consider opening some layers.
  • Open layers must be explicit and documented, or every shortcut becomes a precedent.
Unit and ArchUnit Tests ArchitectureRulesTest.javaArchitectureExamplesTest.java 
package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.domain.JavaClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ClassFileImporter;
import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses;
import static com.tngtech.archunit.library.Architectures.layeredArchitecture;

/** The architecture of the examples, enforced by ArchUnit on every build. */
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    private final JavaClasses classes = new ClassFileImporter()
            .withImportOption(ImportOption.Predefined.DO_NOT_INCLUDE_TESTS)
            .importPackages("com.handbook.architecture");

    @Test
    void groceryLayersOnlyCallDownwards() {
        layeredArchitecture().consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
                .layer("Web").definedBy("..layered.grocery.web..")
                .layer("Service").definedBy("..layered.grocery.service..")
                .layer("Repository").definedBy("..layered.grocery.repository..")
                .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
                .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
                .whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreNeverDependsOnAdapters() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.domain..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.port..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..hexagonal.checkout.adapter..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void cleanArchitectureDependencyRulePointsInwards() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.entities..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..", "..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.usecase..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..clean.coupon.adapters..")
                .check(classes);
    }

    @Test
    void billingModuleDoesNotDependOnOrdering() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.billing..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..modular.shop.ordering..")
                .check(classes);
    }
}

package com.handbook.architecture;

import com.handbook.architecture.clean.coupon.entities.Coupon;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill.RefillPrescription;
import com.handbook.architecture.clean.refill.RefillPrescription.Prescription;
import com.handbook.architecture.eventdriven.dlq.RetryingConsumer;
import com.handbook.architecture.eventdriven.iot.MeterWindowing;
import com.handbook.architecture.eventdriven.iot.MeterWindowing.Reading;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.adapter.out.InMemoryOrderRepository;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.CheckoutService;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.domain.Order;
import com.handbook.architecture.hexagonal.checkout.port.in.PlaceOrderUseCase.PlaceOrderCommand;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.rules.LayerRules;
import com.handbook.architecture.layered.rules.LayerRules.Dependency;
import com.handbook.architecture.modular.cycles.ModuleGraph;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ArchitectureExamplesTest {

    @Test
    void hexagonCoreRunsWithTestAdaptersOnly() {
        List<String> sms = new ArrayList<>();
        var core = new CheckoutService((c, p, r) -> p < 1000, new InMemoryOrderRepository(), (phone, m) -> sms.add(m));
        assertThat(core.placeOrder(new PlaceOrderCommand("C", "P", 500)).status()).isEqualTo(Order.Status.PAID);
        assertThat(core.placeOrder(new PlaceOrderCommand("C", "P", 5000)).status()).isEqualTo(Order.Status.PAYMENT_DECLINED);
        assertThat(sms).hasSize(2);
    }

    @Test
    void couponEntityCapsDiscount() {
        var coupon = new Coupon("X", 50, 0, 10_000, LocalDate.of(2030, 1, 1));
        assertThat(coupon.evaluate(100_000, LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1))).isEqualTo(new Coupon.Discount(10_000));
    }

    @Test
    void controlledSubstancesAlwaysNeedADoctor() {
        var repo = RefillPrescription.inMemory(Map.of("R", new Prescription("R", "P", "D", 5, LocalDate.of(2030, 1, 1), true)));
        assertThat(RefillPrescription.refill(repo, "R", "P", LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1)))
                .isInstanceOf(RefillPrescription.NeedsDoctor.class);
    }

    @Test
    void lateEventsLandInTheirEventTimeWindow() {
        var w = new MeterWindowing(300, 10);
        w.accept(new Reading("M", 10, 2));
        w.accept(new Reading("M", 320, 4));
        w.accept(new Reading("M", 250, 4)); // late
        assertThat(w.advanceWatermark(300)).singleElement().extracting(MeterWindowing.WindowResult::avgKw).isEqualTo(3.0);
    }

    @Test
    void poisonMessageGoesToDlqAndOthersContinue() {
        List<String> handled = new ArrayList<>();
        var consumer = new RetryingConsumer<String>(e -> {
            if (e.equals("bad")) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("x");
            }
            handled.add(e);
        }, 2);
        consumer.consume(List.of("a", "bad", "b"));
        assertThat(handled).containsExactly("a", "b");
        assertThat(consumer.deadLetters()).hasSize(1);
    }

    @Test
    void upwardDependencyIsAViolation() {
        var rules = new LayerRules().layer("w").layer("s");
        assertThat(rules.violations(List.of(new Dependency("s.A", "w.B")))).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(rules.violations(List.of(new Dependency("w.B", "s.A")))).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void cycleIsDetected() {
        assertThat(new ModuleGraph().dependsOn("a", "b").dependsOn("b", "a").findCycle()).isPresent();
        assertThat(new ModuleGraph().dependsOn("a", "b").buildOrder()).containsExactly("b", "a");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Package by layer (controller/, service/, repository/) vs. package by feature (orders/, customers/ with layers inside each). Package by feature scales better and leads naturally to a modular monolith.
  • Enforce layers with ArchUnit (layeredArchitecture(), see the tests above) or Java modules (JPMS).
  • DTO mapping between layers with records and MapStruct; keep JPA entities out of API responses.
  • Evolve towards Hexagonal or Clean when the domain logic grows and you want it independent of persistence.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Layering Spring MVC / Spring Boot @Controller → @Service → @Repository stereotypes Jakarta EE JAX-RS resources → EJB/CDI services → JPA OSI / TCP-IP network stacks Each layer uses only the one below Classic enterprise apps (n-tier) Web tier, application tier, data tier on separate servers

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Simple, universally understood Tends to become database-centric (design starts from tables) Clear separation of technical concerns Changes often cut through all layers (a new field touches every one) Easy to test layers in isolation Sinkhole layers that only forward Good default for CRUD-heavy apps Business logic leaks into controllers or repositories

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Fat controllers

Rules in controllers can't be reused by other channels (Example 2) and are hard to test. Controllers translate; services decide.

Anemic domain with transaction scripts everywhere

Services full of if statements over data-only entities. Fine for simple CRUD; for rich domains, move rules into domain objects (see Clean Architecture).

Leaking persistence types upward

Returning JPA entities from controllers couples your API to your schema and triggers lazy-loading surprises. Map to DTOs.

Upward dependencies

A repository importing a web DTO creates cycles and breaks layering. Catch it automatically (see the coding challenge and ArchUnit).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Layers are technical, not business, boundaries. They tell you how code is organized, not what it does. In large systems, slice by business capability first (modules or services), then layer inside each slice.

Where layered architecture breaks down. When the core logic is complex, the dependency of business on persistence (service → repository implementation) makes the domain hard to test and evolve. Dependency inversion (the service owns a repository interface) is the first step toward Hexagonal/Clean.

Governance. Write the rules down (closed/open layers, allowed dependencies) and enforce them with ArchUnit in CI. Unenforced rules decay within months.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design / architecture round)
docs.text:
"For a CRUD-heavy internal app, I'd use classic layering: REST controllers translate HTTP, services hold use cases and transaction boundaries, repositories handle persistence. I'd package by feature with layers inside, map entities to DTOs at the edge, and enforce layer rules with ArchUnit. Read-only reporting can use an open query layer to avoid pass-through services. If the domain logic grows complex, I'd invert the persistence dependency and move toward hexagonal."

War story: the controller that knew too much

An insurance portal's quote controller contained 1,100 lines of pricing logic. When the company launched a broker API, a developer copied the logic into a second controller. Six months later the two channels quoted different prices for the same customer, because a tax change had only been applied to one copy. A regulator asked why. Fix: pricing moved to a QuoteService used by both controllers; ArchUnit rule "controllers may not contain classes ending in Calculator"; a test comparing both channels' quotes. Lesson: business rules live in the business layer, once.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Layered Hexagonal Clean Modular Monolith Organizes by Technical layer Core vs. adapters Concentric policy levels Business module Domain depends on DB? Usually yes No (ports) No (gateways) Depends on inner style Best for CRUD, simple domains Many integrations, testability Complex domains, long-lived apps Large codebases, many teams

See Hexagonal, Clean, Modular Monolith and the in-process Facade.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Presentation → Business → Persistence; dependencies point down.
  • Controllers translate; services decide (and own transactions); repositories store.
  • Closed vs. open layers; avoid sinkholes.
  • Package by feature; DTOs at the edge; ArchUnit to enforce.
  • Next step for complex domains: invert dependencies (Hexagonal/Clean).

docs.text:

  • Add a phone-bot front end to Example 2 that books "tomorrow at 9".
  • Add an ArchUnit rule: classes in ..service.. must not use java.sql directly.
