docs.title: Command
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Command turns a request ("do this") into an object. Once it's an object, you can queue it, log it, retry it, send it over the network, replay it later, and undo it. Use it for undo/redo, job queues, scheduled operations, offline-first apps, macros and audit trails.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: when a button directly calls doc.delete(0, 7), the action is gone the moment it runs. You can't undo it (what was deleted?), you can't queue it for later, and you can't send it to a server when the network comes back. If the action is instead an object (new Delete(doc, 0, 7)) holding everything needed to run it, and to reverse it, all of those become easy.

Formal definition (GoF):

Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant order slip

The waiter writes your order on a slip (command) and puts it on the kitchen rail (queue). The chef (receiver) cooks orders in sequence. The slip can be read again for the bill (log), corrected (undo: "cancel the dessert"), or re-made if dropped (retry). The waiter (invoker) never needs to know how to cook.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class Command { <<interface>> +execute() +undo() } class ConcreteCommand { -Receiver receiver -params +execute() +undo() } class Receiver { +action() } class Invoker { -history +run(Command) } class Client Command <|.. ConcreteCommand ConcreteCommand --> Receiver Invoker o--> Command Client ..> ConcreteCommand : creates Client ..> Invoker : hands command to Participant Responsibility Command execute() (and optionally undo()) Concrete command Holds the receiver and parameters; calls the receiver Receiver Does the actual work (Document, Ledger) Invoker Runs commands and may store, queue, retry or undo them (Editor, CommandProcessor) Client Creates commands and gives them to the invoker

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
deleteButton.onClick(() -> doc.delete(selectionStart, selectionLength));   // can't undo: what was deleted?
payButton.onClick(() -> ledger.debit(acc, amount));                         // runs now or never; no queue, no retry
  • No undo: nothing remembers what happened.
  • No queueing or scheduling: the action is a method call, not data.
  • UI tied to business logic: buttons know how operations are done.

docs.title: Example 1: Undo / Redo in a Document Editor (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A Google-Docs-style editor supports unlimited undo and redo. Each edit is a command that knows how to reverse itself: an insert is undone by deleting the inserted text; a delete is undone by re-inserting the text it removed (which it must remember). A new edit after an undo clears the redo history, as every editor does.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2 direction LR state "undo stack" as U state "redo stack" as R [*] --> U : run(cmd) / execute, push, clear redo U --> R : undo() / pop, cmd.undo(), push to redo R --> U : redo() / pop, cmd.execute(), push to undo

Full Code:

EditCommand.javaEditor.javaDocument.javaEditorDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor;

/** Command: an edit as an object, with enough information to reverse itself. */
public interface EditCommand {

    void execute();

    void undo();

    String label();

    record Insert(Document doc, int position, String text) implements EditCommand {
        public void execute() { doc.insert(position, text); }
        public void undo() { doc.delete(position, text.length()); }
        public String label() { return "insert '" + text + "'"; }
    }

    final class Delete implements EditCommand {
        private final Document doc;
        private final int position;
        private final int length;
        private String removed; // (1)!

        public Delete(Document doc, int position, int length) {
            this.doc = doc;
            this.position = position;
            this.length = length;
        }

        public void execute() { removed = doc.delete(position, length); }
        public void undo() { doc.insert(position, removed); }
        public String label() { return "delete " + length + " chars"; }
    }
}
  1. The command remembers what it removed during execute() so undo() can put it back. Commands often need a little state like this.
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Invoker: runs commands and keeps the undo/redo history. */
public class Editor {

    private final Deque<EditCommand> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<EditCommand> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void run(EditCommand command) {
        command.execute();
        undoStack.push(command);
        redoStack.clear(); // (1)!
    }

    public String undo() {
        if (undoStack.isEmpty()) {
            return "nothing to undo";
        }
        EditCommand c = undoStack.pop();
        c.undo();
        redoStack.push(c);
        return "undid " + c.label();
    }

    public String redo() {
        if (redoStack.isEmpty()) {
            return "nothing to redo";
        }
        EditCommand c = redoStack.pop();
        c.execute();
        undoStack.push(c);
        return "redid " + c.label();
    }
}
  1. A new edit invalidates the redo history: redoing an old edit on top of a new one would corrupt the document.
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor;

/** Receiver: knows how to change text; knows nothing about undo. */
public class Document {

    private final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();

    public void insert(int position, String s) {
        text.insert(position, s);
    }

    public String delete(int position, int length) {
        String removed = text.substring(position, position + length);
        text.delete(position, position + length);
        return removed;
    }

    public int length() {
        return text.length();
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return '"' + text.toString() + '"';
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor;

import com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor.EditCommand.Delete;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor.EditCommand.Insert;

public class EditorDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Docs SaaS: Undo / Redo ===");
        Document doc = new Document();
        Editor editor = new Editor();

        editor.run(new Insert(doc, 0, "Hello world"));
        System.out.println("type           -> " + doc);
        editor.run(new Insert(doc, 5, ", dear"));
        System.out.println("insert         -> " + doc);
        editor.run(new Delete(doc, 0, 7));
        System.out.println("delete         -> " + doc);

        System.out.println(editor.undo() + " -> " + doc);
        System.out.println(editor.undo() + " -> " + doc);
        System.out.println(editor.redo() + " -> " + doc);
        editor.run(new Insert(doc, doc.length(), "!"));
        System.out.println("new edit       -> " + doc);
        System.out.println(editor.redo());
    }
}

Output:

=== Docs SaaS: Undo / Redo ===
type           -> "Hello world"
insert         -> "Hello, dear world"
delete         -> "dear world"
undid delete 7 chars -> "Hello, dear world"
undid insert ', dear' -> "Hello world"
redid insert ', dear' -> "Hello, dear world"
new edit       -> "Hello, dear world!"
nothing to redo

Why Command here:

  • Undo needs objects that remember what they did.
  • The Editor (invoker) manages history without knowing what an insert or delete is.
  • New edit types (format bold, insert image) plug in with their own undo().

docs.title: Example 2: Nightly Batch of Scheduled Payments (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank lets customers schedule transfers, bill payments and mobile recharges. At night, a batch job executes them. Commands are data (records), so they can be stored in a database, audited and replayed. Mobile clients sometimes resend the same instruction after a timeout, so each command has an ID, and duplicates are skipped. Failed commands (insufficient funds) go to a dead-letter queue for customer notification, without stopping the batch.

Design:

flowchart LR App[Mobile / net banking] -->|submit| Q[(Command queue)] Q --> P[CommandProcessor<br/>de-duplicate by id] P -->|execute| L[Ledger] P -->|failure| D[(Dead-letter queue)] P -->|audit| A[(Audit log)]

Full Code:

CommandProcessor.javaPaymentCommand.javaLedger.javaBankingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking;

import com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking.PaymentCommand.*;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.Set;

/** Invoker: queues commands, executes them later, audits, de-duplicates and dead-letters. */
public class CommandProcessor {

    private final Ledger ledger;
    private final Queue<PaymentCommand> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Set<String> processed = new HashSet<>();
    private final List<String> deadLetters = new ArrayList<>();

    public CommandProcessor(Ledger ledger) {
        this.ledger = ledger;
    }

    public void submit(PaymentCommand command) {
        queue.add(command); // (1)!
    }

    public void runBatch() {
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            PaymentCommand c = queue.poll();
            if (!processed.add(c.id())) { // (2)!
                System.out.println("  skip duplicate " + c.id());
                continue;
            }
            try {
                execute(c);
                System.out.println("  done " + c);
            } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                deadLetters.add(c.id() + ": " + e.getMessage());
                System.out.println("  FAILED " + c.id() + " -> dead-letter queue");
            }
        }
    }

    private void execute(PaymentCommand c) {
        switch (c) { // (3)!
            case Transfer t -> { ledger.debit(t.from(), t.amountInr()); ledger.credit(t.to(), t.amountInr()); }
            case PayBill b -> { ledger.debit(b.from(), b.amountInr()); ledger.credit("BILLER:" + b.biller(), b.amountInr()); }
            case MobileRecharge r -> { ledger.debit(r.from(), r.amountInr()); ledger.credit("TELCO:" + r.phone(), r.amountInr()); }
        }
    }

    public List<String> deadLetters() {
        return deadLetters;
    }
}
  1. Submit now, execute later: the request is stored as an object. In production this queue is a database table or a Kafka topic.
  2. Idempotency: the command's ID makes a resent command harmless. This matters far more than undo in real payment systems.
  3. Commands here are pure data, and the processor dispatches with an exhaustive switch over a sealed interface. This "commands as data + handler" style is how CQRS command handlers and job queues usually look.
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking;

/** Commands as plain data: easy to persist, queue, audit and replay. */
public sealed interface PaymentCommand {

    String id();

    record Transfer(String id, String from, String to, long amountInr) implements PaymentCommand {
    }

    record PayBill(String id, String from, String biller, long amountInr) implements PaymentCommand {
    }

    record MobileRecharge(String id, String from, String phone, long amountInr) implements PaymentCommand {
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Receiver: the actual money movement. */
public class Ledger {

    private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>(Map.of("ACC-1", 10_000L, "ACC-2", 500L));

    public void debit(String account, long amount) {
        long balance = balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L);
        if (balance < amount) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds in " + account);
        }
        balances.put(account, balance - amount);
    }

    public void credit(String account, long amount) {
        balances.merge(account, amount, Long::sum);
    }

    public long balance(String account) {
        return balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking;

import com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking.PaymentCommand.*;

public class BankingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Nightly Batch of Scheduled Payments ===");
        Ledger ledger = new Ledger();
        CommandProcessor processor = new CommandProcessor(ledger);

        processor.submit(new Transfer("CMD-1", "ACC-1", "ACC-2", 2_000));
        processor.submit(new PayBill("CMD-2", "ACC-1", "ELECTRICITY-BESCOM", 1_450));
        processor.submit(new MobileRecharge("CMD-3", "ACC-2", "98450-00001", 3_000));
        processor.submit(new Transfer("CMD-1", "ACC-1", "ACC-2", 2_000)); // resent by a retrying client

        System.out.println("Running batch:");
        processor.runBatch();
        System.out.println("ACC-1 balance: INR " + ledger.balance("ACC-1"));
        System.out.println("ACC-2 balance: INR " + ledger.balance("ACC-2"));
        System.out.println("Dead letters : " + processor.deadLetters());
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Nightly Batch of Scheduled Payments ===
Running batch:
  done Transfer[id=CMD-1, from=ACC-1, to=ACC-2, amountInr=2000]
  done PayBill[id=CMD-2, from=ACC-1, biller=ELECTRICITY-BESCOM, amountInr=1450]
  FAILED CMD-3 -> dead-letter queue
  skip duplicate CMD-1
ACC-1 balance: INR 6550
ACC-2 balance: INR 2500
Dead letters : [CMD-3: insufficient funds in ACC-2]

Why Command here:

  • Requests must be stored, scheduled, audited and replayed, so they need to be data.
  • De-duplication by command ID makes retries safe.
  • Failures are isolated per command (dead-letter), not per batch.

docs.title: Example 3: Offline Driver App (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: Drivers lose signal in tunnels, basements and rural roads. The driver app must keep working: "start trip" and "end trip" are recorded as commands with their original timestamps and IDs, queued in an outbox while offline, and replayed in order when the network returns. Flaky networks sometimes deliver the same action twice, so the server applies each action ID only once. Fares must use the real trip times, not the replay time.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant D as Driver participant A as DriverApp (invoker) participant O as Outbox participant S as TripServer (receiver) D->>A: StartTrip (09:09) Note over A: offline A->>O: queue D->>A: EndTrip (09:31) A->>O: queue Note over A: back online A->>S: replay StartTrip @09:09 A->>S: replay EndTrip @09:31 S->>S: ignore duplicates by id

Full Code:

DriverApp.javaDriverAction.javaTripServer.javaOfflineDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.offline;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** Invoker on the phone: sends immediately when online, queues when offline, replays in order. */
public class DriverApp {

    private final Consumer<DriverAction> server;
    private final List<DriverAction> outbox = new ArrayList<>();
    private boolean online = true;

    public DriverApp(Consumer<DriverAction> server) {
        this.server = server;
    }

    public void setOnline(boolean online) {
        this.online = online;
        System.out.println(online ? "[network] back online, replaying " + outbox.size() + " action(s)" : "[network] lost signal");
        if (online) {
            outbox.forEach(server); // (1)!
            outbox.clear();
        }
    }

    public void perform(DriverAction action) {
        if (online) {
            server.accept(action);
        } else {
            outbox.add(action);
            System.out.println("  queued offline: " + action.getClass().getSimpleName() + " at " + action.at());
        }
    }
}
  1. Replay in the original order, so the server sees start before end. Real apps persist the outbox to local storage (SQLite) so it survives an app restart.
package com.handbook.behavioral.command.offline;

/** Commands recorded on the phone while offline. Each carries an id and the time it happened. */
public sealed interface DriverAction {

    String id();

    String at();

    record AcceptTrip(String id, String at, String tripId) implements DriverAction {
    }

    record ArrivedAtPickup(String id, String at, String tripId) implements DriverAction {
    }

    record StartTrip(String id, String at, String tripId, String otp) implements DriverAction {
    }

    record EndTrip(String id, String at, String tripId, double km) implements DriverAction {
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.command.offline;

import com.handbook.behavioral.command.offline.DriverAction.*;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Receiver on the server: applies actions idempotently using the action id. */
public class TripServer {

    private final Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();

    public void apply(DriverAction action) {
        if (!seen.add(action.id())) {
            System.out.println("  server: ignored duplicate " + action.id());
            return;
        }
        String what = switch (action) {
            case AcceptTrip a -> "trip " + a.tripId() + " accepted";
            case ArrivedAtPickup a -> "driver at pickup for " + a.tripId();
            case StartTrip s -> "trip " + s.tripId() + " started (OTP " + s.otp() + " verified)";
            case EndTrip e -> "trip " + e.tripId() + " ended, " + e.km() + " km, fare INR " + Math.round(50 + 14 * e.km());
        };
        System.out.println("  server @" + action.at() + ": " + what);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.command.offline;

import com.handbook.behavioral.command.offline.DriverAction.*;

public class OfflineDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Driver App Through a Tunnel ===");
        TripServer server = new TripServer();
        DriverApp app = new DriverApp(server::apply);

        app.perform(new AcceptTrip("A1", "09:00", "TRIP-77"));
        app.perform(new ArrivedAtPickup("A2", "09:07", "TRIP-77"));
        app.setOnline(false);
        app.perform(new StartTrip("A3", "09:09", "TRIP-77", "4821"));
        app.perform(new EndTrip("A4", "09:31", "TRIP-77", 8.4));
        app.setOnline(true);
        server.apply(new EndTrip("A4", "09:31", "TRIP-77", 8.4)); // a flaky network re-sends A4
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Driver App Through a Tunnel ===
  server @09:00: trip TRIP-77 accepted
  server @09:07: driver at pickup for TRIP-77
[network] lost signal
  queued offline: StartTrip at 09:09
  queued offline: EndTrip at 09:31
[network] back online, replaying 2 action(s)
  server @09:09: trip TRIP-77 started (OTP 4821 verified)
  server @09:31: trip TRIP-77 ended, 8.4 km, fare INR 168
  server: ignored duplicate A4

Why Command here:

  • Actions must outlive the moment they happen: queued, persisted, replayed.
  • Each command carries its own context (time, IDs), so replays are accurate.
  • The same command objects travel from phone to server, which is the basis of offline-first sync.
Unit Tests: CommandTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.command;

import com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking.CommandProcessor;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking.Ledger;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.banking.PaymentCommand.Transfer;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.cart.CartCommands.*;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor.Document;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor.EditCommand.Delete;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor.EditCommand.Insert;
import com.handbook.behavioral.command.editor.Editor;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class CommandTest {

    @Test
    void undoRestoresEveryPreviousState() {
        Document doc = new Document();
        Editor editor = new Editor();
        editor.run(new Insert(doc, 0, "abc"));
        editor.run(new Delete(doc, 1, 1));
        assertThat(doc).hasToString("\"ac\"");
        editor.undo();
        assertThat(doc).hasToString("\"abc\"");
        editor.undo();
        assertThat(doc).hasToString("\"\"");
        assertThat(editor.undo()).isEqualTo("nothing to undo");
    }

    @Test
    void newEditClearsRedo() {
        Document doc = new Document();
        Editor editor = new Editor();
        editor.run(new Insert(doc, 0, "a"));
        editor.undo();
        editor.run(new Insert(doc, 0, "b"));
        assertThat(editor.redo()).isEqualTo("nothing to redo");
    }

    @Test
    void duplicateCommandsExecuteOnce() {
        Ledger ledger = new Ledger();
        CommandProcessor p = new CommandProcessor(ledger);
        p.submit(new Transfer("X", "ACC-1", "ACC-2", 100));
        p.submit(new Transfer("X", "ACC-1", "ACC-2", 100));
        p.runBatch();
        assertThat(ledger.balance("ACC-1")).isEqualTo(9_900);
    }

    @Test
    void macroUndoIsAllOrNothing() {
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        Macro m = new Macro(List.of(new AddItem(cart, "A", 1), new AddItem(cart, "B", 2)));
        m.execute();
        m.undo();
        assertThat(cart).hasToString("{}");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Lambdas as commands Runnable, Callable, Supplier are commands without undo: executor.submit(() -> sendEmail(order)) Commands as data + handler (Example 2) Records + sealed interface + switch; serializable; the CQRS style Undoable commands (Example 1) execute() + undo(); commands store what they need to reverse Macro commands (coding challenge) A composite command that runs steps in order and undoes them in reverse Compensating commands When undo is impossible (an email was sent), issue a new command that compensates (send a correction); see Saga

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Command JDK Runnable, Callable submitted to ExecutorService; TimerTask Swing Action / AbstractAction (one action used by a menu item, a toolbar button and a shortcut) and UndoManager / UndoableEdit Spring Batch Tasklet, Step Spring Shell / picocli CLI commands as objects Axon Framework @CommandHandler with command objects (CQRS) Message queues Kafka/RabbitMQ messages carrying commands ("ReserveStock") to handlers Hystrix (legacy) HystrixCommand: every remote call wrapped as a command object

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Undo/redo, queueing, scheduling, logging and retries More classes (one per operation) unless you use lambdas or records Decouples who asks from who does Undo logic can be hard (or impossible for external side effects) Commands can be composed (macros) Command history uses memory; bound it Serializable commands enable distributed and offline processing Replaying old commands after schema changes needs versioning

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Non-idempotent replays

Queued commands get retried and duplicated. Without an ID and de-duplication (Examples 2 and 3), retries double-charge customers.

Undo that doesn't really undo

"Undo send email" is impossible. Be honest: offer compensation (send a correction) or a delay before executing (Gmail's "Undo send" just waits a few seconds).

Commands that capture mutable state

A command holding a reference to a mutable Cart may see different data when it runs later. Capture values (IDs, amounts) at creation time.

Unbounded history

Infinite undo stacks in long editing sessions eat memory. Limit them, or compact old commands into snapshots (see Memento).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Commands vs. events. A command is a request that may be rejected ("ReserveStock", imperative). An event is a fact that already happened ("StockReserved", past tense). CQRS systems receive commands, validate them against the current state, and emit events. Mixing the two up leads to confusing systems; be precise in design reviews.

Command queues at scale. Persist commands before acknowledging (transactional outbox), process with at-least-once delivery, make handlers idempotent, partition by entity (account ID) to keep per-entity ordering, and route poison commands to a dead-letter queue with alerting.

Collaborative editing. Undo in a multi-user editor is hard: Alice's undo must not revert Bob's later edits. Real editors (Google Docs, Figma) use Operational Transformation or CRDTs, transforming commands against concurrent ones. Mentioning this shows depth.

Versioning. Stored commands outlive code. Include a schema version in each command and keep handlers able to read old versions, or migrate the queue during deploys.

War story: the batch that paid twice

A bank's scheduled-payments batch crashed halfway through. The operator re-ran the whole batch. Commands had no IDs, so the first half executed again: about 8,000 customers paid their bills twice, and refunds took a week. Fix: every command got a unique ID stored with a "processed" marker in the same database transaction as the ledger update; the processor skips processed IDs; re-running a batch became safe by design. Lesson: if a command can be stored, it can be replayed. Idempotency isn't optional.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Command Strategy Memento Chain of Responsibility Object represents A request (what to do) An algorithm (how to do it) A state snapshot A handler Typical use Undo, queue, log, schedule Swap behavior Restore state Decide who handles Undo approach Inverse operation N/A Restore a snapshot N/A

Command + Memento: undo by restoring a snapshot when an inverse operation is hard to write. Command + Composite: macro commands. Command + Observer: command handlers publish events.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Request as an object: queue it, log it, schedule it, retry it, undo it.
  • Receiver does the work; invoker runs and stores commands.
  • Undo/redo = two stacks; a new command clears redo.
  • Stored commands need IDs + idempotency and versioning.
  • Command ≠ event: a request vs. a fact.
editor.run(new Insert(doc, 0, "Hello")); editor.undo(); editor.redo();

docs.title: Interpreter
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐

TL;DR

Interpreter represents the grammar of a small language as a tree of objects, where each node knows how to evaluate itself. Use it for small, stable domain-specific languages (DSLs): promo rules, pricing formulas, search filters, schedules. Business people write the rules; your code runs them.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: marketing changes promotion rules every week: "carts over INR 999 in electronics, or for gold members, except in Leh". If every rule is Java code, every change needs a developer, a review and a deployment. If rules are text in a small language that your system can interpret, marketing can change them through an admin screen.

Formal definition (GoF):

Given a language, define a representation for its grammar along with an interpreter that uses the representation to interpret sentences in the language.

How it works:

  1. Parse the text into an abstract syntax tree (AST): one object per grammar construct.
  2. Interpret: call eval() / matches() on the root; each node evaluates its children and combines the results.
Grammar part Node type Example Terminal (no children) A value or a leaf test cart_total >= 999, a number, a variable Non-terminal (has children) Combines other expressions AND, OR, +, max(a, b)

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Musical notation

Sheet music is a small language. Notes are terminals; bars, repeats and chords combine them. A musician (the interpreter) reads the score and produces sound. Composers write new pieces without changing the musician.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram class Expression { <<interface>> +interpret(Context) } class TerminalExpression { +interpret(Context) } class NonTerminalExpression { -Expression left -Expression right +interpret(Context) } class Context class Client Expression <|.. TerminalExpression Expression <|.. NonTerminalExpression NonTerminalExpression o--> Expression Client --> Expression : builds AST (via a parser) Client --> Context Participant Responsibility Expression interpret(context) Terminal expression Leaf of the grammar (a comparison, a number) Non-terminal expression Composite node (AND, +, function call) Context Input data (cart fields, variables, date and time) Parser Turns text into the AST (not part of GoF's pattern, but always needed in practice)

The AST is a Composite; the interpreter is a recursive walk over it.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
boolean offerApplies(Cart c) {
    // Changed every week by a developer, after a ticket from marketing:
    return c.total() >= 999 && (c.category().equals("electronics") || c.tier().equals("gold"))
            && !c.city().equals("Leh");
}
  • Every rule change is a code change and a deployment.
  • Business users can't see, test or own the rules.
  • Rules can't vary per country or campaign without more ifs.

docs.title: Example 1: Promo Rules Written by Marketing (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: An e-commerce site's promotions team defines eligibility rules in an admin UI using a tiny language: comparisons (>=, ==), AND, OR, NOT and parentheses. Rules are stored as text, parsed once when saved (so typos are rejected immediately), and evaluated against every cart. AND must bind tighter than OR, as in every programming language, or rules will silently mean something else.

Design:

flowchart TB A1[AND] --> A2[AND] A1 --> N[NOT] A2 --> C1["cart_total >= 999"] A2 --> O[OR] O --> C2["category == 'electronics'"] O --> C3["member_tier == 'gold'"] N --> C4["city == 'Leh'"]

Full Code:

Rule.javaRuleParser.javaPromoDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.promo;

import java.util.Map;

/** Abstract syntax tree for promo rules. Each node interprets itself against a cart context. */
public sealed interface Rule {

    boolean matches(Map<String, Object> cart); // (1)!

    record And(Rule left, Rule right) implements Rule {
        public boolean matches(Map<String, Object> c) { return left.matches(c) && right.matches(c); }
        public String toString() { return "(" + left + " AND " + right + ")"; }
    }

    record Or(Rule left, Rule right) implements Rule {
        public boolean matches(Map<String, Object> c) { return left.matches(c) || right.matches(c); }
        public String toString() { return "(" + left + " OR " + right + ")"; }
    }

    record Not(Rule inner) implements Rule {
        public boolean matches(Map<String, Object> c) { return !inner.matches(c); }
        public String toString() { return "NOT " + inner; }
    }

    record Compare(String field, String op, Object value) implements Rule { // (2)!
        public boolean matches(Map<String, Object> c) {
            Object actual = c.get(field);
            if (actual == null) {
                return false;
            }
            if (value instanceof Double expected) {
                double a = ((Number) actual).doubleValue();
                return switch (op) {
                    case ">" -> a > expected;
                    case ">=" -> a >= expected;
                    case "<" -> a < expected;
                    case "<=" -> a <= expected;
                    case "==" -> a == expected;
                    default -> throw new IllegalStateException(op);
                };
            }
            return switch (op) {
                case "==" -> actual.toString().equals(value);
                case "!=" -> !actual.toString().equals(value);
                default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Operator " + op + " needs a number");
            };
        }

        public String toString() { return field + " " + op + " " + (value instanceof String ? "'" + value + "'" : value); }
    }
}
  1. The interpreter method. Every node evaluates itself against the cart context; non-terminals delegate to their children.
  2. The terminal expression: a single comparison. A missing field means "no match" rather than an error, which is a deliberate rule-language decision.
package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.promo;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/**
 * Recursive-descent parser. Grammar:
 * <pre>
 *   expr    := term ( OR term )*
 *   term    := factor ( AND factor )*
 *   factor  := NOT factor | '(' expr ')' | compare
 *   compare := IDENT OP ( NUMBER | 'string' )
 * </pre>
 */
public final class RuleParser {

    private static final Pattern TOKEN = Pattern.compile(
            "\\s*(?:(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)|'([^']*)'|(>=|<=|==|!=|>|<|\\(|\\))|([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z_0-9]*))");

    private final List<String> tokens = new ArrayList<>();
    private int pos;

    private RuleParser(String text) {
        Matcher m = TOKEN.matcher(text);
        int end = 0;
        while (m.lookingAt()) {
            if (m.group(2) != null) {
                tokens.add("'" + m.group(2)); // mark strings with a leading quote
            } else {
                tokens.add(m.group().strip());
            }
            end = m.end();
            m.region(end, text.length());
        }
        if (!text.substring(end).isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unexpected input at: " + text.substring(end));
        }
    }

    public static Rule parse(String text) {
        RuleParser p = new RuleParser(text);
        Rule rule = p.expr();
        if (p.pos != p.tokens.size()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unexpected token: " + p.tokens.get(p.pos));
        }
        return rule;
    }

    private Rule expr() {
        Rule left = term();
        while (accept("OR")) {
            left = new Rule.Or(left, term());
        }
        return left;
    }

    private Rule term() {
        Rule left = factor();
        while (accept("AND")) {
            left = new Rule.And(left, factor());
        }
        return left;
    }

    private Rule factor() {
        if (accept("NOT")) {
            return new Rule.Not(factor());
        }
        if (accept("(")) {
            Rule inner = expr();
            expect(")");
            return inner;
        }
        String field = next();
        String op = next();
        String raw = next();
        Object value = raw.startsWith("'") ? raw.substring(1) : Double.valueOf(raw);
        return new Rule.Compare(field, op, value);
    }

    private boolean accept(String token) {
        if (pos < tokens.size() && tokens.get(pos).equalsIgnoreCase(token)) {
            pos++;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    private void expect(String token) {
        if (!accept(token)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected " + token);
        }
    }

    private String next() {
        if (pos >= tokens.size()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unexpected end of rule");
        }
        return tokens.get(pos++);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.promo;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class PromoDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Promo Rules Written by Marketing ===");
        String text = "cart_total >= 999 AND (category == 'electronics' OR member_tier == 'gold') AND NOT city == 'Leh'";
        Rule rule = RuleParser.parse(text);
        System.out.println("Rule text : " + text);
        System.out.println("Parsed AST: " + rule);

        List<Map<String, Object>> carts = List.of(
                Map.of("cart_total", 1499, "category", "electronics", "member_tier", "silver", "city", "Pune"),
                Map.of("cart_total", 1200, "category", "fashion", "member_tier", "gold", "city", "Delhi"),
                Map.of("cart_total", 650, "category", "electronics", "member_tier", "gold", "city", "Pune"),
                Map.of("cart_total", 5000, "category", "electronics", "member_tier", "gold", "city", "Leh"));
        for (Map<String, Object> cart : carts) {
            System.out.printf("total=%-5s category=%-12s tier=%-7s city=%-6s -> %s%n",
                    cart.get("cart_total"), cart.get("category"), cart.get("member_tier"), cart.get("city"),
                    rule.matches(cart) ? "OFFER APPLIES" : "no offer");
        }
        try {
            RuleParser.parse("cart_total >= ");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Bad rule rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Promo Rules Written by Marketing ===
Rule text : cart_total >= 999 AND (category == 'electronics' OR member_tier == 'gold') AND NOT city == 'Leh'
Parsed AST: ((cart_total >= 999.0 AND (category == 'electronics' OR member_tier == 'gold')) AND NOT city == 'Leh')
total=1499  category=electronics  tier=silver  city=Pune   -> OFFER APPLIES
total=1200  category=fashion      tier=gold    city=Delhi  -> OFFER APPLIES
total=650   category=electronics  tier=gold    city=Pune   -> no offer
total=5000  category=electronics  tier=gold    city=Leh    -> no offer
Bad rule rejected: Unexpected end of rule

The printed AST makes precedence visible: the parser grouped OR inside the parentheses and AND everywhere else, exactly as written.

Why Interpreter here:

  • Rules change weekly and belong to business users.
  • A small grammar (4 constructs) is easy to parse, document and test.
  • Parsing on save gives immediate feedback; evaluation per cart is a cheap tree walk.

docs.title: Example 2: Tariff Formulas (Telecom)
docs.text:
Scenario: A telecom operator's pricing team defines postpaid bills as formulas: rental, plus extra minutes beyond the free allowance, plus extra data beyond the free GB, and roaming capped at a maximum. Tariffs change with every marketing campaign and regulatory update. Formulas are stored in the product catalogue and evaluated for millions of customers at month-end, so they're parsed once and the AST is reused.

Design:

flowchart TB P1["+"] --> P2["+"] P1 --> M2["*"] P2 --> R[rental] P2 --> M1["*"] M1 --> MX1["max(minutes - free_minutes, 0)"] M1 --> PM[per_min] M2 --> MX2["max(data_gb - free_gb, 0)"] M2 --> PG[per_gb]

Full Code:

Formula.javaFormulaParser.javaBillingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.billing;

import java.util.Map;

/** Arithmetic expression AST: numbers, variables, + - * /, and max/min functions. */
public sealed interface Formula {

    double eval(Map<String, Double> vars);

    record Num(double value) implements Formula {
        public double eval(Map<String, Double> v) { return value; }
    }

    record Var(String name) implements Formula {
        public double eval(Map<String, Double> v) {
            Double value = v.get(name);
            if (value == null) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown variable: " + name);
            }
            return value;
        }
    }

    record BinOp(char op, Formula left, Formula right) implements Formula {
        public double eval(Map<String, Double> v) {
            double a = left.eval(v), b = right.eval(v);
            return switch (op) {
                case '+' -> a + b;
                case '-' -> a - b;
                case '*' -> a * b;
                case '/' -> a / b;
                default -> throw new IllegalStateException();
            };
        }
    }

    record Call(String fn, Formula a, Formula b) implements Formula {
        public double eval(Map<String, Double> v) {
            return switch (fn) {
                case "max" -> Math.max(a.eval(v), b.eval(v));
                case "min" -> Math.min(a.eval(v), b.eval(v));
                default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown function: " + fn);
            };
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.billing;

/**
 * expr   := term (('+'|'-') term)*
 * term   := factor (('*'|'/') factor)*
 * factor := NUMBER | IDENT | IDENT '(' expr ',' expr ')' | '(' expr ')'
 */
public final class FormulaParser {

    private final String s;
    private int i;

    private FormulaParser(String s) {
        this.s = s.replace(" ", "");
    }

    public static Formula parse(String text) {
        FormulaParser p = new FormulaParser(text);
        Formula f = p.expr();
        if (p.i != p.s.length()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unexpected '" + p.s.charAt(p.i) + "' at " + p.i);
        }
        return f;
    }

    private Formula expr() {
        Formula f = term();
        while (i < s.length() && (s.charAt(i) == '+' || s.charAt(i) == '-')) {
            char op = s.charAt(i++);
            f = new Formula.BinOp(op, f, term());
        }
        return f;
    }

    private Formula term() {
        Formula f = factor();
        while (i < s.length() && (s.charAt(i) == '*' || s.charAt(i) == '/')) {
            char op = s.charAt(i++);
            f = new Formula.BinOp(op, f, factor());
        }
        return f;
    }

    private Formula factor() {
        if (s.charAt(i) == '(') {
            i++;
            Formula f = expr();
            i++; // ')'
            return f;
        }
        int start = i;
        if (Character.isDigit(s.charAt(i))) {
            while (i < s.length() && (Character.isDigit(s.charAt(i)) || s.charAt(i) == '.')) {
                i++;
            }
            return new Formula.Num(Double.parseDouble(s.substring(start, i)));
        }
        while (i < s.length() && (Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(i)) || s.charAt(i) == '_')) {
            i++;
        }
        String name = s.substring(start, i);
        if (i < s.length() && s.charAt(i) == '(') {
            i++;
            Formula a = expr();
            i++; // ','
            Formula b = expr();
            i++; // ')'
            return new Formula.Call(name, a, b);
        }
        return new Formula.Var(name);
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.billing;

import java.util.Map;

public class BillingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Telecom: Tariff Formulas Configured by the Pricing Team ===");
        // Stored in the product catalogue, not in code:
        String postpaid = "rental + max(minutes - free_minutes, 0) * per_min + max(data_gb - free_gb, 0) * per_gb";
        String roaming = "min(minutes * intl_rate, cap)";
        Formula bill = FormulaParser.parse(postpaid);
        Formula roam = FormulaParser.parse(roaming);

        Map<String, Double> light = Map.of("rental", 399.0, "minutes", 250.0, "free_minutes", 300.0,
                "per_min", 1.0, "data_gb", 18.0, "free_gb", 20.0, "per_gb", 50.0);
        Map<String, Double> heavy = Map.of("rental", 399.0, "minutes", 420.0, "free_minutes", 300.0,
                "per_min", 1.0, "data_gb", 26.5, "free_gb", 20.0, "per_gb", 50.0);

        System.out.printf("Light user bill : INR %.2f%n", bill.eval(light));
        System.out.printf("Heavy user bill : INR %.2f%n", bill.eval(heavy));
        System.out.printf("Roaming 30 min  : INR %.2f%n", roam.eval(Map.of("minutes", 30.0, "intl_rate", 25.0, "cap", 999.0)));
        System.out.printf("Roaming 90 min  : INR %.2f (capped)%n", roam.eval(Map.of("minutes", 90.0, "intl_rate", 25.0, "cap", 999.0)));
    }
}

Output:

=== Telecom: Tariff Formulas Configured by the Pricing Team ===
Light user bill : INR 399.00
Heavy user bill : INR 844.00
Roaming 30 min  : INR 750.00
Roaming 90 min  : INR 999.00 (capped)

Heavy user: 399 + (420 − 300) × 1 + (26.5 − 20) × 50 = 399 + 120 + 325 = INR 844.

Money and double

The demo uses double to keep the grammar small. A real billing interpreter evaluates with BigDecimal and an explicit rounding rule per tariff.

Why Interpreter here:

  • Pricing is data owned by the pricing team, not code.
  • Parse once, evaluate millions of times: the AST is built at load time.
  • New functions (ceil, if) are new node types; existing formulas keep working.

docs.title: Example 3: Warehouse Receiving Hours (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A logistics network has hundreds of warehouses and hubs, each with receiving hours like MON-FRI 09:00-18:00, SAT 10:00-14:00, or night hubs with FRI-MON 22:00-23:59 (wrapping around the weekend). Trucks are routed only to sites that will accept them on arrival. Hours are edited by site managers as text, and the routing engine must interpret them.

Design:

flowchart LR S["schedule"] --> W1["window: MON-FRI 09:00-18:00"] S --> W2["window: SAT 10:00-14:00"] Q["isOpen(SATURDAY, 15:00)?"] --> S S -->|"any window contains it?"| A[false: wait]

Full Code:

OpeningHours.javaHoursDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.hours;

import java.time.DayOfWeek;
import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * Interprets expressions like "MON-FRI 09:00-18:00, SAT 10:00-14:00".
 * Grammar: schedule := rule (',' rule)* ; rule := days ' ' time '-' time ; days := DAY | DAY '-' DAY
 */
public final class OpeningHours {

    private record Window(Set<DayOfWeek> days, LocalTime from, LocalTime to) { // terminal-level expression
        boolean contains(DayOfWeek day, LocalTime t) {
            return days.contains(day) && !t.isBefore(from) && t.isBefore(to);
        }
    }

    private final List<Window> windows = new ArrayList<>(); // non-terminal: OR of windows

    private OpeningHours() {
    }

    public static OpeningHours parse(String text) {
        OpeningHours h = new OpeningHours();
        for (String rule : text.split(",")) {
            String[] parts = rule.strip().split(" ");
            String[] times = parts[1].split("-");
            h.windows.add(new Window(days(parts[0]), LocalTime.parse(times[0]), LocalTime.parse(times[1])));
        }
        return h;
    }

    private static Set<DayOfWeek> days(String spec) {
        String[] range = spec.split("-");
        DayOfWeek from = day(range[0]);
        DayOfWeek to = range.length == 2 ? day(range[1]) : from;
        Set<DayOfWeek> result = EnumSet.noneOf(DayOfWeek.class);
        for (DayOfWeek d = from; ; d = d.plus(1)) {
            result.add(d);
            if (d == to) {
                return result;
            }
        }
    }

    private static DayOfWeek day(String abbrev) {
        for (DayOfWeek d : DayOfWeek.values()) {
            if (d.name().startsWith(abbrev)) {
                return d;
            }
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown day: " + abbrev);
    }

    public boolean isOpen(DayOfWeek day, LocalTime time) {
        return windows.stream().anyMatch(w -> w.contains(day, time));
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.hours;

import java.time.DayOfWeek;
import java.time.LocalTime;

public class HoursDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Warehouse Receiving Hours ===");
        OpeningHours bhiwandi = OpeningHours.parse("MON-FRI 09:00-18:00, SAT 10:00-14:00");
        OpeningHours nightHub = OpeningHours.parse("FRI-MON 22:00-23:59");

        Object[][] arrivals = {
                {DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY, "11:30"}, {DayOfWeek.SATURDAY, "15:00"},
                {DayOfWeek.SUNDAY, "10:00"}, {DayOfWeek.SUNDAY, "22:30"}};
        for (Object[] a : arrivals) {
            DayOfWeek day = (DayOfWeek) a[0];
            LocalTime t = LocalTime.parse((String) a[1]);
            System.out.printf("Truck %-9s %s -> Bhiwandi: %-6s Night hub: %s%n", day, t,
                    bhiwandi.isOpen(day, t) ? "accept" : "wait", nightHub.isOpen(day, t) ? "accept" : "wait");
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Warehouse Receiving Hours ===
Truck WEDNESDAY 11:30 -> Bhiwandi: accept Night hub: wait
Truck SATURDAY  15:00 -> Bhiwandi: wait   Night hub: wait
Truck SUNDAY    10:00 -> Bhiwandi: wait   Night hub: wait
Truck SUNDAY    22:30 -> Bhiwandi: wait   Night hub: accept

Why Interpreter here:

  • A familiar notation (like OpenStreetMap's opening_hours) that site managers already understand.
  • The grammar is tiny: windows (terminals) combined by "any of" (a non-terminal).
  • Edge cases (week wrap-around, exclusive end times) are handled once, in the interpreter, and tested.
Unit Tests: InterpreterTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter;

import com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.billing.FormulaParser;
import com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.hours.OpeningHours;
import com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.promo.RuleParser;
import com.handbook.behavioral.interpreter.roman.Roman;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.DayOfWeek;
import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class InterpreterTest {

    @Test
    void andBindsTighterThanOr() {
        var rule = RuleParser.parse("a == 'x' OR b == 'y' AND c == 'z'");
        assertThat(rule.matches(Map.of("a", "x", "b", "n", "c", "n"))).isTrue();
        assertThat(rule.toString()).isEqualTo("(a == 'x' OR (b == 'y' AND c == 'z'))");
    }

    @Test
    void missingFieldsDoNotMatch() {
        assertThat(RuleParser.parse("total > 1").matches(Map.of())).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void formulaRespectsPrecedenceAndFunctions() {
        assertThat(FormulaParser.parse("2 + 3 * 4").eval(Map.of())).isEqualTo(14.0);
        assertThat(FormulaParser.parse("(2 + 3) * 4").eval(Map.of())).isEqualTo(20.0);
        assertThat(FormulaParser.parse("max(x - 10, 0)").eval(Map.of("x", 4.0))).isEqualTo(0.0);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> FormulaParser.parse("y + 1").eval(Map.of())).hasMessageContaining("Unknown variable");
    }

    @Test
    void openingHoursWrapAroundTheWeek() {
        var h = OpeningHours.parse("SAT-MON 08:00-10:00");
        assertThat(h.isOpen(DayOfWeek.SUNDAY, LocalTime.of(9, 0))).isTrue();
        assertThat(h.isOpen(DayOfWeek.TUESDAY, LocalTime.of(9, 0))).isFalse();
        assertThat(h.isOpen(DayOfWeek.MONDAY, LocalTime.of(10, 0))).isFalse(); // end is exclusive
    }

    @Test
    void romanNumerals() {
        assertThat(Roman.interpret("XIV")).isEqualTo(14);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Roman.interpret("ABC")).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Sealed interfaces + records for ASTs (all examples): concise, immutable nodes with exhaustive pattern matching.
  • Separate evaluation from the tree with a Visitor or switch: eval(node) as a switch over sealed node types lets you add operations (pretty-print, optimize, translate to SQL) without touching the nodes.
  • Compile instead of interpret: turn the AST into a lambda tree once (Predicate<Cart>), and evaluation becomes plain method calls.
  • Don't write a parser for big languages: use ANTLR for real grammars, or embed an existing expression engine: Spring Expression Language (SpEL), MVEL, JEXL, or a rules engine (Drools). For JSON-friendly rules, consider JSONLogic or CEL (Common Expression Language).

Never eval untrusted code

Embedding a general-purpose scripting engine (Nashorn, Groovy, full SpEL with type access) for business rules lets a rule author run arbitrary code on your servers. A small custom grammar or a sandboxed language (SpEL SimpleEvaluationContext, CEL) is far safer.
