Cron expressions (CronExpression.parse) JPA / Hibernate JPQL / HQL (parsed into an AST, translated to SQL) Spring Data Query derivation from method names (findByStatusAndTotalGreaterThan) Thymeleaf, Freemarker Template expressions

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Business users own the rules; changes without deployments Grammars grow; large languages become hard to maintain as hand-written classes Each grammar rule is one small class (easy to extend) Performance: tree walking is slower than compiled code for hot paths ASTs can be analysed: validated, explained, translated to SQL You now maintain a language: docs, error messages, versioning, tooling Natural fit with Composite and Visitor Security risk if the language can do too much

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Accidental general-purpose language

Rules start simple, then someone needs loops, then variables, then functions. Stop early: keep the grammar declarative and small, or adopt an established engine.

Silent precedence bugs

A OR B AND C must mean A OR (B AND C). Test precedence explicitly (see andBindsTighterThanOr) and show users the parsed tree.

Parsing on every evaluation

Parse once (on save or load), cache the AST, and evaluate many times.

Unhelpful errors

"Parse error" isn't enough for business users. Report position and expected token, and validate fields against a known schema at save time.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Rules platforms. At scale, rule DSLs grow into platforms: an editor with autocomplete, validation against a schema of available fields, versioning with effective dates, simulation ("how many of last week's orders would this rule have matched?"), audit of who changed what, and a kill switch. Interviews for SAP-style or fintech roles love this discussion.

Rules → SQL. Because the AST is data, you can translate it with a visitor: evaluate in memory for one cart, or generate a WHERE clause to find all matching customers in the database. Use bind parameters, never string concatenation.

Performance. For millions of evaluations, compile the AST into lambdas or bytecode once (SpEL has a compiler mode). Order AND operands by cost and selectivity so cheap checks short-circuit first.

Safety. Bound evaluation (depth limits, maximum expression size, timeouts), and whitelist functions. Treat rules as code: review, test and stage them.

War story: the OR that gave everything away

A rule meant "electronics AND (gold OR platinum)" was typed as category == 'electronics' AND tier == 'gold' OR tier == 'platinum'. The interpreter correctly parsed it as (electronics AND gold) OR platinum, so every platinum customer got 20% off everything, including gold coins. The promo ran for 6 hours before finance noticed. Fix: the editor now displays the parsed tree with explicit parentheses before saving, requires parentheses when AND and OR are mixed, and runs a simulation against yesterday's orders showing how many would match. Lesson: a correct interpreter isn't enough. Make the meaning visible to the people writing rules.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Interpreter Composite Visitor Specification Focus Evaluating sentences of a language Part-whole trees Operations over a structure Combinable business rules in code Input Text (parsed) Objects Objects Objects (built in code) Relationship AST is a Composite Structure Adds operations to an AST A code-only cousin of Interpreter (no parser)

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Grammar as classes; sentences as trees; evaluation as a tree walk.
  • Terminals (leaves) and non-terminals (combine children); the AST is a Composite.
  • Parse once, evaluate many; test precedence.
  • Keep grammars small; use ANTLR, SpEL or CEL for anything bigger; never eval untrusted code.
  • Real life: regex, SpEL, JPQL, cron expressions.
Rule r = RuleParser.parse("cart_total >= 999 AND NOT city == 'Leh'"); r.matches(cart);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add an IN operator to the promo language: city IN ('Pune', 'Delhi').
  • Write a visitor (or switch) that converts a promo Rule into a SQL WHERE clause with bind parameters.
  • Switch Formula evaluation to BigDecimal with half-up rounding to 2 decimals.
  • Support overnight windows like MON-FRI 22:00-06:00 in OpeningHours.

Command Next: Iterator

docs.title: Iterator
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Iterator gives a standard way to walk through the elements of a collection one at a time, without exposing how the collection is stored. Java has it built in (Iterator, Iterable, for-each, streams). Write your own when the data is paginated, merged, generated, or traversed in different orders.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a bank statement lives behind an API that returns 50 transactions per page. Callers want "all transactions" in a simple loop. They shouldn't handle cursors, page boundaries, or when to fetch the next page, and they shouldn't download all 10,000 transactions if they only show the first 4.

Formal definition (GoF):

Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.

Java's built-in version:

public interface Iterator<E> { boolean hasNext(); E next(); default void remove() {...} }
public interface Iterable<T> { Iterator<T> iterator(); }   // anything Iterable works in for-each

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A TV remote's channel button

You press "next channel" without knowing whether channels come from cable, satellite or the internet, or how they're stored in the TV's memory. Different buttons (next, favourites only, last watched) give different traversals of the same channel list.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram class Iterable~T~ { <<interface>> +iterator() Iterator~T~ } class Iterator~T~ { <<interface>> +hasNext() boolean +next() T } class ConcreteCollection { +iterator() Iterator~T~ } class ConcreteIterator { -position / cursor state +hasNext() boolean +next() T } Iterable <|.. ConcreteCollection Iterator <|.. ConcreteIterator ConcreteCollection ..> ConcreteIterator : creates Participant Responsibility Iterator hasNext() / next(); keeps the traversal state (position, cursor) Iterable (aggregate) Creates a fresh iterator on each iterator() call Client Loops without knowing the storage or traversal details

Because each iterator has its own state, several traversals can run at the same time over the same collection.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
String cursor = null;
do {
    Page page = api.fetch(account, cursor);         // pagination logic in every caller
    for (Txn t : page.items()) {
        if (shown++ == 4) break;                     // break only exits the inner loop...
        print(t);
    }
    cursor = page.nextCursor();
} while (cursor != null && shown < 4);              // ...so every caller re-implements stopping
  • Traversal logic duplicated in every caller.
  • Callers depend on the storage format (pages and cursors).
  • Easy to fetch too much or too little.

docs.title: Example 1: Statement with Lazy Pagination (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A banking app shows a 4-line "mini statement" on the home screen and a full statement on another screen. The core banking API is cursor-paginated (3 per page here; usually 50–100). The mini statement must fetch only what it needs (one or two pages), while the full statement must get everything, using the same simple loop and the same stream API.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Caller (stream.limit(4)) participant I as Transactions iterator participant A as StatementApi C->>I: hasNext() I->>A: fetch(cursor=null) A-->>I: txns 1-3, next=3 C->>I: next() x3 C->>I: hasNext() I->>A: fetch(cursor=3) A-->>I: txns 4-6, next=6 C->>I: next() (4th) Note over C: limit reached, page 3 is never fetched

Full Code:

Transactions.javaStatementApi.javaStatementDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement;

import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement.StatementApi.Page;
import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement.StatementApi.Txn;

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import java.util.stream.StreamSupport;

/** Iterable view over ALL transactions; pages are fetched lazily as the caller iterates. */
public class Transactions implements Iterable<Txn> {

    private final StatementApi api;
    private final String account;

    public Transactions(StatementApi api, String account) {
        this.api = api;
        this.account = account;
    }

    @Override
    public Iterator<Txn> iterator() {
        return new Iterator<>() { // (1)!
            private Iterator<Txn> current = Collections.emptyIterator();
            private String cursor;
            private boolean lastPageLoaded;

            @Override
            public boolean hasNext() {
                while (!current.hasNext() && !lastPageLoaded) { // (2)!
                    Page page = api.fetch(account, cursor);
                    current = page.items().iterator();
                    cursor = page.nextCursor();
                    lastPageLoaded = cursor == null;
                }
                return current.hasNext();
            }

            @Override
            public Txn next() {
                if (!hasNext()) {
                    throw new NoSuchElementException();
                }
                return current.next();
            }
        };
    }

    public Stream<Txn> stream() {
        return StreamSupport.stream(spliterator(), false); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Every call to iterator() returns a new iterator with its own cursor, so two screens can iterate independently.
  2. The page-fetching loop lives here, once: fetch a page only when the current one is used up. A while (not if) handles empty pages correctly.
  3. Iterable gives you spliterator() for free, so the collection works with streams too, and limit() really does stop fetching.
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Remote API that returns transactions one page at a time (cursor-based pagination). */
public class StatementApi {

    public record Txn(int no, String description, long amountInr) {
    }

    public record Page(List<Txn> items, String nextCursor) {
    }

    private static final int PAGE_SIZE = 3;
    private static final int TOTAL = 8;
    private int calls;

    public Page fetch(String account, String cursor) {
        calls++;
        int start = cursor == null ? 0 : Integer.parseInt(cursor);
        System.out.println("  [api] GET /accounts/" + account + "/txns?cursor=" + cursor);
        List<Txn> items = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = start; i < Math.min(start + PAGE_SIZE, TOTAL); i++) {
            items.add(new Txn(i + 1, i % 2 == 0 ? "UPI to grocery" : "Salary credit", i % 2 == 0 ? -450 - i : 85_000));
        }
        String next = start + PAGE_SIZE < TOTAL ? String.valueOf(start + PAGE_SIZE) : null;
        return new Page(items, next);
    }

    public int calls() {
        return calls;
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement;

public class StatementDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Statement with Lazy Pagination ===");
        StatementApi api = new StatementApi();
        Transactions txns = new Transactions(api, "SB-1001");

        System.out.println("Mini statement (first 4 only):");
        txns.stream().limit(4).forEach(t -> System.out.println("  #" + t.no() + " " + t.description() + " " + t.amountInr()));
        System.out.println("API calls so far: " + api.calls());

        System.out.println("Full statement total:");
        long total = 0;
        for (StatementApi.Txn t : txns) { // the same Iterable works in a for-each loop
            total += t.amountInr();
        }
        System.out.println("  net INR " + total + ", API calls so far: " + api.calls());
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Statement with Lazy Pagination ===
Mini statement (first 4 only):
  [api] GET /accounts/SB-1001/txns?cursor=null
  #1 UPI to grocery -450
  #2 Salary credit 85000
  #3 UPI to grocery -452
  [api] GET /accounts/SB-1001/txns?cursor=3
  #4 Salary credit 85000
API calls so far: 2
Full statement total:
  [api] GET /accounts/SB-1001/txns?cursor=null
  [api] GET /accounts/SB-1001/txns?cursor=3
  [api] GET /accounts/SB-1001/txns?cursor=6
  net INR 338188, API calls so far: 5

The mini statement needed 2 API calls; the full statement made 3 more, all hidden behind a for-each loop.

Why Iterator here:

  • Hides pagination: callers see one sequence.
  • Lazy: pages are fetched on demand, so short reads are cheap.
  • Plugs into for-each and streams by implementing Iterable.

docs.title: Example 2: Merged Home Feed (Social Media)
docs.text:
Scenario: A social app's home feed combines posts from friends, groups and followed pages. Each source already returns posts newest first. The feed must show one combined, newest-first list, but only one screen (6 posts) at a time, without loading every source fully. This is a k-way merge, the same algorithm databases use to merge sorted runs.

Design:

flowchart LR F["friends: 1009, 1004, 1001"] --> H{{"max-heap of<br/>each source's next post"}} G["groups: 1008, 1002"] --> H P["pages: 1006, 1005, 1003"] --> H H --> O["feed: 1009, 1008, 1006, 1005, 1004, 1003 ..."]

Full Code:

FeedMerger.javaFeedDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.feed;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Merges several newest-first sources into one newest-first feed (k-way merge), lazily. */
public class FeedMerger implements Iterator<FeedMerger.Post> {

    public record Post(long timestamp, String source, String text) {
    }

    private record Head(Post post, Iterator<Post> rest) {
    }

    private final PriorityQueue<Head> heap =
            new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingLong((Head h) -> h.post().timestamp()).reversed()); // (1)!

    public FeedMerger(List<Iterator<Post>> sources) {
        for (Iterator<Post> s : sources) {
            if (s.hasNext()) {
                heap.add(new Head(s.next(), s));
            }
        }
    }

    @Override
    public boolean hasNext() {
        return !heap.isEmpty();
    }

    @Override
    public Post next() {
        Head top = heap.poll();
        if (top == null) {
            throw new NoSuchElementException();
        }
        if (top.rest().hasNext()) {
            heap.add(new Head(top.rest().next(), top.rest())); // (2)!
        }
        return top.post();
    }
}
  1. A heap holds the next post of each source, newest on top: O(log k) per post for k sources.
  2. After taking a post, refill the heap from the same source. Each source is read only as far as needed.
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.feed;

import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.feed.FeedMerger.Post;

import java.util.List;

public class FeedDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Social Media: Home Feed from Three Sources ===");
        List<Post> friends = List.of(new Post(1009, "friends", "Riya posted holiday photos"),
                new Post(1004, "friends", "Kabir changed his profile picture"),
                new Post(1001, "friends", "Neel shared a recipe"));
        List<Post> groups = List.of(new Post(1008, "groups", "Pune Runners: Sunday 10K route"),
                new Post(1002, "groups", "Java India: Virtual threads meetup"));
        List<Post> pages = List.of(new Post(1006, "pages", "City Metro: new line opens"),
                new Post(1005, "pages", "Weather: heavy rain alert"),
                new Post(1003, "pages", "Library: new arrivals"));

        FeedMerger feed = new FeedMerger(List.of(friends.iterator(), groups.iterator(), pages.iterator()));
        for (int i = 0; i < 6 && feed.hasNext(); i++) { // the UI only asks for one screen
            Post p = feed.next();
            System.out.printf("  t=%d [%-7s] %s%n", p.timestamp(), p.source(), p.text());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Social Media: Home Feed from Three Sources ===
  t=1009 [friends] Riya posted holiday photos
  t=1008 [groups ] Pune Runners: Sunday 10K route
  t=1006 [pages  ] City Metro: new line opens
  t=1005 [pages  ] Weather: heavy rain alert
  t=1004 [friends] Kabir changed his profile picture
  t=1003 [pages  ] Library: new arrivals

Why Iterator here:

  • An iterator built from other iterators: composition without materializing lists.
  • The UI just calls next() until the screen is full.
  • Works the same whether sources are lists, database cursors, or remote paginated APIs.

docs.title: Example 3: Playlist Play Modes (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: A music app plays the same playlist in order, on repeat (infinitely), or shuffled. The player only knows "give me the next song". Shuffle must be reproducible given a seed, so a "shuffle session" can be resumed on another device and tested deterministically.

Design:

classDiagram class Playlist { -List~String~ songs +play(Mode, seed) Iterator~String~ } class InOrder["songs.iterator()"] class RepeatAll["infinite cycling iterator"] class Shuffle["seeded shuffled copy"] Playlist ..> InOrder : IN_ORDER Playlist ..> RepeatAll : REPEAT_ALL Playlist ..> Shuffle : SHUFFLE

Full Code:

Playlist.javaPlaylistDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.playlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;
import java.util.Random;

/** One collection, several traversal strategies: each mode is a different Iterator. */
public class Playlist {

    public enum Mode { IN_ORDER, REPEAT_ALL, SHUFFLE }

    private final List<String> songs;

    public Playlist(List<String> songs) {
        this.songs = List.copyOf(songs);
    }

    public Iterator<String> play(Mode mode, long seed) {
        return switch (mode) {
            case IN_ORDER -> songs.iterator();
            case REPEAT_ALL -> new Iterator<>() { // (1)!
                private int i;
                public boolean hasNext() { return !songs.isEmpty(); }
                public String next() {
                    if (songs.isEmpty()) {
                        throw new NoSuchElementException();
                    }
                    return songs.get(i++ % songs.size());
                }
            };
            case SHUFFLE -> {
                List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(songs);
                Collections.shuffle(order, new Random(seed)); // (2)!
                yield order.iterator();
            }
        };
    }
}
  1. An infinite iterator: hasNext() is always true for a non-empty playlist. Callers must bound it (the demo takes 6). Streams do this well: Stream.generate(...).limit(n).
  2. A seeded shuffle is reproducible: the same seed gives the same order. Store the seed to resume a session elsewhere.
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.playlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;

public class PlaylistDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Road Trip Playlist ===");
        Playlist playlist = new Playlist(List.of("Kesariya", "Lose Yourself", "Bohemian Rhapsody", "Tum Hi Ho"));

        for (Playlist.Mode mode : Playlist.Mode.values()) {
            Iterator<String> it = playlist.play(mode, 42);
            List<String> next6 = new ArrayList<>();
            while (it.hasNext() && next6.size() < 6) {
                next6.add(it.next());
            }
            System.out.printf("%-10s -> %s%n", mode, next6);
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Road Trip Playlist ===
IN_ORDER   -> [Kesariya, Lose Yourself, Bohemian Rhapsody, Tum Hi Ho]
REPEAT_ALL -> [Kesariya, Lose Yourself, Bohemian Rhapsody, Tum Hi Ho, Kesariya, Lose Yourself]
SHUFFLE    -> [Tum Hi Ho, Lose Yourself, Kesariya, Bohemian Rhapsody]

Why Iterator here:

  • Several traversals of one collection: the essence of the pattern.
  • The player depends on Iterator<String>, not on the mode.
  • New modes (smart shuffle that avoids repeating an artist) are new iterators.
Unit Tests: IteratorTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.iterator;

import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.feed.FeedMerger;
import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.playlist.Playlist;
import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.ring.RingBuffer;
import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement.StatementApi;
import com.handbook.behavioral.iterator.statement.Transactions;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class IteratorTest {

    @Test
    void paginationIsLazyAndComplete() {
        StatementApi api = new StatementApi();
        Transactions txns = new Transactions(api, "A");
        assertThat(txns.stream().limit(2).count()).isEqualTo(2);
        assertThat(api.calls()).isEqualTo(1);
        assertThat(txns.stream().count()).isEqualTo(8);
        Iterator<StatementApi.Txn> it = txns.iterator();
        while (it.hasNext()) {
            it.next();
        }
        assertThatThrownBy(it::next).isInstanceOf(NoSuchElementException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void feedIsSortedNewestFirst() {
        var a = List.of(new FeedMerger.Post(5, "a", ""), new FeedMerger.Post(1, "a", ""));
        var b = List.of(new FeedMerger.Post(4, "b", ""), new FeedMerger.Post(3, "b", ""));
        FeedMerger m = new FeedMerger(List.of(a.iterator(), b.iterator()));
        List<Long> times = new ArrayList<>();
        m.forEachRemaining(p -> times.add(p.timestamp()));
        assertThat(times).containsExactly(5L, 4L, 3L, 1L);
    }

    @Test
    void shuffleIsReproducibleWithSeed() {
        Playlist p = new Playlist(List.of("a", "b", "c", "d"));
        List<String> first = new ArrayList<>();
        List<String> second = new ArrayList<>();
        p.play(Playlist.Mode.SHUFFLE, 7).forEachRemaining(first::add);
        p.play(Playlist.Mode.SHUFFLE, 7).forEachRemaining(second::add);
        assertThat(first).isEqualTo(second).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("a", "b", "c", "d");
    }

    @Test
    void ringBufferKeepsNewest() {
        RingBuffer<Integer> r = new RingBuffer<>(2);
        r.add(1);
        r.add(2);
        r.add(3);
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        r.forEach(out::add);
        assertThat(out).containsExactly(2, 3);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Variation Notes External iterator (hasNext/next) Caller controls the loop; can stop, interleave, merge (Example 2) Internal iterator (forEach(consumer), streams) Collection controls the loop; concise; harder to stop early or interleave Lazy / generated Pages fetched on demand (Example 1), infinite sequences (Example 3) Fail-fast Throws ConcurrentModificationException if the collection changes during iteration (ArrayList, coding challenge) Weakly consistent Never throws; may or may not reflect changes (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList snapshots) Spliterator Iterator that can split for parallel streams

Modern Java helpers: Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next), Stream.generate, Iterator.forEachRemaining, Enumeration.asIterator(), and takeWhile/dropWhile for lazy stopping.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Iterator JDK collections Every Collection.iterator(); ListIterator (bidirectional, with set/add) JDK Scanner (an Iterator<String> over input), BufferedReader.lines(), Files.walk(), DirectoryStream JDBC ResultSet.next(): a database cursor is an iterator Spring Data Slice / Page with hasNext(); Stream<T> repository methods backed by DB cursors Spring Batch ItemReader.read(): an iterator over input records (files, DB, Kafka) Kafka ConsumerRecords iteration; poll() loops AWS SDK v2 Paginators (listObjectsV2Paginator) that hide continuation tokens, exactly like Example 1

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Hides storage and traversal details Custom iterators are easy to get subtly wrong (hasNext side effects, empty pages) Multiple simultaneous and different traversals External iterators are more verbose than streams Lazy: works with huge, remote or infinite data Fail-fast behavior is best-effort, not a concurrency guarantee Uniform loop syntax (for-each, streams) Iterators over remote data hide latency and errors

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Modifying a collection while iterating

for (x : list) list.remove(x) throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use iterator.remove(), removeIf, or collect changes and apply them afterwards.

next() without hasNext() semantics

next() must throw NoSuchElementException at the end, and hasNext() must be idempotent (calling it twice must not skip elements or fetch twice).

Leaking resources

Iterators over files or DB cursors must be closed. Prefer Stream with try-with-resources (try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(p))).

Infinite iterators in eager code

toList() on an infinite iterator never returns. Always bound them (limit).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Pagination design. Prefer cursor-based (keyset) pagination over offset pagination for large or changing datasets: offsets skip or duplicate items when data changes, and OFFSET 100000 is slow. Cursors encode the last seen key (created_at, id). Example 1's iterator works unchanged with either.

Streaming large results. Don't load 10 million rows into a List. Stream them: JDBC fetch size, Spring Data Stream<T> inside a transaction, Spring Batch chunking, or reactive streams with back-pressure (Flux), where the consumer controls how fast the producer goes.

Merging sorted streams (Example 2) is everywhere: LSM-tree compaction, external merge sort, timeline services, log aggregation. Know the complexity: O(n log k).

Concurrency. Choose collection iterators deliberately: fail-fast for single-threaded code (bugs show up quickly), weakly consistent (ConcurrentHashMap) or snapshot (CopyOnWriteArrayList) for concurrent readers.

War story: the export that ate the heap

A "download all transactions" feature for business customers called repository.findAll(accountId) and built a CSV from the resulting List. It worked for two years, until a large merchant with 9 million transactions clicked the button. The JVM ran out of memory and the pod restarted mid-business-day, taking other customers' requests with it. Fix: replaced with a streaming iterator: a keyset-paginated query (1,000 rows per page) feeding a streaming CSV writer that wrote straight to the HTTP response; constant memory regardless of size. Lesson: if the size of a collection depends on a customer, iterate lazily.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Iterator Composite Visitor Generator / Stream Purpose Traverse elements sequentially Structure of parts and wholes Operations over elements Lazily produce elements Who controls the loop Caller (external) N/A The structure / visitor Caller pulls (limit) Typical combo Iterating a Composite tree (DFS/BFS iterator) Traversed by Iterator or Visitor Often uses an Iterator internally Implemented with an Iterator

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Sequential access without exposing structure: Iterator (cursor) + Iterable (collection).
  • Custom iterators shine for pagination, merging, generation, multiple traversal orders.
  • Fail-fast (ConcurrentModificationException) vs. weakly consistent iterators.
  • Lazy iteration keeps memory flat; close resource-backed iterators.
  • Real life: ResultSet, Spring Batch ItemReader, AWS SDK paginators.
for (Txn t : new Transactions(api, "SB-1001")) { ... }   // pages fetched lazily

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a "smart shuffle" mode that never plays the same artist twice in a row.
  • Make Transactions retry a failed page fetch once before giving up.
  • Implement an in-order iterator for a binary search tree using a stack.
  • Return a Stream<Post> from FeedMerger using Spliterators.spliteratorUnknownSize.

docs.title: Mediator
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Mediator centralizes how a group of objects interact. Instead of talking to each other directly, they talk to a mediator that coordinates them. Use it when many objects have tangled, many-to-many communication: dispatch systems, chat rooms, UI forms, auctions, air-traffic-style coordination.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: on a checkout form, choosing a country must reset the state list, change the postcode hint and disable the Pay button; choosing a state and a valid postcode must enable Pay. If each widget calls the others directly, every widget knows every other widget: N widgets means up to N×(N−1) dependencies, and adding one field means editing all of them.

Formal definition (GoF):

Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact. Mediator promotes loose coupling by keeping objects from referring to each other explicitly, and it lets you vary their interaction independently.

flowchart LR subgraph Without["Without mediator: N x N links"] A1[Country] <--> B1[State] A1 <--> C1[Postcode] A1 <--> D1[Pay] B1 <--> C1 B1 <--> D1 C1 <--> D1 end subgraph With["With mediator: N links"] A2[Country] <--> M((Form mediator)) B2[State] <--> M C2[Postcode] <--> M D2[Pay] <--> M end

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Air traffic control

Pilots don't negotiate runways with each other. Each pilot talks only to the control tower, and the tower sequences take-offs and landings. Adding a new plane doesn't require it to know every other plane.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram     class Mediator {         <<interface>>         +notify(sender, event)     }     class ConcreteMediator {         -ColleagueA a         -ColleagueB b         +notify(sender, event)     }     class Colleague {         #Mediator mediator     }     class ColleagueA     class ColleagueB     Mediator <|.. ConcreteMediator     Colleague <|-- ColleagueA     Colleague <|-- ColleagueB     Colleague --> Mediator     ConcreteMediator --> ColleagueA     ConcreteMediator --> ColleagueB Participant Responsibility Mediator Interface colleagues use to report events or requests Concrete mediator Knows the colleagues and the coordination rules Colleagues Know only the mediator; do their own job and report to it

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
class CountrySelect {
    StateSelect state; PostcodeField postcode; PayButton pay;   // knows everyone
    void onChange(String c) {
        state.setOptions(STATES.get(c)); state.clear();
        postcode.setHint(c.equals("India") ? "PIN" : "PLZ"); postcode.clear();
        pay.setEnabled(false);
    }
}
class StateSelect { PayButton pay; PostcodeField postcode; ... }   // ...and so on
  • Tight many-to-many coupling: components can't be reused on another form.
  • Rules are scattered across components; "when is Pay enabled?" has no single answer.
  • Adding a field touches several classes.

docs.title: Example 1: Dispatch Center (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: Riders request trips; drivers become available or busy. Matching rules (nearest available driver, queue riders when everyone is busy, assign the queue when a driver finishes) change often: surge zones, driver ratings, women-only rides. Riders and drivers must never know about each other until matched. All of this belongs in the dispatch center, the mediator.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant M as Meera (rider) participant D as CityDispatch (mediator) participant S as Sunita (driver) M->>D: requestRide() D-->>M: all busy, queued S->>D: tripFinished() D->>S: assign(Meera) D->>M: Sunita arriving in 8 min

Full Code:

Dispatch.javaDispatchDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.dispatch;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Mediator + colleagues. Riders and drivers never reference each other directly. */
public final class Dispatch {

    private Dispatch() {
    }

    public interface DispatchCenter { // (1)!
        void register(Driver driver);
        void requestRide(Rider rider);
        void tripFinished(Driver driver);
    }

    public static final class Driver {
        private final String name;
        private final int locationKm; // position on a 1-D road, to keep the demo simple
        private final DispatchCenter center;
        private boolean available = true;

        public Driver(String name, int locationKm, DispatchCenter center) {
            this.name = name;
            this.locationKm = locationKm;
            this.center = center;
            center.register(this);
        }

        void assign(Rider rider) {
            available = false;
            System.out.println("  " + name + ": heading to " + rider.name());
        }

        public void finishTrip() {
            available = true;
            center.tripFinished(this); // (2)!
        }

        public String name() { return name; }
    }

    public static final class Rider {
        private final String name;
        private final int locationKm;
        private final DispatchCenter center;

        public Rider(String name, int locationKm, DispatchCenter center) {
            this.name = name;
            this.locationKm = locationKm;
            this.center = center;
        }

        public void requestRide() {
            center.requestRide(this);
        }

        void notifyAssigned(Driver d, int etaMin) {
            System.out.println("  " + name + ": " + d.name() + " arriving in " + etaMin + " min");
        }

        void notifyWaiting() {
            System.out.println("  " + name + ": all drivers busy, you're in the queue");
        }

        public String name() { return name; }
    }

    public static final class CityDispatch implements DispatchCenter {
        private final List<Driver> drivers = new ArrayList<>();
        private final List<Rider> waiting = new ArrayList<>();

        public void register(Driver driver) {
            drivers.add(driver);
        }

        public void requestRide(Rider rider) {
            System.out.println(rider.name() + " requests a ride at km " + rider.locationKm);
            Optional<Driver> nearest = drivers.stream().filter(d -> d.available)
                    .min(Comparator.comparingInt(d -> Math.abs(d.locationKm - rider.locationKm))); // (3)!
            nearest.ifPresentOrElse(d -> match(d, rider), () -> {
                waiting.add(rider);
                rider.notifyWaiting();
            });
        }

        public void tripFinished(Driver driver) {
            System.out.println(driver.name() + " finished a trip");
            if (!waiting.isEmpty()) {
                match(driver, waiting.removeFirst());
            }
        }

        private void match(Driver d, Rider r) {
            int etaMin = Math.max(1, Math.abs(d.locationKm - r.locationKm) * 2);
            d.assign(r);
            r.notifyAssigned(d, etaMin);
        }
    }
}
  1. The mediator interface: what colleagues can tell the center.
  2. Colleagues report events to the mediator. A driver finishing a trip doesn't look for riders itself.
  3. The matching rule lives in one place. Switching to "highest-rated nearby driver" changes only the mediator.
package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.dispatch;

import com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.dispatch.Dispatch.*;

public class DispatchDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Dispatch Center ===");
        CityDispatch center = new CityDispatch();
        Driver ramesh = new Driver("Ramesh", 2, center);
        Driver sunita = new Driver("Sunita", 9, center);

        new Rider("Asha", 8, center).requestRide();
        new Rider("Vikram", 3, center).requestRide();
        new Rider("Meera", 5, center).requestRide();
        sunita.finishTrip();
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Dispatch Center ===
Asha requests a ride at km 8
  Sunita: heading to Asha
  Asha: Sunita arriving in 2 min
Vikram requests a ride at km 3
  Ramesh: heading to Vikram
  Vikram: Ramesh arriving in 2 min
Meera requests a ride at km 5
  Meera: all drivers busy, you're in the queue
Sunita finished a trip
  Sunita: heading to Meera
  Meera: Sunita arriving in 8 min

Why Mediator here:

  • Many riders and many drivers, coordinated by one set of rules.
  • Riders and drivers are simple; all coordination (matching, queueing) is in the center.
  • The rules can change (or be A/B tested) without touching rider or driver code.

docs.title: Example 2: Incident Channel (SaaS Team Chat)
docs.text:
Scenario: A Slack-style chat app runs an #incident-payments channel during an outage. Members (engineers and an alert bot) post messages; the room delivers them to everyone else, sends push notifications for @mentions, and enforces mutes (the noisy alert bot gets muted). Members never hold references to each other: they join a room and talk through it.

Design:

flowchart LR P[priya] -- say --> R((ChatRoom<br/>#incident-payments)) A[arjun] -- say --> R B[alertbot] -- say --> R R -- deliver --> P R -- deliver --> A R -- "push: @mention" --> P R -. "blocked: muted" .-x B

Full Code:

ChatRoom.javaChatDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.chat;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** Mediator: routes messages, handles @mentions and mutes. Members only talk to the room. */
public class ChatRoom {

    private static final Pattern MENTION = Pattern.compile("@(\\w+)");

    private final String channel;
    private final Map<String, Member> members = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Set<String> muted = new HashSet<>();

    public ChatRoom(String channel) {
        this.channel = channel;
    }

    public Member join(String name) {
        Member m = new Member(name, this);
        members.put(name, m);
        broadcast("system", name + " joined #" + channel);
        return m;
    }

    public void mute(String name) {
        muted.add(name);
    }

    void send(Member from, String text) {
        if (muted.contains(from.name())) {
            System.out.println("  [room] blocked message from muted member " + from.name());
            from.receive("system", "you are muted in #" + channel);
            return;
        }
        broadcast(from.name(), text);
        Matcher m = MENTION.matcher(text);
        while (m.find()) {
            Member target = members.get(m.group(1));
            if (target != null) {
                target.notify(from.name() + " mentioned you in #" + channel);
            }
        }
    }

    private void broadcast(String from, String text) {
        members.values().stream().filter(m -> !m.name().equals(from)).forEach(m -> m.receive(from, text));
    }

    public static class Member {
        private final String name;
        private final ChatRoom room;

        Member(String name, ChatRoom room) {
            this.name = name;
            this.room = room;
        }

        public String name() { return name; }

        public void say(String text) { room.send(this, text); }

        void receive(String from, String text) {
            if (name.equals("priya")) { // only print one member's view to keep the demo short
                System.out.println("  [priya's screen] " + from + ": " + text);
            }
        }

        void notify(String text) {
            System.out.println("  [push to " + name + "] " + text);
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.chat;

public class ChatDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS: #incident-payments Channel ===");
        ChatRoom room = new ChatRoom("incident-payments");
        ChatRoom.Member priya = room.join("priya");
        ChatRoom.Member arjun = room.join("arjun");
        ChatRoom.Member bot = room.join("alertbot");

        bot.say("p99 latency on /charge is 4.2s");
        arjun.say("@priya can you check the gateway dashboard?");
        priya.say("on it, looks like the bank is degraded");
        room.mute("alertbot");
        bot.say("p99 latency on /charge is 4.3s");
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS: #incident-payments Channel ===
  [priya's screen] system: priya joined #incident-payments
  [priya's screen] system: arjun joined #incident-payments
  [priya's screen] system: alertbot joined #incident-payments
  [priya's screen] alertbot: p99 latency on /charge is 4.2s
  [priya's screen] arjun: @priya can you check the gateway dashboard?
  [push to priya] arjun mentioned you in #incident-payments
  [room] blocked message from muted member alertbot

(Only Priya's screen is printed, plus pushes and room actions, to keep the output short.)

Why Mediator here:

  • Classic many-to-many communication reduced to many-to-one.
  • Policies (mentions, mutes, later retention and moderation) live in the room.
  • Members can be people, bots or integrations; the room treats them the same way.

docs.title: Example 3: Checkout Address Form (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: An international checkout form has country, state, postcode and a Pay button. Choosing a country loads that country's states, resets the state and postcode, and changes the postcode hint (6-digit PIN for India, 5-digit PLZ for Germany). Pay is enabled only when a state is chosen and the postcode has the right length for the selected country. The same field components are reused across many forms.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> NoCountry NoCountry --> CountryChosen : country.set() CountryChosen --> Complete : state + valid postcode Complete --> CountryChosen : country changed (reset) Complete --> [*] : Pay enabled

Full Code:

CheckoutForm.javaFormDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.form;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Mediator for a checkout form. Widgets only tell the form "I changed";
 * the form decides what other widgets must do.
 */
public class CheckoutForm {

    private static final Map<String, List<String>> STATES = Map.of(
            "India", List.of("Karnataka", "Maharashtra"), "Germany", List.of("Bavaria", "Berlin"));

    public final Field country = new Field("country", this);
    public final Field state = new Field("state", this);
    public final Field postcode = new Field("postcode", this);
    public final Field payButton = new Field("pay", this);

    public CheckoutForm() {
        state.enabled = false;
        payButton.enabled = false;
    }

    void changed(Field source) { // (1)!
        switch (source.name) {
            case "country" -> {
                state.options = STATES.getOrDefault(country.value, List.of());
                state.value = null;
                state.enabled = !state.options.isEmpty();
                postcode.hint = country.value.equals("India") ? "6-digit PIN" : "5-digit PLZ";
                postcode.value = null;
            }
            case "state", "postcode" -> { /* fall through to validation below */ }
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(source.name);
        }
        payButton.enabled = state.value != null && postcode.value != null
                && postcode.value.length() == (country.value.equals("India") ? 6 : 5);
    }

    public String render() {
        return "country=%s | state=%s %s | postcode=%s (%s) | Pay %s".formatted(
                country.value, state.value, state.enabled ? state.options : "(disabled)",
                postcode.value, postcode.hint, payButton.enabled ? "ENABLED" : "disabled");
    }

    public static class Field {
        final String name;
        final CheckoutForm form;
        String value;
        boolean enabled = true;
        List<String> options = List.of();
        String hint = "";

        Field(String name, CheckoutForm form) {
            this.name = name;
            this.form = form;
        }

        public void set(String newValue) {
            if (!enabled) {
                throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is disabled");
            }
            value = newValue;
            form.changed(this); // the field knows only the mediator
        }
    }
}
  1. All coordination rules in one method. "When is Pay enabled?" has exactly one answer, here.
package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.form;

public class FormDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Checkout Address Form ===");
        CheckoutForm form = new CheckoutForm();
        System.out.println("start          : " + form.render());
        form.country.set("India");
        System.out.println("pick India     : " + form.render());
        form.state.set("Karnataka");
        form.postcode.set("560034");
        System.out.println("state + PIN    : " + form.render());
        form.country.set("Germany");
        System.out.println("switch country : " + form.render());
        form.state.set("Berlin");
        form.postcode.set("10115");
        System.out.println("state + PLZ    : " + form.render());
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Checkout Address Form ===
start          : country=null | state=null (disabled) | postcode=null () | Pay disabled
pick India     : country=India | state=null [Karnataka, Maharashtra] | postcode=null (6-digit PIN) | Pay disabled
state + PIN    : country=India | state=Karnataka [Karnataka, Maharashtra] | postcode=560034 (6-digit PIN) | Pay ENABLED
switch country : country=Germany | state=null [Bavaria, Berlin] | postcode=null (5-digit PLZ) | Pay disabled
state + PLZ    : country=Germany | state=Berlin [Bavaria, Berlin] | postcode=10115 (5-digit PLZ) | Pay ENABLED

Why Mediator here:

  • This is the GoF's original motivating example (dialog boxes).
  • Fields are reusable and dumb; the form knows how they depend on each other.
  • Business rules for the form are testable without a UI (see the unit tests).
Unit Tests: MediatorTest.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.mediator;

import com.handbook.behavioral.mediator.form.CheckoutForm;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class MediatorTest {

    @Test
    void stateIsDisabledUntilCountryChosen() {
        CheckoutForm form = new CheckoutForm();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> form.state.set("Karnataka")).hasMessageContaining("disabled");
        form.country.set("India");
        form.state.set("Karnataka");
        assertThat(form.render()).contains("state=Karnataka");
    }

    @Test
    void changingCountryResetsDependentFieldsAndPayButton() {
        CheckoutForm form = new CheckoutForm();
        form.country.set("India");
        form.state.set("Karnataka");
        form.postcode.set("560034");
        assertThat(form.render()).endsWith("Pay ENABLED");
        form.country.set("Germany");
        assertThat(form.render()).contains("state=null", "postcode=null").endsWith("Pay disabled");
    }

    @Test
    void wrongPostcodeLengthKeepsPayDisabled() {
        CheckoutForm form = new CheckoutForm();
        form.country.set("Germany");
        form.state.set("Berlin");
        form.postcode.set("560034");
        assertThat(form.render()).endsWith("Pay disabled");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Event-based mediator: colleagues publish events (CountryChanged) to a mediator or an in-process event bus that routes them to handlers. Looser, but the flow is harder to follow.
  • Command/query mediator: in-process request routing (mediator.send(new PlaceOrderCommand(...)) finds the one handler). Popular in .NET (MediatR) and used in Java with Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher or small custom dispatchers. It decouples controllers from handlers.
  • UI frameworks: a form's controller or view-model (MVC/MVVM) is usually the mediator between widgets.
  • Keep it focused: one mediator per collaboration (a form, a room, a dispatch zone), not one per application.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Mediator Spring MVC DispatcherServlet coordinates handler mappings, adapters, view resolvers and exception resolvers Spring ApplicationEventPublisher / ApplicationEventMulticaster (event-based mediator between beans) JDK java.util.Timer (schedules tasks that never know each other); ExecutorService mediates between submitters and worker threads Swing / JavaFX Dialog and controller classes coordinating widgets Messaging Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) are mediators at system scale Workflow engines Camunda, Temporal: orchestrators that mediate between services

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Loose coupling: colleagues know only the mediator The mediator can grow into a god object Interaction rules in one place: easy to change and test Single point of failure or bottleneck (at system scale) Colleagues become reusable Logic moves from many small places into one complex place Many-to-many becomes one-to-many Indirection makes the flow harder to trace than direct calls

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
The god mediator

A MainController mediating 40 widgets and every business rule is unmaintainable. Split by collaboration (address section, payment section) or move domain rules into domain objects.

Colleagues bypassing the mediator

One shortcut (state.payButton.enable()) brings the tangled dependencies back. Colleagues shouldn't hold references to each other at all.

Event loops

A mediator reacting to "state changed" by setting the state again (which fires "state changed"...) loops forever. Guard re-entrant updates.

Hidden ordering assumptions

With event-based mediators, handlers run in some order. If correctness depends on it, make the order explicit.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Orchestration is Mediator at system scale. A saga orchestrator (or Temporal/Camunda workflow) is a mediator between services: services know only the orchestrator's commands and events, never each other. The trade-off against choreography (services react to each other's events directly, Observer-style) is the same as in-process: centralized, visible flow and a potential bottleneck vs. decentralized, flexible flow that's harder to trace.

Orchestration (Mediator) Choreography (Observer) Flow visibility One place shows the whole flow Spread across services Coupling Services coupled to the orchestrator Services coupled to event schemas Change Change the orchestrator Change several services Failure handling Centralized compensation Each service handles its part

Scaling a mediator. Dispatch systems partition the mediator (one dispatcher per city or geo-cell) to avoid a global bottleneck; chat systems shard rooms across servers. The mediator's state (available drivers, room membership) must be partitioned too.

Testing. The mediator holds the interesting rules, so test it heavily with fake colleagues (as MediatorTest does for the form).

War story: the form that charged the wrong currency

A travel site's checkout widgets talked to each other directly. When a new "billing country" field was added, it updated the currency label but nobody updated the payment widget's currency code, because that link existed only in the old shipping-country widget. Customers who changed billing country saw prices in euros but were charged the same number in dollars. Fix: introduced a form mediator owning all cross-field rules (country to currency to payment), with the payment amount and currency computed in exactly one place, and unit tests for every field combination. Lesson: when "X must stay in sync with Y" rules are spread across components, one will be missed. Centralize them.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Mediator Observer Facade Chain of Responsibility Direction Two-way: colleagues ↔ mediator One-way: subject → observers One-way: client → facade → subsystems Along a chain Who knows whom Colleagues know only the mediator; it knows them Subject knows observers through an interface Subsystems don't know the facade Each handler knows the next Purpose Coordinate peers Notify about changes Simplify a subsystem Find a handler

A mediator is often implemented with Observer (colleagues publish events, the mediator subscribes).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Peers talk to a mediator, not to each other: many-to-many becomes many-to-one.
  • Coordination rules in one place; colleagues become simple and reusable.
  • Watch for the god mediator; one per collaboration.
  • vs Observer: coordinate vs. notify. vs Facade: two-way peers vs. one-way simplification.
  • System scale: orchestrators, message brokers, DispatcherServlet.
void changed(Field source) { /* the only place that knows how fields depend on each other */ }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Change dispatch to prefer drivers with a rating above 4.5 when two are equally close.
  • Add thread-safety to AuctionHouse and test with 100 concurrent bidders on virtual threads.
  • Add a "billing address same as shipping" checkbox to CheckoutForm and handle it in the mediator.

Iterator Next: Memento

docs.title: Memento
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Memento captures an object's internal state in a snapshot so it can be restored later, without exposing that state to anyone else. Use it for undo, version history, checkpoints and rollbacks, and saving drafts to resume later.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a designer wants to go back to "v1 draft" of a canvas. To restore it, someone must have saved every shape, colour and the background. If the version-history code copies the canvas's private fields itself, the canvas loses encapsulation: every change to its internals breaks the history code. Memento lets the canvas make its own snapshot, hand it out as an opaque object, and later restore from it.

Formal definition (GoF):

Without violating encapsulation, capture and externalize an object's internal state so that the object can be restored to this state later.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A game's save point

At a checkpoint the game saves your level, health and inventory into a save slot. You can't read or edit the save file (it's opaque to you), but you can load it to go back. The save slots (caretaker) just store saves; only the game (originator) knows what's inside.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram     class Originator {         -state         +save() Memento         +restore(Memento)     }     class Memento {         -state (private to Originator)     }     class Caretaker {         -List~Memento~ history     }     Originator ..> Memento : creates / reads     Caretaker o--> Memento : stores only Participant Responsibility Originator Creates a memento of its current state; restores from one Memento Immutable snapshot; contents visible only to the originator Caretaker Keeps mementos (undo stack, version list, database) but never inspects them

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
class VersionHistory {
    void saveVersion(Canvas c) {
        versions.add(new ArrayList<>(c.shapes));   // needs access to Canvas internals
        backgrounds.add(c.background);             // forgets the new 'grid' field added last week
    }
}
  • Breaks encapsulation: the history must know (and keep up with) the canvas's internals.
  • Incomplete snapshots when fields are added.
  • Shared mutable state if the copy isn't deep enough.

docs.title: Example 1: Named Version History (Design SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A Figma/Canva-style design tool lets designers save named versions ("v1 draft", "v2 dark theme") and restore any of them. The client changes their mind a lot. The canvas's internal model evolves constantly (layers, effects, grids), so the version-history service must not depend on it: it just stores labelled, opaque snapshots.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant D as Designer participant C as Canvas (originator) participant H as VersionHistory (caretaker) D->>C: save("v1 draft") C-->>H: Snapshot (opaque) D->>C: edits... D->>C: save("v2 dark theme") C-->>H: Snapshot D->>H: get("v1 draft") H-->>C: restore(snapshot)

Full Code:

Canvas.javaVersionHistory.javaCanvasDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.canvas;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Originator: a design canvas. Only it can create and read its snapshots. */
public class Canvas {

    public record Shape(String kind, int x, int y, String color) {
    }

    private final List<Shape> shapes = new ArrayList<>();
    private String background = "white";

    public void add(Shape s) { shapes.add(s); }

    public void recolorAll(String color) {
        shapes.replaceAll(s -> new Shape(s.kind(), s.x(), s.y(), color));
    }

    public void setBackground(String bg) { this.background = bg; }

    /** Memento: immutable, and its contents are private to Canvas (nested class, private accessors). */
    public static final class Snapshot { // (1)!
        private final List<Shape> shapes;
        private final String background;
        private final String label;

        private Snapshot(List<Shape> shapes, String background, String label) {
            this.shapes = List.copyOf(shapes); // (2)!
            this.background = background;
            this.label = label;
        }

        public String label() { return label; } // the only thing the caretaker may see
    }

    public Snapshot save(String label) {
        return new Snapshot(shapes, background, label);
    }

    public void restore(Snapshot s) {
        shapes.clear();
        shapes.addAll(s.shapes);
        background = s.background;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "bg=" + background + " " + shapes.stream().map(s -> s.kind() + "(" + s.color() + ")").toList();
    }
}
  1. The memento is a nested class with private fields. Outer classes in Java can read a nested class's private members, but nobody else can. That's how Java enforces "only the originator sees the state".
  2. Defensive copy at snapshot time. The shapes are immutable records, so a shallow copy of the list is enough.
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.canvas;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Caretaker: stores snapshots, never looks inside them. */
public class VersionHistory {

    private final List<Canvas.Snapshot> versions = new ArrayList<>();

    public void keep(Canvas.Snapshot s) {
        versions.add(s);
    }

    public Canvas.Snapshot get(String label) {
        return versions.stream().filter(v -> v.label().equals(label)).findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No version " + label));
    }

    public List<String> labels() {
        return versions.stream().map(Canvas.Snapshot::label).toList();
    }
}

package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.canvas;

import com.handbook.behavioral.memento.canvas.Canvas.Shape;

public class CanvasDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Design SaaS: Named Version History ===");
        Canvas canvas = new Canvas();
        VersionHistory history = new VersionHistory();

        canvas.add(new Shape("logo", 10, 10, "blue"));
        canvas.add(new Shape("headline", 10, 80, "black"));
        history.keep(canvas.save("v1 draft"));

        canvas.setBackground("navy");
        canvas.recolorAll("white");
        history.keep(canvas.save("v2 dark theme"));

        canvas.add(new Shape("banner", 0, 200, "orange"));
        canvas.recolorAll("pink"); // the client hates it
        System.out.println("current      : " + canvas);
        System.out.println("versions     : " + history.labels());

        canvas.restore(history.get("v2 dark theme"));
        System.out.println("restore v2   : " + canvas);
        canvas.restore(history.get("v1 draft"));
        System.out.println("restore v1   : " + canvas);
    }
}

Output:

=== Design SaaS: Named Version History ===
current      : bg=navy [logo(pink), headline(pink), banner(pink)]
versions     : [v1 draft, v2 dark theme]
restore v2   : bg=navy [logo(white), headline(white)]
restore v1   : bg=white [logo(blue), headline(black)]

Why Memento here:

  • Full-state snapshots are simpler and safer than writing an inverse for every possible edit.
  • The caretaker stays independent of the canvas internals.
  • Snapshots are immutable, so they're safe to keep and share.

docs.title: Example 2: Safe Substitutions and "Undo Clear Cart" (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: When an item is out of stock, a grocery app tries a multi-step substitution: remove the item, add a replacement, apply a bundle coupon. If any step fails (the replacement is also out of stock), the cart must return to exactly how it was. Separately, "Clear cart" shows a toast with UNDO for a few seconds. Both use a checkpoint taken just before the change.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> Checkpoint : checkpoint() Checkpoint --> Step1 : remove paneer Step1 --> Step2 : add tofu Step2 --> Step3 : apply coupon Step3 --> Done : success Step2 --> Rollback : failure Step3 --> Rollback : failure Rollback --> [*] : rollback(checkpoint)

Full Code:

Cart.javaCartDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.cart;

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Originator with a checkpoint/rollback API, used around risky multi-step changes. */
public class Cart {

    private final Map<String, Integer> items = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private String coupon;

    public record Checkpoint(Map<String, Integer> items, String coupon) { // (1)!
        public Checkpoint {
            items = Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(items)); // keeps order, unlike Map.copyOf
        }
    }

    public Checkpoint checkpoint() {
        return new Checkpoint(items, coupon);
    }

    public void rollback(Checkpoint c) {
        items.clear();
        items.putAll(c.items());
        coupon = c.coupon();
    }

    public void add(String sku, int qty) { items.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum); }

    public void remove(String sku) { items.remove(sku); }

    public void clear() { items.clear(); coupon = null; }

    public void applyCoupon(String code) { coupon = code; }

    public int size() { return items.size(); }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return items + (coupon == null ? "" : " coupon=" + coupon);
    }
}
  1. A record as memento: immutable and simple. It's public here because callers need to hold it; its contents are copies, so holding it can't change the cart. (If you also want to hide the contents, use the nested-class approach from Example 1.)
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.cart;

public class CartDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Safe Substitutions and 'Undo Clear Cart' ===");
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        cart.add("MILK-1L", 2);
        cart.add("PANEER-200G", 1);
        cart.add("ATTA-5KG", 1);
        System.out.println("cart             : " + cart);

        // A multi-step substitution: paneer out of stock -> swap for tofu + apply a bundle coupon
        Cart.Checkpoint before = cart.checkpoint();
        try {
            cart.remove("PANEER-200G");
            cart.add("TOFU-200G", 1);
            cart.applyCoupon("SWAP10");
            throw new IllegalStateException("TOFU-200G also out of stock"); // step 3 fails
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            cart.rollback(before);
            System.out.println("substitution failed (" + e.getMessage() + "), rolled back");
        }
        System.out.println("cart             : " + cart);

        Cart.Checkpoint undo = cart.checkpoint();
        cart.clear();
        System.out.println("after clear      : " + cart + "   [toast: Cart cleared. UNDO]");
        cart.rollback(undo);
        System.out.println("after UNDO       : " + cart);
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Safe Substitutions and 'Undo Clear Cart' ===
cart             : {MILK-1L=2, PANEER-200G=1, ATTA-5KG=1}
substitution failed (TOFU-200G also out of stock), rolled back
cart             : {MILK-1L=2, PANEER-200G=1, ATTA-5KG=1}
after clear      : {}   [toast: Cart cleared. UNDO]
after UNDO       : {MILK-1L=2, PANEER-200G=1, ATTA-5KG=1}

A bug this example caught

The first version of Checkpoint used Map.copyOf, which doesn't keep insertion order (and its iteration order changes between JVM runs). After a rollback, the cart showed items in a different order. A memento must restore the state exactly, including order where users can see it.

Why Memento here:

  • All-or-nothing multi-step changes with an in-memory checkpoint, like a database savepoint.
  • Undo for destructive actions without writing an inverse of "clear".
  • The cart decides what's in its checkpoint; callers just hold it.

docs.title: Example 3: Resume a Booking on Another Device (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hotel booking takes 4 steps. Users often start on a phone and finish on a laptop. The wizard's state is saved as a draft token (a serialized memento) stored against the user's account. The token is opaque to the server (it doesn't parse it) and versioned: drafts saved by an older app version must be rejected cleanly instead of being misread.

Design:

flowchart LR P["Phone: BookingWizard<br/>step 3, city, dates"] -->|"saveDraft()"| T["opaque token<br/>(Base64)"] T --> S[("User drafts store<br/>(caretaker)")] S --> L["Laptop: BookingWizard.resume(token)"] L --> C[Continue at step 3]

Full Code:

BookingWizard.javaBookingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.booking;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Base64;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Originator: a 4-step hotel booking wizard. Its memento is an opaque, versioned token
 * that can be stored server-side and resumed on another device.
 */
public class BookingWizard {

    private static final int FORMAT_VERSION = 2;
    private final Map<String, String> answers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private int step = 1;

    public void answer(String field, String value) {
        answers.put(field, value);
        step++;
    }

    public String saveDraft() { // (1)!
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("v=" + FORMAT_VERSION + ";step=" + step);
        answers.forEach((k, v) -> sb.append(';').append(k).append('=').append(v));
        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().encodeToString(sb.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }

    public static BookingWizard resume(String token) {
        String raw = new String(Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(token), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        BookingWizard w = new BookingWizard();
        for (String part : raw.split(";")) {
            String[] kv = part.split("=", 2);
            switch (kv[0]) {
                case "v" -> {
                    if (Integer.parseInt(kv[1]) != FORMAT_VERSION) { // (2)!
                        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Draft from an older app version; please start again");
                    }
                }
                case "step" -> w.step = Integer.parseInt(kv[1]);
                default -> w.answers.put(kv[0], kv[1]);
            }
        }
        return w;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "step " + step + "/4 " + answers;
    }
}
  1. The memento leaves the process as an opaque string. Only BookingWizard knows the format. Production code would use JSON with a schema and sign or encrypt the token so it can't be tampered with.
  2. Versioned mementos: a draft from an old format is rejected with a friendly message (or migrated) instead of producing a corrupt wizard.
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento.booking;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Base64;

public class BookingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: Resume a Hotel Booking on Another Device ===");
        BookingWizard onPhone = new BookingWizard();
        onPhone.answer("city", "Goa");
        onPhone.answer("dates", "2026-12-27..2026-12-31");
        System.out.println("phone  : " + onPhone);

        String token = onPhone.saveDraft(); // stored against the user's account
        System.out.println("draft token stored (" + token.length() + " chars)");

        BookingWizard onLaptop = BookingWizard.resume(token);
        System.out.println("laptop : " + onLaptop);
        onLaptop.answer("guests", "2 adults");
        System.out.println("laptop : " + onLaptop);

        String oldToken = Base64.getUrlEncoder().encodeToString("v=1;step=2;city=Pune".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        try {
            BookingWizard.resume(oldToken);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("old draft: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: Resume a Hotel Booking on Another Device ===
phone  : step 3/4 {city=Goa, dates=2026-12-27..2026-12-31}
draft token stored (64 chars)
laptop : step 3/4 {city=Goa, dates=2026-12-27..2026-12-31}
laptop : step 4/4 {city=Goa, dates=2026-12-27..2026-12-31, guests=2 adults}
old draft: Draft from an older app version; please start again

Why Memento here:

  • The wizard's state must outlive the session and the device.
  • The caretaker (drafts store) treats drafts as blobs, so the wizard can evolve freely.
  • Versioning is how mementos survive app updates.
Unit Tests: MementoTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.behavioral.memento;

import com.handbook.behavioral.memento.booking.BookingWizard;
import com.handbook.behavioral.memento.canvas.Canvas;
import com.handbook.behavioral.memento.cart.Cart;
import com.handbook.behavioral.memento.history.BoundedHistory;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class MementoTest {

    @Test
    void snapshotIsNotAffectedByLaterChanges() {
        Canvas c = new Canvas();
        c.add(new Canvas.Shape("a", 0, 0, "red"));
        Canvas.Snapshot s = c.save("v1");
        c.recolorAll("blue");
        c.restore(s);
        assertThat(c.toString()).contains("a(red)");
    }

    @Test
    void cartRollbackRestoresItemsAndCoupon() {
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        cart.add("A", 1);
        var cp = cart.checkpoint();
        cart.applyCoupon("X");
        cart.clear();
        cart.rollback(cp);
        assertThat(cart).hasToString("{A=1}");
    }

    @Test
    void draftRoundTripsThroughToken() {
        BookingWizard w = new BookingWizard();
        w.answer("city", "Goa");
        assertThat(BookingWizard.resume(w.saveDraft()).toString()).isEqualTo(w.toString());
    }

    @Test
    void boundedHistoryDropsOldest() {
        BoundedHistory<Integer> h = new BoundedHistory<>(2);
        h.push(1);
        h.push(2);
        h.push(3);
        assertThat(h.pop()).contains(3);
        assertThat(h.pop()).contains(2);
        assertThat(h.pop()).isEmpty();
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Variation Notes Nested class with private fields (Example 1) Strong encapsulation: only the originator can read it Record memento (Example 2) Simple and immutable; contents visible but can't change the originator Serialized memento (Example 3) JSON/Protobuf/bytes for persistence or transfer; needs versioning and integrity protection Incremental mementos Store diffs instead of full copies for large states (with periodic full snapshots) Bounded history (coding challenge) Keep the last N; drop the oldest

Memento vs. Command for undo:

Memento (snapshot) Command (inverse operation) Undo by Restoring the whole state Running an inverse of each operation Easy when State is small, or operations are hard to reverse State is big, and operations are easy to reverse Memory Higher (full copies) Lower (just the operations) Combined Commands store a memento of what they change, or snapshots every N commands to speed up undo

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Memento JDK java.io.Serializable (serialized state); Swing UndoManager with StateEdit (state snapshots) Databases Savepoints (Connection.setSavepoint() / rollback(savepoint)) Spring Web Flow / Spring Session Saving conversation or session state to resume Spring Batch ExecutionContext saved per step so a failed job restarts from the checkpoint Kafka Streams / Flink State snapshots and checkpoints for fault-tolerant stream processing Event sourcing Snapshots of an aggregate to avoid replaying every event Browsers / editors History API state objects; autosave drafts

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Preserves encapsulation while enabling undo/restore Memory/storage cost of snapshots, especially for large state Simplifies the originator (no inverse logic needed) Snapshots of objects with references to external resources (connections, files) are tricky Caretaker independent of the originator's internals Serialized mementos need versioning and security Natural fit for checkpoints, drafts and versions Frequent snapshots can be slow; consider incremental ones

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Shallow snapshots of mutable state

If the memento shares a mutable list with the originator, later edits change the "snapshot". Copy mutable parts (or use immutable data). See Prototype on deep vs. shallow copies.

Trusting serialized mementos from clients

A draft token sent to the browser can be edited ("price=1"). Sign it (HMAC), encrypt it, or store mementos server-side and give the client only an ID.

Unbounded history

Snapshotting a big canvas on every keystroke eats memory. Bound the history, snapshot periodically, or store diffs.

Restoring identity and side effects

A memento restores state, not the world: emails sent and payments made aren't undone. Restoring a cart doesn't release stock reserved in another service.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Checkpointing in distributed processing. Spark, Flink and Kafka Streams periodically snapshot operator state (mementos) to durable storage; on failure they restore the last checkpoint and replay input from a matching offset. The key insight: a snapshot is only useful together with a position in the input, so the system can resume exactly once.

Event sourcing snapshots. Aggregates rebuilt from events can be slow to load after millions of events. Store a snapshot every N events (a memento) and replay only newer events. Snapshots must be versioned, because the aggregate's shape changes over time.

Storage design for version history. Full copies are simple but expensive; content-addressed storage (like Git: snapshots are trees of hashed, shared blobs) gives cheap versions with structural sharing. Google Docs stores operations and periodic snapshots.

Security and privacy. Mementos may contain personal data; apply the same retention and deletion rules (GDPR "right to be forgotten" must also delete old versions and drafts).

War story: the draft that set its own price

A travel site stored booking-wizard drafts in a client-side cookie as Base64 JSON, including the quoted price, so the user could resume later. A curious user decoded the cookie, edited the price from INR 18,000 to INR 1,800, re-encoded it and resumed. The checkout trusted the draft's price. Fix: drafts moved server-side (the client keeps only an opaque ID); prices are always re-quoted at checkout; any remaining client-side state is HMAC-signed and rejected if modified. Lesson: a memento that leaves your process is untrusted input. Sign it, encrypt it, or keep it on the server.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Memento Command Prototype Event Sourcing Stores A state snapshot An operation A copy to create new objects All changes as events Undo by Restore snapshot Inverse operation N/A Replay to an earlier point Encapsulation Strong (opaque) N/A N/A Events are public facts

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Snapshot state, restore later, keep encapsulation.
  • Originator creates and restores; memento is immutable and opaque; caretaker stores without reading.
  • Copy mutable state deeply and keep order; bound the history.
  • Persisted mementos need versioning and integrity.
  • Memento = snapshot undo; Command = inverse-operation undo.
Snapshot v1 = canvas.save("v1"); ...; canvas.restore(v1);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add redo to BoundedHistory.
  • Sign BookingWizard tokens with HMAC-SHA256 and reject modified ones.
  • Make VersionHistory store diffs between consecutive canvas snapshots.

Mediator Next: Observer

docs.title: Null Object
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Behavioral Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Null Object is a real object that does "nothing" (or a safe default) in place of null. Callers use it like any other object, without null checks. Use it for optional collaborators: no coupon, audit disabled, guest user, no-op logger. Combine it with Optional at boundaries where absence must be visible.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a cart may or may not have a coupon. If the coupon is null, every piece of code that touches it needs if (coupon != null): price calculation, receipts, analytics, emails. Forget one check and you get a NullPointerException in production. Tony Hoare, who invented null references, called them his "billion-dollar mistake".

Definition (Bobby Woolf, Pattern Languages of Program Design 3):

Provide an object as a surrogate for the lack of an object of a given type. The Null Object provides intelligent do-nothing behavior, hiding the details from its collaborators.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A placeholder seat card
