coding-interview/run-all.sh          # runs all 12, writes outputs/
coding-interview/run-all.sh --check  # what CI runs: fails on any failure or changed output

docs.title: 1. Unbreakable Thread-Safe Singleton
docs.text: L2 ★★★ · Holder idiom, double-checked locking + volatile, reflection & serialization defence

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Write a lazily initialised, thread-safe Singleton. Then show how reflection and serialization can create a second instance, and defend against both.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Singleton page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
The holder idiom gives lazy, lock-free initialisation, because the JVM runs a class initialiser exactly once and synchronizes it for you. Double-checked locking is the version interviewers ask you to write by hand, and its field must be volatile. Defences: a constructor guard (reflection) and readResolve() (serialization). An enum singleton gets both defences from the JVM. See Singleton.

sequenceDiagram participant T1 as Thread 1 participant T2 as Thread 2 participant C as IdGenerator.class T1->>C: instance == null? yes T2->>C: instance == null? yes T1->>C: synchronized: still null → create, publish (volatile write) T2->>C: synchronized: re-check → not null → reuse

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why private static final class Holder { static final Config INSTANCE = new Config(); } Holder is only initialised on the first getInstance() call. JVM class initialisation is thread-safe, so this needs no locks and no volatile. private static volatile IdGenerator instance Without volatile, another thread could see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object, because the constructor writes and the reference write can be reordered. IdGenerator local = instance Reading into a local variable means only one volatile read on the fast path. It's a small optimisation that java.util itself uses. if (created) throw new IllegalStateException(...) Reflection can call a private constructor with setAccessible(true). The guard makes the second call fail. private Object readResolve() { return getInstance(); } Deserialization creates a new object. readResolve replaces it with the real instance. enum Registry { INSTANCE } Constructor.newInstance refuses enums, and enum serialization is by name, so the enum form is safe by construction.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space getInstance (after init) O(1), no locking O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/SingletonDefended.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

100 concurrent getInstance() calls -> same object: true
reflection attack blocked: use Config.getInstance()
deserialized copy is the same instance: true
enum singleton: INSTANCE (reflection on enums throws by design)
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Double-checked locking without volatile. It's broken under the Java Memory Model.
  • Making the whole getInstance() method synchronized. It's correct, but every call pays for a lock.
  • Putting mutable global state in a singleton. It makes tests order-dependent. Prefer a DI-managed singleton bean.
  • Forgetting that a singleton is "one per class loader", not one per cluster.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Singleton vs Spring singleton bean?

A Spring singleton is one instance per application context, created and injected by the container. It's testable (you can inject a fake) and doesn't need a static accessor. The GoF Singleton enforces one instance per class loader with a static method, which hides the dependency.

How do you unit-test code that uses a singleton?

Don't call getInstance() inside business logic. Inject the instance through the constructor. If that isn't possible, add a package-private reset hook for tests, or wrap the singleton behind an interface.

docs.title: 2. Builder with Validation
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · Required vs optional params, defaults, cross-field validation, immutability

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build an immutable HttpRequest with two required fields (method, url) and several optional ones (headers, body, timeout, retries). Invalid combinations ("GET with a body", "POST without a body", retries > 5) must be rejected, with all the errors reported at once.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Builder page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Put the required parameters into the builder's entry point (HttpRequest.post(url)) so they can't be forgotten, and the optional ones into fluent methods with defaults. build() is the single place for cross-field validation, so an invalid object can never exist. See Builder.

flowchart LR A["HttpRequest.post(url)"] --> B[".body(...)"] --> C[".timeout(3s)"] --> D{"build(): validate all"} D -->|ok| R[immutable HttpRequest record] D -->|errors| X["IllegalStateException<br/>'url must be http(s); GET must not have a body; ...'"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why static Builder post(String url) { return new Builder("POST", url); } Static entry points per method name the required parameters, and read well: HttpRequest.get(url). private Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(10) Defaults live in the builder, so callers set only what differs. Builder header(...) { ...; return this; } Returning this enables chaining. List<String> errors = ...; if (!errors.isEmpty()) throw ... Collect all the problems and report them together. A caller fixing a config file wants to see every error at once. HttpRequest { headers = Map.copyOf(headers); } The record's compact constructor copies the map, so the builder can be reused without changing objects it already built.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space build() O(h) for h headers O(h)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/BuilderPattern.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

HttpRequest[method=GET, url=https://api.example.com/orders, headers={Accept=application/json}, body=null, timeout=PT10S, retries=2]
HttpRequest[method=POST, url=https://api.example.com/orders, headers={}, body={"sku":"A1"}, timeout=PT3S, retries=0]
invalid request rejected: url must be http(s); GET must not have a body; retries must be 0..5
built object is immutable
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Making every field optional, including the ones that must be set. Then new Builder().build() compiles and fails at run time.
  • Validating in each setter only. Cross-field rules (GET + body) can only be checked in build().
  • Returning a mutable object from build(), or sharing the builder's map with it.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Builder vs telescoping constructors vs JavaBeans setters?

Telescoping constructors become unreadable (new Req("GET", url, null, null, 10, 0)). JavaBeans setters allow half-built, mutable objects. A Builder gives readable, validated, immutable objects at the cost of one extra class.

How does Lombok's @Builder compare?

It generates the boilerplate, but it doesn't enforce required parameters or cross-field validation. You still add a custom build(), or validate in the constructor that the builder calls.

docs.title: 3. Factory Without a Switch
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Registry of Suppliers, OCP, runtime extension

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: createNotifier(channel) is a switch that grows with every new channel (email, SMS, push and so on). Refactor it so that adding a channel doesn't edit the factory, and new channels can even be registered at run time.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Factory Method page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Replace the switch with a map from key to constructor (Map<String, Supplier<Notifier>>). Creation becomes a lookup, and extension becomes a register call. This is the same idea as Spring injecting Map<String, Notifier> beans by name, or ServiceLoader plugins. See Factory Method.

classDiagram class NotifierFactory { -Map~String, Supplier~ registry +register(channel, Supplier) NotifierFactory +create(channel) Notifier } class Notifier { <<interface>> +send(to, msg) String } Notifier <|.. EmailNotifier Notifier <|.. SmsNotifier Notifier <|.. PushLambda NotifierFactory ..> Notifier : creates

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Map<String, Supplier<? extends Notifier>> registry Constructor references (EmailNotifier::new) are Suppliers, so the map stores "how to create", not instances. registry.putIfAbsent(...) != null → throw Registering the same key twice is almost always a bug, so fail fast. throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown channel ... known: " + ...) Listing the valid keys in the error message saves the on-call engineer a lot of time. register("push", () -> (to, msg) -> ...) A new channel added at run time, without editing or recompiling the factory.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space create O(1) O(k) registered types

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/FactoryRegistry.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

EMAIL ana@example.com: order shipped
SMS +15550100: order shipped
PUSH device-42: order shipped
unknown channel 'fax', known: [email, push, sms]
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Storing instances instead of suppliers in the map, which accidentally shares stateful objects.
  • Calling toLowerCase() without Locale.ROOT. In the Turkish locale, "EMAIL" lowercases to a dotless ı.
  • Building a registry for two types that will never change. That's YAGNI; a switch is fine.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you do this in Spring?

Annotate each implementation @Component("email") and inject Map<String, Notifier>. Spring fills it with bean name → bean. New channel = new class, and no edits anywhere else.

Factory Method vs Abstract Factory vs this?

Factory Method: a subclass decides which product to create. Abstract Factory: creates families of related products. A registry is the pragmatic, data-driven form of a simple factory.

docs.title: 4. Strategy: Pluggable Discount Rules
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · Functional interface, lambdas as strategies, composite strategy

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Checkout applies a discount rule chosen by customer tier: percentage, flat amount above a threshold, buy-3-get-the-cheapest-free, or the best of several rules. Adding a rule must not change Checkout.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Strategy page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Extract the varying part into a one-method interface. Each rule is an implementation, and in modern Java often just a lambda from a static factory method. The context (Checkout) receives its strategies and never asks "which one is this?". Combining strategies (bestOf) is itself a strategy. See Strategy.

classDiagram class Checkout { -Map~String, DiscountStrategy~ byTier +total(Cart) long } class DiscountStrategy { <<functional interface>> +discountCents(Cart) long +percent(int)$ +flatAbove(long, long)$ +bestOf(DiscountStrategy...)$ } Checkout --> DiscountStrategy

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why @FunctionalInterface interface DiscountStrategy One abstract method means any lambda can be a strategy, and tests can pass cart -> 100. static DiscountStrategy percent(int pct) { return cart -> ...; } Static factories on the interface give the rules readable names without a class per rule. bestOf(DiscountStrategy... strategies) Strategies compose. Composite plus Strategy is a very common interview follow-up. Math.min(strategy.discountCents(cart), cart.subtotal()) The context enforces global invariants, such as never charging a negative total, so no individual rule can break them. byTier.getOrDefault(tier, DiscountStrategy.none()) A Null Object strategy instead of if (strategy != null).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space total(cart) O(items × strategies) O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/StrategyPricing.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

GUEST    subtotal=6500 total=6500
SILVER   subtotal=6500 total=6000
GOLD     subtotal=6500 total=5850
PLATINUM subtotal=6500 total=5000
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using double for money. Use minor units (long cents) or BigDecimal.
  • Letting strategies reach into the context's internals. Pass them only what they need (the cart).
  • A strategy interface with many methods, most of them unused. Keep it to one method (ISP).

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Strategy vs State?

They have the same structure, but different intent. A Strategy is chosen by the client and doesn't change on its own. A State is changed by the object itself as it moves through a lifecycle. Each state knows the next one.

Which SOLID principles does Strategy support?

OCP (new rules without editing Checkout), DIP (Checkout depends on the interface) and SRP (each rule lives in its own place).

docs.title: 5. Observer: Type-Safe Event Bus
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Subscribe by type, unsubscribe handle, failure isolation, CopyOnWriteArrayList

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement an in-process event bus. Listeners subscribe to a specific event type, can unsubscribe, and a listener that throws must not stop the others from receiving the event.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Observer page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Keep a map from event class to listener list. publish looks up the event's class and calls each listener inside its own try/catch. Returning an AutoCloseable from subscribe gives a clean way to unsubscribe and avoids the lapsed-listener memory leak. See Observer.

sequenceDiagram participant P as Publisher participant B as EventBus participant E as email listener participant A as analytics participant L as loyalty (throws) P->>B: publish(OrderPlaced A-1) B->>E: accept B->>A: accept B->>L: accept → exception B-->>B: record error, continue

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why <E extends Event> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) The generic type ties the listener's parameter to the event type, so the compiler stops a cancel-handler subscribing to placed events. event -> listener.accept(type.cast(event)) The wrapper does one checked cast, so the map can store a uniform Consumer<? super Event>. targets = List.copyOf(...) under the lock, then call outside it Never call foreign code while holding a lock: a listener that subscribes or publishes could deadlock. catch (RuntimeException e) { errors.add(...) } Failure isolation: one broken subscriber can't break the publisher or the other subscribers. return () -> listeners.get(type).remove(wrapper) The unsubscribe handle removes exactly the wrapper that was added.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space publish O(listeners of that type) O(listeners) subscribe / unsubscribe O(1) / O(listeners) -

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/ObserverEventBus.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

email: thanks for A-1
analytics: +4200
analytics: +1000
refund: A-1 (changed mind)
isolated errors: [OrderPlaced: loyalty service down, OrderPlaced: loyalty service down]
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Iterating a plain ArrayList while a listener unsubscribes, which throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Never unsubscribing. Long-lived buses keep short-lived listeners (and everything they reference) alive.
  • Letting one listener's exception propagate to the publisher.
  • Assuming delivery is asynchronous or ordered without saying so. This bus is synchronous and in registration order.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you make delivery asynchronous?

Submit each listener call to an Executor (virtual threads work well). Then you must decide on ordering per listener, back-pressure (bounded queues) and error handling (dead-letter logging). Spring's @EventListener with @Async does this.

In-process observer vs Kafka?

In-process: fast and simple, but events are lost on a crash and stay inside one JVM. Kafka: durable, replayable, and works across services, at the cost of infrastructure and eventual consistency. To publish reliably after a DB commit, use the transactional outbox.

docs.title: 6. Decorator: Retry + Cache + Log
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Wrapping, ordering of decorators, composition over inheritance

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A remote PriceService is slow and sometimes times out. Add retries, caching and logging without changing it, and without a subclass for every combination (RetryingCachingLoggingPriceService...).

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Decorator page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Each concern is a class that implements the same interface and wraps another instance of it. Stack them like layers. Order matters: logging outside caching logs every call, while caching outside retrying means a cached price never retries. See Decorator.

flowchart LR C[client] --> L[Logging] --> CA[Caching] --> R["Retrying (3)"] --> RS[RemotePriceService] RS -. timeout .-> R R -. retry .-> RS

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why abstract static class PriceDecorator implements PriceService { protected final PriceService inner; } The base decorator holds the wrapped component. Each concrete decorator overrides only what it adds. for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) try { return inner... } catch (...) { last = e; } Retries rethrow the last failure, so the caller sees the real cause. In production, add exponential backoff and retry only on transient errors. cache.computeIfAbsent(sku, inner::priceCents) If inner throws, nothing is cached and the exception propagates, so a failure is never cached by mistake. new Logging(new Caching(new Retrying(remote, 3)), log) The composition is the configuration. Reorder the constructor calls to change the behaviour.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space cached call O(1) O(distinct SKUs) uncached call O(attempts) remote calls -

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/DecoratorPipeline.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

apple  = 500
apple  = 500
banana = 600
remote calls = {apple=2, banana=2}
log: price(apple) = 500
log: price(apple) = 500
log: price(banana) = 600
without Retrying: timeout for kiwi
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Subclassing for every combination, which leads to a class explosion.
  • Putting the cache inside the retry, so every retry hits the cache miss path again, or caching exceptions.
  • Forgetting that a decorator must forward every interface method. Large interfaces make that painful, so consider a dynamic proxy (problem 11).

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Decorator vs Proxy vs Adapter?

They have similar structure but different intent. A Decorator adds behaviour and can be stacked. A Proxy controls access (lazy loading, caching, remote access, security) and usually keeps the same behaviour. An Adapter changes the interface.

Where do you see decorators in the JDK and Spring?

BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(...)), Collections.unmodifiableList(...), Spring's TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy, and Resilience4j's Decorators.ofSupplier(...).withRetry(...).withCircuitBreaker(...).

docs.title: 7. Command: Undo / Redo Editor
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Command objects, two stacks, captured state for undo

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a text editor that supports insert and delete with unlimited undo and redo. A new edit after an undo must discard the redo history.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Command page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Turn each action into an object that can execute() and undo() itself. The editor keeps two stacks: run pushes onto undo, undo moves a command onto redo, and redo moves it back. A new command clears redo, because the history has branched. See Command.

stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> Executed: run(cmd) → push undo, clear redo Executed --> Undone: undo() → pop undo, cmd.undo(), push redo Undone --> Executed: redo() → pop redo, cmd.execute(), push undo

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); String name(); } Commands are first-class objects you can store, log, queue, replay or send over a network. private String removed; // captured at execute time Delete can only undo if it remembers what it deleted. Commands capture the state they need. void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); } Clearing redo on a new command is the rule most people forget. Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>() ArrayDeque as a stack: push/pop at the head.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space run / undo / redo O(1) + cost of the edit O(history length)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/CommandUndoRedo.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

after 3 commands : 'World'
undo             : 'Hello World'
undo             : 'Hello'
redo             : 'Hello World'
new command      : 'Hello World!'  (redo history cleared: redo() = false)
undo everything  : ''
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Not clearing the redo stack after a new command.
  • Storing a full snapshot of the document for every command. That's the Memento approach: simple, but O(document) memory per step.
  • Commands that aren't self-contained, for example an undo that depends on the cursor's current position rather than the recorded one.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Command vs Memento for undo?

Command stores how to reverse each change, which is small and needs reversible operations. Memento stores snapshots of state, which is simple and works for any change, but uses more memory. Real editors often combine them: commands, plus periodic snapshots to rebuild from quickly.

How would you limit the history to 100 steps?

Use a bounded deque: after pushing, if undo.size() > 100, remove the oldest with undo.removeLast().

docs.title: 8. State: Vending Machine
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Sealed states, transitions return the next state, illegal actions

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A vending machine behaves differently depending on its state: Idle, HasMoney(credit) or SoldOut. Support insert, select and refund. It should give change, ask for more money, and refuse coins when it's sold out.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full State page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Replace if (state == X && action == Y) ladders with one type per state. Each state implements the actions that are legal for it and returns the next state. Defaults on the interface handle the illegal ones. With sealed records the states are immutable and the full set of states is known to the compiler. See State.

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Idle Idle --> HasMoney: insert HasMoney --> HasMoney: insert (add credit) / select (not enough) HasMoney --> Idle: select (stock left) / refund HasMoney --> SoldOut: select (last item) SoldOut --> SoldOut: insert (return coins)

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why sealed interface State permits Idle, HasMoney, SoldOut The state set is closed and visible. A pattern-matching switch over State would be exhaustive. default State select(Machine m) { m.say("cannot select in " + this); return this; } Illegal actions are handled once, in the interface. Each state overrides only the actions it supports. record HasMoney(int credit) State-specific data (the credit) lives in the state, not as a nullable field on the machine. return m.stock == 0 ? new SoldOut() : new Idle(); The transition logic sits next to the behaviour that causes it. state = state.select(this) The context just delegates and stores whatever comes back.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space each action O(1) O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/StateVendingMachine.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

Idle[]                 cannot select in Idle[]
Idle[]                 credit 100
HasMoney[credit=100]   need 50 more
HasMoney[credit=100]   credit 200
HasMoney[credit=200]   dispensed, change 50
Idle[]                 credit 50
HasMoney[credit=50]    refunded 50
Idle[]                 credit 200
HasMoney[credit=200]   dispensed, change 50
SoldOut[]              sold out, returned 100
final state: SoldOut[]
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Keeping several booleans (hasMoney, soldOut) that can contradict each other. One state value avoids that.
  • Letting the context decide transitions in a big switch, which spreads one state's rules across methods.
  • Using mutable singleton state objects that carry per-machine data, so machines share credit by accident.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you persist this state machine (for example, an order lifecycle in a DB)?

Store the state name plus its data in columns. Rebuild the state object when loading. Enforce allowed transitions in the domain, and optionally with a DB check or an optimistic version column so that two concurrent transitions can't both win.

When would you use Spring State Machine instead?

For large, configurable workflows with guards, actions, hierarchical states and persistence. For a handful of states, hand-written sealed types are clearer and easier to test.

docs.title: 9. Chain of Responsibility: Request Pipeline
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Handlers with next, short-circuiting, pre/post processing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Every API request passes authentication → rate limiting → validation → handler. Any step may reject the request with its own status code. Steps must be addable and reorderable, and one step must also run after the handler (audit).

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Chain of Responsibility page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Each handler receives the request and a next link. It either returns a response itself (short-circuit) or calls next.proceed(request). Code placed after next.proceed runs on the way back, which is how servlet filters, Spring HandlerInterceptors and Netty pipelines work. See Chain of Responsibility.

sequenceDiagram participant C as client participant T as timing participant A as auth participant R as rateLimit participant V as validate participant H as handler C->>T: request T->>A: next.proceed A->>R: token ok R->>V: under limit V-->>T: 400 empty body (short-circuit) T-->>C: 400 (logged on the way back)

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why interface Handler { Response handle(Request r, Chain next); } A handler doesn't know which step comes next, only that there is one. return handlers.get(index).handle(r, new Chain(handlers, index + 1, terminal)) Each Chain is an immutable cursor into the list, so the same chain object can serve concurrent requests. validTokens.contains(r.token()) ? next.proceed(r) : new Response(401, ...) Short-circuiting: a failed check never reaches later steps. Response resp = next.proceed(r); log.add(...); return resp; Post-processing: the timing handler sees the final status of every request, including rejected ones.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per request O(handlers) O(handlers) call depth

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/ChainOfResponsibility.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

ana  -> 201 created for ana
eve  -> 401 bad token
bob  -> 400 empty body
ana  -> 201 created for ana
ana  -> 429 slow down
audit (post-processing): [ana -> 201, eve -> 401, bob -> 400, ana -> 201, ana -> 429]
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting to call next.proceed, so the request silently stops.
  • Putting the order-dependent logic inside the handlers. Keep ordering in the chain configuration, with auth before rate limiting before validation.
  • Keeping per-request state in handler fields. That's a race once requests are concurrent. (The rate limiter's map here would need ConcurrentHashMap in production.)

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Where is this pattern in Spring?

The Servlet FilterChain (Spring Security is a chain of about 15 filters), HandlerInterceptor pre/post handlers, WebFlux WebFilter, and ExchangeFilterFunction on WebClient.

Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator?

Both wrap calls. A decorator always delegates and adds behaviour. A chain handler may decide not to delegate (handle or reject), and the chain is usually built from a configurable list.

docs.title: 10. Composite + Visitor: Expression Tree
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · Recursive sealed types, pattern-matching switch, record deconstruction

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Model arithmetic expressions such as (x + 2) * (3 + -1) as a tree. Implement evaluate, pretty-print and simplify (y * 1 + 0 → y, and constant folding). New operations must not require editing the node classes.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: This problem combines two patterns. Watch them side by side before you code: the tree (Composite) and the operation that walks it (Visitor).

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Composite: leaves (Num, Var) and branches (Add, Mul, Neg) share one type, so operations recurse uniformly. Visitor: put operations outside the nodes. In Java 21 a switch over a sealed interface, with record patterns, replaces the classic double-dispatch visitor. The compiler checks that every node type is handled. See Composite and Visitor.

flowchart TB M["Mul"] --> A1["Add"] M --> A2["Add"] A1 --> X["Var x"] A1 --> N2["Num 2"] A2 --> N3["Num 3"] A2 --> NG["Neg"] NG --> N1["Num 1"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why sealed interface Expr permits Num, Var, Add, Mul, Neg A closed hierarchy: the compiler knows every node type. return switch (e) { case Num n -> ...; case Add a -> eval(a.left()) + eval(a.right()); ... } An exhaustive switch with no default. Adding a Div node makes every operation fail to compile until it's handled, which is exactly what you want. case Add(Expr l, Expr r) -> { ... } Record patterns (Java 21) deconstruct a node in the case label. if (a instanceof Num(double x) && x == 0) yield b; Nested patterns read like the algebra rule: "0 + b = b". case Neg(Neg(Expr inner)) -> simplify(inner); Patterns can match nested shapes, such as double negation, in one case. check(eval(simplify(e2), env) == eval(e2, env)) Property-style check: simplification must preserve the value.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space eval / show / simplify O(nodes) O(depth) recursion

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/CompositeExpression.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

(x + 2) * (3 + -1) = 12.0   with x=4
(y * 1 + 0) * (2 + 3) = 50.0   with y=10
simplify: (y * 1 + 0) * (2 + 3)  ->  y * 5
unbound variable z
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Adding eval(), show() and simplify() as methods on every node class. Each new operation then edits every class.
  • Using default -> in a switch over a sealed type. It turns off the exhaustiveness check that is the whole point.
  • Recursing on very deep trees without thinking about stack depth. Mention an explicit stack for untrusted input.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Classic Visitor (accept/visit) vs pattern matching?

The classic visitor uses double dispatch: node.accept(visitor) calls visitor.visitAdd(this). It needs an accept method on every node and a visitor interface. With sealed types and pattern-matching switch, you get the same 'operations outside the nodes' benefit with much less code.

What's the expression problem?

With OO subclassing, adding types is easy and adding operations is hard. With visitors or pattern matching, the opposite is true. Choose based on which changes more often in your domain.

docs.title: 11. Proxy: Caching & Lazy Loading
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · java.lang.reflect.Proxy, InvocationHandler, virtual proxy

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Add result caching to any interface without writing a class per interface, and create an expensive service lazily, only when it's first used.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Proxy page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
A JDK dynamic proxy generates a class at run time that implements the interfaces you pass and routes every call to one InvocationHandler.invoke(proxy, method, args). That single handler can add caching, timing, security or transactions to any interface. Spring AOP and Mockito work this way. A virtual proxy holds a factory and builds the real object on first use. See Proxy.

sequenceDiagram participant C as client participant P as $Proxy (generated) participant H as CachingHandler participant T as SlowCatalog C->>P: describe("A1") P->>H: invoke(method=describe, args=[A1]) H->>T: MISS → method.invoke(target) C->>P: describe("A1") P->>H: invoke(...) H-->>C: HIT → cached value

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[]{type}, handler) This generates a class implementing type. It works for interfaces only; class proxies need ByteBuddy or CGLIB, which is what Spring uses for @Configuration. if (method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) return method.invoke(target, args) equals, hashCode and toString are also routed through the handler, so don't cache them. List<Object> key = [methodName, args...] A cache key built from method plus arguments. List.equals and hashCode make it a valid map key. method.invoke(target, args) Reflective call to the real object. In production, unwrap InvocationTargetException so callers see the original exception. private ProductCatalog real() { if (real == null) real = factory.get(); ... } Virtual proxy: lazy creation. This version isn't thread-safe; use a holder or a lock if the proxy is shared.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space cached call O(args) to build the key O(distinct calls)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
java coding-interview/src/DynamicProxy.java      # JDK 21+ single-file launcher, no build needed

MISS [describe, A1]
HIT  [describe, A1]
MISS [stock, A1]
HIT  [stock, A1]
MISS [describe, B2]
real calls = 3 (5 requests)
proxy class = generated $Proxy
lazy created? false
after first call, created? true
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting a JDK proxy to work on a concrete class. It only implements interfaces.
  • Self-invocation: inside the target, this.otherMethod() bypasses the proxy. That's the classic "@Transactional doesn't work" bug in Spring.
  • Caching methods with side effects, or with mutable arguments used as keys.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Why doesn't @Transactional work when a method calls another method in the same class?

Spring applies @Transactional with a proxy around the bean. A call from inside the bean (this.save()) goes straight to the target and skips the proxy, so no transaction starts. Fix it by moving the method to another bean, injecting the bean's own proxy, or using AspectJ weaving.

JDK proxy vs CGLIB/ByteBuddy?

JDK proxies implement interfaces, using built-in reflection. CGLIB and ByteBuddy subclass the target class at run time, so they work without interfaces, but they can't proxy final classes or methods. Spring Boot defaults to class-based proxies.

docs.title: 12. Adapter: Integrating Payment SDKs
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · Object adapter, unit/error translation, anti-corruption layer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Checkout depends on PaymentGateway.charge(orderId, amountCents, currency). Integrate a legacy bank SDK (rupees as double, numeric status codes, checked exceptions) and a third-party client (map-based requests, string statuses) without changing checkout.

docs.title: See the pattern in motion
docs.text: Before you write any code, watch the pattern this problem is built on. Switch to Without it to see the bug the pattern prevents. Read the full Adapter page.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Write one adapter per vendor that implements our interface and wraps their client. It translates units (cents ↔ rupees), requests (map building), results (codes → our PaymentResult) and errors (checked exceptions → domain failures). Vendor quirks never leak into the domain. At the architecture level this is an anti-corruption layer. See Adapter.

classDiagram class PaymentGateway { <<interface>> +charge(orderId, cents, currency) PaymentResult } PaymentGateway <|.. LegacyBankAdapter PaymentGateway <|.. StripeAdapter LegacyBankAdapter --> LegacyBankSdk : wraps StripeAdapter --> StripeLikeClient : wraps Checkout --> PaymentGateway

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why sdk.pay(orderId, amountCents / 100.0) Unit translation is confined to the adapter. The domain stays on exact minor units. The legacy double is the vendor's problem, kept at the edge. catch (Exception e) { return new PaymentResult(false, null, e.getMessage()); } The vendor's checked exception becomes a domain result instead of leaking throws Exception into checkout. code == 0 ? ... : "CODE_" + code Map vendor codes to our error vocabulary in one place. A real adapter would use a proper code table. if (!currency.equals("INR")) return ... UNSUPPORTED_CURRENCY Adapters also enforce the vendor's capabilities, so callers get a clear error instead of a mysterious failure from the SDK.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space charge O(1) + vendor call O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Letting vendor types (status codes, SDK exceptions, double amounts) appear in domain signatures.
  • Adapting by inheritance (a class adapter that extends the SDK class), which couples you to SDK internals and its constructor.
  • Putting business rules in the adapter. It should translate, not decide.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you test an adapter?

Use contract tests against the vendor's sandbox, or a recorded stub (WireMock) for the HTTP shape. Unit-test the translation rules (units, code mapping, error mapping) with a fake SDK object, as this demo does.

Adapter vs Facade?

An adapter makes one existing interface fit the one you expect. A facade simplifies many interfaces behind one new, smaller interface.

docs.title: Concurrency Patterns
docs.text:
Concurrency patterns solve coordination between threads: sharing work, sharing data safely, and waiting for results, without races, deadlocks or wasted CPU. Every example in this section runs on Java 21 and uses virtual threads where they make sense.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Producer-Consumer Decouple work producers from workers with a buffer and back-pressure ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Thread Pool Reuse a bounded set of threads for many tasks ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Future / Promise Represent a result that will be available later; compose async steps ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Read-Write Lock Many concurrent readers, exclusive writers ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Immutable Object Share data between threads with no locks at all ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Double-Checked Locking Lazy, thread-safe initialization with minimal locking ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Virtual Threads Millions of cheap threads for blocking I/O (Java 21) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Guarded Suspension & Balking Wait until a condition holds, or skip work that's already in progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Active Object Give an object its own thread and queue; callers get futures, no locks ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Fork/Join Split CPU-bound work recursively across cores with work stealing ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅

The three questions behind every concurrency bug

Visibility: will other threads see my write? Atomicity: can another thread see a half-done update? Ordering: can the JVM or CPU reorder my operations? The Java Memory Model's happens-before rules answer all three. Every pattern here is a way to get those guarantees right.

docs.title: Active Object
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An Active Object owns its own thread. Callers don't run its methods; they drop requests into its queue and get a Future back. One scheduler thread executes the requests in order, so the object's state needs no locks. Use it for a shared resource that must be accessed one request at a time (a wallet, a printer, a device, a subscriber's state), especially when callers shouldn't block.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between threads, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a wallet receives thousands of cashback credits and payment debits from different threads. With locks, every method must be carefully synchronized; a slow operation holds the lock and blocks callers; and a missed lock somewhere corrupts the balance. What if only one thread ever touched the wallet, and everyone else just sent it messages?

Definition (Lavender & Schmidt, Active Object, 1996; POSA2):

Decouples method execution from method invocation to enhance concurrency and simplify synchronized access to an object that resides in its own thread of control.

The actor model (Erlang, Akka/Pekko, Orleans) is the same idea taken further: everything is an active object with a mailbox, and actors only communicate by messages.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A bank teller window with a token system

Customers don't walk into the vault. They take a token (a future), drop their request slip in the tray (the activation queue), and sit down. One teller (the scheduler thread) processes slips in order. Customers are free to read the paper while they wait, and the vault never has two people in it.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram direction LR class Proxy { +credit(paise) CompletableFuture } class ActivationQueue { <<BlockingQueue>> } class Scheduler { <<single thread>> +run() } class Servant { -balancePaise +doCredit() } class Future { <<CompletableFuture>> } Proxy --> ActivationQueue : enqueue MethodRequest Scheduler --> ActivationQueue : dequeue Scheduler --> Servant : execute Proxy ..> Future : returns Scheduler ..> Future : completes Participant Responsibility In the examples Proxy Public API; turns calls into requests; returns futures WalletActor.credit() Method request A captured call The lambda passed to supplyAsync Activation queue Buffers requests (bounded = back-pressure) The executor's queue Scheduler Single thread that dequeues and runs requests newSingleThreadExecutor() Servant The real state and logic, confined to the scheduler thread balancePaise Future Lets callers wait for or chain the result CompletableFuture

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class Wallet {
    private long balance;
    public void credit(long p) { balance += p; }                       // not atomic: lost updates
    public synchronized boolean debit(long p) { ... }                  // locked, but credit isn't
    public synchronized String statement() { Thread.sleep(200); ... }  // slow call blocks every debit
}
  • Every method must get locking right, forever.
  • Slow operations block all callers.
  • Callers can't do anything else while waiting.

docs.title: Example 1: Wallet as an Active Object (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payments app credits INR 1 cashback on 1,000 transactions in a burst, while the user tries 15 debits of INR 100. The balance must end exactly right, no debit may overdraw, and callers (request threads) must not block on a lock.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as 1,000 caller threads participant P as WalletActor (proxy) participant Q as Queue participant S as Scheduler thread C->>P: credit(100) P->>Q: enqueue P-->>C: CompletableFuture (immediately) S->>Q: take S->>S: balance += 100 (no lock) S-->>C: complete future

Full Code:

WalletActor.javaWalletDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.wallet;

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

/** Active Object: a proxy whose methods enqueue requests that ONE scheduler thread executes. */
public final class WalletActor implements AutoCloseable {

    private final ExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // (1)!
    private long balancePaise; // touched only by the scheduler thread: no locks, no volatile
    private int operations;

    public CompletableFuture<Long> credit(long paise) { // (2)!
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            balancePaise += paise;
            operations++;
            return balancePaise;
        }, scheduler);
    }

    public CompletableFuture<Boolean> debit(long paise) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            operations++;
            if (paise > balancePaise) {
                return false; // the check and the update can't interleave with anything else
            }
            balancePaise -= paise;
            return true;
        }, scheduler);
    }

    public CompletableFuture<String> statement() {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "balance=" + balancePaise + " after " + operations + " ops", scheduler);
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        scheduler.close(); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. The scheduler: one thread, one queue. All state is confined to it ("thread confinement"), so plain fields are safe.
  2. The proxy method returns at once with a future. The lambda is the method request.
  3. close() lets queued requests finish and stops the thread (ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19).
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.wallet;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class WalletDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: A Wallet as an Active Object ===");
        try (WalletActor wallet = new WalletActor(); var callers = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<CompletableFuture<Boolean>> debits = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                callers.submit(() -> wallet.credit(100));                    // 1,000 cashback credits of INR 1
            }
            callers.close();                                                 // all credits enqueued
            for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
                debits.add(wallet.debit(10_000));                           // 15 attempts to spend INR 100
            }
            long approved = debits.stream().filter(CompletableFuture::join).count();
            System.out.println("Debits of INR 100 approved: " + approved + " of 15 (balance allows exactly 10)");
            System.out.println("Statement: " + wallet.statement().get());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: A Wallet as an Active Object ===
Debits of INR 100 approved: 10 of 15 (balance allows exactly 10)
Statement: balance=0 after 1015 ops

Why an active object here:

  • Check-then-act (if balance >= amount then subtract) is atomic by construction.
  • No locks to forget; the scheduler thread is the only writer.
  • Callers get futures they can combine (thenCompose) instead of blocking.

docs.title: Example 2: Shared Label Printer with Back-Pressure (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A warehouse packing station has one thermal printer shared by six packers' terminals. Labels must print one at a time, in submission order. While the printer warms up, jobs queue; if more than 3 are waiting, new jobs are rejected with a clear message so packers retry instead of the queue growing without limit.

Design:

flowchart LR T1[Terminal 1] --> Q T2[Terminal 2] --> Q T3[...] --> Q Q[["Bounded queue (3)"]] --> W[Printer worker thread] --> P[(Thermal printer)] Q -. full .-> R[Reject: retry later]

Full Code:

LabelPrinter.javaPrinterDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.printer;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

/** A shared thermal printer: one worker, a BOUNDED activation queue, futures for each job. */
public final class LabelPrinter implements AutoCloseable {

    private final ThreadPoolExecutor worker;
    private final List<String> printed = new ArrayList<>(); // worker-thread only
    private final CountDownLatch paperLoaded;

    public LabelPrinter(int queueCapacity, CountDownLatch paperLoaded) {
        this.paperLoaded = paperLoaded;
        this.worker = new ThreadPoolExecutor(1, 1, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(queueCapacity), new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); // (1)!
    }

    public CompletableFuture<Integer> print(String awb) {
        try {
            return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
                await();
                printed.add(awb);
                return printed.size();
            }, worker);
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // (2)!
            return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new IllegalStateException("printer queue full, retry " + awb + " later"));
        }
    }

    public CompletableFuture<List<String>> printedSoFar() {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> List.copyOf(printed), worker);
    }

    private void await() {
        try {
            paperLoaded.await();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        worker.close();
    }
}
  1. A bounded activation queue plus AbortPolicy. An unbounded queue would hide overload until memory runs out.
  2. Rejection becomes a failed future, so callers handle it like any other result.
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.printer;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class PrinterDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Shipping-Label Printer with a Bounded Queue ===");
        CountDownLatch paper = new CountDownLatch(1); // printer is warming up
        try (LabelPrinter printer = new LabelPrinter(3, paper)) {
            List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> jobs = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
                jobs.add(printer.print("AWB-" + i));
            }
            paper.countDown();
            for (int i = 0; i < jobs.size(); i++) {
                CompletableFuture<Integer> job = jobs.get(i);
                String outcome = job.handle((n, err) -> err == null ? "printed as label #" + n : "REJECTED: " + err.getMessage()).join();
                System.out.println("AWB-" + (i + 1) + ": " + outcome);
            }
            System.out.println("Print order: " + printer.printedSoFar().join());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Shipping-Label Printer with a Bounded Queue ===
AWB-1: printed as label #1
AWB-2: printed as label #2
AWB-3: printed as label #3
AWB-4: printed as label #4
AWB-5: REJECTED: printer queue full, retry AWB-5 later
Print order: [AWB-1, AWB-2, AWB-3, AWB-4]

Why an active object here:

  • The device is inherently single-threaded; the pattern mirrors reality.
  • FIFO ordering of jobs comes for free.
  • The bounded queue gives explicit back-pressure (one job printing + 3 waiting, the 5th is rejected).

docs.title: Example 3: Per-Subscriber Ordering at Scale (Telecom)
docs.text:
Scenario: A telecom processes 20,000 recharge events per second. For each subscriber, "recharge → activate data pack → send SMS" must happen in order, but different subscribers should be processed in parallel. One single-threaded actor per subscriber (millions of them) would be wasteful; instead, each key gets a lightweight "virtual actor": a chain of futures executed on a shared pool.

Design:

flowchart LR E[Recharge events] --> K{Key = MSISDN} K -->|+91...01| C1["chain: recharge → activate → SMS"] K -->|+91...02| C2["chain: recharge → activate → SMS"] K -->|+91...03| C3["chain: recharge → activate → SMS"] C1 & C2 & C3 --> P[(Shared pool, 8 threads)]

Full Code:

KeyedSerialExecutor.javaTelecomDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.keyed;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.Executor;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Many lightweight active objects: tasks for the SAME key run in order; different keys run in parallel. */
public final class KeyedSerialExecutor {

    private final Executor pool;
    private final Map<String, CompletableFuture<?>> tails = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public KeyedSerialExecutor(Executor pool) {
        this.pool = pool;
    }

    public <T> CompletableFuture<T> submit(String key, Supplier<T> task) {
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        CompletableFuture<T>[] next = new CompletableFuture[1];
        tails.compute(key, (k, tail) -> { // (1)!
            CompletableFuture<?> previous = tail == null ? CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null) : tail;
            next[0] = previous.handleAsync((ignored, err) -> task.get(), pool); // (2)!
            return next[0];
        });
        return next[0];
    }
}
  1. compute atomically appends the new task to this key's tail future.
  2. The new task starts only when the previous one for the same key finishes (even if it failed); other keys don't wait.
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.keyed;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class TelecomDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Telecom: Per-Subscriber Ordering for Recharge Events ===");
        Map<String, List<String>> applied = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        try (var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            KeyedSerialExecutor executor = new KeyedSerialExecutor(pool);
            List<CompletableFuture<?>> all = new ArrayList<>();
            String[] subscribers = {"+919845000001", "+919845000002", "+919845000003"};
            String[] steps = {"recharge INR 299", "activate 1.5GB/day", "send SMS"};
            for (String step : steps) {
                for (String msisdn : subscribers) {
                    all.add(executor.submit(msisdn, () -> {
                        applied.computeIfAbsent(msisdn, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(step);
                        return null;
                    }));
                }
            }
            CompletableFuture.allOf(all.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
        }
        new TreeMap<>(applied).forEach((msisdn, log) -> System.out.println(msisdn + " -> " + log));
        System.out.println("Each subscriber's steps stayed in order while subscribers were processed in parallel.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Telecom: Per-Subscriber Ordering for Recharge Events ===
+919845000001 -> [recharge INR 299, activate 1.5GB/day, send SMS]
+919845000002 -> [recharge INR 299, activate 1.5GB/day, send SMS]
+919845000003 -> [recharge INR 299, activate 1.5GB/day, send SMS]
Each subscriber's steps stayed in order while subscribers were processed in parallel.

Why keyed active objects here:

  • Ordering is needed per key, not globally, which is the same reason Kafka partitions by key.
  • A shared pool keeps thread count fixed regardless of subscriber count.
  • This is how Orleans "virtual actors" and Akka's sharded entities scale to millions of instances.
Unit Tests: ActiveObjectTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject;

import com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.generic.Actor;
import com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.keyed.KeyedSerialExecutor;
import com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.printer.LabelPrinter;
import com.handbook.concurrency.activeobject.wallet.WalletActor;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ActiveObjectTest {

    @Test
    void walletNeverOverdrawsUnderConcurrency() throws Exception {
        try (WalletActor w = new WalletActor(); var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            w.credit(500).get();
            List<CompletableFuture<Boolean>> results = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                results.add(pool.submit(() -> w.debit(100)).get());
            }
            assertThat(results.stream().filter(CompletableFuture::join).count()).isEqualTo(5);
        }
    }

    @Test
    void fullPrinterQueueRejectsInsteadOfBlocking() {
        CountDownLatch paper = new CountDownLatch(1);
        try (LabelPrinter p = new LabelPrinter(1, paper)) {
            p.print("a");
            p.print("b");
            CompletableFuture<Integer> third = p.print("c");
            paper.countDown();
            assertThat(third).isCompletedExceptionally();
        }
    }

    @Test
    void keyedExecutorPreservesPerKeyOrder() {
        List<Integer> seen = java.util.Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        try (var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            KeyedSerialExecutor ex = new KeyedSerialExecutor(pool);
            List<CompletableFuture<?>> all = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
                int n = i;
                all.add(ex.submit("k", () -> seen.add(n)));
            }
            CompletableFuture.allOf(all.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
        }
        assertThat(seen).isSorted().hasSize(200);
    }

    @Test
    void actorSerializesAccessToPlainState() throws Exception {
        try (Actor<int[]> a = new Actor<>(new int[1]); var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                pool.submit(() -> a.ask(s -> ++s[0]));
            }
            pool.close();
            assertThat(a.ask(s -> s[0]).get()).isEqualTo(1_000);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Single-thread executor + CompletableFuture The simplest Java active object (Examples 1–2) Virtual-thread scheduler Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(Thread.ofVirtual().factory()): thousands of active objects without thousands of OS threads Keyed serial executor Per-key ordering on a shared pool (Example 3) Actors Akka/Pekko (AbstractBehavior), Orleans-style virtual actors, Vert.x verticles (event-loop-confined state) Event loop Netty, Node.js, Vert.x: one thread per loop runs all handlers for its channels: active objects at the I/O layer Alternative For short critical sections, a ReentrantLock or atomics are simpler and faster

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Active Object JDK Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(..., executor), Swing's Event Dispatch Thread (SwingUtilities.invokeLater) Akka / Apache Pekko Actors with mailboxes; ask returns a CompletionStage Vert.x Verticles: state confined to an event loop; vertx.eventBus().request(...) Netty EventLoop: each channel's handlers run on one thread Android Looper + Handler (main thread message queue) Kafka Streams One stream thread per partition set: per-key ordering, no locks in processors

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons No locks: state is confined to one thread Every call pays queueing and a thread hop Callers don't block; futures compose Throughput capped by one thread per object Natural ordering and bounded-queue back-pressure Debugging async flows and stack traces is harder Scales to many objects with virtual threads/keyed executors Deadlock risk if an actor waits (join()) on its own future or another actor waiting on it

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Blocking inside the scheduler

A request that calls future.join() on another request to the same active object deadlocks: the only thread is waiting for itself. Compose with thenCompose instead of blocking.

Leaking the servant

Returning the mutable internal object (return balancesMap) lets callers touch it from other threads. Return copies or immutable values.

Unbounded mailboxes

newSingleThreadExecutor() has an unbounded queue. Under sustained overload, latency and memory grow silently. Use a bounded queue and a rejection policy (Example 2).

Keyed executors that never forget keys

KeyedSerialExecutor keeps one tail future per key forever. In production, remove the entry when its tail completes (or use a bounded, sharded set of single-thread lanes).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Throughput math. One active object processes 1 / service_time requests per second. If a wallet operation takes 50 µs, that's ~20,000 ops/s per wallet, which is plenty per user but a hard ceiling for a global object. Shard: one active object per account (keyed), not one for the whole bank.

Failure handling. Decide what a failed request does to the object. Erlang/Akka "let it crash": a supervisor restarts the actor with clean state. In a plain Java active object, catch exceptions per request (the future fails), and never let one request corrupt the shared state halfway: validate first, then mutate.

Same idea, distributed. A Kafka partition with one consumer is an active object for all keys in that partition: messages are its mailbox, the consumer thread its scheduler. That's why "partition by entity id" gives per-entity ordering and lock-free processing in stream processors.

War story: the wallet that deadlocked at midnight

A wallet actor's applyCashback request called statement().join() to log the new balance. statement() was enqueued on the same single thread, behind the request waiting for it. The first cashback after deployment froze the wallet; the midnight cashback batch then queued 2 million requests behind it and the service ran out of memory. Fix: compose (thenCompose) instead of join() inside the actor; a bounded mailbox; and an ArchUnit rule forbidding join()/get() in actor classes. Lesson: never block an active object on itself.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Active Object Monitor (synchronized) Producer-Consumer Thread Pool Who runs the method The object's own thread The caller's thread Consumer threads Any pool thread Synchronization Thread confinement Locks Queue None (tasks must be independent) Caller blocks? No (future) Yes, while waiting for the lock Only when the queue is full No Ordering FIFO per object None guaranteed FIFO per queue None

Active Object = Producer-Consumer (the queue) + Future/Promise (the result) + Command (the request) + thread confinement.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Own thread + queue + futures; callers enqueue, never execute.
  • State confined to one thread: no locks.
  • Bound the mailbox; reject or shed when full.
  • Never block the actor on its own future: compose.
  • Per-key ordering at scale: keyed lanes / partitions.
CompletableFuture<Long> credit(long p) { return supplyAsync(() -> balance += p, singleThread); }

docs.text:

  • Make KeyedSerialExecutor remove a key when its last task completes.
  • Give LabelPrinter a priority lane for express shipments.
