docs.title: Guarded Suspension & Balking
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Both patterns handle "a method can only run when a condition (the guard) is true". Guarded Suspension waits until the guard becomes true; Balking gives up immediately if it isn't. Wait when the condition will soon be true and the caller needs the result (a rider waiting for a packed order). Balk when the work is already being done or isn't needed (a second "run settlement" click).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between threads, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a rider arrives at the restaurant before the food is ready. Checking in a loop (while (!ready) {}) burns a CPU core; sleeping a fixed second wastes time or misses the moment. Separately, a nightly settlement job is triggered by the scheduler, by an operator and by a retry at the same time. Running it three times means three payouts.

Definitions (Doug Lea, Concurrent Programming in Java; Mark Grand, Patterns in Java):

Guarded Suspension: if a precondition for an operation isn't met, suspend the calling thread until it is, then proceed.

Balking: if an object is not in an appropriate state for an operation, return immediately without doing it.

Both are the building blocks of every blocking queue, latch, future and "only one at a time" job you'll ever use.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The pickup counter and the lift button

Guarded suspension: you wait at the pickup counter (not pacing around the kitchen) and the staff call your name when the order is ready. Balking: pressing a lift's call button when it's already lit does nothing. The lift is already coming; a second request is pointless.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart TB subgraph GS["Guarded Suspension"] A1["synchronized method"] --> G1{"guard true?"} G1 -- no --> W["wait() / await()<br/>releases the lock"] --> G1 G1 -- yes --> R1["do the work"] N["another thread changes state<br/>then notifyAll() / signalAll()"] -.-> W end subgraph BK["Balking"] A2["method"] --> G2{"state OK?<br/>(compareAndSet)"} G2 -- no --> X["return immediately"] G2 -- yes --> R2["do the work, then reset state"] end Element Guarded Suspension Balking Guard Condition that will become true (item available, order packed) State that makes the call pointless (already running, not dirty) When false Block (with a timeout) Return a "not done" result Java tools synchronized + wait/notifyAll, Lock + Condition, BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet, tryLock(), a state field

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
while (!counter.isPacked(orderId)) { }               // busy-wait: 100% CPU, and maybe never sees the change (no visibility)
while (!counter.isPacked(orderId)) Thread.sleep(1000); // up to 1 s late, and still racy

if (!running) { running = true; settle(); running = false; }   // check-then-act race: two threads both see false
  • Busy waiting wastes CPU and may spin forever without volatile/locks.
  • Sleep-polling adds latency.
  • Check-then-act without atomicity lets duplicates through.

docs.title: Example 1: Riders Wait for Packed Orders (Food Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A cloud kitchen hands 1,500 orders an hour to riders. Riders arrive early; each waits for their order. If the kitchen hasn't packed an order within the rider's slot, the rider must be released and reassigned rather than waiting forever. Thousands of waiting riders are modelled as virtual threads.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant R1 as Rider (ORD-501) participant R2 as Rider (ORD-999) participant C as PickupCounter participant K as Kitchen R1->>C: awaitPickup(501, 2s) → wait() R2->>C: awaitPickup(999, 200ms) → wait() K->>C: markPacked(501, B3) → notifyAll() C-->>R1: shelf B3 Note over R2: guard still false → keeps waiting C-->>R2: timeout → null (reassign)

Full Code:

PickupCounter.javaDeliveryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.delivery;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Guarded Suspension: a rider waits until the guard "order is packed" becomes true. */
public final class PickupCounter {

    private final Map<String, String> packed = new HashMap<>(); // orderId -> shelf

    public synchronized void markPacked(String orderId, String shelf) {
        packed.put(orderId, shelf);
        notifyAll(); // (1)!
    }

    public synchronized String awaitPickup(String orderId, long timeoutMs) throws InterruptedException {
        long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeoutMs * 1_000_000;
        while (!packed.containsKey(orderId)) { // (2)!
            long remainingMs = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000;
            if (remainingMs <= 0) {
                return null; // (3)!
            }
            wait(remainingMs);
        }
        return packed.remove(orderId);
    }
}
  1. notifyAll, not notify: riders wait for different orders, so waking just one might wake the wrong one.
  2. The guard is re-checked in a while loop after every wake-up (spurious wake-ups, or another order was packed).
  3. A timeout turns "wait forever" into a decision the caller can act on.
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.delivery;

public class DeliveryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Food Delivery: Riders Wait at the Counter Until the Order Is Packed ===");
        PickupCounter counter = new PickupCounter();
        String[] result = new String[2];

        Thread rider1 = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            try {
                result[0] = counter.awaitPickup("ORD-501", 2_000);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });
        Thread rider2 = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            try {
                result[1] = counter.awaitPickup("ORD-999", 200); // kitchen never finishes this one in time
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });

        Thread.sleep(100); // kitchen is still cooking; riders are suspended, not spinning
        counter.markPacked("ORD-501", "shelf B3");
        rider1.join();
        rider2.join();
        System.out.println("Rider for ORD-501 picked up from: " + result[0]);
        System.out.println("Rider for ORD-999 got: " + result[1] + " -> timed out, reassigned to another pickup");
    }
}

Output:

=== Food Delivery: Riders Wait at the Counter Until the Order Is Packed ===
Rider for ORD-501 picked up from: shelf B3
Rider for ORD-999 got: null -> timed out, reassigned to another pickup

Why guarded suspension here:

  • The rider needs the result and it will usually arrive soon.
  • Waiting threads release the lock and use no CPU.
  • Timeouts keep the system live when the guard never comes true.

docs.title: Example 2: Balking Duplicate Settlement Runs (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment aggregator settles merchant balances nightly. The scheduler fires at 23:00; operators sometimes click "run now"; the workflow engine retries on a timeout. A second concurrent run would pay merchants twice. Duplicate triggers must return immediately (not queue up and run again afterwards).

Design:

flowchart LR S[Scheduler 23:00] --> J{compareAndSet false→true} O[Ops: Run now] --> J W[Workflow retry] --> J J -- won --> RUN[Settle batch] J -- lost --> B[Balk: return false] RUN --> RESET[running = false]

Full Code:

SettlementJob.javaSettlementDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.settlement;

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Balking: if the job is already running, a new trigger returns immediately instead of waiting. */
public final class SettlementJob {

    private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    private final AtomicInteger batchesSettled = new AtomicInteger();
    private final CountDownLatch holdOpen;

    public SettlementJob(CountDownLatch holdOpen) {
        this.holdOpen = holdOpen;
    }

    /** @return true if this call ran the settlement, false if it balked. */
    public boolean trigger() throws InterruptedException {
        if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) { // (1)!
            return false;
        }
        try {
            holdOpen.await(); // simulates a long settlement run
            batchesSettled.incrementAndGet();
            return true;
        } finally {
            running.set(false); // (2)!
        }
    }

    public boolean isRunning() {
        return running.get();
    }

    public int batchesSettled() {
        return batchesSettled.get();
    }
}
  1. Atomic check-and-set: exactly one caller can flip false → true. Everyone else balks.
  2. Reset in finally, so a failed run doesn't block every future run.
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.settlement;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class SettlementDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Balking Duplicate Settlement Triggers ===");
        CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        SettlementJob job = new SettlementJob(release);

        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            Future<Boolean> cron = pool.submit(job::trigger);   // scheduler fires at 23:00
            while (!job.isRunning()) {
                Thread.onSpinWait();                             // wait until the scheduled run has started
            }
            List<Future<Boolean>> others = new ArrayList<>();
            others.add(pool.submit(job::trigger));               // ops clicks "run now"
            others.add(pool.submit(job::trigger));               // a retry from the orchestrator
            int balked = 0;
            for (Future<Boolean> f : others) {
                balked += f.get() ? 0 : 1;                       // they return at once, no waiting
            }
            System.out.println("While running: " + balked + " duplicate triggers balked immediately");
            release.countDown();
            System.out.println("Scheduled run settled? " + cron.get());
        }
        System.out.println("Batches settled: " + job.batchesSettled() + " (never twice: no double payouts)");
        System.out.println("Next night's trigger runs again: " + new SettlementJob(new CountDownLatch(0)).trigger());
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Balking Duplicate Settlement Triggers ===
While running: 2 duplicate triggers balked immediately
Scheduled run settled? true
Batches settled: 1 (never twice: no double payouts)
Next night's trigger runs again: true

Why balking here:

  • A second run adds no value and real risk (double payouts).
  • Callers get an instant answer ("already running") instead of piling up.
  • Across several instances, the same idea becomes a distributed lock or leader election.

docs.title: Example 3: Start Playback When Enough Is Buffered (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: A video player must not start until 6 seconds are buffered, or viewers see stalls in the first seconds, which is the biggest churn driver. On a weak network the player waits at most 150 ms before switching to a lower bitrate. The network thread appends 2-second segments as they arrive.

Design:

flowchart LR N[Network thread] -->|"append(2s) + signalAll"| B[(PlaybackBuffer)] P[Player] -->|"awaitPlayable(6s, timeout)"| B B -->|true| Play[Start playback] B -->|false| Drop[Lower bitrate, retry]

Full Code:

PlaybackBuffer.javaBufferDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.buffer;

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

/** Guarded suspension with Lock/Condition: playback waits until enough seconds are buffered. */
public final class PlaybackBuffer {

    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition enoughBuffered = lock.newCondition(); // (1)!
    private int bufferedSeconds;

    public void append(int seconds) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            bufferedSeconds += seconds;
            enoughBuffered.signalAll();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    /** @return true if playback can start, false if we should show a spinner / drop quality. */
    public boolean awaitPlayable(int neededSeconds, long timeoutMs) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            long nanos = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(timeoutMs);
            while (bufferedSeconds < neededSeconds) {
                if (nanos <= 0) {
                    return false;
                }
                nanos = enoughBuffered.awaitNanos(nanos); // (2)!
            }
            return true;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}
  1. A Condition is a named wait set. One lock can have several (notFull, notEmpty), so you signal only the threads that care.
  2. awaitNanos returns the time remaining, which makes correct timeouts inside a while loop easy.
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.buffer;

public class BufferDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Start Playback Only When 6 Seconds Are Buffered ===");
        PlaybackBuffer good = new PlaybackBuffer();
        Thread network = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
                good.append(2); // 2-second segments arriving
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(20);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    return;
                }
            }
        });
        System.out.println("Fast network: playable within 2s? " + good.awaitPlayable(6, 2_000));
        network.join();

        PlaybackBuffer slow = new PlaybackBuffer();
        slow.append(2); // only one segment before the network drops
        boolean playable = slow.awaitPlayable(6, 150);
        System.out.println("Weak network: playable within 150ms? " + playable + " -> switch to 480p and retry");
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Start Playback Only When 6 Seconds Are Buffered ===
Fast network: playable within 2s? true
Weak network: playable within 150ms? false -> switch to 480p and retry

Why guarded suspension here:

  • The player should react the moment the guard is met, not on the next polling tick.
  • The timeout encodes a product decision (degrade quality rather than stall).
  • Lock/Condition work well with virtual threads, which don't pin a carrier while waiting.
Unit Tests: GuardedSuspensionTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.guarded;

import com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.buffer.PlaybackBuffer;
import com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.delivery.PickupCounter;
import com.handbook.concurrency.guarded.settlement.SettlementJob;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class GuardedSuspensionTest {

    @Test
    void riderReceivesShelfOnceOrderIsPacked() throws Exception {
        PickupCounter counter = new PickupCounter();
        Thread kitchen = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> counter.markPacked("O", "A1"));
        assertThat(counter.awaitPickup("O", 5_000)).isEqualTo("A1");
        kitchen.join();
    }

    @Test
    void waitingTimesOut() throws Exception {
        assertThat(new PickupCounter().awaitPickup("never", 50)).isNull();
        assertThat(new PlaybackBuffer().awaitPlayable(1, 50)).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void concurrentTriggersBalk() throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        SettlementJob job = new SettlementJob(release);
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            Future<Boolean> first = pool.submit(job::trigger);
            while (!job.isRunning()) {
                Thread.onSpinWait();
            }
            assertThat(pool.submit(job::trigger).get()).isFalse();
            release.countDown();
            assertThat(first.get()).isTrue();
        }
        assertThat(job.batchesSettled()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes wait/notifyAll Built in; one wait set per object; must hold the monitor Lock + Condition Several wait sets, awaitNanos, interruptible and fair options Ready-made guarded objects BlockingQueue.take/poll(timeout), CountDownLatch.await, CompletableFuture.get(timeout), Semaphore.acquire Balking with tryLock() if (!lock.tryLock()) return; for "skip if busy" sections Balking with state if (!dirty) return; (autosave), if (closed) return; (idempotent close()) Virtual threads (Java 21+) Waiting is cheap, so blocking designs scale again; prefer ReentrantLock over synchronized around long waits until JDK 24's fix for monitor pinning

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Guarded Suspension / Balking JDK ArrayBlockingQueue (two Conditions: notEmpty, notFull), FutureTask.get, CountDownLatch, Thread.join JDK balking AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet idioms, Closeable.close() "has no effect if already closed", ExecutorService.shutdown() Spring @Scheduled with ShedLock (@SchedulerLock) balks duplicate runs across instances Kafka KafkaConsumer.poll(timeout) guarded waiting; consumer wakeup() Netty / OkHttp Connection pools wait for a free connection with a timeout

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons No CPU wasted while waiting Easy to get wrong (if vs while, notify vs notifyAll, missed signals) Reacts immediately when the guard changes Waiting forever without timeouts causes hangs Balking prevents duplicate, harmful work Balking can silently drop requests that should have run later Foundation of all blocking concurrency utilities Hand-rolled versions are rarely better than JDK ones

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
if instead of while

After waking, another thread may already have consumed what you were waiting for, or the wake-up was spurious. Always re-check the guard in a loop (coding challenge).

Waiting without a timeout

If the notifier crashes, waiters hang forever. Use wait(ms), awaitNanos or poll(timeout) and handle the "not ready" outcome.

notify() with different guards

notify wakes one arbitrary waiter. If waiters wait for different things, the wrong one may wake and go back to sleep: a missed signal. Use notifyAll or separate Conditions.

Balking that should have been queuing

If a skipped request carries new data (a new file to process), balking loses it. Then you want "run again once afterwards" (a dirty flag) or a queue.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Why the lock is released. wait() atomically releases the monitor and suspends; on wake-up it re-acquires the monitor before returning. That atomicity is what prevents a lost wake-up between "check guard" and "start waiting". Hand-rolled alternatives with volatile flags and sleep reintroduce exactly that race.

Balking across machines. A JVM-local AtomicBoolean only balks within one instance. With three replicas, use a database row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), a lease in Redis/ZooKeeper, ShedLock, or a Kubernetes CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. And still make the job idempotent, because leases can expire mid-run.

Observability. Track how long threads wait on guards and how often callers balk or time out. A rising balk rate means a job is overrunning its schedule; rising wait times are an early capacity signal.

War story: double payouts on a Friday night

A payments team protected settlement with if (!running) { running = true; ... } on a plain boolean. When the scheduler and an operator's "run now" arrived within a millisecond, both threads saw false. 1,200 merchants were paid twice; recovering the money took three weeks. Fix: AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet locally, ShedLock across instances, and an idempotency key per merchant per settlement date in the payout table. Lesson: balking needs an atomic check-and-set, and money movement needs idempotency as a second line of defence.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Guarded Suspension Balking Producer-Consumer Double-Checked Locking Guard false → Wait Return Producer/consumer wait on full/empty Lock, check again Typical guard "Data ready" "Already running / nothing to do" Buffer capacity "Already initialized" Relationship Basis of blocking queues Basis of idempotent triggers Two guarded suspensions Balking on the fast path

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Guarded suspension: guard false → wait (in a while loop, with a timeout).
  • Balking: guard false → return (atomic compareAndSet).
  • notifyAll unless all waiters share one guard; or use separate Conditions.
  • Prefer JDK utilities: BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, CompletableFuture.
  • Across machines: leases/locks plus idempotency.
synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException { while (q.isEmpty()) wait(); return q.poll(); }

docs.text:
• Rewrite PickupCounter with ReentrantLock and one Condition per order.
  • Add a "run again after the current run" flag to SettlementJob instead of pure balking.
  • Implement BoundedMailbox with notFull and notEmpty conditions.

Virtual Threads Next: Active Object

docs.title: Immutable Object
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🔴 Advanced Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An immutable object can't change after it's built. "Changes" create new objects. Immutable objects are automatically thread-safe, can be shared freely and cached, and make reasoning easy. In Java: records (with defensive copies), final fields, List.copyOf, java.time, BigDecimal, String.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: an order snapshot is shared with billing, the warehouse and the email service, each on its own thread. If the snapshot is mutable, any of them (or the cart UI that created it) can change it while others are reading, and you need locks everywhere. If it's immutable, nobody can change it, so nobody needs a lock. Every reader sees exactly what was agreed at checkout.

Definition:

An object whose state cannot be modified after construction. To "change" it, create a new object with the new state (a "wither" or copy-on-write).

The rules (from Java Concurrency in Practice and Effective Java Item 17):

  1. All fields final (records do this for you).
  2. No setters or other mutators.
  3. The class can't be subclassed in a way that adds mutability (final class or record).
  4. Defensive copies of mutable inputs (lists, arrays, Date) in the constructor, and never hand out internal mutable objects.
  5. this doesn't escape during construction.

Follow these and the Java Memory Model guarantees that any thread sees the fully constructed state (final-field semantics), even without synchronization.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A printed receipt

Once a receipt is printed, it doesn't change. Copies can go to the customer, the accountant and the auditor, and they'll always agree. If something needs correcting, you issue a new document (a credit note); you don't scribble on the old receipt.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class Money { <<record, immutable>> +BigDecimal amount +Currency currency +plus(Money) Money +allocate(n) List~Money~ } class Client Client ..> Money : operations return NEW instances Technique Purpose record / final fields No reassignment after construction Compact constructor validation Invalid objects can't exist List.copyOf, Map.copyOf Defensive copy in, unmodifiable out Withers (withX(...)) Create modified copies AtomicReference<Immutable> Swap whole snapshots atomically

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class Order {
    private List<Line> lines;               // mutable list, shared
    public List<Line> getLines() { return lines; }        // caller can add lines
    public void setLines(List<Line> lines) { this.lines = lines; }  // caller keeps a reference
}
// Billing reads total while the cart UI is still adding lines -> invoice != charged amount.
  • Shared mutable state: races, locks everywhere.
  • Aliasing bugs: changing "my" list changes yours.
  • Objects can enter invalid states halfway through updates.

docs.title: Example 1: Money as an Immutable Value (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A banking app splits bills, sums transactions and converts currencies across many threads. Money must never lose a paisa: splitting INR 100 three ways must give 33.34 + 33.33 + 33.33, not 99.99. Amounts like INR 10.005 are invalid. A single Money instance (INR 1) is shared by a million parallel additions without any locks.

Design:

flowchart LR A["Money INR 100.00"] -->|"allocate(3)"| B["[33.34, 33.33, 33.33]"] B -->|"reduce(plus)"| C["Money INR 100.00 (new object)"] A -.->|unchanged| A

Full Code:

Money.javaMoneyDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.money;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Currency;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

/** Immutable value object: every operation returns a NEW Money. Safe to share across threads. */
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {

    public Money { // (1)!
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);
    }

    public static Money inr(String amount) {
        return new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), Currency.getInstance("INR"));
    }

    public Money plus(Money other) { // (2)!
        requireSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);
    }

    /** Split into n parts that add back up EXACTLY: the extra paise go to the first parts. */
    public List<Money> allocate(int parts) {
        BigDecimal unit = BigDecimal.ONE.movePointLeft(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()); // 0.01
        BigDecimal base = amount.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(parts), currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.DOWN);
        BigDecimal remainder = amount.subtract(base.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(parts)));
        int extra = remainder.divide(unit, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY).intValue();
        List<Money> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < parts; i++) {
            result.add(new Money(i < extra ? base.add(unit) : base, currency));
        }
        return List.copyOf(result);
    }

    private void requireSameCurrency(Money other) {
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot add " + other.currency + " to " + currency);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return currency.getCurrencyCode() + " " + amount.toPlainString();
    }
}
  1. The compact constructor validates and normalizes (scale to 2 for INR). An invalid Money can never exist, so no method needs to re-check.
  2. Every operation returns a new Money. Nothing is ever modified, so instances can be shared across threads with no locks.
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.money;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class MoneyDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Splitting a Bill and Summing in Parallel ===");
        Money dinner = Money.inr("100.00");
        List<Money> shares = dinner.allocate(3);
        System.out.println("INR 100 split 3 ways : " + shares);
        System.out.println("Shares add back up   : " + shares.stream().reduce(Money.inr("0"), Money::plus));

        Money oneRupee = Money.inr("1.00"); // shared by all threads, no locks needed
        Money total = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000).parallel()
                .mapToObj(i -> oneRupee)
                .reduce(Money.inr("0"), Money::plus); // (1)!
        System.out.println("1,000,000 x INR 1 in parallel: " + total);
        System.out.println("Original still INR 1.00      : " + oneRupee);

        try {
            Money.inr("10.005");
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected INR 10.005: fractions of a paisa are not money");
        }
    }
}
  1. A parallel reduction over a shared object: safe because plus never mutates. With a mutable accumulator this would be a race.

Output:

=== Banking: Splitting a Bill and Summing in Parallel ===
INR 100 split 3 ways : [INR 33.34, INR 33.33, INR 33.33]
Shares add back up   : INR 100.00
1,000,000 x INR 1 in parallel: INR 1000000.00
Original still INR 1.00      : INR 1.00
Rejected INR 10.005: fractions of a paisa are not money

Why immutability here:

  • Money is a value: two INR 5.00s are the same thing, so equals/hashCode by value (records give this).
  • Thread-safe by construction for parallel computations.
  • Validation in one place, the constructor, so invalid amounts can't exist.

docs.title: Example 2: Order Snapshot Shared by Services (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: At checkout, the order is frozen into a snapshot and handed to billing, warehouse, email and analytics, all running concurrently. The cart UI keeps its own mutable list (customers sometimes add items after paying, by mistake), and that must not change what was charged. Amendments (adding a screen guard after checkout) create a new snapshot.

Design:

flowchart LR Cart["Mutable cart list (UI)"] -->|"List.copyOf at construction"| S["OrderSnapshot (immutable)"] S --> B[Billing thread] S --> W[Warehouse thread] S --> E[Email thread] S --> A[Analytics thread] S -->|"withLine(...)"| S2["New amended snapshot"]

Full Code:

OrderSnapshot.javaOrderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

/** What the customer agreed to at checkout. Shared with billing, warehouse and email threads. */
public record OrderSnapshot(String orderId, Instant placedAt, List<Line> lines) {

    public record Line(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInr) {
    }

    public OrderSnapshot {
        lines = List.copyOf(lines); // (1)!
    }

    public int totalInr() {
        return lines.stream().mapToInt(l -> l.qty() * l.unitPriceInr()).sum();
    }

    public OrderSnapshot withLine(Line extra) { // (2)!
        var copy = new java.util.ArrayList<>(lines);
        copy.add(extra);
        return new OrderSnapshot(orderId, placedAt, copy);
    }
}
  1. Defensive copy in, unmodifiable out: List.copyOf copies the caller's list (later cart changes can't leak in) and returns an unmodifiable list (callers can't modify it). Record components alone aren't enough: a record holding an ArrayList is shallowly immutable.
  2. A wither: the "change" produces a new snapshot; the original is untouched for everyone still using it.
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order;

import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order.OrderSnapshot.Line;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class OrderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Order Snapshot Shared by Four Services ===");
        List<Line> cart = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Line("PHONE-CASE", 1, 499), new Line("CHARGER-65W", 1, 1_899)));
        OrderSnapshot snapshot = new OrderSnapshot("ORD-77", Instant.parse("2026-10-13T10:15:30Z"), cart);

        cart.add(new Line("SNEAKY-ADDON", 1, 9_999)); // the cart UI keeps changing after checkout...
        System.out.println("Cart changed after checkout; snapshot total still INR " + snapshot.totalInr());

        try {
            snapshot.lines().add(new Line("HACK", 1, 1));
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("Snapshot lines cannot be modified");
        }

        try (ExecutorService services = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<String>> results = List.of(
                    services.submit(() -> "billing  : invoice INR " + snapshot.totalInr()),
                    services.submit(() -> "warehouse: pick " + snapshot.lines().size() + " lines"),
                    services.submit(() -> "email    : receipt for " + snapshot.orderId()),
                    services.submit(() -> "analytics: revenue " + snapshot.totalInr()));
            for (Future<String> f : results) {
                System.out.println(f.get()); // no locks: nothing can change
            }
        }

        OrderSnapshot amended = snapshot.withLine(new Line("SCREEN-GUARD", 1, 299));
        System.out.println("Amended copy total INR " + amended.totalInr() + ", original still INR " + snapshot.totalInr());
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Order Snapshot Shared by Four Services ===
Cart changed after checkout; snapshot total still INR 2398
Snapshot lines cannot be modified
billing  : invoice INR 2398
warehouse: pick 2 lines
email    : receipt for ORD-77
analytics: revenue 2398
Amended copy total INR 2697, original still INR 2398

Why immutability here:

  • One agreed version of the order, shared by many threads without coordination.
  • No aliasing bugs from the cart UI.
  • Amendments are explicit new versions, which is good for auditing.

docs.title: Example 3: Lock-Free Config Snapshots (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: An API gateway enforces per-tenant rate limits read on every request (here 400,000 reads), while an admin tool updates the limits. The per-minute limit and burst must always be consistent with each other (burst = rpm / 10, and burst ≤ rpm). With an immutable snapshot inside an AtomicReference, readers never lock: they grab the current snapshot in one step and use it for the whole request.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant R as Request threads participant A as AtomicReference participant U as Admin update R->>A: get() snapshot v5 (600/60) U->>U: build snapshot v6 (1200/120) off to the side U->>A: updateAndGet (atomic swap) R->>A: get() snapshot v6 Note over R: each request sees v5 or v6, never a mix

Full Code:

RateLimitConfig.javaConfigDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.config;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

/** Lock-free configuration: readers get an immutable snapshot; updates swap the whole snapshot. */
public final class RateLimitConfig {

    public record Snapshot(int version, int requestsPerMinute, int burst) { // (1)!
        public Snapshot {
            if (burst > requestsPerMinute) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("burst cannot exceed the per-minute limit");
            }
        }

        Snapshot withLimits(int rpm, int burst) {
            return new Snapshot(version + 1, rpm, burst);
        }
    }

    private final AtomicReference<Snapshot> current = new AtomicReference<>(new Snapshot(1, 600, 60));

    public Snapshot get() {
        return current.get(); // (2)!
    }

    public void update(int rpm, int burst) {
        current.updateAndGet(s -> s.withLimits(rpm, burst)); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. An immutable snapshot record with its invariant enforced in the constructor. An invalid config can't even be built, so it can't be published.
  2. Reading is a single volatile read: wait-free, no locks.
  3. updateAndGet applies the change atomically (retrying if another update raced). The update function must be side-effect free, because it may run more than once.
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.config;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class ConfigDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS API: Rate-Limit Config Updated While Serving Traffic ===");
        RateLimitConfig config = new RateLimitConfig();
        AtomicInteger reads = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger invalid = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5)) {
            for (int r = 0; r < 4; r++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                        RateLimitConfig.Snapshot s = config.get(); // one consistent snapshot per request
                        if (s.burst() > s.requestsPerMinute() || s.burst() * 10 != s.requestsPerMinute()) {
                            invalid.incrementAndGet();
                        }
                        reads.incrementAndGet();
                    }
                });
            }
            ex.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 1_000; i++) {
                    int rpm = (i % 2 == 0) ? 600 : 1_200;
                    config.update(rpm, rpm / 10);
                }
            });
        }
        System.out.println("Requests served       : " + reads.get());
        System.out.println("Config versions       : " + config.get().version());
        System.out.println("Inconsistent configs  : " + invalid.get());
        System.out.println("Locks taken by readers: 0");
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS API: Rate-Limit Config Updated While Serving Traffic ===
Requests served       : 400000
Config versions       : 1001
Inconsistent configs  : 0
Locks taken by readers: 0

Why immutability here:

  • The read path is hot: no locks, no contention.
  • Consistency comes from swapping whole snapshots, not from locking fields.
  • Rollback is easy: keep the previous snapshot and swap it back.
Unit Tests: ImmutableTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.immutable;

import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.config.RateLimitConfig;
import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.money.Money;
import com.handbook.concurrency.immutable.order.OrderSnapshot;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ImmutableTest {

    @Test
    void allocationNeverLosesPaise() {
        for (int parts = 1; parts <= 7; parts++) {
            Money total = Money.inr("100.00").allocate(parts).stream().reduce(Money.inr("0"), Money::plus);
            assertThat(total).isEqualTo(Money.inr("100.00"));
        }
    }

    @Test
    void moneyIsAValue() {
        assertThat(Money.inr("5")).isEqualTo(Money.inr("5.00")); // scale normalized in the constructor
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Money.inr("1").plus(new Money(java.math.BigDecimal.ONE, java.util.Currency.getInstance("USD"))))
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void snapshotIsIsolatedFromCallerList() {
        List<OrderSnapshot.Line> lines = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new OrderSnapshot.Line("A", 1, 10)));
        OrderSnapshot s = new OrderSnapshot("O", Instant.EPOCH, lines);
        lines.clear();
        assertThat(s.totalInr()).isEqualTo(10);
    }

    @Test
    void invalidConfigIsRejectedAndOldSnapshotKept() {
        RateLimitConfig c = new RateLimitConfig();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> c.update(10, 100)).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
        assertThat(c.get().version()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Tool Notes Records (Java 16+) Final fields, value equals/hashCode, compact constructors for validation; shallowly immutable, so copy mutable components List.of/copyOf, Map.of/copyOf, Set.of Truly unmodifiable; null not allowed; copyOf returns the same instance if it's already immutable Collections.unmodifiableList(list) A view: if the original list changes, the view shows it. Not a copy java.time (LocalDate, Instant, Duration) Immutable replacements for Date/Calendar BigDecimal, String, wrapper types Immutable values Withers order.withLine(...); with many fields, builders with toBuilder() Persistent collections (Vavr, PCollections) Efficient "modified copies" via structural sharing

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Immutable JDK String, Integer and other wrappers, BigDecimal, java.time.*, Path, URI, Optional JDK collections List.of, Map.of, Set.of, Stream.toList() Spring HttpHeaders.readOnlyHttpHeaders, ResponseEntity, MediaType; immutable @ConfigurationProperties with constructor binding (records) Jackson Deserializes records and immutable classes via constructors Kafka Records sent are effectively immutable once handed to the producer Guava ImmutableList, ImmutableMap

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Thread-safe without locks New object per change: allocation and GC (usually cheap) Safe to share, cache, use as map keys Large objects copied on every change can be expensive Invariants checked once, at construction Deeply nested updates are verbose without lenses/withers Easy reasoning, no aliasing bugs Some frameworks (JPA entities) expect mutability

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Shallow immutability

record Order(List<Line> lines) is not immutable if lines is an ArrayList: callers can still change it. Copy in the compact constructor (List.copyOf).

Leaking mutable internals

Returning an internal Date, array or list lets callers change your "immutable" object (see the coding challenge). Return copies or immutable types.

Collections.unmodifiableList is a view, not a copy

If the backing list changes, so does the "unmodifiable" view. Use List.copyOf.

Escaping this in the constructor

Registering this with a listener inside the constructor lets other threads see a partially constructed object, voiding the final-field guarantee.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Final-field semantics. The JMM guarantees that once a constructor finishes, any thread that gets a reference to the object sees the correctly initialized values of its final fields, without synchronization, as long as this didn't escape. That's why immutable objects can be published through data races (e.g., a non-volatile field) and still be safe.

Immutability at architecture scale: event sourcing (events are immutable facts), Kafka logs, CRDTs, Git, and container images are all immutable data. Systems built on immutable data are easier to cache, replicate, audit and debug.

Performance reality. Short-lived small objects are almost free on modern JVMs (TLAB allocation, young-gen GC). Profile before introducing mutable "optimizations". For big structures with frequent small changes, use persistent data structures or confine mutation to one thread and publish immutable snapshots.

War story: the invoice that didn't match the charge

An e-commerce checkout passed the same mutable Order object to the payment thread and the invoice thread. A "recommended add-on" widget on the confirmation page added an item to the same object a few hundred milliseconds after payment. The payment charged the old total; the invoice, generated slightly later, included the add-on. About 0.3% of invoices didn't match the charged amount, and every one was a support ticket and a manual credit note. Fix: checkout now creates an immutable OrderSnapshot (record + List.copyOf) that payment, invoicing and email all receive; add-ons after payment create a separate order. Lesson: anything shared between threads, or meant to represent "what was agreed", should be immutable.

docs.text: Immutable Object Read-Write Lock Prototype Flyweight Thread safety Inherent, no locks Locks N/A Requires immutability Changes New objects In place under a write lock Copy then modify Never (shared) Relationship Basis for safe sharing Alternative when mutation is needed Copying mutable objects Flyweights must be immutable

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Can't change after construction; changes create new objects.
  • Thread-safe for free; great keys, cache entries and shared snapshots.
  • Records are shallowly immutable: List.copyOf mutable components.
  • Don't leak internals; prefer java.time over Date.
  • Config pattern: immutable snapshot + AtomicReference swap.
record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) { Money plus(Money o) { return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency); } }

docs.title: Producer-Consumer
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Concurrency Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Producers put work into a shared buffer (queue); consumers take work out and process it, at their own pace. The buffer decouples the two sides, smooths bursts, and, when it's bounded, applies back-pressure so fast producers can't overwhelm slow consumers. In Java, use a BlockingQueue.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: orders arrive at a dark store in bursts (a hundred at 7 pm, ten at 3 pm). Pickers work at a steady pace. If the order system hands each order directly to a picker, it has to wait when all pickers are busy, or orders get lost. A queue between them lets orders arrive at any rate and lets pickers take the next one when they're free. If the queue fills up, the system knows it's overloaded and can slow intake.

Definition:

Separate the code that produces work from the code that consumes it, connected by a thread-safe buffer. Producers block (or are rejected) when the buffer is full; consumers block when it's empty.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant's order rail

Waiters (producers) clip orders onto the rail. Cooks (consumers) take the next ticket when they're ready. If the rail is full, waiters stop taking new tables for a moment (back-pressure). Waiters never need to know which cook will cook the order.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
flowchart LR P1[Producer 1] -->|put| Q[("Bounded BlockingQueue<br/>capacity N")] P2[Producer 2] -->|put| Q Q -->|take| C1[Consumer 1] Q -->|take| C2[Consumer 2] Q -->|take| C3[Consumer 3] Participant Responsibility Producer Creates work items and puts/offers them Buffer Thread-safe queue; bounded to apply back-pressure Consumer takes/polls items and processes them Shutdown signal Poison pill, interrupt, or a "done" flag

BlockingQueue methods, the interview table:

Throws Returns special value Blocks Times out Insert add(e) offer(e) → false put(e) offer(e, t, unit) Remove remove() poll() → null take() poll(t, unit)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();          // not thread-safe
// producer
orders.add(order);
// consumer
while (true) {
    if (!orders.isEmpty()) {                     // busy-waiting burns CPU
        Order o = orders.remove(0);              // race: two consumers take the same order,
        pick(o);                                 // or one gets IndexOutOfBoundsException
    }
}
  • Races on an unsynchronized list.
  • Busy-waiting wastes CPU.
  • Unbounded growth: a burst eventually causes OutOfMemoryError.

docs.title: Example 1: Dark-Store Order Picking (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Order intake produces pick tasks; three pickers (consumers) collect items. The queue holds at most 5 waiting tasks; when it's full, intake blocks until a picker frees a slot, so the floor never has an ever-growing backlog. At closing time, the system must stop pickers cleanly after the last order.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant I as Order intake (producer) participant Q as ArrayBlockingQueue(5) participant P as Pickers x3 (consumers) I->>Q: put(ORD-1..ORD-5) I->>Q: put(ORD-6) blocks: queue full P->>Q: take() ORD-1 Q-->>I: space available, ORD-6 queued I->>Q: put(STOP) x3 (poison pills) P->>Q: take() STOP, exit

Full Code:

PickingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.picking;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Dark store: the order intake produces pick tasks; 3 pickers consume them. */
public class PickingDemo {

    record PickTask(String orderId, int items) {
    }

    private static final PickTask POISON_PILL = new PickTask("STOP", 0); // (1)!

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery Dark Store: Order Picking ===");
        BlockingQueue<PickTask> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(5); // (2)!
        AtomicInteger maxDepth = new AtomicInteger();
        Map<String, Integer> pickedBy = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        AtomicInteger itemsPicked = new AtomicInteger();
        int pickers = 3;

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int p = 1; p <= pickers; p++) {
                String picker = "picker-" + p;
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    while (true) {
                        PickTask task = queue.take(); // (3)!
                        if (task == POISON_PILL) {
                            return null;
                        }
                        Thread.sleep(5); // walking the aisles
                        itemsPicked.addAndGet(task.items());
                        pickedBy.merge(picker, 1, Integer::sum);
                    }
                });
            }

            for (int i = 1; i <= 30; i++) { // the producer: order intake
                queue.put(new PickTask("ORD-" + i, i % 4 + 1)); // blocks when 5 tasks are waiting
                maxDepth.accumulateAndGet(queue.size(), Math::max);
            }
            for (int p = 0; p < pickers; p++) {
                queue.put(POISON_PILL); // one pill per consumer
            }
        } // waits for all pickers to finish

        int orders = pickedBy.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("Orders picked       : " + orders);
        System.out.println("Items picked        : " + itemsPicked.get());
        System.out.println("Queue never above 5 : " + (maxDepth.get() <= 5));
        System.out.println("All pickers worked  : " + (pickedBy.size() == pickers));
    }
}
  1. A poison pill: a special item that tells a consumer to stop. Send one per consumer. Compared with ==, so a real order can never be mistaken for it.
  2. Bounded to 5. This is what creates back-pressure; an unbounded queue just hides overload until memory runs out.
  3. take() blocks while the queue is empty: no busy-waiting. With virtual threads, a blocked consumer costs almost nothing.

Output:

=== Grocery Dark Store: Order Picking ===
Orders picked       : 30
Items picked        : 75
Queue never above 5 : true
All pickers worked  : true

The demo prints only what's guaranteed (totals, the queue bound). Which picker took which order varies from run to run, as it should.

Why Producer-Consumer here:

  • Arrival rate (bursty) and processing rate (steady) are decoupled.
  • The bound gives natural back-pressure on intake.
  • Adding a picker is adding a consumer; the producer doesn't change.

docs.title: Example 2: Batched GPS Ingestion (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: 200 delivery riders' phones send GPS pings constantly. Writing each ping with its own INSERT overwhelms the database. Instead, rider connections (many producers) put pings on a queue, and one writer (consumer) drains up to 100 at a time and writes them in a single batch insert. Under light load, batches are small and latency stays low; under heavy load, batches grow automatically.

Design:

flowchart LR R1[Rider 1] --> Q[(LinkedBlockingQueue)] R2[Rider 2] --> Q R3[... 200 riders] --> Q Q -->|"poll(20 ms) + drainTo(99)"| W[Batch writer] W -->|"1 INSERT with up to 100 rows"| DB[(Database)]

Full Code:

GpsIngestDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.gps;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Many riders' phones produce GPS pings; one writer batches them into the database. */
public class GpsIngestDemo {

    record Ping(String rider, double lat, double lng) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Batched GPS Ingestion ===");
        BlockingQueue<Ping> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
        AtomicBoolean producersDone = new AtomicBoolean();
        AtomicInteger written = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger batches = new AtomicInteger();
        AtomicInteger biggestBatch = new AtomicInteger();

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            pool.submit(() -> { // single consumer: batch writer
                List<Ping> batch = new ArrayList<>(100);
                while (!producersDone.get() || !queue.isEmpty()) {
                    Ping first = queue.poll(20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // wait briefly for the first item
                    if (first == null) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    batch.add(first);
                    queue.drainTo(batch, 99); // (1)!
                    written.addAndGet(batch.size()); // one INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ...
                    batches.incrementAndGet();
                    biggestBatch.accumulateAndGet(batch.size(), Math::max);
                    batch.clear();
                }
                return null;
            });

            try (ExecutorService riders = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                for (int r = 0; r < 200; r++) { // 200 riders x 25 pings
                    String rider = "R" + r;
                    riders.submit(() -> {
                        for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
                            queue.put(new Ping(rider, 12.9 + i * 0.0001, 77.6));
                        }
                        return null;
                    });
                }
            }
            producersDone.set(true);
        }

        System.out.println("Pings received      : 5000");
        System.out.println("Pings written       : " + written.get());
        System.out.println("Batch size <= 100   : " + (biggestBatch.get() <= 100));
        System.out.println("Fewer DB writes than pings: " + (batches.get() < 5_000));
    }
}
  1. drainTo grabs everything already waiting (up to a limit) in one call: the key to adaptive batching. Wait for the first item with a timeout, then take whatever else is ready.

Output:

=== Logistics: Batched GPS Ingestion ===
Pings received      : 5000
Pings written       : 5000
Batch size <= 100   : true
Fewer DB writes than pings: true

Why Producer-Consumer here:

  • Many producers, one consumer: a classic fan-in.
  • The consumer turns a stream of tiny writes into efficient batches.
  • Producers never wait for the database; the queue absorbs the difference.

docs.title: Example 3: Webhook Intake with Back-pressure (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment gateway sends webhooks (payment.captured, refund.created) to a merchant's server. The HTTP handler must respond fast, so it only enqueues the event and returns 202 Accepted; a worker processes events afterwards. If the queue is full (worker down or slow), the handler returns 503 within milliseconds, and the gateway retries later. That's back-pressure across a network boundary.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant G as Payment gateway participant H as HTTP handler (producer) participant Q as Queue (capacity 3) participant W as Worker (consumer) G->>H: POST evt_1..evt_3 H->>Q: offer() ok H-->>G: 202 Accepted G->>H: POST evt_4 H->>Q: offer(10 ms) fails: full H-->>G: 503 (retry later) W->>Q: poll() evt_1..evt_3 G->>H: retry evt_4 H-->>G: 202

Full Code:

WebhookDemo.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.webhooks;

import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

/** Payment webhooks: accept fast, process later, and push back (HTTP 503) when the buffer is full. */
public class WebhookDemo {

    record Webhook(String id, String event) {
    }

    private final BlockingQueue<Webhook> inbox = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);

    int receive(Webhook w) throws InterruptedException { // the HTTP handler: producer
        boolean accepted = inbox.offer(w, 10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // (1)!
        return accepted ? 202 : 503;
    }

    void drain() { // the worker: consumer
        Webhook w;
        while ((w = inbox.poll()) != null) {
            System.out.println("  processed " + w.id() + " " + w.event());
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Webhook Intake with Back-pressure ===");
        WebhookDemo service = new WebhookDemo();
        String[] events = {"payment.captured", "payment.failed", "refund.created", "payment.captured", "dispute.opened"};
        for (int i = 0; i < events.length; i++) {
            Webhook w = new Webhook("evt_" + (i + 1), events[i]);
            int status = service.receive(w);
            System.out.println("POST " + w.id() + " -> " + status + (status == 503 ? " (gateway will retry later)" : " Accepted"));
        }
        System.out.println("Worker catches up:");
        service.drain();
        System.out.println("Retry of evt_4 -> " + service.receive(new Webhook("evt_4", "payment.captured")));
    }
}
  1. offer with a timeout never blocks an HTTP thread for long. A full queue becomes a fast, explicit "try again later" instead of a hung request.

Output:

=== Payments: Webhook Intake with Back-pressure ===
POST evt_1 -> 202 Accepted
POST evt_2 -> 202 Accepted
POST evt_3 -> 202 Accepted
POST evt_4 -> 503 (gateway will retry later)
POST evt_5 -> 503 (gateway will retry later)
Worker catches up:
  processed evt_1 payment.captured
  processed evt_2 payment.failed
  processed evt_3 refund.created
Retry of evt_4 -> 202

In-memory queues lose data on crash

Accepted-but-unprocessed webhooks are gone if the process dies. In production, persist them first (a database table or Kafka topic) and return 202 only after the write. The in-memory queue is fine for work you can afford to lose or rebuild.

Why Producer-Consumer here:

  • Fast acknowledgement, slow processing.
  • Explicit back-pressure (503) pushes the problem back to a sender that knows how to retry.
  • The worker can be restarted or scaled independently.
Unit Test: ProducerConsumerTest.java 
package com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer;

import com.handbook.concurrency.producerconsumer.buffer.BoundedBuffer;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Timeout;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ProducerConsumerTest {

    @Test
    @Timeout(10)
    void manyProducersAndConsumersLoseNothing() throws Exception {
        BoundedBuffer<Integer> buffer = new BoundedBuffer<>(8);
        Set<Integer> received = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 2_500; i++) {
                        received.add(buffer.take());
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
            for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) {
                int base = p * 2_500;
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 2_500; i++) {
                        buffer.put(base + i);
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
        }
        assertThat(received).hasSize(10_000);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Queue Bounded? Notes ArrayBlockingQueue Yes (fixed array) One lock; predictable memory; optional fairness LinkedBlockingQueue Optional (default unbounded!) Separate put/take locks: higher throughput. Always pass a capacity LinkedTransferQueue No transfer() waits until a consumer takes the item (hand-off) SynchronousQueue Zero capacity Direct hand-off; used by Executors.newCachedThreadPool() PriorityBlockingQueue No Consumers get the highest-priority item first (express orders) DelayQueue No Items become available after a delay (retries, scheduled reminders) LMAX Disruptor Ring buffer Lock-free, very high throughput (trading systems)

Virtual threads (Java 21): blocking take()/put() is cheap on virtual threads, so "one virtual thread per consumer" or "per producer" is fine even at large scale. Bound the queue (and the downstream resource), not the threads.

Shutdown options: poison pills (Example 1), a "done" flag plus a timed poll (Example 2), or interrupting consumers (executor.shutdownNow()), where consumers must handle InterruptedException by exiting.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Producer-Consumer JDK ThreadPoolExecutor (submitters produce tasks into a BlockingQueue; worker threads consume) Logback / Log4j2 AsyncAppender / async loggers: application threads produce log events, a background thread writes them Spring Batch ItemReader → chunk → ItemWriter Kafka / RabbitMQ / SQS The same pattern across processes; consumer groups are pools of consumers Netty Event loops consuming I/O events Reactive Streams Publisher/Subscriber with request(n) back-pressure

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Decouples production and consumption rates Extra latency (items wait in the buffer) Absorbs bursts In-memory buffers lose data on crash Back-pressure with bounded queues Shutdown and error handling need care Easy to scale consumers Ordering only per queue; parallel consumers process out of order Enables batching Unbounded queues hide overload until OOM

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Unbounded queues

new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() has a capacity of Integer.MAX_VALUE. Under sustained overload it grows until the JVM dies. Always bound and decide what happens when full (block, reject, drop oldest).

Swallowing InterruptedException

catch (InterruptedException e) {} inside a consumer loop makes it impossible to stop. Restore the flag (Thread.currentThread().interrupt()) and exit.

One poison pill for many consumers

Only one consumer gets it; the others block forever. Send one per consumer, or have the consumer that receives it put it back.

Slow consumers and ordering

With several consumers, items for the same entity (same order, same account) may be processed out of order. Partition by key (one queue per partition) if order matters.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Sizing. Little's Law again: queue length ≈ arrival rate × time in queue. Choose capacity from the latency you can tolerate, not from memory alone: a queue that holds 10 minutes of work means 10-minute-old results.

What to do when full: block the producer (in-process, trusted producers), reject with a retryable error (network edges, as in Example 3), drop (metrics, telemetry), or shed load by priority. Make the policy explicit and observable (queue depth, wait time, rejections).

From in-process to distributed. The same pattern at system scale is a message broker. Kafka adds durability, replay, partition-level ordering and consumer groups; SQS adds visibility timeouts and dead-letter queues. Consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

Batching trade-off. Bigger batches mean higher throughput and higher latency. Adaptive batching (Example 2) gives small batches under light load and large ones under heavy load. Add a max wait time so items never sit too long.

War story: the async logger that took down checkout

A team switched to an asynchronous log appender with an unbounded queue to "make logging free". During an incident, a downstream log collector slowed down; the queue grew to 9 GB of log events, triggered long GC pauses, and then an OutOfMemoryError on every checkout pod at once. Fix: a bounded queue (8,192 events) with "discard DEBUG/INFO when 80% full, never block on ERROR", plus a metric and alert on queue depth. Lesson: every queue is a decision about overload. "Unbounded" is a decision too: the decision to crash later.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Producer-Consumer Thread Pool Observer / Pub-Sub Pipeline Core idea Buffer between producers and consumers Workers consuming a task queue (a specific Producer-Consumer) Notify all subscribers Chain of producer-consumer stages Delivery Each item to one consumer One worker per task Every subscriber gets each event Each stage to the next Back-pressure Bounded queue Bounded queue + rejection policy Usually none (reactive streams add it) Bounded queues between stages

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Producers → bounded BlockingQueue → consumers.
  • put/take block; offer/poll with timeouts for back-pressure at edges.
  • Shutdown: poison pill per consumer or interrupts; never swallow InterruptedException.
  • drainTo for batching; partition by key for ordering.
  • wait() in a loop, prefer notifyAll().
BlockingQueue<Task> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100); q.put(task); Task t = q.take();

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Use a PriorityBlockingQueue so express orders are picked first.
  • Rewrite BoundedBuffer with ReentrantLock and two Conditions.
  • Add a max wait (50 ms) to the GPS writer so partial batches are flushed promptly.
