  2. final stops subclasses from changing the workflow. They may only change what is created. This is Factory Method working together with Template Method.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class RoadLogistics extends LogisticsPlanner {

    @Override
    protected Transport createTransport() {
        return new Truck();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class RailLogistics extends LogisticsPlanner {

    @Override
    protected Transport createTransport() {
        return new FreightTrain();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class AirLogistics extends LogisticsPlanner {

    @Override
    protected Transport createTransport() {
        return new CargoPlane();
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

/** Product interface. */
public interface Transport {

    String name();

    int costPerKmInr();

    int speedKmph();
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public record Truck() implements Transport {
    public String name() { return "Truck"; }
    public int costPerKmInr() { return 18; }
    public int speedKmph() { return 50; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public record FreightTrain() implements Transport {
    public String name() { return "Train"; }
    public int costPerKmInr() { return 8; }
    public int speedKmph() { return 60; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public record CargoPlane() implements Transport {
    public String name() { return "Plane"; }
    public int costPerKmInr() { return 95; }
    public int speedKmph() { return 700; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics;

public class LogisticsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Shipment Planning ===");
        print(new RoadLogistics(), "SHP-1", "Bengaluru->Mysuru", 145);
        print(new RailLogistics(), "SHP-2", "Delhi->Mumbai", 1400);
        print(new AirLogistics(), "SHP-3", "Chennai->Guwahati", 2650);
    }

    private static void print(LogisticsPlanner planner, String id, String route, int km) {
        System.out.println(planner.plan(id, route, km)); // same call, different transport
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Shipment Planning ===
SHP-1 Bengaluru->Mysuru    via Truck |  145 km | cost INR   2610 | ETA  3 h
SHP-2 Delhi->Mumbai        via Train | 1400 km | cost INR  11200 | ETA 24 h
SHP-3 Chennai->Guwahati    via Plane | 2650 km | cost INR 251750 | ETA  4 h

One workflow (plan), three transports. The trade-off is visible in the numbers: the plane is about 22× the cost of the train for a 6× faster delivery.

Why Factory Method here:

  • The algorithm is fixed and the object it needs varies. That's the textbook GoF case.
  • Adding drones means one new subclass; plan() doesn't change. The unit test below proves it with an anonymous DroneLogistics.
  • Each subclass can be tested on its own.
Unit Test: LogisticsPlannerTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod;

import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.AirLogistics;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.LogisticsPlanner;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.RoadLogistics;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.logistics.Transport;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class LogisticsPlannerTest {

    @Test
    void subclassesDecideTheTransport() {
        assertThat(new RoadLogistics().plan("S", "A->B", 100)).contains("Truck", "cost INR   1800");
        assertThat(new AirLogistics().plan("S", "A->B", 1400)).contains("Plane", "ETA  2 h");
    }

    @Test
    void newTransportNeedsOnlyANewSubclass() {
        LogisticsPlanner drone = new LogisticsPlanner() {
            @Override
            protected Transport createTransport() {
                return new Transport() {
                    public String name() { return "Drone"; }
                    public int costPerKmInr() { return 40; }
                    public int speedKmph() { return 80; }
                };
            }
        };
        assertThat(drone.plan("S", "A->B", 10)).contains("Drone", "cost INR    400", "ETA  1 h");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 3: Pluggable Payment Processors (Banking / Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payments team runs checkout for a large e-commerce site. It supports UPI (no fee), cards (2% merchant fee) and wallets (regulatory limit of INR 10,000 per transaction). Net banking is being built by another team and isn't live yet. Payment methods are switched on per country and per merchant through configuration, so the factory can't be a hard-coded switch. It has to be a registry that's filled at start-up, and asking for a method that isn't registered must fail fast with a clear error.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Bootstrap / Config participant F as PaymentProcessorFactory participant C as Checkout participant P as CardProcessor B->>F: register(UPI, UpiProcessor::new) B->>F: register(CARD, CardProcessor::new) B->>F: register(WALLET, WalletProcessor::new) C->>F: create(CARD) F->>P: supplier.get() F-->>C: PaymentProcessor C->>P: pay("ORD-102", 2400) P-->>C: SUCCESS fee=48 C->>F: create(NET_BANKING) F-->>C: UnsupportedPaymentMethodException

Full Code:

PaymentProcessorFactory.javaCheckoutDemo.javaProcessorsSupporting types 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Registry-based factory: new payment methods are added by registering a
 * supplier, not by editing a switch statement (Open/Closed Principle).
 */
public final class PaymentProcessorFactory {

    private final Map<PaymentMethod, Supplier<? extends PaymentProcessor>> registry =
            new EnumMap<>(PaymentMethod.class); // (1)!

    public PaymentProcessorFactory register(PaymentMethod method,
                                            Supplier<? extends PaymentProcessor> supplier) {
        registry.put(method, supplier);
        return this; // fluent registration
    }

    public PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod method) {
        Supplier<? extends PaymentProcessor> supplier = registry.get(method);
        if (supplier == null) {
            throw new UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(method); // (2)!
        }
        return supplier.get(); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. EnumMap is a compact, fast array-backed map for enum keys. Each value is a Supplier, which is a factory method passed as a value. UpiProcessor::new is a constructor reference.
  2. Fail fast with a domain exception. A null return would turn into a confusing NullPointerException far away from the cause.
  3. The supplier is called on every request, so each caller gets a new processor. Register a supplier that returns a shared instance if the processor is stateless and expensive to build.
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class CheckoutDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Checkout with Pluggable Processors ===");
        PaymentProcessorFactory factory = new PaymentProcessorFactory()
                .register(PaymentMethod.UPI, UpiProcessor::new)
                .register(PaymentMethod.CARD, CardProcessor::new)
                .register(PaymentMethod.WALLET, WalletProcessor::new);

        pay(factory, "ORD-101", PaymentMethod.UPI, 450);
        pay(factory, "ORD-102", PaymentMethod.CARD, 2400);
        pay(factory, "ORD-103", PaymentMethod.WALLET, 12000);
        pay(factory, "ORD-104", PaymentMethod.NET_BANKING, 999);
    }

    private static void pay(PaymentProcessorFactory factory, String orderId,
                            PaymentMethod method, int amountInr) {
        String prefix = "%s %-11s INR %5d -> ".formatted(orderId, method, amountInr);
        try {
            PaymentResult result = factory.create(method).pay(orderId, amountInr);
            System.out.println(prefix + (result.success()
                    ? "SUCCESS " + result.detail() + " fee=INR " + result.feeInr()
                    : "FAILED  " + result.detail()));
        } catch (UnsupportedPaymentMethodException e) {
            System.out.println(prefix + "ERROR   " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public interface PaymentProcessor {

    PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr);
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class UpiProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        return PaymentResult.ok(0, "UPI-" + orderId); // UPI has no merchant fee
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    private static final int FEE_PERCENT = 2;

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        return PaymentResult.ok(amountInr * FEE_PERCENT / 100, "CARD-" + orderId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class WalletProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {

    private static final int WALLET_LIMIT_INR = 10_000;

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr) {
        if (amountInr > WALLET_LIMIT_INR) {
            return PaymentResult.failed("wallet limit INR " + WALLET_LIMIT_INR + " exceeded");
        }
        return PaymentResult.ok(0, "WAL-" + orderId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public enum PaymentMethod { UPI, CARD, WALLET, NET_BANKING }

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public record PaymentResult(boolean success, int feeInr, String detail) {

    public static PaymentResult ok(int feeInr, String reference) {
        return new PaymentResult(true, feeInr, "ref=" + reference);
    }

    public static PaymentResult failed(String reason) {
        return new PaymentResult(false, 0, reason);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments;

public class UnsupportedPaymentMethodException extends RuntimeException {

    public UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(PaymentMethod method) {
        super("No processor registered for " + method);
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Checkout with Pluggable Processors ===
ORD-101 UPI         INR   450 -> SUCCESS ref=UPI-ORD-101 fee=INR 0
ORD-102 CARD        INR  2400 -> SUCCESS ref=CARD-ORD-102 fee=INR 48
ORD-103 WALLET      INR 12000 -> FAILED  wallet limit INR 10000 exceeded
ORD-104 NET_BANKING INR   999 -> ERROR   No processor registered for NET_BANKING

Three outcomes worth noticing: a normal success, a business failure handled by the product itself (wallet limit), and a configuration failure caught by the factory (net banking isn't registered).

Why Factory Method here:

  • The set of products is decided by configuration, not by code, so a registry is the natural fit.
  • Open/Closed for real: the net-banking team adds register(NET_BANKING, NetBankingProcessor::new) and touches nothing else.
  • Tests can register a fake for any method (see canSwapInATestDouble below).
  • This is exactly how Spring injects Map<String, PaymentProcessor>; see section 6.
Unit Test: PaymentProcessorFactoryTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.factorymethod;

import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.CardProcessor;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.PaymentMethod;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.PaymentProcessorFactory;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.PaymentResult;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.UnsupportedPaymentMethodException;
import com.handbook.creational.factorymethod.payments.UpiProcessor;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class PaymentProcessorFactoryTest {

    private final PaymentProcessorFactory factory = new PaymentProcessorFactory()
            .register(PaymentMethod.UPI, UpiProcessor::new)
            .register(PaymentMethod.CARD, CardProcessor::new);

    @Test
    void createsRegisteredProcessor() {
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.CARD)).isInstanceOf(CardProcessor.class);
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.CARD).pay("O1", 1000))
                .isEqualTo(new PaymentResult(true, 20, "ref=CARD-O1"));
    }

    @Test
    void returnsANewInstanceEachTime() {
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.UPI)).isNotSameAs(factory.create(PaymentMethod.UPI));
    }

    @Test
    void canSwapInATestDouble() {
        factory.register(PaymentMethod.UPI, () -> (orderId, amount) -> PaymentResult.failed("bank down"));
        assertThat(factory.create(PaymentMethod.UPI).pay("O1", 10).success()).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void unknownMethodFailsFast() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> factory.create(PaymentMethod.NET_BANKING))
                .isInstanceOf(UnsupportedPaymentMethodException.class)
                .hasMessage("No processor registered for NET_BANKING");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Static factory methods on the type itself. Modern Java APIs prefer these to public constructors (Effective Java, Item 1):

List<String> names = List.of("a", "b");       // immutable list
Optional<User> user = Optional.ofNullable(u);
Path path = Path.of("/tmp", "x.txt");
Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

Naming conventions: of, from, valueOf, getInstance, newInstance, create, getType / newType.

Factory method on an interface (Java 8+): the coding challenge below puts FareCalculator.of(type) right on the interface, with lambdas as the products.

Spring does the registry for you. Name each bean after the enum value and inject a map:

public interface PaymentProcessor { PaymentResult pay(String orderId, int amountInr); }

@Component("UPI")  class UpiProcessor  implements PaymentProcessor { /* ... */ }
@Component("CARD") class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { /* ... */ }

@Service
class PaymentProcessorFactory {
    private final Map<String, PaymentProcessor> processors; // bean name -> bean

    PaymentProcessorFactory(Map<String, PaymentProcessor> processors) {
        this.processors = processors;
    }

    PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod method) {
        PaymentProcessor p = processors.get(method.name());
        if (p == null) throw new UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(method);
        return p;
    }
}

Adding a payment method is now one new @Component class, and nothing else changes. Combine this with @ConditionalOnProperty to switch methods on per environment.

ServiceLoader for plug-ins. ServiceLoader.load(PaymentProcessor.class) discovers implementations on the classpath (from META-INF/services or module-info provides). It's how JDBC drivers and many JDK SPIs are found.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example Form JDK Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale) Static factory picks a subclass by locale JDK List.of, Map.of, EnumSet.of Static factory; EnumSet.of returns RegularEnumSet or JumboEnumSet depending on size JDK Collection.iterator() Classic GoF: each collection subclass creates its own iterator JDK URLStreamHandlerFactory, ThreadFactory Factory interfaces you plug in JDK DriverManager.getConnection(url), ServiceLoader Registry/discovery-based Spring FactoryBean<T>, @Bean methods, BeanFactory.getBean() The container is one big factory Spring RestClient.builder(), WebClient.create() Static factory methods Hibernate SessionFactory.openSession() Factory method on a long-lived factory SLF4J LoggerFactory.getLogger(...) Static factory with a pluggable back-end

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Callers depend on an interface, not on concrete classes More classes: one per product, plus creators in the GoF form New products without editing client code (OCP) A factory with a giant switch just moves the if/else, unless it's sealed/exhaustive or a registry Creation logic (validation, caching, pooling) in one place Indirection makes it harder to "jump to definition" in an IDE Easy to swap in test doubles The GoF subclass form uses inheritance, which is rigid. Prefer composition (pass a Supplier) when you can Static factories can have descriptive names and return cached instances or subtypes Static factories can't be overridden or mocked easily

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
The 'god factory'

One ObjectFactory.create(String type) that builds everything in the app is a service locator in disguise. Keep one factory per product family.

Returning null for unknown types

It turns a clear configuration error into a NullPointerException three layers away. Throw a domain exception with the bad key in the message (Example 3).

Stringly typed keys

create("upi") vs create("UPI") bugs. Use an enum (or sealed types) as the key, and convert external strings once at the boundary.

Factory for a single class

If there is, and will only ever be, one implementation, a factory is ceremony. YAGNI. Add it when the second implementation shows up.

Calling the factory method from a constructor

In the GoF form, if the base class constructor calls the abstract createX(), the subclass's fields aren't initialized yet. Call it lazily, or from a method (as plan() does).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Which form to pick:

Situation Choose Fixed, small set of types known at compile time Static factory + sealed + exhaustive switch Shared workflow, only one collaborator varies, a class hierarchy already exists GoF Factory Method (with a final template method) Types are switched on by config, tenant or feature flag, or contributed by other teams/modules Registry (Map<K, Supplier<T>>, Spring map injection, ServiceLoader) Several related products that must match Move up to Abstract Factory

Factories as a seam for operational concerns. Because every instance goes through one point, the factory is where you add metrics (processor.created{method=CARD}), circuit breakers (wrap the product in a Resilience4j-decorated proxy), feature flags (return the new implementation for 5% of traffic), and caching of stateless products.

Feature-flagged migrations. Migrating from an old payment provider to a new one? Register both and let the factory decide per request:

PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod m, String merchantId) {
    if (m == CARD && flags.isEnabled("new-card-gateway", merchantId)) {
        return newCardGateway.get();
    }
    return registry.get(m).get();
}

That's the Strangler Fig pattern at class level. Roll out per merchant, roll back instantly.

Testing strategy. Unit-test each product on its own; test the factory's mapping (every enum value maps to something, using @EnumSource as in Example 1's test); test the clients with a fake registry.

War story: the missing default that charged the wrong fee

A checkout service picked a fee calculator with an old-style switch statement that ended in default: return new StandardFeeCalculator();. A new BNPL (buy now, pay later) method was added to the enum. Nobody updated the switch, and BNPL silently fell through to the standard card fee calculator. For three weeks BNPL merchants were charged 2% instead of the contracted 3.5%, a revenue leak only found in a quarterly audit. Fix: replaced it with a switch expression with no default, so the compiler flags unhandled constants, and added a parameterized test over PaymentMethod.values() asserting each one maps to a calculator. Lesson: "silent default" in a factory is a bug waiting to happen. Make missing cases a compile error or a loud failure.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Simple constructor Creates One product A family of related products One complex product, step by step One known class Decides Which class Which family How it's put together Nothing to decide Typical API create(type) / overridden createX() ui.button(), ui.checkbox() Order.builder().item(..).build() new Order(...) Use when Type varies at runtime Products must be consistent with each other Many optional params, immutability One implementation, simple setup

Works well with: Template Method (Example 2), Strategy (the products are often strategies), Singleton (cache stateless products), Prototype (factory clones a template instead of calling new).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Hide new behind a method; callers get an interface.
  • Three forms: static factory, GoF (subclass overrides createX()), registry (Map<K, Supplier<T>>).
  • OCP: new product = new class (+ registration), no edits to callers.
  • No silent default: use sealed/enum switch expressions, or throw on unknown keys.
  • JDK: List.of, Calendar.getInstance, Collection.iterator(). Spring: FactoryBean, map injection.
static Notification create(Channel c) { return switch (c) { case EMAIL -> new Email(); case SMS -> new Sms(); case PUSH -> new Push(); }; }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a WHATSAPP channel to Example 1. Notice which line fails to compile first.
  • Add a DroneLogistics creator to Example 2 as a real class with its own test.
  • Rewrite Example 3 as a Spring Boot app using Map<String, PaymentProcessor> injection.
  • Make PaymentProcessorFactory cache stateless processors and prove it with a test.

Singleton Next: Abstract Factory

docs.title: Object Pool
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Object Pool keeps a set of expensive, reusable objects and lends them out instead of creating and destroying one per request. Use it for objects that are costly to create or limited in number (database connections, licensed sessions, GPU workers). Don't use it for ordinary objects; the JVM allocates those faster than any pool.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: opening a database connection takes a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake and authentication, around 20–100 ms. A banking API handling 2,000 requests per second can't afford that on every request. The database also allows only so many connections. So you open a fixed number once and lend them to requests, taking them back afterwards.

Definition: Object Pool isn't one of the 23 GoF patterns, but it's a classic creational pattern that appears in every production Java system:

Manage a set of initialized objects that are ready to use. Clients acquire an object from the pool, use it, and release it back instead of destroying it.

The pool decides how many objects exist (bounded), when they're created (eagerly or lazily), and whether a returned object is still healthy.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A library's study rooms

A university library has 10 bookable study rooms. You borrow a key, use the room, and return the key. The library cleans the room between users (reset), takes a broken room out of service (validation), and if all rooms are taken you wait at the desk for a while (timeout). Building a new room for each student would be absurd.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram class ObjectPool~T~ { -BlockingQueue~T~ idle -int maxSize +acquire(timeout) T +release(T) } class PooledObject { +reset() +isValid() boolean } class Client ObjectPool o-- PooledObject : idle objects Client ..> ObjectPool : acquire / release Client ..> PooledObject : uses while borrowed Participant Responsibility Pool Tracks idle and in-use objects, enforces the maximum, creates objects on demand, validates and resets them Pooled object The expensive resource. Must be resettable to a clean state Client Acquires, uses and always releases (ideally via try-with-resources)

The lifecycle of a pooled object:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Idle : created (eagerly or on demand) Idle --> InUse : acquire() InUse --> Idle : release() + reset() InUse --> Destroyed : broken / too old / too many uses Idle --> Destroyed : fails validation / idle too long Destroyed --> [*]

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public BigDecimal balance(long accountId) throws SQLException {
    try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass)) { // new connection EVERY call
        return queryBalance(c, accountId);
    }
}

What goes wrong:

  • Latency. Each request pays 20–100 ms just to connect.
  • Overload. A traffic spike opens thousands of connections and the database falls over (too many connections).
  • No back-pressure. Nothing limits concurrency, so the system degrades for everyone instead of making some requests wait.

docs.title: Example 1: Connection Pool for a Ledger Service (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank's ledger service reads balances and runs transfers against a database that allows this service at most 2 connections (a small number to keep the demo readable; real pools are often 10–50). Connections are opened lazily, reused, reset when returned (any open transaction is rolled back), validated when borrowed (a dropped connection is thrown away), and callers who can't get one within 100 ms get a clear error rather than hanging.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant S as Transfer request participant P as ConnectionPool participant Q as Idle queue participant D as Database S->>P: acquire(100 ms) P->>Q: poll() alt idle connection available Q-->>P: conn#1 (validate) else below max P->>D: open new connection else pool exhausted P->>Q: poll(100 ms) Q-->>P: timeout P-->>S: TimeoutException end S->>D: queries... S->>P: lease.close() P->>P: reset() then back to idle queue

Full Code:

ConnectionPool.javaDbConnection.javaBankingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.banking;

import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class ConnectionPool {

    private final BlockingQueue<DbConnection> idle; // (1)!
    private final AtomicInteger created = new AtomicInteger();
    private final int maxSize;

    public ConnectionPool(int maxSize) {
        this.maxSize = maxSize;
        this.idle = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(maxSize);
    }

    /** A borrowed connection. Closing the lease returns it to the pool. */
    public final class Lease implements AutoCloseable { // (2)!
        private final DbConnection connection;
        private boolean returned;

        private Lease(DbConnection connection) {
            this.connection = connection;
        }

        public DbConnection connection() {
            return connection;
        }

        @Override
        public void close() {
            if (!returned) {
                returned = true;
                release(connection);
            }
        }
    }

    public Lease acquire(long timeoutMs) throws InterruptedException, TimeoutException {
        DbConnection c = idle.poll();
        while (c != null && !c.isValid()) { // (3)!
            System.out.println("  [pool] evicting broken connection #" + c.id());
            created.decrementAndGet();
            c = idle.poll();
        }
        if (c == null && created.incrementAndGet() <= maxSize) { // (4)!
            c = new DbConnection();
        } else if (c == null) {
            created.decrementAndGet();
            c = idle.poll(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // (5)!
            if (c == null) {
                throw new TimeoutException("No connection available within " + timeoutMs + " ms (max " + maxSize + ")");
            }
        }
        return new Lease(c);
    }

    private void release(DbConnection c) {
        c.reset(); // (6)!
        idle.offer(c);
    }

    public String stats() {
        return "created=%d idle=%d max=%d".formatted(created.get(), idle.size(), maxSize);
    }
}
  1. A bounded BlockingQueue holds idle connections. It's thread-safe and supports "wait up to N ms", which is all a pool needs.
  2. The lease implements AutoCloseable, so try (var lease = pool.acquire(..)) returns the connection even if the code throws. Leaked connections are the most common pool bug. The returned flag makes double-close harmless.
  3. Validate on borrow. A connection broken by a network drop is evicted and its slot freed.
  4. Lazy creation, bounded by maxSize. The atomic counter makes "check and reserve a slot" a single step, so two threads can't both create the last connection.
  5. At the limit, wait for a connection to come back, but only for timeoutMs. This is the pool's back-pressure.
  6. Reset on release. The next borrower must never inherit an open transaction, session variables or a different schema.
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.banking;

/** Stand-in for a real JDBC connection: expensive to open, can break. */
public class DbConnection {

    private static int opened = 0;

    private final int id;
    private boolean broken;
    private boolean inTransaction;

    DbConnection() {
        this.id = ++opened;
        System.out.println("  [db] opening connection #" + id + " (TCP + TLS + auth, ~50 ms)");
    }

    public int id() { return id; }

    public String query(String sql) {
        inTransaction = sql.startsWith("BEGIN") || inTransaction;
        return "conn#" + id + " ran: " + sql;
    }

    boolean isValid() { return !broken; }

    void reset() { inTransaction = false; } // roll back anything left open

    boolean inTransaction() { return inTransaction; }

    void simulateNetworkDrop() { broken = true; }

    void close() { System.out.println("  [db] closing connection #" + id); }
}

package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.banking;

import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;

public class BankingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Connection Pool for the Ledger Service ===");
        ConnectionPool pool = new ConnectionPool(2);

        try (var lease = pool.acquire(100)) {
            System.out.println(lease.connection().query("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1"));
        }
        try (var lease = pool.acquire(100)) {
            System.out.println(lease.connection().query("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=2") + "  <- reused");
        }
        System.out.println("Stats: " + pool.stats());

        System.out.println("-- two transfers at once, then a third request --");
        var a = pool.acquire(100);
        var b = pool.acquire(100);
        System.out.println(a.connection().query("BEGIN; UPDATE accounts ..."));
        System.out.println(b.connection().query("BEGIN; UPDATE accounts ..."));
        try {
            pool.acquire(100);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            System.out.println("Third request: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        a.close();
        System.out.println("Returned connection reset (no open transaction)? " + !a.connection().inTransaction());
        b.connection().simulateNetworkDrop();
        b.close();

        System.out.println("-- after a network drop --");
        try (var lease = pool.acquire(100)) {
            System.out.println(lease.connection().query("SELECT 1"));
        }
        try (var lease1 = pool.acquire(100); var lease2 = pool.acquire(100)) {
            System.out.println("Healthy pair: #" + lease1.connection().id() + " and #" + lease2.connection().id());
        }
        System.out.println("Stats: " + pool.stats());
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Connection Pool for the Ledger Service ===
  [db] opening connection #1 (TCP + TLS + auth, ~50 ms)
conn#1 ran: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1
conn#1 ran: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=2  <- reused
Stats: created=1 idle=1 max=2
-- two transfers at once, then a third request --
  [db] opening connection #2 (TCP + TLS + auth, ~50 ms)
conn#1 ran: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts ...
conn#2 ran: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts ...
Third request: No connection available within 100 ms (max 2)
Returned connection reset (no open transaction)? true
-- after a network drop --
conn#1 ran: SELECT 1
  [pool] evicting broken connection #2
  [db] opening connection #3 (TCP + TLS + auth, ~50 ms)
Healthy pair: #1 and #3
Stats: created=2 idle=2 max=2

Follow the connection IDs: #1 is opened once and reused; #2 is opened only when two transfers overlap; the third request times out instead of overloading the database; and the broken #2 is evicted and replaced by #3.

Why Object Pool here:

  • Connections are expensive to create and limited by the database.
  • The pool provides reuse, a hard concurrency limit, health checks and clean state, all in one place.
  • In production you'd use HikariCP (Spring Boot's default), which does all of this and much more. This example shows what it does internally.

docs.title: Example 2: Pre-Warmed Transcoder Workers (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: A video platform transcodes every upload into several resolutions. A transcoder loads codec libraries and allocates GPU memory on start-up, which is slow, and the machine's GPU can only run 3 at once. Uploads arrive in bursts (here, 30 at once, each handled on its own virtual thread). The pool is pre-warmed with 3 transcoders at start-up, so no upload pays the start-up cost and the GPU is never oversubscribed.

Design:

flowchart LR U1[upload-1] --> P U2[upload-2] --> P U3[...] --> P U30[upload-30] --> P subgraph P[TranscoderPool, size 3] T1[Transcoder 1] T2[Transcoder 2] T3[Transcoder 3] end P --> GPU[(GPU)]

Full Code:

TranscoderPool.javaTranscoder.javaStreamingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.streaming;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Fixed-size, pre-warmed pool: all workers are created up front. */
public class TranscoderPool {

    private final BlockingQueue<Transcoder> available;
    private final List<Transcoder> all = new ArrayList<>();
    private final AtomicInteger inUse = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger peakInUse = new AtomicInteger();

    public TranscoderPool(int size) {
        available = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(size);
        for (int i = 1; i <= size; i++) { // (1)!
            Transcoder t = new Transcoder(i);
            all.add(t);
            available.add(t);
        }
    }

    public void run(String video) throws InterruptedException {
        Transcoder t = available.take(); // (2)!
        peakInUse.accumulateAndGet(inUse.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
        try {
            t.transcode(video);
        } finally {
            inUse.decrementAndGet();
            available.put(t); // (3)!
        }
    }

    public int created() { return all.size(); }

    public int peakInUse() { return peakInUse.get(); }

    public int totalJobs() { return all.stream().mapToInt(Transcoder::jobsDone).sum(); }
}
  1. Eager (pre-warmed) creation: pay the cost at start-up, never during a request. Good when the objects are always needed and slow to create.
  2. take() blocks until a transcoder is free. With virtual threads, blocking is cheap: 27 waiting uploads cost almost nothing.
  3. Returned in finally, so a failed transcode never loses a worker.
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.streaming;

/** Expensive worker: loads codecs and allocates GPU buffers on creation. */
public class Transcoder {

    private final int id;
    private int jobsDone;

    public Transcoder(int id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    public void transcode(String video) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(20); // stand-in for real encoding work
        jobsDone++;
    }

    public int id() { return id; }

    public int jobsDone() { return jobsDone; }
}

package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.streaming;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class StreamingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Transcoding Uploads with 3 Pooled Workers ===");
        TranscoderPool pool = new TranscoderPool(3);

        try (ExecutorService uploads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 30; i++) {
                String video = "upload-" + i + ".mp4";
                uploads.submit(() -> {
                    pool.run(video);
                    return null;
                });
            }
        } // waits for all 30 uploads

        System.out.println("Uploads transcoded : " + pool.totalJobs());
        System.out.println("Transcoders created: " + pool.created());
        System.out.println("Never more than 3 busy at once: " + (pool.peakInUse() <= 3));
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Transcoding Uploads with 3 Pooled Workers ===
Uploads transcoded : 30
Transcoders created: 3
Never more than 3 busy at once: true

30 uploads, 3 transcoders, never more than 3 busy at once. The pool turned a burst into an orderly queue.

Why Object Pool here:

  • Workers are expensive to start and the hardware allows only a fixed number.
  • The pool doubles as a concurrency limiter: it's the GPU's admission control.
  • Virtual threads + a pool is a clean modern combination: threads are cheap, so you limit the resource, not the threads.

docs.title: Example 3: Licensed GDS Sessions with a Refresh Policy (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: An online travel agency searches fares through an airline Global Distribution System (GDS) such as Amadeus or Sabre. Each session requires a slow login, and the contract licenses only 2 concurrent sessions. Sessions also go stale, so the provider recommends logging out and back in after a number of uses. The pool reuses sessions, enforces the licence limit, and retires a session after 3 uses (like HikariCP's maxLifetime).

Design:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> LoggedIn : login (licence taken) LoggedIn --> Searching : borrow Searching --> LoggedIn : give back (uses < 3) Searching --> LoggedOut : give back (uses = 3) LoggedOut --> [*] : licence freed

Full Code:

GdsSessionPool.javaGdsSession.javaTravelDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.travel;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Pool with a "max uses" refresh policy, like connection max-lifetime settings. */
public class GdsSessionPool {

    private final int licences;
    private final int maxUsesPerSession;
    private final Deque<GdsSession> idle = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private int live;
    private int nextId = 1;

    public GdsSessionPool(int licences, int maxUsesPerSession) {
        this.licences = licences;
        this.maxUsesPerSession = maxUsesPerSession;
    }

    public <T> T withSession(Function<GdsSession, T> work) { // (1)!
        GdsSession s = borrow();
        try {
            return work.apply(s);
        } finally {
            giveBack(s);
        }
    }

    private synchronized GdsSession borrow() {
        if (!idle.isEmpty()) {
            return idle.pop();
        }
        if (live == licences) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("All " + licences + " GDS licences in use");
        }
        live++;
        return new GdsSession("S" + nextId++);
    }

    private synchronized void giveBack(GdsSession s) {
        if (s.uses() >= maxUsesPerSession) { // (2)!
            s.logout();
            live--;
        } else {
            idle.push(s);
        }
    }
}
  1. withSession(work) is the "execute around" idiom: the pool borrows, runs your code and always gives back. Callers can't forget to return a session. Only borrow and giveBack are synchronized, so the slow search itself runs without holding the lock.
  2. Retirement policy: sessions that hit the use limit are logged out instead of being reused, which frees the licence for a fresh login.
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.travel;

/**
 * A session with an airline Global Distribution System. Logging in is slow and the
 * airline licenses only a fixed number of concurrent sessions.
 */
public class GdsSession {

    private final String id;
    private int uses;

    GdsSession(String id) {
        this.id = id;
        System.out.println("  [gds] login " + id + " (2 s handshake, uses 1 licence)");
    }

    public String search(String route) {
        uses++;
        return id + " fares " + route + " (use " + uses + ")";
    }

    String id() { return id; }

    int uses() { return uses; }

    void logout() {
        System.out.println("  [gds] logout " + id + " after " + uses + " uses (refresh policy)");
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.objectpool.travel;

import java.util.List;

public class TravelDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: Licensed GDS Session Pool (2 licences, refresh after 3 uses) ===");
        GdsSessionPool pool = new GdsSessionPool(2, 3);

        for (String route : List.of("BLR-DEL", "DEL-DXB", "BOM-LHR", "MAA-SIN", "HYD-BKK")) {
            String fares = pool.withSession(s -> s.search(route));
            System.out.println(fares);
        }

        System.out.println("-- a long search holds a session while another request arrives --");
        String nested = pool.withSession(outer -> {
            String first = outer.search("CCU-NRT");
            String second = pool.withSession(inner -> inner.search("GOI-DOH"));
            return first + " | " + second;
        });
        System.out.println(nested);
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: Licensed GDS Session Pool (2 licences, refresh after 3 uses) ===
  [gds] login S1 (2 s handshake, uses 1 licence)
S1 fares BLR-DEL (use 1)
S1 fares DEL-DXB (use 2)
  [gds] logout S1 after 3 uses (refresh policy)
S1 fares BOM-LHR (use 3)
  [gds] login S2 (2 s handshake, uses 1 licence)
S2 fares MAA-SIN (use 1)
S2 fares HYD-BKK (use 2)
-- a long search holds a session while another request arrives --
  [gds] login S3 (2 s handshake, uses 1 licence)
  [gds] logout S2 after 3 uses (refresh policy)
S2 fares CCU-NRT (use 3) | S3 fares GOI-DOH (use 1)

S1 serves 3 searches and is retired (its logout line prints before the third result because giveBack runs before the result is printed). The nested search shows two sessions in use at once: S2 for the outer search and a fresh login S3 for the inner one.

Why Object Pool here:

  • Sessions are slow to create and contractually limited: the pool enforces the licence.
  • Retirement keeps sessions fresh without callers knowing.
  • Execute-around makes leaks impossible by design.
Unit Tests: ObjectPoolTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.creational.objectpool;

import com.handbook.creational.objectpool.banking.ConnectionPool;
import com.handbook.creational.objectpool.generic.ObjectPool;
import com.handbook.creational.objectpool.streaming.TranscoderPool;
import com.handbook.creational.objectpool.travel.GdsSessionPool;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ObjectPoolTest {

    @Test
    void connectionPoolReusesAndLimits() throws Exception {
        ConnectionPool pool = new ConnectionPool(1);
        int firstId;
        try (var lease = pool.acquire(10)) {
            firstId = lease.connection().id();
        }
        try (var lease = pool.acquire(10)) {
            assertThat(lease.connection().id()).isEqualTo(firstId);
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> pool.acquire(10)).isInstanceOf(TimeoutException.class);
        }
    }

    @Test
    void leaseCanBeClosedTwiceSafely() throws Exception {
        ConnectionPool pool = new ConnectionPool(1);
        var lease = pool.acquire(10);
        lease.close();
        lease.close();
        assertThat(pool.stats()).contains("idle=1");
    }

    @Test
    void transcoderPoolNeverExceedsItsSize() {
        TranscoderPool pool = new TranscoderPool(2);
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> { pool.run("v"); return null; });
            }
        }
        assertThat(pool.totalJobs()).isEqualTo(10);
        assertThat(pool.peakInUse()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);
    }

    @Test
    void gdsPoolRejectsBeyondLicences() {
        GdsSessionPool pool = new GdsSessionPool(1, 10);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> pool.withSession(a -> pool.withSession(b -> "x")))
                .hasMessageContaining("licences");
    }

    @Test
    void genericPoolValidatesAndResets() throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger created = new AtomicInteger();
        ObjectPool<StringBuilder> pool = new ObjectPool<>(1,
                () -> { created.incrementAndGet(); return new StringBuilder(); },
                sb -> !sb.toString().equals("broken"), sb -> {});
        StringBuilder sb = pool.borrow(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        sb.append("broken");
        pool.giveBack(sb);
        pool.borrow(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // broken one is discarded
        assertThat(created).hasValue(2);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Variation Notes Lazy vs. eager (pre-warmed) Lazy saves resources at low load; eager avoids first-request latency (minimumIdle in HikariCP) Validate on borrow / on return / in the background Borrow-time checks are safest; background checks keep borrow fast Max lifetime / max uses / idle timeout Retire objects before infrastructure (firewalls, load balancers) kills them silently Lease objects (AutoCloseable) try-with-resources guarantees release Execute-around (withX(work)) The pool controls the whole borrow/use/return cycle Semaphore-limited pools (challenge) A Semaphore enforces the maximum, and a queue holds idle objects

Virtual threads change the thread-pool story, not the resource-pool story

With Java 21 virtual threads you should stop pooling threads (create one per task; they're cheap). But you still pool the resources those threads use: database connections, HTTP connections, GPU workers. If anything, virtual threads make resource pools more important, because a million cheap threads can easily overwhelm a database. Use pools or Semaphores to cap concurrent access.

Don't pool cheap objects. Pooling ordinary objects (DTOs, small buffers) to "help the GC" was common advice in the early 2000s. Modern JVM allocation is a pointer bump, and young-generation GC is extremely efficient. Pools add contention, complexity, and bugs (stale state, leaks). Pool only when creation is expensive (I/O, native memory) or the count must be limited.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Pooled resource HikariCP (Spring Boot default), Apache DBCP, c3p0 JDBC connections Apache HttpClient PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager, OkHttp ConnectionPool, JDK HttpClient HTTP keep-alive connections Netty PooledByteBufAllocator Direct (off-heap) byte buffers Lettuce / Jedis (JedisPool) Redis connections Apache Commons Pool 2 GenericObjectPool Anything; the general-purpose pool library java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor Platform threads (see Thread Pool in the Concurrency section) Jakarta EE Stateless EJB pools, JCA connection pools JDK Integer.valueOf(-128..127) cache (a fixed pool of immutable objects; really Flyweight)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Removes expensive creation from the request path Leaks: a borrower that doesn't return an object shrinks the pool forever Bounds concurrency to what the downstream can handle Stale state: forgetting to reset leaks data between borrowers Back-pressure with timeouts instead of overload Contention: the pool becomes a bottleneck if it's too small Central place for health checks and retirement Sizing is hard: too small means waiting, too big overloads the downstream Pointless (and harmful) for cheap objects

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Connection leaks

A code path that forgets to release (an exception before close()) slowly drains the pool until every request times out. Always use try-with-resources or execute-around. Turn on leak detection (HikariCP's leakDetectionThreshold).

Not resetting state

A connection returned mid-transaction, or with SET search_path changed, poisons the next borrower. Reset on release (Example 1) and validate on borrow.

Holding a pooled object during slow work

Borrowing a DB connection, then calling a slow external API before running the query, keeps the connection idle-but-taken. Acquire late, release early.

Pool size = thread count

"200 Tomcat threads, so 200 DB connections" overloads most databases. A common starting point for HikariCP is connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count, which is often 10–20, not hundreds. Measure.

Waiting forever

take() without a timeout turns a downstream outage into a thread pile-up. Always bound the wait (connectionTimeout) and fail fast.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Sizing with Little's Law. Average connections in use = throughput × average time holding a connection. At 1,000 requests/s with each request holding a connection for 5 ms, you need about 5 connections on average; add headroom for bursts (say 10–15). If the math says you need 200, the fix is usually shorter hold times (better queries, release earlier), not a bigger pool.

Fleet-wide limits. A pool of 20 in each of 50 pods means 1,000 connections to one database. Pool sizing is a system-level decision: sum over all instances, or put a proxy in front (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) that multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections.

Observability. Export pool metrics (HikariCP exposes them to Micrometer): active, idle, pending threads, acquire-time percentiles, timeouts. Alert on pending > 0 for minutes and acquire p99 rising, which are early warnings before timeouts.

Bulkheads. Separate pools per downstream or per workload (critical payments vs. reporting queries) so one slow dependency can't drain the pool everyone needs. This is the Bulkhead pattern, covered in the microservices section.

Retirement matters. Firewalls and cloud load balancers silently drop idle TCP connections (often after 350 s on AWS NLBs). Set the pool's max lifetime and idle timeout below infrastructure timeouts, or borrowers get dead connections.

War story: Black Friday and the 30-second hang

An e-commerce checkout called a fraud-scoring API while holding a database connection (it opened a transaction, called fraud, then wrote the order). On Black Friday the fraud API slowed from 50 ms to 4 s. Every checkout thread held a connection for 4 s, the pool of 30 drained in under a second, and connectionTimeout was the default 30 seconds, so threads piled up waiting. The whole site, including product pages that only needed a quick read, timed out. Fix: moved the fraud call before acquiring the connection; set connectionTimeout to 2 s with a clear error; split pools for checkout and catalogue reads (a bulkhead); added an alert on pending connection requests. Lesson: the pool reflects how you use it. Hold time drives everything, so acquire late and release early.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Object Pool Flyweight Singleton Prototype Objects Many, reusable, mutable while borrowed Many, shared, immutable One Many copies Exclusive use? Yes: one borrower at a time No: shared by everyone at once No Each copy is its own Purpose Avoid expensive creation, limit count Save memory One global instance Avoid expensive setup Example DB connections Integer.valueOf cache, glyphs Config Templates

Related: Thread Pool (a pool of workers), Bulkhead (separate pools to isolate failures), Factory Method (the pool's create step), Proxy (a pooled connection's close() often returns it to the pool instead of closing it; HikariCP wraps connections in a proxy to do exactly that).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Borrow, use, return expensive or limited objects instead of creating them per request.
  • Bounded (max size), validated (on borrow), reset (on return), timeouts (never wait forever).
  • Prevent leaks with try-with-resources or execute-around.
  • Size with Little's Law and think fleet-wide; hold time matters more than pool size.
  • Don't pool cheap objects. With virtual threads, pool resources, not threads.
try (var lease = pool.acquire(100)) { lease.connection().query("SELECT 1"); } // auto-returned

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add leak detection to ConnectionPool: log a warning if a lease isn't closed within 1 second.
  • Add an idle timeout to GdsSessionPool (log out sessions unused for N seconds).
  • Replace ConnectionPool with HikariCP in a Spring Boot app and look at its metrics in /actuator/metrics.
  • Load-test TranscoderPool with sizes 1–6 and plot throughput against pool size.

Prototype Next: Structural Patterns

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing, already-configured object instead of building from scratch. Use it when setting up an object is expensive or complex, and most new objects are "the same as that one, with small changes". The hard part is deep vs. shallow copy.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a hospital's "Complete Blood Count" report has a fixed list of tests and reference ranges, loaded from a slow master-data service. Every patient gets one. Rebuilding it from scratch for each patient is slow and repetitive. Copying a ready-made template and filling in the patient details is fast and simple, as long as the copy doesn't share anything mutable with the template.

Formal definition (GoF):

Specify the kinds of objects to create using a prototypical instance, and create new objects by copying this prototype.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Photocopying a form

A clinic doesn't typeset a new intake form for each patient. It keeps one master copy and photocopies it. Each patient writes on their copy. If the clinic instead handed everyone the same sheet of paper (a shallow copy), every patient would be writing on top of each other.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class Prototype { <<interface>> +copy() Prototype } class ConcretePrototype { -fields +ConcretePrototype(ConcretePrototype source) +copy() ConcretePrototype } class PrototypeRegistry { -Map~String, Prototype~ templates +newInstance(key) Prototype } class Client Prototype <|.. ConcretePrototype PrototypeRegistry o-- Prototype Client ..> PrototypeRegistry : newInstance("CBC") Client ..> Prototype : copy() Participant Responsibility Prototype Declares the copy operation (copy(), or a copy constructor) ConcretePrototype Copies itself correctly, deep-copying mutable parts Registry (optional) Stores named, pre-configured prototypes and hands out copies Client Asks for a copy and customizes it

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// Rebuilding the template for every patient
LabReport report = new LabReport("Complete Blood Count",
        masterData.loadTests("CBC"));        // slow remote call, every time

// ...or "reusing" the template directly
LabReport report = templates.get("CBC");    // NOT a copy!
report.record("WBC", "6.1");                // every future patient now sees WBC=6.1

What goes wrong:

  • Repeated expensive setup. The same data is loaded and assembled again and again.
  • Shared mutable state. Handing out the template itself (or a shallow copy) leaks one patient's data into the next report, a serious privacy incident in healthcare.

docs.title: Example 1: Lab Reports from Templates (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital lab runs thousands of panels a day: blood counts, lipid profiles and so on. Each panel has a fixed set of tests and reference ranges that come from a master-data service. When a sample arrives, a technician needs a fresh report for that patient. The templates are loaded once into a registry; each new report is a deep copy, so results for one patient can never appear on another's report.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant T as Technician UI participant R as ReportTemplateRegistry participant P as CBC template participant C as Copy for P-1001 T->>R: newReport("CBC") R->>P: copy() P->>C: new LabReport(this): deep-copies each TestResult R-->>T: fresh report T->>C: forPatient("P-1001").record("WBC", "6.1") Note over P: Template still says WBC=pending

Full Code:

LabReport.javaReportTemplateRegistry.javaLabDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.healthcare;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** A lab report. Templates are configured once and copied for each patient. */
public class LabReport {

    public static final class TestResult {
        private final String test;
        private final String referenceRange;
        private String value = "pending";

        public TestResult(String test, String referenceRange) {
            this.test = test;
            this.referenceRange = referenceRange;
        }

        TestResult(TestResult other) { // copy constructor
            this(other.test, other.referenceRange);
            this.value = other.value;
        }

        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return "%s=%s (ref %s)".formatted(test, value, referenceRange);
        }
    }

    private final String panel;
    private final List<TestResult> results;
    private String patientId = "-";

    public LabReport(String panel, List<TestResult> results) {
        this.panel = panel;
        this.results = new ArrayList<>(results);
    }

    private LabReport(LabReport source) { // (1)!
        this.panel = source.panel;
        this.patientId = source.patientId;
        this.results = new ArrayList<>();
        for (TestResult r : source.results) {
            this.results.add(new TestResult(r)); // (2)!
        }
    }

    public LabReport copy() { // (3)!
        return new LabReport(this);
    }

    public LabReport forPatient(String patientId) {
        this.patientId = patientId;
        return this;
    }

    public LabReport record(String test, String value) {
        results.stream().filter(r -> r.test.equals(test)).findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Test not in panel: " + test))
                .value = value;
        return this;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "%s [%s] %s".formatted(panel, patientId, results);
    }
}
  1. A private copy constructor does the real work. Making it private keeps copy() as the one public way to clone.
  2. Deep copy: each TestResult is mutable (its value changes), so each one is copied. Copying only the list would leave both reports pointing at the same TestResult objects.
  3. copy() returns the concrete type, so callers don't need a cast (unlike Object.clone()).
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.healthcare;

import com.handbook.creational.prototype.healthcare.LabReport.TestResult;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Prototype registry: configured templates by name; callers always get a copy. */
public class ReportTemplateRegistry {

    private final Map<String, LabReport> templates = new HashMap<>();

    public ReportTemplateRegistry() {
        // Imagine these coming from a slow master-data service; it happens once.
        templates.put("CBC", new LabReport("Complete Blood Count", List.of(
                new TestResult("Hemoglobin", "13.5-17.5 g/dL"),
                new TestResult("WBC", "4.5-11.0 x10^9/L"),
                new TestResult("Platelets", "150-450 x10^9/L"))));
        templates.put("LIPID", new LabReport("Lipid Profile", List.of(
                new TestResult("LDL", "<100 mg/dL"),
                new TestResult("HDL", ">40 mg/dL"))));
    }

    public LabReport newReport(String code) {
        LabReport template = templates.get(code);
        if (template == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown panel " + code);
        }
        return template.copy(); // (1)!
    }

    public String template(String code) {
        return templates.get(code).toString();
    }
}
  1. The registry never returns the template itself, only a copy.
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.healthcare;

public class LabDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital Lab: Reports from Templates ===");
        ReportTemplateRegistry registry = new ReportTemplateRegistry();

        LabReport asha = registry.newReport("CBC").forPatient("P-1001")
                .record("Hemoglobin", "14.2").record("WBC", "6.1");
        LabReport vikram = registry.newReport("CBC").forPatient("P-1002")
                .record("Hemoglobin", "11.9");
        LabReport lipid = registry.newReport("LIPID").forPatient("P-1001")
                .record("LDL", "132");

        System.out.println(asha);
        System.out.println(vikram);
        System.out.println(lipid);
        System.out.println("Template untouched: " + registry.template("CBC"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital Lab: Reports from Templates ===
Complete Blood Count [P-1001] [Hemoglobin=14.2 (ref 13.5-17.5 g/dL), WBC=6.1 (ref 4.5-11.0 x10^9/L), Platelets=pending (ref 150-450 x10^9/L)]
Complete Blood Count [P-1002] [Hemoglobin=11.9 (ref 13.5-17.5 g/dL), WBC=pending (ref 4.5-11.0 x10^9/L), Platelets=pending (ref 150-450 x10^9/L)]
Lipid Profile [P-1001] [LDL=132 (ref <100 mg/dL), HDL=pending (ref >40 mg/dL)]
Template untouched: Complete Blood Count [-] [Hemoglobin=pending (ref 13.5-17.5 g/dL), WBC=pending (ref 4.5-11.0 x10^9/L), Platelets=pending (ref 150-450 x10^9/L)]

Why Prototype here:

  • Templates are expensive to assemble (master data) and cheap to copy.
  • The registry gives "named templates" that the lab can extend without code changes.
  • A deep copy guarantees patient data never leaks between reports.

docs.title: Example 2: Product Variants (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: A fashion marketplace lists a T-shirt in many sizes and colours. Each variant shares the title, long description, image gallery and most attributes, and differs only in SKU, size and sometimes price. Sellers upload one base listing; the catalogue service generates the variants by copying it and changing a few fields. Editing one variant (adding a size attribute) must never change the base listing or another variant.

Design:

flowchart LR B["Base listing<br/>title, description,<br/>3 images, material=cotton"] -->|"variant(S)"| S[TSHIRT-S-BLK] B -->|"variant(M)"| M[TSHIRT-M-BLK] B -->|"variant(XL, INR 649)"| XL[TSHIRT-XL-BLK]

Full Code:

ProductListing.javaFashionCatalogDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.ecommerce;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * A product listing with lots of shared data (description, images, attributes).
 * Variants (size/colour) are created by copying a base listing and changing a few fields.
 */
public class ProductListing {

    private String sku;
    private final String title;
    private final String description;
    private final List<String> imageUrls;
    private final Map<String, String> attributes;
    private int priceInr;

    public ProductListing(String sku, String title, String description,
                          List<String> imageUrls, Map<String, String> attributes, int priceInr) {
        this.sku = sku;
        this.title = title;
        this.description = description;
        this.imageUrls = new ArrayList<>(imageUrls);
        this.attributes = new LinkedHashMap<>(attributes);
        this.priceInr = priceInr;
    }

    /** Copy constructor: the preferred way to implement Prototype in Java. */
    public ProductListing(ProductListing other) { // (1)!
        this(other.sku, other.title, other.description,
                other.imageUrls, other.attributes, other.priceInr); // (2)!
    }

    public ProductListing variant(String sku, String attribute, String value, int priceInr) {
        ProductListing copy = new ProductListing(this);
        copy.sku = sku;
        copy.attributes.put(attribute, value);
        copy.priceInr = priceInr;
        return copy;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "%-12s %-18s INR %4d %s images=%d".formatted(sku, title, priceInr, attributes, imageUrls.size());
    }
}
  1. A public copy constructor is the idiomatic Java Prototype (Effective Java, Item 13 recommends it over clone()): explicit, type-safe, works with final fields, and doesn't need Cloneable.
  2. It delegates to the main constructor, which already makes defensive copies of the list and map. Strings and int are immutable, so sharing them is safe.
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.ecommerce;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class FashionCatalogDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: T-shirt Variants from One Base Listing ===");
        ProductListing base = new ProductListing("TSHIRT-BASE", "Organic Cotton Tee",
                "Soft, breathable, 180 GSM organic cotton.",
                List.of("front.jpg", "back.jpg", "fabric.jpg"),
                Map.of("material", "cotton"), 599);

        List<ProductListing> variants = List.of(
                base.variant("TSHIRT-S-BLK", "size", "S", 599),
                base.variant("TSHIRT-M-BLK", "size", "M", 599),
                base.variant("TSHIRT-XL-BLK", "size", "XL", 649));

        variants.forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("Base listing unchanged: " + base);
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: T-shirt Variants from One Base Listing ===
TSHIRT-S-BLK Organic Cotton Tee INR  599 {material=cotton, size=S} images=3
TSHIRT-M-BLK Organic Cotton Tee INR  599 {material=cotton, size=M} images=3
TSHIRT-XL-BLK Organic Cotton Tee INR  649 {material=cotton, size=XL} images=3
Base listing unchanged: TSHIRT-BASE  Organic Cotton Tee INR  599 {material=cotton} images=3

Why Prototype here:

  • Variants are "the base, plus a few changes", which is exactly what copying expresses.
  • Adding size to a variant's attributes doesn't affect the base, because each copy has its own map.
  • Sellers manage one listing; the system generates the rest.

docs.title: Example 3: Workspace Templates and the Shallow-Copy Bug (SaaS)
docs.text:
Scenario: A project-management SaaS (Jira/Asana-style) lets companies define board templates, such as "Product Launch" with standard columns and starter tasks. When a team starts a launch, it gets its own board copied from the template and adds team-specific tasks. A real incident at a company like this: a "copy" shared its column lists with the template, so one team's tasks appeared in every board created afterwards. This example shows the correct deep copy and reproduces the bug.

Design:

flowchart TB subgraph Deep["Deep copy (correct)"] T1[Template] --> L1[To Do list A] C1[Team copy] --> L2[To Do list B] end subgraph Shallow["Shallow copy (bug)"] T2[Template] --> L3[To Do list A] C2[Team copy] --> L3 end

Full Code:

Board.javaTask.javaWorkspaceDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.saas;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Workspace board: columns of tasks. Deep-copied when a team uses a template. */
public class Board {

    private final String name;
    private final Map<String, List<Task>> columns = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    public Board(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public Board column(String column, Task... tasks) {
        columns.put(column, new ArrayList<>(List.of(tasks)));
        return this;
    }

    public Board addTask(String column, Task task) {
        columns.get(column).add(task);
        return this;
    }

    /** Deep copy of the mutable structure; tasks are immutable so they are shared. */
    public Board copyAs(String newName) {
        Board copy = new Board(newName);
        columns.forEach((col, tasks) -> copy.columns.put(col, new ArrayList<>(tasks))); // (1)!
        return copy;
    }

    /** The bug we are protecting against: a shallow copy shares the column lists. */
    public Board shallowCopyAs(String newName) {
        Board copy = new Board(newName);
        copy.columns.putAll(columns); // (2)!
        return copy;
    }

    public int taskCount() {
        return columns.values().stream().mapToInt(List::size).sum();
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(name).append(" (").append(taskCount()).append(" tasks)");
        columns.forEach((col, tasks) -> sb.append("\n  ").append(col).append(": ")
                .append(tasks.stream().map(Task::title).toList()));
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
  1. New list for each column. The Task objects inside are immutable records, so they can safely be shared. Deep-copy what's mutable, share what's immutable.
  2. putAll copies the map, but the values are the same list objects, so adding a task to the copy also adds it to the template.
package com.handbook.creational.prototype.saas;

/** Immutable leaf: safe to share between copies, no need to clone. */
public record Task(String title, String assigneeRole) {
}

package com.handbook.creational.prototype.saas;

public class WorkspaceDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS: New Team Workspaces from a Template ===");
        Board template = new Board("Template: Product Launch")
                .column("To Do", new Task("Write PRD", "PM"), new Task("Threat model", "Security"))
                .column("Doing")
                .column("Done");

        Board payments = template.copyAs("Payments Team Launch")
                .addTask("To Do", new Task("PCI checklist", "Compliance"));
        Board search = template.copyAs("Search Team Launch");

        System.out.println(payments);
        System.out.println(search);
        System.out.println("Template still has " + template.taskCount() + " tasks");

        System.out.println("--- with a shallow copy (the bug) ---");
        Board buggy = template.shallowCopyAs("Buggy Team Launch")
                .addTask("To Do", new Task("Team-only task", "Dev"));
        System.out.println("Template now has " + template.taskCount() + " tasks (leaked from " + buggy.taskCount() + "-task copy)");
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS: New Team Workspaces from a Template ===
Payments Team Launch (3 tasks)
  To Do: [Write PRD, Threat model, PCI checklist]
  Doing: []
  Done: []
Search Team Launch (2 tasks)
  To Do: [Write PRD, Threat model]
  Doing: []
  Done: []
Template still has 2 tasks
--- with a shallow copy (the bug) ---
Template now has 3 tasks (leaked from 3-task copy)

The last line shows the bug: the template went from 2 to 3 tasks because the shallow copy shared its lists.

Why Prototype here:

  • Templates are complex nested structures that users configure through the UI, so there's no code that could "build" them from scratch.
  • Copying preserves exactly what the admin configured.
  • The example makes the depth of the copy visible, which is the one thing that decides whether Prototype is safe.
Unit Tests: PrototypeTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.creational.prototype;

import com.handbook.creational.prototype.cart.Cart;
import com.handbook.creational.prototype.ecommerce.ProductListing;
import com.handbook.creational.prototype.healthcare.ReportTemplateRegistry;
import com.handbook.creational.prototype.saas.Board;
import com.handbook.creational.prototype.saas.Task;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class PrototypeTest {

    @Test
    void registryHandsOutIndependentCopies() {
        ReportTemplateRegistry registry = new ReportTemplateRegistry();
        String before = registry.template("CBC");
        var a = registry.newReport("CBC").forPatient("A").record("WBC", "7.0");
        var b = registry.newReport("CBC").forPatient("B");
        assertThat(a).isNotSameAs(b);
        assertThat(a.toString()).contains("WBC=7.0");
        assertThat(b.toString()).contains("WBC=pending");
        assertThat(registry.template("CBC")).isEqualTo(before);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> registry.newReport("XRAY")).hasMessageContaining("Unknown panel");
    }

    @Test
    void variantsDoNotChangeTheBaseListing() {
        ProductListing base = new ProductListing("BASE", "Tee", "d", List.of("a.jpg"), Map.of("material", "cotton"), 100);
        String before = base.toString();
        ProductListing xl = base.variant("XL", "size", "XL", 120);
        assertThat(xl.toString()).contains("size=XL", "INR  120");
        assertThat(base.toString()).isEqualTo(before);
    }

    @Test
    void deepCopyIsIndependentButShallowCopyLeaks() {
        Board template = new Board("T").column("To Do", new Task("a", "PM"));
        template.copyAs("Deep").addTask("To Do", new Task("b", "Dev"));
        assertThat(template.taskCount()).isEqualTo(1);

        template.shallowCopyAs("Shallow").addTask("To Do", new Task("c", "Dev"));
        assertThat(template.taskCount()).isEqualTo(2); // documents the bug
    }

    @Test
    void cartCopyIsDeep() {
        Cart original = new Cart("C").add("MILK", 2);
        Cart copy = original.copy();
        copy.line(0).setQuantity(9);
        assertThat(original.toString()).isEqualTo("C [MILKx2]");
        assertThat(copy.toString()).isEqualTo("C [MILKx9]");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Technique Verdict Copy constructor new X(other) ✅ Preferred. Explicit, type-safe, works with final fields Static copy factory X.copyOf(other) ✅ Same benefits, and can return a subtype or cached instance copy() method (Example 1) ✅ Good when callers have only the interface type (polymorphic copy) Object.clone() + Cloneable ⚠️ Avoid in new code: shallow by default, bypasses constructors, checked CloneNotSupportedException, doesn't work with final fields Serialization round-trip ⚠️ Deep, but slow, and requires everything to be Serializable; fine in tests only Immutable objects (records) ✅ Often removes the need to copy at all. Share them, and use "withers" for changes

Immutability is the best Prototype. If TestResult were an immutable record and changes returned new instances, copying the list (or using List.copyOf) would be enough. Prefer immutable leaves and deep-copy only the mutable containers, as Example 3 does with Task.

Copying arrays and collections:

int[] a2 = a.clone();                 // arrays: clone() is fine (shallow for object arrays)
List<Item> l2 = new ArrayList<>(l);   // new list, SAME Item objects (shallow)
List<Item> l3 = l.stream().map(Item::copy).toList();  // deep
Map<K, List<V>> deep = new HashMap<>();
src.forEach((k, v) -> deep.put(k, new ArrayList<>(v))); // deep one level

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example JDK Object.clone() / Cloneable; ArrayList.clone(), HashMap.clone() (shallow); array clone() JDK Copy constructors: new ArrayList<>(collection), new HashMap<>(map), new String(chars) JDK List.copyOf, Map.copyOf, EnumSet.copyOf (static copy factories) Spring prototype bean scope: a new instance every time the bean is requested (named after this pattern, though it creates rather than copies) Spring BeanDefinition "parent" definitions: child beans inherit and override a template definition Jackson objectMapper.copy(), JsonNode.deepCopy() Others Protobuf message.toBuilder(), game engines cloning entity prefabs, document editors' "duplicate slide"

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Avoids repeating expensive setup (I/O, computation, configuration) Deep vs. shallow copy is easy to get wrong, and the bugs are subtle Create objects whose exact class you don't know (polymorphic copy()) Circular references make deep copies tricky Registry of templates is configurable at runtime, without new classes Every new mutable field must be added to the copy logic Works well with user-configured objects (templates, presets) clone() in Java is badly designed; you need to know the pitfalls

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Shallow copies of mutable fields

The single biggest Prototype bug (Example 3). Every mutable field (collections, arrays, Date, mutable objects) needs its own copy. Immutable fields (String, records, LocalDate) can be shared.

Handing out the prototype itself

A registry that returns templates.get(key) instead of templates.get(key).copy() makes every caller share one object.

clone() surprises

super.clone() copies fields bit for bit without running constructors, so final fields that need deep copies can't be reassigned, and invariants set up in constructors are skipped.

Forgetting new fields

Someone adds List<String> tags to the class and not to the copy constructor; now copies share tags. Guard it with a test that mutates every field of the copy and checks the original.

Copying identity

IDs, database keys, version numbers and audit timestamps usually must not be copied. Reset them in the copy (Example 1 resets nothing because patient ID is set right after; in real code, reset it in the copy constructor).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Copy semantics are part of the API contract. Document whether a copy is deep or shallow and which fields are reset (IDs, timestamps, version). In code review, look for every mutable field and ask "who else holds a reference to this?"

Prefer immutability over clever copying. Immutable value objects (records, List.copyOf) make sharing safe and copying trivial. In large systems the long-term fix for copy bugs is to make leaves immutable and keep mutation inside a few aggregate roots.

Copy-on-write and persistent data structures. For read-heavy shared state (configuration, routing tables), keep an immutable snapshot and replace it atomically on change: AtomicReference<Config> + build-new-then-swap. Readers never see a half-updated object and never need locks. CopyOnWriteArrayList does the same for lists.

Templates in multi-tenant SaaS. Store templates as data (JSON) and create instances by copying, while recording the template version in each copy. Later you can answer "which teams were created from v3 of the template?" and offer migrations.
