Performance. Copying is usually far cheaper than recreating objects that need I/O. For large object graphs, measure: a deep copy of a huge graph can be more expensive than rebuilding, and a lazy copy-on-write scheme may be better.

War story: one tenant's settings in another tenant's workspace

A B2B SaaS created new customer workspaces by copying a "default workspace" object held in memory. The copy constructor copied the Map<String, Object> of settings with new HashMap<>(settings), but some values were nested mutable maps (notification rules). When customer A edited their notification rules, the shared nested map changed, and every workspace created afterwards on that pod got A's rules, including A's internal email addresses. Fix: settings moved to immutable records; templates stored as JSON and deserialized for each new workspace; a test now mutates every field of a copy and asserts the template is unchanged. Lesson: "deep enough" isn't one level deep. Copy depth must match the depth of mutability.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Prototype Builder Factory Method Singleton Creates by Copying an existing object Step-by-step assembly Choosing a class Returning the one instance Best when Setup is expensive or user-configured Many optional parameters Type depends on input Exactly one instance needed Key risk Shallow-copy bugs Forgetting fields in toBuilder() Silent defaults Global mutable state

Shallow vs. deep copy, the classic interview table:

Shallow copy Deep copy Top-level object New New Primitive / immutable fields Copied (safe) Copied (safe) Mutable referenced objects Shared Copied recursively Cost Cheap Proportional to graph size Java default Object.clone(), new ArrayList<>(list) You write it

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Create by copying a configured object; great when setup is expensive.
  • Deep-copy mutable fields, share immutable ones. Shallow copies leak changes.
  • Prefer copy constructors / copy() over clone() + Cloneable.
  • Registry = named templates that always hand out copies.
  • Immutability is the best defence: immutable objects can be shared freely.
public LabReport copy() { return new LabReport(this); } // copy ctor deep-copies results

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Make LabReport.TestResult an immutable record and simplify the copy logic.
  • Add a tags list to ProductListing and write the "mutate every field" test first.
  • Add nested sub-tasks to Board and handle the deeper copy.
  • Implement copy() for a graph with cycles using an IdentityHashMap.

docs.title: Singleton
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🔴 Advanced Creational Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Singleton makes sure a class has exactly one instance and gives everyone a single global point of access to it. Use it for things that really are one-per-application, like configuration, an ID sequence or an audit trail. Prefer letting a DI container (Spring) manage the "one instance" rule whenever you can.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: some objects only make sense once. If two parts of your app each build their own configuration object, they might read different values. If two threads each create their own ID generator, they'll hand out duplicate IDs. If every service writes to its own audit log, auditors can't see one ordered trail.

Formal definition (GoF):

Ensure a class only has one instance, and provide a global point of access to it.

Two responsibilities:

  1. Control instantiation: nobody outside the class can call new.
  2. Provide access: a well-known way (getInstance() or INSTANCE) to reach the one object.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The country's President

A country has exactly one sitting President at a time. You don't "create" a new President when you need one; you go through a well-known channel (the President's office) and reach the same person everyone else reaches. The constitution (the private constructor) stops anyone from appointing a second one.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class Singleton { -static Singleton instance -Singleton() +static getInstance() Singleton +businessMethod() } class ClientA class ClientB ClientA ..> Singleton : getInstance() ClientB ..> Singleton : getInstance() Singleton --> Singleton : holds the only instance Participant Responsibility Singleton Holds the single instance in a static field, hides its constructor, exposes getInstance() Client Never calls new; always asks the class for the shared instance

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class ConfigLoader {
    private final Map<String, String> settings;

    public ConfigLoader() {                 // anyone can call new
        settings = loadFromDisk();          // expensive I/O every time
    }
    // ...
}

// Somewhere in CheckoutService
ConfigLoader cfg1 = new ConfigLoader();     // reads file
// Somewhere in DeliveryService
ConfigLoader cfg2 = new ConfigLoader();     // reads file AGAIN; may see a different version

What goes wrong:

  • Wasted work. The file or remote config is read over and over.
  • Inconsistent state. Two copies can disagree if the file changes between reads.
  • Broken invariants. With a counter (an ID generator), two instances means duplicate IDs.

And the "obvious" lazy fix isn't thread-safe:

public static ConfigLoader getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {          // two threads can both see null here...
        instance = new ConfigLoader(); // ...and both create an instance
    }
    return instance;
}

docs.title: 5. Three Real-World Examples
docs.text: Each example uses a different Singleton implementation, so by the end you'll have seen the three you should know for interviews: enum, holder idiom and double-checked locking.

docs.title: Example 1: Store Configuration (Grocery Delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery delivery app (think Blinkit/Instacart) has a checkout service and a delivery-slot service. Both need the same business settings: the delivery fee (INR 30), the free-delivery threshold (INR 499) and feature flags such as express delivery. Loading the settings is expensive (in production it's a call to a config server), and every service must see the same values. Otherwise the cart page and the checkout page could show different delivery fees, which leads straight to customer complaints.

Design:

classDiagram class StoreConfig { <<enumeration>> INSTANCE -Map~String,String~ settings +getInt(key) int +isEnabled(feature) boolean } class CheckoutService { +deliveryFee(subtotal) int +checkout(cartId, subtotal) String } class DeliverySlotService { +expressAvailable() boolean } CheckoutService --> StoreConfig : INSTANCE DeliverySlotService --> StoreConfig : INSTANCE

Full Code:

StoreConfig.javaCheckoutService.javaDeliverySlotService.javaGroceryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Application-wide store configuration, loaded exactly once.
 * The enum form is the simplest thread-safe Singleton in Java and is
 * immune to reflection and serialization attacks.
 */
public enum StoreConfig {
    INSTANCE; // (1)!

    private final Map<String, String> settings;

    StoreConfig() { // (2)!
        System.out.println("[StoreConfig] Loading configuration (runs once)...");
        // In production this would come from a file, Spring Cloud Config or a DB.
        this.settings = Map.of(
                "delivery.fee.inr", "30",
                "free.delivery.above.inr", "499",
                "feature.express.delivery", "true");
    }

    public int getInt(String key) {
        String value = settings.get(key);
        if (value == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown config key: " + key);
        }
        return Integer.parseInt(value);
    }

    public boolean isEnabled(String feature) {
        return Boolean.parseBoolean(settings.getOrDefault("feature." + feature, "false"));
    }
}
  1. An enum with one constant is a Singleton. The JVM guarantees that INSTANCE is created exactly once, lazily (on first access to the enum class) and thread-safely.
  2. Enum constructors are implicitly private. Reflection cannot call them: Constructor.newInstance throws IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

public class CheckoutService {

    private final StoreConfig config = StoreConfig.INSTANCE; // (1)!

    public int deliveryFee(int subtotalInr) {
        int freeAbove = config.getInt("free.delivery.above.inr");
        return subtotalInr >= freeAbove ? 0 : config.getInt("delivery.fee.inr");
    }

    public String checkout(int cartId, int subtotalInr) {
        int fee = deliveryFee(subtotalInr);
        return "Cart #%d subtotal=INR %d -> delivery fee=INR %d, total=INR %d"
                .formatted(cartId, subtotalInr, fee, subtotalInr + fee);
    }

    StoreConfig config() {
        return config;
    }
}
  1. The first line that touches StoreConfig triggers class initialization, and that's when the constructor runs and the "Loading configuration" line prints.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

public class DeliverySlotService {

    private final StoreConfig config = StoreConfig.INSTANCE;

    public boolean expressAvailable() {
        return config.isEnabled("express.delivery");
    }

    StoreConfig config() {
        return config;
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery;

public class GroceryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery Checkout Demo ===");

        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService(); // first use triggers loading
        DeliverySlotService slots = new DeliverySlotService();

        System.out.println(checkout.checkout(1, 350));
        System.out.println(checkout.checkout(2, 620));
        System.out.println("Express delivery available: " + slots.expressAvailable());
        System.out.println("Same config instance in both services? "
                + (checkout.config() == slots.config()));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery Checkout Demo ===
[StoreConfig] Loading configuration (runs once)...
Cart #1 subtotal=INR 350 -> delivery fee=INR 30, total=INR 380
Cart #2 subtotal=INR 620 -> delivery fee=INR 0, total=INR 620
Express delivery available: true
Same config instance in both services? true

Notice that the loading message appears once, even though two services use the config, and only after the demo header. That shows the enum Singleton is lazy.

Why Singleton here:

  • Config is expensive to load and must be loaded once.
  • Every service must see identical values.
  • The enum form is the shortest correct implementation, and it's safe against reflection and serialization.
  • Joshua Bloch (Effective Java, Item 3): "a single-element enum type is often the best way to implement a singleton."
Unit Test: StoreConfigTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton;

import com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery.CheckoutService;
import com.handbook.creational.singleton.grocery.StoreConfig;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class StoreConfigTest {

    @Test
    void enumSingletonIsTheSameInstance() {
        assertThat(StoreConfig.valueOf("INSTANCE")).isSameAs(StoreConfig.INSTANCE);
    }

    @Test
    void deliveryIsFreeAboveThreshold() {
        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService();
        assertThat(checkout.deliveryFee(350)).isEqualTo(30);
        assertThat(checkout.deliveryFee(499)).isZero();
    }

    @Test
    void unknownKeyFailsFast() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> StoreConfig.INSTANCE.getInt("missing"))
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("missing");
    }
}

docs.title: Example 2: Transaction ID Generator (Banking / Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment switch for a bank's Bengaluru node issues an ID for every UPI/card transaction, such as TXN-BLR-0000001. At peak it processes thousands of payments per second on virtual threads. Two transactions with the same ID would be a serious reconciliation incident, so the sequence must be unique and gap-free within the node. There must be exactly one sequence per JVM, and it must be safe to use from thousands of threads at once.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant T1 as Virtual Thread 1 participant T2 as Virtual Thread 2 participant G as TransactionIdGenerator<br/>(Holder.INSTANCE) participant A as AtomicLong T1->>G: getInstance().nextId() G->>A: incrementAndGet() A-->>G: 1 G-->>T1: TXN-BLR-0000001 T2->>G: getInstance().nextId() G->>A: incrementAndGet() A-->>G: 2 G-->>T2: TXN-BLR-0000002

Full Code:

TransactionIdGenerator.javaPaymentsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.payments;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

/**
 * Issues unique, ordered transaction IDs for one payment node.
 * Uses the Initialization-on-demand Holder idiom: lazy, thread-safe, no locks.
 */
public final class TransactionIdGenerator {

    private final AtomicLong sequence = new AtomicLong(); // (1)!
    private final String branchCode;

    private TransactionIdGenerator(String branchCode) { // (2)!
        this.branchCode = branchCode;
    }

    private static final class Holder { // (3)!
        private static final TransactionIdGenerator INSTANCE = new TransactionIdGenerator("BLR");
    }

    public static TransactionIdGenerator getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE; // (4)!
    }

    public String nextId() {
        return "TXN-%s-%07d".formatted(branchCode, sequence.incrementAndGet());
    }
}
  1. The Singleton guarantees one object. AtomicLong makes that object's state thread-safe. You need both: a Singleton with a plain long++ would still hand out duplicates.
  2. The private constructor stops new TransactionIdGenerator(...) from outside.
  3. Initialization-on-demand holder idiom. The JVM doesn't initialize the nested Holder class until getInstance() first touches it, and class initialization is guaranteed thread-safe by the JLS (§12.4.2). You get lazy loading with no synchronized and no volatile.
  4. After the first call this is a plain static field read, about as fast as Java gets.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.payments;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class PaymentsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Transaction ID Generator ===");
        TransactionIdGenerator generator = TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance();
        System.out.println("First ID  : " + generator.nextId());
        System.out.println("Second ID : " + generator.nextId());

        int threads = 1_000;
        int idsPerThread = 10;
        Set<String> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

        System.out.println("Generating 10,000 IDs from 1,000 virtual threads...");
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < idsPerThread; i++) {
                        // every thread asks for "the" generator; all get the same object
                        ids.add(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance().nextId());
                    }
                });
            }
        } // close() waits for all tasks to finish

        System.out.println("Unique IDs : " + ids.size());
        System.out.println("Duplicates : " + (threads * idsPerThread - ids.size()));
        System.out.println("Next ID    : " + generator.nextId());
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Transaction ID Generator ===
First ID  : TXN-BLR-0000001
Second ID : TXN-BLR-0000002
Generating 10,000 IDs from 1,000 virtual threads...
Unique IDs : 10000
Duplicates : 0
Next ID    : TXN-BLR-0010003

10,000 concurrent requests, 0 duplicates, and the next ID continues exactly where the sequence left off (2 + 10,000 + 1 = 10,003).

Why Singleton here:

  • Uniqueness is a business invariant: two generators means two sequences means duplicate IDs.
  • The holder idiom gives lazy, lock-free access, so there's no contention even with thousands of threads.
  • The singleton is per JVM. Across nodes, the branch code (BLR) keeps IDs globally unique. (In a real cluster you'd use a Snowflake-style ID or a DB sequence. See the deep dive.)
Unit Test: TransactionIdGeneratorTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton;

import com.handbook.creational.singleton.payments.TransactionIdGenerator;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class TransactionIdGeneratorTest {

    @Test
    void getInstanceAlwaysReturnsSameObject() {
        assertThat(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance())
                .isSameAs(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance());
    }

    @Test
    void idsAreUniqueUnderConcurrency() {
        Set<String> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 500; t++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                        ids.add(TransactionIdGenerator.getInstance().nextId());
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        assertThat(ids).hasSize(10_000);
        assertThat(ids).allMatch(id -> id.matches("TXN-BLR-\\d{7}"));
    }
}

docs.title: Example 3: Patient Record Audit Trail (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital information system must record every read and write of a patient record, as required by health-data regulations (for example HIPAA, or India's DPDP Act). Doctors view records, nurses update vitals, and the prescription module writes prescriptions. Compliance auditors need one ordered trail across all modules, not a separate log per module. The audit store is expensive to open, so it should only be created when first needed.

Design:

classDiagram class AuditLogger { -static volatile AuditLogger instance -List~String~ entries -AuditLogger() +static getInstance() AuditLogger +record(user, action, patientId) +entries() List~String~ } class PatientRecordService { +view(user, patientId) +updateVitals(user, patientId) } class PrescriptionService { +prescribe(user, patientId) } PatientRecordService ..> AuditLogger PrescriptionService ..> AuditLogger

Full Code:

AuditLogger.javaPatientRecordService.javaPrescriptionService.javaHealthcareDemo.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Central audit trail for access to patient records (compliance requirement:
 * every read/write must be recorded in one ordered log).
 * Implemented with lazy Double-Checked Locking.
 */
public final class AuditLogger {

    private static volatile AuditLogger instance; // (1)!

    private final List<String> entries = new ArrayList<>();

    private AuditLogger() {
        if (instance != null) { // (2)!
            throw new IllegalStateException("Use AuditLogger.getInstance()");
        }
        System.out.println("[AuditLogger] Opening audit store...");
    }

    public static AuditLogger getInstance() {
        AuditLogger local = instance; // (3)!
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (AuditLogger.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) {
                    instance = local = new AuditLogger();
                }
            }
        }
        return local;
    }

    public synchronized void record(String user, String action, String patientId) {
        entries.add("#%03d %-10s %-14s patient=%s"
                .formatted(entries.size() + 1, user, action, patientId));
    }

    public synchronized List<String> entries() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(entries));
    }
}
  1. volatile is mandatory. Without it, the JIT or CPU may publish the reference before the constructor finishes. Another thread could then see a non-null but half-built object. volatile creates a happens-before edge between the write and later reads.
  2. Reflection guard. If someone uses setAccessible(true) to call the constructor after the instance exists, it fails loudly instead of quietly creating a second audit trail.
  3. Reading the volatile field into a local means the common path (already initialized) does one volatile read instead of two. This is the form recommended in Effective Java, Item 83.
package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

public class PatientRecordService {

    public void view(String user, String patientId) {
        AuditLogger.getInstance().record(user, "VIEW_RECORD", patientId);
    }

    public void updateVitals(String user, String patientId) {
        AuditLogger.getInstance().record(user, "UPDATE_VITALS", patientId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

public class PrescriptionService {

    public void prescribe(String user, String patientId) {
        AuditLogger.getInstance().record(user, "PRESCRIBE", patientId);
    }
}

package com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare;

public class HealthcareDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital: Patient Record Audit Trail ===");
        PatientRecordService records = new PatientRecordService();
        PrescriptionService prescriptions = new PrescriptionService();

        records.view("dr.mehta", "P-1001");
        records.updateVitals("nurse.anna", "P-1001");
        prescriptions.prescribe("dr.mehta", "P-1001");
        records.view("dr.khan", "P-2002");

        System.out.println("Audit trail:");
        AuditLogger.getInstance().entries().forEach(e -> System.out.println("  " + e));
        System.out.println("Single audit store? "
                + (AuditLogger.getInstance() == AuditLogger.getInstance()));
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital: Patient Record Audit Trail ===
[AuditLogger] Opening audit store...
Audit trail:
  #001 dr.mehta   VIEW_RECORD    patient=P-1001
  #002 nurse.anna UPDATE_VITALS  patient=P-1001
  #003 dr.mehta   PRESCRIBE      patient=P-1001
  #004 dr.khan    VIEW_RECORD    patient=P-2002
Single audit store? true

Two different services wrote into one ordered trail, with continuous sequence numbers.

Why Singleton here:

  • Regulations require one complete, ordered trail.
  • The store is expensive to open, so lazy creation (DCL) avoids paying for it in modules that never audit.
  • DCL is the version interviewers most often ask you to write and explain (volatile, two null checks).
  • The reflection guard shows you know how a Singleton can be broken.
Unit Test: AuditLoggerTest.java 
package com.handbook.creational.singleton;

import com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare.AuditLogger;
import com.handbook.creational.singleton.healthcare.PatientRecordService;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class AuditLoggerTest {

    @Test
    void servicesShareOneAuditTrail() {
        int before = AuditLogger.getInstance().entries().size();
        new PatientRecordService().view("dr.test", "P-9");
        assertThat(AuditLogger.getInstance().entries()).hasSize(before + 1);
    }

    @Test
    void reflectionCannotCreateSecondInstance() throws Exception {
        AuditLogger.getInstance(); // make sure the instance exists
        Constructor<AuditLogger> ctor = AuditLogger.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
        ctor.setAccessible(true);
        assertThatThrownBy(ctor::newInstance)
                .isInstanceOf(InvocationTargetException.class)
                .hasCauseInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example Notes JDK Runtime.getRuntime() Classic eager Singleton JDK java.awt.Desktop.getDesktop(), System.console() One per JVM JDK Collections.emptyList(), Comparator.naturalOrder() Shared immutable instances JDK Enum constants, Boolean.TRUE Built-in singletons Spring Default bean scope is singleton One instance per ApplicationContext, not per JVM, and without a private constructor Spring @Configuration classes CGLIB proxies make @Bean methods return the same instance Logging LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class) Cached per name (a Multiton) Hibernate SessionFactory Expensive; built once per app Kafka KafkaProducer Thread-safe; recommended to share one instance

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Guarantees one instance, so invariants hold (unique IDs, one config) Global state: hidden dependencies make code harder to reason about Lazy creation saves start-up time and memory Hard to unit-test: you can't easily swap in a mock; state leaks between tests Single point of access, no passing it around Violates Single Responsibility (manages its own lifecycle and does business work) Can be made lock-free (holder, enum) Becomes a bottleneck if it holds a contended lock Only "single" per class loader. In app servers or with multiple class loaders you can get several Doesn't scale across JVMs or pods; that needs a distributed solution

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Forgetting volatile in double-checked locking

Without volatile, another thread can see a partially constructed object. The code passes every test on your laptop and fails at 3 a.m. under load on a many-core server.

Reflection and serialization attacks

setAccessible(true) can call a private constructor. Deserializing creates a new object. Defend with a constructor guard and readResolve(), or just use an enum.

Mutable shared state

A Singleton holding a HashMap that many threads write to is a race condition with a global access point. Make its state immutable, or use concurrent structures (AtomicLong, ConcurrentHashMap).

Singleton as a service locator / god object

AppContext.getInstance().getOrderService().getRepo()... hides dependencies and couples everything to one class. Prefer constructor injection.

Thinking it's 'one per system'

In Kubernetes with 10 pods you have 10 singletons. A per-JVM AtomicLong sequence across pods produces duplicate IDs. That's exactly why Example 2 includes a node code.

Testing pain

Tests share the same instance, so test order changes results. Workarounds: inject the singleton through an interface, or let Spring manage the scope so you can use @MockitoBean.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Java Memory Model view. instance = new AuditLogger() is really three steps: allocate memory, run the constructor, publish the reference. Without a happens-before edge, steps 2 and 3 may be reordered. volatile (JSR-133, Java 5+) forbids that reordering. Class initialization (holder and enum) is protected by the JVM's initialization lock, which gives the same guarantee for free. That's why holder and enum are preferred.

Prefer container-managed singletons. In a Spring Boot service, write a plain class with a public constructor and let Spring make it a singleton bean:

@Service                       // singleton scope by default
public class TransactionIdService {
    private final AtomicLong sequence = new AtomicLong();
    public String nextId() { return "TXN-%07d".formatted(sequence.incrementAndGet()); }
}

You get one instance, constructor injection, easy mocking, and lifecycle hooks (@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy), without the downsides of global static state.

Distributed "singletons". When you need one of something across a cluster:

Need Tool Unique IDs across nodes Snowflake / ULID / UUIDv7, DB sequences, Redis INCR One scheduled job runner ShedLock, Quartz clustered mode, Kubernetes CronJob One leader Leader election (ZooKeeper, etcd, Kubernetes Lease, Spring Integration LockRegistryLeaderInitiator) One shared config Spring Cloud Config, Consul, AWS AppConfig, with refresh events

How to defend it in a design review: "This object enforces an invariant that only holds if there's one instance (a sequence or an ordered log). It's per-JVM by design, it's lock-free, it has no mutable state that can be seen from outside, and it's injected through an interface so tests can replace it. For cross-node uniqueness we rely on X."

When NOT to use it: to avoid passing parameters; for request- or user-specific data; for anything that needs different configurations in tests; for caches that should be bounded or evicted (use Caffeine instead).

War story: duplicate invoice numbers after scaling out

A billing service generated invoice numbers with a Singleton AtomicLong that was seeded from MAX(invoice_no) at start-up. It worked perfectly for two years on one VM. During a migration to Kubernetes, the service was scaled to 3 replicas. Each pod seeded from the same max and started issuing the same numbers. Finance found 1,200 duplicate invoices at month-end close. Fix: switched to a database sequence (nextval) with an allocation size of 50 per pod (Hibernate pooled optimizer) and added a unique constraint on invoice_no. Lesson: a Singleton is a per-process guarantee. Write down that assumption, and add a database constraint as the last line of defense.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Singleton Static utility class Spring singleton bean Monostate Instances 1 per class loader 0 1 per ApplicationContext Many objects, shared static state Can implement interfaces ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ Polymorphism / mocking Hard ❌ ✅ Easy Hard Lazy init ✅ N/A ✅ (@Lazy) ❌ Holds state ✅ Should not ✅ ✅ Use for Real one-per-process invariants Pure functions (Math, Collections) Almost every service in a Spring app Rarely; legacy code

Patterns that often use Singleton: Abstract Factory (one factory per family), Facade (one entry point), Flyweight factory, Object Pool manager, State objects without fields.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One instance + global access. Private constructor, static holder, getInstance().
  • Best forms: enum (safest) or the holder idiom (lazy, lock-free).
  • DCL needs volatile. Say "happens-before" and "partially constructed object".
  • Breakers: reflection, serialization, cloning. Enum beats all three.
  • One per class loader / per JVM, never per cluster. In Spring, prefer singleton-scoped beans.
public enum Config { INSTANCE; public String get(String k) { return "..."; } }

docs.text:
• Rewrite Example 1 using the holder idiom and compare the two.
  • Remove volatile from AuditLogger and explain, in writing, what could go wrong.
  • Add implements Serializable to TransactionIdGenerator, serialize and deserialize it, and show that you get a second instance. Then fix it with readResolve().
  • Turn TransactionIdGenerator into a Spring @Service and write a test that mocks it.

docs.title: Enterprise & DDD Patterns
docs.text:
These patterns sit between the GoF classics and the architecture styles. They answer the questions every business application hits on day one: how objects get their collaborators, how domain objects are loaded and saved, how several changes commit together, how to model concepts precisely, where consistency boundaries go, and how one part of the domain tells the others that something happened.

They come mostly from Martin Fowler's Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) and Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design (2003), and they are what Spring, JPA/Hibernate and Spring Data implement for you. Knowing them is the difference between using @Transactional and JpaRepository and understanding them.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Dependency Injection (IoC) Classes get collaborators from outside, so they can be swapped and tested ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Repository Collection-like access to aggregates; business logic free of SQL ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Unit of Work & Identity Map Commit many changes atomically; one object per row per transaction ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Value Object Model concepts like Quantity or PhoneNumber precisely, instead of primitives ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Aggregate Consistency boundaries: what must be true at commit, and what can be eventual ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Domain Events Aggregates announce what happened; other modules react after commit ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅

docs.title: How they fit together
docs.text:
flowchart LR DI[Dependency Injection] -->|wires| UC[Use case / application service] UC -->|loads & saves via| R[Repository] UC -->|commits via| UOW[Unit of Work] R -->|returns| AG[Aggregate] AG -->|built from| VO[Value Objects] AG -->|records| DE[Domain Events] UOW -->|after commit| DE DE -->|to other services| OUT[Transactional Outbox]

A typical request in a hexagonal Spring service: the controller calls a use case (wired by DI) that opens a unit of work (@Transactional), loads an aggregate through its repository, calls a command method that checks invariants using value objects and records domain events, saves, commits, and then dispatches the events.

docs.title: Suggested learning order
docs.text:
1. Dependency Injection: the foundation for everything else.
  2. Value Object → Aggregate: how to model the domain.
  3. Repository → Unit of Work & Identity Map: how to persist it.
  4. Domain Events: how aggregates communicate, leading into the microservices patterns.

The one-sentence interview answer

"I keep business rules in aggregates built from value objects, load and save them through repositories, make each use case one unit of work, let aggregates raise domain events that are handled after commit, and wire it all with constructor injection so every piece is testable on its own."

Modular Monolith Start: Dependency Injection

docs.title: Aggregate
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Enterprise / DDD Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An Aggregate is a cluster of objects (a root entity plus the entities and values inside it) that is loaded, changed and saved as one unit, so its business rules are always true. Outsiders may only talk to the root. Use it to decide what must be consistent immediately (inside one aggregate, one transaction) versus eventually (between aggregates, via events).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: an order has lines. A rule says "max 4 dozen mangoes per order during the flash sale" and "COD orders can't exceed INR 20,000". If any code can grab order.getLines() and add to it, or update order_line rows directly, those rules are only as strong as the most careless caller. In the other direction, if you make the boundary too big (a Customer that contains every order ever), every new order loads thousands of objects and two phones ordering at once conflict.

Definition (Eric Evans, DDD; Vaughn Vernon, Effective Aggregate Design):

A cluster of associated objects treated as a unit for the purpose of data changes. Each aggregate has a root and a boundary. Outside objects may hold references only to the root. Invariants within the boundary are enforced on every change.

Vernon's four rules of thumb:

  1. Model true invariants inside the boundary (rules that must hold at the end of every transaction).
  2. Design small aggregates.
  3. Reference other aggregates by identity only.
  4. Use eventual consistency (domain events) between aggregates.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A sealed tiffin box

A tiffin (lunch box) has several compartments, but you hand over, carry and wash it as one thing. Nobody reaches in to swap the dal while it's in the delivery bag. The dabbawala doesn't carry your whole kitchen, just the tiffin (small aggregate), and the label on it is your address, not your house (reference by id).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram direction LR class Order { <<aggregate root>> -OrderId id -CustomerId customerId -List~Line~ lines -Status status +add(sku, price, qty) +markPacked() +total() } class Line { <<entity, internal>> -sku -qty } class Quantity { <<value>> } class Customer { <<another aggregate>> } Order "1" *-- "many" Line : owns Line --> Quantity Order ..> Customer : by id only Concept Responsibility Aggregate root The only entry point; public methods enforce all invariants Internal entities / values Can't be referenced or modified from outside (no public constructors, read-only views) Boundary One transaction changes one aggregate; one repository per root References to other aggregates By id (CustomerId), never by object

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Order order = orderRepo.findById(id);
order.getLines().add(new OrderLine("ALPHONSO-1DZ", 5));   // bypasses the flash-sale limit
orderLineRepo.save(new OrderLine(orderId, "TV-32", 1));    // bypasses the COD cap, and the order total is now wrong
  • Invariants checked "somewhere", so in practice nowhere.
  • Repositories per table let anyone change part of the cluster.
  • No clear transaction boundary, so concurrent changes interleave.

docs.title: Example 1: The Order Aggregate (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: During the Alphonso mango sale, each order may have at most 4 dozen, cash-on-delivery orders are capped at INR 20,000, and nothing can be added once the order is packed. Orders are edited by the customer app, customer-support tools and the substitutions service; all of them must obey the rules.

Design:

flowchart LR App[Customer app] --> R Support[Support tool] --> R Subs[Substitution service] --> R subgraph Aggregate boundary R["Order (root)<br/>add / markPacked"] --> L1[Line] R --> L2[Line] end

Full Code:

Order.javaOrderAggregateDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.grocery;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

/** Aggregate root. The ONLY way to change lines is through Order, so its rules always hold. */
public final class Order {

    public enum Status { OPEN, PACKED }

    /** Entity inside the aggregate: identified by SKU within this order, never shared. */
    public static final class Line {
        private final String sku;
        private final long unitPaise;
        private int qty;

        private Line(String sku, long unitPaise, int qty) { // (1)!
            this.sku = sku;
            this.unitPaise = unitPaise;
            this.qty = qty;
        }

        public String sku() { return sku; }
        public int qty() { return qty; }
        public long subtotal() { return unitPaise * qty; }
        public String toString() { return sku + " x" + qty; }
    }

    static final int FLASH_SALE_LIMIT_PER_SKU = 4;
    static final long MAX_ORDER_PAISE = 2_000_000; // INR 20,000 cash-on-delivery cap

    private final String id;
    private final String customerId; // (2)!
    private final List<Line> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    private Status status = Status.OPEN;

    public Order(String id, String customerId) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id);
        this.customerId = Objects.requireNonNull(customerId);
    }

    public void add(String sku, long unitPaise, int qty) { // (3)!
        if (status != Status.OPEN) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("order " + id + " is " + status + "; cannot add " + sku);
        }
        Line line = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.sku.equals(sku)).findFirst().orElse(null);
        int newQty = (line == null ? 0 : line.qty) + qty;
        if (newQty > FLASH_SALE_LIMIT_PER_SKU) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("max " + FLASH_SALE_LIMIT_PER_SKU + " of " + sku + " per order");
        }
        if (total() + unitPaise * qty > MAX_ORDER_PAISE) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("order total would exceed INR 20,000 COD cap");
        }
        if (line == null) {
            lines.add(new Line(sku, unitPaise, qty));
        } else {
            line.qty = newQty;
        }
    }

    public void markPacked() {
        if (lines.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("cannot pack an empty order");
        }
        status = Status.PACKED;
    }

    public long total() { return lines.stream().mapToLong(Line::subtotal).sum(); }
    public List<Line> lines() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(lines); } // (4)!
    public Status status() { return status; }
    public String customerId() { return customerId; }
}
  1. Line's constructor is private: only Order can create lines.
  2. The customer is another aggregate, so it's referenced by id.
  3. Every invariant is checked in the root's command method, against the whole aggregate's state.
  4. Callers get a read-only view; they can look but not touch.
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.grocery;

public class OrderAggregateDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: The Order Aggregate Guards Its Own Rules ===");
        Order order = new Order("ORD-9", "CUST-7");
        order.add("ALPHONSO-1DZ", 89_900, 2);
        order.add("ALPHONSO-1DZ", 89_900, 2);
        order.add("MILK-1L", 6_800, 3);
        System.out.println("Lines " + order.lines() + ", total INR " + order.total() / 100);
        attempt("5th dozen of mangoes", () -> order.add("ALPHONSO-1DZ", 89_900, 1));
        attempt("INR 18,000 TV in a grocery order", () -> order.add("TV-32", 1_800_000, 1));
        attempt("edit lines from outside", () -> order.lines().clear());
        order.markPacked();
        attempt("add after packing", () -> order.add("BREAD", 4_500, 1));
        System.out.println("Final: " + order.status() + " " + order.lines() + ", total INR " + order.total() / 100);
    }

    private static void attempt(String what, Runnable r) {
        try {
            r.run();
            System.out.println("  " + what + ": allowed?!");
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("  " + what + ": rejected (" + (e.getMessage() == null ? e.getClass().getSimpleName() : e.getMessage()) + ")");
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: The Order Aggregate Guards Its Own Rules ===
Lines [ALPHONSO-1DZ x4, MILK-1L x3], total INR 3800
  5th dozen of mangoes: rejected (max 4 of ALPHONSO-1DZ per order)
  INR 18,000 TV in a grocery order: rejected (order total would exceed INR 20,000 COD cap)
  edit lines from outside: rejected (UnsupportedOperationException)
  add after packing: rejected (order ORD-9 is PACKED; cannot add BREAD)
Final: PACKED [ALPHONSO-1DZ x4, MILK-1L x3], total INR 3800

Why an aggregate here:

  • Rules that span lines (per-SKU limit, total cap) need the whole cluster to evaluate.
  • One root means one place to read the rules, and one place to test them.
  • The repository saves Order as a unit, so lines and totals never diverge.

docs.title: Example 2: Card Account with Holds (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A credit card with a INR 50,000 limit receives pre-authorisations (hotel, fuel), captures (often for less than the hold) and reversals. The invariant is posted balance + open holds ≤ limit, and it must hold even with authorisations arriving from different payment networks at the same moment. The account and its holds therefore form one aggregate, saved with a version number.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Held : authorise (if available) Held --> Posted : capture (≤ hold) Held --> Released : release / expiry Posted --> [*] Released --> [*]

Full Code:

CardAccount.javaCardAccountDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.banking;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Invariant: balance + all open holds <= credit limit. Holds are internal to the aggregate. */
public final class CardAccount {

    private final String cardId;
    private final long limitPaise;
    private long postedPaise;
    private final Map<String, Long> holds = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // authCode -> amount
    private long version;

    public CardAccount(String cardId, long limitPaise) {
        this.cardId = cardId;
        this.limitPaise = limitPaise;
    }

    public long available() {
        return limitPaise - postedPaise - holds.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
    }

    public boolean authorise(String authCode, long paise) { // (1)!
        if (paise > available()) {
            return false;
        }
        holds.put(authCode, paise);
        version++;
        return true;
    }

    public void capture(String authCode, long finalPaise) { // (2)!
        Long held = holds.remove(authCode);
        if (held == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("unknown or already settled auth " + authCode);
        }
        if (finalPaise > held) {
            holds.put(authCode, held);
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capture " + finalPaise + " exceeds hold " + held);
        }
        postedPaise += finalPaise;
        version++;
    }

    public void release(String authCode) {
        if (holds.remove(authCode) != null) {
            version++;
        }
    }

    public long version() { return version; }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return cardId + "[posted=" + postedPaise / 100 + ", holds=" + holds.size() + ", available=" + available() / 100 + "]";
    }
}
  1. The limit check uses posted amounts and all open holds, which is only possible because the holds live inside the aggregate.
  2. Capture moves money from a hold to posted; it can't exceed the hold.
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.banking;

public class CardAccountDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Credit Card Account as One Consistency Boundary ===");
        CardAccount card = new CardAccount("CARD-4111", 5_000_000); // INR 50,000 limit
        System.out.println("Hotel pre-auth 30,000 : " + card.authorise("A1", 3_000_000) + " -> " + card);
        System.out.println("Fuel pre-auth 2,000   : " + card.authorise("A2", 200_000) + " -> " + card);
        System.out.println("Laptop 25,000         : " + card.authorise("A3", 2_500_000) + " -> " + card);
        card.capture("A1", 2_400_000);   // final hotel bill lower than the hold
        System.out.println("Hotel captured 24,000 -> " + card);
        card.release("A2");              // fuel station sent a reversal
        System.out.println("Fuel released         -> " + card);
        System.out.println("Laptop retried        : " + card.authorise("A3", 2_500_000) + " -> " + card);
        System.out.println("Version after 5 state changes: " + card.version() + " (used for optimistic locking on save)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Credit Card Account as One Consistency Boundary ===
Hotel pre-auth 30,000 : true -> CARD-4111[posted=0, holds=1, available=20000]
Fuel pre-auth 2,000   : true -> CARD-4111[posted=0, holds=2, available=18000]
Laptop 25,000         : false -> CARD-4111[posted=0, holds=2, available=18000]
Hotel captured 24,000 -> CARD-4111[posted=24000, holds=1, available=24000]
Fuel released         -> CARD-4111[posted=24000, holds=0, available=26000]
Laptop retried        : true -> CARD-4111[posted=24000, holds=1, available=1000]
Version after 5 state changes: 5 (used for optimistic locking on save)

Why an aggregate here:

  • The invariant spans several objects (account + holds), so they belong together.
  • The version makes concurrent authorisations on the same card serialize via optimistic locking: one wins, the other reloads and re-checks.
  • Statements and rewards are separate aggregates that react to events, so they don't bloat this one.

docs.title: Example 3: Seats in a Show (Entertainment)
docs.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform sells seats for 12,000 shows a day; a blockbuster's first-day shows sell out in minutes. A booking for several seats must be all-or-nothing (a family of four doesn't want three seats), no seat may be sold twice, and a show can't exceed capacity. Customers and payments are separate aggregates referenced by id.

Design:

flowchart LR subgraph "Show aggregate (one per show)" S[Show root] --> Seats["seat → CustomerId"] end S -.->|by id| C[(Customer aggregate)] S -.->|event: SeatsBooked| P[(Payment aggregate)]

Full Code:

Show.javaShowDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** A small aggregate: one show's seats. Customers and payments are referenced by ID only. */
public final class Show {

    public record ShowId(String value) { }

    public record CustomerId(String value) { }

    private final ShowId id;
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<String, CustomerId> bookedSeats = new TreeMap<>(); // seat -> customer id (1)!

    public Show(ShowId id, int capacity) {
        this.id = id;
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    public void book(CustomerId customer, String... seats) { // (2)!
        for (String seat : seats) {
            if (bookedSeats.containsKey(seat)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("seat " + seat + " already taken; nothing booked");
            }
        }
        if (bookedSeats.size() + seats.length > capacity) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("show " + id.value() + " is full");
        }
        for (String seat : seats) {
            bookedSeats.put(seat, customer);
        }
    }

    public Map<String, CustomerId> bookedSeats() { return Map.copyOf(bookedSeats); }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return id.value() + " " + bookedSeats.keySet() + " (" + bookedSeats.size() + "/" + capacity + ")";
    }
}
  1. The aggregate stores ids of other aggregates, never Customer objects.
  2. Check everything first, then mutate: a multi-seat booking is atomic within the aggregate.
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema;

import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema.Show.CustomerId;
import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema.Show.ShowId;

public class ShowDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Entertainment: Booking Seats in a Show Aggregate ===");
        Show show = new Show(new ShowId("STARLIGHT-AUDI3-2026-05-01-21:00"), 4);
        show.book(new CustomerId("C-1"), "F7", "F8");
        System.out.println("C-1 booked      -> " + show);
        try {
            show.book(new CustomerId("C-2"), "F9", "F8"); // F8 is taken
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("C-2 F9+F8       -> " + e.getMessage() + " -> " + show);
        }
        show.book(new CustomerId("C-2"), "F9", "F10");
        System.out.println("C-2 F9+F10      -> " + show);
        try {
            show.book(new CustomerId("C-3"), "A1");
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("C-3 A1          -> " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Entertainment: Booking Seats in a Show Aggregate ===
C-1 booked      -> STARLIGHT-AUDI3-2026-05-01-21:00 [F7, F8] (2/4)
C-2 F9+F8       -> seat F8 already taken; nothing booked -> STARLIGHT-AUDI3-2026-05-01-21:00 [F7, F8] (2/4)
C-2 F9+F10      -> STARLIGHT-AUDI3-2026-05-01-21:00 [F10, F7, F8, F9] (4/4)
C-3 A1          -> show STARLIGHT-AUDI3-2026-05-01-21:00 is full

Why an aggregate here:

  • "No double booking" is a true invariant of one show, so one show is the boundary.
  • Different shows never contend: the platform scales by spreading shows across shards.
  • Payment happens afterwards, driven by a SeatsBooked domain event; if it fails, a compensating action releases the seats.
Unit Tests: AggregateTest.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate;

import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.banking.CardAccount;
import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema.Show;
import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema.Show.CustomerId;
import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.cinema.Show.ShowId;
import com.handbook.enterprise.aggregate.grocery.Order;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class AggregateTest {

    @Test
    void orderEnforcesPerSkuLimitAcrossAdds() {
        Order o = new Order("O", "C");
        o.add("A", 100, 3);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> o.add("A", 100, 2)).hasMessageContaining("max 4");
        assertThat(o.lines()).singleElement().extracting(Order.Line::qty).isEqualTo(3);
    }

    @Test
    void linesCannotBeModifiedFromOutside() {
        Order o = new Order("O", "C");
        o.add("A", 100, 1);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> o.lines().clear()).isInstanceOf(UnsupportedOperationException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void cardNeverExceedsLimitIncludingHolds() {
        CardAccount card = new CardAccount("C", 1_000);
        assertThat(card.authorise("a", 700)).isTrue();
        assertThat(card.authorise("b", 400)).isFalse();
        card.capture("a", 500);
        assertThat(card.authorise("b", 400)).isTrue();
        assertThat(card.available()).isEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void bookingIsAllOrNothing() {
        Show show = new Show(new ShowId("S"), 10);
        show.book(new CustomerId("1"), "A1");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> show.book(new CustomerId("2"), "A2", "A1")).isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class);
        assertThat(show.bookedSeats()).containsOnlyKeys("A1");
    }
}

docs.text: Variation Notes Mutable root, private internals Classic OO style (Examples 1–3) with JPA @Entity + @OneToMany(cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true) Immutable aggregates Records with methods returning a new aggregate version; repository saves the new version Event-sourced aggregates State rebuilt from events; commands emit new events after checking invariants (Event Sourcing) Sealed state types sealed interface OrderState permits Open, Packed, Delivered: illegal transitions don't compile Spring Data AbstractAggregateRoot registerEvent(...) inside the root; events published on save() jMolecules @AggregateRoot, @Entity, @ValueObject annotations + ArchUnit rules to verify DDD structure

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Aggregates Spring Data One repository per aggregate root; AbstractAggregateRoot, @DomainEvents; Spring Data JDBC is explicitly aggregate-oriented (saves the whole aggregate) JPA Cascades and orphanRemoval approximate the boundary; @Version for concurrency Axon Framework @Aggregate, @CommandHandler, @EventSourcingHandler Event stores One stream per aggregate instance (order-ORD-9), with expected-version appends

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Invariants enforced in one place, always Choosing boundaries is hard and domain-specific Clear transaction and locking unit Cross-aggregate rules become eventually consistent Small aggregates scale and rarely conflict More events and coordination code Maps naturally to microservices, shards and event streams ORMs push toward big object graphs; you must resist

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Giant aggregates

Customer containing all orders, addresses, payments and reviews: slow loads, huge saves and constant optimistic-lock conflicts. See the coding challenge.

Exposing internals

Returning a mutable List<Line> or public setters on internal entities lets callers break invariants. Return read-only views and expose intention-revealing commands.

Modifying two aggregates in one transaction

Tempting and sometimes acceptable inside one service, but it hides coupling and fails across services. Prefer one aggregate per transaction plus domain events.

Object references across aggregates

@ManyToOne Customer customer inside Order invites lazy-loading and cascades across boundaries. Store CustomerId.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Finding the boundary. Ask: "Which rules must be true at the end of this transaction, and which can be true a few seconds later?" Only the first group justifies putting objects together. "Show can't be double-booked" is immediate; "customer gets a confirmation email" can be eventual.

Concurrency is the real test. If two users regularly modify the same aggregate at the same time and get version conflicts, the aggregate is too big or the operations should be commutative. Seat booking per show is fine; "one aggregate for the whole cinema chain" is not.

Aggregates and services. An aggregate never spans services. A service usually owns a few aggregate types; each is a natural unit for sharding (by aggregate id), for event streams and for idempotency keys.

War story: the shopping cart that couldn't take two items

A grocery app modelled Customer as one aggregate containing carts, orders, addresses and wallet. When households shared an account, two phones adding items at the same time hit optimistic-lock failures on Customer; the app retried silently and dropped items. Order placement for long-time customers took 1.8 s because it loaded five years of history. Fix: Cart, Order, Wallet became separate aggregates referencing CustomerId; the wallet balance update moved to an event handler. Lesson: small aggregates, references by id, events in between.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Aggregate Entity Value Object Repository What Consistency boundary around a cluster Object with identity Immutable, equal by value Loads/saves aggregates Relationship Contains entities and values May be a root or internal Lives inside aggregates One per aggregate root

See also Domain Events (how aggregates talk) and Saga (multi-aggregate business processes).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Cluster + root + boundary; outsiders talk to the root only.
  • Boundary = true invariants that must hold at commit.
  • Small; reference other aggregates by id.
  • One aggregate per transaction; events between aggregates.
  • One repository per root; @Version on the root.
order.add("ALPHONSO-1DZ", 89_900, 2);   // root checks limits, totals, status

  • Add hold expiry to CardAccount (holds older than 7 days are released).
  • Add cancel(CustomerId) to Show that only frees that customer's seats.
