docs.title: Dependency Injection (IoC)
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🔴 Advanced Enterprise Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An object receives the things it depends on from outside (usually through its constructor) instead of creating or looking them up itself. Use it everywhere a class talks to something you might want to swap: databases, payment gateways, clocks, HTTP clients. It is the pattern underneath all of Spring.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a CheckoutService that does new RazorPayGateway() inside its methods is welded to RazorPay. You can't test it without charging a real card, you can't run a demo without network access, and switching to another gateway means editing checkout code. The class is doing two jobs: the business rule and deciding which concrete classes to use.

Definition (Martin Fowler, 2004):

Separate the configuration of services from their use. A separate object, an assembler, populates fields in a class with appropriate implementations of the interfaces it needs.

Inversion of Control (IoC) is the broader idea: the framework or the main method controls object creation, not your class. Dependency Injection is the most common way to achieve it; Service Locator is the other (see the coding challenge for why DI usually wins).

Three injection styles:

Style How Verdict Constructor new CheckoutService(payments, slots, notifier) ✅ Default. Dependencies are explicit, fields can be final, objects are never half-built Setter service.setNotifier(n) For genuinely optional dependencies only Field (@Autowired private X x;) Reflection writes the field ❌ Hides dependencies, can't be final, needs a container even in unit tests

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant kitchen

A chef doesn't grow vegetables or forge knives. The restaurant supplies ingredients and tools to the station. The same chef can cook with organic or regular tomatoes, and a trainee can practise with plastic food, without the chef changing how they cook. The restaurant manager (the composition root) decides what each station gets.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class CheckoutService { -PaymentGateway payments -Notifier notifier +CheckoutService(PaymentGateway, Notifier) +placeOrder() } class PaymentGateway { <<interface>> +charge() } class Notifier { <<interface>> +send() } class RazorPayGateway class FakeGateway class CompositionRoot { +production() CheckoutService } CheckoutService --> PaymentGateway CheckoutService --> Notifier RazorPayGateway ..|> PaymentGateway FakeGateway ..|> PaymentGateway CompositionRoot ..> CheckoutService : creates and injects CompositionRoot ..> RazorPayGateway : creates Participant Responsibility Client (CheckoutService) Business logic. Declares what it needs as constructor parameters typed by interfaces Service interface (PaymentGateway) The abstraction the client depends on (owned by the client's layer, per DIP) Service implementation A concrete class: real, fake, or decorated Injector / composition root The only code that knows concrete classes; builds the object graph once at startup

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class CheckoutService {
    public String placeOrder(Order o) {
        String ref = new RazorPayGateway(System.getenv("RZP_KEY")).charge(o);   // hard-wired
        if (LocalDate.now().getDayOfWeek() == SUNDAY) { ... }                  // hidden clock
        new SmsNotifier().send(o.phone(), "confirmed");                          // hard-wired
        return ref;
    }
}
  • Untestable: every test hits RazorPay and sends a real SMS.
  • Violates DIP and OCP: high-level policy depends on low-level details; new gateway = edit checkout.
  • Hidden dependencies: you only learn it needs RZP_KEY and the system clock by reading every line.

docs.title: Example 1: One Checkout, Two Wirings (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce app places 3,000 orders a minute at peak. The checkout needs a payment gateway, a delivery-slot booker for the dark store, and a notifier. In production it uses RazorPay and SMS; in the sales demo and in tests it must use a fake gateway and record messages instead of sending them, with no change to checkout code.

Design:

flowchart LR Root[CompositionRoot] -->|production| P["CheckoutService(RazorPay, DarkStoreSlots, SMS)"] Root -->|demo / test| D["CheckoutService(FakeGateway, DarkStoreSlots, Recorder)"]

Full Code:

Checkout.javaCompositionRoot.javaGroceryDiDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Ports the checkout needs. The service never decides WHICH implementation it gets. */
public final class Checkout {

    public interface PaymentGateway { String charge(String orderId, long paise); }

    public interface SlotBooker { String book(String pincode); }

    public interface Notifier { void send(String to, String message); }

    /** High-level policy: depends only on the three interfaces, all supplied through the constructor. */
    public static final class CheckoutService {
        private final PaymentGateway payments;
        private final SlotBooker slots;
        private final Notifier notifier;

        public CheckoutService(PaymentGateway payments, SlotBooker slots, Notifier notifier) { // (1)!
            this.payments = payments;
            this.slots = slots;
            this.notifier = notifier;
        }

        public String placeOrder(String orderId, String customer, String pincode, long paise) {
            String paymentRef = payments.charge(orderId, paise);
            String slot = slots.book(pincode);
            notifier.send(customer, "Order " + orderId + " confirmed for " + slot);
            return orderId + " paid (" + paymentRef + "), slot " + slot;
        }
    }

    // ---- Implementations: production-like and demo/test-friendly ----

    public static final class RazorPayGateway implements PaymentGateway {
        public String charge(String orderId, long paise) { return "rzp_" + orderId + "_" + paise; }
    }

    public static final class FakeGateway implements PaymentGateway {
        public String charge(String orderId, long paise) { return "fake-ok"; }
    }

    public static final class DarkStoreSlots implements SlotBooker {
        public String book(String pincode) { return pincode.startsWith("560") ? "Today 18:00-19:00" : "Tomorrow 09:00-10:00"; }
    }

    public static final class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {
        public void send(String to, String message) { System.out.println("  [SMS to " + to + "] " + message); }
    }

    public static final class RecordingNotifier implements Notifier {
        public final List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>();
        public void send(String to, String message) { sent.add(to + ": " + message); }
    }

    private Checkout() {
    }
}
  1. Constructor injection: the three collaborators are interfaces passed in. The fields are final, so a CheckoutService can never exist without them.
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery;

import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.CheckoutService;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.DarkStoreSlots;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.FakeGateway;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.Notifier;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.RazorPayGateway;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.SmsNotifier;

/** The ONE place that knows concrete classes ("pure DI": no framework, just constructors). */
public final class CompositionRoot {

    public static CheckoutService production() { // (1)!
        return new CheckoutService(new RazorPayGateway(), new DarkStoreSlots(), new SmsNotifier());
    }

    public static CheckoutService demo(Notifier notifier) { // (2)!
        return new CheckoutService(new FakeGateway(), new DarkStoreSlots(), notifier);
    }

    private CompositionRoot() {
    }
}
  1. The composition root is the only place that says new RazorPayGateway(). In Spring this role is played by @Configuration classes and component scanning.
  2. A second wiring for demos and tests. Nothing else in the codebase changes.
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery;

import com.handbook.enterprise.di.grocery.Checkout.RecordingNotifier;

public class GroceryDiDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Same CheckoutService, Two Wirings ===");
        System.out.println("Production wiring:");
        System.out.println("  " + CompositionRoot.production().placeOrder("ORD-101", "+91-98450", "560034", 45_900));

        RecordingNotifier recorder = new RecordingNotifier();
        System.out.println("Demo wiring (fake payments, recorded messages):");
        System.out.println("  " + CompositionRoot.demo(recorder).placeOrder("ORD-102", "+91-99001", "110001", 12_000));
        System.out.println("  recorded: " + recorder.sent);
        System.out.println("CheckoutService.java imports no concrete class: swapping needed zero changes to it.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Same CheckoutService, Two Wirings ===
Production wiring:
  [SMS to +91-98450] Order ORD-101 confirmed for Today 18:00-19:00
  ORD-101 paid (rzp_ORD-101_45900), slot Today 18:00-19:00
Demo wiring (fake payments, recorded messages):
  ORD-102 paid (fake-ok), slot Tomorrow 09:00-10:00
  recorded: [+91-99001: Order ORD-102 confirmed for Tomorrow 09:00-10:00]
CheckoutService.java imports no concrete class: swapping needed zero changes to it.

Why DI here:

  • Payment and notification are side effects you must be able to swap for tests and demos.
  • Checkout depends only on interfaces it owns, so it follows DIP.
  • All "which implementation?" decisions live in one file, which is easy to review.

docs.title: Example 2: Injecting the Clock (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank accrues interest on fixed deposits in a nightly batch. When the batch fails, operations rerun it the next morning for the previous business date. Code that calls LocalDate.now() gives a different answer on rerun, and month-end reconciliations break. The fix is to treat time as a dependency.

Design:

flowchart LR Batch["Nightly batch (business date 2025-01-31)"] -->|"Clock.fixed(...)"| Calc[InterestCalculator] Tests -->|"Clock.fixed(...)"| Calc Prod["Live API"] -->|"Clock.systemDefaultZone()"| Calc

Full Code:

FixedDeposit.javaBankingDiDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.banking;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;

/** Interest calculation with time injected instead of hidden inside LocalDate.now(). */
public final class FixedDeposit {

    public record Deposit(String id, long principalPaise, int rateBasisPoints, LocalDate openedOn) {
    }

    /** Hidden dependency: reads the system clock directly, so the result changes every day. */
    public static final class HardWiredInterest {
        public long accruedPaise(Deposit d) {
            long days = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(d.openedOn(), LocalDate.now()); // (1)!
            return d.principalPaise() * d.rateBasisPoints() * days / (10_000L * 365);
        }
    }

    /** Explicit dependency: the clock is a constructor argument. */
    public static final class InterestCalculator {
        private final Clock clock;

        public InterestCalculator(Clock clock) { // (2)!
            this.clock = clock;
        }

        public long accruedPaise(Deposit d) {
            long days = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(d.openedOn(), LocalDate.now(clock));
            return d.principalPaise() * d.rateBasisPoints() * days / (10_000L * 365);
        }
    }

    private FixedDeposit() {
    }
}
  1. LocalDate.now() is a hidden dependency on the system clock: untestable and not reproducible.
  2. java.time.Clock is the JDK's built-in injectable time source. Production passes Clock.systemUTC(); batches and tests pass Clock.fixed(...).
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.banking;

import com.handbook.enterprise.di.banking.FixedDeposit.Deposit;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.banking.FixedDeposit.InterestCalculator;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.ZoneId;

public class BankingDiDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Injecting the Clock into Interest Accrual ===");
        Deposit fd = new Deposit("FD-77", 10_000_000, 725, LocalDate.of(2025, 1, 1)); // INR 1,00,000 at 7.25%
        ZoneId ist = ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata");

        for (String day : new String[] {"2025-01-31", "2025-07-01", "2026-01-01"}) {
            Clock fixed = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse(day + "T06:00:00Z"), ist);
            long paise = new InterestCalculator(fixed).accruedPaise(fd);
            System.out.printf("As of %s: accrued INR %d.%02d%n", day, paise / 100, paise % 100);
        }
        System.out.println("Month-end batch reruns for a past date give the same answer: the clock is an input.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Injecting the Clock into Interest Accrual ===
As of 2025-01-31: accrued INR 595.89
As of 2025-07-01: accrued INR 3595.20
As of 2026-01-01: accrued INR 7250.00
Month-end batch reruns for a past date give the same answer: the clock is an input.

Why DI here:

  • Not every dependency is a "service": time, randomness, IDs and environment variables are dependencies too.
  • Reruns and tests become deterministic.
  • Money stays in integer paise; the only moving part is the injected clock.

docs.title: Example 3: A Tiny IoC Container (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A clinic platform has 40+ services. Wiring them by hand in a composition root grows to hundreds of lines. A container resolves constructors automatically: ask for AppointmentService, it sees the constructor needs a PatientDirectory and a ReminderChannel, finds their bindings, builds them, and caches singletons. It must also fail at startup with a readable message on a missing binding or a circular dependency.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant App participant C as MiniContainer App->>C: get(AppointmentService) C->>C: constructor needs PatientDirectory, ReminderChannel C->>C: get(PatientDirectory) -> bound to EmrDirectory -> new C->>C: get(ReminderChannel) -> bound to WhatsAppChannel -> new C-->>App: new AppointmentService(emr, whatsapp) (cached)

Full Code:

MiniContainer.javaClinic.javaContainerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.container;

import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** A 60-line IoC container: constructor autowiring by type, singletons, cycle detection. */
public final class MiniContainer {

    private final Map<Class<?>, Class<?>> bindings = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<Class<?>, Object> singletons = new HashMap<>();
    private final Deque<Class<?>> resolving = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public <T> MiniContainer bind(Class<T> type, Class<? extends T> impl) { // (1)!
        bindings.put(type, impl);
        return this;
    }

    public <T> T get(Class<T> type) {
        Class<?> impl = bindings.getOrDefault(type, type);
        Object existing = singletons.get(impl);
        if (existing != null) {
            return type.cast(existing);
        }
        if (resolving.contains(impl)) { // (2)!
            List<Class<?>> path = new java.util.ArrayList<>(resolving);
            java.util.Collections.reverse(path);
            path.add(impl);
            throw new IllegalStateException("Circular dependency: "
                    + path.stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).collect(Collectors.joining(" -> ")));
        }
        if (impl.isInterface()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("No binding for " + type.getSimpleName());
        }
        resolving.push(impl);
        try {
            Constructor<?> ctor = impl.getConstructors()[0]; // (3)!
            Object[] args = new Object[ctor.getParameterCount()];
            for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) {
                args[i] = get(ctor.getParameterTypes()[i]);
            }
            Object instance = ctor.newInstance(args);
            singletons.put(impl, instance);
            return type.cast(instance);
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot create " + impl.getSimpleName(), e);
        } finally {
            resolving.pop();
        }
    }
}
  1. A binding maps an interface to an implementation, like a Spring @Bean method or @Component on the implementation.
  2. Cycle detection: if a class is requested while it is still being built, the graph has a cycle. Spring Boot fails startup the same way ("The dependencies of some of the beans form a cycle").
  3. Constructor autowiring by parameter type. Spring does this when a class has a single constructor, no @Autowired needed.
package com.handbook.enterprise.di.container;

/** Healthcare classes that know nothing about the container: plain constructors only. */
public final class Clinic {

    public interface PatientDirectory { String name(String patientId); }

    public interface ReminderChannel { String remind(String name, String when); }

    public static final class EmrDirectory implements PatientDirectory {
        public EmrDirectory() {
        }
        public String name(String patientId) { return patientId.equals("P-9") ? "Asha Rao" : "Unknown"; }
    }

    public static final class WhatsAppChannel implements ReminderChannel {
        public WhatsAppChannel() {
        }
        public String remind(String name, String when) { return "WhatsApp -> " + name + ": appointment " + when; }
    }

    public static final class AppointmentService {
        private final PatientDirectory directory;
        private final ReminderChannel channel;

        public AppointmentService(PatientDirectory directory, ReminderChannel channel) {
            this.directory = directory;
            this.channel = channel;
        }

        public String sendReminder(String patientId, String when) {
            return channel.remind(directory.name(patientId), when);
        }
    }

    // A deliberately broken pair: each needs the other.
    public static final class BillingService {
        public BillingService(InsuranceService insurance) {
        }
    }

    public static final class InsuranceService {
        public InsuranceService(BillingService billing) {
        }
    }

    private Clinic() {
    }
}

package com.handbook.enterprise.di.container;

import com.handbook.enterprise.di.container.Clinic.AppointmentService;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.container.Clinic.BillingService;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.container.Clinic.EmrDirectory;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.container.Clinic.PatientDirectory;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.container.Clinic.ReminderChannel;
import com.handbook.enterprise.di.container.Clinic.WhatsAppChannel;

public class ContainerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: A Tiny IoC Container Autowiring Constructors ===");
        MiniContainer container = new MiniContainer()
                .bind(PatientDirectory.class, EmrDirectory.class)
                .bind(ReminderChannel.class, WhatsAppChannel.class);

        AppointmentService service = container.get(AppointmentService.class);
        System.out.println(service.sendReminder("P-9", "Tue 10:30, Dr. Menon"));
        System.out.println("Same singleton on second lookup: " + (service == container.get(AppointmentService.class)));

        try {
            new MiniContainer().get(AppointmentService.class);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Missing binding  -> " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            container.get(BillingService.class);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Cycle at startup -> " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: A Tiny IoC Container Autowiring Constructors ===
WhatsApp -> Asha Rao: appointment Tue 10:30, Dr. Menon
Same singleton on second lookup: true
Missing binding  -> No binding for PatientDirectory
Cycle at startup -> Circular dependency: BillingService -> InsuranceService -> BillingService

Why a container here:

  • The classes stay plain Java: they don't import the container at all.
  • Wiring errors surface at startup, not on the first patient request.
  • Demystifies Spring: ApplicationContext is this idea plus scopes, proxies, lifecycle callbacks and configuration.

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Pure DI (no framework) A composition root in main. Perfect for libraries, CLIs, Lambdas and small services Reflection containers Spring, Guice, CDI (Jakarta EE). Scan, autowire, manage scopes and proxies at runtime Compile-time DI Dagger, Micronaut, Quarkus (ArC), Spring AOT. Generate wiring code at build time: fast startup, works with GraalVM native images Functional injection Pass a function (Supplier<Instant>, Function<String,Rate>) instead of an interface for one-method dependencies Records as dependency bundles record Deps(PaymentGateway p, Notifier n) when a factory needs many collaborators (but many dependencies is a smell: split the class)

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where DI in action Spring ApplicationContext, @Component + single-constructor autowiring, @Bean methods, @Qualifier, @Profile, ObjectProvider for lazy/optional Jakarta EE / Quarkus CDI @Inject, @ApplicationScoped, @Produces Google Guice / Dagger Module.bind(X.class).to(Y.class), @Provides; Dagger generates the code JDK java.time.Clock, ServiceLoader (a locator, not DI), HttpClient.newBuilder().executor(...) Testing @MockitoBean/@TestConfiguration in Spring Boot tests replace beans in the context

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Testable: pass fakes into constructors Indirection: "where does this come from?" needs IDE support with a container Honest APIs: the constructor lists every dependency Containers add startup time and "magic" (reflection, proxies) Swap implementations per environment without code changes Misconfiguration errors move from compile time to startup time with reflection containers Encourages small, single-purpose classes Easy to over-abstract: an interface for every class "just in case"

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Field injection

@Autowired private PaymentGateway gateway; hides the dependency, prevents final, and forces a Spring context (or reflection) into unit tests. Use a constructor. Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor removes the boilerplate.

Constructor over-injection

Eight constructor parameters isn't a DI problem, it's an SRP problem. DI just makes it visible. Split the class or introduce a facade.

Injecting the container

@Autowired ApplicationContext ctx; ctx.getBean(...) inside business code is the Service Locator anti-pattern wearing DI clothes.

Captive dependency

A singleton holding a request-scoped or prototype bean keeps the first instance forever. Use ObjectProvider<T> or a scoped proxy.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Composition root placement. Only the outermost layer (main, Spring @Configuration, the config package in hexagonal services) should know concrete classes. Your domain and application layers should compile without the framework on the classpath. ArchUnit can enforce that: "classes in ..domain.. must not depend on org.springframework..".

Startup vs. runtime cost. Reflection-based scanning of thousands of beans can take seconds, which matters for autoscaling and serverless. Spring AOT, Micronaut and Dagger move the graph computation to build time. Measure with -Dspring.context.startup / ApplicationStartup before optimizing.

Lifecycles and scopes. Singleton beans must be thread-safe (stateless or immutable). Request/session scopes are implemented with proxies that look up the real instance per call. Lazy beans hide startup failures until first use: prefer eager creation and fail fast.

War story: the Sunday surcharge that only failed on Sundays

A grocery app added a weekend delivery surcharge using LocalDate.now() inside the pricing service. Tests passed Monday to Saturday and failed every Sunday in CI, and nobody could reproduce the bug on weekdays. Worse, the nightly order-reconciliation job ran after midnight and priced Saturday orders as Sunday orders. Fix: Clock became a constructor dependency; the batch injected Clock.fixed(businessDate); tests pinned specific weekdays. Lesson: time, randomness and environment are dependencies. Inject them.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Dependency Injection Service Locator Factory Strategy Who finds the dependency An outside assembler pushes it in The class pulls it from a registry The class asks a factory to create it The caller passes a behaviour Dependencies visible in API ✅ Constructor ❌ Hidden Partly (the factory) ✅ Typical use All application wiring Legacy code, plugin systems Runtime choice of what to create Swapping an algorithm

DI is how you supply Strategies, Repositories, Adapters and Decorators. It is the practical tool for the Dependency Inversion Principle (the "D" in SOLID).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Don't new your collaborators; ask for them in the constructor.
  • Constructor injection by default; avoid field injection.
  • One composition root knows the concrete classes.
  • Clocks, random and env vars are dependencies too.
  • DI pushes, Service Locator pulls (and hides).
public CheckoutService(PaymentGateway payments, Notifier notifier, Clock clock) { ... }

docs.text:
• Add a @Profile-style switch to CompositionRoot driven by an environment variable.
  • Extend MiniContainer with a prototype scope (new instance per get).
  • Find a new SomethingClient() inside a service in your own code and move it to the constructor.

docs.title: Domain Events
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Enterprise / DDD Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Domain Event is an immutable record of something that happened in the business (OrderPlaced, PolicyLapsed), raised by an aggregate and handled by whoever cares, after the change is committed. Use it to keep aggregates small and decoupled: the order says what happened, and loyalty, SMS and the warehouse decide what to do about it.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: placeOrder() starts simple, then grows: award loyalty points, send an SMS, tell the warehouse, update analytics, notify the fraud team. Each addition makes the order module depend on another module, the transaction gets longer, and a failing SMS gateway now blocks orders.

Definition (Eric Evans; Vaughn Vernon, Implementing DDD):

Something that happened in the domain that domain experts care about, modelled as an immutable fact in the past tense. Aggregates publish events; other parts of the system subscribe and react, usually eventually consistent.

Domain event vs integration event:

Domain event Integration event Audience Same service / bounded context, in-process Other services, over a broker Shape Rich, can change with the model Public contract: versioned, minimal, stable Delivery After commit, in memory Through the Transactional Outbox

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A hospital PA announcement

When a baby is born, the nurse doesn't personally phone the paediatrician, the records office, the billing desk and the family. She announces "baby born in room 12". Each team knows what to do when it hears that. The nurse's job stays the same no matter how many teams start listening.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant UC as Use case participant O as Order (aggregate) participant Repo as Repository participant D as Dispatcher participant H1 as Loyalty handler participant H2 as SMS handler UC->>O: place() O->>O: record(OrderPlaced) UC->>Repo: save(order) (transaction) Note over UC,Repo: COMMIT UC->>D: dispatch(order.pullEvents()) D->>H1: OrderPlaced D->>H2: OrderPlaced Participant Responsibility Event Immutable record, past-tense name, ids + the facts handlers need, occurredAt Aggregate Records events as part of a state change; doesn't know the handlers Dispatcher / publisher Delivers events to handlers after commit (Spring ApplicationEventPublisher) Handlers React: update another aggregate, send notifications, write an outbox row

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
    orders.save(o);
    loyaltyService.addPoints(o.customerId(), o.total() / 100);   // order module depends on loyalty
    smsClient.send(o.phone(), "Order confirmed");                  // network call inside the transaction
    warehouseClient.startPicking(o.id());                          // another one
    analytics.track("order_placed", o);                            // and another
}
  • High coupling: every new reaction edits the order module.
  • Long, fragile transactions: an SMS timeout rolls back the order.
  • Side effects can happen even if the commit later fails.

docs.title: Example 1: Order Raises Events, Modules React (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery modular monolith has ordering, loyalty, notifications and warehouse modules. When an order is placed, loyalty awards 1 point per INR 100, notifications send an SMS and the warehouse starts picking. On cancellation only the warehouse cares. New listeners (analytics, referral bonus) are added every quarter, and the ordering team doesn't want to touch their code each time.

Design:

flowchart LR O[Order.place] -->|OrderPlaced| D{Dispatcher} D --> L[Loyalty] D --> S[SMS] D --> W[Warehouse] C[Order.cancel] -->|OrderCancelled| D

Full Code:

DomainEvents.javaOrder.javaGroceryEventsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** Aggregates RECORD events; the application layer DISPATCHES them after a successful commit. */
public final class DomainEvents {

    public sealed interface Event permits OrderPlaced, OrderCancelled { } // (1)!

    public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String customerId, long totalPaise) implements Event { }

    public record OrderCancelled(String orderId, String reason) implements Event { }

    /** Base class for roots: collects events in memory while the transaction runs. */
    public abstract static class AggregateRoot {
        private final List<Event> pending = new ArrayList<>();

        protected void record(Event e) { pending.add(e); } // (2)!

        public List<Event> pullEvents() {
            List<Event> out = List.copyOf(pending);
            pending.clear();
            return out;
        }
    }

    /** In-process publisher: handlers subscribe by event type. */
    public static final class Dispatcher {
        private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Event>>> handlers = new LinkedHashMap<>();

        public <E extends Event> Dispatcher on(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> handler) {
            handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e -> handler.accept(type.cast(e)));
            return this;
        }

        public void dispatch(List<Event> events) {
            for (Event e : events) {
                handlers.getOrDefault(e.getClass(), List.of()).forEach(h -> h.accept(e));
            }
        }
    }

    private DomainEvents() {
    }
}
  1. A sealed hierarchy lists every event this context can raise; records make each one an immutable fact.
  2. The aggregate only records events in memory; publishing is the application layer's job. Spring Data's AbstractAggregateRoot.registerEvent works the same way.
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery;

import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.AggregateRoot;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.OrderCancelled;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.OrderPlaced;

/** The aggregate states WHAT happened; it doesn't know who cares (loyalty, SMS, stock). */
public final class Order extends AggregateRoot {

    private final String id;
    private final String customerId;
    private final long totalPaise;
    private String status = "NEW";

    public Order(String id, String customerId, long totalPaise) {
        this.id = id;
        this.customerId = customerId;
        this.totalPaise = totalPaise;
    }

    public void place() {
        status = "PLACED";
        record(new OrderPlaced(id, customerId, totalPaise));
    }

    public void cancel(String reason) {
        if (!status.equals("PLACED")) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("only placed orders can be cancelled");
        }
        status = "CANCELLED";
        record(new OrderCancelled(id, reason));
    }
}

package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery;

import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.Dispatcher;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.OrderCancelled;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.OrderPlaced;

public class GroceryEventsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Order Raises Events, Other Modules React ===");
        Dispatcher dispatcher = new Dispatcher()
                .on(OrderPlaced.class, e -> System.out.println("  [loyalty]   +" + e.totalPaise() / 10_000 + " points for " + e.customerId()))
                .on(OrderPlaced.class, e -> System.out.println("  [sms]       'Order " + e.orderId() + " confirmed' -> " + e.customerId()))
                .on(OrderPlaced.class, e -> System.out.println("  [warehouse] start picking " + e.orderId()))
                .on(OrderCancelled.class, e -> System.out.println("  [warehouse] stop picking " + e.orderId() + " (" + e.reason() + ")"));

        Order order = new Order("ORD-31", "CUST-5", 1_245_000);
        order.place();
        System.out.println("Use case: order.place() then save in a transaction... committed. Dispatching:");
        dispatcher.dispatch(order.pullEvents()); // (1)!

        order.cancel("customer changed mind");
        System.out.println("Use case: order.cancel() committed. Dispatching:");
        dispatcher.dispatch(order.pullEvents());
        System.out.println("Events left after dispatch: " + order.pullEvents().size());
    }
}
  1. Events are pulled from the aggregate and dispatched after the commit. If the transaction had failed, they'd be discarded with it.

Output:

=== Grocery: Order Raises Events, Other Modules React ===
Use case: order.place() then save in a transaction... committed. Dispatching:
  [loyalty]   +124 points for CUST-5
  [sms]       'Order ORD-31 confirmed' -> CUST-5
  [warehouse] start picking ORD-31
Use case: order.cancel() committed. Dispatching:
  [warehouse] stop picking ORD-31 (customer changed mind)
Events left after dispatch: 0

Why domain events here:

  • Order has zero dependencies on loyalty, SMS or warehouse.
  • New reactions are new handlers; the order module is closed for modification (OCP).
  • Each handler can later move to its own service by switching to integration events.

docs.title: Example 2: Lab Results and Critical Values (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital lab system records 40,000 results a day. A potassium value below 2.5 or above 6.0 mmol/L is critical and must page the on-call doctor within minutes; normal values just go on the patient timeline. Amended results (e.g., a haemolysed sample re-run) must be flagged for review. Events carry the time they happened for the audit trail.

Design:

flowchart LR L[LabOrder.recordPotassium] --> R1["ResultRecorded(critical=false)"] --> T[Timeline] L --> R2["ResultRecorded(critical=true)"] --> P[Page on-call doctor] L --> A["ResultAmended"] --> V[Timeline + reviewer]

Full Code:

LabEvents.javaLabEventsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.healthcare;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Events as immutable facts in past tense, with when they happened, handled via pattern matching. */
public final class LabEvents {

    public sealed interface LabEvent permits ResultRecorded, ResultAmended {
        String patientId();
        Instant occurredAt();
    }

    public record ResultRecorded(String patientId, String test, double value, boolean critical, Instant occurredAt)
            implements LabEvent { }

    public record ResultAmended(String patientId, String test, double oldValue, double newValue, Instant occurredAt)
            implements LabEvent { }

    /** The aggregate: a lab order that knows the critical thresholds. */
    public static final class LabOrder {
        private final String patientId;
        private final Clock clock;
        private final List<LabEvent> events = new ArrayList<>();
        private Double potassium;

        public LabOrder(String patientId, Clock clock) {
            this.patientId = patientId;
            this.clock = clock;
        }

        public void recordPotassium(double mmolPerL) {
            boolean critical = mmolPerL < 2.5 || mmolPerL > 6.0; // (1)!
            if (potassium == null) {
                events.add(new ResultRecorded(patientId, "K+", mmolPerL, critical, clock.instant()));
            } else {
                events.add(new ResultAmended(patientId, "K+", potassium, mmolPerL, clock.instant()));
            }
            potassium = mmolPerL;
        }

        public List<LabEvent> pullEvents() {
            List<LabEvent> out = List.copyOf(events);
            events.clear();
            return out;
        }
    }

    /** Handler with an exhaustive switch: adding a new event type breaks compilation until handled. */
    public static String describe(LabEvent e) {
        return switch (e) { // (2)!
            case ResultRecorded r when r.critical() -> "PAGE on-call doctor: " + r.test() + "=" + r.value() + " for " + r.patientId();
            case ResultRecorded r -> "timeline: " + r.test() + "=" + r.value();
            case ResultAmended a -> "timeline: " + a.test() + " amended " + a.oldValue() + " -> " + a.newValue() + " (notify reviewer)";
        };
    }

    private LabEvents() {
    }
}
  1. The aggregate decides what is critical; the event carries that decision as a fact, so handlers don't re-implement clinical rules.
  2. An exhaustive switch over a sealed interface: add a new event type and every handler that doesn't handle it stops compiling.
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.healthcare;

import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.healthcare.LabEvents.LabOrder;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;

public class LabEventsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: Lab Results as Domain Events ===");
        Clock clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-02-10T03:15:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
        LabOrder ward = new LabOrder("PAT-17", clock);
        ward.recordPotassium(4.1);
        LabOrder icu = new LabOrder("PAT-88", clock);
        icu.recordPotassium(6.8);
        icu.recordPotassium(5.9); // re-run after haemolysed sample

        for (LabOrder order : new LabOrder[] {ward, icu}) {
            order.pullEvents().forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.occurredAt() + " " + LabEvents.describe(e)));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: Lab Results as Domain Events ===
2026-02-10T03:15:00Z timeline: K+=4.1
2026-02-10T03:15:00Z PAGE on-call doctor: K+=6.8 for PAT-88
2026-02-10T03:15:00Z timeline: K+ amended 6.8 -> 5.9 (notify reviewer)

Why domain events here:

  • Events are facts with timestamps, which is exactly what clinical audit needs.
  • Paging, timelines and review queues evolve independently of the lab model.
  • Pattern matching keeps handlers explicit and complete.

docs.title: Example 3: Domain Event to Integration Event (Insurance)
docs.text:
Scenario: When a policy lapses (three missed premiums), the policy service's own modules react in-process (renewals schedules a win-back call, claims blocks new claims). Other services (CRM, marketing, the data lake) also need to know, but must not see underwriter notes or internal risk scores, and they need a stable, versioned contract. The integration event is written to the outbox in the same transaction.

Design:

flowchart LR P[Policy aggregate] -->|"PolicyLapsed: rich, internal"| H[In-process handlers] P --> M[Mapper] -->|"PolicyLapsedV1: public"| OB[(Outbox row)] --> K[[Kafka: insurance.policy.lapsed.v1]]

Full Code:

PolicyEvents.javaPolicyEventsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.insurance;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;

/** Domain events stay internal and rich; integration events are a public, versioned contract. */
public final class PolicyEvents {

    /** Internal: can change freely with the model. Contains data other teams must not depend on. */
    public record PolicyLapsed(String policyId, String customerId, LocalDate lapsedOn, int missedPremiums,
                               String underwriterNotes, double internalRiskScore) { }

    /** Public: what other services may rely on. Stable names, a schema version, no internals. */
    public record PolicyLapsedV1(int schemaVersion, String eventType, String policyId, String customerId, String lapsedOn) { }

    public static PolicyLapsedV1 toIntegrationEvent(PolicyLapsed e) { // (1)!
        return new PolicyLapsedV1(1, "insurance.policy.lapsed.v1", e.policyId(), e.customerId(), e.lapsedOn().toString());
    }

    public static Map<String, String> outboxRow(PolicyLapsedV1 e) { // (2)!
        return Map.of("topic", "insurance.policy.lapsed.v1", "key", e.policyId(),
                "payload", "{\"schemaVersion\":1,\"policyId\":\"" + e.policyId() + "\",\"customerId\":\"" + e.customerId()
                        + "\",\"lapsedOn\":\"" + e.lapsedOn() + "\"}");
    }

    private PolicyEvents() {
    }
}
  1. An explicit mapping from the internal event to the public contract: anything not copied stays private.
  2. The integration event is stored as an outbox row in the same transaction; a relay publishes it to the broker.
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.insurance;

import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.insurance.PolicyEvents.PolicyLapsed;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.insurance.PolicyEvents.PolicyLapsedV1;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class PolicyEventsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Insurance: Domain Event -> Integration Event -> Outbox ===");
        PolicyLapsed internal = new PolicyLapsed("POL-2207", "CUST-41", LocalDate.of(2026, 4, 1), 3,
                "Customer called twice about premium hike", 0.82);
        System.out.println("In-process handlers see : " + internal);
        System.out.println("  [renewals] schedule win-back call; [claims] block new claims on POL-2207");

        PolicyLapsedV1 published = PolicyEvents.toIntegrationEvent(internal);
        System.out.println("Other services receive  : " + published);
        Map<String, String> row = new TreeMap<>(PolicyEvents.outboxRow(published));
        System.out.println("Outbox row (same DB transaction as the lapse): " + row);
        System.out.println("Notes and risk score never leave the policy service.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Insurance: Domain Event -> Integration Event -> Outbox ===
In-process handlers see : PolicyLapsed[policyId=POL-2207, customerId=CUST-41, lapsedOn=2026-04-01, missedPremiums=3, underwriterNotes=Customer called twice about premium hike, internalRiskScore=0.82]
  [renewals] schedule win-back call; [claims] block new claims on POL-2207
Other services receive  : PolicyLapsedV1[schemaVersion=1, eventType=insurance.policy.lapsed.v1, policyId=POL-2207, customerId=CUST-41, lapsedOn=2026-04-01]
Outbox row (same DB transaction as the lapse): {key=POL-2207, payload={"schemaVersion":1,"policyId":"POL-2207","customerId":"CUST-41","lapsedOn":"2026-04-01"}, topic=insurance.policy.lapsed.v1}
Notes and risk score never leave the policy service.

Why two kinds of event here:

  • The internal model can evolve without breaking other teams.
  • Sensitive data is never published by accident.
  • The outbox makes cross-service delivery reliable without distributed transactions.
Unit Tests: DomainEventsTest.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents;

import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.Dispatcher;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.DomainEvents.OrderPlaced;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.grocery.Order;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.healthcare.LabEvents;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.healthcare.LabEvents.LabOrder;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.healthcare.LabEvents.ResultRecorded;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.insurance.PolicyEvents;
import com.handbook.enterprise.domainevents.insurance.PolicyEvents.PolicyLapsed;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DomainEventsTest {

    @Test
    void aggregateRecordsEventsAndPullClearsThem() {
        Order o = new Order("O", "C", 100);
        o.place();
        assertThat(o.pullEvents()).containsExactly(new OrderPlaced("O", "C", 100));
        assertThat(o.pullEvents()).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void dispatcherRoutesByType() {
        List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>();
        Order o = new Order("O", "C", 100);
        o.place();
        o.cancel("x");
        new Dispatcher().on(OrderPlaced.class, e -> seen.add(e.orderId())).dispatch(o.pullEvents());
        assertThat(seen).containsExactly("O");
    }

    @Test
    void criticalResultsPageTheDoctor() {
        LabOrder lab = new LabOrder("P", Clock.systemUTC());
        lab.recordPotassium(2.0);
        var event = lab.pullEvents().get(0);
        assertThat(event).isInstanceOf(ResultRecorded.class);
        assertThat(LabEvents.describe(event)).startsWith("PAGE");
    }

    @Test
    void integrationEventDropsInternalFields() {
        var v1 = PolicyEvents.toIntegrationEvent(new PolicyLapsed("P", "C", LocalDate.EPOCH, 3, "secret", 0.9));
        assertThat(v1.toString()).doesNotContain("secret").doesNotContain("0.9");
        assertThat(v1.schemaVersion()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Record & dispatch after commit (Example 1) Aggregate collects; application dispatches after save commits Static DomainEvents.raise(...) Udi Dahan's original style: convenient but hidden global state; harder to test Spring @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) Handler runs only if the transaction commits; @Async to decouple further Spring Modulith @ApplicationModuleListener + an event publication registry (persisted, retried) between modules Event sourcing Domain events are the state (Event Sourcing) Sealed + records + pattern matching Exhaustive, type-safe event handling (Example 2)

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Domain events Spring ApplicationEventPublisher, @EventListener, @TransactionalEventListener, Spring Data AbstractAggregateRoot / @DomainEvents Spring Modulith Module-to-module events with an outbox-like publication log, Scenario testing API Axon AggregateLifecycle.apply(event), event handlers, sagas Jakarta CDI Event<T>.fire(), @Observes(during = TransactionPhase.AFTER_SUCCESS) Debezium / outbox Integration events leave the database via CDC

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Decouples the aggregate from its consequences Flow is harder to follow ("who handles this?") Small transactions; side effects outside them Eventual consistency between aggregates Natural audit trail and integration point Handler failures need retries and monitoring Easy to add reactions (OCP) Event schemas become contracts to version

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Publishing before commit

Sending the SMS inside the transaction means a later commit failure leaves the customer with a confirmation for an order that doesn't exist (coding challenge). Dispatch after commit, or use an outbox.

Leaking internal events to other services

Publishing domain events straight to Kafka turns every internal refactor into a breaking change and may leak sensitive fields. Map to integration events.

Command disguised as an event

SendSmsEvent is a command with one intended receiver. Events describe what happened (OrderPlaced), not what someone should do.

Fat events vs thin events

Thin events ({orderId}) force every handler to call back for data; fat events (full order) couple consumers to your model. Include what consumers need to act, plus ids.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Delivery guarantees in-process. @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) runs after commit, but if the JVM crashes in between, the event is lost. For must-not-lose reactions inside one service, persist the event (Spring Modulith's publication registry, or your own outbox table) and retry until handlers succeed.

Ordering and idempotency. Handlers should tolerate duplicates (an at-least-once relay) and out-of-order arrival. Include the aggregate id and a sequence/version so consumers can detect gaps or stale events.

Events as the integration backbone. Once integration events flow through a broker, they become the API between teams: give each a schema in a registry (Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema), a topic naming convention (<context>.<aggregate>.<event>.v1) and compatibility rules (backward-compatible changes only).

War story: the confirmation for a phantom order

A grocery checkout sent the "order confirmed" SMS from inside the @Transactional method. On busy evenings, a unique-constraint violation on the invoice number occasionally failed the commit after the SMS was sent. About 200 customers a week waited for orders that didn't exist and then called support. Fix: the aggregate records OrderPlaced; the SMS handler became an @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) reading from a persisted publication log. Lesson: side effects follow the commit, never precede it.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Domain Event Observer Integration Event Command Meaning A business fact "Something changed" callback Business fact as a public contract A request to do something Coupling Aggregate doesn't know handlers Subject holds observer list Producer doesn't know consumers Sender knows the receiver Delivery In-process, after commit Immediate, synchronous Broker via outbox Direct call / queue

Domain events are the domain-level form of Observer; across services they travel via Transactional Outbox to Idempotent Consumers.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Past-tense, immutable business facts raised by aggregates.
  • Record during the change; dispatch after commit.
  • Handlers decouple consequences from the aggregate.
  • Domain events internal; integration events public, versioned, via outbox.
  • Handlers idempotent; events carry ids and occurredAt.
@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT) void on(OrderPlaced e) { sms.send(...); }

docs.text:

  • Make Dispatcher catch handler exceptions so one failing handler doesn't stop the others; log the failure.
  • Map OrderPlaced to an integration event ordering.order.placed.v1 with only ids and total.
