docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Enterprise Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Repository looks like an in-memory collection of domain objects (save, findBySku, lowStock) and hides how they are stored. Use it whenever business logic needs to load or save aggregates, so the logic never contains SQL, JPA queries or HTTP calls to a storage service.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: when a restock rule contains SELECT ... WHERE stock < ? and ResultSet mapping, three things go wrong. You can't unit-test the rule without a database; changing the schema means editing business code; and the same query gets copy-pasted into five services with five slightly different bugs.

Definition (Martin Fowler, PoEAA; Eric Evans, DDD):

Mediates between the domain and data mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects. In DDD, there is one repository per aggregate root.

In a hexagonal service the repository interface is a port in the domain layer; the JDBC/JPA class is an adapter in infrastructure.

Repository vs DAO: a DAO mirrors a table (insertRow, updateColumn) and lives in the data layer. A Repository speaks the domain's language (overdue(asOf), lowStock(threshold)), returns whole aggregates, and its interface belongs to the domain. A repository is often implemented with one or more DAOs.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A library's front desk

You ask the librarian for "the latest edition of Clean Code". You don't care whether it's on shelf 4B, in the basement archive or on loan from another branch. The desk (repository) speaks in books and editions, not in shelf coordinates (tables and rows).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class RestockService { +restockLowItems() } class ProductRepository { <<interface, domain port>> +save(Product) +findBySku(String) Optional~Product~ +lowStock(int) List~Product~ } class InMemoryProductRepository class JdbcProductRepository { -DataSource ds } class Product { <<aggregate root>> } RestockService --> ProductRepository InMemoryProductRepository ..|> ProductRepository JdbcProductRepository ..|> ProductRepository ProductRepository ..> Product Participant Responsibility Aggregate root (Product) The domain object that is loaded and saved as a unit Repository interface Domain-language operations; owned by the domain/application layer Repository implementation SQL/JPA/NoSQL/HTTP details, mapping rows ↔ objects, optimistic locking Client (RestockService) Business logic that only sees the interface

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public List<String> restockLowItems(int threshold) throws SQLException {
    try (var c = dataSource.getConnection();
         var ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT sku, stock FROM product WHERE stock < ?")) {   // SQL in business code
        ps.setInt(1, threshold);
        var rs = ps.executeQuery();
        while (rs.next()) { /* mapping + business rule + UPDATE, all tangled */ }
    }
}
  • Business rule untestable without a database.
  • SRP violation: persistence and policy in one method.
  • Queries duplicated wherever products are needed.

docs.title: Example 1: One Restock Service, Two Adapters (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A dark store tracks 8,000 SKUs. Every 15 minutes a job tops up anything below 10 units. The rule must be unit-tested in milliseconds and run against PostgreSQL in production. Both adapters must behave identically, so a single contract test runs against each.

Design:

flowchart LR S[RestockService] --> P{{ProductRepository port}} P -.-> M[InMemoryProductRepository<br/>unit tests, demos] P -.-> J[JdbcProductRepository<br/>H2 / PostgreSQL]

Full Code:

ProductRepository.javaJdbcProductRepository.javaInMemoryProductRepository.javaRestockService.javaProduct.javaGroceryRepositoryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/** The port: a collection-like interface in the language of the domain. */
public interface ProductRepository { // (1)!

    void save(Product product);

    Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku);

    List<Product> lowStock(int threshold); // (2)!
}
  1. The interface speaks domain language and returns domain objects. No ResultSet, no EntityManager.
  2. An intention-revealing finder. Prefer lowStock(threshold) over a generic findBy(String where).
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Adapter #2: real SQL (H2 here, PostgreSQL in production). All mapping lives here. */
public final class JdbcProductRepository implements ProductRepository {

    private final DataSource ds;

    public JdbcProductRepository(DataSource ds) {
        this.ds = ds;
    }

    public void save(Product p) {
        sql("MERGE INTO product (sku, name, category, price_paise, stock) KEY (sku) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", ps -> { // (1)!
            ps.setString(1, p.sku());
            ps.setString(2, p.name());
            ps.setString(3, p.category());
            ps.setLong(4, p.pricePaise());
            ps.setInt(5, p.stock());
            ps.executeUpdate();
            return null;
        });
    }

    public Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku) {
        return sql("SELECT * FROM product WHERE sku = ?", ps -> {
            ps.setString(1, sku);
            List<Product> found = map(ps.executeQuery());
            return found.stream().findFirst();
        });
    }

    public List<Product> lowStock(int threshold) {
        return sql("SELECT * FROM product WHERE stock < ? ORDER BY sku", ps -> {
            ps.setInt(1, threshold);
            return map(ps.executeQuery());
        });
    }

    private static List<Product> map(ResultSet rs) throws SQLException { // (2)!
        List<Product> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (rs.next()) {
            out.add(new Product(rs.getString("sku"), rs.getString("name"), rs.getString("category"),
                    rs.getLong("price_paise"), rs.getInt("stock")));
        }
        return out;
    }

    private interface Body<T> { T run(PreparedStatement ps) throws SQLException; }

    private <T> T sql(String sql, Body<T> body) {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            return body.run(ps);
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }
}
  1. save is an upsert: callers think "put it in the collection", not "insert vs update".
  2. All row ↔ object mapping is here. Schema changes stop at this file.
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

/** Adapter #1: for unit tests and local demos. */
public final class InMemoryProductRepository implements ProductRepository {

    private final Map<String, Product> rows = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void save(Product product) { rows.put(product.sku(), product); }

    public Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku) { return Optional.ofNullable(rows.get(sku)); }

    public List<Product> lowStock(int threshold) {
        return rows.values().stream().filter(p -> p.stock() < threshold)
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Product::sku)).toList();
    }
}

package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery;

import java.util.List;

/** Application logic written once against the port; works with any adapter. */
public final class RestockService {

    private final ProductRepository products;

    public RestockService(ProductRepository products) {
        this.products = products;
    }

    public List<String> restockLowItems(int threshold, int topUpTo) {
        return products.lowStock(threshold).stream().map(p -> {
            products.save(p.withStock(topUpTo));
            return p.sku() + " " + p.stock() + "->" + topUpTo;
        }).toList();
    }
}

package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery;

/** Domain object. Knows nothing about SQL. */
public record Product(String sku, String name, String category, long pricePaise, int stock) {

    public Product withStock(int newStock) {
        return new Product(sku, name, category, pricePaise, newStock);
    }
}

package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery;

import org.h2.jdbcx.JdbcDataSource;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.List;

public class GroceryRepositoryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: One Restock Service, Two Repository Adapters ===");
        JdbcDataSource ds = new JdbcDataSource();
        ds.setURL("jdbc:h2:mem:catalog;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1");
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE product (sku VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR, category VARCHAR,"
                    + " price_paise BIGINT, stock INT)");
        }
        for (ProductRepository repo : List.of(new InMemoryProductRepository(), new JdbcProductRepository(ds))) {
            repo.save(new Product("MILK-1L", "Toned Milk 1L", "dairy", 6_800, 4));
            repo.save(new Product("ATTA-5KG", "Wheat Atta 5kg", "staples", 28_500, 40));
            repo.save(new Product("EGG-12", "Eggs (12)", "dairy", 9_000, 2));
            List<String> restocked = new RestockService(repo).restockLowItems(10, 50);
            System.out.printf("%-26s restocked %s, MILK-1L stock now %d%n", repo.getClass().getSimpleName(), restocked,
                    repo.findBySku("MILK-1L").orElseThrow().stock());
        }
        System.out.println("RestockService has no SQL and no Map: storage is a detail behind the port.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: One Restock Service, Two Repository Adapters ===
InMemoryProductRepository  restocked [EGG-12 2->50, MILK-1L 4->50], MILK-1L stock now 50
JdbcProductRepository      restocked [EGG-12 2->50, MILK-1L 4->50], MILK-1L stock now 50
RestockService has no SQL and no Map: storage is a detail behind the port.

Why a repository here:

  • The restock rule is tested against the in-memory adapter in microseconds.
  • The same contract test (see Unit Tests) runs against both adapters, so the fake can't drift from reality.
  • Switching PostgreSQL for DynamoDB touches one class.

docs.title: Example 2: Optimistic Locking in the Repository (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A savings account has INR 10,000. The customer withdraws INR 8,000 at an ATM while a UPI payment of INR 7,000 is in flight. Both channels loaded the same balance. Without protection, the second save overwrites the first and the bank loses INR 7,000 (a lost update). The repository rejects stale writes using a version number, like UPDATE account SET ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant ATM participant UPI participant R as AccountRepository ATM->>R: findById (v1, 10,000) UPI->>R: findById (v1, 10,000) ATM->>R: save(balance 2,000, v1) ✅ now v2 UPI->>R: save(balance 3,000, v1) ❌ stale UPI->>R: findById (v2, 2,000) → withdraw 7,000 → insufficient funds

Full Code:

AccountRepository.javaBankingRepositoryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.banking;

import java.util.ConcurrentModificationException;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Repository that protects aggregates with optimistic locking (a version column). */
public final class AccountRepository {

    public record Account(String id, long balancePaise, long version) {
        public Account withdraw(long paise) {
            if (paise > balancePaise) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("insufficient funds");
            }
            return new Account(id, balancePaise - paise, version);
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, Account> table = new HashMap<>();

    public synchronized Optional<Account> findById(String id) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(table.get(id));
    }

    /** Saves only if nobody else saved since we loaded: UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? */
    public synchronized Account save(Account changed) { // (1)!
        Account current = table.get(changed.id());
        long expected = current == null ? 0 : current.version();
        if (changed.version() != expected) {
            throw new ConcurrentModificationException("Account " + changed.id() + " was modified (expected v"
                    + changed.version() + ", found v" + expected + ")");
        }
        Account stored = new Account(changed.id(), changed.balancePaise(), expected + 1);
        table.put(stored.id(), stored);
        return stored;
    }
}
  1. The repository enforces optimistic concurrency: the save succeeds only if the stored version equals the version the caller loaded. JPA does this with @Version.
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.banking;

import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.banking.AccountRepository.Account;

import java.util.ConcurrentModificationException;

public class BankingRepositoryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Repository with Optimistic Locking ===");
        AccountRepository accounts = new AccountRepository();
        accounts.save(new Account("SB-501", 1_000_000, 0));

        Account atm = accounts.findById("SB-501").orElseThrow();    // two channels load v1
        Account upi = accounts.findById("SB-501").orElseThrow();
        System.out.println("ATM and UPI both loaded " + atm);

        System.out.println("ATM saves  -> " + accounts.save(atm.withdraw(800_000)));
        try {
            accounts.save(upi.withdraw(700_000));                   // based on the stale balance
        } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
            System.out.println("UPI rejected: " + e.getMessage());
            Account fresh = accounts.findById("SB-501").orElseThrow(); // (1)!
            try {
                accounts.save(fresh.withdraw(700_000));
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException again) {
                System.out.println("UPI retried on fresh state: " + again.getMessage() + " (no overdraft)");
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. The correct reaction to a version conflict: reload and re-run the business rule on fresh state, never blindly retry the same write.

Output:

=== Banking: Repository with Optimistic Locking ===
ATM and UPI both loaded Account[id=SB-501, balancePaise=1000000, version=1]
ATM saves  -> Account[id=SB-501, balancePaise=200000, version=2]
UPI rejected: Account SB-501 was modified (expected v1, found v2)
UPI retried on fresh state: insufficient funds (no overdraft)

Why a repository here:

  • Concurrency control belongs with persistence, so every caller gets it for free.
  • The aggregate (Account) still enforces its own invariant (no overdraft).
  • Callers work with whole aggregates, never with half-updated rows.

docs.title: Example 3: Domain Finders and a Caching Decorator (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A courier's tracking page is refreshed about 1,000 times per parcel on delivery day. Ops also run an "overdue shipments" report. The tracking lookup should be cached; the report must always be fresh. Because callers depend on the ShipmentRepository interface, caching is added as a decorator without touching them.

Design:

flowchart LR T[Tracking page] --> C[CachingShipmentRepository] O[Ops report] --> C C -->|"byAwb: cache miss only"| D[DbShipmentRepository] C -->|"overdue: always"| D

Full Code:

Shipments.javaLogisticsRepositoryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Intention-revealing finders plus a caching decorator over the repository port. */
public final class Shipments {

    public record Shipment(String awb, String city, LocalDate promised, boolean delivered) {
    }

    public interface ShipmentRepository {
        Optional<Shipment> byAwb(String awb);
        List<Shipment> overdue(LocalDate asOf); // (1)!
    }

    /** Pretend database that counts round trips. */
    public static final class DbShipmentRepository implements ShipmentRepository {
        private final Map<String, Shipment> rows = new HashMap<>();
        public int queries;

        public DbShipmentRepository add(Shipment s) {
            rows.put(s.awb(), s);
            return this;
        }

        public Optional<Shipment> byAwb(String awb) {
            queries++;
            return Optional.ofNullable(rows.get(awb));
        }

        public List<Shipment> overdue(LocalDate asOf) {
            queries++;
            return rows.values().stream().filter(s -> !s.delivered() && s.promised().isBefore(asOf))
                    .sorted(java.util.Comparator.comparing(Shipment::awb)).toList();
        }
    }

    /** Decorator: same port, adds a read-through cache for hot tracking lookups. */
    public static final class CachingShipmentRepository implements ShipmentRepository { // (2)!
        private final ShipmentRepository inner;
        private final Map<String, Optional<Shipment>> cache = new HashMap<>();

        public CachingShipmentRepository(ShipmentRepository inner) {
            this.inner = inner;
        }

        public Optional<Shipment> byAwb(String awb) { return cache.computeIfAbsent(awb, inner::byAwb); }

        public List<Shipment> overdue(LocalDate asOf) { return inner.overdue(asOf); } // reports always go to the DB
    }

    private Shipments() {
    }
}
  1. A domain question as a method (overdue(asOf)), not findByDeliveredFalseAndPromisedBefore. Spring Data can generate either; the domain name reads better at call sites.
  2. A decorator implementing the same port: callers can't tell it's there.
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics;

import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.CachingShipmentRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.DbShipmentRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.Shipment;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.ShipmentRepository;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public class LogisticsRepositoryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Domain Finders and a Caching Repository ===");
        DbShipmentRepository db = new DbShipmentRepository()
                .add(new Shipment("AWB-1", "Pune", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 1), true))
                .add(new Shipment("AWB-2", "Delhi", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2), false))
                .add(new Shipment("AWB-3", "Chennai", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 9), false));
        ShipmentRepository repo = new CachingShipmentRepository(db);

        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
            repo.byAwb("AWB-2"); // customers refreshing the tracking page
        }
        System.out.println("1,000 tracking lookups -> DB queries: " + db.queries);
        System.out.println("Overdue as of 2026-03-05: " + repo.overdue(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 5)).stream()
                .map(s -> s.awb() + " (" + s.city() + ")").toList());
        System.out.println("DB queries after report: " + db.queries);
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Domain Finders and a Caching Repository ===
1,000 tracking lookups -> DB queries: 1
Overdue as of 2026-03-05: [AWB-2 (Delhi)]
DB queries after report: 2

Why a repository here:

  • An interface gives you a seam for cross-cutting concerns (caching, metrics, tenant filters).
  • Finder names document the business questions the system answers.
  • The cached and uncached paths are explicit, not hidden in an ORM's second-level cache.
Unit Tests: RepositoryTest.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.repository;

import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.banking.AccountRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.banking.AccountRepository.Account;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery.InMemoryProductRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery.JdbcProductRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery.Product;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.grocery.ProductRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.CachingShipmentRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.DbShipmentRepository;
import com.handbook.enterprise.repository.logistics.Shipments.Shipment;
import org.h2.jdbcx.JdbcDataSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.ConcurrentModificationException;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.UUID;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class RepositoryTest {

    static List<ProductRepository> adapters() throws Exception {
        JdbcDataSource ds = new JdbcDataSource();
        ds.setURL("jdbc:h2:mem:" + UUID.randomUUID() + ";DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1");
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE product (sku VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR, category VARCHAR,"
                    + " price_paise BIGINT, stock INT)");
        }
        return List.of(new InMemoryProductRepository(), new JdbcProductRepository(ds));
    }

    /** One contract, every adapter: the in-memory fake can't drift from the real one. */
    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("adapters")
    void everyAdapterHonoursTheSameContract(ProductRepository repo) {
        repo.save(new Product("A", "a", "x", 100, 1));
        repo.save(new Product("B", "b", "x", 100, 99));
        repo.save(new Product("A", "a", "x", 100, 5)); // upsert
        assertThat(repo.findBySku("A")).get().extracting(Product::stock).isEqualTo(5);
        assertThat(repo.findBySku("missing")).isEmpty();
        assertThat(repo.lowStock(10)).extracting(Product::sku).containsExactly("A");
    }

    @Test
    void staleWritesAreRejected() {
        AccountRepository repo = new AccountRepository();
        repo.save(new Account("X", 100, 0));
        Account a = repo.findById("X").orElseThrow();
        repo.save(a.withdraw(10));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> repo.save(a.withdraw(20))).isInstanceOf(ConcurrentModificationException.class);
        assertThat(repo.findById("X").orElseThrow().balancePaise()).isEqualTo(90);
    }

    @Test
    void cachingDecoratorHitsTheDatabaseOnce() {
        DbShipmentRepository db = new DbShipmentRepository().add(new Shipment("A", "P", LocalDate.EPOCH, false));
        CachingShipmentRepository repo = new CachingShipmentRepository(db);
        repo.byAwb("A");
        repo.byAwb("A");
        assertThat(db.queries).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Spring Data repositories interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, String>: derived queries, @Query, paging. Fast to write; leaks JPA types into callers unless you wrap it Port + adapter (hexagonal) Your own interface in domain; a Spring Data repository used inside the adapter. Keeps the domain framework-free Specification-based findAll(Specification<T>) for dynamic filters (see Specification) Read-only query repositories For CQRS read models: return DTOs/projections, not aggregates Records as aggregates Immutable records + withX methods; the repository saves the new version

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Repository Spring Data CrudRepository, JpaRepository, MongoRepository, R2dbcRepository, @Repository (also translates exceptions to DataAccessException) Jakarta Data (EE 11) @Repository interfaces with @Find, @Insert, @Query Hibernate / JPA EntityManager is the Unit of Work underneath; @Version for optimistic locking Micronaut Data Compile-time generated repositories Axon / event-sourced systems Repository<Aggregate> that loads by replaying events

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Business logic is storage-agnostic and unit-testable Another layer of interfaces and mapping code Queries live in one place, named by intent Easy to over-generalize into a leaky "generic repository" Seam for caching, auditing, multi-tenancy, optimistic locking Hides query cost: an innocent findAll() can load a million rows One repository per aggregate enforces consistency boundaries Mapping domain ↔ entity is extra work in rich domains

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Generic repository with findBy(String where)

Repository<T>.query(String sql) pushes SQL back into business code and makes every caller depend on the schema. Expose named, typed finders.

Returning IQueryable-style builders or JPA entities everywhere

If callers build CriteriaQuery or touch lazy-loaded @Entity graphs, the repository hides nothing. Lazy-loading outside a transaction becomes LazyInitializationException in a controller.

One repository per table

Repositories are per aggregate root. An OrderLineRepository lets code modify lines without going through Order, bypassing its invariants.

In-memory fakes that don't copy

A HashMap that hands out stored objects lets tests "save" without calling save(). See the coding challenge.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Where transactions go. The repository does not open transactions per call; the application service (use case) owns the transaction boundary (@Transactional) so several repository calls commit together. That's the Unit of Work.

Performance. Design finders for the access patterns you actually have: lowStock(threshold) can use an index on stock; a generic findAll().stream().filter(...) can't. Watch for N+1 queries when aggregates contain collections; use fetch joins or batch loading inside the adapter.

Contract tests for adapters. Write one abstract test suite for the port and run it against the in-memory and the real adapter (Testcontainers PostgreSQL in CI). That is what keeps fakes honest.

War story: the fake that hid a lost update

A team's checkout tests used an in-memory InventoryRepository backed by a HashMap that returned stored objects directly. A refactor dropped a save() call; tests still passed because the mutated object was the stored one. In production with JPA in a read-only transaction, stock never decreased and the store oversold 400 units of mangoes during a sale. Fix: the fake now copies in and out, and the same contract suite runs against the JPA adapter with Testcontainers. Lesson: a fake repository must behave like a database, not like a shared object.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Repository DAO Active Record Unit of Work Speaks in Aggregates, domain terms Tables, rows The object saves itself (order.save()) Changes to track Interface owned by Domain Data layer The entity Infrastructure Best for Rich domains, hexagonal Simple data access CRUD apps (Rails, Panache) Committing many changes atomically

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Collection-like interface for aggregates; hides storage.
  • Interface in the domain, implementation in infrastructure.
  • One repository per aggregate root; named, intention-revealing finders.
  • Optimistic locking (@Version) belongs here; transactions belong in the use case.
  • Contract-test every adapter, including the fake.
interface ProductRepository { void save(Product p); Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku); List<Product> lowStock(int t); }

docs.text:
• Add delete(String sku) to the port and both adapters, with a contract test.
  • Add a version column to JdbcProductRepository and reject stale saves.
  • Add a metrics decorator that counts calls per finder.

docs.title: Unit of Work & Identity Map
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Enterprise Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Unit of Work tracks every object a business transaction creates, changes or deletes, and writes them all in one database transaction at the end. An Identity Map makes sure each record is loaded into exactly one object per unit of work. You use both every day: JPA's EntityManager / Hibernate's Session is a unit of work with an identity map (the persistence context).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: placing a grocery order inserts an order row, inserts several line rows and decrements stock for each product. If every repository call commits on its own and the third write fails, you're left with an order that has no lines, or stock taken for an order that doesn't exist. Separately, if two parts of the same request load the same booking, they get two different objects; one changes the seat, the other still has the old one and may save it back.

Definitions (Martin Fowler, PoEAA):

Unit of Work: maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates the writing out of changes and the resolution of concurrency problems.

Identity Map: ensures that each object gets loaded only once by keeping every loaded object in a map. Looks up objects using the map when referring to them.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A supermarket trolley and the checkout counter

You walk the aisles adding and removing items (registering changes), but nothing is paid for until the checkout (commit). If your card is declined, the whole trolley is rejected, not half of it. And there's only one trolley per shopper: you don't push two trolleys holding different versions of your shopping (identity map).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class UseCase { +place(order) } class UnitOfWork { -List pending +registerNew(obj) +registerDirty(obj) +registerRemoved(obj) +commit() } class IdentityMap~K,V~ { -Map loaded +get(K) V } class Mapper~T~ { <<interface>> +insert() +update() +delete() } UseCase --> UnitOfWork UnitOfWork --> Mapper UnitOfWork --> IdentityMap Participant Responsibility Unit of Work Tracks new / dirty / removed objects; opens one transaction on commit; rolls back on failure Identity Map One in-memory object per database identity within the unit of work Mapper Knows how to write one kind of object (SQL); the unit of work orders and calls them Use case / application service Starts a unit of work, runs business logic, commits

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
orderRepo.insert(order);            // auto-commit #1
for (Line l : lines) {
    lineRepo.insert(l);             // auto-commit #2, #3
    stockRepo.decrement(l.sku(), l.qty());   // auto-commit #4 ... throws: stock would go negative
}
// The order and some lines are already committed. Manual cleanup code? Hope?
  • No atomicity: partial writes survive failures.
  • Many round trips and commits instead of one.
  • Duplicate objects for the same row → lost updates inside one request.

docs.title: Example 1: Order + Lines + Stock, All or Nothing (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: During a mango-season flash sale, a dark store receives 200 orders a minute for a product with limited stock. Placing an order writes the order, its lines and the stock decrements. The database has CHECK (on_hand >= 0). If any write fails, none of them may persist: no orphan orders, no stock taken for a failed order.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant U as OrderPlacement participant W as UnitOfWork participant DB U->>W: registerNew(order), registerNew(line x2), registerDirty(stock x2) U->>W: commit() W->>DB: BEGIN, INSERT order, INSERT lines, UPDATE stock ... alt all succeed W->>DB: COMMIT else CHECK constraint fails W->>DB: ROLLBACK (nothing persists) end

Full Code:

UnitOfWork.javaOrderPlacement.javaGroceryUowDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Collects new/changed/removed objects during a use case and writes them in ONE transaction. */
public final class UnitOfWork {

    /** How to write one kind of object. The unit of work doesn't know SQL itself. */
    public interface Mapper<T> {
        void insert(Connection c, T obj) throws SQLException;
        void update(Connection c, T obj) throws SQLException;
    }

    private record Pending<T>(String kind, T obj, Mapper<T> mapper) {
        void apply(Connection c) throws SQLException {
            if (kind.equals("INSERT")) {
                mapper.insert(c, obj);
            } else {
                mapper.update(c, obj);
            }
        }
    }

    private final DataSource ds;
    private final List<Pending<?>> pending = new ArrayList<>();

    public UnitOfWork(DataSource ds) {
        this.ds = ds;
    }

    public <T> void registerNew(T obj, Mapper<T> mapper) { pending.add(new Pending<>("INSERT", obj, mapper)); } // (1)!

    public <T> void registerDirty(T obj, Mapper<T> mapper) { pending.add(new Pending<>("UPDATE", obj, mapper)); }

    public int commit() {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false); // (2)!
            try {
                for (Pending<?> p : pending) {
                    p.apply(c);
                }
                c.commit();
                return pending.size();
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                c.rollback(); // (3)!
                throw new IllegalStateException("Rolled back " + pending.size() + " changes (SQLState " + e.getSQLState() + ")", e);
            } finally {
                pending.clear();
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }
}
  1. Business code registers changes; nothing is written yet. Hibernate does the same when you persist() or modify a managed entity.
  2. One connection, one transaction, for every pending change.
  3. Any failure rolls back everything, so the database never sees a half-placed order.
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.List;

/** Use case: create an order, its lines and the stock decrements, all-or-nothing. */
public final class OrderPlacement {

    public record Order(String id, String customer) { }

    public record Line(String orderId, String sku, int qty) { }

    public record Stock(String sku, int onHand) { }

    static final UnitOfWork.Mapper<Order> ORDERS = new UnitOfWork.Mapper<>() {
        public void insert(Connection c, Order o) throws SQLException {
            exec(c, "INSERT INTO orders (id, customer) VALUES (?, ?)", o.id(), o.customer());
        }
        public void update(Connection c, Order o) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    };

    static final UnitOfWork.Mapper<Line> LINES = new UnitOfWork.Mapper<>() {
        public void insert(Connection c, Line l) throws SQLException {
            exec(c, "INSERT INTO order_line (order_id, sku, qty) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", l.orderId(), l.sku(), l.qty());
        }
        public void update(Connection c, Line l) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    };

    static final UnitOfWork.Mapper<Stock> STOCK = new UnitOfWork.Mapper<>() {
        public void insert(Connection c, Stock s) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
        public void update(Connection c, Stock s) throws SQLException {
            exec(c, "UPDATE stock SET on_hand = ? WHERE sku = ?", s.onHand(), s.sku());
        }
    };

    private final UnitOfWork uow;

    public OrderPlacement(UnitOfWork uow) {
        this.uow = uow;
    }

    /** Business logic only registers changes; nothing touches the database until commit. */
    public int place(Order order, List<Line> lines, List<Stock> currentStock) {
        uow.registerNew(order, ORDERS);
        for (Line line : lines) {
            uow.registerNew(line, LINES);
            Stock s = currentStock.stream().filter(x -> x.sku().equals(line.sku())).findFirst().orElseThrow();
            uow.registerDirty(new Stock(s.sku(), s.onHand() - line.qty()), STOCK);
        }
        return uow.commit();
    }

    private static void exec(Connection c, String sql, Object... args) throws SQLException {
        try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) {
                ps.setObject(i + 1, args[i]);
            }
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery;

import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement.Line;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement.Order;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement.Stock;
import org.h2.jdbcx.JdbcDataSource;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.List;

public class GroceryUowDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Order + Lines + Stock in One Unit of Work ===");
        JdbcDataSource ds = new JdbcDataSource();
        ds.setURL("jdbc:h2:mem:uow_grocery;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1");
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, customer VARCHAR)");
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE order_line (order_id VARCHAR, sku VARCHAR, qty INT)");
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE stock (sku VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, on_hand INT CHECK (on_hand >= 0))");
            c.createStatement().execute("INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('MANGO-1KG', 3), ('CURD-400G', 10)");
        }

        int written = new OrderPlacement(new UnitOfWork(ds)).place(new Order("O-1", "riya"),
                List.of(new Line("O-1", "MANGO-1KG", 2), new Line("O-1", "CURD-400G", 1)),
                List.of(new Stock("MANGO-1KG", 3), new Stock("CURD-400G", 10)));
        System.out.println("O-1 committed " + written + " changes -> " + snapshot(ds));

        try {
            new OrderPlacement(new UnitOfWork(ds)).place(new Order("O-2", "arjun"),
                    List.of(new Line("O-2", "CURD-400G", 2), new Line("O-2", "MANGO-1KG", 5)), // only 1 mango left
                    List.of(new Stock("MANGO-1KG", 1), new Stock("CURD-400G", 9)));
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("O-2 failed: " + e.getMessage() + ": stock would go negative");
        }
        System.out.println("After O-2 -> " + snapshot(ds) + " (no orphan order, curd untouched)");
    }

    private static String snapshot(JdbcDataSource ds) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            ResultSet o = c.createStatement().executeQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders");
            o.next();
            ResultSet l = c.createStatement().executeQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_line");
            l.next();
            ResultSet s = c.createStatement().executeQuery("SELECT LISTAGG(sku || '=' || on_hand, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY sku) FROM stock");
            s.next();
            return "orders=" + o.getInt(1) + ", lines=" + l.getInt(1) + ", stock[" + s.getString(1) + "]";
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Order + Lines + Stock in One Unit of Work ===
O-1 committed 5 changes -> orders=1, lines=2, stock[CURD-400G=9, MANGO-1KG=1]
O-2 failed: Rolled back 5 changes (SQLState 23513): stock would go negative
After O-2 -> orders=1, lines=2, stock[CURD-400G=9, MANGO-1KG=1] (no orphan order, curd untouched)

Why a unit of work here:

  • One business action = one atomic database transaction.
  • The use case contains no commit/rollback plumbing.
  • Writes are batched at the end, so there are fewer round trips and locks are held for less time.

docs.title: Example 2: Identity Map in a Check-in Session (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: An airline's web check-in page renders several widgets in one request: seat map, baggage, meal choice. Each widget loads the booking. Without an identity map there are three database reads and three separate Booking objects. When the seat widget upgrades the passenger to 3A, the baggage widget still holds 14C and prints the wrong boarding-pass zone.

Design:

flowchart LR S[Seat widget] --> M[(Identity map<br/>PNR-42 → Booking@1)] B[Baggage widget] --> M M -->|first lookup only| DB[(bookings)]

Full Code:

IdentityMap.javaTravelIdentityMapDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.travel;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Ensures each record is loaded once per session: one id -> one in-memory object. */
public final class IdentityMap<K, V> {

    private final Map<K, V> loaded = new HashMap<>();
    private final Function<K, V> loader;

    public IdentityMap(Function<K, V> loader) {
        this.loader = loader;
    }

    public V get(K id) {
        return loaded.computeIfAbsent(id, loader); // (1)!
    }

    public int size() {
        return loaded.size();
    }
}
  1. Load on first access, then always return the same instance. This is why em.find(Booking.class, id) == em.find(Booking.class, id) is true inside one JPA transaction.
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.travel;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class TravelIdentityMapDemo {

    /** A mutable booking, like a JPA entity. */
    static final class Booking {
        final String pnr;
        String seat;
        Booking(String pnr, String seat) { this.pnr = pnr; this.seat = seat; }
    }

    static final Map<String, String> SEATS_TABLE = new HashMap<>(Map.of("PNR-42", "14C"));
    static int dbReads = 0;

    static Booking loadFromDb(String pnr) {
        dbReads++;
        return new Booking(pnr, SEATS_TABLE.get(pnr));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: Identity Map in a Check-in Session ===");

        dbReads = 0;
        Booking forSeatMap = loadFromDb("PNR-42");    // seat-map widget
        Booking forBaggage = loadFromDb("PNR-42");    // baggage widget, same request
        forSeatMap.seat = "3A";                         // passenger upgrades
        System.out.println("Without map: reads=" + dbReads + ", same object=" + (forSeatMap == forBaggage)
                + ", baggage widget still sees seat " + forBaggage.seat + " (stale copy)");

        dbReads = 0;
        IdentityMap<String, Booking> session = new IdentityMap<>(TravelIdentityMapDemo::loadFromDb);
        Booking a = session.get("PNR-42");
        Booking b = session.get("PNR-42");
        a.seat = "3A";
        System.out.println("With map   : reads=" + dbReads + ", same object=" + (a == b) + ", baggage widget sees seat " + b.seat);
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: Identity Map in a Check-in Session ===
Without map: reads=2, same object=false, baggage widget still sees seat 14C (stale copy)
With map   : reads=1, same object=true, baggage widget sees seat 3A

Why an identity map here:

  • Consistency inside a request: everyone sees the same booking state.
  • Fewer reads: the second lookup is free (a first-level cache).
  • Needed by the unit of work to know which object to write for a given row.

docs.title: Example 3: Dirty Checking for an Appraisal Batch (SaaS / ERP)
docs.text:
Scenario: An HR system's appraisal job loads 5,000 employee records, but only about 10% get a raise or transfer. Writing back all 5,000 rows would bloat the audit log and contend with other jobs. The unit of work snapshots each object when loaded and, at flush, issues an UPDATE only for objects whose fields actually changed, and only for those columns.

Design:

flowchart LR L["find(E1..E5)"] --> Snap["snapshot of each on load"] Code["appraisal logic mutates E2, E4"] --> F["flush(): compare current vs snapshot"] F --> U2["UPDATE E2 salary"] F --> U4["UPDATE E4 department"] F -.->|unchanged| X["E1, E3, E5: no SQL"]

Full Code:

DirtyCheckingSession.javaErpDirtyCheckingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.erp;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Hibernate-style dirty checking: snapshot on load, compare on flush, UPDATE only what changed. */
public final class DirtyCheckingSession {

    public static final class Employee { // mutable "managed entity"
        public final String id;
        public String department;
        public long salaryPaise;

        public Employee(String id, String department, long salaryPaise) {
            this.id = id;
            this.department = department;
            this.salaryPaise = salaryPaise;
        }
    }

    private record Snapshot(String department, long salaryPaise) {
        static Snapshot of(Employee e) { return new Snapshot(e.department, e.salaryPaise); }
    }

    private final Map<String, Employee> table;
    private final Map<String, Employee> managed = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // identity map
    private final Map<String, Snapshot> snapshots = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    public DirtyCheckingSession(Map<String, Employee> table) {
        this.table = table;
    }

    public Employee find(String id) {
        return managed.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> {
            Employee row = table.get(k);
            Employee copy = new Employee(row.id, row.department, row.salaryPaise);
            snapshots.put(k, Snapshot.of(copy)); // (1)!
            return copy;
        });
    }

    /** Returns the SQL it would issue. */
    public List<String> flush() {
        List<String> sql = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Employee e : managed.values()) {
            Snapshot before = snapshots.get(e.id);
            List<String> sets = new ArrayList<>();
            if (!before.department().equals(e.department)) {
                sets.add("department='" + e.department + "'");
            }
            if (before.salaryPaise() != e.salaryPaise) {
                sets.add("salary_paise=" + e.salaryPaise);
            }
            if (!sets.isEmpty()) { // (2)!
                sql.add("UPDATE employee SET " + String.join(", ", sets) + " WHERE id='" + e.id + "'");
                table.put(e.id, new Employee(e.id, e.department, e.salaryPaise));
                snapshots.put(e.id, Snapshot.of(e));
            }
        }
        return sql;
    }
}
  1. The snapshot taken at load time, exactly what Hibernate keeps in its persistence context ("loaded state").
  2. Only changed objects produce SQL. Setting a field to its existing value is not a change.
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.erp;

import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.erp.DirtyCheckingSession.Employee;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class ErpDirtyCheckingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== ERP: Annual Appraisal with Dirty Checking ===");
        Map<String, Employee> table = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            table.put("E" + i, new Employee("E" + i, "Finance", 1_200_000_00L));
        }
        DirtyCheckingSession session = new DirtyCheckingSession(table);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            Employee e = session.find("E" + i);
            if (i == 2) {
                e.salaryPaise = 1_320_000_00L;            // 10% raise
            }
            if (i == 4) {
                e.department = "Treasury";                 // transfer
                e.salaryPaise = e.salaryPaise;             // "set" to same value: not a change
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Loaded 5 employees, flush issues:");
        session.flush().forEach(s -> System.out.println("  " + s));
        System.out.println("Second flush with no changes issues " + session.flush().size() + " statements");
    }
}

Output:

=== ERP: Annual Appraisal with Dirty Checking ===
Loaded 5 employees, flush issues:
  UPDATE employee SET salary_paise=132000000 WHERE id='E2'
  UPDATE employee SET department='Treasury' WHERE id='E4'
Second flush with no changes issues 0 statements

Why dirty checking here:

  • Business code just changes objects; it never calls update().
  • Minimal writes: fewer locks, smaller audit trail, less replication traffic.
  • Explains JPA behaviour that surprises people: modifying a managed entity is a save.
Unit Tests: UnitOfWorkTest.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork;

import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.erp.DirtyCheckingSession;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.erp.DirtyCheckingSession.Employee;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement.Line;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement.Order;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.OrderPlacement.Stock;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.grocery.UnitOfWork;
import com.handbook.enterprise.unitofwork.travel.IdentityMap;
import org.h2.jdbcx.JdbcDataSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.UUID;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class UnitOfWorkTest {

    @Test
    void failedCommitLeavesNothingBehind() throws Exception {
        JdbcDataSource ds = new JdbcDataSource();
        ds.setURL("jdbc:h2:mem:" + UUID.randomUUID() + ";DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1");
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, customer VARCHAR)");
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE order_line (order_id VARCHAR, sku VARCHAR, qty INT)");
            c.createStatement().execute("CREATE TABLE stock (sku VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, on_hand INT CHECK (on_hand >= 0))");
            c.createStatement().execute("INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('A', 1)");
        }
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> new OrderPlacement(new UnitOfWork(ds))
                .place(new Order("O", "c"), List.of(new Line("O", "A", 2)), List.of(new Stock("A", 1))))
                .hasMessageContaining("Rolled back 3 changes");
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders");
            rs.next();
            assertThat(rs.getInt(1)).isZero();
        }
    }

    @Test
    void identityMapLoadsOncePerId() {
        AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger();
        IdentityMap<String, Object> map = new IdentityMap<>(id -> {
            loads.incrementAndGet();
            return new Object();
        });
        assertThat(map.get("x")).isSameAs(map.get("x"));
        assertThat(loads).hasValue(1);
    }

    @Test
    void dirtyCheckingUpdatesOnlyChangedColumns() {
        Map<String, Employee> table = new HashMap<>(Map.of("E1", new Employee("E1", "HR", 100), "E2", new Employee("E2", "HR", 100)));
        DirtyCheckingSession s = new DirtyCheckingSession(table);
        s.find("E1").salaryPaise = 200;
        s.find("E2");
        assertThat(s.flush()).containsExactly("UPDATE employee SET salary_paise=200 WHERE id='E1'");
        assertThat(s.flush()).isEmpty();
        assertThat(table.get("E1").salaryPaise).isEqualTo(200);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Caller registration (Example 1) Code explicitly calls registerNew/Dirty. Simple and explicit Object registration / dirty checking (Example 3) The unit of work snapshots on load and detects changes. Hibernate, EclipseLink Spring @Transactional Declares the unit-of-work boundary on a use-case method; the persistence context lives for that transaction Immutable aggregates With records, you save(newVersion) explicitly and the unit of work just batches those calls Event-sourced unit of work Collect new events from several aggregates and append them atomically with expected versions Outbox in the same unit of work Write the outbox row in the same transaction as the business change (Transactional Outbox)

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Unit of Work / Identity Map JPA / Hibernate EntityManager / Session = unit of work; the persistence context = identity map + snapshots; flush(), FlushMode Spring @Transactional, TransactionTemplate, PlatformTransactionManager; Open-Session-in-View (and why to disable it) jOOQ / JDBC No automatic unit of work: DSLContext.transaction(...) gives atomicity, you track changes yourself .NET EF Core DbContext + SaveChanges(): the same pattern, and a common interview comparison Kafka Producer transactions group writes to several partitions into one atomic unit

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Atomic business operations Long units of work hold memory and, if not careful, locks Fewer, batched writes; minimal UPDATEs with dirty checking "Magic" saves: changing a managed entity writes it, sometimes surprisingly Identity map: consistency within a request + first-level cache Dirty checking costs CPU proportional to managed objects Business code free of transaction plumbing Doesn't span services: across services you need a Saga

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Units of work that span user think-time

Keeping a transaction (or JPA persistence context) open while the user fills a form holds locks and connections. Load, close, then use optimistic locking (a version) when the user submits.

Open Session in View

Spring Boot enables it by default (with a warning). Lazy loading in controllers/views fires queries outside your use case, causing N+1 and surprising writes. Set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.

Global identity maps

An identity map guarantees identity, not freshness. Shared across requests it becomes a stale, thread-unsafe cache (coding challenge). Scope it to one unit of work.

Batch jobs with one giant persistence context

Loading 1 million entities in one session exhausts memory and makes every flush slower. Process in chunks: flush() + clear() every N items.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Write ordering. A real unit of work orders writes to satisfy foreign keys: inserts parent-first, deletes child-first. Hibernate uses an action queue sorted by entity type; with hibernate.order_inserts=true and JDBC batching, it groups statements into batches.

Flush vs commit. flush() sends SQL but stays in the transaction; commit() makes it durable. JPQL queries trigger an auto-flush so queries see pending changes (FlushModeType.AUTO), a frequent source of "why did it run an UPDATE before my SELECT?".

Consistency beyond one database. A unit of work is a local transaction. Once a business action spans services, replace "one transaction" with a saga plus an outbox written in the same local unit of work, and idempotent consumers on the other side.

War story: the orphaned orders

A grocery platform's order service used Spring Data repositories without @Transactional on the use case. Each save() committed on its own. During a sale, a stock CHECK constraint failed after the order and two lines were committed: 3,100 orders appeared in customer apps with no items and no payment. Support refunded nothing (nothing was charged) but spent two days explaining "empty orders". Fix: @Transactional on the application service (one unit of work per use case) and an integration test asserting no rows survive a failed placement. Lesson: a repository is not a transaction boundary. The use case is.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Unit of Work Identity Map Repository Saga Purpose Atomic commit of many changes One object per row per session Collection-like access to aggregates Consistency across services Scope One local transaction One unit of work Per aggregate type Many services, long-running In JPA EntityManager + @Transactional Persistence context Spring Data repository Not provided

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Unit of Work: register changes, then one atomic commit (or rollback).
  • Identity Map: one object per row per unit of work; identity, not freshness.
  • JPA EntityManager = both; @Transactional on the use case sets the boundary.
  • Modifying a managed entity is a save (dirty checking).
  • Across services, use a saga + outbox instead.
@Transactional public void place(Order o) { orders.save(o); stock.decrement(o.lines()); } // one unit of work

docs.text:
• Add registerRemoved and order writes: inserts, then updates, then deletes.
  • Make IdentityMap keyed by (type, id) so several entity types can share it.
  • Add a readOnly mode to DirtyCheckingSession that skips snapshots entirely.

Repository Next: Value Object

docs.title: Value Object
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Enterprise / DDD Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Value Object is a small immutable type defined only by its values (Quantity, PhoneNumber, StayPeriod), with no identity of its own. It validates itself and carries the rules that belong to that concept. Use one whenever a primitive (String, long, LocalDate pair) has rules, units or a format. In Java 21 this is usually a record.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: long quantity doesn't say whether it means grams, kilograms or pieces. String phone accepts "098450-12345" and "+91 98450 12345" as two different customers. LocalDate from, LocalDate to lets someone create a stay that ends before it starts. Every service re-implements (slightly differently) the same checks. This is called primitive obsession.

Definition (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design):

An object that describes some characteristic or attribute but carries no concept of identity. Value objects are immutable, compared by value (two Quantity(2 kg) are interchangeable), and should be self-validating and side-effect free.

Value Object vs Entity: an entity (Customer, Order) has an identity that persists while its attributes change. A value (Address, Money, Quantity) is replaced, not modified. Ask: "If every field is equal, are these the same thing?" If yes, it's a value.

This page is the domain modelling view. For the thread-safety view of the same idea, see Immutable Object.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Banknotes

You don't care which ₹500 note you get back, only that it's ₹500: banknotes are compared by value. A forged ₹700 note can't exist (validation). And you never "edit" a note; you exchange it for different ones (immutability). Your bank account, on the other hand, is an entity: it's still your account when the balance changes.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram class Quantity { <<record, value object>> +long amount +Unit unit +plus(Quantity) Quantity +priceFor(long) long } class OrderLine { <<entity part>> +Sku sku +Quantity quantity } OrderLine --> Quantity : holds by value note for Quantity "Validated in the compact constructor;\nequals/hashCode by value; no setters" Property How in Java Immutable record (final fields), withers return new instances Equal by value Records generate equals/hashCode from components; normalise first so equal values compare equal Self-validating Compact constructor throws on invalid input; invalid values can't exist Behaviour-rich Methods like plus, overlaps, masked live on the value, not in services

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
void addToCart(String sku, long qty, String unit) { ... }            // "kg"? "KG"? "Kilogram"?
boolean bedFree(LocalDate from, LocalDate to, LocalDate from2, LocalDate to2) { ... }  // overlap logic copy-pasted
customerRepo.findByPhone(rawInput);                                 // "098450-12345" ≠ "+919845012345"
  • Validation scattered across controllers, services and SQL.
  • Easy to mix units, swap arguments and duplicate records.
  • The domain's vocabulary is invisible in the code.

docs.title: Example 1: Quantity with Units (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery app sells loose vegetables by weight (g/kg) and eggs by count (pieces/dozen). Carts merge quantities from re-orders and substitutions. A past bug added "6 pieces" of eggs to "2 kg" of potatoes in a picking summary. Prices are per kg or per piece, in integer paise.

Design:

flowchart LR A["Quantity(500, GRAM)"] --> P["plus"] B["Quantity(1, KILOGRAM) → normalised to 1000 g"] --> P P --> C["Quantity(1500 g)"] D["Quantity(6, PIECE)"] -.->|different dimension| X["IllegalArgumentException"]

Full Code:

Quantity.javaQuantityDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery;

import java.util.Objects;

/** A quantity of something, with its unit. Equal by value; normalised to the smallest unit. */
public record Quantity(long amount, Unit unit) {

    public enum Unit {
        GRAM(Dimension.MASS, 1), KILOGRAM(Dimension.MASS, 1000), PIECE(Dimension.COUNT, 1), DOZEN(Dimension.COUNT, 12);

        final Dimension dimension;
        final long factor;

        Unit(Dimension dimension, long factor) {
            this.dimension = dimension;
            this.factor = factor;
        }
    }

    enum Dimension { MASS, COUNT }

    public Quantity { // (1)!
        Objects.requireNonNull(unit, "unit");
        if (amount < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity cannot be negative: " + amount);
        }
        long base = Math.multiplyExact(amount, unit.factor);
        amount = base;
        unit = unit.dimension == Dimension.MASS ? Unit.GRAM : Unit.PIECE;
    }

    public static Quantity of(long amount, Unit unit) {
        return new Quantity(amount, unit);
    }

    public Quantity plus(Quantity other) { // (2)!
        if (unit.dimension != other.unit.dimension) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("cannot add " + other + " to " + this);
        }
        return new Quantity(amount + other.amount, unit);
    }

    /** Price for this quantity, given a price per kg or per piece, in paise (rounded half-up). */
    public long priceFor(long paisePerKgOrPiece) {
        long divisor = unit == Unit.GRAM ? 1000 : 1;
        return (amount * paisePerKgOrPiece + divisor / 2) / divisor;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        if (unit == Unit.GRAM) {
            return amount % 1000 == 0 ? amount / 1000 + " kg" : amount + " g";
        }
        return amount + " pc";
    }
}
  1. The compact constructor validates and normalises (1 kg becomes 1000 g, 1 dozen becomes 12 pieces), so record equality works across units.
  2. Operations return new values and enforce the rule "only add like with like".
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery;

import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.DOZEN;
import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.GRAM;
import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.KILOGRAM;
import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.PIECE;

public class QuantityDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Quantity as a Value Object ===");
        Quantity basket = Quantity.of(500, GRAM).plus(Quantity.of(1, KILOGRAM)).plus(Quantity.of(500, GRAM));
        System.out.println("500 g + 1 kg + 500 g = " + basket);
        System.out.println("1 kg equals 1000 g? " + Quantity.of(1, KILOGRAM).equals(Quantity.of(1000, GRAM)));
        System.out.println("1 dozen equals 12 pc? " + Quantity.of(1, DOZEN).equals(Quantity.of(12, PIECE)));
        System.out.println("Tomatoes 750 g at INR 40/kg = " + Quantity.of(750, GRAM).priceFor(4_000) + " paise");
        try {
            Quantity.of(2, KILOGRAM).plus(Quantity.of(6, PIECE));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            Quantity.of(-1, PIECE);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Quantity as a Value Object ===
500 g + 1 kg + 500 g = 2 kg
1 kg equals 1000 g? true
1 dozen equals 12 pc? true
Tomatoes 750 g at INR 40/kg = 3000 paise
Rejected: cannot add 6 pc to 2 kg
Rejected: quantity cannot be negative: -1

Why a value object here:

  • Units become part of the type, not a comment.
  • Pricing and addition rules live in one place.
  • Quantity.of(1, KILOGRAM).equals(Quantity.of(1000, GRAM)), so dedupe and comparisons just work.

docs.title: Example 2: StayPeriod for Bed Allocation (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital's bed manager assigns 600 beds. A stay runs from the admission date until the discharge date; a new patient can be admitted to the same bed on the discharge day. Overlap checks were duplicated across four services, and two of them treated the discharge day as occupied, leaving beds empty for a night.

Design:

gantt dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD title Bed 7 section Stays Current stay [10, 14) :a, 2026-03-10, 4d Next patient [14, 16) :b, 2026-03-14, 2d

Full Code:

StayPeriod.javaStayPeriodDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.healthcare;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.Objects;

/** A half-open date range [admitted, discharged). Rules about stays live here, not in services. */
public record StayPeriod(LocalDate admitted, LocalDate discharged) {

    public StayPeriod {
        Objects.requireNonNull(admitted);
        Objects.requireNonNull(discharged);
        if (!discharged.isAfter(admitted)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("discharge " + discharged + " must be after admission " + admitted);
        }
    }

    public long nights() {
        return ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(admitted, discharged);
    }

    public boolean overlaps(StayPeriod other) { // (1)!
        return admitted.isBefore(other.discharged) && other.admitted.isBefore(discharged);
    }

    public StayPeriod extendTo(LocalDate newDischarge) { // (2)!
        return new StayPeriod(admitted, newDischarge);
    }
}
  1. One correct overlap rule for half-open ranges [start, end), used by everyone.
  2. "Changing" a stay produces a new value; anything holding the old one is unaffected.
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.healthcare;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public class StayPeriodDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: Bed Allocation with a StayPeriod Value Object ===");
        StayPeriod current = new StayPeriod(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 14));
        StayPeriod nextPatient = new StayPeriod(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 14), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 16));
        System.out.println("Bed 7 current stay: " + current.nights() + " nights");
        System.out.println("Next patient admitted on discharge day overlaps? " + current.overlaps(nextPatient));

        StayPeriod extended = current.extendTo(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 15));
        System.out.println("Doctor extends stay -> " + extended.nights() + " nights; now overlaps? " + extended.overlaps(nextPatient));
        System.out.println("Original value unchanged: " + current.nights() + " nights");
        try {
            new StayPeriod(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 12), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 12));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: Bed Allocation with a StayPeriod Value Object ===
Bed 7 current stay: 4 nights
Next patient admitted on discharge day overlaps? false
Doctor extends stay -> 5 nights; now overlaps? true
Original value unchanged: 4 nights
Rejected: discharge 2026-03-12 must be after admission 2026-03-12

Why a value object here:

  • Date-range logic is notoriously easy to get wrong; centralise it once.
  • An invalid stay (discharge on or before admission) can't be constructed.
  • Services ask the domain question (overlaps, nights) instead of comparing dates.

docs.title: Example 3: PhoneNumber Normalisation (Telecom)
docs.text:
Scenario: A telecom's sign-up funnel collects numbers from web, app, retail stores and partner kiosks: "+91 98450 12345", "098450-12345", "9845012345". Stored as raw strings, one person became three subscribers with three SIM KYC records. Logs must never print a full number.

Design:

flowchart LR R1["+91 98450 12345"] --> P["PhoneNumber.parse"] R2["098450-12345"] --> P R3["9845012345"] --> P P --> E["PhoneNumber(+919845012345)"] E --> M["masked() → +9198*****345"]

Full Code:

PhoneNumber.javaPhoneNumberDemo.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.telecom;

/** An Indian mobile number in canonical E.164 form. Parsing normalises every accepted spelling. */
public record PhoneNumber(String e164) {

    public PhoneNumber {
        if (!e164.matches("\\+91[6-9]\\d{9}")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("not a canonical Indian mobile number: " + e164);
        }
    }

    public static PhoneNumber parse(String raw) { // (1)!
        String digits = raw.replaceAll("[^0-9]", "");
        if (digits.length() == 12 && digits.startsWith("91")) {
            digits = digits.substring(2);
        } else if (digits.length() == 11 && digits.startsWith("0")) {
            digits = digits.substring(1);
        }
        if (digits.length() != 10) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("cannot parse '" + raw + "'");
        }
        return new PhoneNumber("+91" + digits);
    }

    public String masked() {
        return e164.substring(0, 5) + "*****" + e164.substring(10);
    }
}
  1. A factory that accepts the messy real-world formats and produces one canonical value. The constructor only accepts canonical form, so every PhoneNumber is valid.
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.telecom;

import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

public class PhoneNumberDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Telecom: De-duplicating Subscribers by PhoneNumber ===");
        List<String> signups = List.of("+91 98450 12345", "098450-12345", "9845012345", "91-9845012345", "+91 70221 99887");
        Set<PhoneNumber> unique = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (String raw : signups) {
            unique.add(PhoneNumber.parse(raw));
        }
        System.out.println(signups.size() + " raw sign-ups -> " + unique.size() + " subscribers: " + unique.stream().map(PhoneNumber::e164).toList());
        System.out.println("Masked for SMS logs: " + unique.stream().map(PhoneNumber::masked).toList());
        for (String bad : List.of("12345", "+91 12345 67890")) {
            try {
                PhoneNumber.parse(bad);
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
                System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Telecom: De-duplicating Subscribers by PhoneNumber ===
5 raw sign-ups -> 2 subscribers: [+919845012345, +917022199887]
Masked for SMS logs: [+9198*****345, +9170*****887]
Rejected: cannot parse '12345'
Rejected: not a canonical Indian mobile number: +911234567890

Why a value object here:

  • Canonical form makes equality, sets and database uniqueness constraints correct.
  • Privacy rules (masked) travel with the value.
  • Parsing happens once at the edge; the rest of the system trusts the type.
Unit Tests: ValueObjectTest.java 
package com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject;

import com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity;
import com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.healthcare.StayPeriod;
import com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.telecom.PhoneNumber;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;

import java.time.LocalDate;

import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.GRAM;
import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.KILOGRAM;
import static com.handbook.enterprise.valueobject.grocery.Quantity.Unit.PIECE;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ValueObjectTest {

    @Test
    void quantitiesAreEqualByValueAcrossUnits() {
        assertThat(Quantity.of(2, KILOGRAM)).isEqualTo(Quantity.of(2000, GRAM)).hasSameHashCodeAs(Quantity.of(2000, GRAM));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> Quantity.of(1, KILOGRAM).plus(Quantity.of(1, PIECE))).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
        assertThat(Quantity.of(250, GRAM).priceFor(6_000)).isEqualTo(1_500);
    }

    @Test
    void halfOpenStaysDoNotOverlapOnTheSameDay() {
        StayPeriod a = new StayPeriod(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1), LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 3));
        assertThat(a.overlaps(new StayPeriod(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 3), LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 4)))).isFalse();
        assertThat(a.overlaps(new StayPeriod(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 4)))).isTrue();
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {"+91 98450 12345", "098450-12345", "9845012345", "919845012345"})
    void everySpellingNormalisesToTheSameNumber(String raw) {
        assertThat(PhoneNumber.parse(raw)).isEqualTo(new PhoneNumber("+919845012345"));
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Records (Java 16+) The natural fit: final fields, value equality, compact constructors Typed IDs record OrderId(UUID value) instead of UUID everywhere (coding challenge) Enums Values with a closed set (Unit, Currency) Sealed interfaces of records Values with variants: sealed interface Discount permits Percent, Flat JPA mapping @Embeddable classes (records supported as embeddables since Hibernate 6.2), or AttributeConverter<PhoneNumber, String> Jackson Records (de)serialise via their canonical constructor; @JsonValue/@JsonCreator for single-field values Project Valhalla (future) value class will give values without identity at the JVM level (no headers, flattening)

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Value objects JDK LocalDate, Instant, Duration, BigDecimal, UUID, Currency, URI, Optional Libraries Joda-Money Money, JSR 354 MonetaryAmount, libphonenumber PhoneNumber Spring MediaType, HttpMethod, DataSize (10MB in config), Duration binding in @ConfigurationProperties JPA @Embeddable / @Embedded, AttributeConverter

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Invalid states can't be represented More types and small files Rules live in one place, close to the data Mapping to DB columns/JSON needs converters Thread-safe and shareable (immutable) Over-wrapping trivial strings adds ceremony Code reads like the domain language Allocation per operation (negligible in practice)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Equality without normalisation

record Quantity(long amount, Unit unit) without normalising makes 1 kg ≠ 1000 g. Normalise in the compact constructor, or write equals yourself.

Mutable value objects

A value with setters shared by two orders means changing one order's address changes the other's. Values must be immutable.

Records holding mutable components

record Basket(List<Item> items) is only shallowly immutable. List.copyOf in the constructor.

Validation in the controller only

If new PhoneNumber(...) accepts anything, every other code path (batch imports, Kafka consumers) can create invalid values. Validate in the constructor.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Parse, don't validate. Convert raw input to value objects at the system edge (controllers, message consumers). After that, code receives PhoneNumber, not String, so the type itself is proof of validation. This removes defensive checks from deep inside services.

Persistence. Map values as embedded columns (quantity_amount, quantity_unit) or converters to one column. Keep the canonical form in the database too, with a unique index (UNIQUE (phone_e164)), so duplicates are impossible at both layers.

APIs and events. Value objects make great contract types: {"amount": 1500, "unit": "GRAM"} is unambiguous. Version them carefully: changing a value's canonical form (e.g., kg → g) is a breaking change for consumers.

War story: three subscribers, one person

A telecom stored raw phone strings from five channels. The fraud team found customers with up to four active SIM KYC profiles because "098450-12345" and "+91 98450 12345" never matched. Regulators asked for a cleanup within 30 days. Fix: a PhoneNumber value object with canonical E.164 form, used by every channel; a migration normalised 18 million rows and merged 410,000 duplicates; a unique index prevents recurrence. Lesson: if a value has a canonical form, make it a type.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Value Object Entity Immutable Object DTO Identity None (equal by value) Yes (id) N/A None Mutability Immutable Mutable over its life Immutable Usually mutable Behaviour Domain rules (plus, overlaps) Domain rules + lifecycle Any None (data carrier) Purpose Model a concept precisely Track something over time Thread safety Move data across boundaries

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • No identity; equal by value; immutable; self-validating.
  • Use a record with a compact constructor that validates and normalises.
  • Put the rules (plus, overlaps, masked) on the value.
  • Parse at the edge; pass types, not strings, inside.
  • Entity = identity over time; value = replace, don't modify.
record PhoneNumber(String e164) { PhoneNumber { if (!e164.matches("\\+91[6-9]\\d{9}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } }

  • Add StayPeriod.split(LocalDate) that returns two consecutive stays.
