docs.title: Design Principles Beyond SOLID
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner 🟡 Intermediate Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

SOLID tells you how to shape classes and dependencies. These seven principles keep the result simple, honest and safe: don't repeat knowledge (DRY), don't be clever (KISS), don't build for imaginary futures (YAGNI), prefer composition to inheritance, talk only to your friends (Law of Demeter), tell objects what to do instead of asking for their data, and fail fast on invalid input.

# Principle One-liner Smell when violated Pattern/tool that helps 1 DRY One authoritative place for each piece of knowledge The same rule copy-pasted and drifting Value objects, Template Method 2 KISS The simplest solution that works Clever code nobody can review Standard library 3 YAGNI Build it when it's needed, not before Unused interfaces, flags, plug-in points Refactoring later 4 Composition over Inheritance Has-a beats is-a for reuse Fragile base class, deep trees Decorator, Strategy 5 Law of Demeter Only talk to your immediate friends a.getB().getC().doX() Facade, Tell-Don't-Ask 6 Tell, Don't Ask Send commands, don't pull data and decide Logic in callers; anemic models Rich domain model 7 Fail Fast Reject invalid state immediately, loudly Wrong results far from the cause Validating constructors

docs.title: 1. DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself
docs.text:
"Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system." (Andy Hunt & Dave Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer, 1999)

Key point: DRY is about knowledge, not about text. Two identical-looking lines that represent different rules are not duplication. One rule written in two different ways is.

❌ Before: copy-pasted rule that drifted✅ After: one value object owns the rule▶ Demo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.other.dry;

/** VIOLATES DRY: the same email rule is copy-pasted, and the copies have already drifted apart. */
public class SignupBefore {
    public boolean canRegister(String email) {
        return email != null && email.contains("@") && email.indexOf('@') > 0;
    }

    public boolean canInvite(String email) {
        return email != null && email.contains("@");          // drifted: accepts "@nobody"
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.dry;

import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** DRY: the single, authoritative representation of "a valid email". Every caller reuses it. */
public record EmailAddress(String value) {
    private static final Pattern SHAPE = Pattern.compile("^[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+$");

    public EmailAddress {
        if (value == null || !SHAPE.matcher(value.strip()).matches()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid email: " + value);
        }
        value = value.strip().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
    }

    public static boolean isValid(String raw) {
        try {
            new EmailAddress(raw);
            return true;
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    public String domain() { return value.substring(value.indexOf('@') + 1); }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.dry;

public class DryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SignupBefore before = new SignupBefore();
        String bad = "@nobody";
        System.out.println("before: register(" + bad + ")=" + before.canRegister(bad) + ", invite(" + bad + ")=" + before.canInvite(bad)
                + "  <-- two copies, two answers");
        System.out.println("after : isValid(" + bad + ")=" + EmailAddress.isValid(bad));
        EmailAddress ok = new EmailAddress("  Ana@Example.COM ");
        System.out.println("after : normalised=" + ok.value() + ", domain=" + ok.domain());
    }
}

before: register(@nobody)=false, invite(@nobody)=true  <-- two copies, two answers
after : isValid(@nobody)=false
after : normalised=ana@example.com, domain=example.com
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs A rule change is one edit, so copies can't drift Wrong abstraction: merging code that only looks alike couples unrelated features. "Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction" (Sandi Metz) Bugs are fixed once Cross-service DRY (shared libraries) couples deploys. Microservices often prefer some duplication Creates meaningful types (EmailAddress) Over-DRY tests become hard to read. Prefer DAMP (Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases) in tests

Rule of three: tolerate the second copy, and extract on the third, once you know what really varies.

docs.title: 2. KISS: Keep It Simple
docs.text:
"Keep it simple, stupid." (attributed to Kelly Johnson, Lockheed Skunk Works, 1960s)

Key point: prefer the solution that is easiest to read, review and change, even if it's less general or less "elegant". Simplicity is about how much a reader has to keep in their head, not about line count.

Code▶ Demo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.other.kiss;

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.BinaryOperator;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** KISS: the same requirement ("is this year a leap year? what is the max?"), solved clever vs simple. */
public final class KissExamples {
    private KissExamples() { }

    // ---- too clever: a generic "strategy factory" for a one-line rule
    public static boolean isLeapClever(int year) {
        Supplier<Function<Integer, BinaryOperator<Boolean>>> factory =
                () -> divisor -> (acc, unused) -> acc && year % divisor == 0;
        boolean by4 = factory.get().apply(4).apply(true, true);
        boolean by100 = factory.get().apply(100).apply(true, true);
        boolean by400 = factory.get().apply(400).apply(true, true);
        return by4 && (!by100 || by400);
    }

    // ---- simple: reads like the rule itself
    public static boolean isLeapSimple(int year) {
        return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
    }

    // ---- hand-rolled loop vs the library: the library is simpler AND already tested
    public static int maxHandRolled(List<Integer> values) {
        int max = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int i = 0; i < values.size(); i++) {
            if (values.get(i) > max) max = values.get(i);
        }
        return max;
    }

    public static int maxSimple(List<Integer> values) {
        return Collections.max(values);
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.kiss;

import java.util.List;

public class KissDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int year : new int[]{1900, 2000, 2024, 2026}) {
            System.out.println(year + " leap? clever=" + KissExamples.isLeapClever(year) + " simple=" + KissExamples.isLeapSimple(year));
        }
        List<Integer> values = List.of(3, 9, 4);
        System.out.println("max: hand-rolled=" + KissExamples.maxHandRolled(values) + " library=" + KissExamples.maxSimple(values));
    }
}

1900 leap? clever=false simple=false
2000 leap? clever=true simple=true
2024 leap? clever=true simple=true
2026 leap? clever=false simple=false
max: hand-rolled=9 library=9
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Faster onboarding and code review "Simple" is subjective. Agree on team conventions Fewer bugs hide in simple code Too simple can mean naive (O(n²) loops, no error handling) Easier to optimise later, once you've measured Sometimes the simple local choice adds global complexity, such as duplicated logic

Signs of violation: generic frameworks written for one use case, reflection or metaprogramming where a method call would do, deeply nested streams, one-letter names, "clever" bit tricks without a measured need.

docs.title: 3. YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It
docs.text:
"Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them." (Ron Jeffries, Extreme Programming, late 1990s)

Key point: speculative features have a cost you pay now: building them, testing them, carrying them along and delaying other work. They usually turn out wrong, because the real requirement differs from the one you guessed.

Code▶ Demo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.other.yagni;

import java.util.Map;

/** YAGNI: the requirement today is "convert INR to USD at a configured rate". */
public final class YagniExamples {
    private YagniExamples() { }

    /** Speculative: plugin registry, provider SPI, caching hooks, multi-hop conversion... none of it requested. */
    public interface RateProvider { double rate(String from, String to); }

    public interface RateCache { Double lookup(String pair); void store(String pair, double rate); }

    public interface ConversionListener { void converted(String from, String to, long in, long out); }

    public static final class OverEngineeredConverter {
        private final Map<String, RateProvider> providers;
        private final RateCache cache;
        private final ConversionListener listener;

        public OverEngineeredConverter(Map<String, RateProvider> providers, RateCache cache, ConversionListener listener) {
            this.providers = providers;
            this.cache = cache;
            this.listener = listener;
        }

        public long convert(String providerName, String from, String to, long minorUnits) {
            String pair = from + "->" + to;
            Double rate = cache.lookup(pair);
            if (rate == null) {
                rate = providers.get(providerName).rate(from, to);
                cache.store(pair, rate);
            }
            long out = Math.round(minorUnits * rate);
            listener.converted(from, to, minorUnits, out);
            return out;
        }
    }

    /** Just enough: one rate, one method. Easy to extend WHEN a real second requirement appears. */
    public record InrToUsd(long usdCentsPerHundredRupees) {
        public long convertPaise(long paise) {
            return Math.round(paise * (double) usdCentsPerHundredRupees / 10_000);
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.yagni;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class YagniDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Double> cacheStore = new HashMap<>();
        var heavy = new YagniExamples.OverEngineeredConverter(
                Map.of("fixed", (from, to) -> 0.012),
                new YagniExamples.RateCache() {
                    public Double lookup(String pair) { return cacheStore.get(pair); }
                    public void store(String pair, double rate) { cacheStore.put(pair, rate); }
                },
                (from, to, in, out) -> { });
        System.out.println("over-engineered: 10000 paise -> " + heavy.convert("fixed", "INR", "USD", 10_000)
                + " USD cents (3 interfaces + 1 class to wire)");
        System.out.println("just enough    : 10000 paise -> " + new YagniExamples.InrToUsd(120).convertPaise(10_000)
                + " USD cents (1 record)");
    }
}

over-engineered: 10000 paise -> 120 USD cents (3 interfaces + 1 class to wire)
just enough    : 10000 paise -> 120 USD cents (1 record)
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Ship sooner, with less code to maintain Some decisions are expensive to reverse (public APIs, data formats, security, i18n). Design those up front The design follows real requirements Needs good tests and a refactoring habit, or "add it later" turns into "rewrite later" Fewer unused abstractions, which serves KISS Can be misused as an excuse for no design at all

YAGNI vs OCP: OCP says "make it easy to extend". YAGNI says "don't add the extension point until it's needed". Together: write simple code now, and refactor to an abstraction when the second variant actually arrives.

docs.title: 4. Composition over Inheritance
docs.text:
"Favor object composition over class inheritance." (Gang of Four, Design Patterns, 1994)

Key point: inheritance gives white-box reuse: the child sees and depends on the parent's internals. Composition gives black-box reuse: you hold a reference to an interface and forward calls to it. You can change it at run time, combine several behaviours, and never depend on how the delegate works internally.

❌ Inheritance: double counting✅ Composition: forwarding wrapper▶ Demo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.other.composition;

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.HashSet;

/**
 * BROKEN by inheritance (Effective Java, Item 18): HashSet.addAll() internally calls add(),
 * so every element added through addAll() is counted twice. The subclass depends on a
 * self-use implementation detail of its parent: the "fragile base class" problem.
 */
public class InstrumentedHashSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    private int addCount = 0;

    @Override
    public boolean add(E e) {
        addCount++;
        return super.add(e);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);
    }

    public int addCount() { return addCount; }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.composition;

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * FIXED by composition: wrap ANY Set and forward to it. We no longer care how the wrapped set
 * implements addAll, and the same wrapper works for HashSet, TreeSet, LinkedHashSet...
 */
public class InstrumentedSet<E> implements Set<E> {
    private final Set<E> delegate;
    private int addCount = 0;

    public InstrumentedSet(Set<E> delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }

    public int addCount() { return addCount; }

    @Override public boolean add(E e) { addCount++; return delegate.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { addCount += c.size(); return delegate.addAll(c); }

    // ---- plain forwarding
    @Override public int size() { return delegate.size(); }
    @Override public boolean isEmpty() { return delegate.isEmpty(); }
    @Override public boolean contains(Object o) { return delegate.contains(o); }
    @Override public Iterator<E> iterator() { return delegate.iterator(); }
    @Override public Object[] toArray() { return delegate.toArray(); }
    @Override public <T> T[] toArray(T[] a) { return delegate.toArray(a); }
    @Override public boolean remove(Object o) { return delegate.remove(o); }
    @Override public boolean containsAll(Collection<?> c) { return delegate.containsAll(c); }
    @Override public boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c) { return delegate.retainAll(c); }
    @Override public boolean removeAll(Collection<?> c) { return delegate.removeAll(c); }
    @Override public void clear() { delegate.clear(); }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return delegate.equals(o); }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return delegate.hashCode(); }
    @Override public String toString() { return delegate.toString(); }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.composition;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.TreeSet;

public class CompositionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        InstrumentedHashSet<String> inherited = new InstrumentedHashSet<>();
        inherited.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        System.out.println("inheritance: added 3, addCount = " + inherited.addCount() + "  <-- double counted");

        InstrumentedSet<String> composed = new InstrumentedSet<>(new TreeSet<>());
        composed.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        System.out.println("composition: added 3, addCount = " + composed.addCount() + "  (wrapping a TreeSet: " + composed + ")");
    }
}

inheritance: added 3, addCount = 6  <-- double counted
composition: added 3, addCount = 3  (wrapping a TreeSet: [a, b, c])
classDiagram direction LR class Set~E~ { <<interface>> } class InstrumentedSet~E~ { -Set~E~ delegate -int addCount } Set <|.. InstrumentedSet InstrumentedSet o-- Set : wraps any Set HashSet <|-- InstrumentedHashSet : fragile ✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Immune to the parent's self-use changes Boilerplate forwarding methods (Lombok @Delegate and Kotlin by help) Works with any implementation of the interface Identity: wrapper != delegate, which matters for equals and callbacks (the "SELF problem") Behaviour can be swapped or stacked at run time (Decorator) More objects and indirection

When inheritance is still right: a real "is-a" relationship, inside one package or team, with a parent designed and documented for extension (AbstractList, Template Method bases, sealed hierarchies of data types).

docs.title: 5. Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge)
docs.text:
"Only talk to your immediate friends." (Ian Holland, Northeastern University, Demeter project, 1987)

Key point: a method m of object O should only call methods on: O itself, m's parameters, objects m creates, and O's direct fields. Chained calls into someone else's internals (customer.getWallet().setCents(...)) couple you to the whole structure.

Code▶ Demo + Output Paperboy.java (before vs after)
package com.handbook.principles.other.demeter;

public class Paperboy {
    private long collected;

    /** VIOLATES LoD: reaches through customer into the wallet ("train wreck" a.getB().getC()). */
    public void collectBefore(Customer customer, long due) {
        Wallet wallet = customer.getWallet();
        if (wallet.getCents() >= due) {
            wallet.setCents(wallet.getCents() - due);
            collected += due;
        }
    }

    /** FOLLOWS LoD: only talks to its direct collaborator. */
    public void collectAfter(Customer customer, long due) {
        collected += customer.pay(due);
    }

    public long collected() { return collected; }
}
Customer.java
package com.handbook.principles.other.demeter;

/** Exposes its wallet (Before) AND offers a behaviour that hides it (After). */
public class Customer {
    private final String name;
    private final Wallet wallet;

    public Customer(String name, Wallet wallet) {
        this.name = name;
        this.wallet = wallet;
    }

    public String name() { return name; }

    /** Before-style accessor: leaks the internal structure. */
    public Wallet getWallet() { return wallet; }

    /** After: the customer decides how to pay; callers only talk to their direct friend. */
    public long pay(long cents) {
        if (wallet.getCents() < cents) throw new IllegalStateException(name + " cannot pay " + cents);
        wallet.setCents(wallet.getCents() - cents);
        return cents;
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.demeter;

public class DemeterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Customer ana = new Customer("Ana", new Wallet(1_000));
        Paperboy boy = new Paperboy();
        boy.collectBefore(ana, 300);
        System.out.println("before: paperboy rummaged in the wallet, wallet now " + ana.getWallet().getCents());
        boy.collectAfter(ana, 300);
        System.out.println("after : customer paid, wallet now " + ana.getWallet().getCents() + ", collected " + boy.collected());
        try {
            boy.collectAfter(ana, 5_000);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("after : the rule lives with the data -> " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

before: paperboy rummaged in the wallet, wallet now 700
after : customer paid, wallet now 400, collected 600
after : the rule lives with the data -> Ana cannot pay 5000
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Internal structure can change without breaking callers Can lead to many small wrapper methods on the middle object Rules live with the data (the "insufficient funds" check is in one place) Fluent APIs and streams are fine: list.stream().map().filter() returns the same kind of object and isn't a violation Easier mocking: one collaborator, not a chain Data-transfer objects and records are meant to be navigated

docs.title: 6. Tell, Don't Ask
docs.text:
"Rather than asking an object for data and acting on that data, we should instead tell an object what to do." (Andy Hunt & Dave Thomas, IEEE Software, 2003; popularised by Martin Fowler)

Key point: if the caller does if (obj.getX() …) obj.setY(…), the decision belongs inside obj. That keeps behaviour next to the data it depends on (encapsulation) and stops callers from re-implementing the rule differently.

Code▶ Demo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.other.telldontask;

/** The object that owns the data also owns the decision. */
public class Thermostat {
    private final int targetCelsius;
    private boolean heating;

    public Thermostat(int targetCelsius) { this.targetCelsius = targetCelsius; }

    // ---- ASK style: getters let callers pull the data and make the decision outside
    public int getTargetCelsius() { return targetCelsius; }

    public void setHeating(boolean heating) { this.heating = heating; }

    public boolean isHeating() { return heating; }

    // ---- TELL style: give the object the new fact; it decides what that means
    public void onTemperatureReading(int currentCelsius) {
        heating = currentCelsius < targetCelsius - 1;     // 1 degree hysteresis, in ONE place
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.telldontask;

public class TellDontAskDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // ASK: the caller duplicates the rule (and here forgets the hysteresis)
        Thermostat asked = new Thermostat(21);
        int reading = 20;
        if (reading < asked.getTargetCelsius()) asked.setHeating(true);
        System.out.println("ask : reading " + reading + " -> heating " + asked.isHeating() + "  (rule re-implemented by the caller)");

        // TELL: the thermostat applies its own rule
        Thermostat told = new Thermostat(21);
        told.onTemperatureReading(reading);
        System.out.println("tell: reading " + reading + " -> heating " + told.isHeating() + " (thermostat's own 1-degree hysteresis)");
        told.onTemperatureReading(18);
        System.out.println("tell: reading 18 -> heating " + told.isHeating());
    }
}

ask : reading 20 -> heating true  (rule re-implemented by the caller)
tell: reading 20 -> heating false (thermostat's own 1-degree hysteresis)
tell: reading 18 -> heating true
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Rich domain model; one place for each rule Queries are still needed for display, reports and serialization. CQS (separate commands from queries) is the balance Fewer getters/setters, which fights the anemic domain model Taken to extremes, objects collect unrelated behaviour (an SRP violation) Simpler callers, easier to test the rule Some logic really spans several objects. Put it in a domain service

docs.title: 7. Fail Fast
docs.text:
"Fail fast… makes failures immediate and visible." (Jim Shore, IEEE Software, 2004)

Key point: detect invalid input or state at the earliest point, usually the constructor or method entry, and throw a clear exception. A failure far from its cause, like a negative invoice three services later, is much harder to diagnose.

❌ Fail slow✅ Fail fast▶ Demo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.other.failfast;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;

/** FAIL SLOW: accepts anything; the error surfaces much later as a wrong number, far from its cause. */
public class LenientReservation {
    private final LocalDate checkIn;
    private final LocalDate checkOut;

    public LenientReservation(LocalDate checkIn, LocalDate checkOut) {
        this.checkIn = checkIn;
        this.checkOut = checkOut;
    }

    public long priceCents(long perNightCents) {
        return ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(checkIn, checkOut) * perNightCents;   // negative nights -> negative invoice
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.failfast;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Objects;

/** FAIL FAST: an invalid Reservation can never exist, so nothing downstream has to re-check it. */
public record Reservation(String guest, LocalDate checkIn, LocalDate checkOut, int guests) {
    public Reservation {
        Objects.requireNonNull(guest, "guest");
        Objects.requireNonNull(checkIn, "checkIn");
        Objects.requireNonNull(checkOut, "checkOut");
        if (guest.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("guest must not be blank");
        if (!checkOut.isAfter(checkIn)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("checkOut " + checkOut + " must be after checkIn " + checkIn);
        if (guests < 1 || guests > 8) throw new IllegalArgumentException("guests must be 1..8 but was " + guests);
    }

    public long nights() { return checkIn.until(checkOut).getDays(); }
}

package com.handbook.principles.other.failfast;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public class FailFastDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDate in = LocalDate.of(2025, 3, 10);
        LocalDate out = LocalDate.of(2025, 3, 7);       // typo: before check-in

        System.out.println("fail slow: price = " + new LenientReservation(in, out).priceCents(5_000) + " cents  <-- refund by accident");
        try {
            new Reservation("Ana", in, out, 2);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("fail fast: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("valid    : " + new Reservation("Ana", in, in.plusDays(3), 2).nights() + " nights");
    }
}

fail slow: price = -15000 cents  <-- refund by accident
fail fast: checkOut 2025-03-07 must be after checkIn 2025-03-10
valid    : 3 nights
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Bugs surface near their cause, with a precise message Not always right at system edges. A UI or batch job may prefer to collect all errors (Notification pattern / Bean Validation) Invalid objects can't exist, so downstream code needn't re-check Fragile if over-applied to optional or noisy data (for example parsing third-party feeds) Spring Boot does it at startup (@ConfigurationProperties + @Validated) Needs good error handling and translation at the boundary (RFC 9457 ProblemDetail)

JDK examples: Objects.requireNonNull, fail-fast iterators (ConcurrentModificationException), List.of rejecting null, and record compact constructors.

docs.title: 8. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
DRY vs WET vs AHA, and when is duplication OK?

WET means "Write Everything Twice" (a violation). AHA means "Avoid Hasty Abstractions" (Kent C. Dodds), and it supports the rule of three. Duplication is fine when the copies represent different knowledge that happens to look the same today, or across service boundaries where a shared library would couple deploys.

Doesn't YAGNI conflict with OCP?

They are balanced against each other: write the simplest code now, and when a real second variant arrives, refactor to an abstraction (OCP). Good tests make that refactoring cheap. Design up front only for decisions that are expensive to reverse.

Is method chaining always a Law of Demeter violation?

No. LoD is about reaching into the structure of other objects. Fluent builders, streams and Optional chains return the same or a related abstraction, so they don't expose structure. order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() does.

Give a real example where composition beat inheritance.

java.util.Collections.synchronizedList and unmodifiableList wrap any List instead of subclassing each implementation. Spring's TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy and Java I/O streams (BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(...))) work the same way, as Decorators.

Fail fast vs defensive programming?

Defensive programming tolerates bad input and tries to continue. Fail fast refuses bad input loudly. Inside your own code, fail fast (invariants, preconditions). At untrusted boundaries, validate everything, collect the errors, and respond gracefully.

docs.title: 9. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • DRY: one home for each piece of knowledge; rule of three; avoid the wrong abstraction.
  • KISS: optimise for the reader; use the standard library.
  • YAGNI: build what's needed now; refactor when the need is real.
  • Composition > inheritance: wrap an interface; avoid fragile base classes.
  • LoD: no train wrecks; fluent chains are fine.
  • Tell, Don't Ask: put the decision where the data is.
  • Fail fast: validate in constructors; collect errors only at UX edges.

docs.title: How to Use This Handbook
docs.text:
This handbook is written for three readers at once. Pick the path that fits you; you can switch at any time.

Every pattern page has the same 13 sections

So once you've read one page, you know where everything is on every other page. Start with Singleton; it's the reference page.

docs.title: Beginner path
docs.text:
Who: students, freshers, engineers with 0–2 years of experience.

  1. Read OOP & SOLID Refresher first. Patterns are just SOLID applied to recurring problems.
  2. Skim the UML Cheat Sheet so the diagrams make sense.
  3. On each pattern page, read sections 1–5 (intent, analogy, structure, naive approach, the 3 examples) and section 13 (revision card).
  4. Run every example yourself. Change one thing and predict the new output before you run it.
  5. Do the 🟢 tab in the Interview Corner.

Suggested order: Singleton → Factory Method → Builder → Strategy → Observer → Decorator → Adapter → Facade → Template Method → State.

docs.title: Experienced path
docs.text:
Who: engineers with 5–15+ years, tech leads, architects.

  1. Skip the analogies. Go straight to section 5 and look at how each example is put together.
  2. Spend most of your time on sections 6–10: modern Java variants, framework internals, trade-offs, pitfalls, the senior deep dive and the war story.
  3. Use section 11 to sharpen how you explain the differences between similar patterns. This is where design reviews are won.
  4. Go through the microservices and architecture sections. That's where 10–15-year interviews spend most of their time.

  • Week 2: Behavioral (Strategy, Observer, State, Command, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method).

docs.title: The Four Pillars of OOP
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Foundations Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Encapsulation protects state, Abstraction hides complexity behind a contract, Inheritance reuses and specialises behaviour, and Polymorphism lets one call do different things depending on the object. Every design pattern in this handbook is a combination of these four.

flowchart LR E[🔒 Encapsulation<br/>protect invariants] --> A[🎭 Abstraction<br/>depend on what, not how] A --> P[🔀 Polymorphism<br/>one call, many behaviours] I[🧬 Inheritance<br/>is-a reuse] --> P P --> DP[Design patterns<br/>Strategy, State, Decorator, …] Pillar Question it answers Java tools Overuse risk Encapsulation Who can change this state, and how? private, validated methods, immutable records, defensive copies Getter/setter-only classes (anemic) Abstraction What does the caller need to know? interface, abstract class, modules Abstractions with one implementation forever Inheritance What is shared, and what is specialised? extends, abstract, final, sealed Fragile base classes, deep hierarchies Polymorphism Which behaviour runs for this object? Overriding, overloading, generics, switch patterns Clever dispatch that's hard to follow

docs.title: 1. Encapsulation
docs.text:
Definition. Bundle data with the operations on it, and hide the internal state so it can only change through methods that enforce the object's rules (its invariants). Encapsulation is about protecting invariants, not just about making fields private and adding getters and setters.

Key features: private fields; behaviour methods instead of setters; validation in the constructor and methods; immutable or read-only views of internal collections (List.copyOf, unmodifiableList); package-private helpers.

CodeDemo + Output 
package com.handbook.principles.oop.encapsulation;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Encapsulation: state is private and can only change through methods that protect the invariant
 * "balance is never negative". Callers cannot reach in and set the balance directly.
 */
public class BankAccount {
    private final String id;
    private long balanceCents;
    private final List<String> history = new ArrayList<>();

    public BankAccount(String id, long openingCents) {
        if (openingCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("opening balance must be >= 0");
        this.id = id;
        this.balanceCents = openingCents;
        history.add("open " + openingCents);
    }

    public void deposit(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("deposit must be positive");
        balanceCents += cents;
        history.add("deposit " + cents);
    }

    public void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("withdrawal must be positive");
        if (cents > balanceCents) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds: balance " + balanceCents + ", requested " + cents);
        balanceCents -= cents;
        history.add("withdraw " + cents);
    }

    public long balanceCents() { return balanceCents; }

    public String id() { return id; }

    /** Read-only view: callers can look at the history but cannot rewrite it. */
    public List<String> history() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(history); }
}

package com.handbook.principles.oop.encapsulation;

public class EncapsulationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BankAccount account = new BankAccount("ACC-1", 10_000);
        account.deposit(2_500);
        account.withdraw(4_000);
        System.out.println("balance = " + account.balanceCents());
        try {
            account.withdraw(1_000_000);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            account.history().add("withdraw 999999");
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("history is read-only to callers");
        }
        System.out.println("history = " + account.history());
    }
}

balance = 8500
rejected: insufficient funds: balance 8500, requested 1000000
history is read-only to callers
history = [open 10000, deposit 2500, withdraw 4000]
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Invariants can't be broken from outside, so there are fewer "impossible" states More methods to write than with public fields You can change the internal representation without affecting callers Too much hiding can make debugging and serialization awkward One place to add validation, logging or thread-safety Frameworks (JPA, Jackson) sometimes want no-arg constructors or setters, so you have to balance purity against tooling

Pitfall: leaking mutable internals

public List<String> getHistory() { return history; } lets callers change the list and bypass every rule. Return an unmodifiable view or a copy, and copy incoming mutable arguments.

docs.title: 2. Abstraction
docs.text:
Definition. Expose what something does and hide how it does it. Callers depend on a simplified model (an interface or abstract class), and the complexity lives behind it.

Key features: interfaces or abstract classes as contracts; names in the caller's language (put, get), not the implementation's (gzipThenWriteToBucket); implementations you can swap.

AbstractionImplementationsDemo + Output FileStorage.java
package com.handbook.principles.oop.abstraction;

import java.util.Optional;

/** Abstraction: callers see WHAT storage does, not HOW (disk, memory, S3...). */
public interface FileStorage {
    void put(String key, byte[] content);

    Optional<byte[]> get(String key);

    String describe();
}
ReportArchiver.java (client knows only the abstraction)
package com.handbook.principles.oop.abstraction;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

/** Client written against the abstraction only. */
public class ReportArchiver {
    private final FileStorage storage;

    public ReportArchiver(FileStorage storage) { this.storage = storage; }

    public String archiveAndReadBack(String name, String body) {
        storage.put(name, body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return storage.get(name).map(b -> new String(b, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)).orElse("<missing>");
    }
}
InMemoryStorage.java
package com.handbook.principles.oop.abstraction;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

public class InMemoryStorage implements FileStorage {
    private final Map<String, byte[]> files = new HashMap<>();

    public void put(String key, byte[] content) { files.put(key, content.clone()); }

    public Optional<byte[]> get(String key) { return Optional.ofNullable(files.get(key)).map(byte[]::clone); }

    public String describe() { return "in-memory (" + files.size() + " files)"; }
}
CompressingStorage.java
package com.handbook.principles.oop.abstraction;

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.zip.GZIPInputStream;
import java.util.zip.GZIPOutputStream;

/** A very different implementation hidden behind the same abstraction: gzip on the way in, gunzip on the way out. */
public class CompressingStorage implements FileStorage {
    private final FileStorage delegate;

    public CompressingStorage(FileStorage delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }

    public void put(String key, byte[] content) {
        ByteArrayOutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (GZIPOutputStream gz = new GZIPOutputStream(out)) {
            gz.write(content);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
        }
        delegate.put(key, out.toByteArray());
    }

    public Optional<byte[]> get(String key) {
        return delegate.get(key).map(bytes -> {
            try (GZIPInputStream gz = new GZIPInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes))) {
                return gz.readAllBytes();
            } catch (IOException e) {
                throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
            }
        });
    }

    public String describe() { return "gzip over " + delegate.describe(); }
}

package com.handbook.principles.oop.abstraction;

public class AbstractionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String body = "Q3 revenue report. ".repeat(3);
        for (FileStorage storage : new FileStorage[]{new InMemoryStorage(), new CompressingStorage(new InMemoryStorage())}) {
            String readBack = new ReportArchiver(storage).archiveAndReadBack("q3.txt", body);
            System.out.println(storage.describe() + " -> round trip ok: " + readBack.equals(body));
        }
    }
}

in-memory (1 files) -> round trip ok: true
gzip over in-memory (1 files) -> round trip ok: true
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Callers stay simple and stable Every abstraction leaks eventually (Joel Spolsky's "Law of Leaky Abstractions"), for example the latency of remote storage Implementations can be swapped (memory, disk, S3, compressed) Too many layers make the code hard to follow Enables DIP and testing with fakes A poor abstraction is worse than none: it constrains every implementation

Encapsulation vs Abstraction: encapsulation hides data to protect it; abstraction hides complexity to simplify use. BankAccount is mainly encapsulation; FileStorage is mainly abstraction.

docs.title: 3. Inheritance
docs.text:
Definition. A subclass reuses and specialises a parent class (an "is-a" relationship). The subclass inherits fields and methods, can override behaviour, and can be used wherever the parent is expected (see LSP).

Key features: extends (a single class), abstract hooks, protected members for subclasses, final to forbid overriding, sealed to restrict who may extend, and super(...) constructor chaining.

CodeDemo + Output Vehicle.java (template method + abstract hook)
package com.handbook.principles.oop.inheritance;

/**
 * Inheritance: shared state and behaviour live in the base class; subclasses specialise.
 * The template method describe() is final so subclasses can't break the format, only fill in the hook.
 */
public abstract class Vehicle {
    private final String plate;
    private final int wheels;

    protected Vehicle(String plate, int wheels) {
        this.plate = plate;
        this.wheels = wheels;
    }

    /** Hook that subclasses must provide. */
    protected abstract long tollCents();

    public final String describe() {
        return getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + plate + " (" + wheels + " wheels) toll=" + tollCents();
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.oop.inheritance;

public class Car extends Vehicle {
    public Car(String plate) { super(plate, 4); }

    @Override
    protected long tollCents() { return 250; }
}

package com.handbook.principles.oop.inheritance;

public class Truck extends Vehicle {
    private final int axles;

    public Truck(String plate, int axles) {
        super(plate, axles * 2 + 2);
        this.axles = axles;
    }

    @Override
    protected long tollCents() { return 400L * axles; }   // specialised rule
}

package com.handbook.principles.oop.inheritance;

import java.util.List;

public class InheritanceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Vehicle> lane = List.of(new Car("KA-01-1234"), new Truck("MH-12-9876", 3));
        lane.forEach(v -> System.out.println(v.describe()));
    }
}

Car KA-01-1234 (4 wheels) toll=250
Truck MH-12-9876 (8 wheels) toll=1200
classDiagram class Vehicle { <<abstract>> -String plate -int wheels #tollCents()* long +describe() String } Vehicle <|-- Car Vehicle <|-- Truck class Truck { -int axles } ✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Shared code is written once Tight coupling. Subclasses depend on parent internals (the fragile base class problem) Natural for true "is-a" taxonomies Single inheritance only; deep trees become rigid Template Method gives controlled extension points Easy to break LSP; changes in the parent ripple to every child

Pitfall: the fragile base class

A subclass that overrides methods the parent calls internally depends on implementation details. The classic case is InstrumentedHashSet extends HashSet, which counts elements twice because addAll calls add. See the runnable demo under Composition over Inheritance. Design for inheritance (document self-use, make hooks protected abstract, make the rest final) or forbid it.

docs.title: 4. Polymorphism
docs.text:
Definition. "Many forms": the same call produces different behaviour depending on the type.

Kind Resolved at Java mechanism Subtype (runtime) Run time (dynamic dispatch) Overriding methods from an interface or superclass Ad-hoc (compile time) Compile time Method overloading: same name, different parameter types Parametric Compile time Generics (List<T>) Pattern-based (Java 21) Run time, checked at compile time switch with type patterns over a sealed hierarchy CodeDemo + Output Payment.java (sealed, each subtype overrides feeCents)
package com.handbook.principles.oop.polymorphism;

/** Sealed hierarchy: the compiler knows every subtype, enabling exhaustive switch (Java 21). */
public sealed interface Payment permits Payment.Card, Payment.Upi, Payment.Cash {

    long amountCents();

    /** Runtime (subtype) polymorphism: each subtype overrides fee(). */
    long feeCents();

    record Card(long amountCents, String last4) implements Payment {
        public long feeCents() { return amountCents * 2 / 100; }       // 2%
    }

    record Upi(long amountCents, String vpa) implements Payment {
        public long feeCents() { return 0; }
    }

    record Cash(long amountCents) implements Payment {
        public long feeCents() { return 0; }
    }
}
Receipt.java (overloading + exhaustive switch)
package com.handbook.principles.oop.polymorphism;

/** Compile-time (ad-hoc) polymorphism: overloading picks a method by the static argument types. */
public final class Receipt {
    private Receipt() { }

    public static String line(String label, long cents) { return label + ": " + cents + " cents"; }

    public static String line(String label, double percent) { return label + ": " + percent + "%"; }

    /** Pattern-matching switch over a sealed type: no default branch needed, adding a subtype is a compile error here. */
    public static String channel(Payment p) {
        return switch (p) {
            case Payment.Card c -> "card ending " + c.last4();
            case Payment.Upi u -> "UPI " + u.vpa();
            case Payment.Cash cash -> "cash";
        };
    }
}

package com.handbook.principles.oop.polymorphism;

import java.util.List;

public class PolymorphismDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Payment> payments = List.of(new Payment.Card(10_000, "4242"), new Payment.Upi(5_000, "ana@bank"), new Payment.Cash(700));
        for (Payment p : payments) {
            System.out.println(Receipt.channel(p) + " | " + Receipt.line("amount", p.amountCents()) + " | " + Receipt.line("fee", p.feeCents()));
        }
        System.out.println(Receipt.line("card fee rate", 2.0));
    }
}

card ending 4242 | amount: 10000 cents | fee: 200 cents
UPI ana@bank | amount: 5000 cents | fee: 0 cents
cash | amount: 700 cents | fee: 0 cents
card fee rate: 2.0%
✅ Pros ⚠️ Cons / Trade-offs Removes if/else type checks, which enables OCP Behaviour is spread across classes, so "what runs here?" needs an IDE New subtypes plug in without changing callers Overloading combined with autoboxing or varargs can pick surprising methods A sealed + switch makes the compiler check every case Virtual dispatch is slightly slower (the JIT usually removes it)

docs.title: 5. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
Encapsulation vs abstraction: what's the difference?

Encapsulation is about hiding data and enforcing invariants (private fields plus validated methods). Abstraction is about hiding complexity behind a contract (an interface). A class can show both: FileStorage abstracts how files are stored; BankAccount encapsulates its balance.

Is a class with private fields and public getters/setters encapsulated?

Barely. If every field has a setter, any caller can put the object in an invalid state. Real encapsulation exposes behaviour (withdraw, deposit) that keeps the invariants, and avoids unconditional setters.

Overloading vs overriding?

Overloading means the same name with different parameters in the same class, chosen at compile time from static types. Overriding means the same signature in a subclass, chosen at run time from the object's real type. Static, private and final methods can't be overridden.

Why is 'favour composition over inheritance' so common?

Inheritance couples the child to the parent's implementation and fixes the relationship at compile time. Composition couples only to an interface, can be changed at run time, and can combine several behaviours. Use inheritance for real "is-a" relationships that you designed for extension.

Abstract class vs interface in modern Java?

Interfaces can have default, static and private methods but no instance state. Abstract classes can hold state and constructors and protected members, but a class can extend only one. Use an interface for a capability or contract, and an abstract class for a partial implementation that shares state, such as a Template Method base.

docs.title: 6. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Encapsulation: protect invariants; expose behaviour, not setters; avoid leaking mutable internals.
  • Abstraction: depend on what, not how; interfaces at boundaries.
  • Inheritance: real "is-a" only; design for it or mark it final; beware the fragile base class.
  • Polymorphism: overriding (runtime), overloading (compile time), generics, sealed + switch (exhaustive).

docs.title: OOP, SOLID & Design Principles
docs.text:
Design patterns are named, proven ways of applying a small set of principles. If you understand why a principle exists, which problem it solves and what it costs, most patterns will feel obvious. Each principle below has its own page with the definition and origin, signs of violation, a runnable before/after Java example with real output, pros, cons and trade-offs, when (not) to apply it, related patterns, interview Q&A and a revision card.

All examples are runnable

The code lives in the code/principles Maven module (com.handbook.principles). It's covered by unit tests, and its output is captured by code/run-demos.sh, so every output block on these pages is real.

flowchart TB OOP["🧱 OOP pillars<br/>Encapsulation · Abstraction · Inheritance · Polymorphism"] SOLID["🏛️ SOLID<br/>SRP · OCP · LSP · ISP · DIP"] OTHER["🧭 Design principles<br/>DRY · KISS · YAGNI · Composition · LoD · Tell-Don't-Ask · Fail Fast"] PAT["🧩 Design patterns<br/>Strategy, Decorator, Factory, Observer, …"] OOP --> SOLID --> PAT OTHER --> PAT

docs.title: The four pillars of OOP
docs.text: Pillar One-liner Java tool Deep dive Encapsulation Hide state, expose behaviour that protects invariants private fields, validated methods, read-only views Encapsulation Abstraction Depend on what, not how interface, abstract class Abstraction Inheritance Reuse and specialise via "is-a" extends, final, sealed (use sparingly) Inheritance Polymorphism One call, many behaviours Overriding, overloading, generics, sealed + switch Polymorphism

docs.title: SOLID at a glance
docs.text: Principle Statement Violation smell Main benefit Main cost Patterns that apply it S Single Responsibility One reason (actor) to change *Manager, mixed imports, "and…and" Focused, testable classes More classes Facade, Strategy, Repository O Open/Closed Extend by adding code, not editing it Repeated instanceof/switch on type Lower regression risk Must guess the axis of change Strategy, Decorator, Template Method L Liskov Substitution Subtypes are drop-in replacements UnsupportedOperationException overrides Trustworthy polymorphism Some hierarchies must be redesigned Null Object, Proxy, Template Method I Interface Segregation No client depends on unused methods Fat interfaces, stubbed methods Compile-time capability checks Interface proliferation Adapter, Facade, role interfaces D Dependency Inversion Policy owns abstractions; details implement them new/static calls to infrastructure Swappable, fast-to-test core Indirection and wiring Hexagonal, Factory, DI container Before/after in one line eachHow SOLID principles reinforce each other Principle ❌ Before ✅ After SRP Invoice computes tax, prints and saves Invoice + TaxCalculator + InvoicePrinter + InvoiceRepository OCP AreaCalculator with an instanceof chain Shape.area(); Triangle added with no edits LSP Square extends Rectangle breaks setWidth Immutable Rectangle and Square records under a sealed Shape ISP OfficeMachine { print; scan; fax } Printer, Scanner, Fax role interfaces DIP OrderNotifier news up EmailSender OrderNotifier(MessageSender) with Email, SMS or a fake injected flowchart LR SRP[SRP<br/>small cohesive classes] --> ISP[ISP<br/>small cohesive interfaces] ISP --> DIP[DIP<br/>depend on those interfaces] DIP --> OCP[OCP<br/>new implementations plug in] LSP[LSP<br/>implementations are substitutable] --> OCP

docs.title: Other principles you'll be asked about
docs.text:
Principle Meaning Interview sound bite Deep dive DRY Don't Repeat Yourself "Every piece of knowledge has one authoritative place, but I avoid the wrong abstraction." DRY KISS Keep It Simple "The simplest design that meets today's requirements, optimised for the reader." KISS YAGNI You Aren't Gonna Need It "I don't add extension points until a second use case appears." YAGNI Composition over inheritance Prefer "has-a" to "is-a" "Inheritance is the strongest coupling in Java; composition lets me swap behaviour at run time." Composition Law of Demeter Talk only to your immediate friends "Avoid a.getB().getC().doX() chains." LoD Tell, Don't Ask Command objects; don't pull data and decide "The decision belongs where the data is." Tell-Don't-Ask Fail Fast Reject invalid state immediately "An invalid object should never exist." Fail Fast

Want to see what happens when these principles are ignored? See Anti-Patterns.

Interview favourite

"Which SOLID principle does the Strategy pattern support?" Mainly Open/Closed (new strategies without editing the context) and Dependency Inversion (the context depends on the strategy interface). It also helps Single Responsibility, because each algorithm lives in its own class.

Is SOLID still relevant with functional programming and records?

Yes. The ideas carry over even where the mechanics change. A Function<Order, Money> parameter is a one-method interface (ISP + DIP); passing a different lambda is OCP; records with compact constructors give encapsulation and fail-fast; sealed hierarchies are a deliberate alternative to OCP-by-interface (the expression problem).

Can you over-apply SOLID?

Yes. You get interfaces with one implementation, five-class chains for a one-line rule, and abstractions guessed on the wrong axis. Balance SOLID with KISS and YAGNI: apply it where change actually happens and at I/O boundaries.
