docs.text:
Used for State, Saga and order lifecycles.

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> CREATED CREATED --> PAID : payment captured CREATED --> CANCELLED : payment failed PAID --> PACKED PACKED --> OUT_FOR_DELIVERY OUT_FOR_DELIVERY --> DELIVERED DELIVERED --> [*] CANCELLED --> [*]

In interviews

You don't need perfect UML. Interviewers want to see classes, their responsibilities, and the relationships between them (especially interface vs. implementation). Boxes and arrows on a whiteboard, labelled clearly, are enough.

docs.title: D: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate SOLID Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

High-level policy should not depend on low-level details. Both should depend on abstractions, and the abstraction belongs to the high-level side. Dependency injection is the most common way to achieve this.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to see the design that follows the principle. Switch to Breaks it to see the "before" version that violates it. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Definition & Origin
docs.text:
"A. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. B. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions." (Robert C. Martin, 1996)

The word inversion refers to the direction of the source-code dependency. In traditional layered code, the policy (OrderNotifier) imports the detail (EmailSender). After DIP, the detail imports an interface owned by the policy (MessageSender). The arrow now points towards the business logic. This is the foundation of Hexagonal, Onion and Clean Architecture.

DIP ≠ DI ≠ IoC

  • DIP is a design principle about the direction of dependencies.
  • DI (Dependency Injection) is a technique: dependencies are passed in, usually through the constructor, instead of created inside the class.
  • IoC (Inversion of Control) is a broader idea: a framework calls your code. A DI container (Spring) is one form of IoC.

You can do DI without DIP (injecting a concrete class) and DIP without a container (wiring by hand in main).

docs.title: 2. The Problem It Solves
docs.text:
• Can't switch implementations. Moving from email to SMS, or MySQL to Postgres, means editing business code.
  • Can't unit-test. The policy creates the real EmailSender, so tests send real email or need bytecode-mocking tricks.
  • Changes ripple upwards. A change in a low-level library breaks high-level modules.
  • The domain is tied to frameworks and can't be reused or compiled on its own.

docs.title: 3. Key Features & How to Spot a Violation
docs.text: Signal Fix new ConcreteThing() for a collaborator inside business logic Inject it through the constructor as an interface Business classes import javax.mail, a JDBC driver or an HTTP client Define a port interface in the domain and implement it in an adapter Static calls to infrastructure (Database.getConnection()) Replace them with an injected dependency Tests need Mockito mockStatic or mockConstruction The dependency is hard-wired

docs.title: 4. Generic Example: Order Notifications
5. Pros
docs.text:
• Swap implementations (email/SMS/push, real/fake) without touching business code.
  • Fast unit tests. Pass a lambda or fake; no container, network or mocking framework needed.
  • Stable core. The domain doesn't depend on volatile infrastructure, so infrastructure upgrades don't ripple inwards.
  • Parallel development. You can build the domain against the interface before the adapter exists.
  • It enables OCP. New details plug in behind the abstraction.

docs.title: 6. Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text:
• More types and indirection. An interface with exactly one implementation forever is ceremony.
  • Wiring has to live somewhere: main, a factory or a DI container. Containers add magic and startup cost.
  • Leaky abstractions. If the interface mirrors one vendor's API (sendViaSes(...)), the inversion is only in name. Design the port in the domain's language.
  • Debugging. "Go to implementation" can lead to several candidates; runtime wiring errors replace compile errors.

docs.title: 7. When to Apply / When Not To
docs.text: Invert when… Depend directly when… The dependency does I/O (DB, network, file, clock, random) It's a stable value type or the JDK (String, List, BigDecimal) You need to unit-test the policy in isolation It's a pure, deterministic helper with no side effects More than one implementation exists or is likely It's a small script with no business core to protect

docs.title: 8. Related Patterns & Frameworks
docs.text:
• Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters): ports are DIP abstractions, adapters are details.
  • Factory, Abstract Factory and Service Locator (an alternative to DI, usually worse) create the details.
  • Strategy, Repository, Adapter.
  • Spring IoC, Guice, Dagger, Jakarta CDI; the JDK ServiceLoader (SPI) is DIP at the module level.

docs.title: 9. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
What exactly is 'inverted'?

The source-code dependency between the policy and the detail. Control flow still goes policy → detail at runtime, but at compile time the detail depends on the policy's interface. That's why the interface should live in the high-level package, not next to the implementation.

Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?

It makes dependencies explicit and final, makes the object fully initialised (fail fast), lets tests use plain new without reflection, and makes "too many dependencies" (an SRP smell) obvious in the constructor signature.

Should every class have an interface?

No. Introduce an interface at architectural boundaries (I/O, external systems, volatile policies) or when you have a second implementation. One interface per class "just because" is noise. Mockito can mock classes anyway.

How do you handle the system clock under DIP?

Inject java.time.Clock (or your own TimeSource) instead of calling Instant.now(). Production uses Clock.systemUTC(); tests use Clock.fixed(...). Do the same for random numbers and UUID generation.

docs.title: 10. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Policy owns the interface; details implement it. The arrow points towards the business logic.
  • DIP (principle) ≠ DI (technique) ≠ IoC (framework calls you).
  • Smell: new/static calls to infrastructure inside business code.
  • Constructor injection + interfaces at I/O boundaries. Don't add interfaces everywhere.

docs.title: I: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner SOLID Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, role-based interfaces to one "fat" interface.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to see the design that follows the principle. Switch to Breaks it to see the "before" version that violates it. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Definition & Origin
docs.text:
"Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use." (Robert C. Martin, 1996)

Martin came up with ISP while consulting for Xerox. A single Job class served print, staple and fax jobs, so every small change recompiled and redeployed everything. Splitting it into role interfaces, one per client need, fixed that. ISP is SRP applied to interfaces: SRP is cohesion from the implementer's side, ISP is cohesion from the client's side.

docs.title: 2. The Problem It Solves
docs.text:
• Implementers forced to stub methods with throw new UnsupportedOperationException(). That's also an LSP violation.
  • Unnecessary coupling. A client that only prints still depends on fax() and is affected when it changes.
  • Bloated test doubles. A mock of a 20-method interface for a test that uses one method.
  • Unclear capabilities. The type system says "can scan" when the object can't.

docs.title: 3. Key Features & How to Spot a Violation
docs.text: Signal Fix Implementations full of UnsupportedOperationException / empty methods Split the interface by capability Each client uses a different subset of methods One interface per client role Interfaces named *Service with 15+ unrelated methods Group by use case: OrderReader, OrderWriter… Mocks that stub one method out of many The client only needs a narrow role interface

docs.title: 4. Generic Example: Office Machines
5. Pros
docs.text:
• Errors move from runtime to compile time. You can't call scan() on something that can't scan.
  • Less coupling. Clients recompile and retest only when their role changes.
  • Simple test doubles. A one-method interface is a lambda.
  • Clearer intent. Method parameters say exactly what capability they need (Printer, not OfficeMachine).

docs.title: 6. Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text:
• Interface proliferation. Too many one-method interfaces fragment the model and make it harder to discover.
  • Implementations still have to be coherent. A class implementing 8 small interfaces may be breaking SRP instead.
  • API stability. For a public library, a broader, stable interface can be easier to evolve, using default methods.
  • Aggregation is sometimes handy. You can keep interface OfficeMachine extends Printer, Scanner, Fax {} for clients that really need all three.

docs.title: 7. When to Apply / When Not To
docs.text: Split an interface when different clients use different subsets or when implementers start stubbing methods. Don't split a cohesive interface that every client uses entirely (such as Iterator's hasNext/next).

docs.title: 8. Related Patterns & Frameworks
docs.text:
• Adapter can expose a narrow role over a wide class. Facade is the client-side aggregation of roles.
  • Proxy and Decorator are easier to write over small interfaces.
  • JDK: Readable/Appendable/Closeable/AutoCloseable, java.util.function.*, Comparable.
  • Spring Data: Repository → CrudRepository → ListCrudRepository. You can extend just Repository and declare only the methods you need.
  • CQRS applies ISP at the architecture level: read and write models are separate interfaces.

docs.title: 9. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
ISP vs SRP?

SRP: an implementation should have one reason to change. ISP: a client shouldn't depend on methods it doesn't use. They often lead to the same split, seen from opposite sides.

How do default methods affect ISP?

default methods let you add to an interface without breaking implementers, which helps library evolution. But they can hide fat interfaces. A default that throws UnsupportedOperationException is still an ISP/LSP smell.

Show ISP in a Spring codebase.

Split a huge UserService into UserQueries (read) and UserCommands (write). One bean implements both. The read-only controller injects UserQueries, so it can't call a mutating method by accident, and its test needs only a read stub.

docs.title: 10. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • No client should depend on methods it doesn't use.
  • Smell: UnsupportedOperationException stubs; fat *Service interfaces; huge mocks.
  • Fix: role interfaces, implemented together where needed.
  • Don't go too far: avoid fragmenting a cohesive interface.

docs.title: L: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate SOLID Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Subtypes must be usable anywhere their base type is expected, without the caller noticing. If code written against Rectangle breaks when you pass it a Square, then Square is not a behavioural subtype of Rectangle.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to see the design that follows the principle. Switch to Breaks it to see the "before" version that violates it. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Definition & Origin
docs.text:
"If for each object o1 of type S there is an object o2 of type T such that for all programs P defined in terms of T, the behavior of P is unchanged when o1 is substituted for o2, then S is a subtype of T." (Barbara Liskov, 1987 keynote "Data Abstraction and Hierarchy"; formalised with Jeannette Wing, 1994)

In practice LSP is design by contract applied to inheritance (Bertrand Meyer). A subtype must:

Rule Meaning Violation example Preconditions cannot be strengthened Accept at least everything the parent accepts Parent accepts any amount > 0; child throws for amount > 1000 Postconditions cannot be weakened Guarantee at least what the parent guarantees Parent's sort() returns sorted data; child returns it "mostly sorted" Invariants must be preserved Keep every rule the parent keeps Square changes height when you set width History constraint Don't allow state changes the parent forbids An immutable parent with a mutable child No new checked exceptions Throw only what the parent declares (or subtypes of it) Java enforces this for checked exceptions; it doesn't for UnsupportedOperationException

docs.title: 2. The Problem It Solves
docs.text: Polymorphism only works if you can trust the abstraction. When subtypes break the contract, callers start adding if (x instanceof Square) checks. That destroys OCP, spreads knowledge of the subtypes everywhere, and creates bugs that only show up for some runtime types.

docs.title: 3. Key Features & How to Spot a Violation
docs.text:
• An overridden method throws UnsupportedOperationException or does nothing ("refused bequest").
  • Callers check instanceof before calling a base-class method.
  • An override ignores or changes the meaning of its arguments.
  • Tests that pass for the base class fail for a subclass. A good trick is to run the base class's test suite against every subtype.
  • "Is-a" is true in the real world (a square is a rectangle) but not in behaviour.

docs.title: 4. Generic Example: Rectangle and Square
5. Pros
docs.text:
• Trustworthy polymorphism. Callers program against the base type and never type-check.
  • OCP keeps working. New subtypes plug in safely.
  • Reusable tests. One contract test suite covers every implementation.
  • Better models. LSP pushes you towards immutability and composition, which are simpler to reason about.

docs.title: 6. Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text:
• It's hard to check. The compiler checks method signatures, not behaviour, so you need contracts, docs and tests.
  • It limits reuse by inheritance. Some "obvious" hierarchies (Square/Rectangle, Penguin/Bird.fly) have to be redesigned.
  • The JDK breaks it on purpose. List.of(...) returns a List whose add throws. That's a trade-off: the List interface marks those methods as optional operations in its docs, so the contract is loosened on purpose.
  • More types. Splitting hierarchies (for example Bird versus FlyingBird) adds interfaces.

docs.title: 7. When to Apply / When Not To
docs.text: LSP isn't optional whenever you use subtype polymorphism. The real question is whether to use inheritance at all. Prefer composition or interfaces when the child would have to remove or contradict parent behaviour. Use final classes, sealed hierarchies and records so subtyping happens only where you intend it.

docs.title: 8. Related Patterns & Frameworks
docs.text:
• Template Method, Strategy, Proxy and Decorator all rely on substitutable implementations.
  • Null Object is a well-behaved substitute that keeps the contract instead of returning null.
  • Composition over inheritance (Design Principles) is the usual fix.
  • Spring AOP proxies and JPA lazy-loading proxies only work because they are LSP-compliant subtypes or implementations.

docs.title: 9. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
Explain LSP with a non-shape example.

Bird.fly() with a Penguin subclass that throws. Fix it by splitting the capability: Bird with a separate FlyingBird interface, so only birds that can fly promise fly(). Another example: ReadOnlyAccount extends Account whose withdraw throws.

Does Java enforce LSP?

Only partly. It enforces signature rules: covariant return types, no broader checked exceptions, and no reduced visibility. It can't enforce behavioural rules like preconditions, postconditions and invariants. Those come from contracts and tests.

Is Collections.unmodifiableList an LSP violation?

Strictly, yes: add() throws. The Collection API documents mutators as optional operations, so the contract allows it. It's a pragmatic trade-off that avoids splitting every collection interface into read and write halves. Kotlin and Guava split List and MutableList partly for this reason.

How do you test for LSP?

Write an abstract contract test class with the base type's expected behaviour, and subclass the test for each implementation. Any implementation that fails the inherited tests violates LSP.

docs.title: 10. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • A subtype must be a drop-in replacement, behaviourally and not just in signature.
  • Contract rules: preconditions can't be stronger, postconditions can't be weaker, invariants are kept.
  • Smells: UnsupportedOperationException overrides, instanceof checks, empty overrides.
  • Fixes: immutable values, sibling types under a shared interface, composition, sealed.

docs.title: O: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate SOLID Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. You add new behaviour by adding new code (a new class) instead of editing working, tested code.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to see the design that follows the principle. Switch to Breaks it to see the "before" version that violates it. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Definition & Origin
docs.text:
"Software entities (classes, modules, functions, etc.) should be open for extension, but closed for modification." (Bertrand Meyer, Object-Oriented Software Construction, 1988)

Meyer's original version relied on implementation inheritance. Robert C. Martin restated it in the 1990s in its modern form: depend on abstractions (interfaces), so that new implementations plug in without touching the code that uses them. "Closed" doesn't mean the source is frozen. It means the module's behaviour can be extended without changing its source.

docs.title: 2. The Problem It Solves
docs.text:
• Growing if/else and switch chains on a type code, copied into every place that needs type-specific behaviour.
  • Regression risk. Every new variant means editing, re-testing and redeploying code that already worked.
  • Merge hotspots. Every feature team edits the same central method.
  • No third-party extension. A library user can't add a variant without forking the library.

docs.title: 3. Key Features & How to Spot a Violation
docs.text:
Signal What it tells you instanceof / switch (type) chains outside one factory The behaviour belongs to the types, not to the caller The same type switch appears in several places Every new type means N edits (shotgun surgery) A method ends in else throw new IllegalArgumentException("unsupported") The method is a closed list of options Adding a feature always edits the same core file That core file is not closed

Mechanisms that make code open for extension: interfaces plus polymorphism, the Strategy pattern, plugins or ServiceLoader, template methods (hooks), decorators, event listeners, and configuration-driven rules.

docs.title: 4. Generic Example: Area Calculator
5. Pros
docs.text:
• Lower regression risk. Code that already works isn't touched again.
  • Independent extension. Teams, and even third parties, can add variants in parallel.
  • Behaviour lives with the data. Each shape knows its own area, so the code is cohesive.
  • Testability. You test each variant in isolation, and you can test the calculator with a stub Shape.

docs.title: 6. Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text:
• You must guess the axis of change. An abstraction protects against one kind of change. If you guess wrong, the abstraction itself has to change. Martin calls this strategic closure.
  • More indirection. Readers jump from an interface to its implementations.
  • The expression problem. With an interface it's easy to add new types but hard to add new operations (you'd have to edit every class). With a sealed interface + switch it's the reverse: adding operations is easy, and the compiler lists every switch to update when you add a type. Pick the side that matches how your domain changes.
  • Over-engineering. Adding plug-in points nobody needs violates YAGNI. Wait until you've seen the second variant.

docs.title: 7. When to Apply / When Not To
docs.text: Apply OCP when… Hold off when… You've already added the 2nd or 3rd variant of something There's only one variant and no sign of more Variants are owned by different teams or plugins The set of cases is fixed by nature (days of the week, HTTP methods) Each new variant risks breaking a central method A closed sealed hierarchy with exhaustive switch is clearer

docs.title: 8. Related Patterns & Frameworks
docs.text:
• Strategy, Template Method, Decorator, Observer, Visitor (the operations-side answer to the expression problem), Factory Method.
  • Spring: injecting List<SomeHandler> beans; HandlerInterceptor, BeanPostProcessor and @Conditional auto-configuration are all OCP extension points.
  • JDK: ServiceLoader plugins, Comparator, java.util.function interfaces.

docs.title: 9. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
If the code is 'closed for modification', how do you fix bugs?

OCP is about adding features, not bug fixes. You always fix bugs in place. The goal is that new requirements of the anticipated kind arrive as new code.

Is a switch statement always an OCP violation?

No. A single switch in a factory that maps config to objects is fine, because it's the one place that knows about all the types. The problem is the same switch repeated across the codebase. With Java 21, a switch over a sealed type is a deliberate choice: the compiler enforces exhaustiveness, so adding a type gives you a compile error instead of a silent bug.

How does OCP relate to Strategy and DIP?

Strategy is the most common mechanism for OCP. DIP is what makes it work: the high-level code depends on the abstraction, so new low-level strategies don't affect it.

Give a real framework example.

Spring Security's filter chain: you add a custom OncePerRequestFilter bean without changing Spring's code. The same goes for JUnit 5 extensions (@ExtendWith) and Servlet filters.

docs.title: 10. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Extend by adding code, not by editing working code.
  • Smell: repeated instanceof or switch on a type, and else throw unsupported.
  • Tools: interface + polymorphism, Strategy, Decorator, plugins.
  • Trade-off: the expression problem. Interfaces make new types easy; sealed + switch makes new operations easy.
  • Apply after the second variant, not the first.

docs.title: S: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner SOLID Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. Put together the things that change for the same reason, and keep apart the things that change for different reasons.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to see the design that follows the principle. Switch to Breaks it to see the "before" version that violates it. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Definition & Origin
docs.text:
"A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor." (Robert C. Martin, Clean Architecture, 2017)

Robert C. Martin coined SRP in the early 2000s, building on the older ideas of cohesion (Tom DeMarco, Meilir Page-Jones) and separation of concerns (Dijkstra). People often misread it as "a class should do one thing". The precise version is about reasons to change: who asks for changes to this code? If finance asks for tax changes, marketing asks for invoice layout changes and ops asks for storage changes, one class serving all three has three reasons to change.

docs.title: 2. The Problem It Solves
docs.text:
• Merge conflicts and accidental breakage. Two teams editing one class for unrelated reasons step on each other.
  • Fragile tests. To test the tax rule you have to set up printing and a database.
  • No reuse. You can't reuse the printing without dragging the persistence along.
  • Shotgun redeploys. A one-line tax change redeploys printing and storage code that didn't change.

docs.title: 3. Key Features & How to Spot a Violation
docs.text: Signal What it tells you The class name contains And / Manager / Util / Processor The class has no single concept behind it Imports from many unrelated layers (SQL + HTTP + PDF + mail) It touches several actors' concerns Methods fall into groups that never use each other's fields Low cohesion: the groups want to be separate classes You describe it with "…and…and…" Each "and" is a candidate responsibility Unrelated change requests keep landing in the same file That's the textbook symptom

docs.title: 4. Generic Example: an Invoice
5. Pros
docs.text:
• High cohesion, low coupling. Each class is small and easy to understand.
  • Cheap, focused tests. You can test TaxCalculator with no printer and no database.
  • Safer change. A change for one actor can't break another actor's feature.
  • Reuse. CsvInvoicePrinter can be used anywhere an Invoice exists.
  • Parallel work. Different people can own different classes without merge conflicts.

docs.title: 6. Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text:
• More classes and files. Over-applied, you get "class explosion" and have to jump through five files to follow one flow.
  • Indirection. Someone has to wire the pieces together, usually a small service or the DI container.
  • Judgement is needed. "Reason to change" isn't mechanical. Splitting by technical step (validate/save/send) rather than by actor can scatter one business concept across many classes.
  • Premature splitting violates YAGNI. If only one actor ever changes this code, one class is fine.

docs.title: 7. When to Apply / When Not To
docs.text: Apply SRP when… Hold off when… Different stakeholders change different parts It's a small script or prototype with one owner A class has grown past a few hundred lines with method clusters The "responsibilities" always change together Tests need unrelated setup Splitting would just move code between files with no independent reason to change

docs.title: 8. Related Patterns & Frameworks
docs.text:
• Facade puts a single entry point over many single-responsibility classes.
  • Strategy (InvoicePrinter) pulls a varying responsibility out into its own type.
  • Repository isolates persistence. Command gives one action one class.
  • Spring stereotypes (@Controller / @Service / @Repository) are SRP at the layer level.
  • At the architecture level, SRP is the Common Closure Principle and the basis of microservice boundaries.

docs.title: 9. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
What does 'one reason to change' actually mean?

One actor (a person, team or stakeholder role) whose requests drive changes to the class. A class with three methods is fine if one actor owns all of them. A class with one method can still violate SRP if two actors fight over it.

Doesn't SRP lead to too many tiny classes?

It can, if you split by verb instead of by actor. Split when you see independent change, not in advance. A cohesive class with ten methods for one actor beats ten one-method classes.

How do you refactor a God class towards SRP?

1) Group methods by the fields they use (a cohesion analysis). 2) Write characterization tests. 3) Use Extract Class for each group and leave a delegating method behind. 4) Point callers at the new classes. 5) Delete the delegates.

How does SRP relate to microservices?

It's the same idea at a larger scale. A service should be owned by one team or bounded context and change for one business reason. Otherwise you get a distributed monolith, where every feature needs coordinated deploys.

docs.title: 10. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One actor, one reason to change, not "one method".
  • Smells: *Manager/*Util, mixed imports, "and" in the description, unrelated changes in the same file.
  • Fix: Extract Class by actor, then wire the pieces with a thin service or DI.
  • Don't over-split. Wait for real, independent change.

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
This section turns the handbook into an interview plan. Pattern pages already end with an Interview Corner (beginner, mid-level, senior and a coding challenge) and a STAR story. The pages here add company-specific preparation, low-level design (LLD) problems with full code, system design patterns, and the top 100 questions in one place.

About company pages

Interview processes differ by team, level, country and year, and companies change them often. The company pages describe commonly reported formats and how design-pattern knowledge is typically tested there; they aren't official descriptions. Always check the company's own careers pages and ask your recruiter what your loop looks like.

docs.title: What you'll find here
docs.text:
• Company guides

    Google, Microsoft, Amazon, SAP, and service companies (TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, Accenture, Capgemini and others): format, what's evaluated, 15 practice questions each, and a 4-week plan.

    Google · Microsoft · Amazon · SAP · Service companies

  • LLD problems

    12 classic machine-coding problems (Parking Lot, Elevator, Vending Machine, LRU Cache, Splitwise, BookMyShow-style booking and more), each with requirements, patterns, class diagram, runnable code and output.

    LLD problems

  • System design patterns

    The building blocks (caching, sharding, consistent hashing, queues, replication) and how microservice patterns combine in classic designs.

    System design patterns

  • Top 100 questions

    The most frequently asked design-pattern, architecture and microservices questions, with short answers and links to the full explanations.

    Top 100

docs.title: Which patterns matter at which level
docs.text: Level Expectation Must know Should know Fresher / 0–2 years Explain and code the classics; SOLID Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, Decorator, Template Method Facade, Proxy, Command, State, Iterator Mid / 3–7 years Choose patterns for LLD problems; Spring internals; basic microservices All GoF essentials + Chain of Responsibility, Composite, State, Producer-Consumer, Thread Pool Circuit Breaker, Saga, Outbox, API Gateway, CQRS Senior / 8–15 years Trade-offs, architecture, distributed systems, leading design reviews Hexagonal/Clean, modular monolith, all resilience and data-consistency patterns, observability Event sourcing, service mesh, migration strategies, anti-patterns and their cost

docs.title: A four-week plan (any company)
docs.text:
Week Focus Use these pages 1 OOP, SOLID, creational and structural patterns; code each example yourself OOP & SOLID, Creational, Structural 2 Behavioral and concurrency patterns; 4 LLD problems under time pressure (45 min each) Behavioral, Concurrency, LLD problems 3 Microservices and architecture; 2 system design mocks Microservices, Architecture, System design patterns 4 Company-specific prep, STAR stories, top 100 questions, revision Company page, Top 100, Cheat sheet

In every design interview

  1. Clarify requirements and constraints before drawing anything.
  2. Name the pattern only after describing the problem it solves ("the pricing rules change per campaign, so I'll isolate them behind a strategy").
  3. State the trade-off (what it costs) and an alternative you rejected.
  4. Write code that runs: small, tested pieces beat a big diagram.

Glossary Next: Google

docs.title: Amazon: Design Patterns in Interviews
docs.text:
Commonly reported, not official

Based on Amazon's public interview guidance and widely shared candidate experiences. Details vary by team and level. Confirm with your recruiter.

docs.title: What the process commonly looks like
docs.text:
• An online assessment (coding, sometimes work-style questions) or phone screen, then an interview loop (often 4–5 interviews).
  • Rounds cover coding, object-oriented / low-level design (common for SDE I/II), system design (SDE II and above), and behavioral questions in every round.
  • Amazon publishes its Leadership Principles (Customer Obsession, Ownership, Dive Deep, Bias for Action, and others) and its interview guidance says behavioral questions are based on them. One interviewer, often called the Bar Raiser, is from outside the hiring team.

docs.title: Where design patterns show up
docs.text: Situation Pattern knowledge that helps LLD: "design a locker system / parking lot / vending machine" State, Strategy, Factory Method, Singleton (and its pitfalls) Extensibility follow-ups ("now add a new payment type") Open/closed with Strategy/Factory, Decorator System design (orders, inventory, notifications) Saga, Outbox, Idempotent Consumer, CQRS, queues Operational excellence Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Rate Limiter, Tracing

docs.title: What interviewers look for
docs.text:
Signal What strong looks like LLD Clear entities and responsibilities, extensible where requirements will change, working code for the core flow System design Requirements and scale first, simple design that works, then bottlenecks, failure modes and cost Leadership Principles Specific STAR stories with your actions, data, and results; real trade-offs and mistakes Ownership Talks about operating what you build: monitoring, on-call, fixing root causes

Prepare two stories per Leadership Principle

Interviewers ask follow-ups ("what data did you use?", "what would you do differently?"). Each STAR tie-in at the end of the pattern pages in this handbook is a template; replace it with your own experience.

docs.title: 15 practice questions (with model answers)
docs.text:
1. Design an Amazon Locker-style package locker system.

Lockers with sizes (S/M/L), allocation Strategy (smallest fitting), codes with expiry, locker State (free/reserved/occupied), notifications via Observer; concurrency on allocation.

2. Design a vending machine.

State machine: Idle → HasMoney → Dispensing; coin handling; out-of-stock; refunds. See the Vending Machine LLD.

3. Your checkout calls payment, inventory and shipping. How do you keep them consistent?

Orchestrated Saga with compensations, Outbox for events, idempotent handlers, timeouts and PENDING states.

4. How do you avoid charging a customer twice when the client retries?

Idempotency-Key stored with the response; unique constraints; replay the stored response. See Idempotent Consumer.

5. Add a new discount type to a pricing engine without modifying existing code.

Each discount is a Strategy/Specification; a registry or chain applies them; new type = new class + registration. See the Discount Engine LLD.

6. Design a notification service for order updates (email, SMS, push).

Channel Strategy + Factory, templates (Template Method), preferences, retries and DLQ, dedupe keys, rate limits. See the Notification LLD.

7. Your service depends on a slow third-party API. How do you protect it?

Timeouts, Circuit Breaker with fallback, Bulkhead, caching, async processing via queues.

8. Design a system to show 'customers who bought this also bought'.

Event stream of orders → batch/stream job computing co-occurrence → read model per product (CQRS) in a key-value store, cached at the edge.

9. Singleton: when is it acceptable and what are the risks?

For truly single, stateless or immutable resources (config, registries) via DI; risks are hidden global state, testing pain, and false assumptions of uniqueness across JVMs. See Singleton.

10. Design an inventory service that never oversells during a flash sale.

Atomic conditional decrements (UPDATE ... SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0), reservations with TTL, a queue for the hottest SKUs, rate limits per user, and reconciliation.

11. How would you find the cause of rising p99 latency in production?

Metrics to find which endpoint, tracing to find the slow hop, logs for that trace; check recent deploys and dependencies (Dive Deep).

12. Observer vs. pub/sub messaging?

Observer is in-process and synchronous by default; pub/sub uses a broker for decoupled, asynchronous, durable delivery across services. See Event-Driven.

13. Design a parking garage pricing system that changes per hour, weekend and vehicle type.

Composable pricing rules (Strategy + Chain or Decorator), config-driven rates, injectable clock for tests.

14. Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team's design (Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit).

STAR: your data-driven argument, how you disagreed respectfully, the decision, how you committed, and the outcome either way.

15. Tell me about a production issue you owned end to end (Ownership, Dive Deep).

STAR: detection, mitigation first, root cause with evidence, long-term fix (tests, alarms, runbooks), and what you changed in the team's process.

Week Do 1 Coding fundamentals; 2 LLD problems (Parking Lot, Vending Machine) with working code 2 4 more LLD problems; patterns: State, Strategy, Observer, Factory, Decorator 3 System design: orders, inventory, notifications; Saga, Outbox, Idempotency, Circuit Breaker 4 2 STAR stories per Leadership Principle; mock loop with a "bar raiser" style interviewer

docs.title: Google: Design Patterns in Interviews
docs.text:
Commonly reported, not official

This page summarizes publicly shared candidate experiences and Google's own general hiring guidance. Formats vary by role, level and location and change over time. Confirm the details of your loop with your recruiter.

docs.title: What the process commonly looks like
docs.text:
• Coding interviews dominate for software engineers: data structures and algorithms, written in a shared doc or editor, with emphasis on correctness, complexity and clear code.
  • System design is commonly added for experienced (roughly L5+) candidates.
  • Behavioral / "Googleyness & leadership" conversations explore collaboration, ambiguity and impact.
  • Google's careers site describes evaluating general cognitive ability, role-related knowledge, leadership and "Googleyness". Feedback is typically reviewed by a hiring committee rather than decided by one interviewer.

docs.title: Where design patterns show up
docs.text:
Google interviews rarely ask "define the Visitor pattern". Patterns show up implicitly:

Situation Pattern knowledge that helps A coding problem with extensible rules ("now support a new type of discount") Strategy, Factory Method, open/closed design Iterating complex structures lazily Iterator, generators, Composite Designing an API or library Builder, Immutable Object, Facade Concurrency follow-ups Producer-Consumer, Thread Pool, Read-Write Lock System design Rate Limiter, caching, sharding, CQRS, Circuit Breaker

docs.title: What interviewers look for
docs.text:
Signal What strong looks like Problem solving Clarifies, explores examples, chooses a sound approach, states complexity Code quality Readable names, small functions, correct edge cases, no over-engineering Testing Walks through examples, finds own bugs, mentions test cases Communication Thinks aloud, takes hints well, explains trade-offs Design (senior) Requirements → API → data model → scaling → failure modes, with numbers

Pattern advice for Google-style coding rounds

Use patterns only when they simplify the solution. An interface plus two implementations for an extensibility follow-up is great; a factory of builders for a 30-line problem is not. Say why you chose the structure.

docs.title: 15 practice questions (with model answers)
docs.text:
1. Design an iterator that flattens a nested list of integers lazily.

Keep a stack of iterators; hasNext() advances until the top iterator yields an integer, pushing nested lists as you meet them. O(1) amortized per element, O(depth) memory. This is Iterator over a Composite.

2. Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. How would you make it thread-safe?

HashMap + doubly linked list (or LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true and removeEldestEntry). Thread safety: a single lock is simplest; for high concurrency, shard into N segments by key hash. See the LRU Cache LLD.

3. A pricing function grows a new if every sprint. Refactor it.

Extract each rule into a PricingRule Strategy (or Specification + action), register rules in a list or map, and test each independently. New rules don't touch existing code.

4. Design a rate limiter for an API used by millions of clients.

Token bucket per key, Redis with atomic Lua scripts for global limits, local buckets for hot paths, 429 with Retry-After. See Rate Limiter.

5. Make an expensive, immutable configuration object available everywhere, loaded once.

Lazy holder idiom or an enum singleton; better, dependency injection with a single instance. Immutable, so no locking after construction. See Singleton and Immutable Object.

6. Implement an event system where components subscribe to typed events.

Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<?>>>, type-safe subscribe/publish, copy-on-write lists for concurrent publishing, and unsubscribe handles to avoid leaks. See Observer.

7. Design a bounded blocking queue without java.util.concurrent collections.

Array + head/tail indices + ReentrantLock with two Conditions (notFull, notEmpty); always wait in a while loop. See Producer-Consumer.

8. Design a text editor's undo/redo.

Command objects with execute/undo on two stacks, or Memento snapshots for complex state; merge consecutive typing commands.

9. How would you parse and evaluate expressions like price > 100 AND category = 'fruit'?

Tokenize → recursive-descent parser → AST of composite nodes → evaluate with an Interpreter or Visitor. Discuss precedence and error messages.

10. Design a URL shortener. Which parts would you cache and how?

ID generation (counter + base62 or random with collision check), key-value store sharded by key, cache-aside for hot links with TTL, 301 vs 302 trade-off, analytics via async events. See System design patterns.

11. A service calls three backends; p99 latency is too high. What do you do?

Call in parallel (Future/Promise), add per-call timeouts and hedged requests for idempotent reads, cache, and make optional calls degradable. See BFF.

12. How do you guarantee only one instance runs a scheduled job across a cluster?

Leader election (lease in a DB/etcd/ZooKeeper with fencing tokens), or a DB row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), not a JVM singleton.

13. Builder vs. telescoping constructors vs. static factories: when each?

Static factories for simple named creation; builders for many optional parameters and validation across fields; avoid telescoping constructors. See Builder.

14. Design a thread-safe counter used by 64 threads at very high rate.

LongAdder (striped cells) beats AtomicLong under contention; reads sum the cells. Explain the trade-off (reads are not atomic snapshots).

15. Tell me about a time you simplified an over-engineered design.

STAR: what the abstraction cost (onboarding, bugs), the evidence you gathered, how you removed it safely (tests first), the measurable result. See the anti-patterns page: Anti-Patterns.

docs.title: 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Do 1 30 algorithm problems (arrays, hashing, two pointers, trees, graphs); code cleanly with small helper classes 2 20 more problems + 4 design-flavoured coding problems (iterator, LRU, rate limiter, event bus) from this handbook 3 Concurrency patterns; 2 system design mocks (URL shortener, news feed) using System design patterns 4 Mock interviews with a timer; 5 STAR stories; revise the cheat sheet

docs.title: Low-Level Design (LLD) Problems
docs.text:
Machine-coding and object-oriented design rounds (common at Amazon, Microsoft, Flipkart, Uber, Swiggy, and in senior rounds at service companies) ask you to design and code a small system in 45–90 minutes. Below are 12 classic problems, each with requirements, the patterns that fit, a class diagram, complete runnable code, real output, and the follow-up questions interviewers usually ask.

A repeatable approach for any LLD round

  1. Clarify requirements (5 min): actors, use cases, what's out of scope. Write them down.
  2. Identify entities and their responsibilities (5 min): nouns become classes, verbs become methods.
  3. Find what varies and isolate it behind an interface (pricing, allocation, notifications): that's where patterns appear.
  4. Code the core flow first, then edge cases, then extensions. Keep it compiling and runnable.
  5. Talk about concurrency, testing and extensibility at the end.
# Problem Key patterns Interview frequency 1 Parking Lot Strategy (allocation, pricing), enums for types ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 2 Elevator System State, Strategy (dispatch), SCAN ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 3 Vending Machine State (sealed types) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 4 LRU Cache HashMap + doubly linked list; locking ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 5 Splitwise Strategy (split types), greedy settlement ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 6 Snake and Ladder Builder, Strategy (dice) ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 7 Library Management Strategy (fines), Observer (reservations) ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 8 Movie Ticket Booking Seat holds with expiry, atomic all-or-nothing ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 9 Notification System Strategy, Factory, Template Method, Decorator ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 10 Logging Framework Chain of Responsibility, Strategy, hierarchy ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 11 Grocery Discount Engine Specification, Strategy, combination policy ⭐⭐⭐⭐ 12 Tic-Tac-Toe O(1) win detection ⭐⭐⭐⭐

docs.title: 1. Parking Lot
docs.text:
Requirements: multiple floors; spot sizes small/medium/large; bikes, cars and trucks (a vehicle fits its size or larger); issue a ticket on entry; charge on exit (first 30 minutes free, then per started hour by vehicle type); show free spots; reject reused tickets. Patterns: Strategy for allocation and pricing, so rules can change per lot.

Watch the design handle the demo scenario step by step, with the matching code lit up. Switch to Naive design to see a simpler design fail. Open in the explorer

classDiagram class ParkingLot { +park(vehicle, time) Optional~Ticket~ +exit(ticketId, time) Receipt +freeSpots(type) long } class AllocationStrategy { <<interface>> +choose(spots, vehicle) Optional~Spot~ } class PricingStrategy { <<interface>> +feePaise(type, duration) long } class Spot { id floor size parked } class Ticket { id vehicle spotId entry } ParkingLot --> AllocationStrategy ParkingLot --> PricingStrategy ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" Spot ParkingLot --> Ticket ParkingLot.javaParkingLotDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.parkinglot;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Parking lot LLD. Patterns: Strategy (spot allocation, pricing), Factory-style creation of spots
 * per floor, and a small state model per spot (free/occupied).
 */
public final class ParkingLot {

    public enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }

    public enum SpotSize {
        SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE;

        boolean fits(VehicleType v) {
            return switch (v) {
                case BIKE -> true;
                case CAR -> this != SMALL;
                case TRUCK -> this == LARGE;
            };
        }
    }

    public record Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) {
    }

    public static final class Spot {
        final String id;
        final int floor;
        final SpotSize size;
        Vehicle parked;

        Spot(String id, int floor, SpotSize size) {
            this.id = id;
            this.floor = floor;
            this.size = size;
        }

        boolean isFree() {
            return parked == null;
        }
    }

    public record Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, String spotId, Instant entry) {
    }

    public record Receipt(String ticketId, String plate, Duration parked, long feePaise) {
    }

    /** Strategy: which free spot to give a vehicle. */
    public interface AllocationStrategy {
        Optional<Spot> choose(List<Spot> spots, Vehicle vehicle);
    }

    /** Strategy: how much to charge. */
    public interface PricingStrategy {
        long feePaise(VehicleType type, Duration parked);
    }

    /** Nearest floor first, and the smallest spot that fits (keeps large spots for trucks). */
    public static AllocationStrategy nearestSmallestFit() {
        return (spots, v) -> spots.stream()
                .filter(Spot::isFree)
                .filter(s -> s.size.fits(v.type()))
                .min((a, b) -> a.floor != b.floor ? Integer.compare(a.floor, b.floor) : a.size.compareTo(b.size));
    }

    /** First 30 minutes free, then a per-hour rate by vehicle type, rounded up to whole hours. */
    public static PricingStrategy hourly(Map<VehicleType, Long> ratePerHourPaise) {
        return (type, parked) -> {
            if (parked.compareTo(Duration.ofMinutes(30)) <= 0) {
                return 0;
            }
            long hours = (parked.toMinutes() + 59) / 60;
            return hours * ratePerHourPaise.get(type);
        };
    }

    private final List<Spot> spots = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Spot> spotById = new HashMap<>();
    private final AllocationStrategy allocation;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private int nextTicket = 1;

    public ParkingLot(AllocationStrategy allocation, PricingStrategy pricing) {
        this.allocation = allocation;
        this.pricing = pricing;
    }

    public ParkingLot addFloor(int floor, int small, int medium, int large) {
        add(floor, SpotSize.SMALL, small);
        add(floor, SpotSize.MEDIUM, medium);
        add(floor, SpotSize.LARGE, large);
        return this;
    }

    private void add(int floor, SpotSize size, int count) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
            Spot s = new Spot("F" + floor + "-" + size.name().charAt(0) + i, floor, size);
            spots.add(s);
            spotById.put(s.id, s);
        }
    }

    public synchronized Optional<Ticket> park(Vehicle vehicle, Instant at) {
        return allocation.choose(spots, vehicle).map(spot -> {
            spot.parked = vehicle;
            Ticket t = new Ticket("T-" + nextTicket++, vehicle, spot.id, at);
            active.put(t.id(), t);
            return t;
        });
    }

    public synchronized Receipt exit(String ticketId, Instant at) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);
        if (t == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown or already used ticket " + ticketId);
        }
        spotById.get(t.spotId()).parked = null;
        Duration parked = Duration.between(t.entry(), at);
        return new Receipt(t.id(), t.vehicle().plate(), parked, pricing.feePaise(t.vehicle().type(), parked));
    }

    public synchronized long freeSpots(VehicleType type) {
        return spots.stream().filter(Spot::isFree).filter(s -> s.size.fits(type)).count();
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.parkinglot;

import com.handbook.lld.parkinglot.ParkingLot.Vehicle;
import com.handbook.lld.parkinglot.ParkingLot.VehicleType;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Map;

public class ParkingLotDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var lot = new ParkingLot(ParkingLot.nearestSmallestFit(), ParkingLot.hourly(Map.of(
                VehicleType.BIKE, 1_000L, VehicleType.CAR, 4_000L, VehicleType.TRUCK, 10_000L)))
                .addFloor(0, 1, 1, 0)
                .addFloor(1, 0, 1, 1);
        Instant nine = Instant.parse("2026-10-14T09:00:00Z");

        System.out.println("=== LLD: Parking lot ===");
        var bike = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-B-1", VehicleType.BIKE), nine).orElseThrow();
        var car1 = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-1", VehicleType.CAR), nine).orElseThrow();
        var car2 = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-2", VehicleType.CAR), nine).orElseThrow();
        var truck = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-T-1", VehicleType.TRUCK), nine.plusSeconds(600));
        System.out.println("bike  -> " + bike.spotId() + " (smallest fitting spot on the nearest floor)");
        System.out.println("car 1 -> " + car1.spotId());
        System.out.println("car 2 -> " + car2.spotId());
        System.out.println("truck -> " + truck.map(t -> t.spotId()).orElse("FULL"));
        System.out.println("free spots for cars now: " + lot.freeSpots(VehicleType.CAR));
        System.out.println("another car -> " + lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01-C-3", VehicleType.CAR), nine)
                .map(t -> t.spotId()).orElse("FULL"));

        System.out.println(lot.exit(bike.id(), nine.plusSeconds(20 * 60)) + "  (first 30 min free)");
        System.out.println(lot.exit(car1.id(), nine.plusSeconds(2 * 3600 + 5 * 60)) + "  (3 started hours)");
        try {
            lot.exit(car1.id(), nine.plusSeconds(3 * 3600));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("re-using a ticket: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

=== LLD: Parking lot ===
bike  -> F0-S1 (smallest fitting spot on the nearest floor)
car 1 -> F0-M1
car 2 -> F1-M1
truck -> F1-L1
free spots for cars now: 0
another car -> FULL
Receipt[ticketId=T-1, plate=KA01-B-1, parked=PT20M, feePaise=0]  (first 30 min free)
Receipt[ticketId=T-2, plate=KA01-C-1, parked=PT2H5M, feePaise=12000]  (3 started hours)
re-using a ticket: unknown or already used ticket T-2

Follow-ups: concurrency at entry gates (synchronized here; per-floor locks or a DB row lock in a real system), electric-vehicle spots with chargers (a new SpotSize capability or a spot feature set), lost tickets, payments as a separate service, display boards (Observer).

docs.title: 2. Elevator System
docs.text:
Requirements: N elevators; hall calls (floor + direction) and car calls (button inside); serve requests efficiently; don't reverse while there are stops ahead. Patterns: State (direction per car), Strategy (dispatcher), SCAN scheduling.

Watch the design handle the demo scenario step by step, with the matching code lit up. Switch to Naive design to see a simpler design fail. Open in the explorer

classDiagram class ElevatorSystem { +hallCall(floor, dir) +carCall(car, floor) +tick() } class Car { id floor direction stops +step() } class Dispatcher { <<interface>> +choose(cars, floor, dir) Car } ElevatorSystem "1" *-- "*" Car ElevatorSystem --> Dispatcher ElevatorSystem.javaElevatorDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.elevator;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * Elevator LLD. Patterns: State (each car's direction), Strategy (which car serves a hall call),
 * and the SCAN ("elevator") algorithm: keep moving in one direction while there are stops ahead.
 */
public final class ElevatorSystem {

    public enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

    public static final class Car {
        final String id;
        int floor;
        Direction direction = Direction.IDLE;
        final TreeSet<Integer> stops = new TreeSet<>();

        Car(String id, int floor) {
            this.id = id;
            this.floor = floor;
        }

        /** One tick: move one floor toward the next stop in the current direction (SCAN). */
        String step() {
            if (stops.isEmpty()) {
                direction = Direction.IDLE;
                return id + "@" + floor + " idle";
            }
            if (direction == Direction.IDLE) {
                direction = stops.first() >= floor ? Direction.UP : Direction.DOWN;
            }
            if (direction == Direction.UP && stops.ceiling(floor) == null) {
                direction = Direction.DOWN; // nothing above: reverse
            } else if (direction == Direction.DOWN && stops.floor(floor) == null) {
                direction = Direction.UP;
            }
            if (stops.remove(floor)) {
                return id + "@" + floor + " doors open";
            }
            floor += direction == Direction.UP ? 1 : -1;
            if (stops.remove(floor)) {
                return id + "@" + floor + " doors open";
            }
            return id + "@" + floor + " moving " + direction;
        }
    }

    /** Strategy for assigning a hall call to a car. */
    public interface Dispatcher {
        Car choose(List<Car> cars, int floor, Direction wanted);
    }

    /** Prefer an idle car or one already heading toward the floor in the same direction; then nearest. */
    public static Dispatcher nearestSuitable() {
        return (cars, floor, wanted) -> cars.stream()
                .min((a, b) -> Integer.compare(cost(a, floor, wanted), cost(b, floor, wanted)))
                .orElseThrow();
    }

    private static int cost(Car c, int floor, Direction wanted) {
        int distance = Math.abs(c.floor - floor);
        boolean onTheWay = (c.direction == Direction.UP && wanted == Direction.UP && floor >= c.floor)
                || (c.direction == Direction.DOWN && wanted == Direction.DOWN && floor <= c.floor);
        if (c.direction == Direction.IDLE || onTheWay) {
            return distance;
        }
        return distance + 100; // busy in the other direction: last resort
    }

    private final List<Car> cars = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Dispatcher dispatcher;

    public ElevatorSystem(Dispatcher dispatcher, int... startFloors) {
        this.dispatcher = dispatcher;
        for (int i = 0; i < startFloors.length; i++) {
            cars.add(new Car("E" + (i + 1), startFloors[i]));
        }
    }

    public String hallCall(int floor, Direction wanted) {
        Car car = dispatcher.choose(cars, floor, wanted);
        car.stops.add(floor);
        return "hall call " + floor + " " + wanted + " -> " + car.id;
    }

    public void carCall(String carId, int floor) {
        cars.stream().filter(c -> c.id.equals(carId)).findFirst().orElseThrow().stops.add(floor);
    }

    public List<String> tick() {
        return cars.stream().map(Car::step).toList();
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.elevator;

import com.handbook.lld.elevator.ElevatorSystem.Direction;

public class ElevatorDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var building = new ElevatorSystem(ElevatorSystem.nearestSuitable(), 0, 8);

        System.out.println("=== LLD: Elevator system (2 cars, SCAN scheduling) ===");
        System.out.println(building.hallCall(3, Direction.UP));
        System.out.println(building.hallCall(7, Direction.DOWN));
        for (int t = 1; t <= 4; t++) {
            if (t == 2) {
                building.carCall("E1", 6); // passenger who got in at 3 presses 6
                System.out.println("   (passenger in E1 presses 6)");
            }
            System.out.println("t=" + t + " " + building.tick());
        }
        System.out.println(building.hallCall(5, Direction.UP) + "  (E1 is moving up past 5)");
        for (int t = 5; t <= 7; t++) {
            System.out.println("t=" + t + " " + building.tick());
        }
    }
}

=== LLD: Elevator system (2 cars, SCAN scheduling) ===
hall call 3 UP -> E1
hall call 7 DOWN -> E2
t=1 [E1@1 moving UP, E2@7 doors open]
   (passenger in E1 presses 6)
t=2 [E1@2 moving UP, E2@7 idle]
t=3 [E1@3 doors open, E2@7 idle]
t=4 [E1@4 moving UP, E2@7 idle]
hall call 5 UP -> E1  (E1 is moving up past 5)
t=5 [E1@5 doors open, E2@7 idle]
t=6 [E1@6 doors open, E2@7 idle]
t=7 [E1@6 idle, E2@7 idle]

Follow-ups: capacity/weight limits, express elevators serving certain floors, peak-hour strategies (up-peak in the morning), emergency mode (a state that overrides all), and making tick() driven by a scheduler thread.

docs.title: 3. Vending Machine
docs.text:
Requirements: accept ₹1/2/5/10 coins; select a product; dispense if paid enough and in stock; return change with the fewest coins; cancel and refund. Pattern: State, with sealed types and pattern matching so each state's behaviour is explicit.

Watch the design handle the demo scenario step by step, with the matching code lit up. Switch to Naive design to see a simpler design fail. Open in the explorer

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Idle Idle --> HasMoney: insert coin HasMoney --> HasMoney: insert coin / select (not enough, sold out) HasMoney --> Idle: select (dispense + change) HasMoney --> Idle: cancel (refund) VendingMachine.javaVendingMachineDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.vending;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Vending machine LLD. Pattern: State. Each state decides how to react to the same events
 * (insert coin, select, cancel), which removes the big if/else on a status field.
 */
public final class VendingMachine {

    public record Product(String name, int priceRupees) {
    }

    sealed interface State permits Idle, HasMoney {
    }

    record Idle() implements State {
    }

    record HasMoney(int credit) implements State {
    }

    private static final int[] COINS = {10, 5, 2, 1};

    private final Map<String, Product> slots = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private State state = new Idle();

    public VendingMachine load(String slot, Product product, int quantity) {
        slots.put(slot, product);
        stock.put(slot, quantity);
        return this;
    }

    public String insert(int coin) {
        if (coin != 1 && coin != 2 && coin != 5 && coin != 10) {
            return "rejected coin ₹" + coin;
        }
        state = switch (state) {
            case Idle i -> new HasMoney(coin);
            case HasMoney m -> new HasMoney(m.credit() + coin);
        };
        return "credit ₹" + ((HasMoney) state).credit();
    }

    public String select(String slot) {
        return switch (state) {
            case Idle i -> "insert coins first";
            case HasMoney m -> {
                Product p = slots.get(slot);
                if (p == null) {
                    yield "no such slot " + slot;
                }
                if (stock.get(slot) == 0) {
                    yield p.name() + " sold out, credit ₹" + m.credit() + " kept";
                }
                if (m.credit() < p.priceRupees()) {
                    yield p.name() + " costs ₹" + p.priceRupees() + ", insert ₹" + (p.priceRupees() - m.credit()) + " more";
                }
                stock.merge(slot, -1, Integer::sum);
                state = new Idle();
                yield "dispensed " + p.name() + change(m.credit() - p.priceRupees());
            }
        };
    }

    public String cancel() {
        if (state instanceof HasMoney m) {
            state = new Idle();
            return "refunded" + change(m.credit());
        }
        return "nothing to refund";
    }

    /** Greedy change-making works for canonical coin systems like 10/5/2/1. */
    private static String change(int amount) {
        if (amount == 0) {
            return "";
        }
        List<Integer> coins = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int c : COINS) {
            while (amount >= c) {
                coins.add(c);
                amount -= c;
            }
        }
        return ", change " + coins;
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.vending;

import com.handbook.lld.vending.VendingMachine.Product;

public class VendingMachineDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var vm = new VendingMachine()
                .load("A1", new Product("Masala chips", 20), 2)
                .load("B1", new Product("Mango juice", 35), 0);

        System.out.println("=== LLD: Vending machine (State pattern) ===");
        System.out.println("select A1       -> " + vm.select("A1"));
        System.out.println("insert ₹10      -> " + vm.insert(10));
