docs.title: Service Companies: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, Accenture, Capgemini and Others
docs.text:
Commonly reported, not official

Based on publicly shared candidate experiences. Hiring drives, tests and rounds change by year, role, campus vs. lateral hiring, and client project. Check the company's careers portal and your recruiter's instructions.

docs.title: What the process commonly looks like
docs.text:
Freshers (campus and off-campus drives)

  • An online test: aptitude (quantitative, logical, verbal) plus a coding section; some companies use national hiring tests or named programmes for different salary bands.
  • A technical interview: core Java/OOP, data structures, SQL, a few design patterns (Singleton, Factory, MVC), and your final-year project.
  • An HR interview: communication, relocation, shifts, career goals.

Experienced (lateral hiring, 2–15 years)

  • One or two technical rounds focused on the job description: Java 8–21 features, Spring Boot, REST, JPA/Hibernate, microservices, SQL, sometimes cloud (AWS/Azure) and DevOps basics.
  • Often a client or project round for a specific account, testing practical problem solving and communication.
  • A managerial / HR round.

docs.title: Where design patterns show up
docs.text: Question style Typical expectation "What design patterns have you used?" Name 3–5 with where and why in your project (Singleton for config, Factory for payment types, Builder for DTOs, Strategy for rules, Observer/events) "Write a thread-safe Singleton" Double-checked locking with volatile, holder idiom, or enum; explain each. See Singleton "Patterns used in Spring?" Singleton scope, Factory (BeanFactory), Proxy (AOP, @Transactional), Template (JdbcTemplate), Observer (ApplicationEvent), Front Controller (DispatcherServlet) "Microservices patterns you've used" API Gateway, Service Discovery (Eureka), Config Server, Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j), Saga basics, distributed tracing "Explain MVC" Model/View/Controller in Spring MVC with DispatcherServlet, controllers, view resolvers

docs.title: What interviewers look for
docs.text: Signal What strong looks like Fundamentals Clear, correct definitions with a small code example Practical experience Concrete examples from your projects, not textbook lists Spring Boot/microservices (lateral) How things work under the hood (auto-configuration, proxies, transactions) and what you configured Communication Structured answers, honest about what you don't know Client readiness Explains trade-offs simply; asks clarifying questions

docs.title: 15 practice questions (with model answers)
docs.text:
1. What is a design pattern? Name the three GoF categories.

A reusable solution to a common design problem. Creational (object creation), Structural (composition of classes/objects), Behavioral (communication and responsibilities).

2. Write a thread-safe Singleton in Java.

Enum singleton (enum Config { INSTANCE; }), or the holder idiom (private static class Holder { static final Config I = new Config(); }), or double-checked locking with a volatile field. See Singleton.

3. How can a Singleton be broken? How do you prevent it?

Reflection, serialization, cloning and multiple class loaders. Use an enum; or guard the constructor, implement readResolve, and don't implement Cloneable.

4. Factory vs. Abstract Factory?

Factory creates one product type (choosing the subclass); Abstract Factory creates families of related products. See Factory Method and Abstract Factory.

5. Which design patterns does Spring use?

Singleton (default bean scope), Factory (BeanFactory, FactoryBean), Proxy (AOP, @Transactional), Template Method (JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate), Observer (ApplicationEventPublisher), Adapter (HandlerAdapter), Front Controller (DispatcherServlet), Strategy (resource loading, PlatformTransactionManager).

6. Explain the Builder pattern. Where have you used it?

Step-by-step construction of complex objects, avoiding telescoping constructors; e.g. Lombok @Builder for DTOs, HttpRequest.newBuilder(). See Builder.

7. What is the Observer pattern? Real example?

Subjects notify registered observers on change; e.g. Spring @EventListener for OrderPlacedEvent sending emails. See Observer.

8. Strategy pattern with an example.

Interchangeable algorithms behind an interface: PaymentStrategy with UpiPayment, CardPayment; chosen at runtime. See Strategy.

9. What is MVC and how does Spring MVC implement it?

DispatcherServlet (front controller) routes to @Controller methods (controller), which return model data and a view name (or a body for REST); views render the model.

10. What are microservices? Name 5 patterns you've used.

Small, independently deployable services around business capabilities. Patterns: API Gateway, Service Discovery, Config Server, Circuit Breaker, Distributed Tracing.

11. How does a circuit breaker work in Spring Boot?

Resilience4j @CircuitBreaker(name, fallbackMethod): CLOSED → OPEN after failure-rate threshold → HALF_OPEN after wait → CLOSED if trial calls succeed. See Circuit Breaker.

12. How do you handle transactions across microservices?

Not with a single DB transaction: use the Saga pattern (orchestration or choreography) with compensating actions, plus the outbox for reliable events.

13. Difference between Adapter and Facade?

Adapter makes an incompatible interface fit another; Facade provides a simpler interface over a complex subsystem. See Comparisons.

14. What is SOLID? Explain one principle with code.

Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. E.g. Open/closed: add a new DiscountRule class without editing the checkout. See OOP & SOLID.

15. Explain your project's architecture.

Prepare a 2-minute answer: business purpose, main modules/services, tech stack, how a request flows, data storage, one design decision you made and why, and one problem you solved. Draw it if allowed.

docs.title: Preparation tips
docs.text:
• Know your own project deeply: architecture, your module, patterns used and why, a bug you fixed, how you deployed it.
  • Code by hand: Singleton (3 ways), Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Producer-Consumer, LRU cache.
  • Spring internals: bean lifecycle, scopes, @Transactional proxy pitfalls, auto-configuration, profiles.
  • SQL: joins, group by/having, indexes, N+1 problem in JPA.
  • Communication: answer in a structure (definition → example → where you used it → trade-off).

docs.title: 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Do 1 Aptitude practice (freshers) or Java 8–21 features (lateral); OOP & SOLID; Singleton, Factory, Builder 2 Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter, Facade, Template Method, MVC; Spring patterns 3 Spring Boot + microservices patterns: gateway, discovery, config, circuit breaker, saga, tracing 4 Project explanation, mock technical + HR interviews, Top 100 questions

docs.title: System Design Patterns
docs.text: System design rounds ask you to design a large system (a URL shortener, a feed, checkout, ride-hailing) in 45–60 minutes. Interviewers don't expect a perfect design; they look for a structured approach, sound building blocks, numbers, and trade-offs. This page collects the building blocks and shows how the microservices and architecture patterns from this handbook combine in classic designs.

docs.title: 1. A framework for the round
docs.text:
Step Time What to do 1. Requirements 5 min Functional (core use cases only), non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency), out of scope 2. Estimates 5 min Users, requests/s (average and peak), storage per day/year, bandwidth, read:write ratio 3. API 5 min Key endpoints or events with request/response shapes 4. Data model 5 min Entities, keys, access patterns → choice of store 5. High-level design 10 min Clients → edge → services → data; draw the main flow 6. Deep dives 15 min The 2–3 hardest parts: hot keys, consistency, fan-out, failure handling 7. Wrap-up 5 min Bottlenecks, monitoring, what you'd do next, trade-offs you made

Say the trade-off out loud

"I'll use cache-aside with a 60-second TTL. That means a price change can show for up to a minute on product pages, but checkout re-reads from the database, so customers are never charged a stale price."

docs.title: Caching strategies
docs.text:
Strategy How Good for Watch out for Cache-aside (lazy loading) App reads cache; on miss, reads DB and fills cache Most read-heavy data Stale data until TTL; stampede on hot key expiry (use locks or early refresh) Read-through Cache library loads from DB on miss Same, less app code Same as cache-aside Write-through Write to cache and DB synchronously Read-after-write consistency Slower writes Write-behind Write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously Very write-heavy counters Data loss on cache failure Refresh-ahead Refresh hot keys before expiry Predictable hot keys Wasted refreshes

Invalidation: delete the key on writes (not update) to avoid races; use short TTLs as a safety net; version keys (product:42:v7) for bulk changes.

docs.title: Consistent hashing
docs.text:
Spreading keys across cache or database nodes with hash(key) % N moves almost every key when N changes. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring; adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes even out the distribution.

ConsistentHashRing.javaConsistentHashingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.lld.systemdesign;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.SortedMap;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/**
 * Consistent hashing with virtual nodes: keys and nodes are hashed onto a ring; a key belongs to
 * the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys, instead of
 * nearly all of them with {@code hash(key) % N}.
 */
public final class ConsistentHashRing {

    private final TreeMap<Long, String> ring = new TreeMap<>();
    private final int virtualNodes;

    public ConsistentHashRing(int virtualNodes) {
        this.virtualNodes = virtualNodes;
    }

    public void addNode(String node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) {
            ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node);
        }
    }

    public void removeNode(String node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) {
            ring.remove(hash(node + "#" + i));
        }
    }

    public String nodeFor(String key) {
        SortedMap<Long, String> tail = ring.tailMap(hash(key));
        return tail.isEmpty() ? ring.firstEntry().getValue() : tail.get(tail.firstKey());
    }

    /** First 8 bytes of MD5: stable across JVMs and well distributed (not for security). */
    static long hash(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            long h = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
                h = (h << 8) | (d[i] & 0xff);
            }
            return h;
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    public static Map<String, Integer> distribution(ConsistentHashRing ring, int keys) {
        Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < keys; i++) {
            counts.merge(ring.nodeFor("cart:" + i), 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return counts;
    }
}

package com.handbook.lld.systemdesign;

public class ConsistentHashingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int keys = 100_000;
        var ring = new ConsistentHashRing(200);
        for (String n : new String[] {"cache-1", "cache-2", "cache-3", "cache-4"}) {
            ring.addNode(n);
        }
        String[] before = new String[keys];
        for (int i = 0; i < keys; i++) {
            before[i] = ring.nodeFor("cart:" + i);
        }

        System.out.println("=== System design: consistent hashing for a cart cache cluster ===");
        System.out.println("4 nodes, 200 virtual nodes each: " + ConsistentHashRing.distribution(ring, keys));

        ring.addNode("cache-5");
        int moved = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < keys; i++) {
            if (!ring.nodeFor("cart:" + i).equals(before[i])) {
                moved++;
            }
        }
        System.out.printf("add cache-5 -> %.1f%% of keys moved (ideal 1/5 = 20%%)%n", moved * 100.0 / keys);

        int movedModulo = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < keys; i++) {
            int h = Math.floorMod(("cart:" + i).hashCode(), 4);
            int h5 = Math.floorMod(("cart:" + i).hashCode(), 5);
            if (h != h5) {
                movedModulo++;
            }
        }
        System.out.printf("with hash %% N instead: %.1f%% of keys would move%n", movedModulo * 100.0 / keys);
    }
}

=== System design: consistent hashing for a cart cache cluster ===
4 nodes, 200 virtual nodes each: {cache-1=25169, cache-2=23658, cache-3=24689, cache-4=26484}
add cache-5 -> 21.5% of keys moved (ideal 1/5 = 20%)
with hash % N instead: 80.1% of keys would move

Used by: Cassandra and DynamoDB-style partitioning, Memcached clients, load balancers with session affinity, CDNs.

docs.title: Other patterns worth naming
docs.text: Pattern One-liner Leader election One instance does a job (lease in etcd/ZooKeeper/DB) with fencing tokens so a stale leader can't write Back-pressure Bounded queues; slow consumers push back instead of collapsing (Producer-Consumer) Write-ahead log Append before applying; recover by replaying (databases, Kafka, Event Sourcing) Bloom filter Probabilistic "definitely not present" checks to skip disk/DB lookups Snowflake IDs 64-bit time-ordered IDs: timestamp + machine ID + sequence; no central counter Fan-out on write vs. read Precompute feeds for most users; compute on read for celebrities with millions of followers Hedged requests Send a backup request after p95 latency to cut tail latency (reads only) Geo-partitioning Keep users' data in their region for latency and data residency

docs.title: 3. Classic designs and the patterns inside them
URL shortener
docs.text:
flowchart LR C[Client] --> GW[API Gateway<br/>rate limit per key] GW --> W[Write service<br/>ID gen + base62] GW --> R[Redirect service] R --> CA[(Cache<br/>cache-aside)] CA -.miss.-> DB[(KV store<br/>sharded by code)] W --> DB R -->|click event| Q[[Kafka]] --> AN[Analytics]
  • Estimates: 100M new URLs/month ≈ 40 writes/s; reads 100× → 4,000/s, cache hit rate > 90%.
  • Patterns: rate limiter, cache-aside, consistent hashing for the KV store, event-driven analytics, 302 (trackable) vs. 301 (cacheable) redirects.

docs.title: E-commerce checkout
docs.text:
flowchart LR App --> GW[Gateway] --> BFF[Mobile BFF] --> CO[Checkout service] CO -->|saga| INV[Inventory] CO -->|saga| PAY[Payment] CO -->|saga| DEL[Delivery] CO -->|outbox| K[[Kafka]] K --> N[Notifications] K --> RM[Order history<br/>CQRS read model]
  • Patterns: BFF, Saga with a pivot at payment, Outbox, Idempotency keys, CQRS for order history, Circuit Breaker on payment, flash-sale stock with atomic conditional updates.
  • See the Capstone for a runnable version.

docs.title: News feed / timeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR P[Post service] -->|PostCreated| K[[Kafka]] K --> FO[Fan-out workers] FO --> FC[(Feed cache per user<br/>Redis lists)] U[User] --> FS[Feed service] --> FC FS -.celebrity posts.-> PS[(Posts store)]
  • Patterns: fan-out on write for normal users, on read for celebrities (hybrid), Producer-Consumer workers, cache per user, ranking as a Strategy, pagination with cursors.

docs.title: Ride-hailing (matching and tracking)
docs.text:
flowchart LR D[Driver app<br/>location every 4s] --> LS[Location service] --> GEO[(Geo index<br/>geohash/H3 cells)] R[Rider app] --> M[Matching service] --> GEO M --> T[Trip service<br/>state machine] T -->|TripCompleted| K[[Kafka]] --> B[Billing] M --> ETA[ETA service<br/>circuit breaker + fallback]
  • Patterns: State for trips, geo-sharding, Circuit Breaker with estimate fallback, event-driven billing, idempotent fare charging, tracing across async hops.

docs.title: Notification platform
docs.text:
flowchart LR S[Domain services] -->|events| K[[Kafka]] --> NS[Notification service] NS --> PREF[(Preferences)] NS --> D{Dedupe + rate limit} D --> Q1[[email queue]] --> E[Email provider] D --> Q2[[sms queue]] --> SMS[SMS provider] D --> Q3[[push queue]] --> PU[Push provider] Q1 & Q2 & Q3 -.failures.-> DLQ[[DLQ]]
  • Patterns: Strategy per channel, Template Method for messages, idempotent dedupe, rate limiting per user, bulkheads per provider, DLQs. See the Notification LLD.

docs.title: Chat / messaging
docs.text: • Patterns: WebSocket gateways with session routing (consistent hashing by user), messages persisted per conversation (partitioned by conversation ID for ordering), delivery receipts as events, offline push via the notification platform, idempotent client message IDs to avoid duplicates on reconnect.

docs.title: Distributed rate limiter, cache, or job scheduler
docs.text:
• Rate limiter: token buckets in Redis with Lua, local fallback (Rate Limiter).
  • Distributed cache: consistent hashing, replication for hot keys, eviction (LRU), cache-aside.
  • Job scheduler: jobs table with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, leader election for the scheduler loop, idempotent jobs, retries with backoff, DLQ.

docs.title: 4. Numbers worth remembering
docs.text:
Operation Order of magnitude L1 cache / main memory reference ~1 ns / ~100 ns Read 1 MB sequentially from memory ~10 µs (varies by hardware) SSD random read ~16–100 µs Round trip within a data centre ~0.5 ms Redis GET over the network ~0.5–1 ms Simple indexed DB query ~1–10 ms Round trip across continents ~100–150 ms Quick math Value 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s 1M requests/day ≈ 12 requests/s average; plan peaks at 2–10× 1 KB × 1B records ≈ 1 TB

Estimation example: grocery orders

5M orders/day → ~58 orders/s average; evening peak 5× → ~300/s. Each order ~2 KB with lines → 10 GB/day → ~3.6 TB/year (before indexes and replicas). Order-history reads 10× writes → ~3,000 reads/s at peak: a CQRS read model plus cache handles it comfortably.

LLD problems Next: Top 100 questions

docs.title: Top 100 Design Pattern, Architecture & Microservices Questions
docs.text:
The questions asked most often in Java interviews, from campus drives to senior design rounds, with short model answers. Each links to the page with full explanations, three worked examples and code. Levels: 🟢 beginner, 🟡 mid-level, 🔴 senior.

How to practise

Cover the answer, say yours out loud in under 60 seconds, then compare. If you can't, read the linked page's Quick Revision Card.

docs.title: OOP & SOLID (1–8)
docs.text:
1. 🟢 What are the four pillars of OOP?

Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism. See OOP & SOLID.

2. 🟢 What does SOLID stand for?

Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.

3. 🟢 Composition vs. inheritance: which and why?

Prefer composition: it changes behavior at runtime and avoids fragile base classes and subclass explosions. Inherit only for true is-a relationships.

4. 🟡 Give an example of violating Liskov substitution.

Square extends Rectangle where setWidth also changes height; code expecting a rectangle breaks. Model them separately or make them immutable.

5. 🟡 How does dependency inversion relate to dependency injection?

DIP: high-level code depends on abstractions it owns. DI is a technique to supply implementations (constructor injection, Spring).

6. 🟢 What is a design pattern? Name the GoF categories.

A reusable solution to a recurring design problem. Creational, structural, behavioral.

7. 🟡 When should you NOT use a design pattern?

When the problem it solves isn't present yet (YAGNI); patterns add indirection. See Anti-Patterns.

8. 🔴 How do you decide which pattern fits a problem?

Identify what varies and what must stay stable, then pick the pattern that isolates that variation. See the Pattern Selection Guide.

docs.title: Creational (9–20)
docs.text:
9. 🟢 How do you write a thread-safe Singleton?

Enum, holder idiom, or double-checked locking with volatile. See Singleton.

10. 🟡 Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

Without it, another thread can see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object due to reordering. See Double-Checked Locking.

11. 🟡 How can a Singleton be broken?

Reflection, serialization, cloning, multiple class loaders. Enums resist the first three.

12. 🔴 Is Singleton an anti-pattern?

Global mutable state and hidden dependencies make it one when misused; a single instance managed by DI is fine.

13. 🟢 Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory?

Factory Method creates one product; Abstract Factory creates families of related products. See Factory Method, Abstract Factory.

14. 🟢 Static factory method vs. constructor?

Static factories have names, can cache or return subtypes (List.of, Optional.of); constructors always create a new exact type.

15. 🟢 Why use the Builder pattern?

Many optional parameters, immutability, readable construction and validation in build(). See Builder.

16. 🟡 Builder vs. Java records?

Records are perfect for small immutable data; builders still help with many optional fields or step-wise validation.

17. 🟡 What is the Prototype pattern? Shallow vs. deep copy?

Create objects by copying a template. Shallow copies share mutable fields; deep copies duplicate them. Avoid clone(); prefer copy constructors. See Prototype.

18. 🟡 When is an Object Pool useful?

For expensive, limited resources (DB connections, threads); not for cheap objects. See Object Pool.

19. 🟡 Which creational patterns does Spring use?

Singleton scope, BeanFactory/FactoryBean, prototype scope, builders (RestClient.builder()).

20. 🔴 How would you design a plugin system that creates implementations at runtime?

A factory registry (map of type → supplier) populated via ServiceLoader or Spring beans; no switch statements.

docs.title: Structural (21–34)
docs.text:
21. 🟢 What is the Adapter pattern?

Converts one interface into another clients expect, e.g. InputStreamReader. See Adapter.

22. 🟢 What is the Decorator pattern?

Wraps an object with the same interface to add behavior; stackable. BufferedInputStream. See Decorator.

23. 🟡 Decorator vs. Proxy?

Decorator adds behavior; Proxy controls access (lazy, remote, security, caching). See Comparisons.

24. 🟢 What is the Facade pattern?

A simple entry point over a complex subsystem, e.g. JdbcTemplate. See Facade.

25. 🟡 Adapter vs. Facade?

Adapter makes one interface fit another; Facade simplifies many interfaces into one.

26. 🟡 How do Spring proxies work, and why doesn't @Transactional work on self-invocation?

Spring wraps beans in JDK or CGLIB proxies; internal this.method() calls bypass the proxy. See Proxy.

27. 🟡 What is the Composite pattern?

Treat individual objects and groups uniformly in a tree (menus, file systems, org charts). See Composite.

28. 🟡 What is the Bridge pattern?

Separates abstraction from implementation so both vary independently (JDBC API + drivers). See Bridge.

29. 🟡 What is the Flyweight pattern? JDK example?

Share intrinsic state among many objects; Integer.valueOf cache, string interning. See Flyweight.

30. 🟢 Why is Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b true but 128 false?

Integer.valueOf caches −128..127 (Flyweight); 128 creates new objects. Use equals.

31. 🟡 Which structural patterns are in Java I/O?

Decorator (buffered/data streams), Adapter (InputStreamReader), Facade-like utilities (Files).

32. 🔴 How would you add caching to a service without changing its code?

A caching Proxy/Decorator implementing the same interface, or Spring @Cacheable (proxy-based).

33. 🔴 What's an Anti-Corruption Layer and how does it relate to Adapter/Facade?

A system-level translation boundary combining adapters, facades and translators to keep a foreign model out of your domain. See ACL.

34. 🟡 What is the Service Locator, and why is DI preferred?

A registry you ask for dependencies; it hides dependencies and complicates tests. DI makes them explicit.

docs.title: Behavioral (35–54)
docs.text:
35. 🟢 What is the Strategy pattern?

Interchangeable algorithms behind an interface, chosen at runtime (payment methods, pricing). See Strategy.

36. 🟡 Strategy vs. State?

Strategy is chosen by the client and rarely changes itself; State objects change the context's state as part of behavior. See Comparisons.

37. 🟢 What is the Observer pattern?

Subscribers are notified of changes in a subject; Spring events, listeners. See Observer.

38. 🟡 How do you avoid memory leaks with observers?

Unsubscribe (return a handle), weak references, or scoped lifecycles.

39. 🟢 What is the Template Method pattern?

A base class defines the algorithm skeleton; subclasses fill steps. AbstractList, JdbcTemplate callbacks. See Template Method.

40. 🟡 Template Method vs. Strategy?

Inheritance with hooks vs. composition with swappable algorithms. Prefer Strategy for flexibility.

41. 🟢 What is the Command pattern?

Encapsulate a request as an object: queue it, log it, undo it. See Command.

42. 🟡 How do you implement undo/redo?

Commands with undo() on two stacks, or Memento snapshots. See Memento.

43. 🟡 What is Chain of Responsibility? Where in Java/Spring?

Pass a request along handlers until handled; servlet filters, Spring Security filter chain. See Chain of Responsibility.

44. 🟡 What is the State pattern? Example?

Behavior changes with internal state; order lifecycle, vending machine. See State.

45. 🟡 What is the Iterator pattern?

Sequential access without exposing internals; Iterator, Spliterator. See Iterator.

46. 🟡 What is the Mediator pattern?

Objects communicate via a mediator instead of directly; chat rooms, air traffic control, UI dialogs. See Mediator.

47. 🔴 What is the Visitor pattern and when is it worth it?

Add operations to a stable class hierarchy without modifying it (compilers, ASTs); sealed types + pattern matching are a modern alternative. See Visitor.

48. 🟡 What is the Memento pattern?

Capture and restore an object's state without exposing internals (drafts, undo). See Memento.

49. 🔴 What is the Interpreter pattern?

Represent a grammar as classes and evaluate sentences (rules engines, filters). See Interpreter.

50. 🟡 What is the Null Object pattern?

A do-nothing implementation instead of null checks. See Null Object.

51. 🟡 What is the Specification pattern?

Business rules as composable predicates (and, or, not); Spring Data Specification. See Specification.

52. 🟡 Which behavioral patterns does Spring use?

Template Method (JdbcTemplate), Observer (events), Strategy (PlatformTransactionManager), Chain (filters), Command-like (Runnable tasks).

53. 🔴 How do you design a rules engine for discounts?

Specification for eligibility, Strategy for calculation, a combination policy (stackable vs. exclusive). See the Discount Engine LLD.

54. 🔴 Observer vs. publish/subscribe with a broker?

Observer is in-process and synchronous; pub/sub is distributed, async and durable. See Event-Driven.

docs.title: Concurrency (55–66)
docs.text:
55. 🟢 What is the Producer-Consumer pattern?

Producers put work in a bounded queue; consumers take it; back-pressure via blocking. See Producer-Consumer.

56. 🟡 How do you size a thread pool?

CPU-bound: ~number of cores; I/O-bound: cores × (1 + wait/compute), or virtual threads. See Thread Pool.

57. 🟡 Why is Executors.newFixedThreadPool risky in production?

Its queue is unbounded; under overload, memory grows until OOM. Use a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor with a rejection policy.

58. 🟡 Future vs. CompletableFuture?

Future only blocks for results; CompletableFuture composes async steps (thenApply, thenCombine, allOf) and handles errors. See Future/Promise.

59. 🟡 When do you use a read-write lock?

Many readers, few writers, and non-trivial read work. See Read-Write Lock.

60. 🟢 Why are immutable objects thread-safe?

Their state can't change after construction (with final fields and safe publication), so no synchronization is needed. See Immutable Object.

61. 🟡 What are virtual threads and when should you use them?

Lightweight JVM-managed threads (Java 21) for high-concurrency blocking I/O; not for CPU-bound work. See Virtual Threads.

62. 🔴 What is pinning with virtual threads?

A virtual thread blocked inside synchronized (before JDK 24) or native code holds its carrier thread; use ReentrantLock for long blocking sections on older JDKs.

63. 🟡 synchronized vs. ReentrantLock?

ReentrantLock adds tryLock, timeouts, fairness and multiple conditions; synchronized is simpler and auto-releases.

64. 🟡 What does volatile guarantee?

Visibility and ordering (happens-before) for a variable, not atomicity of compound actions.

65. 🔴 How do you avoid deadlocks?

Consistent lock ordering, timeouts (tryLock), fewer locks, immutable data, message passing.

66. 🟡 AtomicLong vs. LongAdder?

LongAdder stripes counters to reduce contention under heavy writes; reads sum cells.

docs.title: Architecture (67–76)
docs.text:
67. 🟢 What is layered architecture?

Presentation → business → persistence, dependencies pointing down. See Layered.

68. 🟡 What is hexagonal architecture?

A core with ports (interfaces it owns) and adapters for technologies on both sides. See Hexagonal.

69. 🟡 What is Clean Architecture's dependency rule?

Source dependencies point inward: entities ← use cases ← adapters ← frameworks. See Clean.

70. 🟡 Hexagonal vs. Clean vs. Onion?

Same principle (domain at the center, dependencies inward); different vocabulary and emphasis.

71. 🟡 What is a modular monolith?

One deployable with enforced business modules, each with a public API and private internals. See Modular Monolith.

72. 🔴 Monolith or microservices for a new product?

Usually a modular monolith first; extract services when there's a clear reason (scaling, team autonomy, compliance).

73. 🟡 What is event-driven architecture?

Components communicate via events through a broker; producers don't know consumers. See Event-Driven.

74. 🔴 How do you enforce architecture rules?

ArchUnit tests, Spring Modulith verification, build modules, code review checklists.

75. 🔴 What is an architecture decision record (ADR)?

A short document capturing a decision, its context, options and consequences, kept with the code.

76. 🟡 What is MVC and how does Spring MVC implement it?

DispatcherServlet (front controller) → @Controller → model + view (or response body for REST).

docs.title: Microservices (77–100)
docs.text:
77. 🟢 What are microservices?

Small, independently deployable services around business capabilities, each owning its data. See Microservices.

78. 🟡 How do you decide service boundaries?

DDD bounded contexts, business capabilities, data ownership, team ownership. See Decomposition.

79. 🟢 What does an API gateway do?

Single entry point: routing, auth, rate limiting, request IDs, TLS. See API Gateway.

80. 🟡 API gateway vs. BFF?

Gateway: generic edge concerns; BFF: backend tailored to one client type. See BFF.

81. 🟡 Client-side vs. server-side discovery?

Caller queries the registry and picks an instance vs. a load balancer/DNS picks. See Service Discovery.

82. 🟢 What is a circuit breaker? States?

Stops calls to a failing dependency: CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN. See Circuit Breaker.

83. 🟡 How do retries cause outages?

They multiply load (retry storms) and duplicate non-idempotent operations. Use backoff, jitter, budgets and idempotency. See Retry / Timeout / Bulkhead.

84. 🟡 What is a bulkhead?

Limit concurrent calls per dependency so one slow dependency can't exhaust shared resources.

85. 🟡 Token bucket vs. sliding window rate limiting?

Token bucket allows bursts with an average rate; sliding window counts precisely over a moving period. See Rate Limiter.

86. 🟡 How do you handle transactions across services?

Saga: local transactions + compensations, orchestrated or choreographed.

87. 🔴 Orchestration vs. choreography?

Central coordinator (visible flow, easier error handling) vs. event reactions (looser coupling, harder to follow).

88. 🟡 What is the dual-write problem and the outbox fix?

DB write + broker publish can't be atomic; write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it. See Outbox.

89. 🟡 How do you make a consumer idempotent?

Record processed message IDs with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect. See Idempotent Consumer.

90. 🟡 What is CQRS?

Separate write models from query-shaped read models updated from events. See CQRS.

91. 🔴 What is event sourcing? Pros and cons?

Store state as events; audit and time travel vs. complexity and schema evolution. See Event Sourcing.

92. 🟢 Why database per service?

Loose coupling and independent evolution; joins become API composition or read models. See Database per Service.

93. 🟡 How do you migrate a monolith to microservices?

Strangler Fig: facade, extract capability by capability, gradual rollout, retire legacy code.

94. 🟡 What is a service mesh?

Sidecar proxies + control plane for mTLS, traffic control and telemetry. See Sidecar / Service Mesh.

95. 🟡 How does distributed tracing work?

Trace and span IDs propagated in headers (W3C traceparent), spans collected into a tree. See Distributed Tracing.

96. 🟢 How do you manage configuration across environments?

Externalized config (config server/ConfigMaps), profiles, secrets in a vault, refresh for flags. See Config Server.

97. 🟡 What is an anti-corruption layer?

A translation layer that keeps legacy or external models out of your domain. See ACL.

98. 🔴 How do you guarantee exactly-once processing?

You don't get exactly-once delivery; you get exactly-once effect with an outbox + idempotent consumers + idempotent external calls.

99. 🔴 How do you test microservices?

Unit tests per service, consumer-driven contract tests (Pact), integration tests with Testcontainers, a few end-to-end tests, chaos testing for resilience.

100. 🔴 Design checkout for a grocery app. Which patterns do you use?

Gateway + BFF, saga (reserve → pay → schedule) with outbox and idempotency keys, circuit breakers and timeouts on payment, CQRS for order history, tracing, rate limits for flash sales. See the Capstone.

docs.title: Microservices Patterns
docs.text:
Microservices patterns solve the problems that appear when one application becomes many independently deployed services: how to split it, how clients reach it, how services find and call each other safely, how data stays consistent without shared transactions, how to migrate from a monolith, and how to see what's going on.

Every page has three real-world examples from different industries (grocery, banking, travel, healthcare, streaming, ride-hailing, insurance, logistics), full code, real output, a coding challenge, and a "system design round" answer.

How the code runs

The examples are plain Java 21 simulations of distributed systems, so you can run every one in milliseconds with ./run-demos.sh, with no Docker, Kafka or Kubernetes needed. Time is controlled with a FakeClock, randomness is seeded, and databases are real H2 in-memory databases with real JDBC transactions. Where the production version uses Spring Boot (Resilience4j, Spring Kafka, JdbcTemplate, Micrometer Tracing, @ConfigurationProperties), the page shows a class from the spring-reference module. CI compiles that module, but it isn't run, because it needs real infrastructure. YAML snippets for Spring Cloud Gateway, Istio and similar tools are references and are labelled as such.

docs.title: Suggested learning order
docs.text:
1. Foundations: Decomposition → Database per Service → API Gateway.
  2. Calling other services safely: Retry / Timeout / Bulkhead → Circuit Breaker → Service Discovery → Rate Limiter.
  3. Data consistency: Transactional Outbox → Idempotent Consumer → Saga → CQRS → Event Sourcing.
  4. Migration and operations: Strangler Fig → Anti-Corruption Layer → Distributed Tracing → Config Server → Sidecar / Service Mesh → BFF.
  5. Data, scale and operations: Cache-Aside → Materialized View → Sharding → Competing Consumers → Backpressure → Leader Election → Health Check → Deployment Strategies → Ambassador → Gateway Aggregation.

The microservices interview in one sentence

Almost every system design answer combines the same moves: gateway at the edge, a database per service, sagas + outbox + idempotent consumers for consistency, CQRS read models for heavy queries, timeouts/circuit breakers/bulkheads on every call, and tracing to see it all. If you can explain why each is needed, and what it costs, you can handle most microservices rounds.

Microservices are a trade-off, not an upgrade

They buy team autonomy and independent scaling at the cost of distributed-systems complexity. For a small team or an unclear domain, a modular monolith is often the better start, and the patterns in the Architecture section apply either way.

docs.title: Ambassador
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An Ambassador is a helper proxy deployed next to a client (same host or pod) that handles the client's outbound connectivity: auth, retries, timeouts, routing, sharding, TLS and metrics. The client just calls localhost. Use it when you can't (or don't want to) change the client: legacy apps, third-party binaries, or many languages that all need the same connection logic.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a 2009 loan-servicing application must call a partner bank's new API, which requires an API key, request ids and tolerance for frequent 503s. The app's HTTP client can't add headers or retry, and nobody can safely rebuild it. Separately, a Node.js, a Python and a Java service all need the same sharded-Redis logic, and three implementations drift.

Definition (Microsoft Azure Architecture Center; Burns & Oppenheimer, Design Patterns for Container-based Distributed Systems):

Create helper services that send network requests on behalf of a consumer service or application. An ambassador service can be thought of as an out-of-process proxy co-located with the client.

Ambassador vs sidecar vs gateway: a sidecar is the general idea of a helper container next to the app (inbound and outbound). An ambassador is a sidecar specialised for the app's outbound calls. An API gateway is a shared inbound proxy in front of many services.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A country's ambassador

A visiting minister doesn't learn the host country's protocol, language and paperwork. The ambassador handles introductions, translations and retries ("the minister is busy, come back at 3"), so the minister just says what they want.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph "Pod / host"       App["Legacy app<br/>(calls http://localhost:9000)"] --> Amb["Ambassador<br/>auth · retries · timeouts · TLS · metrics"]     end     Amb -->|HTTPS + API key| Ext[(Partner API)]     Amb -->|shard routing| R1[(Redis 1)] & R2[(Redis 2)] Participant Responsibility Client application Business logic; calls a local, simple endpoint Ambassador Connectivity concerns for outbound calls; deployed and versioned with the client Remote service(s) The real dependency: partner API, cache cluster, database Configuration Endpoints, credentials, retry policy: owned by platform/ops, not the app

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Legacy app: patch the 15-year-old HTTP library to add headers and retries → risky release, no tests
Each language: re-implement shard routing, token refresh, retries → five slightly different bugs
  • Changing legacy or third-party code is risky or impossible.
  • Cross-cutting connection logic is duplicated per language.
  • Ops can't change retry policy or endpoints without app releases.

docs.title: Example 1: Auth and Retries for a Legacy App (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The loan-servicing app checks EMIs against a partner bank's API. The partner requires an Authorization header and returns 503 under load. The app can only be reconfigured, not rebuilt. An ambassador on localhost:9000 adds the key and a request id, retries 5xx up to 3 times, and logs every attempt; the app's base URL is the only change.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant App as Legacy app participant A as Ambassador (localhost:9000) participant P as Partner API App->>A: GET /loans/LN-7781/emi A->>P: GET https://api.partner-bank.example/... + Authorization + X-Request-Id P-->>A: 503 A->>P: retry P-->>A: 503 A->>P: retry P-->>A: 200 EMI INR 18,450 A-->>App: 200

Full Code:

PartnerAmbassador.javaLegacyAppDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.legacy;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Runs next to the legacy app (localhost:9000). Adds what the app can't: auth, retries, timeouts, logs. */
public final class PartnerAmbassador implements Function<Request, Response> {

    private final Function<Request, Response> remotePartner;
    private final String apiKey;
    private final int maxAttempts;
    public final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();

    public PartnerAmbassador(Function<Request, Response> remotePartner, String apiKey, int maxAttempts) {
        this.remotePartner = remotePartner;
        this.apiKey = apiKey;
        this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts;
    }

    @Override
    public Response apply(Request fromLegacyApp) {
        Request outbound = fromLegacyApp
                .withPath("https://api.partner-bank.example" + fromLegacyApp.path()) // (1)!
                .withHeader("Authorization", "ApiKey " + apiKey)                    // (2)!
                .withHeader("X-Request-Id", "req-" + Math.abs(fromLegacyApp.path().hashCode() % 10_000));
        Response last = null;
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            last = remotePartner.apply(outbound);
            log.add("attempt " + attempt + " -> " + last.status());
            if (last.status() < 500) {
                return last;
            }
        }
        return last; // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Routing: the app calls a local path; the ambassador knows the real host (and could switch it without the app noticing).
  2. Credentials live with the ambassador, managed by ops (from a secret store), not compiled into the app.
  3. Retries only on 5xx; client errors (4xx) are returned at once. Real ambassadors also enforce timeouts and backoff.
package com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.legacy;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class LegacyAppDemo {

    /** The 2009 loan-servicing app: plain HTTP to a configured base URL, no retries, no auth support. */
    static String legacyCheckEmi(Function<Request, Response> http) {
        Response r = http.apply(Request.get("/loans/LN-7781/emi", Map.of()));
        return r.status() + " " + r.body();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: An Ambassador Gives a Legacy App Auth and Retries ===");
        int[] calls = {0};
        Function<Request, Response> partner = req -> {
            calls[0]++;
            if (req.header("Authorization") == null) {
                return Response.of(401, "missing credentials");
            }
            return calls[0] < 3 ? Response.of(503, "busy") : Response.of(200, "EMI INR 18,450 due 05-Oct");
        };

        System.out.println("Legacy app -> partner directly : " + legacyCheckEmi(partner));
        calls[0] = 0;
        PartnerAmbassador ambassador = new PartnerAmbassador(partner, "k-live-91f2", 3);
        System.out.println("Legacy app -> localhost:9000   : " + legacyCheckEmi(ambassador));
        System.out.println("Ambassador log: " + ambassador.log);
        System.out.println("Legacy code unchanged: only its base URL config moved to http://localhost:9000.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: An Ambassador Gives a Legacy App Auth and Retries ===
Legacy app -> partner directly : 401 missing credentials
Legacy app -> localhost:9000   : 200 EMI INR 18,450 due 05-Oct
Ambassador log: [attempt 1 -> 503, attempt 2 -> 503, attempt 3 -> 200]
Legacy code unchanged: only its base URL config moved to http://localhost:9000.

Why an ambassador here:

  • The legacy code doesn't change at all, which removes the riskiest part of the project.
  • Retry and timeout policy can be tuned by ops per environment.
  • Every outbound call is logged and measured in one place.

docs.title: Example 2: A Sharding Proxy for Redis (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The cart service (and four other services in three languages) store carts in a Redis cluster of 3 shards. Instead of embedding a cluster-aware client everywhere, each pod runs an ambassador (Envoy's Redis proxy, twemproxy) on localhost:6379 that hashes keys to shards. Adding a shard is a proxy config change.

Design:

flowchart LR C["cart service<br/>(plain Redis client → localhost:6379)"] --> A["Ambassador<br/>hash(key) % 3"] A --> S0[(shard 0)] A --> S1[(shard 1)] A --> S2[(shard 2)]

Full Code:

CacheShardProxy.javaShardProxyDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.shardproxy;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Like twemproxy/Envoy Redis proxy: the app talks to ONE local endpoint; the ambassador picks the shard. */
public final class CacheShardProxy {

    private final List<Map<String, String>> shards;
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> hitsPerShard = new HashMap<>();

    public CacheShardProxy(int shardCount) {
        this.shards = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < shardCount; i++) {
            shards.add(new HashMap<>());
        }
    }

    private int shardFor(String key) { // (1)!
        return Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), shards.size());
    }

    public void set(String key, String value) {
        int s = shardFor(key);
        hitsPerShard.merge(s, 1, Integer::sum);
        shards.get(s).put(key, value);
    }

    public String get(String key) {
        int s = shardFor(key);
        hitsPerShard.merge(s, 1, Integer::sum);
        return shards.get(s).get(key);
    }

    public Map<Integer, Integer> hitsPerShard() {
        return new java.util.TreeMap<>(hitsPerShard);
    }
}
  1. Sharding logic lives only in the ambassador. Production proxies use consistent hashing so adding shards moves few keys.
package com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.shardproxy;

public class ShardProxyDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Cart Service Talks to localhost:6379, the Ambassador Shards ===");
        CacheShardProxy redis = new CacheShardProxy(3);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 9_000; i++) {
            redis.set("cart:CUST-" + i, "{items:" + (i % 7) + "}");
        }
        System.out.println("cart:CUST-42 -> " + redis.get("cart:CUST-42"));
        System.out.println("Operations per shard: " + redis.hitsPerShard());
        System.out.println("The cart service has no shard map, no cluster client, and no code change when shards are added.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Cart Service Talks to localhost:6379, the Ambassador Shards ===
cart:CUST-42 -> {items:0}
Operations per shard: {0=3000, 1=3001, 2=3000}
The cart service has no shard map, no cluster client, and no code change when shards are added.

Why an ambassador here:

  • One implementation of routing for every language.
  • Apps use the simplest possible client (single-node Redis protocol).
  • Topology changes (new shards, failover) don't require app releases. See Sharding.

docs.title: Example 3: Token Caching for an SMS Gateway (Telecom)
docs.text:
Scenario: A notifications service sends 50 SMS per minute through a gateway that requires OAuth2 client-credentials tokens valid for 1 hour. Requesting a new token per SMS would hammer the auth server and add 200 ms per message. The ambassador caches the token and refreshes it 5 minutes before expiry, so no request ever carries an expired token. (This is the coding challenge's solution.)

Design:

flowchart LR App["notifications app"] -->|"POST /sms (no auth)"| A["Ambassador<br/>cached Bearer token"] A -->|"refresh at expiry − 5 min"| Auth[(Auth server)] A -->|"Authorization: Bearer tok-N"| G[(SMS gateway)]

Full Code:

TokenAmbassador.javaTokenAmbassadorDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.token;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Coding challenge solution: an ambassador that caches an OAuth2 client-credentials token and refreshes it early. */
public final class TokenAmbassador {

    public record Token(String value, Instant expiresAt) { }

    private final Supplier<Token> authServer;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration refreshMargin;
    private Token cached;
    private int tokenRequests;

    public TokenAmbassador(Supplier<Token> authServer, Clock clock, Duration refreshMargin) {
        this.authServer = authServer;
        this.clock = clock;
        this.refreshMargin = refreshMargin;
    }

    public synchronized String authorizationHeader() {
        if (cached == null || !clock.instant().isBefore(cached.expiresAt().minus(refreshMargin))) {
            cached = authServer.get();
            tokenRequests++;
        }
        return "Bearer " + cached.value();
    }

    public int tokenRequests() {
        return tokenRequests;
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.token;

import com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.token.TokenAmbassador.Token;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class TokenAmbassadorDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Challenge: Token Caching in the Ambassador (SMS gateway, 1-hour tokens) ===");
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-01T09:00:00Z");
        int[] issued = {0};
        TokenAmbassador ambassador = new TokenAmbassador(
                () -> new Token("tok-" + ++issued[0], clock.instant().plus(Duration.ofHours(1))), clock, Duration.ofMinutes(5));

        for (int minute = 0; minute <= 120; minute++) {
            for (int sms = 0; sms < 50; sms++) {
                ambassador.authorizationHeader(); // 50 SMS per minute from the app
            }
            if (minute == 0 || minute == 54 || minute == 55 || minute == 120) {
                System.out.println("t=+" + minute + "min header: " + ambassador.authorizationHeader());
            }
            clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(1));
        }
        System.out.println("6,050 SMS sent, token requests to the auth server: " + ambassador.tokenRequests()
                + " (refreshed 5 minutes before each expiry)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Challenge: Token Caching in the Ambassador (SMS gateway, 1-hour tokens) ===
t=+0min header: Bearer tok-1
t=+54min header: Bearer tok-1
t=+55min header: Bearer tok-2
t=+120min header: Bearer tok-3
6,050 SMS sent, token requests to the auth server: 3 (refreshed 5 minutes before each expiry)

Why an ambassador here:

  • Token lifecycle (fetch, cache, refresh, rotate secrets) is infrastructure, not business logic.
  • The app stays free of OAuth libraries and secrets.
  • Refreshing early avoids a burst of 401s at every expiry.
Unit Tests: AmbassadorTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.legacy.PartnerAmbassador;
import com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.shardproxy.CacheShardProxy;
import com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.token.TokenAmbassador;
import com.handbook.microservices.ambassador.token.TokenAmbassador.Token;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class AmbassadorTest {

    @Test
    void ambassadorAddsAuthAndRetriesServerErrors() {
        int[] calls = {0};
        PartnerAmbassador a = new PartnerAmbassador(r -> {
            calls[0]++;
            assertThat(r.header("Authorization")).isEqualTo("ApiKey k");
            return calls[0] == 1 ? Response.of(502, "") : Response.of(200, "ok");
        }, "k", 3);
        assertThat(a.apply(Request.get("/x", Map.of())).status()).isEqualTo(200);
        assertThat(calls[0]).isEqualTo(2);
    }

    @Test
    void clientErrorsAreNotRetried() {
        int[] calls = {0};
        PartnerAmbassador a = new PartnerAmbassador(r -> {
            calls[0]++;
            return Response.of(404, "");
        }, "k", 3);
        a.apply(Request.get("/x", Map.of()));
        assertThat(calls[0]).isEqualTo(1);
    }

    @Test
    void shardProxyRoundTrips() {
        CacheShardProxy p = new CacheShardProxy(4);
        p.set("k", "v");
        assertThat(p.get("k")).isEqualTo("v");
    }

    @Test
    void tokenIsReusedUntilTheRefreshMargin() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        TokenAmbassador t = new TokenAmbassador(() -> new Token("t", clock.instant().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(10))), clock, Duration.ofMinutes(2));
        t.authorizationHeader();
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(7));
        t.authorizationHeader();
        assertThat(t.tokenRequests()).isEqualTo(1);
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(1));
        t.authorizationHeader();
        assertThat(t.tokenRequests()).isEqualTo(2);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Kubernetes pod (reference) 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: loan-servicing }
spec:
  containers:
    - name: legacy-app
      image: registry.example/loan-servicing:2009.4
      env: [{ name: PARTNER_BASE_URL, value: "http://localhost:9000" }]
    - name: partner-ambassador           # Envoy, or a small Spring Cloud Gateway app
      image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.31.2
      ports: [{ containerPort: 9000 }]
      volumeMounts: [{ name: envoy-config, mountPath: /etc/envoy }]
  volumes:
    - name: envoy-config
      configMap: { name: partner-ambassador-config }
Variation Notes Envoy as ambassador Retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, TLS origination, Redis/Mongo/Postgres protocol filters Database ambassadors PgBouncer (connection pooling), Cloud SQL Auth Proxy (IAM auth + TLS), ProxySQL Service mesh egress Istio ServiceEntry + DestinationRule for external calls: a mesh-managed ambassador Library instead For one modern Java service, Resilience4j + a Spring RestClient interceptor is simpler Dapr A sidecar exposing bindings, state and pub/sub over a local API

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Ambassador Envoy / Istio Sidecar proxies handling egress; ServiceEntry, DestinationRule, retry policies Google Cloud Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, AlloyDB Auth Proxy PgBouncer / ProxySQL Connection pooling and routing for databases Twemproxy / Envoy Redis Sharding proxies for Redis/Memcached Dapr Sidecar APIs for state, pub/sub, secrets, bindings AWS ECS/EKS sidecars like the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry collector (telemetry ambassador)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons No changes to legacy or third-party clients Extra hop: added latency (small on localhost, but non-zero) One implementation for many languages Another process to deploy, monitor and upgrade Ops control policies without app releases Debugging spans two processes Credentials isolated from app code Overkill for a single modern service where a library would do

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Retrying non-idempotent calls

An ambassador retrying POST /payments on a timeout can pay twice. Retry only idempotent methods, or require idempotency keys.

Retries in both app and ambassador

3 app retries × 3 ambassador retries = 9 calls per request during an outage. Retry in one layer only.

Ambassador becomes a business-logic dumping ground

Transforming payloads, applying pricing rules or enriching data in the proxy hides behaviour from the team that owns it. Keep it to connectivity.

Startup and shutdown ordering

The app may start before its ambassador is ready, or the ambassador may exit first during shutdown and drop in-flight calls. Use Kubernetes native sidecars (restartPolicy: Always init containers) or readiness gates.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
When to choose it. Ambassador wins when the client can't change, or when the same connectivity logic must serve many runtimes. For a fleet of Spring Boot services, a shared library (or a mesh) is usually cheaper. Many organisations use ambassadors as a migration tool: wrap the legacy app now, replace it later (Strangler Fig).

Latency budget. A localhost hop adds ~50–200 µs plus serialization. Fine for most calls; noticeable for chatty protocols. Use Unix domain sockets or keep-alive connections, and avoid double TLS.

Ownership. The ambassador's config is code: version it, review it, test it (contract tests against the partner sandbox), and roll it out with the app so a policy change can be rolled back with the release.

War story: the retry that paid twice

A team put an ambassador in front of a legacy billing app and enabled "retry on timeout" for all methods. During a partner slowdown, POST /debits timed out after 2 s but had succeeded on the partner side. The ambassador retried; 1,900 customers were debited twice. Fix: retries limited to GET/PUT; POST /debits now carries an idempotency key the ambassador generates once per app request and the partner honours. Lesson: transparent retries are only safe for idempotent operations.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Ambassador Sidecar / Mesh API Gateway Anti-Corruption Layer Direction Outbound from one client Inbound + outbound Inbound to many services Model translation Deployed Next to the client Next to every service At the edge Inside the service (or as a service) Concern Connectivity Connectivity, security, telemetry Routing, auth, limits for clients Domain language

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner / Service Companies🟡 Mid-Level🔴 Senior / FAANG / SAP💻 Coding Challenge

Q1. What is the Ambassador pattern?

A helper proxy next to a client that handles its outbound calls (auth, retries, routing), so the client just calls localhost.

Q2. Ambassador vs API Gateway?

The ambassador sits next to one client for outbound calls; the gateway sits in front of many services for inbound calls.

Q3. Give a real example.

Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, PgBouncer, or an Envoy sidecar adding retries and TLS.

Q4. Why use it for legacy apps?

You get modern connectivity features without changing the legacy code.

Q5. Is the ambassador a sidecar?

Yes, a sidecar specialised for outbound connectivity.

Q1. What should an ambassador not do?

Business logic or data transformation; keep it to connectivity.

Q2. Where should retries live: app or ambassador?

In one layer only, and only for idempotent operations.

Q3. How do you handle secrets?

The ambassador fetches them from a secret store; the app never sees them.

Q4. What's the cost?

An extra hop, an extra process to operate, and more complex debugging.

Q5. Ambassador vs library?

A library is simpler for one language you control; an ambassador is language-agnostic and works for code you can't change.

Q1. "Migrate 40 legacy apps to a new partner API with OAuth2 and mTLS."

Standard ambassador image (Envoy + token sidecar) per app; config per partner in Git; contract tests in CI; roll out app by app; observability via the ambassador's metrics.

Q2. "How do you prevent retry amplification across layers?"

Retry budgets, one retrying layer per call path, deadlines propagated in headers, and circuit breakers at the ambassador.

Q3. "How do you make ambassador config changes safe?"

Version with the app, canary them, validate against a sandbox, and keep metrics on retries/timeouts per route.

Q4. "When does a mesh replace ambassadors?"

When most services are on Kubernetes and need the same policies: the mesh's sidecars become ambassadors managed centrally.

Q5. "How do you measure the ambassador's overhead?"

Compare client-side latency with and without it (or ambassador-reported upstream time vs app-observed time); watch CPU and connection counts.

Problem: Build an ambassador that adds an OAuth2 bearer token to every SMS request, fetching a new token only when needed and refreshing it 5 minutes before it expires. Show how many token requests 2 hours of traffic need.

Solution

See TokenAmbassador.java and TokenAmbassadorDemo.java in Example 3.

Key points to say: cache the token with its expiry; refresh at expiresAt − margin so requests in flight never carry an expired token; make the refresh synchronized (or single-flight) so concurrent requests don't all fetch a token; handle a 401 by forcing one refresh and retrying once.

Behavioural tie-in (STAR) for experienced candidates

  • S: A legacy loan app couldn't call a partner's new API (auth headers, frequent 503s), and rewriting it was a 9-month estimate.
  • T: Integrate within one quarter without touching the legacy code.
  • A: Deployed an Envoy-based ambassador with API-key injection, idempotent-only retries, timeouts and metrics; changed only the app's base URL; added contract tests against the partner sandbox.
  • R: Live in 5 weeks; partner call success rate rose from 91% to 99.8%; the same ambassador image was reused for three other legacy apps.

docs.title: 13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Out-of-process helper next to the client for outbound calls.
  • Auth, retries, timeouts, TLS, routing, sharding, metrics.
  • Great for legacy/third-party code and polyglot fleets.
  • Retry only idempotent calls; retry in one layer.
  • Connectivity only, never business logic.
app → http://localhost:9000 → ambassador → https://partner-api (+ auth, retries, TLS)

docs.text:
• Add a per-attempt timeout and exponential backoff to PartnerAmbassador.
  • Make TokenAmbassador force a refresh and retry once on a 401.
  • Switch CacheShardProxy to consistent hashing and count keys moved when adding a shard.
