docs.title: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An anti-corruption layer is a translation boundary between your domain model and an external or legacy system with a different model. It converts their data, codes and protocols into your concepts (and back), so their quirks never leak into your code. It's the Adapter and Facade patterns applied at the scale of whole systems (a Domain-Driven Design strategic pattern).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the new catalog service reads products from a 25-year-old ERP: fields like MAT_NO with 18-digit zero padding, prices as "1.299,00", units KGM/ST, and DEL_FLAG = "X" for inactive. If those details spread through the new code, the new service becomes as hard to change as the ERP, and replacing the ERP later means touching everything. That's the "corruption".

Definition (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design):

Create an isolating layer to provide clients with functionality in terms of their own domain model. The layer talks to the other system through its existing interface, requiring little or no modification to the other system.

Typical ACL building blocks:

Part Role Facade Simplifies the foreign system's API (many calls → one) Adapter Talks the foreign protocol (SOAP, XML, fixed-width files, RFC) Translator Maps foreign data and codes to domain objects, and back

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
An interpreter and customs desk at a border

Travellers (data) from another country arrive with their own language, units and documents. At the border they're translated and checked: miles become kilometres, unknown items are held for inspection. Inside the country, nobody has to speak the foreign language.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR subgraph Ours["Our bounded context"] D[Domain services] --> P[Port: ProductCatalog] end P --> ACL[Anti-corruption layer<br/>facade + adapter + translator] ACL --> L[Legacy ERP / partner API<br/>foreign model] Participant Responsibility Our domain Uses only its own types (Product, Money, Unit) ACL Calls the foreign system; translates in both directions; rejects or flags what can't be mapped Foreign system Unchanged; often not under our control

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// Deep inside the pricing service...
if ("X".equals(row.get("DEL_FLAG")) || row.get("BASE_UOM").equals("ST")) { ... }
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal(row.get("PRICE").replace(".", "").replace(",", "."));
// ...repeated in cart, search and recommendations. Replacing the ERP = rewriting all of them.

docs.title: Example 1: Products from a Legacy ERP (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The catalog service needs product data from the ERP's material master. The ACL zero-pads SKUs for the ERP, strips padding on the way back, title-cases descriptions, maps unit codes to an enum, parses European-format prices into paise, and turns DEL_FLAG into a boolean. Unknown materials become Optional.empty().

Full Code:

ErpProductTranslator.javaErpAclDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.acl.erp;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * The anti-corruption layer between our catalog and a decades-old ERP. The ERP's cryptic fields,
 * zero-padded codes, comma decimals and status flags stop here; the rest of our code only sees
 * our own Product model.
 */
public final class ErpProductTranslator {

    public enum Unit { KILOGRAM, PIECE, LITRE }

    /** Our domain model: clean names, types and invariants. */
    public record Product(String sku, String name, Unit unit, long pricePaise, boolean active) {
    }

    /** The ERP's interface, as it is. We don't control it. */
    public interface LegacyErp {
        Map<String, String> readMaterial(String materialNumber);
    }

    private final LegacyErp erp;

    public ErpProductTranslator(LegacyErp erp) {
        this.erp = erp;
    }

    public Optional<Product> product(String sku) {
        Map<String, String> raw = erp.readMaterial(String.format("%018d", Long.parseLong(sku.replace("SKU-", "")))); // (1)!
        if (raw.isEmpty()) {
            return Optional.empty();
        }
        return Optional.of(new Product(
                "SKU-" + Long.parseLong(raw.get("MAT_NO")),       // strip the zero padding
                titleCase(raw.get("MAT_DESC").trim()),
                unit(raw.get("BASE_UOM")),                       // (2)!
                new BigDecimal(raw.get("PRICE").replace(".", "").replace(',', '.'))
                        .movePointRight(2).longValueExact(),     // (3)!
                !"X".equals(raw.get("DEL_FLAG"))));              // (4)!
    }

    private static Unit unit(String erpCode) {
        return switch (erpCode) {
            case "KGM" -> Unit.KILOGRAM;
            case "ST", "PCE" -> Unit.PIECE;
            case "LTR" -> Unit.LITRE;
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unmapped ERP unit " + erpCode);
        };
    }

    private static String titleCase(String upper) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (String w : upper.toLowerCase().split(" ")) {
            sb.append(Character.toUpperCase(w.charAt(0))).append(w.substring(1)).append(' ');
        }
        return sb.toString().trim();
    }
}
  1. Our SKU format → the ERP's 18-digit, zero-padded material number. The ERP's key format never leaves the ACL.
  2. Explicit code mapping; an unmapped unit fails loudly instead of silently becoming wrong data.
  3. "1.299,00" (thousands dot, decimal comma) → 129900 paise, with exact decimal arithmetic.
  4. The ERP's soft-delete flag becomes a meaningful domain property.
package com.handbook.microservices.acl.erp;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class ErpAclDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ErpProductTranslator.LegacyErp erp = materialNumber -> switch (materialNumber) {
            case "000000000000012345" -> Map.of("MAT_NO", "000000000000012345", "MAT_DESC", "ALPHONSO MANGO PREMIUM   ",
                    "BASE_UOM", "KGM", "PRICE", "1.299,00", "DEL_FLAG", "");
            case "000000000000012346" -> Map.of("MAT_NO", "000000000000012346", "MAT_DESC", "COCONUT WATER",
                    "BASE_UOM", "LTR", "PRICE", "89,50", "DEL_FLAG", "X");
            default -> Map.of();
        };
        var catalog = new ErpProductTranslator(erp);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: reading products from a legacy ERP through an ACL ===");
        System.out.println("ERP says   : " + new TreeMap<>(erp.readMaterial("000000000000012345")));
        System.out.println("We see     : " + catalog.product("SKU-12345").orElseThrow());
        System.out.println("We see     : " + catalog.product("SKU-12346").orElseThrow());
        System.out.println("Unknown SKU: " + catalog.product("SKU-99999"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: reading products from a legacy ERP through an ACL ===
ERP says   : {BASE_UOM=KGM, DEL_FLAG=, MAT_DESC=ALPHONSO MANGO PREMIUM   , MAT_NO=000000000000012345, PRICE=1.299,00}
We see     : Product[sku=SKU-12345, name=Alphonso Mango Premium, unit=KILOGRAM, pricePaise=129900, active=true]
We see     : Product[sku=SKU-12346, name=Coconut Water, unit=LITRE, pricePaise=8950, active=false]
Unknown SKU: Optional.empty

Why an ACL here:

  • The ERP's conventions are confined to one class with focused tests.
  • Replacing the ERP later means writing a new translator, not changing the catalog domain.

docs.title: Example 2: Policies from Legacy XML (Insurance)
docs.text:
Scenario: The new claims service needs policy data from a legacy policy-admin system that returns XML with tags like POL_REF, CVR_CD, EXP_DT (yyyyMMdd). The ACL parses it securely (no external entities), maps cover codes to an enum, converts dates, and produces a Policy with behaviour (coversOn(date)). Unknown cover codes are rejected at the boundary.

Full Code:

PolicyXmlTranslator.javaPolicyAclDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.acl.insurance;

import org.w3c.dom.Document;
import org.w3c.dom.Element;
import org.w3c.dom.NodeList;

import javax.xml.XMLConstants;
import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory;
import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Translates the legacy policy-admin system's XML (its own vocabulary, date format and codes)
 * into our claims service's Policy model. Only this class knows the XML exists.
 */
public final class PolicyXmlTranslator {

    public enum CoverType { COMPREHENSIVE, THIRD_PARTY }

    public record Policy(String number, String holder, CoverType cover, LocalDate validUntil, List<String> namedDrivers) {
        public boolean coversOn(LocalDate date) {
            return !date.isAfter(validUntil);
        }
    }

    private static final DateTimeFormatter LEGACY_DATE = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyyMMdd");

    public Policy translate(String xml) {
        try {
            DocumentBuilderFactory factory = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
            factory.setFeature(XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, true); // (1)!
            factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true);
            Document doc = factory.newDocumentBuilder()
                    .parse(new ByteArrayInputStream(xml.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)));
            Element root = doc.getDocumentElement();
            List<String> drivers = new ArrayList<>();
            NodeList nodes = root.getElementsByTagName("DRV_NM");
            for (int i = 0; i < nodes.getLength(); i++) {
                drivers.add(nodes.item(i).getTextContent().trim());
            }
            return new Policy(
                    text(root, "POL_REF").replace("/", "-"),
                    text(root, "INS_NM"),
                    switch (text(root, "CVR_CD")) { // (2)!
                        case "01" -> CoverType.COMPREHENSIVE;
                        case "02" -> CoverType.THIRD_PARTY;
                        default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown cover code " + text(root, "CVR_CD"));
                    },
                    LocalDate.parse(text(root, "EXP_DT"), LEGACY_DATE), // (3)!
                    List.copyOf(drivers));
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("cannot translate policy XML: " + e.getMessage(), e);
        }
    }

    private static String text(Element root, String tag) {
        return root.getElementsByTagName(tag).item(0).getTextContent().trim();
    }
}
  1. Secure XML parsing: disallow DOCTYPE/external entities (XXE attacks). The boundary is also a security boundary.
  2. Codes → domain enum; anything unknown is an error, not a guess.
  3. Legacy date format converted once into LocalDate.
package com.handbook.microservices.acl.insurance;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public class PolicyAclDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String legacyXml = """
                <PLCY_RSP>
                  <POL_REF>MTR/2025/004417</POL_REF>
                  <INS_NM>Ravi Kumar</INS_NM>
                  <CVR_CD>01</CVR_CD>
                  <EXP_DT>20261231</EXP_DT>
                  <DRVRS><DRV_NM>Ravi Kumar</DRV_NM><DRV_NM>Anita Kumar</DRV_NM></DRVRS>
                </PLCY_RSP>
                """;
        var translator = new PolicyXmlTranslator();

        System.out.println("=== Insurance: claims service reads policies from a legacy XML system ===");
        var policy = translator.translate(legacyXml);
        System.out.println("Policy: " + policy);
        System.out.println("Accident on 2026-11-02 covered? " + policy.coversOn(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2)));
        System.out.println("Accident on 2027-01-05 covered? " + policy.coversOn(LocalDate.of(2027, 1, 5)));
        try {
            translator.translate(legacyXml.replace("<CVR_CD>01", "<CVR_CD>07"));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Unknown code rejected at the boundary: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Insurance: claims service reads policies from a legacy XML system ===
Policy: Policy[number=MTR-2025-004417, holder=Ravi Kumar, cover=COMPREHENSIVE, validUntil=2026-12-31, namedDrivers=[Ravi Kumar, Anita Kumar]]
Accident on 2026-11-02 covered? true
Accident on 2027-01-05 covered? false
Unknown code rejected at the boundary: cannot translate policy XML: unknown cover code 07

Why an ACL here:

  • The claims domain talks about Policy, CoverType and coverage dates, not XML tags.
  • Bad or unexpected data is stopped at the edge, where it's easy to log and investigate.

docs.title: Example 3: One Status Model for Many Carriers (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: Each delivery partner reports status in its own vocabulary: QuickDrop uses OFD/DL/NDR; BlueKite uses 1–4 and 9. A per-carrier mapping translates them into our ShipmentStatus. Inputs are normalized ("dl " → DL). An unmapped code becomes UNKNOWN with an alert, instead of crashing the tracking pipeline.

Full Code:

CarrierStatusTranslator.javaCarrierAclDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.acl.logistics;

import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Each delivery partner reports status in its own vocabulary. One adapter per partner maps it to
 * OUR status model; unknown codes become UNKNOWN (and an alert) instead of crashing the pipeline.
 */
public final class CarrierStatusTranslator {

    public enum ShipmentStatus { PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, FAILED_ATTEMPT, UNKNOWN }

    public record CarrierEvent(String carrier, String awb, String rawStatus) {
    }

    public record TrackingUpdate(String trackingId, ShipmentStatus status) {
    }

    private static final Map<String, Map<String, ShipmentStatus>> MAPPINGS = Map.of( // (1)!
            "QuickDrop", Map.of("PU", ShipmentStatus.PICKED_UP, "IT", ShipmentStatus.IN_TRANSIT,
                    "OFD", ShipmentStatus.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, "DL", ShipmentStatus.DELIVERED,
                    "NDR", ShipmentStatus.FAILED_ATTEMPT),
            "BlueKite", Map.of("1", ShipmentStatus.PICKED_UP, "2", ShipmentStatus.IN_TRANSIT,
                    "3", ShipmentStatus.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, "4", ShipmentStatus.DELIVERED,
                    "9", ShipmentStatus.FAILED_ATTEMPT));

    public TrackingUpdate translate(CarrierEvent event) {
        ShipmentStatus status = MAPPINGS.getOrDefault(event.carrier(), Map.of())
                .getOrDefault(event.rawStatus().trim().toUpperCase(), ShipmentStatus.UNKNOWN); // (2)!
        if (status == ShipmentStatus.UNKNOWN) {
            System.out.println("    ALERT: unmapped status '" + event.rawStatus() + "' from " + event.carrier());
        }
        return new TrackingUpdate(event.carrier() + ":" + event.awb(), status); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Mappings are data, one table per partner. Onboarding a new carrier means adding a mapping, not changing domain code.
  2. Normalize, then map; unknown codes get a safe default plus an alert, because a tracking page showing "unknown" beats a stopped pipeline.
  3. Our own tracking ID scheme, independent of each carrier's AWB format.
package com.handbook.microservices.acl.logistics;

import com.handbook.microservices.acl.logistics.CarrierStatusTranslator.CarrierEvent;

import java.util.List;

public class CarrierAclDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var acl = new CarrierStatusTranslator();
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: two carriers, one status model ===");
        for (CarrierEvent e : List.of(
                new CarrierEvent("QuickDrop", "771020", "OFD"),
                new CarrierEvent("BlueKite", "BK-55", "3"),
                new CarrierEvent("QuickDrop", "771020", "dl "),
                new CarrierEvent("BlueKite", "BK-56", "9"),
                new CarrierEvent("BlueKite", "BK-57", "7"))) {
            System.out.printf("%-9s %-7s %-4s -> %s%n", e.carrier(), e.awb(), "'" + e.rawStatus() + "'", acl.translate(e));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: two carriers, one status model ===
QuickDrop 771020  'OFD' -> TrackingUpdate[trackingId=QuickDrop:771020, status=OUT_FOR_DELIVERY]
BlueKite  BK-55   '3'  -> TrackingUpdate[trackingId=BlueKite:BK-55, status=OUT_FOR_DELIVERY]
QuickDrop 771020  'dl ' -> TrackingUpdate[trackingId=QuickDrop:771020, status=DELIVERED]
BlueKite  BK-56   '9'  -> TrackingUpdate[trackingId=BlueKite:BK-56, status=FAILED_ATTEMPT]
    ALERT: unmapped status '7' from BlueKite
BlueKite  BK-57   '7'  -> TrackingUpdate[trackingId=BlueKite:BK-57, status=UNKNOWN]

Why an ACL here:

  • Many external models, one internal model; the rest of the system never learns about carriers' codes.
  • Fail-soft vs. fail-hard is a deliberate choice per boundary (insurance codes: reject; tracking codes: flag).
Unit Tests: AntiCorruptionLayerTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.acl.erp.ErpProductTranslator;
import com.handbook.microservices.acl.erp.ErpProductTranslator.Unit;
import com.handbook.microservices.acl.logistics.CarrierStatusTranslator;
import com.handbook.microservices.acl.logistics.CarrierStatusTranslator.CarrierEvent;
import com.handbook.microservices.acl.logistics.CarrierStatusTranslator.ShipmentStatus;
import com.handbook.microservices.acl.outbound.LegacyOrderExporter;
import com.handbook.microservices.acl.outbound.LegacyOrderExporter.OrderLine;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class AntiCorruptionLayerTest {

    @Test
    void erpFieldsAreTranslatedIntoDomainTypes() {
        var acl = new ErpProductTranslator(n -> Map.of("MAT_NO", n, "MAT_DESC", "RICE", "BASE_UOM", "ST",
                "PRICE", "1.000,50", "DEL_FLAG", ""));
        var p = acl.product("SKU-7").orElseThrow();
        assertThat(p.sku()).isEqualTo("SKU-7");
        assertThat(p.unit()).isEqualTo(Unit.PIECE);
        assertThat(p.pricePaise()).isEqualTo(100_050);
        assertThat(p.active()).isTrue();
    }

    @Test
    void unknownCarrierCodesBecomeUnknown() {
        var update = new CarrierStatusTranslator().translate(new CarrierEvent("BlueKite", "1", "42"));
        assertThat(update.status()).isEqualTo(ShipmentStatus.UNKNOWN);
    }

    @Test
    void fixedWidthRecordsHaveExactLength() {
        String r = LegacyOrderExporter.toRecord(new OrderLine("O-1", "Élodie", 3, LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 2)));
        assertThat(r).hasSize(41).contains("ELODIE").endsWith("00003260102");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Ports and adapters: define a port in your domain (ProductCatalog), and implement it in the ACL. See Hexagonal Architecture.
  • ACL as a separate service: when several services need the same legacy system, an "integration service" owns the translation (and caching) once.
  • Mapping libraries: MapStruct generates compile-time mappers for the boring field-to-field part; keep code mappings and rules explicit.
  • Event translation: translate legacy events (CDC rows, IDocs, flat files) into clean domain events before publishing to your event bus.
  • Contract tests: record real responses from the foreign system and test the translator against them.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Anti-corruption layer DDD context maps "ACL" relationship between bounded contexts Apache Camel / Spring Integration Message translators, content enrichers, normalizers (EIP) SAP Integration Suite, MuleSoft Integration platforms often acting as ACLs MapStruct Generated mappers inside ACL code Strangler migrations ACL between new services and the old system

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Domain model stays clean and independent Extra layer to build and maintain Foreign system can be replaced behind it Translation adds latency and possibly caching complexity One place for validation, security and logging of foreign data Can become a bottleneck if one team owns all ACLs Easy to test with recorded responses Mapping gaps discovered only with real data

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Leaky ACL

Returning the foreign DTO "for now" or adding getRawField() lets foreign concepts creep back into the domain. The ACL's public API must use only your types.

Silent defaults

Mapping unknown codes to a plausible value ("07" → COMPREHENSIVE) creates wrong data that surfaces months later. Fail loudly, or map to an explicit UNKNOWN plus an alert.

Business logic in the translator

The ACL translates and validates the shape of data. Business rules (is this claim payable?) belong in the domain.

No tests against real samples

Legacy systems have edge cases nobody documented. Build a corpus of real (anonymized) messages and run the translator against all of them in CI.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Context mapping. In DDD terms, use an ACL when you're downstream of a model you can't influence (legacy, vendor, partner) and don't want to conform. If the upstream offers a well-designed Open Host Service / Published Language, a thinner ACL may suffice; if both teams cooperate closely, a shared kernel or partnership might be better.

ACL in migrations. During a strangler migration, the ACL lets new services use the legacy system's data in new terms. When the legacy capability is replaced, only the ACL's implementation changes.

Ownership and scaling. Per-service ACLs keep autonomy; a shared integration service avoids duplicating complex legacy access (connection limits, licensing, caching). Choose based on how many consumers there are and how complex the access is.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• ACL API exposes only domain types; foreign DTOs never escape.
  • Explicit mappings for codes and units; unknowns fail or are flagged deliberately.
  • Secure parsing (XXE-safe XML, size limits), input validation, logging of rejected records.
  • Translator tests against a corpus of real samples; contract tests with the foreign system.
  • Timeouts, retries and caching for calls to the foreign system.
  • Metrics for translation failures and unknown codes.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Our new services integrate with the legacy ERP and with carrier APIs through anti-corruption layers. Each ACL exposes a port in our domain language, like ProductCatalog.product(sku) or TrackingUpdate, and inside does the protocol calls, field and code mappings, unit and currency conversion, and validation. Unknown codes are rejected or flagged depending on the risk. Translators are tested against recorded real messages. When we retire the ERP, we replace the ACL implementation; nothing in the domain changes."

War story: the unit that cost a fortune

A retailer's replenishment service read ERP order quantities directly. One supplier's materials used unit CS (case of 24) instead of ST (piece). The code assumed pieces everywhere. A store ordered "12" bottles of oil and received 12 cases (288 bottles), for weeks, across 80 stores, before anyone noticed the overstock. Fix: an ACL that converts all ERP quantities into base units with explicit conversion factors, rejecting unknown units; a report of rejected records reviewed daily. Lesson: foreign units and codes are where silent, expensive errors live. Translate them explicitly, once.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Anti-Corruption Layer Adapter Facade Gateway / BFF Scale System boundary (bounded contexts) One interface One subsystem Edge of the system Main job Translate models Convert interfaces Simplify Route / shape for clients Protects Our domain model Calling code Clients from complexity Services from clients

See Adapter, Facade, Strangler Fig and Decomposition.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Translate at the boundary; the domain sees only its own types.
  • Facade + adapter + translator, at system scale (DDD).
  • Explicit code/unit mappings; unknowns rejected or flagged, never guessed.
  • Secure parsing and validation at the edge.
  • Makes the legacy system replaceable.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add support for the ERP unit CS (case of 24) by converting quantities to pieces.
  • Add a third carrier with string statuses ("Delivered", "Out for delivery") to the logistics ACL.
  • Write the reverse translator for insurance: Policy → legacy XML, and test the round trip.

Config Server Next: Cache-Aside

docs.title: API Gateway
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

An API gateway is the single entry point for clients: it routes each request to the right service and handles cross-cutting edge concerns (authentication, rate limiting, TLS, request IDs, canary routing) in one place. Clients see one stable API; services stay simple and can move, split or scale behind it.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a grocery mobile app talks to catalog, cart, order and payment services. Without a gateway, the app needs every service's address, each service re-implements token validation and rate limiting, and moving or splitting a service means shipping a new app version (and waiting weeks for users to update). A gateway puts one front door in front of all of them.

Definition (microservices.io):

Implement an API gateway that is the single entry point for all clients. The gateway handles requests by routing them to the appropriate service, or by fanning out to multiple services.

Typical gateway responsibilities:

Concern Example Routing /orders/** → order-service; strip or rewrite paths Authentication Validate JWTs / API keys once; pass identity downstream (X-Customer-Id) Rate limiting / quotas Per client, per API key, per tenant Observability Request IDs, trace headers, access logs, metrics Traffic management Canary releases, A/B tests, blue-green Protocol translation REST ↔ gRPC, WebSocket upgrade Edge security TLS termination, WAF, IP allow-lists, CORS

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A hotel reception desk

Guests don't wander the corridors looking for housekeeping or the restaurant manager. Reception checks who you are (authentication), sends your request to the right department (routing), and politely says "please wait" when the kitchen is overwhelmed (rate limiting). Departments can be reorganized without guests noticing.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     App[Mobile app] --> GW[API Gateway<br/>TLS, auth, rate limit,<br/>routing, request IDs]     Web[Web app] --> GW     Partner[Partner API client] --> GW     GW -->|/catalog/**| C[Catalog service]     GW -->|/cart/**| K[Cart service]     GW -->|/orders/**| O[Order service]     GW -->|/payments/**| P[Payment service] Participant Responsibility Clients Know one host and one API Gateway Edge concerns + routing; no business logic Services Business capabilities; trust identity headers from the gateway (inside a private network or with mTLS)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
mobile app ──► catalog.internal:8081   (needs to know every host)
           ──► cart.internal:8082       (each service validates JWTs its own way)
           ──► orders.internal:8083     (each service has its own rate limiter, or none)
Split order-service in two?  → release a new app and wait for users to update.
  • Clients coupled to internal topology.
  • Duplicated edge logic (auth, rate limiting) with inconsistent behavior.
  • Internal services exposed to the internet.

docs.title: Example 1: Mobile API Gateway (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery app has public endpoints (browse the catalog) and private ones (cart, orders). The gateway routes by path prefix, strips the prefix (services don't care about their public URL), validates the session token once, passes the customer ID downstream, and tags every request with an ID for log correlation. Unknown paths return 404 at the edge without touching any service.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant A as App participant G as Gateway participant O as order-service A->>G: GET /orders/ORD-9 (Bearer tok-asha) G->>G: route match /orders, validate token → CUST-42 G->>O: GET /ORD-9 + X-Customer-Id: CUST-42 + X-Request-Id: req-4 O-->>G: 200 G-->>A: 200 + X-Request-Id: req-4

Full Code:

MobileGateway.javaHttp.java (support)MobileGatewayDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.gateway.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Single entry point for the mobile app: routing, authentication, prefix stripping, request IDs. */
public class MobileGateway {

    private record Route(String prefix, Function<Request, Response> service, boolean requiresLogin) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Route> routes = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, String> sessions = Map.of("tok-asha", "CUST-42"); // token -> customer
    private int requestCounter;

    public MobileGateway route(String prefix, Function<Request, Response> service, boolean requiresLogin) {
        routes.put(prefix, new Route(prefix, service, requiresLogin));
        return this;
    }

    public Response handle(Request req) {
        String requestId = "req-" + (++requestCounter);
        Route route = routes.values().stream()
                .filter(r -> req.path().startsWith(r.prefix())).findFirst().orElse(null); // (1)!
        if (route == null) {
            return Response.of(404, "no route for " + req.path()).withHeader("X-Request-Id", requestId);
        }
        Request forwarded = req.withPath(req.path().substring(route.prefix().length())) // (2)!
                .withHeader("X-Request-Id", requestId);
        if (route.requiresLogin()) {
            String auth = req.header("Authorization");
            String customer = auth == null ? null : sessions.get(auth.replace("Bearer ", ""));
            if (customer == null) {
                return Response.of(401, "login required").withHeader("X-Request-Id", requestId); // (3)!
            }
            forwarded = forwarded.withHeader("X-Customer-Id", customer); // (4)!
        }
        return route.service().apply(forwarded).withHeader("X-Request-Id", requestId);
    }
}
  1. Route matching by prefix (first match wins; order specific routes first).
  2. Path rewriting: services see /ORD-9, not the public /orders/ORD-9, so the public API can change without touching services.
  3. Authentication at the edge: invalid requests never reach a service.
  4. Identity propagation: services trust X-Customer-Id from the gateway. Only safe if services aren't reachable directly (private network, mTLS); the gateway must also strip any client-supplied copy of that header.
package com.handbook.microservices.support;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Minimal HTTP request/response records so gateways, BFFs and sidecars can be shown without a web server. */
public final class Http {

    private Http() {
    }

    public record Request(String method, String path, Map<String, String> headers, String body) {
        public Request {
            headers = Map.copyOf(headers);
        }

        public static Request get(String path, Map<String, String> headers) {
            return new Request("GET", path, headers, "");
        }

        public String header(String name) {
            return headers.get(name);
        }

        public Request withPath(String newPath) {
            return new Request(method, newPath, headers, body);
        }

        public Request withHeader(String name, String value) {
            Map<String, String> h = new LinkedHashMap<>(headers);
            h.put(name, value);
            return new Request(method, path, h, body);
        }
    }

    public record Response(int status, Map<String, String> headers, String body) {
        public Response {
            headers = Map.copyOf(headers);
        }

        public static Response of(int status, String body) {
            return new Response(status, Map.of(), body);
        }

        public Response withHeader(String name, String value) {
            Map<String, String> h = new LinkedHashMap<>(headers);
            h.put(name, value);
            return new Response(status, h, body);
        }

        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return status + " " + body + (headers.isEmpty() ? "" : " " + new java.util.TreeMap<>(headers));
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.gateway.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;

public class MobileGatewayDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Mobile API Gateway ===");
        MobileGateway gateway = new MobileGateway()
                .route("/catalog", r -> Response.of(200, "catalog-service saw " + r.path()), false)
                .route("/cart", r -> Response.of(200, "cart-service: cart of " + r.header("X-Customer-Id")), true)
                .route("/orders", r -> Response.of(200, "order-service: orders of " + r.header("X-Customer-Id") + " at " + r.path()), true);

        Map<String, String> loggedIn = Map.of("Authorization", "Bearer tok-asha");
        System.out.println("GET /catalog/products/MANGO   -> " + gateway.handle(Request.get("/catalog/products/MANGO", Map.of())));
        System.out.println("GET /cart (no token)          -> " + gateway.handle(Request.get("/cart", Map.of())));
        System.out.println("GET /cart (logged in)         -> " + gateway.handle(Request.get("/cart", loggedIn)));
        System.out.println("GET /orders/ORD-9 (logged in) -> " + gateway.handle(Request.get("/orders/ORD-9", loggedIn)));
        System.out.println("GET /admin/users              -> " + gateway.handle(Request.get("/admin/users", loggedIn)));
    }
}

Output (happy and failure paths):

=== Grocery: Mobile API Gateway ===
GET /catalog/products/MANGO   -> 200 catalog-service saw /products/MANGO {X-Request-Id=req-1}
GET /cart (no token)          -> 401 login required {X-Request-Id=req-2}
GET /cart (logged in)         -> 200 cart-service: cart of CUST-42 {X-Request-Id=req-3}
GET /orders/ORD-9 (logged in) -> 200 order-service: orders of CUST-42 at /ORD-9 {X-Request-Id=req-4}
GET /admin/users              -> 404 no route for /admin/users {X-Request-Id=req-5}

Why a gateway here:

  • One host and API for the app; internal services can move freely.
  • Authentication and request IDs implemented once.
  • Public/private routes are a gateway configuration decision.

docs.title: Example 2: Open-Banking Partner Gateway (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank exposes account APIs to licensed fintech partners. Each partner has an API key and a quota in its contract (BudgetApp: 3 requests/minute in this demo; real quotas are higher). The gateway rejects unknown keys, counts requests per partner per minute, returns X-RateLimit-Remaining so partners can pace themselves, and answers 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After when the quota is used up, protecting the core banking systems behind it.

Design:

flowchart LR P[Partner request + X-Api-Key] --> K{Known key?} K -->|no| E401[401] K -->|yes| Q{Within this minute's quota?} Q -->|no| E429["429 + Retry-After"] Q -->|yes| S[accounts-service] --> R["200 + X-RateLimit-Remaining"]

Full Code:

OpenBankingGateway.javaOpenBankingDemo.javaFakeClock.java (support) 
package com.handbook.microservices.gateway.openbanking;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Partner-facing gateway: API keys, per-partner quotas, rate-limit headers. */
public class OpenBankingGateway {

    public record Partner(String name, int requestsPerMinute) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Partner> apiKeys;
    private final Function<Request, Response> accountsService;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Map<String, Integer> used = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Instant> windowStart = new HashMap<>();

    public OpenBankingGateway(Map<String, Partner> apiKeys, Function<Request, Response> accountsService, Clock clock) {
        this.apiKeys = apiKeys;
        this.accountsService = accountsService;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public Response handle(Request req) {
        Partner partner = apiKeys.get(req.header("X-Api-Key"));
        if (partner == null) {
            return Response.of(401, "invalid API key");
        }
        Instant minute = clock.instant().truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.MINUTES); // (1)!
        if (!minute.equals(windowStart.get(partner.name()))) {
            windowStart.put(partner.name(), minute);
            used.put(partner.name(), 0);
        }
        int count = used.merge(partner.name(), 1, Integer::sum);
        int remaining = Math.max(0, partner.requestsPerMinute() - count);
        if (count > partner.requestsPerMinute()) {
            long retryAfter = 60 - clock.instant().getEpochSecond() % 60;
            return Response.of(429, "quota exceeded").withHeader("Retry-After", String.valueOf(retryAfter)); // (2)!
        }
        return accountsService.apply(req.withHeader("X-Partner", partner.name()))
                .withHeader("X-RateLimit-Remaining", String.valueOf(remaining)); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. A fixed window per partner per minute, using an injected Clock so the demo is deterministic. See Rate Limiter for token buckets and sliding windows.
  2. 429 + Retry-After tells well-behaved clients exactly when to retry.
  3. Rate-limit headers let partners slow down before they hit the limit.
package com.handbook.microservices.gateway.openbanking;

import com.handbook.microservices.gateway.openbanking.OpenBankingGateway.Partner;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;

public class OpenBankingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Open-Banking API Gateway for Fintech Partners ===");
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T10:00:05Z");
        OpenBankingGateway gw = new OpenBankingGateway(
                Map.of("key-budgetapp", new Partner("BudgetApp", 3), "key-lender", new Partner("QuickLender", 100)),
                r -> Response.of(200, "balance for " + r.header("X-Partner")), clock);

        Map<String, String> budgetApp = Map.of("X-Api-Key", "key-budgetapp");
        for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
            System.out.println("BudgetApp call " + i + " -> " + gw.handle(Request.get("/accounts/SB-1/balance", budgetApp)));
            clock.advanceMillis(5_000);
        }
        System.out.println("Unknown key       -> " + gw.handle(Request.get("/accounts/SB-1/balance", Map.of("X-Api-Key", "stolen"))));
        clock.advanceMillis(45_000); // next minute
        System.out.println("Next minute       -> " + gw.handle(Request.get("/accounts/SB-1/balance", budgetApp)));
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.support;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;

/** A controllable clock so time-based patterns (timeouts, windows, TTLs) give deterministic output. */
public final class FakeClock extends Clock {

    private Instant now;

    public FakeClock(Instant start) {
        this.now = start;
    }

    public static FakeClock at(String isoInstant) {
        return new FakeClock(Instant.parse(isoInstant));
    }

    public void advance(Duration d) {
        now = now.plus(d);
    }

    public void advanceMillis(long ms) {
        advance(Duration.ofMillis(ms));
    }

    @Override
    public Instant instant() {
        return now;
    }

    @Override
    public ZoneId getZone() {
        return ZoneOffset.UTC;
    }

    @Override
    public Clock withZone(ZoneId zone) {
        return this;
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Open-Banking API Gateway for Fintech Partners ===
BudgetApp call 1 -> 200 balance for BudgetApp {X-RateLimit-Remaining=2}
BudgetApp call 2 -> 200 balance for BudgetApp {X-RateLimit-Remaining=1}
BudgetApp call 3 -> 200 balance for BudgetApp {X-RateLimit-Remaining=0}
BudgetApp call 4 -> 429 quota exceeded {Retry-After=40}
Unknown key       -> 401 invalid API key
Next minute       -> 200 balance for BudgetApp {X-RateLimit-Remaining=2}

Why a gateway here:

  • Contractual quotas enforced consistently for every partner and every API.
  • Core banking is protected from partner traffic spikes.
  • Partner identity and usage are measured at one place (billing, audit).

docs.title: Example 3: Tenant-Aware Routing (SaaS ERP)
docs.text:
Scenario: A SaaS ERP hosts tenants in regional shards for data residency (EU customers in eu-1, US customers in us-2). Each tenant has its own subdomain (acme.erp.example.com). The gateway resolves the tenant from the Host header and routes to its shard. During planned maintenance of a shard, its tenants get a clear 503 with Retry-After, while tenants on other shards are unaffected. Unknown subdomains get a 404 at the edge.

Design:

flowchart LR A["acme.erp.example.com"] --> G{Gateway: tenant from Host} B["globex.erp.example.com"] --> G G -->|acme → eu-1| EU[(eu-1 shard)] G -->|"globex → us-2 (maintenance)"| M["503 Retry-After: 120"]

Full Code:

TenantGateway.javaTenantGatewayDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.gateway.tenancy;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Multi-tenant SaaS: resolve the tenant from the Host header and route to its regional shard. */
public class TenantGateway {

    private final Map<String, String> tenantToShard;
    private final Map<String, Function<Request, Response>> shards;
    private final Set<String> shardsDown;

    public TenantGateway(Map<String, String> tenantToShard, Map<String, Function<Request, Response>> shards, Set<String> shardsDown) {
        this.tenantToShard = tenantToShard;
        this.shards = shards;
        this.shardsDown = shardsDown;
    }

    public Response handle(Request req) {
        String host = req.header("Host");                       // acme.erp.example.com
        String tenant = host == null ? "" : host.split("\\.")[0]; // (1)!
        String shard = tenantToShard.get(tenant);
        if (shard == null) {
            return Response.of(404, "unknown tenant '" + tenant + "'");
        }
        if (shardsDown.contains(shard)) {
            return Response.of(503, "shard " + shard + " under maintenance").withHeader("Retry-After", "120"); // (2)!
        }
        return shards.get(shard).apply(req.withHeader("X-Tenant", tenant)); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Tenant resolution at the edge. Real systems also validate that the authenticated user belongs to this tenant.
  2. Shard-level maintenance mode without touching the shard.
  3. The tenant context travels as a header (and in the token) so every service can enforce isolation.
package com.handbook.microservices.gateway.tenancy;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

public class TenantGatewayDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== SaaS ERP: Tenant-Aware Routing to Regional Shards ===");
        TenantGateway gw = new TenantGateway(
                Map.of("acme", "eu-1", "globex", "us-2", "initech", "us-2"),
                Map.of("eu-1", r -> Response.of(200, "eu-1 served invoices for " + r.header("X-Tenant")),
                        "us-2", r -> Response.of(200, "us-2 served invoices for " + r.header("X-Tenant"))),
                Set.of("us-2"));

        for (String host : new String[] {"acme.erp.example.com", "globex.erp.example.com", "hooli.erp.example.com"}) {
            System.out.printf("%-24s -> %s%n", host, gw.handle(Request.get("/invoices", Map.of("Host", host))));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== SaaS ERP: Tenant-Aware Routing to Regional Shards ===
acme.erp.example.com     -> 200 eu-1 served invoices for acme
globex.erp.example.com   -> 503 shard us-2 under maintenance {Retry-After=120}
hooli.erp.example.com    -> 404 unknown tenant 'hooli'

Why a gateway here:

  • Data residency and sharding are invisible to clients.
  • Operational controls (maintenance, migrations of a tenant between shards) are routing changes.
  • Tenant context is established once, at the edge.
Unit Tests: ApiGatewayTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.gateway.grocery.MobileGateway;
import com.handbook.microservices.gateway.openbanking.OpenBankingGateway;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ApiGatewayTest {

    @Test
    void gatewayStripsPrefixAndPropagatesIdentity() {
        MobileGateway gw = new MobileGateway().route("/orders", r -> Response.of(200, r.path() + "|" + r.header("X-Customer-Id")), true);
        Response res = gw.handle(Request.get("/orders/1", Map.of("Authorization", "Bearer tok-asha")));
        assertThat(res.body()).isEqualTo("/1|CUST-42");
        assertThat(res.headers()).containsKey("X-Request-Id");
    }

    @Test
    void quotaResetsEachMinute() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        var gw = new OpenBankingGateway(Map.of("k", new OpenBankingGateway.Partner("p", 1)), r -> Response.of(200, "ok"), clock);
        var req = Request.get("/x", Map.of("X-Api-Key", "k"));
        assertThat(gw.handle(req).status()).isEqualTo(200);
        assertThat(gw.handle(req).status()).isEqualTo(429);
        clock.advanceMillis(60_000);
        assertThat(gw.handle(req).status()).isEqualTo(200);
    }
}

        - id: catalog
          uri: lb://catalog-service          # load-balanced via service discovery
          predicates: [ "Path=/catalog/**" ]
          filters: [ "StripPrefix=1" ]
        - id: orders
          uri: lb://order-service
          predicates: [ "Path=/orders/**" ]
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1
            - name: RequestRateLimiter       # Redis token bucket
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
                key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"
      # JWT validation: spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server + spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri
Option Notes Spring Cloud Gateway Java/Spring, reactive, rich filters; good if your team is Spring-heavy Kong, NGINX, Envoy, Traefik High-performance, plugin ecosystems; language-agnostic Cloud gateways (AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, GCP API Gateway/Apigee) Managed, with API keys, quotas, developer portals Kubernetes Gateway API / Ingress Declarative routing at the cluster edge BFF One gateway per client type. See Backend for Frontend

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Gateway Spring Cloud Gateway Routes, predicates, filters (StripPrefix, RequestRateLimiter, CircuitBreaker, Retry) Netflix Zuul (legacy) The original Java microservice gateway Envoy / Istio ingress gateway Edge proxy in service meshes Kong / Apigee / AWS API Gateway API management: keys, quotas, monetization, portals

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons One entry point; clients decoupled from topology Single point of failure: needs HA, autoscaling and fast config rollback Edge concerns implemented once Extra hop: a little latency Safe place for canaries, quotas, auth Can become a bottleneck team if every change needs gateway edits Hides internal services from the internet Temptation to put business logic in it

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Business logic in the gateway

Discount rules or order validation in gateway filters create a hidden monolith that every team depends on. Keep the gateway to edge concerns; use a BFF or a service for aggregation and logic.

Trusting identity headers from clients

If services trust X-Customer-Id and the gateway doesn't strip client-supplied copies, anyone can impersonate anyone. Strip, then set, and keep services off the public network.

One giant shared gateway config

Hundreds of routes owned by one team slows everyone. Use per-team route ownership (GitOps), or per-client BFFs.

No timeouts or circuit breakers at the edge

A slow service ties up gateway connections and can take down all routes. Set per-route timeouts and circuit breakers.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Availability. The gateway is on every request path: run it in several zones, autoscale on connections and CPU, keep it stateless (rate-limit state in Redis or local approximations), and roll configuration out gradually with instant rollback.

Security layering. TLS and WAF at the edge, authentication (JWT validation with cached keys), coarse authorization (scopes), then fine-grained authorization in services. Zero-trust networks add mTLS between gateway and services so header-based identity can't be spoofed internally.

Gateway vs. service mesh. The gateway handles north-south traffic (clients → services); a mesh handles east-west traffic (service ↔ service: mTLS, retries, telemetry). Many platforms use both. See Sidecar / Service Mesh.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Multi-zone, autoscaled, stateless gateway instances; health checks and fast config rollback.
  • Per-route timeouts, retries only for idempotent requests, circuit breakers.
  • Authentication at the edge; strip and set identity headers; mTLS to services.
  • Rate limits per client/key/tenant with 429 + Retry-After.
  • Request IDs and trace propagation (W3C traceparent); access logs with latency and status.
  • Route ownership and review process; contract tests for public APIs.
  • Canary/blue-green routing with automatic rollback on error-rate increase.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Clients hit a single API gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway or Envoy) behind a load balancer. It terminates TLS, validates JWTs, applies per-user and per-API-key rate limits, adds request and trace IDs, and routes by path to internal services discovered through the registry. It has no business logic. It's stateless and multi-zone; rate-limit counters live in Redis. For different clients I'd add thin BFFs behind it. Each route has timeouts and a circuit breaker so one slow service can't exhaust gateway resources."

War story: the header that granted admin

A marketplace's gateway validated JWTs and set X-User-Role for downstream services, but didn't remove that header if the client sent it. An internal admin endpoint was accidentally exposed through a new route. A security researcher sent X-User-Role: ADMIN with a normal user token, and the service trusted it. Fix: the gateway now strips all X-User-* headers from incoming requests before setting its own; services verify a signed internal token (or mTLS identity) instead of plain headers; new routes require a security review. Lesson: identity propagated in headers is only as safe as the guarantee that clients can't set them.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: API Gateway BFF Service Mesh Facade Traffic North-south (clients → services) North-south, per client type East-west (service ↔ service) In-process Logic Edge concerns only Client-specific aggregation and shaping Network concerns (mTLS, retries) Simplified API over classes Count One (or a few) One per client type One sidecar per pod Any

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Single entry point: routing + edge concerns (auth, rate limits, TLS, IDs, canaries).
  • No business logic in the gateway.
  • Strip client-supplied identity headers; mTLS internally.
  • HA, stateless, timeouts and circuit breakers per route.
  • Gateway = north-south; mesh = east-west; BFF = per client type.
- id: orders
  uri: lb://order-service
  predicates: [ "Path=/orders/**" ]
  filters: [ "StripPrefix=1" ]

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Make MobileGateway strip any client-supplied X-Customer-Id header and add a test for it.
  • Add a per-route timeout to the gateway using CompletableFuture.orTimeout.
  • Move a tenant from us-2 to eu-1 with a routing change, and design how data moves with it.

docs.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A BFF is a small backend dedicated to one client experience (mobile, TV, web, partners). It calls the general-purpose services, then aggregates, trims and reshapes the data into exactly what that client renders. Each client team owns its BFF, so they can change screens without waiting for the service teams.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the same catalog, progress and recommendation services feed a phone app on mobile data, a 4K TV app and a web site. One generic API means either the phone downloads huge payloads it throws away, or each client makes 5 round trips and stitches data together on a slow network. Adding fields "for the TV" bloats the API for everyone.

Definition (Sam Newman, who named the pattern):

Rather than have a general-purpose API backend, have one backend per user experience.

What a BFF does:

  • Aggregates: one client call → several service calls (often in parallel).
  • Shapes: picks fields, image sizes, formats and copy for that UI.
  • Adapts: handles client-specific auth flows, versions and caching.
  • Does not own business rules or data; those stay in the services.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A tailor vs. ready-made clothes

The fabric mill (services) produces the same cloth for everyone. A tailor (BFF) cuts and stitches it for one customer's measurements. A child and an adult get garments from the same fabric, each fitted exactly, and the mill doesn't care about anybody's size.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     M[Mobile app] --> MB[Mobile BFF<br/>owned by mobile team]     T[TV app] --> TB[TV BFF<br/>owned by TV team]     P[Partners] --> PB[Partner BFF<br/>owned by API team]     MB --> C[Catalog]     MB --> G[Progress]     TB --> C     TB --> G     TB --> R[Recommendations]     MB --> R     PB --> A[Accounts] Participant Responsibility Client Renders UI; ideally one call per screen BFF Aggregation, shaping, client-specific concerns; no business rules Downstream services Business capabilities and data, client-agnostic API gateway (optional, in front) Generic edge concerns: TLS, auth, rate limiting

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
One generic API for all clients:
  Phone on 3G:  GET /titles?ids=...   (full synopsis + 1920 px artwork it never shows)
                GET /progress/P-7
                GET /recommendations/P-7      → 3 round trips, ~2x the bytes
  TV team needs "hero banner": adds fields to the shared API → phone pays for them too.
  Every change to the shared API needs every client team to agree.

docs.title: Example 1: Mobile vs. TV Home Screens (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: Same three services; two very different screens. The mobile BFF returns two compact rows with 320 px thumbnails and a progress percentage. The TV BFF returns an autoplay hero banner, genres, and 1920 px artwork for every tile. Each team changes its BFF on its own release schedule.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant App as Mobile app participant BFF as Mobile BFF participant C as Catalog participant P as Progress participant R as Recommendations App->>BFF: GET /mobile/home BFF->>P: progress(P-7) BFF->>R: forProfile(P-7) BFF->>C: byId(...) for each title BFF-->>App: compact JSON (211 chars)

Full Code:

MobileBff.javaTvBff.javaStreamingBackends.javaJson.java (support)StreamingBffDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.CatalogService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.ProgressService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.RecommendationService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.Title;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

import java.util.Map;

/** Owned by the mobile team: small images, few fields, one round trip, metered-data friendly. */
public final class MobileBff {

    private final CatalogService catalog;
    private final ProgressService progress;
    private final RecommendationService recommendations;

    public MobileBff(CatalogService catalog, ProgressService progress, RecommendationService recommendations) {
        this.catalog = catalog;
        this.progress = progress;
        this.recommendations = recommendations;
    }

    public Map<String, Object> homeScreen(String profileId) {
        var continueWatching = progress.progress(profileId).entrySet().stream()
                .map(e -> {
                    Title t = catalog.byId(e.getKey());
                    return card(t, Json.obj("percent", e.getValue() * 100 / t.minutes())); // (1)!
                }).toList();
        var forYou = recommendations.forProfile(profileId).stream()
                .limit(2) // (2)!
                .map(id -> card(catalog.byId(id), Json.obj()))
                .toList();
        return Json.obj("continue", continueWatching, "forYou", forYou);
    }

    private static Map<String, Object> card(Title t, Map<String, Object> extra) {
        Map<String, Object> card = Json.obj("id", t.id(), "name", t.name(), "img", t.artwork().get("320")); // (3)!
        card.putAll(extra);
        return card;
    }
}
  1. The BFF computes display values (percent watched) so the client stays dumb.
  2. Mobile shows two cards; the TV shows the whole row. The decision lives with the team that owns the screen.
  3. Only the small image: on metered mobile data, bytes matter.
package com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.CatalogService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.ProgressService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.RecommendationService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.Title;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

import java.util.Map;

/** Owned by the TV team: big artwork, an autoplay hero banner, more rows for a 10-foot screen. */
public final class TvBff {

    private final CatalogService catalog;
    private final ProgressService progress;
    private final RecommendationService recommendations;

    public TvBff(CatalogService catalog, ProgressService progress, RecommendationService recommendations) {
        this.catalog = catalog;
        this.progress = progress;
        this.recommendations = recommendations;
    }

    public Map<String, Object> homeScreen(String profileId) {
        var recs = recommendations.forProfile(profileId);
        Title hero = catalog.byId(recs.get(0));
        return Json.obj(
                "hero", Json.obj("name", hero.name(), "art", hero.artwork().get("1920"), // (1)!
                        "autoplay", hero.trailerUrl()),
                "continue", progress.progress(profileId).keySet().stream().map(id -> tile(catalog.byId(id))).toList(),
                "forYou", recs.stream().map(id -> tile(catalog.byId(id))).toList()); // (2)!
    }

    private static Map<String, Object> tile(Title t) {
        return Json.obj("id", t.id(), "name", t.name(), "genre", t.genre(), "art", t.artwork().get("1920"));
    }
}
  1. A TV-only concept (autoplay hero banner) that the mobile API never has to carry.
  2. Large artwork and genres for a 10-foot UI.

package com.handbook.microservices.support;

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** Renders maps, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and null as compact JSON (insertion order kept). */
public final class Json {

    private Json() {
    }

    /** An ordered map from alternating keys and values: {@code obj("id", 1, "name", "x")}. */
    public static Map<String, Object> obj(Object... keyValues) {
        Map<String, Object> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < keyValues.length; i += 2) {
            map.put((String) keyValues[i], keyValues[i + 1]);
        }
        return map;
    }

    public static String of(Object value) {
        if (value == null) {
            return "null";
        }
        if (value instanceof String s) {
            return "\"" + s.replace("\"", "\\\"") + "\"";
        }
        if (value instanceof Number || value instanceof Boolean) {
            return value.toString();
        }
        if (value instanceof Map<?, ?> m) {
            return m.entrySet().stream()
                    .map(e -> of(String.valueOf(e.getKey())) + ":" + of(e.getValue()))
                    .collect(Collectors.joining(",", "{", "}"));
        }
        if (value instanceof Collection<?> c) {
            return c.stream().map(Json::of).collect(Collectors.joining(",", "[", "]"));
        }
        return of(value.toString());
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.CatalogService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.ProgressService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.streaming.StreamingBackends.RecommendationService;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

public class StreamingBffDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var catalog = new CatalogService();
        var progress = new ProgressService();
        var recs = new RecommendationService();

        System.out.println("=== Streaming: one backend, two BFFs ===");
        String mobile = Json.of(new MobileBff(catalog, progress, recs).homeScreen("P-7"));
        String tv = Json.of(new TvBff(catalog, progress, recs).homeScreen("P-7"));

        System.out.println("GET /mobile/home ->");
        System.out.println("  " + mobile);
        System.out.println("GET /tv/home ->");
        System.out.println("  " + tv);
        System.out.println("Payload size: mobile " + mobile.length() + " chars, tv " + tv.length() + " chars");
        System.out.println("Same 3 backend services, each screen gets exactly what it renders.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: one backend, two BFFs ===
GET /mobile/home ->
  {"continue":[{"id":"T2","name":"City of Rain","img":"img/T2-320.jpg","percent":75}],"forYou":[{"id":"T1","name":"Monsoon Express","img":"img/T1-320.jpg"},{"id":"T3","name":"Spice Route","img":"img/T3-320.jpg"}]}
GET /tv/home ->
  {"hero":{"name":"Monsoon Express","art":"img/T1-1920.jpg","autoplay":"video/T1-trailer.m3u8"},"continue":[{"id":"T2","name":"City of Rain","genre":"Drama","art":"img/T2-1920.jpg"}],"forYou":[{"id":"T1","name":"Monsoon Express","genre":"Thriller","art":"img/T1-1920.jpg"},{"id":"T3","name":"Spice Route","genre":"Documentary","art":"img/T3-1920.jpg"},{"id":"T4","name":"Byte Club","genre":"Comedy","art":"img/T4-1920.jpg"}]}
Payload size: mobile 211 chars, tv 423 chars
Same 3 backend services, each screen gets exactly what it renders.

Why a BFF here:

  • The phone gets half the payload in one round trip.
  • TV-only features don't leak into the mobile contract.
  • Downstream services stay generic and reusable.

docs.title: Example 2: Order Details for Web vs. Mobile (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: The desktop order page shows items, totals, a full tracking timeline and "review your purchase" prompts, so the web BFF calls three services. The mobile order card shows one summary line and the delivery time, so the mobile BFF calls two services and never touches the review service. Formatting money (₹1,447.00) is done once, server-side.

Design:

flowchart LR W[Web] --> WB[Web BFF] --> O[Orders] WB --> S[Shipping] WB --> RV[Reviews] M[Mobile] --> MB[Mobile BFF] --> O MB --> S

Full Code:

WebBff.javaMobileOrderBff.javaOrderBackends.javaOrderBffDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.Line;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.OrderService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.ReviewService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.ShippingService;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

import java.util.Map;

/** Desktop order page: everything on one wide screen, including the tracking timeline and review prompts. */
public final class WebBff {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final ShippingService shipping;
    private final ReviewService reviews;

    public WebBff(OrderService orders, ShippingService shipping, ReviewService reviews) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.shipping = shipping;
        this.reviews = reviews;
    }

    public Map<String, Object> orderPage(String orderId) {
        var order = orders.get(orderId);
        var shipment = shipping.forOrder(orderId);
        var prompts = reviews.prompts(order.customerId(), order.lines().stream().map(Line::sku).toList()); // (1)!
        return Json.obj(
                "order", order.id(),
                "items", order.lines().stream()
                        .map(l -> Json.obj("name", l.name(), "qty", l.qty(), "price", rupees(l.pricePaise())))
                        .toList(),
                "total", rupees(order.lines().stream().mapToLong(l -> l.qty() * l.pricePaise()).sum()),
                "tracking", Json.obj("carrier", shipment.carrier(), "status", shipment.status(),
                        "timeline", shipment.scans()),
                "reviewSkus", prompts.stream().filter(p -> p.eligible()).map(p -> p.sku()).toList());
    }

    static String rupees(long paise) { // (2)!
        return String.format("₹%,d.%02d", paise / 100, paise % 100);
    }
}
  1. Only the web BFF depends on the review service. If it's down, the mobile app is unaffected.
  2. Presentation formatting (currency, locale) belongs in the BFF, not in every client.
package com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.OrderService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.ShippingService;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

import java.util.Map;

/** Mobile order card: a one-line summary and live status. No review service call at all. */
public final class MobileOrderBff {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final ShippingService shipping;

    public MobileOrderBff(OrderService orders, ShippingService shipping) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.shipping = shipping;
    }

    public Map<String, Object> orderCard(String orderId) {
        var order = orders.get(orderId);
        var shipment = shipping.forOrder(orderId);
        int items = order.lines().stream().mapToInt(l -> l.qty()).sum();
        return Json.obj(
                "order", order.id(),
                "summary", items + " items · " + WebBff.rupees(order.lines().stream()
                        .mapToLong(l -> l.qty() * l.pricePaise()).sum()), // (1)!
                "status", "Arriving by " + shipment.eta()); // (2)!
    }
}
  1. A pre-rendered summary string: the app just displays it.
  2. UX copy can change without an app release.

package com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.OrderService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.ReviewService;
import com.handbook.microservices.bff.ecommerce.OrderBackends.ShippingService;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

public class OrderBffDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var orders = new OrderService();
        var shipping = new ShippingService();

        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: order details for web vs. mobile ===");
        String web = Json.of(new WebBff(orders, shipping, new ReviewService()).orderPage("ORD-9"));
        String mobile = Json.of(new MobileOrderBff(orders, shipping).orderCard("ORD-9"));
        System.out.println("Web BFF    (3 backend calls) -> " + web);
        System.out.println("Mobile BFF (2 backend calls) -> " + mobile);
        System.out.printf("Mobile payload is %d%% of the web payload%n", mobile.length() * 100 / web.length());
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: order details for web vs. mobile ===
Web BFF    (3 backend calls) -> {"order":"ORD-9","items":[{"name":"Alphonso mangoes 1 kg","qty":2,"price":"₹399.00"},{"name":"Basmati rice 5 kg","qty":1,"price":"₹649.00"}],"total":"₹1,447.00","tracking":{"carrier":"QuickDrop","status":"OUT_FOR_DELIVERY","timeline":["09:40 packed","11:05 left hub","16:10 out for delivery"]},"reviewSkus":["MANGO-1KG"]}
Mobile BFF (2 backend calls) -> {"order":"ORD-9","summary":"3 items · ₹1,447.00","status":"Arriving by 18:30"}
Mobile payload is 24% of the web payload

Why a BFF here:

  • Each client's dependency set is minimal (fewer things that can break a screen).
  • The mobile payload is about a quarter of the web one.
  • Formatting and copy are server-controlled, avoiding app-store release cycles.

docs.title: Example 3: Partner BFF over Internal Accounts (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The internal accounts service returns everything the bank knows: branch code, internal risk score, KYC status. A fintech partner may see only masked account numbers and balances, only for customers who consented, and two contract versions (v1, v2) must run side by side while partners migrate. The partner BFF owns that external contract, so the internal service can evolve freely.

Design:

flowchart LR P[Partner app] -->|/partner/v1 or /v2| PB[Partner BFF] PB --> CS{Consent?} CS -->|no| E[NO_CONSENT] CS -->|yes| A[Internal accounts service] A --> PB PB -->|mask, filter, version| P

Full Code:

PartnerAccountBff.javaPartnerBffDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.bff.partner;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * A BFF for external fintech partners. The internal account record has fields partners must never
 * see; the BFF owns the partner contract, masks data, and serves two contract versions side by side.
 */
public final class PartnerAccountBff {

    /** What the internal accounts service returns (full, internal view). */
    public record InternalAccount(String accountNumber, String holder, long balancePaise, String currency,
                                  String branchCode, int internalRiskScore, String kycStatus) {
    }

    public interface AccountService {
        InternalAccount find(String accountNumber);
    }

    private final AccountService accounts;
    private final Set<String> consentedAccounts;

    public PartnerAccountBff(AccountService accounts, Set<String> consentedAccounts) {
        this.accounts = accounts;
        this.consentedAccounts = consentedAccounts;
    }

    public Map<String, Object> account(String version, String accountNumber) {
        if (!consentedAccounts.contains(accountNumber)) { // (1)!
            return Json.obj("error", "NO_CONSENT");
        }
        InternalAccount a = accounts.find(accountNumber);
        String masked = "XXXX" + a.accountNumber().substring(a.accountNumber().length() - 4); // (2)!
        return switch (version) { // (3)!
            case "v1" -> Json.obj("account", masked, "balance", a.balancePaise() / 100.0);
            case "v2" -> Json.obj("account", masked,
                    "balance", Json.obj("amountMinor", a.balancePaise(), "currency", a.currency()),
                    "holderInitials", initials(a.holder()));
            default -> Json.obj("error", "UNSUPPORTED_VERSION");
        };
    }

    private static String initials(String name) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (String part : name.split(" ")) {
            sb.append(part.charAt(0)).append('.');
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
  1. Consent check at the boundary. External access needs extra rules that internal clients don't.
  2. Masking: partners never receive the full account number.
  3. Versioned contracts live in the BFF; the internal model has one shape.
package com.handbook.microservices.bff.partner;

import com.handbook.microservices.bff.partner.PartnerAccountBff.InternalAccount;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Json;

import java.util.Set;

public class PartnerBffDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PartnerAccountBff.AccountService internal = number -> new InternalAccount(
                number, "Asha Rao", 1_254_075, "INR", "BLR-017", 12, "VERIFIED");

        var bff = new PartnerAccountBff(internal, Set.of("50100012345678"));

        System.out.println("=== Banking: partner BFF over the internal accounts service ===");
        System.out.println("Internal record   : " + internal.find("50100012345678"));
        System.out.println("GET /partner/v1/accounts/..5678 -> " + Json.of(bff.account("v1", "50100012345678")));
        System.out.println("GET /partner/v2/accounts/..5678 -> " + Json.of(bff.account("v2", "50100012345678")));
        System.out.println("GET /partner/v2/accounts/..9999 -> " + Json.of(bff.account("v2", "50100099999999")));
        System.out.println("Branch code, risk score and KYC status never leave the bank.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: partner BFF over the internal accounts service ===
Internal record   : InternalAccount[accountNumber=50100012345678, holder=Asha Rao, balancePaise=1254075, currency=INR, branchCode=BLR-017, internalRiskScore=12, kycStatus=VERIFIED]
GET /partner/v1/accounts/..5678 -> {"account":"XXXX5678","balance":12540.75}
GET /partner/v2/accounts/..5678 -> {"account":"XXXX5678","balance":{"amountMinor":1254075,"currency":"INR"},"holderInitials":"A.R."}
GET /partner/v2/accounts/..9999 -> {"error":"NO_CONSENT"}
Branch code, risk score and KYC status never leave the bank.

Why a BFF here:

  • Data minimization by design: internal fields can't leak by accident.
  • External versioning is isolated from internal refactoring.
  • Partner-specific rules (consent, masking) live in one owned place.
