docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• GraphQL as a BFF: the client asks for exactly the fields it needs; resolvers fan out to services (Spring for GraphQL, Netflix DGS). One GraphQL server per experience, or a federated graph.
  • Parallel fan-out: use CompletableFuture or structured concurrency with virtual threads, each call with its own timeout (see the coding challenge).
  • BFF + gateway: gateway for generic edge concerns, BFFs behind it for shaping.
  • Server-driven UI: the BFF returns layout components ("hero", "row") rather than raw data, so screens change without app releases.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where BFF Netflix Device-specific API adapters over shared services (historically Groovy scripts, later Node and GraphQL federation) SoundCloud Popularized the term with per-platform backends Spring for GraphQL / Netflix DGS GraphQL BFFs in Java Next.js / Remix route handlers Web BFFs colocated with the frontend

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Optimized payloads and fewer round trips per client More services to run and monitor Client teams ship independently Duplication across BFFs (similar aggregation) Generic services stay clean Risk of business logic creeping in Safe place for client auth flows, versioning, masking Fan-out latency is bounded by the slowest dependency

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Business rules in the BFF

If the mobile BFF calculates discounts, the web BFF will eventually calculate them differently. Rules belong in services; BFFs shape.

One BFF per screen, or per developer

A BFF per experience (mobile, TV, web, partners). Dozens of micro-BFFs multiply operational cost for no gain.

Sequential fan-out

Calling five services one after another adds up their latencies. Call independent services in parallel with per-call timeouts and fallbacks.

All-or-nothing pages

If reviews fail, show the product without reviews. Decide which parts are critical and which are optional.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Ownership is the point. A BFF works best when it's owned by the same team as its client (Conway's law used deliberately). If a central API team owns all BFFs, you've rebuilt the bottleneck you were escaping.

Handling duplication. Some duplication between BFFs is the price of independence. Extract shared libraries (clients, auth helpers) or push genuinely shared aggregation into a downstream service, but don't merge BFFs back into one.

Latency and resilience. The BFF's p99 is bounded below by the slowest required dependency. Classify each call as critical or optional, set timeouts below the client's own timeout, use circuit breakers on optional calls, and cache stable data (catalog metadata).

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• One BFF per client experience, owned by that client's team.
  • Parallel fan-out with per-call timeouts; critical vs. optional sections.
  • Circuit breakers and fallbacks for optional data; partial responses flagged (degraded).
  • No business rules; contract tests against downstream services.
  • Response caching where safe (per user/locale); compression.
  • Trace propagation so a slow screen can be traced to the slow service.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Behind the gateway I'd put one BFF per experience: mobile, TV/web, and a partner API. Each is owned by that client's team. A BFF fans out in parallel to the domain services, applies timeouts and fallbacks, and returns exactly the screen's data in one round trip, which matters on mobile networks. Optional sections like recommendations degrade gracefully. BFFs hold no business rules, only aggregation and presentation, so the domain services stay reusable and teams ship independently."

War story: the shared API that served nobody well

A retailer ran one "universal" product API. Over three years every client added fields: the iOS app needed badges, the web needed SEO blocks, kiosks needed printer layouts. The response grew to 140 KB per product; Android on 3G timed out in rural areas. Changing a field needed sign-off from six teams. Fix: mobile and web BFFs, each owned by its client team, over slimmed-down domain services. Mobile responses dropped to 9 KB; release cadence went from monthly to weekly. Lesson: a single API for many very different clients ends up optimized for none of them.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
BFF API Gateway Facade Adapter Purpose Shape data for one client experience Generic edge concerns for all clients Simplify a subsystem Convert one interface to another Aggregates calls Yes Rarely Yes (in-process) No Owned by Client team Platform team Any Any

See API Gateway and the in-process cousin Facade.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One backend per client experience, owned by the client team.
  • Aggregate (in parallel), trim, format. No business rules.
  • Critical vs. optional data; partial responses with fallbacks.
  • Gateway = generic edge; BFF = client-specific shaping. Use both.
  • GraphQL is a popular way to build a BFF.

  • Add a v3 partner contract that includes the IFSC code, without changing InternalAccount.

docs.title: Backpressure & Load Shedding
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Backpressure is how a slow consumer tells a fast producer to slow down, by pulling only what it can handle or by refusing work when its bounded buffer is full. Load shedding is the server-side version: reject excess requests fast so the accepted ones stay fast. Use it everywhere work crosses a speed boundary: reactive streams, queues between services, thread pools, and the front door of an overloaded API. The rule: every buffer is bounded, and you decide what happens when it's full.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: during a sale, orders arrive at 1,000/s but the warehouse picking API handles 600/s. If the service queues everything in memory, the queue grows by 400 items every second: after a minute, new requests wait 40 seconds (most clients have already timed out and retried, adding even more load), and then the JVM runs out of memory. Accepting work you can't finish is worse than refusing it.

Definitions:

Backpressure (Reactive Streams): a subscriber signals demand (request(n)) and a publisher must never send more than was requested.

Load shedding (Google SRE book): when a server is overloaded, it rejects some requests quickly and cheaply, so it can serve the rest within their deadlines.

Mechanism Who slows down Example Pull / demand signalling The producer emits only on request Reactive Streams request(n), Kafka poll() Bounded buffer + block The producer thread waits ArrayBlockingQueue.put, CallerRunsPolicy Bounded buffer + drop Old or new items are discarded Live GPS, metrics, video frames Bounded buffer + reject The caller is told "not now" HTTP 429/503 with Retry-After Concurrency limits Excess requests shed at the door Semaphores, Envoy/Istio limits, adaptive limits

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant that stops seating

When the kitchen is full, a good restaurant stops seating new guests and gives them a waiting time at the door, instead of seating 200 people who'll all wait 90 minutes and leave angry. The kitchen asks the waiters for the next orders only when a cook is free (pull). The host refusing walk-ins is load shedding.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR P[Fast producer] -->|"offer()"| B[["Bounded buffer (capacity N)"]] B -->|"take() at its own pace"| C[Slow consumer] B -. full .-> X{Policy} X --> R["Reject: 429 + Retry-After"] X --> D["Drop oldest / newest"] X --> W["Block the producer"] C -->|"request(n)"| P Element Responsibility Demand signal Consumer tells producer how much it can take (request(n), credits, window size) Bounded buffer Absorbs short bursts; its size caps memory and waiting time Overflow policy Block, drop or reject: a business decision per data type Concurrency limiter Caps in-flight work at the service entrance Retry-After / client backoff Turns rejection into a slower, spread-out retry instead of a storm

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);   // unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue inside
@PostMapping("/pick") void pick(Req r) { pool.submit(() -> pickingApi.call(r)); }   // always "accepted"

Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(1)).subscribe(this::slowWrite);   // no demand control → overflow
  • Unbounded queues turn overload into latency, then memory exhaustion.
  • Callers time out and retry, multiplying the load (a retry storm).
  • Everyone gets slow service instead of most people getting good service.

docs.title: Example 1: Pull-Based GPS Processing (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: Every driver's phone sends a GPS ping every 2 seconds. A map-matching stage snaps pings to roads in batches of 3 and is CPU-heavy. Using the JDK's java.util.concurrent.Flow (the Reactive Streams interfaces), the matcher requests 3 pings, processes them, then requests 3 more. The publisher never pushes more than requested.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant M as Map-matcher (subscriber) participant G as GPS publisher M->>G: request(3) G->>M: p1, p2, p3 M->>M: map-match batch M->>G: request(3) G->>M: p4, p5, p6 M->>G: request(3) G->>M: p7, p8, onComplete

Full Code:

GpsPublisher.javaBatchingSubscriber.javaFlowDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.flow;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Flow;

/** A Reactive-Streams publisher that emits ONLY what the subscriber has requested (pull-based back-pressure). */
public final class GpsPublisher implements Flow.Publisher<String> {

    private final List<String> pings;

    public GpsPublisher(List<String> pings) {
        this.pings = pings;
    }

    @Override
    public void subscribe(Flow.Subscriber<? super String> subscriber) {
        subscriber.onSubscribe(new Flow.Subscription() {
            private int next;
            private boolean done;

            @Override
            public void request(long n) { // (1)!
                for (long i = 0; i < n && next < pings.size(); i++) {
                    subscriber.onNext(pings.get(next++));
                }
                if (next == pings.size() && !done) {
                    done = true;
                    subscriber.onComplete();
                }
            }

            @Override
            public void cancel() {
                next = pings.size();
            }
        });
    }
}
  1. The publisher emits at most n items per request(n). This is Reactive Streams rule 1.1, the heart of backpressure. (Production publishers also avoid unbounded recursion when request is called from onNext; Reactor and RxJava handle that for you.)
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.flow;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Flow;

/** Asks for a batch, processes it, then asks for the next: it never receives more than it can handle. */
public final class BatchingSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<String> {

    private final int batchSize;
    private final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
    private final List<String> current = new ArrayList<>();
    private Flow.Subscription subscription;

    public BatchingSubscriber(int batchSize) {
        this.batchSize = batchSize;
    }

    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) {
        subscription = s;
        log.add("request(" + batchSize + ")");
        s.request(batchSize); // (1)!
    }

    @Override
    public void onNext(String ping) {
        current.add(ping);
        if (current.size() == batchSize) {
            log.add("map-match " + current + " -> request(" + batchSize + ")");
            current.clear();
            subscription.request(batchSize); // (2)!
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable t) {
        log.add("error " + t.getMessage());
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        log.add("complete" + (current.isEmpty() ? "" : ", last partial batch " + current));
    }

    public List<String> log() {
        return log;
    }
}
  1. Initial demand: "I can take 3".
  2. Only after finishing a batch does the subscriber ask for more. Demand, not the producer's speed, sets the pace.
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.flow;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class FlowDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Map-Matching GPS Pings at the Consumer's Pace ===");
        List<String> pings = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 8; i++) {
            pings.add("p" + i);
        }
        BatchingSubscriber matcher = new BatchingSubscriber(3);
        new GpsPublisher(pings).subscribe(matcher);
        matcher.log().forEach(l -> System.out.println("  " + l));
        System.out.println("The publisher never pushed more than the 3 pings requested at a time.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Map-Matching GPS Pings at the Consumer's Pace ===
  request(3)
  map-match [p1, p2, p3] -> request(3)
  map-match [p4, p5, p6] -> request(3)
  complete, last partial batch [p7, p8]
The publisher never pushed more than the 3 pings requested at a time.

Why pull-based backpressure here:

  • The consumer's capacity is the true limit, so it should set the rate.
  • Memory stays bounded no matter how fast pings arrive upstream.
  • WebFlux, Reactor, R2DBC and Kafka consumers all work this way.

docs.title: Example 2: Overflow Policies for a Bounded Buffer (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: An order service hands pick requests to the warehouse's picking API through an in-memory buffer of 4. During a spike, 7 requests arrive before any are consumed. What should happen to the extra 3? The answer depends on the data: orders must not be silently dropped (reject so the client retries); live rider locations can drop stale points; inside one process, the producer thread can simply wait.

Design:

flowchart LR R["pick-1 ... pick-7"] --> B[["buffer (4)"]] B -->|"REJECT_NEW"| X1["pick-5..7 → 429, client retries"] B -->|"DROP_OLDEST"| X2["pick-1..3 dropped, newest kept"] B -->|"CALLER_WAITS"| X3["producer blocks"]

Full Code:

IntakeBuffer.javaOverflowDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.overflow;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** A bounded buffer must decide what happens when it's full: that decision IS the back-pressure policy. */
public final class IntakeBuffer {

    public enum Policy { REJECT_NEW, DROP_OLDEST, CALLER_WAITS }

    private final Deque<String> buffer = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;
    private final Policy policy;

    public IntakeBuffer(int capacity, Policy policy) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.policy = policy;
    }

    /** @return what the producer is told. */
    public String offer(String item) {
        if (buffer.size() < capacity) {
            buffer.add(item);
            return "queued";
        }
        return switch (policy) { // (1)!
            case REJECT_NEW -> "429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After: 2";
            case DROP_OLDEST -> {
                String dropped = buffer.poll();
                buffer.add(item);
                yield "queued (dropped " + dropped + ")";
            }
            case CALLER_WAITS -> "producer blocked until space frees up";
        };
    }

    public Deque<String> contents() {
        return new ArrayDeque<>(buffer);
    }
}
  1. The overflow policy is explicit. Java gives you each one: offer() (reject), put() (block), ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardOldestPolicy (drop oldest), CallerRunsPolicy (the caller does the work, slowing itself down).
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.overflow;

import com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.overflow.IntakeBuffer.Policy;

public class OverflowDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Picking API Is Slow; 7 Requests Arrive for a Buffer of 4 ===");
        for (Policy policy : Policy.values()) {
            IntakeBuffer buffer = new IntakeBuffer(4, policy);
            StringBuilder outcomes = new StringBuilder();
            for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
                String result = buffer.offer("pick-" + i);
                if (i > 4) {
                    outcomes.append("\n    pick-").append(i).append(": ").append(result);
                }
            }
            System.out.println(policy + " -> buffer " + buffer.contents() + outcomes);
        }
        System.out.println("REJECT_NEW for orders (client retries), DROP_OLDEST for live location, CALLER_WAITS inside one process.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Picking API Is Slow; 7 Requests Arrive for a Buffer of 4 ===
REJECT_NEW -> buffer [pick-1, pick-2, pick-3, pick-4]
    pick-5: 429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After: 2
    pick-6: 429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After: 2
    pick-7: 429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After: 2
DROP_OLDEST -> buffer [pick-4, pick-5, pick-6, pick-7]
    pick-5: queued (dropped pick-1)
    pick-6: queued (dropped pick-2)
    pick-7: queued (dropped pick-3)
CALLER_WAITS -> buffer [pick-1, pick-2, pick-3, pick-4]
    pick-5: producer blocked until space frees up
    pick-6: producer blocked until space frees up
    pick-7: producer blocked until space frees up
REJECT_NEW for orders (client retries), DROP_OLDEST for live location, CALLER_WAITS inside one process.

Why explicit policies here:

  • "What happens when full?" is a business decision; make it visible in code.
  • Rejection pushes pressure back to the client, who can back off.
  • Dropping is correct only for data that is superseded by newer data.

docs.title: Example 3: Load Shedding at the Front Door (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank's statement API queries the core-banking database, which can only serve 3 statement queries at a time before latency explodes for payments too. At month-end, customers open statements in bursts. The API holds at most 3 requests in flight and answers the rest immediately with 503 and Retry-After: 1, rather than queueing them until they time out.

Design:

flowchart LR U["5 concurrent requests"] --> L{"Semaphore(3).tryAcquire()"} L -- "3 permits" --> DB[(Core banking)] L -- "no permit" --> S["503 + Retry-After: 1 (in microseconds)"]

Full Code:

ConcurrencyLimiter.javaSheddingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.shedding;

import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Load shedding at the door: at most N requests in flight; the rest are refused fast, not queued forever. */
public final class ConcurrencyLimiter {

    private final Semaphore permits;

    public ConcurrencyLimiter(int maxInFlight) {
        this.permits = new Semaphore(maxInFlight);
    }

    public String handle(Supplier<String> work) {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { // (1)!
            return "503 Service Unavailable (shed, Retry-After: 1)";
        }
        try {
            return work.get();
        } finally {
            permits.release();
        }
    }
}
  1. tryAcquire() never waits: if all permits are taken, the request is shed at once, costing almost nothing. A blocking acquire() would just move the queue somewhere invisible.
package com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.shedding;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class SheddingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Statement API Protects the Core-Banking DB (max 3 in flight) ===");
        ConcurrencyLimiter limiter = new ConcurrencyLimiter(3);
        CountDownLatch slowCoreBanking = new CountDownLatch(1);
        AtomicInteger started = new AtomicInteger();

        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<String>> first = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
                int n = i;
                first.add(pool.submit(() -> limiter.handle(() -> {
                    started.incrementAndGet();
                    try {
                        slowCoreBanking.await();
                    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    }
                    return "200 statement-" + n;
                })));
            }
            while (started.get() < 3) {
                Thread.onSpinWait(); // wait until 3 requests occupy all permits
            }
            System.out.println("request 4 -> " + limiter.handle(() -> "200 statement-4"));
            System.out.println("request 5 -> " + limiter.handle(() -> "200 statement-5"));
            slowCoreBanking.countDown();
            for (Future<String> f : first) {
                System.out.println("in-flight -> " + f.get());
            }
            System.out.println("request 6 -> " + limiter.handle(() -> "200 statement-6") + " (capacity is back)");
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Statement API Protects the Core-Banking DB (max 3 in flight) ===
request 4 -> 503 Service Unavailable (shed, Retry-After: 1)
request 5 -> 503 Service Unavailable (shed, Retry-After: 1)
in-flight -> 200 statement-1
in-flight -> 200 statement-2
in-flight -> 200 statement-3
request 6 -> 200 statement-6 (capacity is back)

Why load shedding here:

  • Protects a shared, fragile dependency (and every other feature that uses it).
  • Accepted requests stay fast; rejected ones fail fast and retry later.
  • Adaptive limiters (Netflix concurrency-limits, Envoy adaptive concurrency) tune the limit automatically from latency.
Unit Tests: BackpressureTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.flow.BatchingSubscriber;
import com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.flow.GpsPublisher;
import com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.overflow.IntakeBuffer;
import com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.overflow.IntakeBuffer.Policy;
import com.handbook.microservices.backpressure.shedding.ConcurrencyLimiter;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class BackpressureTest {

    @Test
    void subscriberControlsTheRate() {
        BatchingSubscriber s = new BatchingSubscriber(2);
        new GpsPublisher(List.of("a", "b", "c")).subscribe(s);
        assertThat(s.log()).containsExactly("request(2)", "map-match [a, b] -> request(2)", "complete, last partial batch [c]");
    }

    @Test
    void fullBufferAppliesItsPolicy() {
        IntakeBuffer reject = new IntakeBuffer(1, Policy.REJECT_NEW);
        reject.offer("a");
        assertThat(reject.offer("b")).startsWith("429");
        IntakeBuffer drop = new IntakeBuffer(1, Policy.DROP_OLDEST);
        drop.offer("a");
        drop.offer("b");
        assertThat(drop.contents()).containsExactly("b");
    }

    @Test
    void limiterAdmitsWhenPermitsAreFree() {
        assertThat(new ConcurrencyLimiter(1).handle(() -> "ok")).isEqualTo("ok");
    }
}

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Memory and latency stay bounded under overload Some requests are rejected or dropped Overload degrades gracefully instead of collapsing Clients must handle 429/503 and retry with backoff Prevents retry storms and cascading failures Choosing limits and buffer sizes needs measurement Makes capacity limits explicit End-to-end backpressure requires every stage to cooperate

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Unbounded queues

Executors.newFixedThreadPool, LinkedBlockingQueue() with no capacity, onBackpressureBuffer() with no size: all accept work forever. Under sustained overload they become latency bombs and then OOMs (coding challenge).

Shedding after doing the work

Rejecting a request after parsing, authenticating and querying the DB saves nothing. Shed as early (and cheaply) as possible.

Retries without backoff or jitter

Rejected clients retrying immediately just recreate the spike. Honour Retry-After, use exponential backoff with jitter, and cap retries.

Blocking a reactive pipeline

A .block() or blocking JDBC call inside a WebFlux handler stalls the event loop, which disables backpressure for everyone on that thread.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Size buffers in time, not items. A buffer is "how much waiting is acceptable": 2 seconds of work at 600/s = 1,200 items. If clients time out after 3 seconds, a queue holding 40 seconds of work is pure waste: everything in it will be served too late.

Prioritize what you keep. Under overload, shed by priority: health checks and payments first, recommendations last. Tag requests with criticality (Google's "criticality" propagation) and shed the cheapest-to-lose classes first.

Propagate deadlines. Pass the remaining time budget downstream (grpc-timeout, a deadline header). A service should drop work whose caller has already given up. That's backpressure by deadline.

War story: the queue that ate the sale

A grocery order service submitted picking calls to Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50). When the picking API slowed during a mango sale, the hidden unbounded queue grew to 1.8 million tasks over 20 minutes. Customers' apps timed out and retried, tripling arrivals. The pods ran out of heap and restarted, losing every queued task. Fix: a bounded queue of 2 seconds' work with AbortPolicy → 429 + Retry-After; client retries with jittered backoff; a semaphore in front of the picking client; dashboards on queue age. Lesson: an unbounded queue doesn't absorb overload, it postpones the crash and makes it bigger.

13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Every buffer is bounded; decide what happens when it's full.
  • Pull (request(n)), block, drop, or reject (429/503 + Retry-After).
  • Shed early and cheaply; keep accepted work fast.
  • Size queues in seconds of work, below client timeouts.
  • Clients: backoff + jitter + retry budgets.

docs.title: Cache-Aside (and Other Caching Patterns)
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Cache-aside: the application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and puts the result in the cache with a TTL; on a write it updates the database and deletes the cache entry. Use it for read-heavy data that tolerates being a few seconds stale (catalogs, profiles, configuration). Add request coalescing for hot keys, and know when write-through or write-behind fit better.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the product page for bananas is viewed 1,000 times a minute during the evening rush, and every view runs the same SELECT. The database's CPU climbs, latency rises for everything else, and you're paying for a bigger database just to answer the same question again and again.

Definition (Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Cache-Aside):

Load data on demand into a cache from a data store. The application is responsible for reading from and writing to the store and keeping the cache consistent.

The family of caching patterns:

Pattern Read path Write path Typical use Cache-aside (lazy loading) App: cache → miss → DB → fill cache App: write DB, delete cache key Most microservices with Redis Read-through Cache library loads from DB on a miss (Usually with write-through) Caffeine LoadingCache, Hazelcast MapLoader Write-through From cache Write cache and DB synchronously Data read right after write Write-behind (write-back) From cache Write cache; flush to DB asynchronously in batches Counters, metrics, likes Refresh-ahead From cache Reload hot keys before they expire Hot keys with expensive loads

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The stock of popular items at the billing counter

A supermarket keeps chewing gum and batteries at the counter (the cache) instead of sending someone to the aisles (the database) each time. When the counter runs out, the cashier fetches more from the aisle (miss → load). When the price changes, the counter stock is relabelled by removing the old tags (invalidate), not by guessing the new price.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     autonumber     participant App     participant Cache as Redis     participant DB     App->>Cache: GET product:BANANA-6     alt hit         Cache-->>App: value     else miss         App->>DB: SELECT ...         DB-->>App: row         App->>Cache: SET product:BANANA-6 value EX 600     end     Note over App,DB: write path     App->>DB: UPDATE price     App->>Cache: DEL product:BANANA-6 Participant Responsibility Application Owns the logic: look up, load on miss, fill, invalidate on write Cache (Redis, Memcached, Caffeine) Fast key-value store with TTLs and eviction Database Source of truth TTL Upper bound on staleness and a safety net for missed invalidations

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public Product get(String sku) {
    return jdbc.queryForObject("SELECT * FROM product WHERE sku = ?", mapper, sku);  // every view hits the DB
}
// or, the opposite mistake:
static final Map<String, Product> CACHE = new HashMap<>();   // per-instance, never expires, never invalidated
  • The database carries load that a cache could absorb 1000×.
  • Home-made per-instance maps: inconsistent between pods, unbounded memory, stale forever.
  • No TTL means one missed invalidation is permanent.

docs.title: Example 1: Product Pages (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery app's product pages are viewed tens of thousands of times an hour, but prices change only a few times a day. A 10-minute TTL is acceptable, except that a price drop must show up immediately (marketing has pushed a notification). The write path updates PostgreSQL, then deletes the Redis key.

Design:

flowchart LR V["1,000 views"] --> C{"cache hit?"} C -- "999 yes" --> R[(Redis)] C -- "1 miss" --> DB[(PostgreSQL)] --> R U["Price update"] --> DB U -->|DEL key| R

Full Code:

ProductCatalog.javaTtlCache.javaCatalogCacheDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Cache-aside: the APPLICATION reads the cache, falls back to the DB, and fills the cache itself. */
public final class ProductCatalog {

    public record Product(String sku, String name, long pricePaise) { }

    private final Map<String, Product> database = new HashMap<>();
    private final TtlCache<Product> cache;
    private int dbReads;

    public ProductCatalog(TtlCache<Product> cache) {
        this.cache = cache;
    }

    public void seed(Product p) {
        database.put(p.sku(), p);
    }

    public Product get(String sku) {
        return cache.get("product:" + sku).orElseGet(() -> { // (1)!
            dbReads++;
            Product fromDb = database.get(sku);
            cache.set("product:" + sku, fromDb, Duration.ofMinutes(10)); // (2)!
            return fromDb;
        });
    }

    public void updatePrice(String sku, long newPaise) {
        Product p = database.get(sku);
        database.put(sku, new Product(sku, p.name(), newPaise)); // 1. write the source of truth
        cache.delete("product:" + sku);                         // 2. invalidate (don't set) (3)!
    }

    public int dbReads() {
        return dbReads;
    }
}
  1. Look in the cache first; only on a miss go to the database.
  2. Fill the cache with a TTL. The TTL bounds staleness even if an invalidation is lost.
  3. Delete, don't set, on writes. Setting the new value from the writer races with concurrent readers and can't handle complex derived values; a delete just forces the next reader to load fresh data.
package com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

/** A minimal Redis stand-in: get / set with TTL / delete. */
public final class TtlCache<V> {

    private record Entry<V>(V value, Instant expiresAt) { }

    private final Map<String, Entry<V>> data = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Clock clock;

    public TtlCache(Clock clock) {
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public Optional<V> get(String key) {
        Entry<V> e = data.get(key);
        if (e == null || !clock.instant().isBefore(e.expiresAt())) {
            data.remove(key);
            return Optional.empty();
        }
        return Optional.of(e.value());
    }

    public void set(String key, V value, Duration ttl) {
        data.put(key, new Entry<>(value, clock.instant().plus(ttl)));
    }

    public void delete(String key) {
        data.remove(key);
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog;

import com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog.ProductCatalog.Product;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class CatalogCacheDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Cache-Aside for Product Pages ===");
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-06-01T18:00:00Z");
        ProductCatalog catalog = new ProductCatalog(new TtlCache<>(clock));
        catalog.seed(new Product("BANANA-6", "Robusta Banana (6)", 4_200));

        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
            catalog.get("BANANA-6"); // evening rush on the product page
        }
        System.out.println("1,000 page views -> DB reads: " + catalog.dbReads());

        catalog.updatePrice("BANANA-6", 3_900);
        long paise = catalog.get("BANANA-6").pricePaise();
        System.out.printf("After price drop, next view shows INR %d.%02d (DB reads: %d)%n", paise / 100, paise % 100, catalog.dbReads());

        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(11));
        catalog.get("BANANA-6");
        System.out.println("11 minutes later the entry expired and was reloaded (DB reads: " + catalog.dbReads() + ")");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Cache-Aside for Product Pages ===
1,000 page views -> DB reads: 1
After price drop, next view shows INR 39.00 (DB reads: 2)
11 minutes later the entry expired and was reloaded (DB reads: 3)

Why cache-aside here:

  • Read-heavy, rarely written data: a near-perfect hit rate.
  • The application controls what is cached and for how long.
  • If Redis is down, the app can still read the database (degraded, not broken).

docs.title: Example 2: Stampede Protection for a New Release (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: When a new episode drops at 12:00, 500 viewers open it in the same second. The metadata isn't cached yet, so all 500 miss and query the database at once: a cache stampede (thundering herd). The fix is request coalescing (single-flight): the first miss loads; everyone else waits for that same load.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant V1 as Viewer 1 participant Vn as Viewers 2..500 participant L as SingleFlightLoader participant DB V1->>L: get(ep-2201) → miss, owns in-flight Vn->>L: get(ep-2201) → miss, join in-flight future L->>DB: ONE query DB-->>L: metadata L-->>V1: value L-->>Vn: same value

Full Code:

SingleFlightLoader.javaStampedeDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.caching.singleflight;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Request coalescing: concurrent misses for the same key share ONE load instead of stampeding the DB. */
public final class SingleFlightLoader<V> {

    private final Map<String, V> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, CompletableFuture<V>> inFlight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Function<String, V> loader;

    public SingleFlightLoader(Function<String, V> loader) {
        this.loader = loader;
    }

    public V get(String key) {
        V cached = cache.get(key);
        if (cached != null) {
            return cached;
        }
        CompletableFuture<V> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
        CompletableFuture<V> existing = inFlight.putIfAbsent(key, mine); // (1)!
        if (existing != null) {
            return existing.join(); // (2)!
        }
        try {
            V value = cache.get(key); // re-check: a load may have finished between our first check and now
            if (value == null) {
                value = loader.apply(key);
            }
            cache.put(key, value);
            mine.complete(value);
            return value;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            mine.completeExceptionally(e);
            throw e;
        } finally {
            inFlight.remove(key);
        }
    }
}
  1. putIfAbsent elects exactly one loader per key; everyone else gets the in-flight future.
  2. Waiters share the result (or the failure) of that single load.
package com.handbook.microservices.caching.singleflight;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class StampedeDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: 500 Viewers Open a Just-Released Episode ===");
        AtomicInteger dbLoads = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch slowDb = new CountDownLatch(1);
        SingleFlightLoader<String> metadata = new SingleFlightLoader<>(id -> {
            dbLoads.incrementAndGet();
            try {
                slowDb.await(); // the metadata query takes a while
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
            return id + ": 'The Monsoon Heist' S2E1, 52 min, 4K";
        });

        List<Future<String>> viewers = new ArrayList<>();
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
                viewers.add(pool.submit(() -> metadata.get("ep-2201")));
            }
            while (dbLoads.get() == 0) {
                Thread.onSpinWait();
            }
            Thread.sleep(100); // let the other 499 requests pile up behind the in-flight load
            slowDb.countDown();
            long served = 0;
            for (Future<String> f : viewers) {
                served += f.get().startsWith("ep-2201") ? 1 : 0;
            }
            System.out.println("Viewers served: " + served);
        }
        System.out.println("Database loads: " + dbLoads.get() + " (without coalescing: up to 500)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: 500 Viewers Open a Just-Released Episode ===
Viewers served: 500
Database loads: 1 (without coalescing: up to 500)

Why coalescing here:

  • Hot keys + cold cache = synchronized misses; this turns N database queries into 1.
  • Caffeine's AsyncLoadingCache does this per JVM; across pods, add a short Redis lock or jittered TTLs.
  • The same idea protects downstream APIs, not just databases.

docs.title: Example 3: Write-Behind View Counters (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: A travel site shows "1,234 people viewed this hotel today". That's 20,000 increments per second at peak across three hotels in this demo. Writing each to the database is wasteful; counters can tolerate losing a second of data on a crash. Increments go to the cache and are flushed as aggregated deltas once per second.

Design:

flowchart LR V["20,000 views/s"] -->|INCR| C[(Cache deltas)] T["every 1 s"] -->|flush| C C -->|"3 UPDATEs: views = views + delta"| DB[(Database)]

Full Code:

WriteBehindCounter.javaWriteBehindDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.caching.writebehind;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** Write-behind: absorb writes in the cache, flush aggregated deltas to the database in batches. */
public final class WriteBehindCounter {

    private final Map<String, Long> pendingDeltas = new HashMap<>(); // the "cache" side
    private final Map<String, Long> database = new TreeMap<>();
    private int dbWrites;

    public synchronized void increment(String hotelId) {
        pendingDeltas.merge(hotelId, 1L, Long::sum); // (1)!
    }

    public synchronized int flush() { // (2)!
        int rows = pendingDeltas.size();
        pendingDeltas.forEach((id, delta) -> database.merge(id, delta, Long::sum));
        dbWrites += rows;
        pendingDeltas.clear();
        return rows;
    }

    public synchronized long pending() {
        return pendingDeltas.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
    }

    public synchronized Map<String, Long> database() {
        return Map.copyOf(database);
    }

    public synchronized int dbWrites() {
        return dbWrites;
    }
}
  1. Writes only touch the in-memory side: microseconds, no DB round trip.
  2. A periodic flush writes one row per key with the aggregated delta.
package com.handbook.microservices.caching.writebehind;

import java.util.Random;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class WriteBehindDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: Hotel Page-View Counters with Write-Behind ===");
        WriteBehindCounter counter = new WriteBehindCounter();
        Random random = new Random(7);
        String[] hotels = {"GOA-BEACH-12", "JAIPUR-FORT-3", "MUNNAR-TEA-8"};

        for (int second = 1; second <= 3; second++) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) {
                counter.increment(hotels[random.nextInt(hotels.length)]);
            }
            System.out.println("t=" + second + "s flush wrote " + counter.flush() + " rows");
        }
        System.out.println("60,000 views -> " + counter.dbWrites() + " DB writes; totals " + new TreeMap<>(counter.database()));

        for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
            counter.increment("GOA-BEACH-12");
        }
        System.out.println("Crash before the next flush would lose " + counter.pending() + " views: fine for counters, never for money.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: Hotel Page-View Counters with Write-Behind ===
t=1s flush wrote 3 rows
t=2s flush wrote 3 rows
t=3s flush wrote 3 rows
60,000 views -> 9 DB writes; totals {GOA-BEACH-12=19956, JAIPUR-FORT-3=20009, MUNNAR-TEA-8=20035}
Crash before the next flush would lose 500 views: fine for counters, never for money.

Why write-behind here:

  • 60,000 increments became 9 database writes.
  • The data is approximate by nature, so a small loss window is acceptable.
  • Never use write-behind for money, orders or anything you can't afford to lose.
Unit Tests: CacheAsideTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog.ProductCatalog;
import com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog.ProductCatalog.Product;
import com.handbook.microservices.caching.catalog.TtlCache;
import com.handbook.microservices.caching.singleflight.SingleFlightLoader;
import com.handbook.microservices.caching.writebehind.WriteBehindCounter;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class CacheAsideTest {

    @Test
    void cacheAsideServesFromCacheAndInvalidatesOnWrite() {
        ProductCatalog c = new ProductCatalog(new TtlCache<>(FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z")));
        c.seed(new Product("A", "a", 100));
        c.get("A");
        c.get("A");
        assertThat(c.dbReads()).isEqualTo(1);
        c.updatePrice("A", 90);
        assertThat(c.get("A").pricePaise()).isEqualTo(90);
    }

    @Test
    void entriesExpireAfterTtl() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        TtlCache<String> cache = new TtlCache<>(clock);
        cache.set("k", "v", Duration.ofSeconds(5));
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
        assertThat(cache.get("k")).isEmpty();
    }

    @Test
    void sequentialMissesAfterFillHitTheCache() {
        AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger();
        SingleFlightLoader<Integer> l = new SingleFlightLoader<>(k -> loads.incrementAndGet());
        l.get("x");
        l.get("x");
        assertThat(loads).hasValue(1);
    }

    @Test
    void writeBehindAggregatesDeltas() {
        WriteBehindCounter c = new WriteBehindCounter();
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            c.increment("h");
        }
        assertThat(c.flush()).isEqualTo(1);
        assertThat(c.database()).containsEntry("h", 100L);
    }
}

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Caching Spring @Cacheable, @CachePut, @CacheEvict, CacheManager (Redis, Caffeine, JCache) Caffeine LoadingCache, AsyncLoadingCache (coalescing), refreshAfterWrite (refresh-ahead), W-TinyLFU eviction Redis SET key value EX ttl NX, DEL, INCRBY, keyspace notifications Hibernate Second-level cache (read-through for entities) CDNs / HTTP Cache-Control: max-age, stale-while-revalidate: cache-aside at the edge

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Huge read offload; sub-millisecond reads Data can be stale (bounded by TTL and invalidation) Cache failure degrades gracefully (fall back to DB) First request after expiry is slow; stampedes on hot keys Only requested data is cached Invalidation logic in every writer, in every service Simple to add to an existing service Cache and DB can't be updated atomically; races exist

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Updating the cache instead of deleting

"Write DB, then SET the new value" races with concurrent writers and readers and can leave the older value in the cache. Delete, and let the next read load.

Caching without a TTL

One lost DEL (network blip, a bug in another service) makes stale data permanent. Always set a TTL.

Cache stampede on hot keys

Popular keys expiring at once flatten the database. Use coalescing, jittered TTLs, refresh-ahead or a short lock.

Caching per-user or rarely reused data

A low hit rate means you pay for Redis and serialization for nothing. Measure hit ratio per cache.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
The stale-set race. Reader misses and loads v1; writer updates the DB to v2 and deletes the key; the slow reader then sets v1. Now the cache is stale until the TTL. Mitigations: short TTLs; versioned sets (only write if the version is newer, coding challenge); "delayed double delete" (delete again after a few hundred ms); or invalidation driven by CDC events, which are ordered per key.

Sizing and eviction. Measure working-set size and hit ratio; choose maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu (or Caffeine's W-TinyLFU) for skewed traffic. Watch big keys (a 5 MB JSON blob) and hot keys (one key at 100k ops/s); split or replicate them.

Consistency budget. Decide per data type how stale is acceptable: product price on a listing page (seconds to minutes), price at checkout (never: read from the source of truth), stock count (show "few left" from cache, but reserve against the database).

War story: the price that wouldn't go down

A grocery app set new prices into Redis right after updating the database. During a festival sale, two price updates for the same product raced: the older one's SET landed last. The listing showed INR 120 while checkout (reading the database) charged INR 99, and 6,000 customers abandoned carts thinking the sale was fake. Fix: writers only DEL; reads fill the cache; TTL cut from 24 h to 10 min; checkout always reads the database. Lesson: the cache is a copy. Invalidate it; don't try to keep it in sync by writing to it.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Cache-Aside Read-Through Write-Through Write-Behind Who loads on miss Application Cache library (Combined with read-through) (Combined with read-through) Write latency DB write + DEL — DB + cache, synchronous Cache only (fast) Data-loss risk None None None Yes, until flush Staleness Up to TTL / race window Up to TTL Low Low in cache, DB lags

Related: CQRS read models are a durable, purpose-built form of cache; Materialized View precomputes query results; Identity Map is per-transaction, not a cache.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Read: cache → miss → DB → SET with TTL.
  • Write: update DB → DEL key.
  • Always a TTL; jitter it; coalesce hot misses.
  • Write-through = safe & synchronous; write-behind = fast & lossy.
  • Never trust the cache for money or stock decisions.
return cache.get(key).orElseGet(() -> { var v = db.load(key); cache.set(key, v, TTL); return v; });

docs.text:

  • Add jitter to the TTL and show expiry times spread out.
  • Add a "flush on shutdown" hook to WriteBehindCounter.
