docs.title: Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and watches the failures. When they cross a threshold it "opens" and fails fast (or serves a fallback) without calling the dependency. After a cool-down it lets a few trial calls through ("half-open") and closes again if they succeed. It stops one sick service from tying up threads everywhere and gives it room to recover.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the payment provider starts timing out after 10 seconds. Every checkout thread now waits 10 s, the thread pool fills up, and checkout stops working for everyone, including requests that never touch payments. Meanwhile, the struggling provider is hammered with retries and can't recover. That's a cascading failure.

Definition (Michael Nygard, Release It!; popularized by Martin Fowler):

Wrap a protected function call in a circuit breaker object, which monitors for failures. Once the failures reach a certain threshold, the circuit breaker trips, and all further calls return with an error, without the protected call being made at all.

The state machine:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> CLOSED CLOSED --> OPEN: failure rate ≥ threshold<br/>(over last N calls, after min calls) OPEN --> HALF_OPEN: wait duration elapsed HALF_OPEN --> CLOSED: trial calls succeed HALF_OPEN --> OPEN: a trial call fails

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The electrical breaker in your home

When a faulty heater draws too much current, the breaker trips and cuts power to that circuit before the wiring catches fire. The rest of the house keeps working. After fixing the heater, you flip the breaker back and see whether it holds.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
Participant Responsibility Caller Calls through the breaker; supplies a fallback Circuit breaker Records outcomes in a sliding window, manages state, fails fast when OPEN Protected dependency Remote service, database, third-party API Fallback Cached data, a default, a queued request, or a clear error

Key configuration (Resilience4j names): slidingWindowSize, minimumNumberOfCalls, failureRateThreshold, waitDurationInOpenState, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState, plus slowCallDurationThreshold / slowCallRateThreshold.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public String pay(String orderId) {
    return paymentHttp.post(orderId); // 10 s read timeout
}
// Provider degrades → 200 checkout threads all blocked for 10 s
// → the thread pool is exhausted → browsing and cart APIs on the same service time out too
// → clients retry → even more blocked threads → total outage

docs.title: 5. Three Real-World Examples
docs.text:
All three examples use the same small breaker, modelled on Resilience4j's count-based state machine:

CircuitBreaker.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * A count-based circuit breaker modelled on Resilience4j's state machine.
 * <pre>
 *   CLOSED --(failure rate >= threshold over the last N calls)--> OPEN
 *   OPEN   --(wait duration elapsed)--> HALF_OPEN
 *   HALF_OPEN --(trial calls succeed)--> CLOSED, --(any trial call fails)--> OPEN
 * </pre>
 */
public final class CircuitBreaker {

    public enum State { CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN }

    public record Config(int windowSize, int minimumCalls, int failureRatePercent,
                         Duration waitInOpen, int trialCalls) {
    }

    public static final class OpenException extends RuntimeException {
        OpenException(String name) {
            super(name + " circuit is OPEN");
        }
    }

    private final String name;
    private final Config config;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Deque<Boolean> window = new ArrayDeque<>(); // true = failure
    private State state = State.CLOSED;
    private Instant openedAt;
    private int trialSuccesses;

    public CircuitBreaker(String name, Config config, Clock clock) {
        this.name = name;
        this.config = config;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public synchronized State state() {
        if (state == State.OPEN && !clock.instant().isBefore(openedAt.plus(config.waitInOpen()))) {
            transition(State.HALF_OPEN); // (1)!
        }
        return state;
    }

    public <T> T call(Supplier<T> action, Function<Throwable, T> fallback) {
        try {
            return call(action);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            return fallback.apply(e); // (2)!
        }
    }

    public <T> T call(Supplier<T> action) {
        if (state() == State.OPEN) {
            throw new OpenException(name); // (3)!
        }
        try {
            T result = action.get();
            record(false);
            return result;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            record(true);
            throw e;
        }
    }

    private synchronized void record(boolean failure) {
        if (state == State.HALF_OPEN) { // (4)!
            if (failure) {
                trip();
            } else if (++trialSuccesses >= config.trialCalls()) {
                window.clear();
                transition(State.CLOSED);
            }
            return;
        }
        window.addLast(failure);
        if (window.size() > config.windowSize()) {
            window.removeFirst();
        }
        long failures = window.stream().filter(f -> f).count();
        if (window.size() >= config.minimumCalls() // (5)!
                && failures * 100 / window.size() >= config.failureRatePercent()) {
            trip();
        }
    }

    private void trip() {
        openedAt = clock.instant();
        transition(State.OPEN);
    }

    private void transition(State to) {
        System.out.println("    [" + name + "] " + state + " -> " + to);
        state = to;
        trialSuccesses = 0;
    }
}
  1. OPEN → HALF_OPEN happens lazily when someone asks for the state after the wait duration.
  2. The fallback receives the exception, so it can tell "circuit open" from "real failure".
  3. Fail fast: no network call, no waiting, so threads are freed immediately.
  4. In HALF_OPEN, one failure re-opens; enough successes close the circuit with a fresh window.
  5. minimumCalls prevents opening on 1 failure out of 1 call (100%) at startup.

docs.title: Example 1: Checkout → Payment Provider (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A window of 4 calls, at least 4 calls before deciding, and a 50% failure threshold. When the provider starts timing out, the breaker opens and orders are queued for retry instead of failing (the customer sees "payment processing"). While OPEN, the provider receives zero calls. After 30 s, a trial call succeeds and the circuit closes.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant C as Checkout participant B as Breaker participant P as Payment provider C->>B: ORD-3, ORD-4 B->>P: calls time out Note over B: 2/4 failed = 50% → OPEN C->>B: ORD-5, ORD-6 B-->>C: fail fast → queued Note over B: +30 s → HALF_OPEN C->>B: ORD-7 B->>P: trial call OK Note over B: 2 trials OK → CLOSED

Full Code:

PaymentClient.javaPaymentBreakerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;

import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Checkout calls the payment provider through a breaker; when it's open, orders are queued, not lost. */
public final class PaymentClient {

    private final CircuitBreaker breaker;
    private final Supplier<String> provider;

    public PaymentClient(CircuitBreaker breaker, Supplier<String> provider) {
        this.breaker = breaker;
        this.provider = provider;
    }

    public String pay(String orderId) {
        return breaker.call(
                () -> orderId + " paid (" + provider.get() + ")",
                e -> orderId + " queued for retry: " + e.getMessage()); // (1)!
    }
}
  1. The fallback queues the payment for a background retry. This is a business decision: the order isn't lost, and the customer is told payment is pending.
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;
import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker.Config;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class PaymentBreakerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T18:00:00Z");
        AtomicBoolean providerDown = new AtomicBoolean(false);
        AtomicInteger providerCalls = new AtomicInteger();

        var breaker = new CircuitBreaker("payment", new Config(4, 4, 50, Duration.ofSeconds(30), 2), clock);
        var client = new PaymentClient(breaker, () -> {
            providerCalls.incrementAndGet();
            if (providerDown.get()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("provider timeout");
            }
            return "txn-ok";
        });

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: checkout -> payment provider ===");
        pay(client, "ORD-1");
        pay(client, "ORD-2");
        System.out.println("-- provider starts timing out --");
        providerDown.set(true);
        pay(client, "ORD-3");
        pay(client, "ORD-4");
        int before = providerCalls.get();
        pay(client, "ORD-5");
        pay(client, "ORD-6");
        System.out.println("Provider calls while OPEN: " + (providerCalls.get() - before) + " (fail fast, no waiting)");

        System.out.println("-- 30 s later, provider has recovered --");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
        providerDown.set(false);
        pay(client, "ORD-7");
        pay(client, "ORD-8");
        pay(client, "ORD-9");
    }

    private static void pay(PaymentClient client, String orderId) {
        System.out.println(client.pay(orderId));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: checkout -> payment provider ===
ORD-1 paid (txn-ok)
ORD-2 paid (txn-ok)
-- provider starts timing out --
ORD-3 queued for retry: provider timeout
    [payment] CLOSED -> OPEN
ORD-4 queued for retry: provider timeout
ORD-5 queued for retry: payment circuit is OPEN
ORD-6 queued for retry: payment circuit is OPEN
Provider calls while OPEN: 0 (fail fast, no waiting)
-- 30 s later, provider has recovered --
    [payment] OPEN -> HALF_OPEN
ORD-7 paid (txn-ok)
    [payment] HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED
ORD-8 paid (txn-ok)
ORD-9 paid (txn-ok)

Why a circuit breaker here:

  • Checkout threads aren't held hostage by a slow provider.
  • The provider gets breathing room to recover.
  • Automatic recovery: no human has to "turn payments back on".

docs.title: Example 2: ETA with a Degraded Fallback (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: The traffic-aware routing engine gives accurate ETAs. During its deploy it returns 503s. Riders still need some ETA, so the fallback estimates from straight-line distance. The example also shows a failed trial: HALF_OPEN → OPEN when the engine is still down, then a successful trial 10 s later.

Full Code:

EtaService.javaEtaBreakerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.ridehailing;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;

import java.util.function.ToIntFunction;

/**
 * The traffic-aware routing engine gives accurate ETAs. If it's unhealthy, the breaker opens and
 * riders get a rougher estimate from straight-line distance instead of an error screen.
 */
public final class EtaService {

    public record Trip(String id, double distanceKm) {
    }

    private final CircuitBreaker breaker;
    private final ToIntFunction<Trip> routingEngine;

    public EtaService(CircuitBreaker breaker, ToIntFunction<Trip> routingEngine) {
        this.breaker = breaker;
        this.routingEngine = routingEngine;
    }

    public String eta(Trip trip) {
        return breaker.call(
                () -> routingEngine.applyAsInt(trip) + " min (live traffic)",
                e -> estimate(trip) + " min (estimate)"); // (1)!
    }

    private static int estimate(Trip trip) {
        return (int) Math.ceil(trip.distanceKm() / 25.0 * 60 * 1.3); // 25 km/h city average, 30% detour
    }
}
  1. A degraded but useful answer, labelled as an estimate so the UI can show "~25 min".
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.ridehailing;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;
import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker.Config;
import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.ridehailing.EtaService.Trip;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;

public class EtaBreakerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T08:00:00Z");
        AtomicBoolean engineHealthy = new AtomicBoolean(true);
        var breaker = new CircuitBreaker("routing", new Config(5, 3, 60, Duration.ofSeconds(10), 1), clock);
        var eta = new EtaService(breaker, trip -> {
            if (!engineHealthy.get()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("routing engine 503");
            }
            return (int) Math.round(trip.distanceKm() * 2.4);
        });

        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: ETA with a degraded fallback ===");
        System.out.println("trip-1 (5 km):  " + eta.eta(new Trip("trip-1", 5)));
        engineHealthy.set(false);
        System.out.println("-- routing engine fails during a deploy --");
        for (int i = 2; i <= 5; i++) {
            System.out.println("trip-" + i + " (8 km):  " + eta.eta(new Trip("trip-" + i, 8)));
        }
        System.out.println("-- 10 s later: one trial call while the engine is still down --");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        System.out.println("trip-6 (8 km):  " + eta.eta(new Trip("trip-6", 8)));
        System.out.println("-- another 10 s: engine is back --");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        engineHealthy.set(true);
        System.out.println("trip-7 (8 km):  " + eta.eta(new Trip("trip-7", 8)));
        System.out.println("Breaker state: " + breaker.state());
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: ETA with a degraded fallback ===
trip-1 (5 km):  12 min (live traffic)
-- routing engine fails during a deploy --
trip-2 (8 km):  25 min (estimate)
    [routing] CLOSED -> OPEN
trip-3 (8 km):  25 min (estimate)
trip-4 (8 km):  25 min (estimate)
trip-5 (8 km):  25 min (estimate)
-- 10 s later: one trial call while the engine is still down --
    [routing] OPEN -> HALF_OPEN
    [routing] HALF_OPEN -> OPEN
trip-6 (8 km):  25 min (estimate)
-- another 10 s: engine is back --
    [routing] OPEN -> HALF_OPEN
    [routing] HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED
trip-7 (8 km):  19 min (live traffic)
Breaker state: CLOSED

Why a circuit breaker here:

  • The app keeps working with lower quality instead of failing.
  • A failed trial re-opens immediately, so the engine isn't flooded the moment the wait ends.

docs.title: Example 3: Personalised Rows with Layered Fallbacks (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: At Friday 9 pm the recommender is overloaded. The home screen must never fail, so the client falls back to the profile's last good recommendations, then to a global "Popular now" row for profiles with no cache. The open breaker also sheds load from the recommender during its worst moment.

Full Code:

RecommendationsClient.javaRecommendationsBreakerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.streaming;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Personalised rows are nice to have. If the recommender is struggling, fall back to the profile's
 * last good response, then to a global "Popular now" row. The home screen never fails.
 */
public final class RecommendationsClient {

    private final CircuitBreaker breaker;
    private final Function<String, List<String>> recommender;
    private final Map<String, List<String>> lastGood = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<String> popularNow;

    public RecommendationsClient(CircuitBreaker breaker, Function<String, List<String>> recommender,
                                 List<String> popularNow) {
        this.breaker = breaker;
        this.recommender = recommender;
        this.popularNow = popularNow;
    }

    public String row(String profileId) {
        return breaker.call(() -> {
            List<String> titles = recommender.apply(profileId);
            lastGood.put(profileId, titles); // (1)!
            return "For you " + titles;
        }, e -> {
            List<String> cached = lastGood.get(profileId);
            return cached != null ? "For you (cached) " + cached : "Popular now " + popularNow; // (2)!
        });
    }
}
  1. Every success refreshes the last-good cache.
  2. Layered fallback: personal cache → global default. Each layer is cheaper and less personal.
package com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.streaming;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;
import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker.Config;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;

public class RecommendationsBreakerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T21:00:00Z");
        AtomicBoolean overloaded = new AtomicBoolean(false);
        var breaker = new CircuitBreaker("recommender", new Config(4, 2, 50, Duration.ofSeconds(60), 1), clock);
        var client = new RecommendationsClient(breaker, profile -> {
            if (overloaded.get()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("recommender overloaded");
            }
            return profile.equals("P-1") ? List.of("Monsoon Express", "Spice Route") : List.of("Byte Club");
        }, List.of("City of Rain", "Monsoon Express"));

        System.out.println("=== Streaming: personalised row with layered fallbacks ===");
        System.out.println("P-1: " + client.row("P-1"));
        System.out.println("-- Friday 9 pm peak: recommender overloaded --");
        overloaded.set(true);
        System.out.println("P-1: " + client.row("P-1"));
        System.out.println("P-2: " + client.row("P-2"));
        System.out.println("P-1: " + client.row("P-1") + "   <- breaker open, recommender not called");
        System.out.println("P-3: " + client.row("P-3"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: personalised row with layered fallbacks ===
P-1: For you [Monsoon Express, Spice Route]
-- Friday 9 pm peak: recommender overloaded --
    [recommender] CLOSED -> OPEN
P-1: For you (cached) [Monsoon Express, Spice Route]
P-2: Popular now [City of Rain, Monsoon Express]
P-1: For you (cached) [Monsoon Express, Spice Route]   <- breaker open, recommender not called
P-3: Popular now [City of Rain, Monsoon Express]

Why a circuit breaker here:

  • Optional features degrade invisibly; viewers still get a full home screen.
  • Load shedding during peaks helps the recommender recover faster.
Unit Tests: CircuitBreakerTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker;
import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker.Config;
import com.handbook.microservices.circuitbreaker.core.CircuitBreaker.State;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class CircuitBreakerTest {

    private final FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
    private final CircuitBreaker breaker = new CircuitBreaker("t", new Config(4, 4, 50, Duration.ofSeconds(10), 1), clock);
    private final Supplier<String> failing = () -> {
        throw new IllegalStateException("boom");
    };

    @Test
    void opensAtFailureRateAndFailsFast() {
        breaker.call(() -> "ok", e -> "fb");
        breaker.call(() -> "ok", e -> "fb");
        breaker.call(failing, e -> "fb");
        assertThat(breaker.state()).isEqualTo(State.CLOSED); // only 3 calls, minimum is 4
        breaker.call(failing, e -> "fb");
        assertThat(breaker.state()).isEqualTo(State.OPEN);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> breaker.call(() -> "ok")).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.OpenException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void halfOpenTrialClosesOrReopens() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
            breaker.call(failing, e -> "fb");
        }
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        assertThat(breaker.state()).isEqualTo(State.HALF_OPEN);
        breaker.call(failing, e -> "fb");
        assertThat(breaker.state()).isEqualTo(State.OPEN);
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        assertThat(breaker.call(() -> "ok", e -> "fb")).isEqualTo("ok");
        assertThat(breaker.state()).isEqualTo(State.CLOSED);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Resilience4j with Spring Boot (the standard choice; Hystrix is in maintenance mode). This class is compiled in the repo's spring-reference module:

PaymentProviderClient.javaapplication.yml (reference) 
package com.handbook.springref.resilience;

import io.github.resilience4j.bulkhead.annotation.Bulkhead;
import io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.annotation.CircuitBreaker;
import io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.annotation.RateLimiter;
import io.github.resilience4j.retry.annotation.Retry;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

/**
 * Resilience4j annotations on a Spring bean. Order of decoration (outermost first) by default:
 * Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ) ).
 * Instances "payment" are configured in application.yml (see the Circuit Breaker page).
 */
@Component
public class PaymentProviderClient {

    private final RestClient http;

    public PaymentProviderClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        this.http = builder.baseUrl("https://payments.example.com").build();
    }

    @Retry(name = "payment")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "queueForLater")
    @RateLimiter(name = "payment")
    @Bulkhead(name = "payment")
    public String charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
        return http.post()
                .uri("/charges")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", orderId) // retries must not double-charge
                .body(new ChargeRequest(orderId, amountPaise))
                .retrieve()
                .body(String.class);
    }

    /** Same parameters plus the exception; called when the call fails or the circuit is open. */
    String queueForLater(String orderId, long amountPaise, Throwable cause) {
        return "QUEUED:" + orderId;
    }

    record ChargeRequest(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
    }
}

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payment:
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED      # or TIME_BASED (last N seconds)
        sliding-window-size: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10
        failure-rate-threshold: 50            # %
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s      # slow calls count as failures...
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 80          # ...when 80% are slow
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3
        record-exceptions: [java.io.IOException, org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException]
        ignore-exceptions: [com.shop.InvalidCardException]   # business errors aren't outages
  retry:
    instances:
      payment: { max-attempts: 3, wait-duration: 200ms, enable-exponential-backoff: true }
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      payment: { max-concurrent-calls: 25 }
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      payment: { limit-for-period: 50, limit-refresh-period: 1s, timeout-duration: 0 }
Variation Notes Count-based vs. time-based window Last N calls vs. last N seconds Slow-call detection Slow responses also trip the breaker (latency, not just errors) Per-host breakers One breaker per downstream instance or region, so one bad host doesn't open the whole service Mesh-level Envoy/Istio outlier detection and connection-pool limits do this without code

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Circuit breaker Resilience4j CircuitBreaker, with Spring Boot annotations and Micrometer metrics Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker Abstraction over Resilience4j (CircuitBreakerFactory) Spring Cloud Gateway CircuitBreaker filter with fallback URI Netflix Hystrix (legacy) The original Java implementation, now in maintenance mode Istio / Envoy Outlier detection + connection pool limits

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Prevents cascading failures and thread exhaustion Tuning thresholds is hard; bad settings flap or never open Fast failure gives a better UX than long waits Fallbacks must be designed per use case Gives the dependency room to recover Per-instance breakers see only local traffic Built-in metrics show dependency health Can hide problems if nobody watches the metrics

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Counting business errors as failures

"Card declined" (HTTP 402/422) is a correct answer, not an outage. Counting it opens the breaker on a busy shopping day. Use ignoreExceptions / recordExceptions.

Breaker without timeouts

A breaker records a failure only when a call ends. Without a timeout, a hung call never ends, so it never counts. Always pair breakers with timeouts.

Retry outside the breaker hammering an open circuit

Retrying CallNotPermittedException is pointless. Configure retries to ignore it, and keep retry counts small.

One breaker for many endpoints

If /search is down but /orders is fine, a shared breaker blocks both. Use breakers per dependency and per operation where behaviour differs.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Composition order. Resilience4j's default aspect order is Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ))))). Retry wraps the breaker, so each retry attempt is counted and an open circuit stops retries quickly. Think about whether that's what you want, and document it.

Fallback design is product design. Options: cached/stale data, default values, degraded computation, queue for later, or a clear error. Payments → queue; recommendations → popular list; balances → error (stale balances are dangerous). Discuss with product owners.

Observability. Export state transitions and failure rates (Micrometer → Prometheus). Alert on OPEN for critical dependencies; dashboards show which dependency is sick across all callers.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Timeouts on every remote call, inside the breaker.
  • Record only infrastructure failures (5xx, timeouts, connection errors); ignore business errors.
  • Slow-call thresholds for latency-driven failures.
  • A meaningful fallback per use case, agreed with product.
  • Metrics + alerts on state transitions; dashboards per dependency.
  • Chaos tests (inject latency/failures) to verify breakers actually open.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Every synchronous dependency call goes through Resilience4j: a timeout, a circuit breaker (e.g. 50% failures or 80% slow calls over the last 20 calls, open for 30 s, 3 trial calls), a bulkhead to cap concurrency, and limited retries with jitter for idempotent calls only. Each has a fallback that makes business sense: recommendations fall back to popular items, payments get queued and confirmed asynchronously. Breaker state is exported as metrics with alerts, so a sick dependency is visible in one dashboard."

War story: the breaker that tripped on success

A food-delivery checkout counted all exceptions as failures, including PromoCodeExpiredException. During a marketing campaign, thousands of users entered an expired promo code. The breaker around the pricing service opened, and all checkouts for 30 s got the fallback "pricing unavailable" error. It kept re-opening for an hour. Fix: ignoreExceptions for business errors; record only timeouts, connection failures and 5xx. Lesson: a circuit breaker should measure the health of the dependency, not the validity of user input.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Circuit Breaker Retry Timeout Bulkhead Rate Limiter Question it answers Is the dependency healthy enough to call? Was this failure transient? How long will I wait? How many concurrent calls? How many calls per period? Protects Caller and dependency UX against blips Caller's threads Other features from one dependency The service from overload

See Retry / Timeout / Bulkhead, Rate Limiter and the in-process State pattern that the breaker is built on.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • CLOSED → OPEN (failure/slow rate over window) → HALF_OPEN (after wait) → CLOSED/OPEN.
  • Fail fast + fallback = no cascading failures.
  • Always with timeouts; ignore business errors.
  • Resilience4j: @CircuitBreaker(name, fallbackMethod).
  • Fallbacks are a product decision.
@CircuitBreaker(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "queueForLater")
public String charge(String orderId, long amount) { ... }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add slow-call detection to CircuitBreaker: calls longer than a threshold count as failures.
  • Add a listener API so state transitions can be exported as metrics.
  • Make HALF_OPEN allow only N concurrent trial calls (others fail fast).

Service Discovery Next: Retry / Timeout / Bulkhead

docs.title: Competing Consumers
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Several identical consumers read from the same queue; each message is delivered to only one of them. Add consumers to add throughput. Use it for background work that arrives faster than one worker can handle (PDFs, emails, webhooks, image processing). Pair it with acknowledgements, visibility timeouts, idempotency and a dead-letter queue.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: every order needs an invoice PDF. At 5 pm a single worker can render 50 per second, but orders arrive at 200 per second; the backlog grows all evening. Running the renderer inside the checkout request makes checkout slow. You want to put the work on a queue and add workers until the queue keeps up, and you want a crashed worker's job to be picked up by someone else.

Definition (Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns):

Create multiple Competing Consumers on a single channel so that the consumers can process multiple messages concurrently. The messaging system ensures each message is delivered to only one consumer.

Two broker models:

Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ, JMS) Log with consumer groups (Kafka, Kinesis) Unit of competition Each message Each partition (one owner at a time) Ordering None across consumers (FIFO queues: per group id) Per partition (per key) Max parallelism Number of consumers Number of partitions Redelivery Visibility timeout / nack Uncommitted offsets re-read after rebalance

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Bank counters with a token display

Customers take a token and wait in one shared queue. Whichever counter is free calls the next token. Opening more counters serves more customers; if a clerk leaves mid-transaction, the customer is called again by another counter.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     P1[Checkout] --> Q[["invoice-jobs queue"]]     P2[Re-issue tool] --> Q     Q --> C1[Worker 1]     Q --> C2[Worker 2]     Q --> C3[Worker 3]     Q -. "after N failures" .-> DLQ[["DLQ"]] Participant Responsibility Producers Put messages on the queue; don't know who processes them Queue / topic Stores messages; hands each to one consumer; redelivers unacked ones Consumers Identical, stateless workers; ack on success; idempotent Dead-letter queue Holds messages that keep failing, for inspection and replay Autoscaler Adds/removes consumers based on queue depth or lag (KEDA, HPA on lag)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@PostMapping("/orders")
public Order place(...) {
    Order o = orders.save(...);
    pdfRenderer.render(o);      // 400 ms inside the request
    emailClient.send(o);        // another 300 ms, and a failure fails the order
    return o;
}
  • Request latency includes slow background work.
  • Spikes overload the service instead of building a queue.
  • A crash loses the work; there's no retry.

docs.title: Example 1: Invoice PDFs with a Worker Pool (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery platform renders 400 invoice PDFs for a batch of evening orders. Four identical workers pull from one queue. Each invoice must be rendered exactly once, and adding a fifth worker should need no code changes, just another instance. Workers stop gracefully when the queue drains (poison-pill shutdown).

Design:

flowchart LR O["400 orders"] --> Q[["LinkedBlockingQueue"]] Q -->|take| W1[worker 1] Q -->|take| W2[worker 2] Q -->|take| W3[worker 3] Q -->|take| W4[worker 4]

Full Code:

InvoiceWorkers.javaInvoiceDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.invoices;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** N identical workers pull from ONE queue; each message goes to exactly one of them. */
public final class InvoiceWorkers {

    private static final String STOP = "__STOP__";

    private final BlockingQueue<String> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();
    private final Map<String, Integer> processedCount = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicInteger inProgress = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger maxParallel = new AtomicInteger();

    public void publish(String orderId) {
        queue.add(orderId);
    }

    public void runWith(int workers) throws InterruptedException {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < workers; i++) {
                queue.add(STOP); // one poison pill per worker, after the real work
            }
            for (int i = 0; i < workers; i++) {
                pool.submit(this::workLoop);
            }
            pool.shutdown();
            pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        }
    }

    private Void workLoop() throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            String orderId = queue.take(); // (1)!
            if (orderId.equals(STOP)) {
                return null;
            }
            int now = inProgress.incrementAndGet();
            maxParallel.accumulateAndGet(now, Math::max);
            Thread.sleep(2); // render the PDF
            processedCount.merge(orderId, 1, Integer::sum);
            inProgress.decrementAndGet();
        }
    }

    public Map<String, Integer> processedCount() {
        return processedCount;
    }

    public int maxParallel() {
        return maxParallel.get();
    }
}
  1. take() removes the message atomically, so two workers can never get the same one. A broker gives the same guarantee across machines.
package com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.invoices;

public class InvoiceDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: 400 Invoice PDFs Shared by 4 Competing Workers ===");
        InvoiceWorkers workers = new InvoiceWorkers();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 400; i++) {
            workers.publish("ORD-" + i);
        }
        workers.runWith(4);
        long once = workers.processedCount().values().stream().filter(n -> n == 1).count();
        System.out.println("Invoices rendered      : " + workers.processedCount().size());
        System.out.println("Rendered exactly once  : " + once);
        System.out.println("Never more than 4 at a time: " + (workers.maxParallel() <= 4) + " (scale by adding workers, not code)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: 400 Invoice PDFs Shared by 4 Competing Workers ===
Invoices rendered      : 400
Rendered exactly once  : 400
Never more than 4 at a time: true (scale by adding workers, not code)

Why competing consumers here:

  • Work items are independent, so any worker can take any job.
  • Throughput scales linearly with workers until the bottleneck moves (CPU, the PDF service).
  • Checkout just enqueues and returns.

docs.title: Example 2: Visibility Timeout and Redelivery (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment gateway sends payment.captured webhooks. A worker receives one, starts settling, and its pod is killed by a deploy before it acknowledges. With an SQS-style queue, the message is hidden for 30 seconds rather than deleted; when the timeout passes without an ack, it becomes visible again and another worker processes it. Because the first attempt might have partly run, settlement is idempotent.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant A as worker-A participant Q as Queue participant B as worker-B A->>Q: receive → evt_91 (hidden 30s) Note over A: crash, no ack B->>Q: receive at +5s → nothing Note over Q: +31s: visibility expired → visible again B->>Q: receive at +36s → evt_91 (attempt 2) B->>B: settle (idempotent by payment id) B->>Q: ack → deleted

Full Code:

VisibilityQueue.javaWebhookDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.visibility;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

/** SQS-style queue: a received message is hidden, not deleted, until the worker acks it. */
public final class VisibilityQueue {

    public record Message(String id, String body, int receiveCount) { }

    private record InFlight(Message message, Instant visibleAgainAt) { }

    private final Deque<Message> visible = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Map<String, InFlight> inFlight = new HashMap<>();
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration visibilityTimeout;

    public VisibilityQueue(Clock clock, Duration visibilityTimeout) {
        this.clock = clock;
        this.visibilityTimeout = visibilityTimeout;
    }

    public void send(String id, String body) {
        visible.add(new Message(id, body, 0));
    }

    public Optional<Message> receive() {
        returnExpired();
        Message m = visible.poll();
        if (m == null) {
            return Optional.empty();
        }
        Message delivered = new Message(m.id(), m.body(), m.receiveCount() + 1);
        inFlight.put(m.id(), new InFlight(delivered, clock.instant().plus(visibilityTimeout))); // (1)!
        return Optional.of(delivered);
    }

    public void ack(String id) {
        inFlight.remove(id); // (2)!
    }

    private void returnExpired() {
        inFlight.values().removeIf(f -> {
            if (!clock.instant().isBefore(f.visibleAgainAt())) {
                visible.addFirst(f.message()); // (3)!
                return true;
            }
            return false;
        });
    }
}
  1. Receiving hides the message for the visibility timeout instead of deleting it.
  2. Only an explicit ack deletes it: no ack, no loss.
  3. Expired in-flight messages go back to the front for another consumer.
package com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.visibility;

import com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.visibility.VisibilityQueue.Message;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

public class WebhookDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: A Worker Crashes Mid-Webhook; Another Finishes It ===");
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-08-15T10:00:00Z");
        VisibilityQueue queue = new VisibilityQueue(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(30));
        queue.send("evt_91", "payment.captured pay_ABC INR 1,499");
        Set<String> settledPayments = new HashSet<>(); // the idempotency record

        Message m1 = queue.receive().orElseThrow();
        System.out.println("worker-A received " + m1.id() + " (attempt " + m1.receiveCount() + ") ... crashed before ack");
        System.out.println("worker-B polls at +5s  : " + queue.receive().map(Message::id).orElse("nothing (message still hidden)"));

        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(31));
        Message m2 = queue.receive().orElseThrow();
        boolean firstTime = settledPayments.add("pay_ABC");
        queue.ack(m2.id());
        System.out.println("worker-B polls at +36s : " + m2.id() + " (attempt " + m2.receiveCount() + "), settled=" + firstTime + ", acked");
        System.out.println("worker-C polls later   : " + queue.receive().map(Message::id).orElse("nothing (done)"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: A Worker Crashes Mid-Webhook; Another Finishes It ===
worker-A received evt_91 (attempt 1) ... crashed before ack
worker-B polls at +5s  : nothing (message still hidden)
worker-B polls at +36s : evt_91 (attempt 2), settled=true, acked
worker-C polls later   : nothing (done)

Why this matters:

  • Delivery is at-least-once: crashes cause redelivery, never silent loss.
  • So consumers must be idempotent (here: a set of settled payment ids).
  • The visibility timeout must exceed the normal processing time, or healthy jobs get processed twice.

docs.title: Example 3: Kafka Consumer Groups and Rebalancing (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: Trip events are on a Kafka topic with 6 partitions, keyed by trip id so each trip's events stay in order. The trip-processing service autoscales from 1 to 7 pods. Kafka divides partitions among group members; when a pod joins or dies, partitions are rebalanced. With more pods than partitions, the extra pod has nothing to do.

Design:

flowchart LR subgraph "trip-events (6 partitions)" P0[p0] & P1[p1] & P2[p2] & P3[p3] & P4[p4] & P5[p5] end P0 & P1 --> A[pod-1] P2 & P3 --> B[pod-2] P4 & P5 --> C[pod-3]

Full Code:

ConsumerGroup.javaConsumerGroupDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.groups;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Kafka-style consumer group: partitions are divided among members; each partition has ONE owner. */
public final class ConsumerGroup {

    private final int partitions;
    private final List<String> members = new ArrayList<>();

    public ConsumerGroup(int partitions) {
        this.partitions = partitions;
    }

    public Map<String, List<Integer>> join(String member) {
        members.add(member);
        return rebalance();
    }

    public Map<String, List<Integer>> leave(String member) {
        members.remove(member);
        return rebalance();
    }

    /** Range assignment, like Kafka's RangeAssignor. */
    private Map<String, List<Integer>> rebalance() { // (1)!
        Map<String, List<Integer>> assignment = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        members.forEach(m -> assignment.put(m, new ArrayList<>()));
        int per = partitions / members.size();
        int extra = partitions % members.size();
        int next = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < members.size(); i++) {
            int count = per + (i < extra ? 1 : 0); // (2)!
            for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
                assignment.get(members.get(i)).add(next++);
            }
        }
        return assignment;
    }

    public static int partitionFor(String key, int partitions) {
        return Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), partitions); // same key -> same partition -> same consumer, in order
    }
}
  1. Every membership change triggers a rebalance: partitions are reassigned so each has exactly one owner in the group.
  2. Range assignment: the first partitions % members consumers get one extra partition.
package com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.groups;

public class ConsumerGroupDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: 'trip-events' (6 partitions) and a Scaling Consumer Group ===");
        ConsumerGroup group = new ConsumerGroup(6);
        System.out.println("pod-1 joins -> " + group.join("pod-1"));
        System.out.println("pod-2 joins -> " + group.join("pod-2"));
        System.out.println("pod-3 joins -> " + group.join("pod-3"));
        group.join("pod-4");
        group.join("pod-5");
        group.join("pod-6");
        System.out.println("pod-7 joins -> " + group.join("pod-7") + "  <- more consumers than partitions: one idles");
        System.out.println("pod-2 dies  -> " + group.leave("pod-2"));
        System.out.println("Trip TRIP-88 always goes to partition " + ConsumerGroup.partitionFor("TRIP-88", 6)
                + ", so its events are processed in order by whoever owns it.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: 'trip-events' (6 partitions) and a Scaling Consumer Group ===
pod-1 joins -> {pod-1=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]}
pod-2 joins -> {pod-1=[0, 1, 2], pod-2=[3, 4, 5]}
pod-3 joins -> {pod-1=[0, 1], pod-2=[2, 3], pod-3=[4, 5]}
pod-7 joins -> {pod-1=[0], pod-2=[1], pod-3=[2], pod-4=[3], pod-5=[4], pod-6=[5], pod-7=[]}  <- more consumers than partitions: one idles
pod-2 dies  -> {pod-1=[0], pod-3=[1], pod-4=[2], pod-5=[3], pod-6=[4], pod-7=[5]}
Trip TRIP-88 always goes to partition 2, so its events are processed in order by whoever owns it.

Why consumer groups here:

  • Competition happens per partition, which preserves per-trip ordering.
  • Parallelism is capped by the partition count: choose it for peak load up front.
  • Failover is automatic: a dead pod's partitions move to survivors.
Unit Tests: CompetingConsumersTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.groups.ConsumerGroup;
import com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.invoices.InvoiceWorkers;
import com.handbook.microservices.competingconsumers.visibility.VisibilityQueue;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class CompetingConsumersTest {

    @Test
    void everyMessageIsProcessedExactlyOnceByTheGroup() throws Exception {
        InvoiceWorkers w = new InvoiceWorkers();
        for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
            w.publish("O" + i);
        }
        w.runWith(3);
        assertThat(w.processedCount()).hasSize(50).allSatisfy((k, v) -> assertThat(v).isEqualTo(1));
        assertThat(w.maxParallel()).isBetween(1, 3);
    }

    @Test
    void unackedMessageReappearsAfterVisibilityTimeout() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        VisibilityQueue q = new VisibilityQueue(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        q.send("m", "x");
        q.receive();
        assertThat(q.receive()).isEmpty();
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        assertThat(q.receive()).get().extracting(VisibilityQueue.Message::receiveCount).isEqualTo(2);
    }

    @Test
    void partitionsAreSplitWithoutOverlap() {
        ConsumerGroup g = new ConsumerGroup(5);
        g.join("a");
        Map<String, List<Integer>> a = g.join("b");
        assertThat(a.get("a")).containsExactly(0, 1, 2);
        assertThat(a.get("b")).containsExactly(3, 4);
        assertThat(a.values().stream().flatMap(List::stream).collect(Collectors.toSet())).hasSize(5);
    }
}

docs.text: Where Competing consumers Kafka Consumer groups, cooperative-sticky rebalancing, max.poll.interval.ms RabbitMQ Multiple consumers on a queue, basic.qos prefetch, manual acks, DLX AWS SQS Visibility timeout, maxReceiveCount → redrive to DLQ, FIFO message groups JMS / ActiveMQ Queue receivers, CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE Spring @KafkaListener(concurrency), @RabbitListener, @SqsListener, DefaultErrorHandler Kubernetes KEDA ScaledObject on Kafka lag / SQS depth

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Horizontal scaling by adding consumers No global ordering across consumers Load levelling: spikes become queue depth, not outages At-least-once delivery: duplicates must be handled Fault tolerance: unacked work is redelivered Poison messages can loop without a DLQ Producers and consumers deploy independently Kafka parallelism capped by partitions; rebalances pause processing

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Non-idempotent consumers

Redelivery after a crash, a rebalance or a visibility timeout is normal. Without idempotency, customers get two emails, or two refunds.

No dead-letter queue

A message that always fails is retried forever, burning capacity and (in Kafka) blocking its partition. Retry a bounded number of times, then dead-letter (coding challenge).

Visibility timeout shorter than processing time

A 30 s job with a 20 s timeout gets processed twice, every time. Size the timeout from p99 processing time, or extend it while working.

Expecting order from a plain queue

Ten consumers process messages in parallel; message 2 may finish before message 1. Use a key-partitioned log or FIFO groups for per-entity order.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Capacity planning. Consumers needed ≈ arrival rate × processing time (Little's law). 200 msg/s × 0.4 s = 80 concurrent jobs. For Kafka, provision partitions for the peak consumer count you'll ever need; increasing partitions later changes key → partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering for in-flight keys.

Rebalance storms. In Kafka, slow processing beyond max.poll.interval.ms makes the broker think the consumer died, triggering rebalances, redelivery and more slowness. Use smaller max.poll.records, cooperative-sticky assignment, static membership (group.instance.id) and offload slow work.

Back-pressure to producers. A queue absorbs spikes, not sustained overload. Alert on age of the oldest message (not just depth), and shed or degrade at the producer when the backlog SLO is breached.

War story: every webhook processed twice

A team moved webhook handling to SQS with the default 30 s visibility timeout. The handler called a slow bank API (p99 45 s). Every slow message became visible again mid-processing and a second worker settled it too: 2,300 merchants were credited twice in one day. Fix: visibility timeout raised to 5 minutes with periodic extension (ChangeMessageVisibility) for long jobs, an idempotency table keyed by payment id, and a DLQ after 5 receives. Lesson: at-least-once is a promise of duplicates. Size timeouts and make consumers idempotent.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Competing Consumers Publish-Subscribe Producer-Consumer Thread Pool Each message goes to One consumer Every subscriber (group) One consumer thread One worker thread Scope Across processes/machines Across services In one process In one process Purpose Scale processing Broadcast events Decouple rates Reuse threads

Kafka does both: consumers in the same group compete; different groups each get every message (pub-sub). See also Producer-Consumer, Idempotent Consumer and Backpressure.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One queue, many identical consumers; each message to one.
  • Ack after success; unacked = redelivered (at-least-once).
  • Consumers idempotent; bounded retries → DLQ.
  • Kafka: one owner per partition; parallelism ≤ partitions; key = order.
  • Scale on lag / oldest-message age.
@KafkaListener(topics = "invoice-jobs", groupId = "invoice-renderer", concurrency = "4") void on(Job j) { ... }

docs.title: Externalized Configuration & Config Server
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Keep configuration outside the deployable artifact, so the same build runs in dev, test and prod with different settings. A config server (or Kubernetes ConfigMaps) serves versioned configuration per service and environment, supports refresh without redeploys, and secrets come from a dedicated secret store. Build once, configure per environment, never commit secrets.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: 40 services × 4 environments. Database URLs, timeouts, feature flags and partner endpoints are baked into each JAR's application.properties. Changing a timeout means rebuilding and redeploying. Someone committed the production DB password to Git. Nobody knows which timeout is actually running in prod.

Definition (The Twelve-Factor App, factor III):

Store config in the environment. An app's config is everything that is likely to vary between deploys (staging, production, developer environments, etc.).

Kind of setting Where it belongs Per-environment values (URLs, pool sizes, timeouts) Config server / ConfigMaps, versioned in Git Feature flags and kill switches Config with refresh, or a feature-flag service Secrets (passwords, API keys, certificates) Secret store (Vault, AWS/GCP/Azure secret managers), never Git Code-level constants that never vary In code

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A restaurant chain's recipe book and daily specials board

Every branch uses the same kitchen equipment (the build). Head office publishes the menu and prices for each city (config per environment) and can change today's specials on the board without retraining cooks (refresh). The safe's combination (secrets) is never written on the board; managers get it from the security office.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     G[(Git repo<br/>application.yml<br/>order-service-prod.yml)] --> CS[Config server]     V[(Vault / Secrets Manager)] -.-> S1     CS --> S1[order-service prod]     CS --> S2[cart-service prod]     G -->|webhook on commit| BUS[[Refresh bus]] --> S1     BUS --> S2 Participant Responsibility Config repository Versioned, reviewed configuration files per app and profile Config server Merges files by precedence; serves them over HTTP Service Loads config at startup; rebinds on refresh; fails fast on invalid config Secret store Holds secrets with access policies, audit and rotation

docs.text:
# src/main/resources/application.properties: built into the JAR
payment.url=https://payments.prod.internal
payment.timeout.ms=5000
db.password=Sup3rS3cret!        # in Git history forever

docs.title: Example 1: Profiles and Precedence (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: One config repo holds application (global defaults), application-prod, order-service and order-service-prod. The server merges them from least to most specific. The demo prints each resolved property with the file it came from, which is exactly what you need when debugging "why is the timeout 800 in prod?".

Full Code:

ConfigServer.javaConfigProfilesDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.config.profiles;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/**
 * A config server (Spring Cloud Config style) backed by a Git repo of property files.
 * For an application and profile it merges, from lowest to highest precedence:
 * application → application-{profile} → {app} → {app}-{profile}.
 */
public final class ConfigServer {

    public record Resolved(Map<String, String> properties, Map<String, String> sourceOf) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Map<String, String>> files = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // "file name" → properties

    public ConfigServer file(String name, Map<String, String> properties) {
        files.put(name, properties);
        return this;
    }

    public Resolved resolve(String app, String profile) {
        List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(List.of( // (1)!
                "application", "application-" + profile, app, app + "-" + profile));
        Map<String, String> merged = new TreeMap<>();
        Map<String, String> source = new TreeMap<>();
        for (String file : order) {
            files.getOrDefault(file, Map.of()).forEach((k, v) -> { // (2)!
                merged.put(k, v);
                source.put(k, file);
            });
        }
        return new Resolved(merged, source);
    }
}
  1. Precedence order, the same as Spring Cloud Config: global → global-profile → app → app-profile.
  2. Later files override earlier ones; we remember the source of each value for debugging.
package com.handbook.microservices.config.profiles;

import java.util.Map;

public class ConfigProfilesDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var server = new ConfigServer()
                .file("application", Map.of(
                        "logging.level", "INFO",
                        "http.timeout.ms", "2000",
                        "tracing.sample.ratio", "0.1"))
                .file("application-prod", Map.of(
                        "logging.level", "WARN"))
                .file("order-service", Map.of(
                        "order.max.items", "50",
                        "payment.url", "http://payment-service"))
                .file("order-service-prod", Map.of(
                        "order.max.items", "100",
                        "http.timeout.ms", "800"));

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: one config repo, many services and environments ===");
        for (String profile : new String[] {"dev", "prod"}) {
            var resolved = server.resolve("order-service", profile);
            System.out.println("order-service [" + profile + "]");
            resolved.properties().forEach((k, v) ->
                    System.out.printf("  %-22s = %-22s (from %s)%n", k, v, resolved.sourceOf().get(k)));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: one config repo, many services and environments ===
order-service [dev]
  http.timeout.ms        = 2000                   (from application)
  logging.level          = INFO                   (from application)
  order.max.items        = 50                     (from order-service)
  payment.url            = http://payment-service (from order-service)
  tracing.sample.ratio   = 0.1                    (from application)
order-service [prod]
  http.timeout.ms        = 800                    (from order-service-prod)
  logging.level          = WARN                   (from application-prod)
  order.max.items        = 100                    (from order-service-prod)
  payment.url            = http://payment-service (from order-service)
  tracing.sample.ratio   = 0.1                    (from application)

Why a config server here:

  • Shared defaults in one place; overrides only where needed.
  • Every change is a reviewed Git commit: who changed the prod timeout and why.

docs.title: Example 2: Refresh Without Restart (Fintech)
docs.text:
Scenario: The UPI partner has an outage. Ops sets upi.enabled=false in Git; the refresh event reaches every instance and the flag flips without a deploy. Later UPI is re-enabled with a temporarily lower limit. Listeners log what changed.

Full Code:

RefreshableConfig.javaFeatureFlagRefreshDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.config.refresh;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.BiConsumer;

/**
 * Holds the current configuration and notifies listeners when a refresh changes a value, like
 * Spring Cloud Bus broadcasting a refresh to every instance and @RefreshScope beans rebinding.
 */
public final class RefreshableConfig {

    private final Map<String, String> values = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<BiConsumer<String, String>> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    private long version;

    public RefreshableConfig(Map<String, String> initial) {
        values.putAll(initial);
    }

    public String get(String key) {
        return values.get(key);
    }

    public void onChange(BiConsumer<String, String> listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
    }

    /** Called when the config server reports a new version (webhook from Git → bus → instance). */
    public synchronized void refresh(Map<String, String> latest) { // (1)!
        version++;
        new TreeMap<>(latest).forEach((k, v) -> {
            if (!v.equals(values.put(k, v))) { // (2)!
                listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(k, v));
            }
        });
    }

    public synchronized long version() {
        return version;
    }
}
  1. Triggered by the config server / Spring Cloud Bus (or a Kubernetes ConfigMap watch).
  2. Only changed keys notify listeners, like EnvironmentChangeEvent in Spring.
package com.handbook.microservices.config.refresh;

import java.util.Map;

public class FeatureFlagRefreshDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var config = new RefreshableConfig(Map.of("upi.enabled", "true", "upi.max.amount", "100000"));
        config.onChange((key, value) -> System.out.println("    [refresh] " + key + " -> " + value));

        System.out.println("=== Fintech: switching a payment method off without a deploy ===");
        System.out.println("pay ₹500 by UPI   : " + pay(config, 500));
        System.out.println("-- the UPI partner reports an outage; ops flips the flag in Git --");
        config.refresh(Map.of("upi.enabled", "false", "upi.max.amount", "100000"));
        System.out.println("pay ₹500 by UPI   : " + pay(config, 500));
        System.out.println("-- partner recovers, with a temporary lower limit --");
        config.refresh(Map.of("upi.enabled", "true", "upi.max.amount", "20000"));
        System.out.println("pay ₹500 by UPI   : " + pay(config, 500));
        System.out.println("pay ₹50,000 by UPI: " + pay(config, 50_000));
        System.out.println("config version " + config.version() + ", zero restarts");
    }

    private static String pay(RefreshableConfig config, long rupees) {
        if (!Boolean.parseBoolean(config.get("upi.enabled"))) {
            return "UPI temporarily unavailable, please use a card";
        }
        if (rupees > Long.parseLong(config.get("upi.max.amount"))) {
            return "amount above the current UPI limit";
        }
        return "paid";
    }
}

Output:

=== Fintech: switching a payment method off without a deploy ===
pay ₹500 by UPI   : paid
-- the UPI partner reports an outage; ops flips the flag in Git --
    [refresh] upi.enabled -> false
pay ₹500 by UPI   : UPI temporarily unavailable, please use a card
-- partner recovers, with a temporary lower limit --
    [refresh] upi.enabled -> true
    [refresh] upi.max.amount -> 20000
pay ₹500 by UPI   : paid
pay ₹50,000 by UPI: amount above the current UPI limit
config version 2, zero restarts

Why refresh here:

  • Kill switches and limits need to change in seconds, not after a 20-minute pipeline.
  • Caution: not every setting is safe to change live (pool sizes, ports). Refresh only what's designed for it.

docs.title: Example 3: Secret References (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: The medical-records service's Git config contains only references (vault:secret/records/db#password). At startup, the service resolves them from Vault (an audited read with a short-lived token), keeps the values only in memory, and masks them in every log.

Full Code:

SecretResolver.javaSecretsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.config.secrets;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Configuration in Git holds only REFERENCES to secrets ({@code vault:path#key}). At startup the
 * service resolves them from the secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) into memory, and every
 * printout masks them.
 */
public final class SecretResolver {

    private static final String PREFIX = "vault:";

    private final Function<String, String> secretStore;

    public SecretResolver(Function<String, String> secretStore) {
        this.secretStore = secretStore;
    }

    public Map<String, String> resolve(Map<String, String> config) {
        Map<String, String> resolved = new TreeMap<>();
        config.forEach((k, v) -> resolved.put(k, v.startsWith(PREFIX) ? secretStore.apply(v.substring(PREFIX.length())) : v)); // (1)!
        return resolved;
    }

    public static Map<String, String> masked(Map<String, String> config, Map<String, String> original) {
        Map<String, String> safe = new TreeMap<>();
        config.forEach((k, v) -> safe.put(k, original.get(k).startsWith(PREFIX) ? "******" : v)); // (2)!
        return safe;
    }
}
  1. Only values with the vault: prefix are resolved; everything else passes through.
  2. Mask secrets in anything printable: logs, actuator endpoints, error messages.
package com.handbook.microservices.config.secrets;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class SecretsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, String> fromGit = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(
                "db.url", "jdbc:postgresql://records-db:5432/records",
                "db.username", "records_svc",
                "db.password", "vault:secret/records/db#password",
                "lab.api.key", "vault:secret/records/lab#apiKey"));
        Map<String, String> vault = Map.of(
                "secret/records/db#password", "s3cr3t-rotated-2026-10",
                "secret/records/lab#apiKey", "lab-key-9f2c");

        var resolver = new SecretResolver(path -> {
            System.out.println("    vault read " + path + " (audited, short-lived token)");
            return vault.get(path);
        });

        System.out.println("=== Healthcare: secrets are references in Git, values only in memory ===");
        System.out.println("committed to Git : " + fromGit);
        Map<String, String> runtime = resolver.resolve(fromGit);
        System.out.println("logged at startup: " + SecretResolver.masked(runtime, fromGit));
        System.out.println("db.password usable by the DataSource: " + (runtime.get("db.password").length() > 0));
    }
}

Output:

=== Healthcare: secrets are references in Git, values only in memory ===
committed to Git : {db.password=vault:secret/records/db#password, db.url=jdbc:postgresql://records-db:5432/records, db.username=records_svc, lab.api.key=vault:secret/records/lab#apiKey}
    vault read secret/records/db#password (audited, short-lived token)
    vault read secret/records/lab#apiKey (audited, short-lived token)
logged at startup: {db.password=******, db.url=jdbc:postgresql://records-db:5432/records, db.username=records_svc, lab.api.key=******}
db.password usable by the DataSource: true

Why a secret store here:

  • Health data regulations require access control and audit for credentials.
  • Rotation happens in Vault; services pick up new values without code changes.
  • A leaked Git repo leaks no passwords.
Unit Tests: ConfigServerTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.config.profiles.ConfigServer;
import com.handbook.microservices.config.validation.CheckoutConfig;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ConfigServerTest {

    @Test
    void mostSpecificFileWins() {
        var server = new ConfigServer()
                .file("application", Map.of("k", "global"))
                .file("svc", Map.of("k", "svc"))
                .file("svc-prod", Map.of("k", "svc-prod"));
        assertThat(server.resolve("svc", "prod").properties()).containsEntry("k", "svc-prod");
        assertThat(server.resolve("svc", "dev").properties()).containsEntry("k", "svc");
        assertThat(server.resolve("other", "dev").properties()).containsEntry("k", "global");
    }

    @Test
    void invalidConfigFailsWithAllErrors() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> CheckoutConfig.bind(Map.of("checkout.max-items", "0")))
                .hasMessageContaining("max-items must be")
                .hasMessageContaining("payment-timeout is missing")
                .hasMessageContaining("payment-url is missing");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Typed configuration in Spring Boot (compiled in the spring-reference module):

package com.handbook.springref.config;

import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;

import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Duration;

/**
 * Typed configuration bound from checkout.* properties (from application.yml, environment
 * variables, or a config server). Register with @EnableConfigurationProperties or
 * @ConfigurationPropertiesScan. Validation in the compact constructor makes startup fail fast;
 * with spring-boot-starter-validation you would use @Validated and @Min/@NotNull instead.
 */
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "checkout")
public record CheckoutProperties(int maxItems, Duration paymentTimeout, URI paymentUrl) {

    public CheckoutProperties {
        if (maxItems < 1 || maxItems > 500) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("checkout.max-items must be 1..500");
        }
        if (paymentTimeout == null || paymentTimeout.isZero()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("checkout.payment-timeout is required");
        }
        if (paymentUrl == null || !"https".equals(paymentUrl.getScheme())) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("checkout.payment-url must be an https URL");
        }
    }
}

# order-service: bootstrap from a config server and Vault (reference)
spring:
  application.name: order-service
  profiles.active: prod
  config.import:
    - "configserver:http://config-server:8888"
    - "vault://"                     # spring-cloud-vault: resolves secret/order-service
checkout:
  max-items: 100
  payment-timeout: 2s
  payment-url: https://payments.internal
Option Notes Spring Cloud Config Git/Vault-backed server, profiles, /actuator/refresh, Spring Cloud Bus Kubernetes ConfigMaps + Secrets Native; mounted as files or env vars; Spring Cloud Kubernetes can reload Consul KV / etcd Key-value config with watches AWS AppConfig / Azure App Configuration Managed config with validation and gradual rollout Feature-flag services (OpenFeature, Unleash, LaunchDarkly) Per-user targeting, experiments, audit External Secrets Operator Syncs cloud secret managers into Kubernetes Secrets

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Externalized configuration Spring Boot @ConfigurationProperties, profiles, spring.config.import, relaxed binding from env vars Spring Cloud Config Config server + @RefreshScope MicroProfile Config (Quarkus, Helidon) @ConfigProperty, config sources by ordinal HashiCorp Vault Dynamic database credentials, leases, rotation Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Secrets, projected volumes

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Build once, deploy anywhere Config server is a dependency at startup (cache it, make it HA) Versioned, reviewed config changes Bad config can break all instances at once Live changes for flags and limits Refresh semantics can be surprising Secrets managed and audited properly More moving parts (server, bus, vault)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Secrets in Git (even encrypted, even in a private repo)

History is forever, and repos get cloned to laptops and CI logs. Use references to a secret store; scan repositories for secrets (gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning).

Config changes without validation or rollout

A typo in a shared application.yml reaches every service at once. Validate on startup (fail fast), and roll out config changes gradually like code.

Everything refreshable

Changing a connection-pool size or a port on a running instance can half-apply. Mark which properties support refresh; restart for the rest.

Environment-specific code paths

if (env.equals("prod")) in code defeats externalized config. Express differences as configuration values.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Config is code. Changes go through pull requests, reviews, CI validation (schema checks, policy-as-code) and gradual rollout (one region or canary instances first). Many outages are config changes, not code changes.

Startup resilience. If the config server is down, can services start? Use fail-fast deliberately: fail for critical config, or start with a cached last-known-good copy. Run the config server HA; consider baking defaults into images.

Secrets lifecycle. Prefer dynamic secrets (Vault issues a database user per service instance with a lease) over long-lived passwords; rotate automatically; use workload identity (Kubernetes service accounts, cloud IAM) to authenticate to the secret store, so there's no "secret zero" in config.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• No environment-specific values or secrets in artifacts; one build for all environments.
  • Config in Git with reviews; history and owners clear.
  • Typed, validated config; fail fast at startup with all errors listed.
  • Refresh only for properties designed for it (flags, limits); others need a restart.
  • Secrets from a secret store via workload identity; rotation; masked in logs and actuator.
  • Config server/ConfigMap changes rolled out gradually and monitored.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Each service is built once and configured per environment. Non-secret config lives in Git and is served by Spring Cloud Config (or ConfigMaps on Kubernetes), with defaults in application.yml and overrides per service and profile. Services bind it into validated @ConfigurationProperties records and fail fast on invalid values. Kill switches and limits are refreshable via the bus; anything else needs a rolling restart. Secrets come from Vault using the pod's service account, with dynamic, rotated database credentials, and they're masked in logs. Config changes go through PRs and canary rollout like code."

War story: the timeout that took down every service

A platform team changed the shared application.yml to reduce http.client.timeout from 5000 to 500 (meaning 500 ms) for one service, but the property was read by all 60 services. Within a minute of the refresh event, every service started timing out calls to slower dependencies; error rates hit 30% across the company. Fix: rolled back the commit; moved the override to the service's own file; added CI checks that flag changes to global config, a staged refresh (one service group at a time), and typed properties with units (500ms). Lesson: a shared configuration file is shared code. Review it, test it, and roll it out gradually.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Config Server ConfigMaps Feature-flag service Secret store Content Any config, per app/profile Any config, per namespace Flags, targeting rules Credentials, keys, certs Live change Refresh via bus File watch / restart Real-time Leases, rotation Audit Git history K8s audit Built-in Built-in, detailed

See Service Discovery (often the same platform, e.g. Consul) and Strangler Fig (feature flags for rollout).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Build once, configure per environment (12-factor).
  • Precedence: global → global-profile → app → app-profile.
  • Typed + validated config, fail fast.
  • Refresh only flags/limits; restart for structural settings.
  • Secrets in a secret store, referenced, masked, rotated.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a region dimension to ConfigServer (order-service-prod-eu) with the right precedence.
  • Make RefreshableConfig reject a refresh that fails validation and keep the old values.
  • Add masking for any key containing password, secret or token, even without a vault: reference.
