docs.title: Decomposition (by Business Capability / Subdomain)
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Split a system into services along business capabilities (what the business does) or DDD subdomains, so each service owns its data and can change and deploy independently. The test of a good boundary: most use cases write inside one service. If a common use case must update data in two services at once, the boundary is probably wrong.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a grocery monolith has catalog, inventory, orders, payments and delivery in one codebase and one database. Every team deploys together, a bad inventory query slows checkout, and a change to the products table breaks four teams. Microservices promise independent teams and deployments, but only if the boundaries are right. Split badly (by technical layer, or by today's org chart) and you get a distributed monolith: all the network problems, none of the independence.

Definitions (microservices.io / DDD):

  • Decompose by business capability: a service per thing the business does (catalog, inventory, ordering, billing), stable over time even as technology and org charts change.
  • Decompose by subdomain (DDD): model the domain, find bounded contexts where a term has one meaning ("Trip" in dispatch vs. billing), and align services with them.
Subdomain type Meaning Strategy Core Where you compete (pricing, matching, recommendations) Build in-house, best engineers Supporting Necessary, specific to you (catalog admin) Build simply, or customize Generic Same for everyone (auth, email, payments gateway) Buy or use a SaaS

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A hospital's departments

A hospital isn't organized by "people who use computers" and "people who use phones". It's organized by capability: emergency, radiology, pharmacy, billing. Each department has its own records and staff, and they coordinate through well-defined requests (a lab order, a discharge summary). A reorganization of managers doesn't move the pharmacy.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph Monolith["Before: one deployable, one DB"]         M[Catalog + Inventory + Orders + Payments] --> DB[(Shared DB)]     end     subgraph Services["After: services by business capability"]         C[Catalog] --> CDB[(catalog DB)]         I[Inventory] --> IDB[(inventory DB)]         O[Ordering] --> ODB[(orders DB)]         O -- "API: canFulfil?" --> I         O -- "event: OrderPlaced" --> I         I -- "event: StockLow" --> C     end Rule Why Each service owns its data No shared tables, so services can change their schema independently Integrate via APIs and events Explicit contracts instead of hidden coupling Most use cases write in one service Avoids distributed transactions A team owns each service end to end Conway's Law: the architecture mirrors communication paths

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Split by technical layer:      web-service, business-service, data-service    <- every feature touches all three
Split by current teams:        Registration, Doctors, Scheduling, Billing, Payments  <- org chart changes yearly
Split by entities (nouns):     CustomerService, ProductService, OrderService   <- "entity services": chatty, anemic
Shared database:               everyone reads/writes the same tables           <- distributed monolith
  • Every feature spans several services: coordinated deployments.
  • Distributed transactions for common use cases.
  • Chatty calls between services that should have been one.

docs.title: Example 1: Grocery Monolith Split by Business Capability (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A quick-commerce company splits its monolith into Catalog (what we sell and how it's shown), Inventory (units in each dark store) and Ordering (the order lifecycle). Ordering checks stock through Inventory's API, never its tables; Inventory announces events (StockLow) that Catalog uses to update the "only 1 left" badge. Each service could now be deployed, scaled and changed by its own team.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant O as Ordering participant I as Inventory participant C as Catalog O->>I: canFulfil(MANGO-1KG, 2)? (API) I-->>O: yes O-)I: OrderPlaced (event) I->>I: reserve 2, 1 left I-)C: StockLow(left=1) (event) C->>C: badge "only 1 left"

Full Code:

GroceryServices.javaEventBus.java (support)GroceryDecompositionDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Three services split by BUSINESS CAPABILITY. Each owns its data (a private map standing in
 * for its own database) and talks to the others only through APIs and events.
 */
public final class GroceryServices {

    private GroceryServices() {
    }

    public record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String sku, int qty) {
    }

    public record StockLow(String sku, int left) {
    }

    /** Catalog: what we sell, how it's described, whether to show it as available. */
    public static class CatalogService {
        private final Map<String, String> products = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", "Alphonso mangoes, 1 kg"));
        private final Map<String, Boolean> showAsAvailable = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", true));

        public CatalogService(EventBus bus) {
            bus.<StockLow>subscribe("inventory.stock-low", e -> { // (1)!
                showAsAvailable.put(e.sku(), e.left() > 0);
                System.out.println("  [catalog] " + e.sku() + " badge -> " + (e.left() > 0 ? "only " + e.left() + " left" : "out of stock"));
            });
        }

        public String describe(String sku) {
            return products.get(sku) + (showAsAvailable.get(sku) ? "" : " (out of stock)");
        }
    }

    /** Inventory: how many units each dark store physically has. */
    public static class InventoryService {
        private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", 3));
        private final EventBus bus;

        public InventoryService(EventBus bus) {
            this.bus = bus;
            bus.<OrderPlaced>subscribe("orders.placed", e -> {
                int left = stock.merge(e.sku(), -e.qty(), Integer::sum);
                System.out.println("  [inventory] reserved " + e.qty() + " x " + e.sku() + ", " + left + " left");
                if (left <= 1) {
                    bus.publish("inventory.stock-low", new StockLow(e.sku(), left));
                }
            });
        }

        public boolean canFulfil(String sku, int qty) { // a synchronous API other services may call
            return stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0) >= qty;
        }
    }

    /** Ordering: the order lifecycle. It asks Inventory through its API, never reads its tables. */
    public static class OrderService {
        private final InventoryService inventoryApi;
        private final EventBus bus;
        private int next = 1;

        public OrderService(InventoryService inventoryApi, EventBus bus) {
            this.inventoryApi = inventoryApi;
            this.bus = bus;
        }

        public String place(String sku, int qty) {
            if (!inventoryApi.canFulfil(sku, qty)) { // (2)!
                return "rejected: not enough " + sku;
            }
            String id = "ORD-" + next++;
            bus.publish("orders.placed", new OrderPlaced(id, sku, qty)); // (3)!
            return "accepted " + id;
        }
    }

    public static List<String> ownership() {
        return List.of(
                "Catalog   owns: product names, descriptions, images, availability badge",
                "Inventory owns: units per dark store, reservations",
                "Ordering  owns: orders, order lifecycle");
    }
}
  1. Catalog reacts to Inventory's events instead of reading Inventory's tables. It keeps its own copy of what it needs (the badge).
  2. A synchronous API call for a question that needs a fresh answer before accepting the order.
  3. An event for something that already happened. Inventory decides what reservation means.
package com.handbook.microservices.support;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * A tiny, synchronous, in-memory stand-in for a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
 * Real brokers are asynchronous and at-least-once; the examples call that out where it matters.
 */
public final class EventBus {

    private final Map<String, List<Consumer<Object>>> subscribers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final boolean log;

    public EventBus(boolean log) {
        this.log = log;
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <T> void subscribe(String topic, Consumer<T> handler) {
        subscribers.computeIfAbsent(topic, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e -> handler.accept((T) e));
    }

    public void publish(String topic, Object event) {
        if (log) {
            System.out.println("  [bus] " + topic + " <- " + event);
        }
        for (Consumer<Object> s : subscribers.getOrDefault(topic, List.of())) {
            s.accept(event);
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery.GroceryServices.*;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;

public class GroceryDecompositionDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Monolith Split by Business Capability ===");
        GroceryServices.ownership().forEach(System.out::println);
        EventBus bus = new EventBus(true);
        CatalogService catalog = new CatalogService(bus);
        InventoryService inventory = new InventoryService(bus);
        OrderService orders = new OrderService(inventory, bus);

        System.out.println("Customer 1 orders 2 mangoes:");
        System.out.println("  -> " + orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 2));
        System.out.println("Customer 2 orders 2 mangoes:");
        System.out.println("  -> " + orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 2));
        System.out.println("Customer 3 orders 1 mango:");
        System.out.println("  -> " + orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 1));
        System.out.println("Catalog page now shows: " + catalog.describe("MANGO-1KG"));
    }
}

Output (happy path and failure path):

=== Grocery: Monolith Split by Business Capability ===
Catalog   owns: product names, descriptions, images, availability badge
Inventory owns: units per dark store, reservations
Ordering  owns: orders, order lifecycle
Customer 1 orders 2 mangoes:
  [bus] orders.placed <- OrderPlaced[orderId=ORD-1, sku=MANGO-1KG, qty=2]
  [inventory] reserved 2 x MANGO-1KG, 1 left
  [bus] inventory.stock-low <- StockLow[sku=MANGO-1KG, left=1]
  [catalog] MANGO-1KG badge -> only 1 left
  -> accepted ORD-1
Customer 2 orders 2 mangoes:
  -> rejected: not enough MANGO-1KG
Customer 3 orders 1 mango:
  [bus] orders.placed <- OrderPlaced[orderId=ORD-2, sku=MANGO-1KG, qty=1]
  [inventory] reserved 1 x MANGO-1KG, 0 left
  [bus] inventory.stock-low <- StockLow[sku=MANGO-1KG, left=0]
  [catalog] MANGO-1KG badge -> out of stock
  -> accepted ORD-2
Catalog page now shows: Alphonso mangoes, 1 kg (out of stock)

Why this boundary:

  • Each capability has its own data and rules (reservation logic stays in Inventory).
  • Catalog stays fast and available even if Inventory is slow: it uses its own copy of the badge.
  • Teams map one-to-one to services.

docs.title: Example 2: One Word, Two Bounded Contexts (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: In a ride-hailing company, Dispatch thinks of a trip as a driver, a pickup location, an ETA and a status. Billing thinks of a trip as base fare, distance fare, time fare and surge. A single shared Trip class (and table) would grow 60 columns, couple both teams, and make every change risky. Instead, each bounded context has its own Trip model, and Dispatch publishes a small, stable TripCompleted event that Billing translates into its model.

Design:

flowchart LR subgraph Dispatch["Dispatch context"] DT["Trip: driverId, pickup lat/lng, etaMinutes, status"] end subgraph Billing["Billing context"] BT["Trip: baseFare, distanceFare, timeFare, surge, total"] end DT -- "TripCompleted(tripId, riderId, km, minutes, city)" --> BT

Full Code:

TripContexts.javaTripContextsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * The word "Trip" means different things in two bounded contexts. Each context has its OWN model;
 * they integrate through a published event, not a shared Trip class or shared table.
 */
public final class TripContexts {

    private TripContexts() {
    }

    // ---------- Dispatch context: moving cars around the city ----------
    public static final class Dispatch {
        public record Trip(String id, String driverId, double pickupLat, double pickupLng, int etaMinutes, String status) { // (1)!
        }

        /** The public contract Dispatch publishes. Deliberately small and stable. */
        public record TripCompleted(String tripId, String riderId, double distanceKm, int durationMin, String city) { // (2)!
        }

        private final List<Consumer<TripCompleted>> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

        public void onTripCompleted(Consumer<TripCompleted> l) {
            listeners.add(l);
        }

        public void complete(Trip trip, String riderId, double km, int minutes) {
            System.out.println("  [dispatch] " + trip.id() + " completed by driver " + trip.driverId() + " (ETA was " + trip.etaMinutes() + " min)");
            listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(new TripCompleted(trip.id(), riderId, km, minutes, "Bengaluru")));
        }
    }

    // ---------- Billing context: charging riders ----------
    public static final class Billing {
        public record Trip(String id, String riderId, int baseFare, int distanceFare, int timeFare, int surge, int totalInr) { // (3)!
        }

        private final List<Trip> invoiced = new ArrayList<>();

        public void handle(Dispatch.TripCompleted e) { // translate THEIR language into OURS
            int base = 50;
            int distance = (int) Math.round(e.distanceKm() * 14);
            int time = e.durationMin() * 2;
            int surge = e.city().equals("Bengaluru") ? 20 : 0;
            Trip t = new Trip(e.tripId(), e.riderId(), base, distance, time, surge, base + distance + time + surge);
            invoiced.add(t);
            System.out.println("  [billing] invoice " + t);
        }

        public List<Trip> invoiced() {
            return invoiced;
        }
    }
}
  1. Dispatch's model: what matters for moving cars.
  2. The published contract between contexts: small, explicit, versioned. It's not either side's internal model.
  3. Billing's model: what matters for charging money. Same word, different concept.
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing.TripContexts.Billing;
import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing.TripContexts.Dispatch;

public class TripContextsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: One Word, Two Bounded Contexts ===");
        Dispatch dispatch = new Dispatch();
        Billing billing = new Billing();
        dispatch.onTripCompleted(billing::handle);

        Dispatch.Trip trip = new Dispatch.Trip("TRIP-77", "DRV-12", 12.9352, 77.6245, 4, "IN_PROGRESS");
        dispatch.complete(trip, "RIDER-5", 8.4, 23);
        System.out.println("Dispatch's Trip has GPS + ETA; Billing's Trip has fare components. Neither knows the other's model.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: One Word, Two Bounded Contexts ===
  [dispatch] TRIP-77 completed by driver DRV-12 (ETA was 4 min)
  [billing] invoice Trip[id=TRIP-77, riderId=RIDER-5, baseFare=50, distanceFare=118, timeFare=46, surge=20, totalInr=234]
Dispatch's Trip has GPS + ETA; Billing's Trip has fare components. Neither knows the other's model.

Why bounded contexts here:

  • The ubiquitous language differs between teams; forcing one model makes both worse.
  • The event is the boundary: each side can evolve its internals freely.
  • Billing can add surge rules without touching Dispatch, and vice versa.

docs.title: Example 3: Checking Candidate Splits Against Use Cases (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: A hospital IT department wants to break up its patient-management system. One architect proposes splitting by current teams (Registration, Doctors, Scheduling, Billing, Payments); another by business capability (PatientRecords, Scheduling, Billing). Before writing code, they check each split against the real use cases: which ones would have to write data owned by two services in one transaction?

Design:

flowchart TB U[Use cases + tables they write/read] --> C{BoundaryChecker} S1[Split A: by teams] --> C S2[Split B: by capability] --> C C --> R1["Split A: 3 cross-service writes"] C --> R2["Split B: 1 cross-service write"]

Full Code:

BoundaryChecker.javaBoundaryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * Checks a proposed service split against the system's use cases: a use case that must WRITE
 * data owned by two services in one transaction is a warning sign (distributed transaction).
 */
public final class BoundaryChecker {

    public record UseCase(String name, Set<String> writes, Set<String> reads) {
    }

    private BoundaryChecker() {
    }

    public static Map<String, String> check(Map<String, String> tableOwner, List<UseCase> useCases) {
        Map<String, String> report = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (UseCase uc : useCases) {
            Set<String> writeOwners = new TreeSet<>();
            uc.writes().forEach(t -> writeOwners.add(tableOwner.get(t)));
            Set<String> readOwners = new TreeSet<>();
            uc.reads().forEach(t -> readOwners.add(tableOwner.get(t)));
            readOwners.removeAll(writeOwners);
            String verdict;
            if (writeOwners.size() > 1) {
                verdict = "WARN writes span " + writeOwners + " -> needs a saga or a different boundary"; // (1)!
            } else if (!readOwners.isEmpty()) {
                verdict = "ok   (reads from " + readOwners + ": API calls or a read model)";
            } else {
                verdict = "ok   (inside " + writeOwners + ")";
            }
            report.put(uc.name(), verdict);
        }
        return report;
    }
}
  1. The heuristic: writes across services in one use case mean a saga (complex) or a wrong boundary. Reads across services are normal (API calls or a local read model).
package com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare.BoundaryChecker.UseCase;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

public class BoundaryDemo {

    static final List<UseCase> USE_CASES = List.of(
            new UseCase("Book appointment", Set.of("appointments", "slots"), Set.of("patients", "doctors")),
            new UseCase("Check in patient", Set.of("appointments"), Set.of("patients")),
            new UseCase("Close consultation + bill", Set.of("appointments", "invoices"), Set.of("tariffs")),
            new UseCase("Pay invoice", Set.of("invoices", "payments"), Set.of()),
            new UseCase("Update allergies", Set.of("patients"), Set.of()));

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital: Checking Two Candidate Service Splits ===");
        Map<String, String> splitByTeam = Map.of( // split along today's org chart
                "patients", "Registration", "appointments", "Scheduling", "slots", "Doctors",
                "doctors", "Doctors", "invoices", "Billing", "payments", "Payments", "tariffs", "Billing");
        Map<String, String> splitByCapability = Map.of( // split along business capabilities
                "patients", "PatientRecords", "appointments", "Scheduling", "slots", "Scheduling",
                "doctors", "Scheduling", "invoices", "Billing", "payments", "Billing", "tariffs", "Billing");

        for (var split : List.of(Map.entry("Split A (by current teams)", splitByTeam),
                Map.entry("Split B (by business capability)", splitByCapability))) {
            System.out.println(split.getKey() + ":");
            BoundaryChecker.check(split.getValue(), USE_CASES)
                    .forEach((uc, verdict) -> System.out.printf("  %-26s %s%n", uc, verdict));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital: Checking Two Candidate Service Splits ===
Split A (by current teams):
  Book appointment           WARN writes span [Doctors, Scheduling] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Check in patient           ok   (reads from [Registration]: API calls or a read model)
  Close consultation + bill  WARN writes span [Billing, Scheduling] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Pay invoice                WARN writes span [Billing, Payments] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Update allergies           ok   (inside [Registration])
Split B (by business capability):
  Book appointment           ok   (reads from [PatientRecords]: API calls or a read model)
  Check in patient           ok   (reads from [PatientRecords]: API calls or a read model)
  Close consultation + bill  WARN writes span [Billing, Scheduling] -> needs a saga or a different boundary
  Pay invoice                ok   (inside [Billing])
  Update allergies           ok   (inside [PatientRecords])

The capability-based split leaves one warning, "Close consultation + bill". That's acceptable if Scheduling publishes ConsultationClosed and Billing creates the invoice asynchronously: the invoice doesn't need to exist in the same transaction. Making that decision explicitly is the point of the exercise.

Why this check:

  • Turns "where should the boundary be?" from opinion into evidence from use cases.
  • Splitting by org chart produced three cross-service writes: a distributed monolith in the making.
  • Cheap to run before writing any service code.
Unit Tests: DecompositionTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.grocery.GroceryServices.*;
import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.healthcare.BoundaryChecker;
import com.handbook.microservices.decomposition.ridehailing.TripContexts;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DecompositionTest {

    @Test
    void servicesCollaborateOnlyThroughApisAndEvents() {
        EventBus bus = new EventBus(false);
        CatalogService catalog = new CatalogService(bus);
        OrderService orders = new OrderService(new InventoryService(bus), bus);
        assertThat(orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 3)).startsWith("accepted");
        assertThat(catalog.describe("MANGO-1KG")).endsWith("(out of stock)");
        assertThat(orders.place("MANGO-1KG", 1)).startsWith("rejected");
    }

    @Test
    void billingTranslatesDispatchEventIntoItsOwnModel() {
        var dispatch = new TripContexts.Dispatch();
        var billing = new TripContexts.Billing();
        dispatch.onTripCompleted(billing::handle);
        dispatch.complete(new TripContexts.Dispatch.Trip("T", "D", 0, 0, 1, "X"), "R", 10, 10);
        assertThat(billing.invoiced()).singleElement().extracting(TripContexts.Billing.Trip::totalInr).isEqualTo(50 + 140 + 20 + 20);
    }

    @Test
    void crossServiceWritesAreFlagged() {
        var report = BoundaryChecker.check(Map.of("a", "S1", "b", "S2"),
                List.of(new BoundaryChecker.UseCase("uc", Set.of("a", "b"), Set.of())));
        assertThat(report.get("uc")).startsWith("WARN");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Modular monolith first. Many teams start with one deployable split into strict modules (Java modules, Spring Modulith, ArchUnit rules), then extract services when a module needs independent scaling or deployment. See Modular Monolith.
  • Event storming workshops to discover domain events, aggregates and bounded contexts with domain experts.
  • Context mapping between bounded contexts: customer/supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, open-host service, published language.
  • Strangler fig to extract services from an existing monolith incrementally. See Strangler Fig.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Tool Helps with Spring Modulith Module boundaries inside one Spring Boot app, module events, verification tests ArchUnit Tests that fail when packages/modules depend on each other illegally Java Platform Module System module-info.java with exports/requires Spring Cloud / Kubernetes Running the resulting services (discovery, config, gateways) Kafka / RabbitMQ Integration events between services

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Independent deployment and scaling per capability Distributed system costs: network failures, latency, eventual consistency Team autonomy: one team, one service, one database Cross-service queries need API composition or read models Failures isolated to one capability Operational overhead: CI/CD, monitoring, on-call per service Each service can use the right technology Wrong boundaries are expensive to fix later

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Splitting by technical layer or by entity

ProductService, CustomerService, OrderService as CRUD wrappers ("entity services") create chatty, anemic services where every feature changes three of them.

Shared database

Services that share tables are one system with extra network hops. Each service must own its data; others get it through APIs or events.

Too many, too small

50 services for 8 engineers means more time on infrastructure than features. Size services to teams and capabilities, not to lines of code.

Splitting before understanding the domain

Boundaries are hardest to get right early. Start with a modular monolith and extract when the seams are clear.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver. Systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Design team boundaries deliberately to get the architecture you want (Team Topologies: stream-aligned teams owning services end to end, platform teams providing paved roads).

Data ownership decides boundaries. Ask "who is allowed to change this data, and what invariants protect it?" An invariant that spans data in two services ("an appointment can't be booked unless the slot is free") belongs inside one service, or it needs a saga and accepts eventual consistency.

Migration path. Strangler fig: put a routing layer in front of the monolith, extract one capability at a time (start with one that has clear data and low coupling), replicate data with CDC during the transition, and delete the monolith code once traffic has moved.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Each service has one owning team and an on-call rotation.
  • Each service has its own database (or schema with enforced access control).
  • Integration contracts (APIs, events) are versioned and covered by contract tests.
  • The most common use cases write in a single service.
  • Cross-service flows have explicit consistency strategies (sagas, events, read models).
  • Observability: distributed tracing, per-service SLOs and dashboards.
  • Independent CI/CD pipelines; a service can deploy without others.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"I'd split by business capability: catalog, inventory, ordering, payments, delivery. Each owns its data; no shared tables. Ordering checks stock through Inventory's API for decisions that must be fresh, and publishes events like OrderPlaced that Inventory and Notifications consume. I'd validate the boundaries against core use cases: placing an order should write mostly within Ordering, with reservation and payment handled by a saga. I'd start as a modular monolith if the team is small, and extract services as scaling or team boundaries require."

War story: the twelve services that always deployed together

A fintech split its monolith into 12 services along its database tables (Customer, Account, Card, Transaction...). Every feature needed changes in 4–6 services, deployed in a strict order. Releases took a full day, and a failed deploy of one service broke the others. They had built a distributed monolith. Fix: re-drew boundaries around capabilities (Onboarding, Cards, Payments, Lending), merged services that always changed together, and introduced events for cross-capability flows. Deploys became independent and went from weekly to 30 per day. Lesson: services that change together belong together. Draw boundaries around change and data ownership, not nouns.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Decomposition by capability Decomposition by subdomain (DDD) Modular monolith Unit Business capability Bounded context Module inside one deployable Driver What the business does The domain model and language Code organization first, deployment later Deployable units Many Many One

Related patterns: Database per Service, Saga, API Gateway, Anti-Corruption Layer, Strangler Fig.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Split by business capability / bounded context, not by layer, entity or org chart.
  • Each service owns its data; integrate with APIs (fresh decisions) and events (facts).
  • Test: common use cases write inside one service.
  • Same word, different models across contexts; integrate with published events.
  • Small team or unclear domain? Start with a modular monolith.
Catalog | Inventory | Ordering | Payments | Delivery   — each with its own DB, team and pipeline

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a Payments service to Example 1 and decide what Ordering needs from it (API or event?).
  • Add a TripCancelled event and teach Billing to charge a cancellation fee.
  • Run the BoundaryChecker on a system you know and share the warnings with your team.

docs.title: Deployment Strategies: Blue-Green, Canary & Feature Toggles
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Separate deploying code from releasing it, and make every release reversible. Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments; canary shifts traffic gradually and rolls back automatically on bad metrics; feature toggles turn features on per user, percentage or segment without redeploying. Use all three: canary or blue-green for every deploy, toggles for risky features, and expand/contract migrations so old and new versions can run side by side.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the team deploys checkout v42 on Friday evening by replacing v41 on every server. A bug for coupon users appears at once, for everyone. Rolling back means another full deploy (15 minutes) while orders fail. Next time, people deploy less often, batches get bigger, and each release gets riskier.

The strategies:

Strategy How Blast radius Rollback Cost Recreate / big bang Stop old, start new 100% Redeploy Low, but has downtime Rolling Replace instances a few at a time Grows over time Roll forward/back gradually Low (Kubernetes default) Blue-green Two full environments; switch the router 100% at switch Instant (switch back) 2× capacity during release Canary Small % of traffic to the new version, then increase 1% → 100% Instant (route back) Needs good metrics Feature toggles Code deployed dark; enabled by configuration Any segment / % Instant (flip flag) Flag debt to clean up

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Opening a new restaurant menu

Blue-green: a second, fully staffed kitchen prepares the new menu; at 7 pm all orders switch to it, and if something's wrong, orders switch back. Canary: the new dish is offered to one table in a hundred first, and the manager watches whether plates come back. Feature toggle: the dish is on the menu card but hidden for most guests, shown to staff and regulars first, and can be removed instantly if a supplier fails.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     U[Users] --> R{Router / gateway / mesh}     R -->|"blue-green: 100% to live colour"| B[Blue v41]     R -.-> G[Green v42]     R -->|"canary: 95%"| S[Stable v41]     R -->|"canary: 5%"| C[Canary v42]     C --> M[(Metrics: errors, latency, business KPIs)]     M -->|"bad → rollback"| R     F[(Flag service)] -->|"isOn(feature, user)"| S & C Element Responsibility Router Load balancer, gateway, ingress or service mesh that controls traffic split Environments / versions Blue + green, or stable + canary Analysis Compares canary vs baseline metrics and decides continue / rollback Flag service Evaluates toggles per request (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature providers) Compatible data Schemas and messages that both versions can read and write (expand/contract)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
1. Stop all v41 instances
2. Run DB migration (rename column)
3. Start v42 everywhere
4. Bug? → revert code, but the column was renamed → v41 can't start either
  • Every user hits every bug immediately.
  • Rollback is a new deploy, and may be impossible after a breaking migration.
  • Releases become rare, big and scary.

docs.title: Example 1: Blue-Green Checkout Release (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: The checkout service runs as two identical environments behind the load balancer. v42 is deployed to the idle (green) environment and smoke-tested with no customer traffic. The router then switches all traffic to green. A coupon bug appears; switching back to blue (still running v41, warm and unchanged) is one step.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Ops participant R as Router participant B as Blue (v41) participant G as Green (v42) Ops->>G: deploy v42 + smoke test Ops->>R: switch → green R->>G: 100% of traffic Note over G: coupon bug! Ops->>R: switch → blue (rollback in seconds) R->>B: 100% of traffic

Full Code:

BlueGreenRouter.javaBlueGreenDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.deployment.bluegreen;

import java.util.function.Function;

/** Two full environments; the router points ALL traffic at one of them. Switching (and rolling back) is one step. */
public final class BlueGreenRouter {

    private Function<String, String> blue;
    private Function<String, String> green;
    private String live = "blue";

    public BlueGreenRouter(Function<String, String> blue) {
        this.blue = blue;
    }

    public void deployToIdle(Function<String, String> newVersion) { // (1)!
        if (live.equals("blue")) {
            green = newVersion;
        } else {
            blue = newVersion;
        }
    }

    public String smokeTestIdle(String request) { // (2)!
        return (live.equals("blue") ? green : blue).apply(request);
    }

    public void switchTraffic() { // (3)!
        live = live.equals("blue") ? "green" : "blue";
    }

    public String handle(String request) {
        return live + ": " + (live.equals("blue") ? blue : green).apply(request);
    }
}
  1. Deploy to the idle colour: customers are unaffected while it starts and warms up.
  2. Smoke-test the idle environment with synthetic requests before any customer sees it.
  3. The release (and the rollback) is a single router change: a DNS weight, a load-balancer target group, a Kubernetes Service selector.
package com.handbook.microservices.deployment.bluegreen;

public class BlueGreenDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Blue-Green Release of the Checkout Service ===");
        BlueGreenRouter router = new BlueGreenRouter(cart -> "total INR 1,240 (v41)");
        System.out.println("Before release   -> " + router.handle("cart-1"));

        router.deployToIdle(cart -> cart.equals("cart-with-coupon") ? "500 NullPointerException (v42)" : "total INR 1,240 (v42)");
        System.out.println("Smoke test green -> " + router.smokeTestIdle("cart-1") + " (no customer traffic yet)");

        router.switchTraffic();
        System.out.println("After switch     -> " + router.handle("cart-1"));
        System.out.println("Coupon user      -> " + router.handle("cart-with-coupon") + "  <- bug found in production");

        router.switchTraffic(); // rollback = flip back; blue is still running v41, warm and unchanged
        System.out.println("Rollback (1 step)-> " + router.handle("cart-with-coupon"));
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Blue-Green Release of the Checkout Service ===
Before release   -> blue: total INR 1,240 (v41)
Smoke test green -> total INR 1,240 (v42) (no customer traffic yet)
After switch     -> green: total INR 1,240 (v42)
Coupon user      -> green: 500 NullPointerException (v42)  <- bug found in production
Rollback (1 step)-> blue: total INR 1,240 (v41)

Why blue-green here:

  • Instant rollback to a warm, known-good environment.
  • The new version is fully started and verified before taking traffic.
  • Simple mental model; good for stateful edge services and big-bang changes that can't be split.

docs.title: Example 2: Canary with Automated Analysis (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: A new fare engine is rolled out in steps: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% of rides, then promoted. At each step, the canary's error rate is compared with the stable baseline (10,000 rides per step); if the canary is worse by more than 0.5 percentage points, the rollout stops and traffic returns to stable. Release 7.3 is healthy; release 7.4 breaks fares for airport pickups.

Design:

flowchart LR S1["1%"] -->|"canary − baseline ≤ 0.5pp"| S2["5%"] --> S3["25%"] --> S4["50%"] --> P["PROMOTE 100%"] S1 -->|"worse"| RB["ROLLBACK to stable"] S2 --> RB S3 --> RB S4 --> RB

Full Code:

CanaryAnalysis.javaCanaryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.deployment.canary;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;

/** Progressive delivery: shift traffic in steps and compare canary vs baseline error rates before each step. */
public final class CanaryAnalysis {

    public record StepResult(int percent, double baselineErrorPct, double canaryErrorPct, String decision) { }

    private final int[] steps;
    private final double maxErrorIncreasePct;

    public CanaryAnalysis(int[] steps, double maxErrorIncreasePct) {
        this.steps = steps;
        this.maxErrorIncreasePct = maxErrorIncreasePct;
    }

    /** Simulates 10,000 requests per step with the given true error probabilities (seeded, so reproducible). */
    public List<StepResult> run(double baselineErrorRate, double canaryErrorRate, long seed) {
        Random random = new Random(seed);
        List<StepResult> results = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int percent : steps) {
            int canaryRequests = 10_000 * percent / 100;
            int baselineRequests = 10_000 - canaryRequests;
            double b = errors(random, baselineRequests, baselineErrorRate) * 100.0 / Math.max(1, baselineRequests);
            double c = errors(random, canaryRequests, canaryErrorRate) * 100.0 / Math.max(1, canaryRequests);
            boolean healthy = c - b <= maxErrorIncreasePct; // (1)!
            boolean last = percent == steps[steps.length - 1];
            results.add(new StepResult(percent, b, c, healthy ? (last ? "PROMOTE to 100%" : "continue") : "ROLLBACK"));
            if (!healthy) {
                break; // (2)!
            }
        }
        return results;
    }

    private static int errors(Random random, int requests, double rate) {
        int n = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) {
            n += random.nextDouble() < rate ? 1 : 0;
        }
        return n;
    }
}
  1. Compare canary to the baseline at the same time, not to last week: both see the same traffic mix and incidents.
  2. Stop at the first bad step. Argo Rollouts / Flagger do this with Prometheus queries as "analysis templates".
package com.handbook.microservices.deployment.canary;

import com.handbook.microservices.deployment.canary.CanaryAnalysis.StepResult;

public class CanaryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: Canary Rollout of a New Fare Engine (steps 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50%, then promote) ===");
        CanaryAnalysis analysis = new CanaryAnalysis(new int[] {1, 5, 25, 50}, 0.5);

        System.out.println("Release 7.3 (healthy):");
        for (StepResult r : analysis.run(0.004, 0.0045, 11)) {
            print(r);
        }
        System.out.println("Release 7.4 (bug: fares fail for airport pickups, ~3% of rides):");
        for (StepResult r : analysis.run(0.004, 0.034, 11)) {
            print(r);
        }
        System.out.println("The bad release was stopped at 1% of rides, automatically, instead of reaching everyone.");
    }

    private static void print(StepResult r) {
        System.out.printf("  %3d%% canary: baseline %.2f%% errors, canary %.2f%% -> %s%n",
                r.percent(), r.baselineErrorPct(), r.canaryErrorPct(), r.decision());
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: Canary Rollout of a New Fare Engine (steps 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50%, then promote) ===
Release 7.3 (healthy):
    1% canary: baseline 0.32% errors, canary 0.00% -> continue
    5% canary: baseline 0.20% errors, canary 0.00% -> continue
   25% canary: baseline 0.37% errors, canary 0.44% -> continue
   50% canary: baseline 0.30% errors, canary 0.54% -> PROMOTE to 100%
Release 7.4 (bug: fares fail for airport pickups, ~3% of rides):
    1% canary: baseline 0.32% errors, canary 4.00% -> ROLLBACK
The bad release was stopped at 1% of rides, automatically, instead of reaching everyone.

Why canary here:

  • A bad release reaches 1% of rides, not 100%.
  • The decision is automatic and metric-driven, not "someone was watching the dashboard".
  • Real traffic finds bugs that tests and staging don't (airport pickups!).

docs.title: Example 3: Feature Toggles for Instant Loans (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A bank ships "instant loan offers" code to production weeks before launch, switched off. Employees see it first (dogfooding), then 10% of customers, then 50%. Each customer's experience must be sticky (the same answer on every visit). When the credit-risk team spots a scoring issue, a kill switch turns it off for everyone in seconds, with no deploy.

Design:

flowchart LR Req["isOn('instant-loans', user, segment)"] --> K{kill switch?} K -- on --> Off[false] K -- off --> Seg{segment targeted?} Seg -- employees --> On[true] Seg -- no --> B{"hash(feature:user) % 100 < percent?"} B -- yes --> On B -- no --> Off

Full Code:

FeatureToggles.javaTogglesDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.deployment.toggles;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.zip.CRC32;

/** Release toggles decoupled from deploys: segment targeting, sticky percentage rollout, and a kill switch. */
public final class FeatureToggles {

    public record Rule(boolean killSwitchOn, Set<String> segments, int percent) { }

    private final Map<String, Rule> rules = new HashMap<>();

    public void set(String feature, Rule rule) {
        rules.put(feature, rule);
    }

    public boolean isOn(String feature, String userId, String segment) {
        Rule r = rules.get(feature);
        if (r == null || r.killSwitchOn()) { // (1)!
            return false;
        }
        if (r.segments().contains(segment)) { // (2)!
            return true;
        }
        return bucket(feature, userId) < r.percent(); // (3)!
    }

    /** Stable 0..99 bucket per (feature, user): the same user always gets the same answer. */
    static int bucket(String feature, String userId) {
        CRC32 crc = new CRC32();
        crc.update((feature + ":" + userId).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return (int) (crc.getValue() % 100);
    }
}
  1. The kill switch is checked first and overrides everything.
  2. Segment targeting: employees, beta testers, one city, one tenant.
  3. Sticky percentage rollout: a stable hash puts each user in a bucket 0–99, so raising 10% → 50% keeps everyone who already had it.
package com.handbook.microservices.deployment.toggles;

import com.handbook.microservices.deployment.toggles.FeatureToggles.Rule;

import java.util.Set;

public class TogglesDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Rolling Out 'Instant Loan Offers' with Feature Toggles ===");
        FeatureToggles toggles = new FeatureToggles();
        toggles.set("instant-loans", new Rule(false, Set.of("employees"), 10)); // code already deployed to everyone

        System.out.println("Employee (dogfooding)  : " + toggles.isOn("instant-loans", "emp-17", "employees"));
        System.out.println("Customers enabled at 10%: " + count(toggles) + " of 10,000");
        System.out.println("cust-123 asks 3 times   : " + toggles.isOn("instant-loans", "cust-123", "retail") + ", "
                + toggles.isOn("instant-loans", "cust-123", "retail") + ", " + toggles.isOn("instant-loans", "cust-123", "retail") + " (sticky)");

        toggles.set("instant-loans", new Rule(false, Set.of("employees"), 50));
        System.out.println("Raised to 50%           : " + count(toggles) + " of 10,000 (everyone from the 10% still has it)");

        toggles.set("instant-loans", new Rule(true, Set.of("employees"), 50)); // credit-risk team spots a scoring issue
        System.out.println("Kill switch flipped     : " + count(toggles) + " of 10,000, employee=" + toggles.isOn("instant-loans", "emp-17", "employees")
                + " (no deploy needed)");
    }

    private static int count(FeatureToggles toggles) {
        int on = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
            on += toggles.isOn("instant-loans", "cust-" + i, "retail") ? 1 : 0;
        }
        return on;
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Rolling Out 'Instant Loan Offers' with Feature Toggles ===
Employee (dogfooding)  : true
Customers enabled at 10%: 1038 of 10,000
cust-123 asks 3 times   : false, false, false (sticky)
Raised to 50%           : 4908 of 10,000 (everyone from the 10% still has it)
Kill switch flipped     : 0 of 10,000, employee=false (no deploy needed)

Why feature toggles here:

  • Deploy ≠ release: code ships continuously; business decides when users see it.
  • Gradual exposure by segment and percentage, with consistent experiences.
  • Fastest possible rollback for a feature (seconds), independent of the deploy pipeline.
Unit Tests: DeploymentStrategiesTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.deployment.bluegreen.BlueGreenRouter;
import com.handbook.microservices.deployment.canary.CanaryAnalysis;
import com.handbook.microservices.deployment.toggles.FeatureToggles;
import com.handbook.microservices.deployment.toggles.FeatureToggles.Rule;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class DeploymentStrategiesTest {

    @Test
    void rollbackRestoresTheOldVersionInOneStep() {
        BlueGreenRouter r = new BlueGreenRouter(x -> "old");
        r.deployToIdle(x -> "new");
        r.switchTraffic();
        assertThat(r.handle("x")).isEqualTo("green: new");
        r.switchTraffic();
        assertThat(r.handle("x")).isEqualTo("blue: old");
    }

    @Test
    void badCanaryIsRolledBackEarly() {
        var results = new CanaryAnalysis(new int[] {1, 5, 25, 100}, 0.5).run(0.001, 0.2, 1);
        assertThat(results.get(results.size() - 1).decision()).isEqualTo("ROLLBACK");
        assertThat(results.get(results.size() - 1).percent()).isLessThan(100);
    }

    @Test
    void togglesAreStickyAndKillSwitchWins() {
        FeatureToggles t = new FeatureToggles();
        t.set("f", new Rule(false, Set.of("beta"), 30));
        boolean first = t.isOn("f", "u1", "x");
        assertThat(t.isOn("f", "u1", "x")).isEqualTo(first);
        assertThat(t.isOn("f", "u2", "beta")).isTrue();
        t.set("f", new Rule(true, Set.of("beta"), 100));
        assertThat(t.isOn("f", "u2", "beta")).isFalse();
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Deployment strategies Kubernetes Rolling updates, readiness-gated rollout, kubectl rollout undo Argo Rollouts / Flagger Canary and blue-green with automated analysis (Prometheus, Datadog) Istio / Linkerd / Envoy Weighted routing, header-based routing, traffic mirroring Spring Cloud Gateway Weight route predicates for canaries (see API Gateway) Feature flags OpenFeature SDK, Unleash, LaunchDarkly, FF4J, Togglz Databases Flyway / Liquibase migrations written in expand/contract style

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Small blast radius and fast rollback Both versions must be compatible (APIs, schemas, messages) Release decisions driven by metrics, not hope Canary needs reliable, low-noise metrics and enough traffic Frequent, small, low-stress releases Blue-green doubles capacity during releases Toggles let business control exposure Toggle sprawl and untested flag combinations

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Breaking schema changes in the same release

Renaming or dropping a column while old instances still run (or might be rolled back to) causes outages and blocks rollback. Use expand → migrate → contract across several releases (coding challenge).

Canary metrics that can't see the bug

Error rate alone won't catch "fares are 10% too low". Include business metrics (average fare, conversion) and compare against the baseline, not a fixed threshold.

Toggles that never die

Every release toggle doubles test paths. Give each an owner and an expiry date; delete the flag and the dead branch after full rollout.

Sticky sessions and caches across versions

Users bouncing between v41 and v42 (non-sticky routing) can see inconsistent behaviour; caches written by v42 in a new format can break v41 after rollback. Version cache keys and message formats.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Compatibility is the real constraint. Any strategy that runs two versions at once (all of them except recreate) requires N and N−1 to coexist: backward-compatible APIs, tolerant readers for messages, additive schema changes, and dual-reading caches. Make "can we roll back?" a release checklist item.

Statistics matter. At 1% of 10,000 requests you only see 100 requests: a 0.4% error rate is noise. Use enough traffic per step, longer bake times for low-volume services, and statistical tests (Kayenta's Mann-Whitney) rather than eyeballing.

Data migrations are releases too. Backfills run as throttled jobs; dual-writes are verified with reconciliation queries before cutting reads over; the contract step is delayed until rollback past it is no longer needed.

War story: the rollback that couldn't roll back

A grocery team released v42 with a Flyway migration that renamed mobile to phone_e164. v42 had a checkout bug; they rolled back to v41, which crashed on startup because its queries referenced mobile. Checkout was down for 34 minutes while engineers wrote and deployed a reverse migration under pressure. Fix: migrations reviewed for expand/contract; CI runs the previous app version's integration tests against the new schema; renames take three releases. Lesson: a deployment strategy is only as reversible as your database changes.

docs.text:
Blue-Green Canary Feature Toggle Strangler Fig Unit switched Whole environment Traffic percentage A feature, per user A route/capability, permanently Rollback Switch back Route back Flip flag Route back to legacy Needs 2× capacity Good metrics Flag service + discipline Facade/router

See Strangler Fig, Config Server (where flags often live), and Health Check (rollouts depend on readiness).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Deploy ≠ release. Make every release reversible.
  • Blue-green: two environments, one switch, instant rollback.
  • Canary: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, compare to baseline, auto-rollback.
  • Toggles: kill switch, segments, sticky % buckets; delete when done.
  • Expand → migrate → contract so N and N−1 always coexist.
if (flags.getBooleanValue("instant-loans", false, ctx)) { ... }   // default off
