docs.title: Distributed Tracing
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Give each request a trace ID at the edge, propagate it (with the current span ID) to every service it touches via headers such as W3C traceparent, and record a span per unit of work. A tracing backend assembles the spans into a tree showing where the time went and where it failed. Logs tell you what happened in one service; traces tell you where in the call chain it happened.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: checkout takes 1.5 s sometimes. The request touches the gateway, order, inventory, payment and an external bank. Each service's logs say "OK" and its average latency looks fine. Which hop is slow, for this request? Without a shared ID, correlating logs across five services by timestamp is guesswork.

Definition (OpenTelemetry):

Traces give us the big picture of what happens when a request is made to an application. A trace is made of one or more spans; each span represents a unit of work.

Concept Meaning Trace The whole journey of one request (one trace ID) Span One operation: name, start, duration, attributes, status, parent span ID Context propagation Passing trace ID + parent span ID across process boundaries (HTTP headers, message headers) traceparent W3C header: 00-<trace-id 32 hex>-<parent-id 16 hex>-<flags> Sampling Recording only a share of traces to control cost

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A parcel's tracking number

The parcel gets one tracking number at pickup. Every hub scans it on arrival and departure, so you can see it spent 14 hours stuck at the Pune sort centre. The tracking number is the trace ID; each scan pair is a span.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     C[Client] --> G[Gateway<br/>starts trace]     G -->|traceparent| O[Order svc]     O -->|traceparent| I[Inventory svc]     O -->|traceparent| P[Payment svc]     P -->|traceparent| K[[Kafka<br/>headers]] --> B[Billing svc]     G & O & I & P & B -.->|spans via OTLP| COL[Collector] --> BE[(Jaeger / Tempo / Zipkin)] Participant Responsibility Instrumentation (OTel agent, Micrometer) Creates spans for HTTP, DB, messaging; injects/extracts headers Propagator Serializes context into headers (W3C, B3) Collector Receives, batches, samples and exports spans Backend Stores and visualizes traces; links to logs and metrics

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
order-service    19:00:00.112 INFO placing order ORD-1
payment-service  19:00:00.140 INFO charging...
payment-service  19:00:01.561 INFO charged
(800 other requests logged in the same second; which "charging..." belongs to ORD-1?)

docs.title: 5. Three Real-World Examples
docs.text:
All examples use a small tracer and the W3C header format:

TraceContext.javaTracer.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core;

import java.util.Random;

/**
 * The W3C Trace Context carried between services in the {@code traceparent} header:
 * {@code 00-<32 hex trace-id>-<16 hex parent span-id>-<flags>} (flags 01 = sampled).
 */
public record TraceContext(String traceId, String spanId, boolean sampled) {

    public static TraceContext parse(String traceparent) {
        String[] parts = traceparent.split("-"); // (1)!
        if (parts.length != 4 || !parts[0].equals("00") || parts[1].length() != 32 || parts[2].length() != 16) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad traceparent: " + traceparent);
        }
        return new TraceContext(parts[1], parts[2], parts[3].equals("01"));
    }

    public String toTraceparent() {
        return "00-" + traceId + "-" + spanId + "-" + (sampled ? "01" : "00");
    }

    public static TraceContext newRoot(Random ids) {
        return new TraceContext(hex(ids, 16), hex(ids, 8), true);
    }

    public TraceContext newChild(Random ids) { // (2)!
        return new TraceContext(traceId, hex(ids, 8), sampled);
    }

    static String hex(Random ids, int bytes) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < bytes; i++) {
            sb.append(String.format("%02x", ids.nextInt(256)));
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
  1. Strict parsing: a malformed header should start a new trace rather than corrupt one.
  2. A child keeps the trace ID and gets a new span ID; the old span ID becomes its parent.
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** A tiny tracer: creates spans, records them when they end, and prints a trace as a tree. */
public final class Tracer {

    public record Span(String traceId, String spanId, String parentId, String service, String name,
                       long startMillis, long endMillis) {
        long duration() {
            return endMillis - startMillis;
        }
    }

    private final Clock clock;
    private final Random ids;
    private final List<Span> finished = new ArrayList<>(); // what a collector (Jaeger, Tempo) receives

    public Tracer(Clock clock, Random ids) {
        this.clock = clock;
        this.ids = ids;
    }

    /** Runs work inside a new span. {@code parent} may be null to start a new trace. */
    public <T> T inSpan(TraceContext parent, String service, String name,
                        Function<TraceContext, T> work) {
        TraceContext ctx = parent == null ? TraceContext.newRoot(ids) : parent.newChild(ids);
        long start = clock.millis();
        try {
            return work.apply(ctx);
        } finally {
            synchronized (finished) {
                finished.add(new Span(ctx.traceId(), ctx.spanId(), parent == null ? null : parent.spanId(),
                        service, name, start, clock.millis()));
            }
        }
    }

    public <T> T inSpan(TraceContext parent, String service, String name, Supplier<T> work) {
        return inSpan(parent, service, name, ctx -> work.get());
    }

    public List<Span> spans() {
        synchronized (finished) {
            return List.copyOf(finished);
        }
    }

    public void printTree(String traceId) {
        List<Span> trace = spans().stream().filter(s -> s.traceId().equals(traceId)).toList();
        long t0 = trace.stream().mapToLong(Span::startMillis).min().orElse(0);
        long t1 = trace.stream().mapToLong(Span::endMillis).max().orElse(t0);
        double msPerChar = Math.max(1, (t1 - t0) / 40.0); // the whole trace fits in 40 characters
        trace.stream().filter(s -> s.parentId() == null).forEach(root -> print(root, trace, t0, msPerChar, 0));
    }

    private void print(Span span, List<Span> trace, long t0, double msPerChar, int depth) {
        int offset = (int) ((span.startMillis() - t0) / msPerChar);
        int width = (int) Math.max(1, Math.round(span.duration() / msPerChar));
        System.out.printf("  %-50s %5d ms |%s%n", "  ".repeat(depth) + span.service() + ": " + span.name(),
                span.duration(), " ".repeat(offset) + "#".repeat(width));
        trace.stream().filter(s -> span.spanId().equals(s.parentId()))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Span::startMillis))
                .forEach(child -> print(child, trace, t0, msPerChar, depth + 1));
    }
}

docs.title: Example 1: Finding the Slow Hop in Checkout (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: One checkout request crosses the gateway, order, inventory and payment services. Each service parses the incoming traceparent, creates a child span and passes its own span ID downstream. The trace tree (with a timeline bar per span) makes the answer obvious: 1.4 s of the 1.5 s is the bank authorization call inside payment-service.

Full Code:

CheckoutTraceDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.Tracer;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Random;

/**
 * One checkout request crosses four services. Each service reads the incoming traceparent header,
 * creates a child span, and passes its own span ID downstream. The collector stitches the tree.
 */
public class CheckoutTraceDemo {

    static FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T19:00:00Z");
    static Tracer tracer = new Tracer(clock, new Random(7));

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: tracing one slow checkout across services ===");
        Request incoming = Request.get("/checkout", Map.of()); // no traceparent: the gateway starts the trace
        String traceId = tracer.inSpan(null, "api-gateway", "POST /checkout", gw -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(5);
            orderService(incoming.withHeader("traceparent", gw.toTraceparent())); // (1)!
            clock.advanceMillis(3);
            return gw.traceId();
        });
        System.out.println("trace-id " + traceId);
        tracer.printTree(traceId);
        System.out.println("The tree shows where the time went: payment-service waiting on the bank.");
    }

    static void orderService(Request req) {
        TraceContext parent = TraceContext.parse(req.header("traceparent")); // (2)!
        tracer.inSpan(parent, "order-service", "placeOrder", ctx -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(10);
            tracer.inSpan(ctx, "inventory-service", "reserve", () -> {
                clock.advanceMillis(40);
                return null;
            });
            paymentService(req.withHeader("traceparent", ctx.toTraceparent()));
            clock.advanceMillis(15);
            return null;
        });
    }

    static void paymentService(Request req) {
        TraceContext parent = TraceContext.parse(req.header("traceparent"));
        tracer.inSpan(parent, "payment-service", "charge", ctx -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(20);
            tracer.inSpan(ctx, "payment-service", "HTTP POST bank /authorize", () -> {
                clock.advanceMillis(1_400); // the slow external call
                return null;
            });
            return null;
        });
    }
}
  1. Inject: the gateway sends its context downstream in the traceparent header.
  2. Extract: each service continues the trace from the incoming header.

Output:

=== Grocery: tracing one slow checkout across services ===
trace-id bba3bf02597de5beb5915af31e40d9b2
  api-gateway: POST /checkout                         1493 ms |########################################
    order-service: placeOrder                         1485 ms |########################################
      inventory-service: reserve                        40 ms |#
      payment-service: charge                         1420 ms | ######################################
        payment-service: HTTP POST bank /authorize    1400 ms |  ######################################
The tree shows where the time went: payment-service waiting on the bank.

Why tracing here:

  • Latency is attributed to a specific hop for a specific request.
  • The tree also shows structure: inventory and payment run sequentially, so parallelizing them is a possible optimization.

docs.title: Example 2: Across Kafka (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: Completing a trip publishes TripCompleted; billing consumes it 2 seconds later on another machine. The producer puts traceparent into the message headers; the consumer extracts it and continues the same trace, so the invoice insert appears under the original HTTP request.

Full Code:

KafkaTracePropagationDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.async;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.Tracer;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.Random;

/**
 * Traces cross asynchronous boundaries too: the producer puts traceparent into the message headers,
 * and the consumer, possibly seconds later on another machine, continues the same trace.
 */
public class KafkaTracePropagationDemo {

    record Message(String topic, Map<String, String> headers, String payload) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T22:00:00Z");
        Tracer tracer = new Tracer(clock, new Random(11));
        Queue<Message> topic = new ArrayDeque<>();

        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: trip completion -> async billing, one trace ===");
        String traceId = tracer.inSpan(null, "trip-service", "POST /trips/TRIP-5/complete", ctx -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(25);
            tracer.inSpan(ctx, "trip-service", "kafka send trips.completed", producer -> {
                topic.add(new Message("trips.completed",
                        Map.of("traceparent", producer.toTraceparent()), "TripCompleted TRIP-5")); // (1)!
                clock.advanceMillis(4);
                return null;
            });
            return ctx.traceId();
        });

        clock.advanceMillis(2_000); // consumer lag
        Message m = topic.poll();
        TraceContext fromHeaders = TraceContext.parse(m.headers().get("traceparent")); // (2)!
        tracer.inSpan(fromHeaders, "billing-service", "kafka receive " + m.topic(), consumer -> {
            clock.advanceMillis(30);
            tracer.inSpan(consumer, "billing-service", "INSERT invoice", () -> {
                clock.advanceMillis(12);
                return null;
            });
            return null;
        });

        System.out.println("message headers: " + m.headers());
        tracer.printTree(traceId);
        System.out.println("billing-service joined trace " + traceId.substring(0, 8) + "... 2 s after the HTTP request ended.");
    }
}
  1. Message headers carry the context just like HTTP headers do.
  2. The consumer extracts it; OpenTelemetry may model this as a child or as a span link for batch consumers.

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: trip completion -> async billing, one trace ===
message headers: {traceparent=00-bab66d36a16606e830490b8d6f70abfb-2d5a670a88b89bb4-01}
  trip-service: POST /trips/TRIP-5/complete             29 ms |#
    trip-service: kafka send trips.completed             4 ms |#
      billing-service: kafka receive trips.completed    42 ms |                                       #
        billing-service: INSERT invoice                 12 ms |                                       #
billing-service joined trace bab66d36... 2 s after the HTTP request ended.

Why propagate through messages:

  • Async flows (sagas, outbox relays) are where "where did it get stuck?" is hardest to answer.
  • Consumer lag becomes visible as a gap in the trace.

docs.title: Example 3: Keeping Context Across Threads (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: The home-screen service fetches three rows in parallel. The current trace lives in a ThreadLocal, so work on a plain executor loses it, and those spans become orphan traces. A context-propagating executor captures the context at submit time and restores it in the worker.

Full Code:

ContextPropagatingExecutor.javaThreadContextDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.threads;

import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;

import java.util.concurrent.Executor;

/**
 * The current trace context usually lives in a ThreadLocal. Work submitted to another thread loses
 * it unless the executor captures the context at submit time and restores it in the worker.
 */
public final class ContextPropagatingExecutor implements Executor {

    public static final ThreadLocal<TraceContext> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

    private final Executor delegate;

    public ContextPropagatingExecutor(Executor delegate) {
        this.delegate = delegate;
    }

    @Override
    public void execute(Runnable task) {
        TraceContext captured = CURRENT.get(); // (1)!
        delegate.execute(() -> {
            TraceContext previous = CURRENT.get();
            CURRENT.set(captured); // (2)!
            try {
                task.run();
            } finally {
                CURRENT.set(previous); // (3)!
            }
        });
    }
}
  1. Capture on the submitting thread.
  2. Restore on the worker thread for the task's duration.
  3. Always restore the previous value. Pooled threads are reused, and leaking context into the next task corrupts traces.
package com.handbook.microservices.tracing.threads;

import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.Executor;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class ThreadContextDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TraceContext request = TraceContext.newRoot(new Random(3));
        ContextPropagatingExecutor.CURRENT.set(request);

        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            System.out.println("=== Streaming: parallel home-screen fetches keep the trace ===");
            System.out.println("request thread trace: " + request.traceId().substring(0, 8) + "...");
            System.out.println("plain executor      : " + fetchAll(pool));
            System.out.println("propagating executor: " + fetchAll(new ContextPropagatingExecutor(pool)));
        } finally {
            ContextPropagatingExecutor.CURRENT.remove();
        }
    }

    private static List<String> fetchAll(Executor executor) {
        List<CompletableFuture<String>> rows = List.of("continue-watching", "trending", "for-you").stream()
                .map(row -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
                    TraceContext ctx = ContextPropagatingExecutor.CURRENT.get();
                    return row + "=" + (ctx == null ? "NO TRACE" : ctx.traceId().substring(0, 8));
                }, executor))
                .toList();
        return rows.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: parallel home-screen fetches keep the trace ===
request thread trace: bb8f12ce...
plain executor      : [continue-watching=NO TRACE, trending=NO TRACE, for-you=NO TRACE]
propagating executor: [continue-watching=bb8f12ce, trending=bb8f12ce, for-you=bb8f12ce]

Why this matters:

  • Async code (CompletableFuture, @Async, reactive) is the most common place traces break.
  • OpenTelemetry's Context.taskWrapping(executor) and Micrometer's ContextExecutorService do exactly this.
Unit Tests: DistributedTracingTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.core.TraceContext;
import com.handbook.microservices.tracing.sampling.RatioSampler;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Random;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class DistributedTracingTest {

    @Test
    void traceparentRoundTripsAndChildKeepsTraceId() {
        TraceContext root = TraceContext.newRoot(new Random(1));
        TraceContext parsed = TraceContext.parse(root.toTraceparent());
        assertThat(parsed).isEqualTo(root);
        TraceContext child = parsed.newChild(new Random(2));
        assertThat(child.traceId()).isEqualTo(root.traceId());
        assertThat(child.spanId()).isNotEqualTo(root.spanId());
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsMalformedHeaders() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> TraceContext.parse("00-abc-def-01")).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void samplingIsDeterministicPerTraceId() {
        RatioSampler sampler = new RatioSampler(0.5);
        String traceId = TraceContext.newRoot(new Random(9)).traceId();
        assertThat(sampler.shouldSampleRoot(traceId)).isEqualTo(sampler.shouldSampleRoot(traceId));
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Spring Boot 3 with Micrometer Tracing (compiled in the spring-reference module):

package com.handbook.springref.tracing;

import io.micrometer.observation.Observation;
import io.micrometer.observation.ObservationRegistry;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

/**
 * With micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel on the classpath, Spring Boot instruments incoming HTTP
 * requests and the auto-configured RestClient.Builder, so traceparent is propagated for free.
 * Custom spans for business steps use the Observation API.
 */
@Service
public class TracedCheckoutService {

    private final RestClient payments;
    private final ObservationRegistry observations;

    public TracedCheckoutService(RestClient.Builder builder, ObservationRegistry observations) {
        this.payments = builder.baseUrl("http://payment-service").build(); // builder carries tracing
        this.observations = observations;
    }

    public String checkout(String orderId) {
        long total = Observation.createNotStarted("checkout.price-cart", observations)
                .lowCardinalityKeyValue("channel", "app") // becomes a span tag and a metric dimension
                .observe(() -> priceCart(orderId));
        return payments.post().uri("/charges/{id}", orderId)
                .body(total)
                .retrieve()
                .body(String.class); // child span + traceparent header added automatically
    }

    private long priceCart(String orderId) {
        return 79_800;
    }
}

# application.yml (reference)
management:
  tracing:
    sampling.probability: 0.1          # 10% head sampling
  otlp:
    tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"  # IDs in every log line
Option Notes OpenTelemetry Java agent Zero-code instrumentation (-javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar) for HTTP, JDBC, Kafka and more Micrometer Tracing (Spring Boot 3) Observation API; bridges to OTel or Brave Head sampling Decide at the root (cheap; may miss rare errors) Tail sampling The collector decides after seeing the whole trace (keep errors and slow traces) Exemplars Link a metric spike to example trace IDs

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Tracing OpenTelemetry The standard API/SDK, OTLP protocol and collector Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Zipkin Open-source backends Spring Boot 3 Micrometer Tracing + ObservationRegistry auto-instrumentation Service meshes Proxies emit spans per hop (apps still forward headers) W3C Trace Context traceparent/tracestate header standard

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Pinpoints slow or failing hops per request Instrumentation gaps break traces Shows real dependency graphs Storage cost; requires sampling at scale Correlates logs, metrics and traces by ID Context propagation across async code needs care Standardized (W3C, OTel) Sensitive data can leak into span attributes

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Broken propagation

One service that doesn't forward traceparent (a hand-built HTTP client, a thread pool, a message without headers) splits every trace in two. Test propagation end to end.

High-cardinality or sensitive attributes

Putting card numbers, emails or full request bodies into span attributes leaks PII into the tracing backend. Use allow-lists for attributes.

Sampling inconsistently

If each service samples independently at 10%, only 1% of traces are complete. Use parent-based sampling (see the coding challenge).

Tracing without logs correlation

Put trace and span IDs in every log line (MDC), so you can jump from a trace to the exact logs.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Three pillars, one ID. Metrics tell you that something is wrong (error rate up), traces tell you where (which hop), logs tell you why (the exception). Wire them together: exemplars on metrics, trace IDs in logs, and service graphs from traces.

Sampling strategy. Head sampling at 1–10% for volume; tail sampling in the collector to always keep errors and slow traces; higher rates for low-traffic critical paths. Budget storage per day.

Baggage. W3C Baggage can carry business context (tenant ID, experiment) across services. It's sent on every hop and visible to every service, so keep it small and non-sensitive.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry agent or Micrometer Tracing in every service; W3C propagation everywhere (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka).
  • Context propagation through executors, @Async, reactive and virtual threads verified.
  • Trace/span IDs in logs (MDC); exemplars on latency metrics.
  • Parent-based head sampling + tail sampling for errors/slow requests.
  • Attribute allow-list; no PII in spans.
  • Collector deployed with batching and back-pressure; backend retention set.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Every service runs the OpenTelemetry agent. The gateway starts a trace and propagates W3C traceparent over HTTP, gRPC and Kafka headers, so a checkout produces one trace across all services and async consumers. Spans go via OTLP to a collector that does tail sampling (keep all errors and requests over 1 s, plus 5% of the rest) and exports to Tempo. Trace IDs are in every log line and metrics have exemplars, so from a latency spike we can click straight to a slow trace and then to its logs."

War story: the trace that ended at the thread pool

A payments team adopted tracing, but traces for refunds always stopped at refund-service. The refund flow used a custom ExecutorService for parallel ledger updates; the context stayed on the request thread. For months, slow refunds were blamed on the ledger database, which looked fine. Fix: wrapped the executor with context propagation; the now-complete traces showed the real culprit: a synchronous call to a fraud-scoring API inside the parallel tasks, with no timeout. Lesson: a trace that stops early hides the actual problem. Verify propagation across every async boundary.

docs.text:
Distributed Tracing Correlation ID in logs Metrics Log aggregation Answers Where in the chain, for one request Which log lines belong together How much / how often What exactly happened Structure Tree of timed spans Flat ID Aggregates Text/events Cost Medium (sampling) Low Low High

See Sidecar / Service Mesh, API Gateway (where traces start), and Saga (where async tracing matters most).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Trace = request journey; span = timed operation with a parent.
  • Propagate traceparent over HTTP, gRPC and message headers.
  • Watch async boundaries (executors, @Async, reactive).
  • Parent-based + tail sampling; IDs in logs; no PII in spans.
  • OpenTelemetry + Jaeger/Tempo; Spring Boot 3 = Micrometer Tracing.

docs.title: Event Sourcing
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Instead of storing the current state and overwriting it, store every change as an immutable event in an append-only log. The current state is derived by replaying the events (sped up with snapshots). You get a complete audit trail, time travel ("what was the state on 1 March?"), and the ability to build new views from history, at the cost of more complexity (schema evolution, replays, eventual consistency of read models).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a CRUD accounts table says the balance is ₹11,200. How did it get there? Which deposit was reversed? What was the balance at month-end for the regulator? The UPDATE destroyed that information. Bolting on audit tables later is error-prone (they drift from reality).

Definition (Martin Fowler):

Event Sourcing ensures that all changes to application state are stored as a sequence of events. Not just can we query these events, we can also use the event log to reconstruct past states.

Core mechanics:

Concept Meaning Event An immutable fact in the past tense: Deposited(₹100) Stream All events of one aggregate, in order (account-ACC-1) Rehydration Rebuilding state by applying events in order Snapshot Saved state at version N, so replay starts there Optimistic concurrency Append only if the stream is still at the expected version Projection A read model built from events (see CQRS)

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Your bank passbook vs. a whiteboard

A whiteboard shows only today's balance; erase and rewrite. A passbook lists every deposit and withdrawal; the balance is the sum. You can check any past balance, find a wrong entry, and correct it with a new entry (a reversal), never by tearing out a page. Accountants have worked this way for centuries.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     C[Command: withdraw ₹25] --> L[Load: snapshot + later events]     L --> A[Aggregate checks rules]     A -->|new events| S[(Event store<br/>append-only)]     S --> P1[Projection: balance view]     S --> P2[Projection: statement]     S --> P3[Projection: fraud analytics] Participant Responsibility Aggregate Rebuilds state from events; decides which new events a command produces Event store Appends events per stream with version checks; reads streams Snapshot store Optional; periodic state copies to bound replay time Projections Read models, rebuildable from the log

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2500 WHERE id = 'ACC-1';
-- History lost. Audit table added later:
INSERT INTO account_audit ...   -- forgotten in one code path → audit no longer matches reality

docs.title: Example 1: Event-Sourced Bank Account (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: An account stream with Opened, Deposited and Withdrawn events. The repository loads the latest snapshot (taken every 4 events) and replays only later events. Two tellers load version 6 at the same time; teller A withdraws first; teller B's append is rejected by optimistic concurrency, reloads, and the rule check now correctly refuses the withdrawal: no double spend.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant A as Teller A participant B as Teller B participant S as Event store A->>S: load (v6) B->>S: load (v6) A->>S: append Withdrawn(10000), expected v6 ✔ → v7 B->>S: append Withdrawn(10000), expected v6 ✘ (now v7) B->>S: reload v7 → balance 1200 → insufficient funds

Full Code:

Account.javaEventStore.javaAccountRepository.javaAccountEventSourcingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import java.util.List;

/**
 * An event-sourced aggregate. State is never stored directly: it is the result of applying every
 * event in order. Commands check rules against that state and return NEW events.
 */
public final class Account {

    public sealed interface Event permits Opened, Deposited, Withdrawn {
    }

    public record Opened(String owner) implements Event {
    }

    public record Deposited(long paise) implements Event {
    }

    public record Withdrawn(long paise) implements Event {
    }

    /** A snapshot: the state as of a version, so replay can start there. */
    public record Snapshot(long version, String owner, long balance) {
    }

    private String owner;
    private long balance;
    private long version;

    public static Account replay(Snapshot snapshot, List<Event> laterEvents) {
        Account a = new Account();
        if (snapshot != null) {
            a.owner = snapshot.owner();
            a.balance = snapshot.balance();
            a.version = snapshot.version();
        }
        laterEvents.forEach(a::apply); // (1)!
        return a;
    }

    private void apply(Event e) { // (2)!
        switch (e) {
            case Opened o -> owner = o.owner();
            case Deposited d -> balance += d.paise();
            case Withdrawn w -> balance -= w.paise();
        }
        version++;
    }

    public List<Event> deposit(long paise) { // (3)!
        if (paise <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
        return List.of(new Deposited(paise));
    }

    public List<Event> withdraw(long paise) {
        if (paise > balance) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        }
        return List.of(new Withdrawn(paise));
    }

    public Snapshot snapshot() {
        return new Snapshot(version, owner, balance);
    }

    public long version() {
        return version;
    }

    public long balance() {
        return balance;
    }
}
  1. State = fold of events, starting from a snapshot if there is one.
  2. apply only changes state; it never validates (past events are facts, even if today's rules differ).
  3. Commands validate and return new events; they don't mutate state directly.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * An append-only store of events per stream (one stream per aggregate). Appends carry the version
 * the writer last saw; if someone else appended first, the write is rejected (optimistic locking).
 */
public final class EventStore<E> {

    public static final class ConcurrencyException extends RuntimeException {
        ConcurrencyException(String stream, long expected, long actual) {
            super(stream + ": expected version " + expected + " but was " + actual);
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, List<E>> streams = new HashMap<>();
    private int reads;

    public synchronized void append(String stream, long expectedVersion, List<E> events) {
        List<E> existing = streams.computeIfAbsent(stream, k -> new ArrayList<>());
        if (existing.size() != expectedVersion) { // (1)!
            throw new ConcurrencyException(stream, expectedVersion, existing.size());
        }
        existing.addAll(events);
    }

    /** Events with version greater than {@code afterVersion} (versions start at 1). */
    public synchronized List<E> read(String stream, long afterVersion) {
        List<E> all = streams.getOrDefault(stream, List.of());
        reads += all.size() - (int) afterVersion;
        return List.copyOf(all.subList((int) afterVersion, all.size()));
    }

    public synchronized int eventsReadSoFar() {
        return reads;
    }
}
  1. Optimistic concurrency: the append fails if someone else appended since we loaded.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Snapshot;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/** Loads aggregates from snapshot + later events, and saves new events with optimistic locking. */
public final class AccountRepository {

    private final EventStore<Event> store;
    private final Map<String, Snapshot> snapshots = new HashMap<>();
    private final int snapshotEvery;

    public AccountRepository(EventStore<Event> store, int snapshotEvery) {
        this.store = store;
        this.snapshotEvery = snapshotEvery;
    }

    public Account load(String id) {
        Snapshot snap = snapshots.get(id);
        return Account.replay(snap, store.read(id, snap == null ? 0 : snap.version()));
    }

    /** Load, run the command, append its events at the version we loaded. */
    public void execute(String id, Function<Account, List<Event>> command) {
        Account account = load(id);
        List<Event> events = command.apply(account);
        store.append(id, account.version(), events);
        Account after = Account.replay(account.snapshot(), events);
        if (after.version() / snapshotEvery > account.version() / snapshotEvery) { // (1)!
            snapshots.put(id, after.snapshot());
        }
    }
}
  1. Take a snapshot when the version crosses a multiple of snapshotEvery.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Opened;

import java.util.List;

public class AccountEventSourcingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EventStore<Event> store = new EventStore<>();
        var repo = new AccountRepository(store, 4);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: an event-sourced account ===");
        store.append("ACC-1", 0, List.of(new Opened("Asha")));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.deposit(10_000));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.withdraw(2_500));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.deposit(4_000));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.withdraw(1_000));
        repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.deposit(700));

        System.out.println("Event stream : " + store.read("ACC-1", 0));
        int before = store.eventsReadSoFar();
        Account loaded = repo.load("ACC-1");
        System.out.println("Balance " + loaded.balance() + " at version " + loaded.version()
                + ", rebuilt by replaying " + (store.eventsReadSoFar() - before) + " event(s) after the snapshot at v4");

        System.out.println("-- two tellers load v6 at the same time --");
        Account tellerA = repo.load("ACC-1");
        Account tellerB = repo.load("ACC-1");
        store.append("ACC-1", tellerA.version(), tellerA.withdraw(10_000));
        System.out.println("Teller A withdrew 10000 -> balance " + repo.load("ACC-1").balance());
        try {
            store.append("ACC-1", tellerB.version(), tellerB.withdraw(10_000));
        } catch (EventStore.ConcurrencyException e) {
            System.out.println("Teller B rejected: " + e.getMessage() + " -> reload and retry");
            try {
                repo.execute("ACC-1", a -> a.withdraw(10_000));
            } catch (IllegalStateException retryFailed) {
                System.out.println("Retry on fresh state: " + retryFailed.getMessage() + " (no double spend)");
            }
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: an event-sourced account ===
Event stream : [Opened[owner=Asha], Deposited[paise=10000], Withdrawn[paise=2500], Deposited[paise=4000], Withdrawn[paise=1000], Deposited[paise=700]]
Balance 11200 at version 6, rebuilt by replaying 2 event(s) after the snapshot at v4
-- two tellers load v6 at the same time --
Teller A withdrew 10000 -> balance 1200
Teller B rejected: ACC-1: expected version 6 but was 7 -> reload and retry
Retry on fresh state: insufficient funds (no double spend)

Why event sourcing here:

  • The ledger is the history; audits and disputes read it directly.
  • Concurrency is handled per stream without row locks.
  • Snapshots keep loading fast as streams grow.

docs.title: Example 2: What the Cart Table Forgets (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: A CRUD cart table shows only what's in each cart now. The event log also knows what was added and removed. Replaying it reveals that avocados are removed right before checkout in carts that still get bought, a signal about price or stock reliability that CRUD would have deleted.

Full Code:

CartEvents.javaCartHistoryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** Cart events, the current cart derived from them, and an insight a CRUD table would have lost. */
public final class CartEvents {

    public sealed interface Event permits ItemAdded, ItemRemoved, CheckedOut {
        String cartId();
    }

    public record ItemAdded(String cartId, String sku) implements Event {
    }

    public record ItemRemoved(String cartId, String sku) implements Event {
    }

    public record CheckedOut(String cartId) implements Event {
    }

    private CartEvents() {
    }

    /** Current state: what a CRUD "cart_items" table would hold. */
    public static Map<String, List<String>> currentCarts(List<Event> log) {
        Map<String, List<String>> carts = new TreeMap<>();
        for (Event e : log) {
            switch (e) {
                case ItemAdded a -> carts.computeIfAbsent(a.cartId(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(a.sku());
                case ItemRemoved r -> carts.get(r.cartId()).remove(r.sku());
                case CheckedOut c -> { }
            }
        }
        return carts;
    }

    /** History-based insight: items removed from carts that were later checked out anyway. */
    public static Map<String, Integer> removedBeforeCheckout(List<Event> log) {
        Map<String, List<String>> removedPerCart = new HashMap<>();
        Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>();
        for (Event e : log) {
            switch (e) {
                case ItemRemoved r -> removedPerCart.computeIfAbsent(r.cartId(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(r.sku());
                case CheckedOut c -> removedPerCart.getOrDefault(c.cartId(), List.of())
                        .forEach(sku -> counts.merge(sku, 1, Integer::sum)); // (1)!
                case ItemAdded a -> { }
            }
        }
        return counts;
    }
}
  1. A new question asked of old data: no schema change, just a new fold over the events.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.CheckedOut;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.ItemAdded;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.cart.CartEvents.ItemRemoved;

import java.util.List;

public class CartHistoryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Event> log = List.of(
                new ItemAdded("C1", "MANGO-1KG"), new ItemAdded("C1", "AVOCADO-2"), new ItemRemoved("C1", "AVOCADO-2"),
                new CheckedOut("C1"),
                new ItemAdded("C2", "AVOCADO-2"), new ItemAdded("C2", "RICE-5KG"), new ItemRemoved("C2", "AVOCADO-2"),
                new CheckedOut("C2"),
                new ItemAdded("C3", "MILK-1L"), new ItemAdded("C3", "BREAD"), new ItemRemoved("C3", "BREAD"));

        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: what the cart table shows vs. what the events know ===");
        System.out.println("Current carts (CRUD view)          : " + CartEvents.currentCarts(log));
        System.out.println("Removed, yet the cart was bought   : " + CartEvents.removedBeforeCheckout(log));
        System.out.println("Insight: avocados are dropped at checkout. Is the price too high, or is stock unreliable?");
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: what the cart table shows vs. what the events know ===
Current carts (CRUD view)          : {C1=[MANGO-1KG], C2=[RICE-5KG], C3=[MILK-1L]}
Removed, yet the cart was bought   : {AVOCADO-2=2}
Insight: avocados are dropped at checkout. Is the price too high, or is stock unreliable?

Why event sourcing here:

  • Business questions nobody thought of at design time can be answered retroactively.
  • Analytics and ML features come from the same source of truth as the app.

docs.title: Example 3: Temporal Queries on a Shipment (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A customer disputes a late delivery and blames the courier. Replaying the shipment's scans up to a point in time shows exactly what the system knew then: at 14:00 the parcel was in transit at Pune; by midnight it was flagged with a weather delay.

Full Code:

ShipmentHistory.javaShipmentTemporalDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.shipment;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

/** Shipment events with timestamps support "what did we know at time T?" queries. */
public final class ShipmentHistory {

    public record Scanned(Instant at, String location, String status) {
    }

    public record State(String location, String status) {
    }

    private final List<Scanned> events;

    public ShipmentHistory(List<Scanned> events) {
        this.events = List.copyOf(events);
    }

    public State current() {
        return stateAt(Instant.MAX);
    }

    public State stateAt(Instant when) { // (1)!
        State state = new State("-", "CREATED");
        for (Scanned e : events) {
            if (e.at().isAfter(when)) {
                break;
            }
            state = new State(e.location(), e.status());
        }
        return state;
    }
}
  1. Time travel: replay only events up to when.
package com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.shipment;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.shipment.ShipmentHistory.Scanned;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

public class ShipmentTemporalDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var history = new ShipmentHistory(List.of(
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T06:10:00Z"), "Mumbai hub", "PICKED_UP"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T13:45:00Z"), "Pune sort centre", "IN_TRANSIT"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T18:20:00Z"), "Pune sort centre", "DELAYED_WEATHER"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-13T09:05:00Z"), "Bengaluru hub", "IN_TRANSIT"),
                new Scanned(Instant.parse("2026-10-13T15:30:00Z"), "Koramangala", "DELIVERED")));

        System.out.println("=== Logistics: temporal queries on a shipment ===");
        System.out.println("Now                         : " + history.current());
        System.out.println("At 2026-10-12 14:00 UTC     : " + history.stateAt(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T14:00:00Z")));
        System.out.println("At 2026-10-12 23:59 UTC     : " + history.stateAt(Instant.parse("2026-10-12T23:59:00Z")));
        System.out.println("Customer says: \"the delay was the courier's fault\" -> the history shows a weather delay at Pune, 18:20.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: temporal queries on a shipment ===
Now                         : State[location=Koramangala, status=DELIVERED]
At 2026-10-12 14:00 UTC     : State[location=Pune sort centre, status=IN_TRANSIT]
At 2026-10-12 23:59 UTC     : State[location=Pune sort centre, status=DELAYED_WEATHER]
Customer says: "the delay was the courier's fault" -> the history shows a weather delay at Pune, 18:20.

Why event sourcing here:

  • "As of" queries are natural; with CRUD they need bitemporal tables.
  • Dispute resolution and SLA penalties rely on exact history.
Unit Tests: EventSourcingTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Deposited;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Event;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.Account.Opened;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.AccountRepository;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.account.EventStore;
import com.handbook.microservices.eventsourcing.upcasting.Upcaster;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class EventSourcingTest {

    @Test
    void stateIsRebuiltFromEventsWithOrWithoutSnapshots() {
        EventStore<Event> store = new EventStore<>();
        store.append("A", 0, List.of(new Opened("x")));
        var repo = new AccountRepository(store, 2);
        repo.execute("A", a -> a.deposit(100));
        repo.execute("A", a -> a.deposit(50));
        assertThat(repo.load("A").balance()).isEqualTo(150);
        assertThat(Account.replay(null, store.read("A", 0)).balance()).isEqualTo(150);
    }

    @Test
    void staleWriterIsRejected() {
        EventStore<Event> store = new EventStore<>();
        store.append("A", 0, List.of(new Opened("x")));
        store.append("A", 1, List.of(new Deposited(1)));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> store.append("A", 1, List.of(new Deposited(1))))
                .isInstanceOf(EventStore.ConcurrencyException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void upcasterConvertsRupeeStringsToPaise() {
        Map<String, Object> v1 = new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(Map.of("type", "PriceSet", "version", 1, "price", "1.05"));
        assertThat(Upcaster.upcast(v1)).containsEntry("amountPaise", 105L).containsEntry("version", 2);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
// Axon Framework (reference): an event-sourced aggregate
@Aggregate
class AccountAggregate {
    @AggregateIdentifier String id;
    long balance;

    @CommandHandler
    void handle(WithdrawCommand cmd) {
        if (cmd.amount() > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        AggregateLifecycle.apply(new Withdrawn(cmd.accountId(), cmd.amount())); // stored + applied
    }

    @EventSourcingHandler
    void on(Withdrawn e) { balance -= e.amount(); }  // used for rehydration
}
Option Notes EventStoreDB (Kurrent) Purpose-built event store: streams, subscriptions, optimistic concurrency Axon Framework + Axon Server Java CQRS/ES framework with snapshots and sagas PostgreSQL table events(stream_id, version, type, payload, PRIMARY KEY(stream_id, version)): the unique key enforces concurrency Kafka Great for distributing events, but weak as the store for per-aggregate loads and optimistic concurrency Java records + sealed interfaces Ideal for events: immutable, exhaustive switch in apply

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Event sourcing Axon Framework @EventSourcingHandler, snapshots, upcasters EventStoreDB Streams with expected-version appends Git Commits are events; a checkout is a replay Database WAL / Kafka log compaction Log-first storage underneath many systems Accounting ledgers Double-entry bookkeeping is event sourcing on paper

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Complete audit trail by design Steep learning curve; unfamiliar to most teams Temporal queries and debugging by replay Event schema evolution is hard (events are forever) New read models from old data Queries need projections (CQRS) Natural fit with event-driven integration GDPR "right to be forgotten" in an immutable log needs crypto-shredding No lost updates (optimistic concurrency per stream) Replays can be slow without snapshots

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Event sourcing the whole system

Use it for aggregates where history matters (ledgers, orders, workflows), not for user profiles or reference data. Mixing styles per service is normal.

Using events as a message bus between services without contracts

Internal domain events (fine-grained, private) are different from integration events (public, stable). Publishing internal events couples other services to your internals.

Validating in apply

If rules change, old events would fail to replay. apply must accept every historical event; validate in command handlers.

Changing or deleting stored events

Fix mistakes with compensating events (DepositReversed). For schema changes, use upcasting (see the coding challenge) or copy-and-transform migrations.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Schema evolution strategies. Weak schemas (tolerant readers ignoring unknown fields), upcasters that convert old versions on read, versioned event types, or copy-transform migrations of whole streams. Keep events small and business-focused to limit change.

GDPR and immutability. Encrypt personal data in events with a per-subject key and delete the key on erasure (crypto-shredding), or keep PII out of events and reference it.

Snapshot policy. Snapshot every N events or when load time exceeds a threshold; snapshots are a cache, so they can be discarded and rebuilt after model changes.

When it pays off. Domains with inherent history (finance, logistics, compliance), complex workflows, or heavy analytics needs. When it doesn't: CRUD-heavy domains, small teams, tight deadlines.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Clear reason (audit, temporal queries, complex domain), scoped to specific aggregates.
  • Event store with per-stream optimistic concurrency (unique (stream, version)).
  • Snapshot policy; replay performance measured.
  • Versioned events + upcasters; tolerant readers.
  • Separate internal domain events from published integration events.
  • PII strategy (crypto-shredding); retention and archival plan.
  • Projections idempotent with checkpoints; rebuild procedure tested.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"For the wallet ledger I'd use event sourcing: each wallet is a stream of Credited/Debited/Reversed events in a PostgreSQL events table with a unique (wallet_id, version) constraint for optimistic concurrency. Commands load a snapshot plus recent events, check the balance rule and append. Events go to Kafka via the outbox and feed projections: balance, statements and fraud features. Corrections are new events, never updates. Snapshots every 100 events keep loads fast, upcasters handle schema changes, and personal data is encrypted per user for erasure."

War story: the event nobody could replay

A logistics company renamed a field in ParcelScanned and deployed. Old events still had the old field name; the next projection rebuild failed halfway through 400 million events, and the tracking page served stale data for 9 hours while engineers wrote an emergency upcaster. Fix: schema-compatibility checks in CI (every historical event version must deserialize), upcasters registered for every change, and a nightly replay of a sample of old streams. Lesson: in event sourcing, old events are part of your API forever. Test them like an API.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Event Sourcing CRUD + audit table Transactional Outbox Memento Source of truth Events Current state Current state Current state History Complete, by design Partial, can drift Published events only Explicit snapshots Temporal queries Natural Hard No Snapshots only

See CQRS (projections), Transactional Outbox, and the in-process Memento and Command patterns.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • State = replay of immutable events; snapshots for speed.
  • Commands validate → new events; apply never validates.
  • Optimistic concurrency per stream (expected version).
  • Corrections are new events; upcasters for schema changes.
  • Pair with CQRS projections for queries.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a DepositReversed event and make the account handle it.
  • Add stateAt(version) to Account (replay only the first N events).
  • Write an upcaster chain v1 → v2 → v3 where v3 adds a region field defaulting to "IN".

CQRS Next: Database per Service

docs.title: Gateway Aggregation
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Gateway Aggregation combines several backend calls into one client request: the client asks once, the gateway fans out (in parallel where possible), merges the results and returns a single response, within a latency budget and with partial results when a backend is slow or down. Use it when clients (especially mobile) would otherwise make many round trips. Keep it to composition: no business rules.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a travel app's trip screen needs flight status, the hotel, the cab and the weather, from four services. On a 4G connection each round trip costs ~300 ms, so the screen takes over a second, drains the battery and breaks when any one call fails. Every client (iOS, Android, web) re-implements the same fan-out.

Definition (Azure Architecture Center, Gateway Aggregation pattern):

Use a gateway to aggregate multiple individual requests into a single request. The gateway receives one request from the client, dispatches requests to the various backend systems, aggregates the results and sends them back to the requesting client.

Where this page fits: the BFF page shows who owns aggregation (one backend per client experience). This page is about how to aggregate well: declarative composition, field-driven fan-out, latency budgets with partial results, and dependency-ordered calls.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A travel agent

Instead of calling the airline, the hotel, the cab company and checking the weather yourself, you call one travel agent who makes those calls in parallel and gives you one itinerary. If the cab company doesn't answer in time, the agent still sends the itinerary with "cab: to be confirmed", rather than making you wait all day.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     autonumber     participant App as Mobile app     participant G as Gateway / aggregator     participant F as Flights     participant H as Hotels     participant C as Cabs     App->>G: GET /itinerary/TRIP-9     par fan-out         G->>F: status         G->>H: booking         G->>C: pickup     end     F-->>G: 120 ms     H-->>G: 90 ms     C-->>G: 60 ms     G-->>App: one merged response (≈ slowest call) Participant Responsibility Client One request per screen/use case Aggregator (gateway, BFF, GraphQL server) Fan-out, per-call timeouts, overall budget, merge, partial-result handling Backend services Own their data; unaware of aggregation Composition spec Which backends and fields make up the response (code or configuration)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// Android client
val flight = api.flight(tripId)      // 300 ms
val hotel  = api.hotel(tripId)       // 300 ms
val cab    = api.cab(tripId)         // 300 ms
val wx     = api.weather(city)       // 300 ms  → 1.2 s, four failure points, repeated on iOS and web
  • Latency adds up over slow networks.
  • Each client duplicates orchestration and error handling.
  • Internal service boundaries leak into public APIs.

docs.title: Example 1: Declarative Itinerary Composition (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: A travel app's trip screen combines four services. The API team keeps the composition in configuration ("gate comes from flights.gate"), so adding a field is a config change reviewed like code, and the gateway calls all four backends in parallel. Latency becomes the slowest backend (120 ms) instead of four mobile round trips.

Design:

flowchart LR App -->|"GET /itinerary"| G["Aggregation spec<br/>flight ← flights.status<br/>gate ← flights.gate<br/>hotel ← hotels.name<br/>..."] G --> F[flights] & H[hotels] & C[cabs] & W[weather]

Full Code:

AggregationSpec.javaItineraryDemo.javaSimCall.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.declarative;

import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core.SimCall;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Aggregation as configuration: which backends to call and which fields to copy into the response. */
public final class AggregationSpec {

    /** "itinerary.flight <- flights.pnrStatus" style mapping. */
    public record FieldMapping(String responseField, String backend, String backendField) { }

    private final List<FieldMapping> mappings;

    public AggregationSpec(List<FieldMapping> mappings) {
        this.mappings = mappings;
    }

    /** Calls every backend in parallel once, then copies mapped fields; latency is the slowest call. */
    public Map<String, Object> execute(Map<String, SimCall> backends, StringBuilder timeline) {
        Map<String, Object> response = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        long slowest = 0;
        for (SimCall call : backends.values()) { // (1)!
            slowest = Math.max(slowest, call.latencyMs());
        }
        for (FieldMapping m : mappings) { // (2)!
            response.put(m.responseField(), backends.get(m.backend()).result().get(m.backendField()));
        }
        timeline.append(backends.size()).append(" backends in parallel, total ").append(slowest).append(" ms");
        return response;
    }
}
  1. Each backend is called once, in parallel: total latency is the maximum, not the sum.
  2. The response shape is driven by mappings, not hand-written merging code.
package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.declarative;

import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core.SimCall;
import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.declarative.AggregationSpec.FieldMapping;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class ItineraryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: One /itinerary Call Instead of Four from the Mobile App ===");
        AggregationSpec spec = new AggregationSpec(List.of( // would live in gateway YAML, owned by the API team
                new FieldMapping("flight", "flights", "status"),
                new FieldMapping("gate", "flights", "gate"),
                new FieldMapping("hotel", "hotels", "name"),
                new FieldMapping("checkIn", "hotels", "checkIn"),
                new FieldMapping("cab", "cabs", "pickup"),
                new FieldMapping("weather", "weather", "summary")));

        Map<String, SimCall> backends = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        backends.put("flights", SimCall.ok("flights", 120, Map.of("status", "6E-2134 on time", "gate", "B12")));
        backends.put("hotels", SimCall.ok("hotels", 90, Map.of("name", "Sea Breeze, Goa", "checkIn", "14:00")));
        backends.put("cabs", SimCall.ok("cabs", 60, Map.of("pickup", "GOI T1, 11:20")));
        backends.put("weather", SimCall.ok("weather", 40, Map.of("summary", "31C, humid")));

        StringBuilder timeline = new StringBuilder();
        Map<String, Object> itinerary = spec.execute(backends, timeline);
        System.out.println("Response: " + itinerary);
        System.out.println("Gateway: " + timeline + "; the app on 4G would have made 4 round trips (~4 x 300 ms).");
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core;

import java.util.Map;

/** A backend call with a known latency, so aggregation timelines are deterministic (virtual milliseconds). */
public record SimCall(String backend, long latencyMs, Map<String, Object> result, boolean fails) {

    public static SimCall ok(String backend, long latencyMs, Map<String, Object> result) {
        return new SimCall(backend, latencyMs, result, false);
    }

    public static SimCall failing(String backend, long latencyMs) {
        return new SimCall(backend, latencyMs, Map.of(), true);
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: One /itinerary Call Instead of Four from the Mobile App ===
Response: {flight=6E-2134 on time, gate=B12, hotel=Sea Breeze, Goa, checkIn=14:00, cab=GOI T1, 11:20, weather=31C, humid}
Gateway: 4 backends in parallel, total 120 ms; the app on 4G would have made 4 round trips (~4 x 300 ms).

Why aggregation here:

  • One round trip over the slow network; the fan-out happens on the fast data-centre network.
  • Composition is visible, reviewable configuration.
  • Backends stay unaware of the screen they serve.

docs.title: Example 2: Field-Driven Fan-Out (E-commerce)
docs.text:
Scenario: The search-results tile shows only name and price; the product page shows name, price, stock, rating and delivery ETA. The reviews service is slow (180 ms). With a fixed "product" endpoint, every search tile would wait for reviews it never displays. With GraphQL-style field selection, the aggregator calls only the backends that own the requested fields.

Design:

flowchart LR T["Search tile: {name, price}"] --> A{Field → owner} P["Product page: {name, price, stock, rating, eta}"] --> A A -->|tile| C[catalog] & PR[pricing] A -->|page| C & PR & I[inventory] & R[reviews] & D[delivery]

Full Code:

FieldDrivenAggregator.javaProductFieldsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.fields;

import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core.SimCall;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/** GraphQL-style: the client names the fields it needs; only the backends that own those fields are called. */
public final class FieldDrivenAggregator {

    private final Map<String, String> fieldOwner; // field -> backend
    private final Map<String, SimCall> backends;

    public FieldDrivenAggregator(Map<String, String> fieldOwner, Map<String, SimCall> backends) {
        this.fieldOwner = fieldOwner;
        this.backends = backends;
    }

    public record Result(Map<String, Object> data, Set<String> backendsCalled, long latencyMs) { }

    public Result query(List<String> fields) {
        Set<String> needed = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (String f : fields) {
            needed.add(fieldOwner.get(f)); // (1)!
        }
        long latency = needed.stream().mapToLong(b -> backends.get(b).latencyMs()).max().orElse(0);
        Map<String, Object> data = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (String f : fields) {
            data.put(f, backends.get(fieldOwner.get(f)).result().get(f));
        }
        return new Result(data, needed, latency);
    }
}
  1. Resolve each requested field to its owning backend; the set of backends to call is derived from the query. This is how GraphQL resolvers and Netflix's federated graph avoid over-fetching.
package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.fields;

import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core.SimCall;
import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.fields.FieldDrivenAggregator.Result;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class ProductFieldsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== E-commerce: Each Screen Asks Only for the Fields It Shows ===");
        FieldDrivenAggregator gateway = new FieldDrivenAggregator(
                Map.of("name", "catalog", "price", "pricing", "stock", "inventory", "rating", "reviews", "eta", "delivery"),
                Map.of("catalog", SimCall.ok("catalog", 30, Map.of("name", "Noise-cancelling earbuds")),
                        "pricing", SimCall.ok("pricing", 25, Map.of("price", "INR 3,999")),
                        "inventory", SimCall.ok("inventory", 40, Map.of("stock", "In stock")),
                        "reviews", SimCall.ok("reviews", 180, Map.of("rating", "4.3 (2,140)")),
                        "delivery", SimCall.ok("delivery", 70, Map.of("eta", "Tomorrow"))));

        Result listTile = gateway.query(List.of("name", "price"));
        System.out.println("Search tile   " + listTile.data() + " -> called " + listTile.backendsCalled() + ", " + listTile.latencyMs() + " ms");
        Result detail = gateway.query(List.of("name", "price", "stock", "rating", "eta"));
        System.out.println("Product page  -> called " + detail.backendsCalled().size() + " backends, " + detail.latencyMs() + " ms (reviews is the slow one)");
        System.out.println("A fixed 'product' endpoint would make every search tile wait 180 ms for reviews it doesn't show.");
    }
}

Output:

=== E-commerce: Each Screen Asks Only for the Fields It Shows ===
Search tile   {name=Noise-cancelling earbuds, price=INR 3,999} -> called [catalog, pricing], 30 ms
Product page  -> called 5 backends, 180 ms (reviews is the slow one)
A fixed 'product' endpoint would make every search tile wait 180 ms for reviews it doesn't show.

Why field-driven aggregation here:

  • Each screen pays only for the data it shows (30 ms vs 180 ms for search tiles).
  • Fewer backend calls under load: search pages are 10× more common than product pages.
  • One endpoint serves many screens without bespoke versions.

docs.title: Example 3: Latency Budget with Partial Results (Insurance)
docs.text:
Scenario: An insurance marketplace shows car-insurance quotes from 5 insurers. Most answer in under 700 ms; one partner API often takes 2 seconds; another sometimes errors. Product's rule: show the page within 800 ms with whatever quotes are available, sorted by price, and list who's missing, rather than fail or make everyone wait for the slowest insurer.

Design:

gantt dateFormat x axisFormat %L ms title Fan-out with an 800 ms budget section Insurers Suraksha General (220) :0, 220 Bharat Shield (640) :0, 640 Raksha Direct (410) :0, 410 Kavach Insure (1900, cut) :crit, 0, 800 Monsoon Mutual (error) :crit, 0, 150

Full Code:

QuoteAggregator.javaQuotesDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.budget;

import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core.SimCall;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

/** Fan out to every insurer, keep whatever answers within the latency budget, and say what's missing. */
public final class QuoteAggregator {

    public record Quote(String insurer, long premiumPaise) { }

    public record Page(List<Quote> quotes, List<String> missing, long respondedAtMs) { }

    private final long budgetMs;

    public QuoteAggregator(long budgetMs) {
        this.budgetMs = budgetMs;
    }

    public Page aggregate(List<SimCall> insurers) {
        List<Quote> quotes = new ArrayList<>();
        List<String> missing = new ArrayList<>();
        long latest = 0;
        for (SimCall call : insurers) {
            if (call.fails()) {
                missing.add(call.backend() + " (error)"); // (1)!
            } else if (call.latencyMs() > budgetMs) {
                missing.add(call.backend() + " (timed out at " + budgetMs + " ms)"); // (2)!
            } else {
                quotes.add(new Quote(call.backend(), (Long) call.result().get("premium")));
                latest = Math.max(latest, call.latencyMs());
            }
        }
        boolean anyMissing = !missing.isEmpty();
        quotes.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::premiumPaise));
        return new Page(quotes, missing, anyMissing ? budgetMs : latest); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. A failing backend becomes a missing section, not a failed page.
  2. A backend slower than the budget is cut off (completeOnTimeout / orTimeout in real code).
  3. The response time is bounded by the budget whenever anything is missing.
package com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.budget;

import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.budget.QuoteAggregator.Page;
import com.handbook.microservices.aggregation.core.SimCall;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class QuotesDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Insurance: Car Insurance Quotes from 5 Insurers within 800 ms ===");
        List<SimCall> insurers = List.of(
                SimCall.ok("Suraksha General", 220, Map.of("premium", 1_245_000L)),
                SimCall.ok("Bharat Shield", 640, Map.of("premium", 1_189_900L)),
                SimCall.ok("Kavach Insure", 1_900, Map.of("premium", 1_099_000L)), // slow partner API
                SimCall.failing("Monsoon Mutual", 150),
                SimCall.ok("Raksha Direct", 410, Map.of("premium", 1_310_500L)));
        Page page = new QuoteAggregator(800).aggregate(insurers);
        page.quotes().forEach(q -> System.out.printf("  %-17s INR %,d%n", q.insurer(), q.premiumPaise() / 100));
        System.out.println("Missing: " + page.missing());
        System.out.println("Page returned at " + page.respondedAtMs() + " ms with partial results, instead of waiting 1,900 ms or failing.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Insurance: Car Insurance Quotes from 5 Insurers within 800 ms ===
  Bharat Shield     INR 11,899
  Suraksha General  INR 12,450
  Raksha Direct     INR 13,105
Missing: [Kavach Insure (timed out at 800 ms), Monsoon Mutual (error)]
Page returned at 800 ms with partial results, instead of waiting 1,900 ms or failing.

Why a budget here:

  • The page's latency is decided by product, not by the slowest partner.
  • Partial results are better than no results for comparison shopping.
  • The "missing" list can drive a "more quotes loading" refresh or partner SLAs.

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Aggregation Spring Spring for GraphQL (@SchemaMapping, @BatchMapping), Spring Cloud Gateway custom filters, WebFlux Mono.zip GraphQL ecosystem Apollo Federation, Netflix DGS, DataLoader API gateways KrakenD (merging backends), Kong and Apigee policies, AWS AppSync JDK CompletableFuture.allOf, completeOnTimeout, orTimeout; virtual threads

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons One round trip for the client: lower latency, less battery The aggregator is a new hop and a potential bottleneck Centralised fan-out, timeouts and fallbacks Couples the aggregator to many backends' APIs Partial results instead of all-or-nothing Risk of business logic creeping into the gateway Hides internal service boundaries from public APIs Harder to cache than single-resource endpoints

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Sequential calls in the aggregator

Calling backends one after another just moves the latency problem to the server. Parallelize everything that doesn't depend on something else (coding challenge).

No per-call timeouts

Without timeouts, the slowest backend sets the page's latency, and a hung backend exhausts the aggregator's threads.

Business rules in the gateway

Discount calculation or eligibility checks in aggregation code create a hidden monolith. Push rules into the owning service.

N+1 fan-out

Fetching ratings for 50 products with 50 calls. Use batch endpoints (@BatchMapping, DataLoader).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Latency math. Parallel latency ≈ max(calls); with dependencies it's the critical path. Tail latency compounds: if each of 5 backends has a 1% chance of a 1-second response, the aggregate is slow ~5% of the time. Budgets, hedging and optional sections keep the tail under control.

Failure semantics are a product decision. For each section: required (fail the page), optional (omit with a marker), or stale-acceptable (serve cached). Write it down per endpoint and test each degraded mode.

Ownership. If one team owns a generic aggregation gateway for everyone, it becomes a bottleneck for every client change. Prefer BFFs owned by client teams, or GraphQL federation where each domain team owns its part of the schema.

War story: the home screen that waited for recommendations

A grocery app's home endpoint aggregated banners, orders, offers and recommendations, with no per-call timeouts. When the recommendations service degraded to 4-second responses, the whole home screen took 4 seconds; app-open conversion dropped 22% in an hour. Fix: 250 ms timeouts per optional section, recommendations made optional with a cached fallback, and a 600 ms overall budget. Lesson: an aggregator is only as fast as its slowest required dependency, so make most dependencies optional.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One client request → parallel fan-out → merged response.
  • Latency = slowest call (or critical path), so parallelize and add timeouts.
  • Overall budget + optional sections = partial results, not failures.
  • Field-driven fan-out avoids over-fetching; batch to avoid N+1.
  • Composition only: no business rules.
