docs.title: Health Check (Liveness & Readiness)
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A service exposes health endpoints that the platform polls: liveness ("is this process broken and needs a restart?") and readiness ("can it take traffic right now?"). Load balancers route only to ready instances; orchestrators restart only non-live ones. Every service needs both, and they must check different things: dependencies belong in readiness, never in liveness.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a pod is "running" but its thread pool is deadlocked, so it returns nothing and the load balancer keeps sending it customers. Another pod is still warming its cache and gets traffic too early, timing out the first thousand requests. And when the database blips, a naïve health check makes Kubernetes restart every pod at once, turning a 1-minute blip into a 5-minute outage.

Definition (microservices.io, Health Check API):

A service has a health check API endpoint (e.g. /health) that returns the health of the service. A monitoring service, service registry or load balancer periodically invokes the endpoint to check the instance and route requests accordingly.

Probe Question Failure means Typical checks Liveness Is the process alive and making progress? Restart the container Event loop / thread pool responsive, no deadlock Readiness Should this instance receive traffic now? Stop routing to it (no restart) Started, caches warm, critical dependencies reachable, not overloaded Startup Has it finished starting? Keep waiting (don't run liveness yet) Initialization done

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A shop's lights and its OPEN sign

The lights being on tells you someone's inside (liveness). The OPEN sign tells you they're ready to serve (readiness). During stock-taking, the lights stay on but the sign is flipped to CLOSED; nobody calls an ambulance just because the shop is closed for an hour. If the shopkeeper collapses (deadlock), that's when you call for help (restart).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     K[kubelet] -->|"/actuator/health/liveness"| P[Pod]     K -->|"/actuator/health/readiness"| P     LB[Service / load balancer] -.->|"routes only if ready"| P     P --> D1[(Database)]     P --> D2[Cache]     P --> D3[Optional: recommendations]     K -->|"liveness failed N times"| R[Restart container] Participant Responsibility Health indicators One per component (DB, cache, broker, disk), each UP/DOWN with details Health groups Liveness and readiness are different groups of indicators Prober kubelet, load balancer, service registry, monitoring Policy Thresholds, periods, timeouts; what to do on failure (restart vs remove from rotation)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@GetMapping("/health")
public String health() {
    jdbcTemplate.queryForObject("SELECT 1", Integer.class);   // used for BOTH liveness and readiness
    restTemplate.getForObject("http://recommendations/health", String.class);  // optional dependency
    return "OK";
}
  • A database blip fails liveness → every pod restarts → cold caches → longer outage.
  • An optional dependency makes the whole service "unhealthy".
  • Every probe from every prober hits the database.

docs.title: Example 1: Liveness vs Readiness Through a Pod's Life (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The grocery catalog service warms an in-memory cache of 200,000 SKUs for 40 seconds at startup. Later, the database fails over for 30 seconds. Later still, a bug deadlocks its worker pool. The probes must keep the cold pod out of rotation, keep pods alive (but out of rotation) during the failover, and restart only the deadlocked pod.

Design:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Starting: container starts Starting --> Serving: cache warm (ready=200) Serving --> OutOfRotation: DB failover (ready=503, live=200) OutOfRotation --> Serving: DB back Serving --> Restarting: deadlock (live=503) Restarting --> Starting

Full Code:

GroceryProbes.javaProbesDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.probes;

import java.util.function.BooleanSupplier;

/** Liveness: "am I broken beyond repair?" Readiness: "can I serve traffic right now?" They answer different questions. */
public final class GroceryProbes {

    private final BooleanSupplier eventLoopResponsive;
    private final BooleanSupplier databaseReachable;
    private final BooleanSupplier catalogCacheWarm;

    public GroceryProbes(BooleanSupplier eventLoopResponsive, BooleanSupplier databaseReachable, BooleanSupplier catalogCacheWarm) {
        this.eventLoopResponsive = eventLoopResponsive;
        this.databaseReachable = databaseReachable;
        this.catalogCacheWarm = catalogCacheWarm;
    }

    public int liveness() { // (1)!
        return eventLoopResponsive.getAsBoolean() ? 200 : 503;
    }

    public int readiness() { // (2)!
        return eventLoopResponsive.getAsBoolean() && databaseReachable.getAsBoolean() && catalogCacheWarm.getAsBoolean() ? 200 : 503;
    }

    /** What the platform does with the two answers. */
    public static String kubernetesAction(int liveness, int readiness) {
        if (liveness != 200) {
            return "RESTART container";
        }
        return readiness == 200 ? "send traffic" : "remove from Service endpoints (no restart)";
    }
}
  1. Liveness checks only the process itself. A restart can fix a deadlock; it can't fix the database.
  2. Readiness includes dependencies and warm-up, because those decide whether this instance should get requests now.
package com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.probes;

public class ProbesDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Liveness vs Readiness Through a Pod's Life ===");
        boolean[] loop = {true};
        boolean[] db = {true};
        boolean[] cache = {false};
        GroceryProbes probes = new GroceryProbes(() -> loop[0], () -> db[0], () -> cache[0]);

        String[] phases = {"starting, cache cold", "cache warmed", "database failover (30s)", "database back", "thread deadlock"};
        for (String phase : phases) {
            switch (phase) {
                case "cache warmed" -> cache[0] = true;
                case "database failover (30s)" -> db[0] = false;
                case "database back" -> db[0] = true;
                case "thread deadlock" -> loop[0] = false;
                default -> { }
            }
            int live = probes.liveness();
            int ready = probes.readiness();
            System.out.printf("%-24s live=%d ready=%d -> %s%n", phase, live, ready, GroceryProbes.kubernetesAction(live, ready));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Liveness vs Readiness Through a Pod's Life ===
starting, cache cold     live=200 ready=503 -> remove from Service endpoints (no restart)
cache warmed             live=200 ready=200 -> send traffic
database failover (30s)  live=200 ready=503 -> remove from Service endpoints (no restart)
database back            live=200 ready=200 -> send traffic
thread deadlock          live=503 ready=503 -> RESTART container

Why two probes here:

  • Cold pods never get traffic; they join only when ready.
  • Dependency problems remove pods from rotation without restarting them.
  • Genuine process failures still get the restart they need.

docs.title: Example 2: Composite Health by Criticality (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payment service depends on its ledger database and primary PSP (critical), plus a fraud-scoring service and an email-receipt service (optional, with fallbacks: rule-based fraud checks, receipts queued for later). The health endpoint must report DEGRADED when an optional dependency fails (still serving, but page the on-call) and DOWN only when a critical one fails.

Design:

flowchart TB H["/health → overall status"] --> L["ledgerDb (critical)"] H --> P["primaryPsp (critical)"] H --> F["fraudScoring (optional)"] H --> E["emailReceipts (optional)"] L & P -->|any DOWN| D[DOWN: stop traffic] F & E -->|any DOWN| G[DEGRADED: serve + alert]

Full Code:

CompositeHealth.javaPaymentsHealthDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Aggregate component health by criticality: a broken optional dependency degrades, a broken critical one is DOWN. */
public final class CompositeHealth {

    public enum Status { UP, DEGRADED, DOWN }

    public record Component(String name, boolean critical, boolean healthy) { }

    public record Report(Status status, Map<String, String> details) { }

    public static Report evaluate(List<Component> components) {
        Map<String, String> details = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        Status overall = Status.UP;
        for (Component c : components) {
            details.put(c.name(), c.healthy() ? "UP" : "DOWN" + (c.critical() ? "" : " (optional)"));
            if (!c.healthy() && c.critical()) {
                overall = Status.DOWN; // (1)!
            } else if (!c.healthy() && overall == Status.UP) {
                overall = Status.DEGRADED; // (2)!
            }
        }
        return new Report(overall, details);
    }
}
  1. Any critical component down makes the service DOWN (not ready).
  2. An optional component down only degrades it: the service keeps serving with a fallback.
package com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite;

import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite.CompositeHealth.Component;
import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite.CompositeHealth.Report;

import java.util.List;

public class PaymentsHealthDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: One Health Endpoint, Components with Different Criticality ===");
        print("Normal day", List.of(new Component("ledgerDb", true, true), new Component("primaryPsp", true, true),
                new Component("fraudScoring", false, true), new Component("emailReceipts", false, true)));
        print("Fraud scorer down", List.of(new Component("ledgerDb", true, true), new Component("primaryPsp", true, true),
                new Component("fraudScoring", false, false), new Component("emailReceipts", false, true)));
        print("Ledger DB down", List.of(new Component("ledgerDb", true, false), new Component("primaryPsp", true, true),
                new Component("fraudScoring", false, true), new Component("emailReceipts", false, false)));
        System.out.println("DEGRADED stays ready (fallback: rule-based fraud check) but pages the on-call; DOWN stops traffic.");
    }

    private static void print(String scenario, List<Component> components) {
        Report r = CompositeHealth.evaluate(components);
        System.out.printf("%-18s -> %-8s %s%n", scenario, r.status(), r.details());
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: One Health Endpoint, Components with Different Criticality ===
Normal day         -> UP       {ledgerDb=UP, primaryPsp=UP, fraudScoring=UP, emailReceipts=UP}
Fraud scorer down  -> DEGRADED {ledgerDb=UP, primaryPsp=UP, fraudScoring=DOWN (optional), emailReceipts=UP}
Ledger DB down     -> DOWN     {ledgerDb=DOWN, primaryPsp=UP, fraudScoring=UP, emailReceipts=DOWN (optional)}
DEGRADED stays ready (fallback: rule-based fraud check) but pages the on-call; DOWN stops traffic.

Why composite health here:

  • Health reflects business impact, not just "is everything green".
  • Optional failures don't take payments offline.
  • Details per component speed up diagnosis (but restrict them to internal callers).

docs.title: Example 3: Cached Deep Checks (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: A streaming catalog service runs 200 pods. Five probers (kubelet, load balancer, mesh, two monitors) hit each pod every second. If every probe ran SELECT 1 against the catalog database, that's 60,000 extra queries a minute just for health. The deep check runs at most once every 10 seconds per pod; probes read the cached result.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Pr as 5 probers (every 1s) participant C as CachedHealthCheck participant DB as Catalog DB Pr->>C: healthy? C->>DB: SELECT 1 (only if last check > 10 s ago) DB-->>C: ok C-->>Pr: cached result Pr->>C: healthy? (×49 more within 10 s) C-->>Pr: cached result (no DB call)

Full Code:

CachedHealthCheck.javaCachedHealthDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.cached;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.function.BooleanSupplier;

/** Run the expensive dependency check at most once per interval; probes read the cached result. */
public final class CachedHealthCheck {

    private final BooleanSupplier expensiveCheck;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration interval;
    private Instant checkedAt = Instant.MIN;
    private boolean lastResult;
    private int executions;

    public CachedHealthCheck(BooleanSupplier expensiveCheck, Clock clock, Duration interval) {
        this.expensiveCheck = expensiveCheck;
        this.clock = clock;
        this.interval = interval;
    }

    public synchronized boolean healthy() {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        if (checkedAt == Instant.MIN || !now.isBefore(checkedAt.plus(interval))) { // (1)!
            lastResult = expensiveCheck.getAsBoolean();
            checkedAt = now;
            executions++;
        }
        return lastResult;
    }

    public int executions() {
        return executions;
    }
}
  1. The expensive check runs only when the cached result is older than the interval; probes always get an instant answer.
package com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.cached;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class CachedHealthDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Probes Every Second, Database Checked Every 10 Seconds ===");
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-11-01T20:00:00Z");
        int[] dbQueries = {0};
        CachedHealthCheck check = new CachedHealthCheck(() -> {
            dbQueries[0]++;
            return true; // SELECT 1 against the catalog DB
        }, clock, Duration.ofSeconds(10));

        int probes = 0;
        for (int second = 0; second < 60; second++) {
            for (int source = 0; source < 5; source++) { // kubelet + load balancer + mesh + 2 monitors
                check.healthy();
                probes++;
            }
            clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        }
        System.out.println("Health probes in one minute: " + probes);
        System.out.println("Queries the database actually received: " + dbQueries[0]);
        System.out.println("Across 200 pods: " + probes * 200 + " probes -> " + dbQueries[0] * 200 + " DB queries per minute");
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Probes Every Second, Database Checked Every 10 Seconds ===
Health probes in one minute: 300
Queries the database actually received: 6
Across 200 pods: 60000 probes -> 1200 DB queries per minute

Why caching here:

  • Health checks must never become a load problem for the dependencies they check.
  • Probe responses stay fast (well under the probe timeout).
  • In production, run the check on a background schedule and have probes only read the result.
Unit Tests: HealthCheckTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.cached.CachedHealthCheck;
import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite.CompositeHealth;
import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite.CompositeHealth.Component;
import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.composite.CompositeHealth.Status;
import com.handbook.microservices.healthcheck.probes.GroceryProbes;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class HealthCheckTest {

    @Test
    void databaseOutageAffectsReadinessOnly() {
        GroceryProbes p = new GroceryProbes(() -> true, () -> false, () -> true);
        assertThat(p.liveness()).isEqualTo(200);
        assertThat(p.readiness()).isEqualTo(503);
    }

    @Test
    void optionalFailureDegradesCriticalFailureIsDown() {
        assertThat(CompositeHealth.evaluate(List.of(new Component("a", true, true), new Component("b", false, false))).status())
                .isEqualTo(Status.DEGRADED);
        assertThat(CompositeHealth.evaluate(List.of(new Component("a", true, false), new Component("b", false, true))).status())
                .isEqualTo(Status.DOWN);
    }

    @Test
    void expensiveCheckRunsOncePerInterval() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        CachedHealthCheck c = new CachedHealthCheck(() -> true, clock, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        c.healthy();
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(9));
        c.healthy();
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        c.healthy();
        assertThat(c.executions()).isEqualTo(2);
    }
}

docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Automatic recovery from stuck processes Wrong probe design causes restart storms Traffic only reaches instances that can serve it Probes add load if they do deep checks Zero-downtime deploys and graceful shutdown Health "green" doesn't guarantee correct behaviour Clear operational signal per component Details endpoints can leak internals if exposed publicly

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Dependencies in liveness

If the database is down, restarting every pod can't fix it; it just adds cold starts, connection storms and longer recovery (coding challenge). Put dependencies in readiness.

Shared dependency failing every pod's readiness

If all pods depend on the same database, readiness also drops all of them, and the service returns load-balancer errors instead of graceful ones. For a shared hard dependency, consider staying ready and serving a degraded response or fast 503s with a clear message.

No startup probe for slow starters

Without one, liveness kills slow-starting JVMs before they finish booting: crash loop.

Exposing health details publicly

show-details: always on a public endpoint reveals versions, hosts and dependency names. Restrict details to authenticated or internal callers.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Readiness is a load-shedding tool. Failing readiness under overload (queue too deep, latency too high) moves traffic to healthier pods. But if every pod reaches the same state, readiness empties the pool: combine it with backpressure and autoscaling instead of relying on it alone.

Liveness should be boring. The most useful liveness checks detect conditions only a restart fixes: deadlocked worker pools, a stuck event loop, an exhausted heap that GC can't recover. If you can't name such a condition, a basic "process responds" check is enough.

Health ≠ correctness. A service can be green and serving wrong prices. Pair probes with SLO-based alerting on real traffic (error rate, latency, business KPIs) and synthetic journeys.

War story: the database blip that became a 12-minute outage

A payments platform's liveness probe ran SELECT 1. A 70-second database failover failed liveness on all 60 pods; Kubernetes restarted them together. Each JVM took 50 seconds to start and then opened 40 connections at once, overloading the freshly promoted database. Pods failed liveness again. The cycle lasted 12 minutes. Fix: liveness = process only; readiness = DB + PSP; a startup probe for the JVM boot; connection-pool warm-up with jitter. Lesson: restarts fix processes, not dependencies.

docs.title: Idempotent Consumer
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Message brokers and clients deliver at-least-once, so the same message or request will arrive more than once. An idempotent consumer makes processing a duplicate harmless, typically by recording processed message IDs (or idempotency keys) in the same transaction as the side effect. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives an exactly-once effect.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a Kafka consumer credits ₹199 to a wallet and crashes before committing its offset; on restart it gets the message again and credits again. A mobile app's "Pay" request times out on a bad network; the app retries; the customer is charged twice. A courier app sends "out for delivery" twice; the customer gets two SMS. Duplicates are normal in distributed systems:

Source of duplicates Example Consumer crash/rebalance before offset commit Kafka redelivers the batch Producer retries Outbox relay republishes after a crash Client retries after a timeout The first request actually succeeded Upstream bugs Partner sends the same webhook twice

Definition (microservices.io):

Implement an idempotent consumer, which is a message consumer that can handle duplicate messages correctly.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A doorman with a guest list

Each guest's invitation has a number. When a guest arrives, the doorman ticks the number off. If someone arrives again with the same invitation (they stepped out and came back), the doorman sees the tick and doesn't hand them a second welcome gift.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR B[[Broker / client]] -->|message id=501| C[Consumer] C --> TX{{One local transaction}} TX --> P[(processed_messages<br/>PRIMARY KEY message_id)] TX --> S[(Business tables)] P -->|duplicate key| SKIP[Skip: already processed] Technique How Processed-message table Insert message ID with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect Idempotency key (APIs) Client sends a unique key; server stores the response and replays it for retries Natural idempotency Design operations to be idempotent: "set status = SHIPPED" vs. "add 1" Version / sequence checks Apply only if the event's version is newer than the stored one TTL dedupe cache Remember keys for a window (Redis SET NX EX) when occasional duplicates are tolerable

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@KafkaListener(topics = "refunds")
void on(RefundIssued e) {
    if (!processedIds.contains(e.id())) {   // check...
        wallet.credit(e.customer(), e.amount());
        processedIds.add(e.id());           // ...then act, in memory, outside the DB transaction
    }
}
// Crash between credit and add → duplicate credit after restart.
// Two instances processing concurrently → both pass the check.

docs.title: Example 1: Wallet Credits with a Processed-Messages Table (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Refund messages credit a customer's wallet. Each message's ID is inserted into processed_messages (primary key) in the same JDBC transaction as the credit (real H2 database). A redelivered message violates the key, the transaction rolls back, and the duplicate is acknowledged without effect.

Full Code:

WalletCreditConsumer.javaWalletDedupeDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.wallet;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;

/**
 * Credits a wallet for each RefundIssued message. The message ID is inserted into
 * processed_messages in the SAME transaction as the credit; a duplicate violates the primary key,
 * the whole transaction rolls back, and the duplicate is acknowledged without effect.
 */
public final class WalletCreditConsumer {

    public static final String[] SCHEMA = {
            "CREATE TABLE wallets (customer VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, balance BIGINT)",
            "CREATE TABLE processed_messages (message_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, processed_at TIMESTAMP)" // (1)!
    };

    private final DataSource db;

    public WalletCreditConsumer(DataSource db) {
        this.db = db;
    }

    /** Returns true if the message had an effect, false if it was a duplicate. */
    public boolean onRefundIssued(String messageId, String customer, long paise) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = db.getConnection()) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (PreparedStatement dedupe = c.prepareStatement(
                    "INSERT INTO processed_messages VALUES (?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)");
                 PreparedStatement credit = c.prepareStatement(
                         "MERGE INTO wallets w USING (VALUES (?, ?)) v(c, amt) ON w.customer = v.c "
                                 + "WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET balance = balance + v.amt "
                                 + "WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (v.c, v.amt)")) {
                dedupe.setString(1, messageId);
                dedupe.executeUpdate(); // (2)!
                credit.setString(1, customer);
                credit.setLong(2, paise);
                credit.executeUpdate();
                c.commit(); // (3)!
                return true;
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                c.rollback();
                if ("23505".equals(e.getSQLState())) { // unique violation: already processed
                    return false;
                }
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. The unique constraint is the guard: the database enforces it even across instances and threads.
  2. Inserting the ID first means a duplicate fails before any business change.
  3. ID and effect commit together. A crash before commit means neither happened, so the redelivery is processed normally.
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.wallet;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class WalletDedupeDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        DataSource db = Db.inMemory("wallet", WalletCreditConsumer.SCHEMA);
        var consumer = new WalletCreditConsumer(db);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: refund messages credited to the wallet exactly once ===");
        String[][] deliveries = {
                {"msg-501", "CUST-42", "19900"},
                {"msg-502", "CUST-42", "4500"},
                {"msg-501", "CUST-42", "19900"}, // redelivered after a consumer rebalance
                {"msg-502", "CUST-42", "4500"},  // redelivered again
        };
        for (String[] d : deliveries) {
            boolean applied = consumer.onRefundIssued(d[0], d[1], Long.parseLong(d[2]));
            System.out.println(d[0] + " ₹" + Long.parseLong(d[2]) / 100 + " -> " + (applied ? "credited" : "duplicate, skipped"));
        }
        System.out.println("Wallet balance: ₹" + Db.count(db, "SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE customer = 'CUST-42'") / 100
                + " (expected ₹244)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: refund messages credited to the wallet exactly once ===
msg-501 ₹199 -> credited
msg-502 ₹45 -> credited
msg-501 ₹199 -> duplicate, skipped
msg-502 ₹45 -> duplicate, skipped
Wallet balance: ₹244 (expected ₹244)

Why this design:

  • Correct under crashes, rebalances and multiple instances.
  • Cheap: one extra insert per message; old IDs can be purged after the broker's redelivery window.

docs.title: Example 2: Idempotency-Key for a Transfer API (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The mobile app sends POST /transfers with an Idempotency-Key. The response is lost on a flaky network; the app retries with the same key and gets the same response (TX-1001), so only one transfer is executed. Reusing the key with a different amount is a client bug and returns 422.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant App participant API as Transfer API participant S as Key store App->>API: POST /transfers (key-7f3a) API->>S: new key → execute → store response API--xApp: 201 (lost on network) App->>API: retry POST /transfers (key-7f3a) API->>S: key exists, same body → stored response API-->>App: 201 TX-1001 (no second transfer)

Full Code:

IdempotencyKeyStore.javaTransferApiDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Server side of the Idempotency-Key header (as used by payment APIs): the first request with a key
 * is executed and its response stored; retries with the same key get the stored response. Reusing a
 * key with a different request body is a client bug and is rejected.
 * Simplified for one thread: in production, first insert the key as IN_PROGRESS with a unique
 * constraint, so a concurrent retry gets 409 Conflict instead of executing the operation twice.
 */
public final class IdempotencyKeyStore {

    public record StoredResponse(String requestFingerprint, int status, String body) {
    }

    private final Map<String, StoredResponse> responses = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public StoredResponse execute(String key, String requestBody, Supplier<StoredResponse> operation) {
        String fingerprint = Integer.toHexString(requestBody.hashCode()); // (1)!
        StoredResponse previous = responses.get(key);
        if (previous != null) {
            if (!previous.requestFingerprint().equals(fingerprint)) {
                return new StoredResponse(fingerprint, 422, "Idempotency-Key reused with a different request"); // (2)!
            }
            return previous; // (3)!
        }
        StoredResponse fresh = operation.get();
        StoredResponse stored = new StoredResponse(fingerprint, fresh.status(), fresh.body());
        responses.put(key, stored);
        return stored;
    }
}
  1. A fingerprint of the request detects key reuse with a different body. Production code uses SHA-256 of the canonical body.
  2. Same key, different request: reject (422) rather than guessing.
  3. A retry gets the original response, including the original transfer ID.
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey;

import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey.IdempotencyKeyStore.StoredResponse;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class TransferApiDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var store = new IdempotencyKeyStore();
        AtomicInteger transfersExecuted = new AtomicInteger();

        System.out.println("=== Banking: POST /transfers with an Idempotency-Key ===");
        String body = "{from: A-100, to: B-200, amount: 5000}";
        StoredResponse first = store.execute("key-7f3a", body,
                () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "transfer TX-" + (1000 + transfersExecuted.incrementAndGet()) + " created"));
        System.out.println("1st attempt (response lost on a flaky mobile network): " + first.status() + " " + first.body());

        StoredResponse retry = store.execute("key-7f3a", body,
                () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "transfer TX-" + (1000 + transfersExecuted.incrementAndGet()) + " created"));
        System.out.println("App retries with the same key                          : " + retry.status() + " " + retry.body());

        StoredResponse misuse = store.execute("key-7f3a", "{from: A-100, to: B-200, amount: 9000}",
                () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "should not run"));
        System.out.println("Same key, different amount                             : " + misuse.status() + " " + misuse.body());
        System.out.println("Transfers actually executed: " + transfersExecuted.get());
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: POST /transfers with an Idempotency-Key ===
1st attempt (response lost on a flaky mobile network): 201 transfer TX-1001 created
App retries with the same key                          : 201 transfer TX-1001 created
Same key, different amount                             : 422 Idempotency-Key reused with a different request
Transfers actually executed: 1

Why idempotency keys here:

  • Clients can safely retry POSTs, which is essential on mobile networks.
  • Payment providers (Stripe, Adyen and others) expose exactly this contract.

docs.title: Example 3: Time-Window Dedupe for SMS (Food delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Status updates arrive from courier apps, sometimes twice within seconds. The notification service remembers orderId:status keys for 24 hours (Redis SET key 1 NX EX 86400), so customers get one SMS per status. Memory stays bounded because keys expire.

Full Code:

SmsDeduplicator.javaSmsDedupeDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.notifications;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Remembers recently sent notification keys for a limited time, like Redis
 * {@code SET key 1 NX EX 86400}. Memory stays bounded because old keys expire; duplicates arriving
 * later than the window are rare and, for notifications, acceptable.
 */
public final class SmsDeduplicator {

    private final Map<String, Instant> seen = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Duration window;
    private final Clock clock;

    public SmsDeduplicator(Duration window, Clock clock) {
        this.window = window;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    /** Atomically "set if absent": true means this key is new and the SMS should be sent. */
    public synchronized boolean firstTime(String dedupeKey) {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        seen.values().removeIf(expiry -> !now.isBefore(expiry)); // (1)!
        return seen.putIfAbsent(dedupeKey, now.plus(window)) == null; // (2)!
    }

    public synchronized int size() {
        return seen.size();
    }
}
  1. Expire old keys, so memory is bounded by traffic within the window.
  2. Set-if-absent is atomic, so concurrent duplicates can't both pass.
package com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.notifications;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class SmsDedupeDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T07:00:00Z");
        var dedupe = new SmsDeduplicator(Duration.ofHours(24), clock);

        System.out.println("=== Food delivery: \"Your order is out for delivery\" SMS ===");
        send(dedupe, "ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(4));
        send(dedupe, "ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY"); // the courier app sent the status twice
        send(dedupe, "ORD-9:DELIVERED");
        send(dedupe, "ORD-10:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
        System.out.println("keys remembered: " + dedupe.size());
        clock.advance(Duration.ofHours(25));
        send(dedupe, "ORD-11:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY");
        System.out.println("keys remembered after 25 h: " + dedupe.size() + " (old keys expired)");
    }

    private static void send(SmsDeduplicator dedupe, String key) {
        System.out.println(key + " -> " + (dedupe.firstTime(key) ? "SMS sent" : "duplicate, not sent"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Food delivery: "Your order is out for delivery" SMS ===
ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> SMS sent
ORD-9:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> duplicate, not sent
ORD-9:DELIVERED -> SMS sent
ORD-10:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> SMS sent
keys remembered: 3
ORD-11:OUT_FOR_DELIVERY -> SMS sent
keys remembered after 25 h: 1 (old keys expired)

Why a TTL window here:

  • A duplicate SMS a day later is unlikely and harmless; a permanent table of every notification key isn't worth it.
  • Choose the window from how late duplicates can realistically arrive.
Unit Tests: IdempotentConsumerTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey.IdempotencyKeyStore;
import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.apikey.IdempotencyKeyStore.StoredResponse;
import com.handbook.microservices.idempotency.wallet.WalletCreditConsumer;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import javax.sql.DataSource;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class IdempotentConsumerTest {

    @Test
    void duplicateMessageHasNoEffect() throws Exception {
        DataSource db = Db.inMemory("t_wallet", WalletCreditConsumer.SCHEMA);
        var consumer = new WalletCreditConsumer(db);
        assertThat(consumer.onRefundIssued("m1", "C", 100)).isTrue();
        assertThat(consumer.onRefundIssued("m1", "C", 100)).isFalse();
        assertThat(Db.count(db, "SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE customer = 'C'")).isEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void idempotencyKeyReturnsStoredResponse() {
        var store = new IdempotencyKeyStore();
        int[] runs = {0};
        StoredResponse a = store.execute("k", "body", () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "run " + ++runs[0]));
        StoredResponse b = store.execute("k", "body", () -> new StoredResponse("", 201, "run " + ++runs[0]));
        assertThat(b.body()).isEqualTo(a.body());
        assertThat(store.execute("k", "other", () -> null).status()).isEqualTo(422);
    }
}

@KafkaListener(topics = "payments.refunds", groupId = "wallet")
@Transactional
public void on(ConsumerRecord<String, String> record) {
    String messageId = new String(record.headers().lastHeader("message-id").value(), UTF_8);
    try {

ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on (order_id, event_type) Version check UPDATE ... WHERE version < :eventVersion (see the replica in Database per Service) Transactional inbox Store incoming messages first, process from the inbox table

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Exactly-once effect on at-least-once infrastructure Extra storage and write per message Safe retries everywhere (clients, relays, consumers) Requires a stable message ID / key from producers Simple, database-enforced correctness Dedupe tables need retention/purging Enables aggressive retry policies TTL-based dedupe can miss very late duplicates

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Dedupe outside the transaction

Recording the ID in Redis and the effect in Postgres (or in memory) creates a crash window between them. Store the ID in the same database transaction as the effect, or make the effect itself idempotent.

Using the payload hash as the ID

Two legitimate refunds of ₹199 to the same customer have identical payloads. Use a producer-assigned unique ID.

Check-then-act in application code

if (!exists(id)) process() races between concurrent consumers. Let a unique constraint or atomic SET NX decide (see the coding challenge).

Idempotent handler, non-idempotent side calls

The handler dedupes, but it also calls an email API before the commit. On retry after a crash, the email is sent again. Move side effects to the outbox or make them idempotent too.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Exactly-once is a property of the whole pipeline. Producer: idempotent producer or outbox with stable IDs. Broker: at-least-once. Consumer: dedupe in the same transaction as effects; external calls with idempotency keys. Any non-idempotent link breaks the chain.

Retention. Keep processed IDs at least as long as duplicates can arrive: broker retention plus your maximum replay window. For replays of months of history, use version checks instead of ID tables.

API idempotency at scale. Store keys with status (IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED + response), scope them per client, expire after 24–72 h, and return 409 for concurrent in-progress requests with the same key.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every message has a unique, stable ID assigned by the producer.
  • Consumers insert the ID with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect.
  • POST APIs that create money movements accept Idempotency-Key; responses are stored and replayed.
  • Side effects (emails, partner calls) go through the outbox or carry idempotency keys.
  • Retention/purge policy for dedupe tables; metrics on duplicate rate.
  • Tests that deliver every message twice, and concurrently.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"I assume at-least-once delivery everywhere. Producers give every event a unique ID through the outbox. Each consumer, in the same database transaction as its side effect, inserts that ID into a processed_messages table with a primary key, so duplicates fail the insert and are skipped, even across instances. Client-facing POST endpoints that move money accept an Idempotency-Key; we store the response and replay it on retries, and reject reuse with a different body. Where possible, operations are naturally idempotent: set-state and versioned upserts instead of increments."

War story: the double payout

A gig-economy platform paid drivers via a Kafka consumer that called the bank's payout API and then committed offsets. A deploy restarted consumers mid-batch; 2,300 payouts were sent again. Drivers were happy; finance spent three weeks recovering the money. Fix: payouts recorded in a payouts table with a unique (driver_id, period) key before calling the bank; the bank call uses the payout ID as its idempotency key; the consumer skips periods already recorded. Lesson: "we'll commit the offset right after" is not a strategy. Make the effect idempotent.

13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Delivery is at-least-once; make effects idempotent.
  • Message ID + unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect.
  • APIs: Idempotency-Key, stored response, 422 on mismatch, 409 while in progress.
  • Prefer naturally idempotent operations (set state, versioned upserts).
  • Outbox (producer) + idempotent consumer = exactly-once effect.

docs.text:
• Add an IN_PROGRESS state to IdempotencyKeyStore and return 409 for concurrent requests with the same key.
  • Purge processed_messages rows older than 7 days in WalletCreditConsumer.

docs.title: Leader Election
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

When several identical instances run but some work must be done by exactly one of them (a scheduled job, a partition owner, a coordinator), they elect a leader, usually by competing for a time-limited lease. Others stand by and take over when the lease expires. Combine it with fencing tokens so a leader that was paused or partitioned can't keep acting after it lost leadership.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the grocery service runs on three pods. At 02:00 a job builds the "substitution report" and emails 800 stores. If every pod runs it, stores get three emails and the database does triple work. If only pod-1 is configured to run it, the job silently stops when pod-1 is rescheduled. You need "exactly one, and always one".

Definition (Azure Architecture Center, Leader Election pattern):

Coordinate the actions performed by a collection of collaborating instances by electing one instance as the leader that assumes responsibility for managing the others or for doing work that must not be duplicated.

Building blocks:

Mechanism How Examples Lease A record with holder + expiry, acquired/renewed atomically Kubernetes Lease, DB row, DynamoDB conditional write, Redis SET NX PX Ephemeral sequential nodes Lowest sequence wins; session loss deletes the node ZooKeeper, etcd (revision-based) Consensus Raft/Paxos elect a leader with majority votes etcd, Consul, Kafka KRaft, CockroachDB Bully / ring algorithms Message-based election among known peers Classic textbook algorithms (coding challenge)

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The baton in a relay race

Only the runner holding the baton may run. The baton is handed over explicitly or, if a runner collapses, the official declares the leg forfeited after a timeout and gives the next runner a new numbered baton. A runner who wakes up with an old baton number isn't allowed back on the track (fencing).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     autonumber     participant P1 as pod-1     participant P2 as pod-2     participant L as Lease store     P1->>L: acquire (holder=pod-1, expires=t+15s) ✅     P2->>L: acquire ❌ (held)     loop every 5s         P1->>L: renew ✅     end     Note over P1: crash     P2->>L: acquire ❌ (until expiry)     P2->>L: acquire after expiry ✅ → pod-2 is leader Participant Responsibility Candidates Identical instances that try to acquire leadership Coordination store Provides an atomic compare-and-set or consensus (DB, etcd, ZooKeeper, Kubernetes API) Lease / term Time-bounded leadership; renewed by the leader; expiry enables failover Fencing token Monotonic number per term, checked by downstream resources

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *")
public void substitutionReport() { ... }   // runs on EVERY replica: 3 emails per store

if (System.getenv("POD_NAME").equals("grocery-0")) { ... }   // stops forever when grocery-0 is down
  • Duplicated work (and duplicated side effects).
  • A hard-coded "leader" is a single point of failure.
  • Home-made "check then claim" races let two pods become leader.

docs.title: Example 1: A Database Lease for a Nightly Job (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Three pods of the grocery service all try to acquire the substitution-report lease every 5 seconds. The lease lasts 15 seconds and is renewed by the holder. When the leader pod is killed without releasing, another pod takes over after the lease expires, never before, so there is never more than one leader.

Design:

flowchart LR P1[pod-1] -->|"UPDATE ... WHERE holder = me OR expired"| T[(lease table)] P2[pod-2] --> T P3[pod-3] --> T T -->|"1 row updated = leader"| R[run report]

Full Code:

DbLease.javaLeaseDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.lease;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Timestamp;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;

/** Leader election with a lease row: whoever holds an unexpired lease is the leader. */
public final class DbLease {

    private final DataSource ds = Db.inMemory("leases",
            "CREATE TABLE lease (name VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, holder VARCHAR, expires_at TIMESTAMP)",
            "INSERT INTO lease VALUES ('substitution-report', NULL, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:00')");
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration ttl;

    public DbLease(Clock clock, Duration ttl) {
        this.clock = clock;
        this.ttl = ttl;
    }

    /** Acquire if free/expired, or renew if we already hold it. One atomic UPDATE: no race. */
    public boolean tryAcquireOrRenew(String pod) {
        String sql = "UPDATE lease SET holder = ?, expires_at = ? "
                + "WHERE name = 'substitution-report' AND (holder = ? OR expires_at < ?)"; // (1)!
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            Timestamp now = Timestamp.from(clock.instant());
            ps.setString(1, pod);
            ps.setTimestamp(2, Timestamp.from(clock.instant().plus(ttl)));
            ps.setString(3, pod);
            ps.setTimestamp(4, now);
            return ps.executeUpdate() == 1; // (2)!
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }
}
  1. Acquire and renew in one conditional UPDATE: it succeeds only if we already hold the lease or it has expired. The database serializes concurrent attempts.
  2. Exactly one pod sees "1 row updated". No read-then-write race.
package com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.lease;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class LeaseDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: One of Three Pods Runs the Substitution Report ===");
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-09-01T02:00:00Z");
        DbLease lease = new DbLease(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(15));
        List<String> pods = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pod-1", "pod-2", "pod-3"));

        for (int tick = 0; tick < 6; tick++) {
            if (tick == 2) {
                pods.remove("pod-1");
                System.out.println("t=" + tick * 5 + "s pod-1 is killed (no graceful release)");
            }
            List<String> leaders = new ArrayList<>();
            for (String pod : pods) {
                if (lease.tryAcquireOrRenew(pod)) {
                    leaders.add(pod);
                }
            }
            System.out.println("t=" + tick * 5 + "s leader(s): " + (leaders.isEmpty() ? "none (lease not yet expired)" : leaders));
            clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: One of Three Pods Runs the Substitution Report ===
t=0s leader(s): [pod-1]
t=5s leader(s): [pod-1]
t=10s pod-1 is killed (no graceful release)
t=10s leader(s): none (lease not yet expired)
t=15s leader(s): none (lease not yet expired)
t=20s leader(s): none (lease not yet expired)
t=25s leader(s): [pod-2]

Why a lease here:

  • Uses infrastructure you already have (the service's database); ShedLock does exactly this.
  • Failover is automatic, bounded by the lease TTL.
  • The gap with no leader (t=10s to t=20s) is the price of never having two.

docs.title: Example 2: Fencing Tokens for the Payout Writer (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payout service writes settlement batches to the bank's SFTP drop folder. Writer A holds leadership, then freezes in a 40-second GC pause. Its lease expires, B becomes leader and writes batch 2. A wakes up, unaware anything happened, and tries to write batch 2 again, which would pay merchants twice. Each lease grant carries an increasing fencing token; the storage rejects writes with an older token.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant A as Writer A participant Lk as Lock service participant B as Writer B participant S as Payout storage A->>Lk: acquire → token 34 A->>S: write(batch-1, 34) ✅ Note over A: GC pause 40 s, lease expires B->>Lk: acquire → token 35 B->>S: write(batch-2, 35) ✅ (highest = 35) A->>S: write(batch-2, 34) ❌ rejected: 34 < 35

Full Code:

FencedStorage.javaFencingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.fencing;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** The storage side of fencing: it rejects writes carrying a token older than one it has already seen. */
public final class FencedStorage {

    private long highestToken;
    private final List<String> written = new ArrayList<>();

    public synchronized boolean write(long fencingToken, String line) {
        if (fencingToken < highestToken) { // (1)!
            return false;
        }
        highestToken = fencingToken;
        written.add(line);
        return true;
    }

    public synchronized List<String> written() {
        return List.copyOf(written);
    }

    /** The lock service: every grant gets a strictly increasing token. */
    public static final class LockService {
        private long nextToken = 33;

        public synchronized long grant(String holder) { // (2)!
            return ++nextToken;
        }
    }
}
  1. The resource enforces safety: a token lower than one it has already accepted means the writer's leadership is over.
  2. Every grant gets a strictly higher token (ZooKeeper's zxid, etcd's revision, a DB sequence).
package com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.fencing;

import com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.fencing.FencedStorage.LockService;

public class FencingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Fencing Tokens Stop a Zombie Leader ===");
        LockService locks = new LockService();
        FencedStorage payoutFile = new FencedStorage();

        long tokenA = locks.grant("payout-writer-A");
        System.out.println("A becomes leader with token " + tokenA + ", writes batch 1: " + payoutFile.write(tokenA, "batch-1 by A"));
        System.out.println("A pauses for 40s (stop-the-world GC); its lease expires");

        long tokenB = locks.grant("payout-writer-B");
        System.out.println("B becomes leader with token " + tokenB + ", writes batch 2: " + payoutFile.write(tokenB, "batch-2 by B"));

        boolean zombie = payoutFile.write(tokenA, "batch-2 by A (duplicate payouts!)");
        System.out.println("A wakes up, still thinks it's leader, writes with token " + tokenA + ": accepted=" + zombie);
        System.out.println("Payout file: " + payoutFile.written());
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Fencing Tokens Stop a Zombie Leader ===
A becomes leader with token 34, writes batch 1: true
A pauses for 40s (stop-the-world GC); its lease expires
B becomes leader with token 35, writes batch 2: true
A wakes up, still thinks it's leader, writes with token 34: accepted=false
Payout file: [batch-1 by A, batch-2 by B]

Why fencing here:

  • A lease guarantees at most one leader at a time only if every holder notices expiry instantly, and GC pauses, network partitions and clock drift break that.
  • Fencing moves the check to the place where damage happens.
  • Martin Kleppmann's critique of Redlock is exactly this: locks without fencing aren't safe for correctness.

docs.title: Example 3: Sequential Nodes Without a Herd (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: Four route-optimizer instances need one leader to assign delivery zones. With ZooKeeper, each creates an ephemeral sequential znode under /election; the lowest sequence is the leader. Instead of everyone watching the leader (and stampeding when it dies), each node watches only its predecessor, so each failure wakes exactly one node.

Design:

flowchart LR A["n_0 optimizer-a (LEADER)"] --- B["n_1 optimizer-b<br/>watches n_0"] --- C["n_2 optimizer-c<br/>watches n_1"] --- D["n_3 optimizer-d<br/>watches n_2"]

Full Code:

SequentialElection.javaDispatchLeaderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.sequential;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** ZooKeeper recipe: ephemeral sequential znodes; lowest sequence leads; each node watches its predecessor only. */
public final class SequentialElection {

    private final TreeMap<Integer, String> znodes = new TreeMap<>(); // seq -> member
    private int nextSeq;
    private final List<String> notifications = new ArrayList<>();

    public int join(String member) {
        int seq = nextSeq++;
        znodes.put(seq, member); // (1)!
        return seq;
    }

    /** Session ends (crash or close): its ephemeral znode disappears and only its watcher is notified. */
    public void sessionExpired(String member) {
        Integer seq = znodes.entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue().equals(member)).map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst().orElseThrow();
        Map.Entry<Integer, String> watcher = znodes.higherEntry(seq); // (2)!
        znodes.remove(seq);
        if (watcher != null) {
            boolean nowLeader = znodes.firstKey().equals(watcher.getKey());
            notifications.add(watcher.getValue() + " notified (predecessor " + member + " gone) -> "
                    + (nowLeader ? "now LEADER" : "watches " + znodes.lowerEntry(watcher.getKey()).getValue()));
        }
    }

    public Optional<String> leader() {
        return znodes.isEmpty() ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of(znodes.firstEntry().getValue());
    }

    public List<String> drainNotifications() {
        List<String> out = List.copyOf(notifications);
        notifications.clear();
        return out;
    }
}
  1. Ephemeral sequential znodes: the sequence orders candidates; the node disappears when the session dies.
  2. Only the next node is notified, which checks whether it's now the lowest (leader) or should watch a new predecessor.
package com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.sequential;

public class DispatchLeaderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Electing the Route-Optimizer Leader with Sequential Nodes ===");
        SequentialElection election = new SequentialElection();
        for (String node : new String[] {"optimizer-a", "optimizer-b", "optimizer-c", "optimizer-d"}) {
            System.out.println(node + " created /election/n_" + String.format("%010d", election.join(node)));
        }
        System.out.println("Leader: " + election.leader().orElseThrow());

        election.sessionExpired("optimizer-c"); // a follower dies
        election.drainNotifications().forEach(n -> System.out.println("  " + n));
        election.sessionExpired("optimizer-a"); // the leader dies
        election.drainNotifications().forEach(n -> System.out.println("  " + n));
        System.out.println("Leader: " + election.leader().orElseThrow() + " (each death woke exactly one node: no herd effect)");
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Electing the Route-Optimizer Leader with Sequential Nodes ===
optimizer-a created /election/n_0000000000
optimizer-b created /election/n_0000000001
optimizer-c created /election/n_0000000002
optimizer-d created /election/n_0000000003
Leader: optimizer-a
  optimizer-d notified (predecessor optimizer-c gone) -> watches optimizer-b
  optimizer-b notified (predecessor optimizer-a gone) -> now LEADER
Leader: optimizer-b (each death woke exactly one node: no herd effect)

Why sequential nodes here:

  • Leadership order is deterministic and fair (first come, first lead).
  • No herd effect: N candidates don't all hit ZooKeeper when the leader dies.
  • Session expiry gives failure detection for free.
Unit Tests: LeaderElectionTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.fencing.FencedStorage;
import com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.lease.DbLease;
import com.handbook.microservices.leaderelection.sequential.SequentialElection;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class LeaderElectionTest {

    @Test
    void onlyOneHolderUntilTheLeaseExpires() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        DbLease lease = new DbLease(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        assertThat(lease.tryAcquireOrRenew("a")).isTrue();
        assertThat(lease.tryAcquireOrRenew("b")).isFalse();
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(11));
        assertThat(lease.tryAcquireOrRenew("b")).isTrue();
        assertThat(lease.tryAcquireOrRenew("a")).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void staleTokensAreFencedOff() {
        FencedStorage s = new FencedStorage();
        assertThat(s.write(5, "x")).isTrue();
        assertThat(s.write(6, "y")).isTrue();
        assertThat(s.write(5, "z")).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void lowestSequenceLeadsAndSuccessionIsOrdered() {
        SequentialElection e = new SequentialElection();
        e.join("a");
        e.join("b");
        e.sessionExpired("a");
        assertThat(e.leader()).contains("b");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Leader election Kubernetes Lease objects; kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler run active/standby Kafka (KRaft) Raft quorum elects the controller; each partition has a leader replica ZooKeeper / Curator LeaderLatch, LeaderSelector recipes Spring Spring Integration LeaderInitiator (JDBC, Redis, ZooKeeper, Hazelcast); ShedLock for @Scheduled Databases PostgreSQL advisory locks (pg_try_advisory_lock), Patroni (Postgres HA via etcd/Consul)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Exactly-one execution without a dedicated special instance A coordination dependency to run and secure Automatic failover Failover gap (up to the lease TTL) with no leader Simple mental model for coordinators and schedulers Leader can become a bottleneck or single point of slowness Works with infrastructure you have (DB, Kubernetes) Correctness needs fencing; clocks and pauses break naïve leases

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Locks without fencing for correctness-critical work

A paused or partitioned ex-leader can still act. If duplicates cost money, the downstream resource must check a fencing token (or the work must be idempotent).

Check-then-claim

if (lease.holder == null) lease.holder = me; as two operations lets two pods win. Use one atomic conditional write.

TTL too short or too long

Too short: GC pauses and slow renewals cause flapping leadership. Too long: slow failover. Renew at ~1/3 of the TTL and size the TTL from observed pauses.

Leader does all the work

If the leader also processes every request, you've built a single-node system with extra steps. Let the leader coordinate (assign work), and the followers do it.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Time is the enemy. Leases rely on the holder noticing expiry before others act. Process pauses (GC, VM migration), clock drift and network delays violate that. Defences: renew early, stop acting when a renewal fails (not when the lease "should" expire), use monotonic clocks locally, and fence every write.

Choose the right store. For correctness (payouts, partition ownership), use a linearizable store with revisions: etcd, ZooKeeper, a single-primary SQL database. Redis single-node SET NX PX is fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work) but not for safety under failover.

Prefer not needing a leader. Idempotent jobs, partitioned work (each pod owns a hash range), or a queue with competing consumers often remove the need for a global leader and its failover gap.

War story: two payout files on a Monday

A payout service used a Redis lock with a 30-second TTL. One Monday a full GC paused the leader for 41 seconds; the standby acquired the lock and generated the payout file; the old leader resumed and uploaded its own copy a minute later. The bank processed both: INR 2.3 crore paid twice to 600 merchants. Fix: etcd-based election with revisions as fencing tokens; the upload step writes the token into the file header and the bank-side importer rejects older tokens; payouts also got idempotency keys per merchant per date. Lesson: a lock tells you who should act; only fencing stops who shouldn't.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Leader Election Balking Competing Consumers Sharding Ensures One instance does the job One concurrent run in a process Each message handled once Each key owned by one shard Scope Cluster One JVM Queue consumers Data Failover Lease expiry / session loss N/A Redelivery Replica promotion

See Guarded Suspension & Balking for the single-JVM version, and Competing Consumers for a leaderless alternative.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • One instance leads; others stand by; lease expiry = failover.
  • Acquire/renew with one atomic conditional write.
  • Leases alone aren't safe: add fencing tokens.
  • Watch predecessors, not the leader (no herd).
  • Often better: idempotent or partitioned work, no leader at all.
UPDATE lease SET holder = :me, expires_at = :now + ttl WHERE name = :job AND (holder = :me OR expires_at < :now);

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a release(pod) method for graceful shutdown and show instant failover.
  • Return a fencing token (a version column) from DbLease.tryAcquireOrRenew.
  • Make the leader in LeaseDemo stop work when a renewal fails, not when the TTL ends.
