docs.title: Materialized View
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Materialized View stores the precomputed result of an expensive query (aggregates, joins, data from several services) so reads become a single cheap lookup. It's refreshed on a schedule or kept up to date incrementally from events. Use it when the same expensive question is asked far more often than the underlying data changes, or when the data needed lives in several services or shards.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the store manager's dashboard shows today's orders and revenue. Computing it means SUM over millions of order lines, run every time 400 managers refresh their screens. The tracking page needs shipment, driver and ETA data that live in three different services; joining them over HTTP on every page view is slow and fragile.

Definition (Azure Architecture Center, Materialized View pattern):

Generate prepopulated views over the data in one or more data stores when the data isn't ideally formatted for required query operations. The view is a disposable cache: it can always be rebuilt from the source of truth.

Refresh strategies:

Strategy How Freshness Cost Full refresh Recompute everything on a schedule (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW) Minutes / hours Proportional to all data Incremental Apply each change (event, CDC row) to the view Seconds Proportional to changes On read, cached Compute on miss, keep with TTL Varies See Cache-Aside

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
The cricket scoreboard

Nobody recounts every ball of the match to know the score. The scorer updates the board after each ball (incremental view). The board can always be reconstructed from the ball-by-ball scorebook (source of truth) if someone suspects a mistake.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph Sources of truth       O[(Orders DB)]       D[(Delivery service)]       P[(Payments service)]     end     O -->|"events / CDC / scheduled query"| B[View builder]     D --> B     P --> B     B --> V[(Materialized view<br/>denormalized, query-shaped)]     Q[Dashboard / page] -->|"one lookup"| V Participant Responsibility Source of truth Normalized data owned by its service; never modified by the view View builder Scheduled job, stream processor or CDC consumer that computes/updates the view Materialized view Denormalized, query-shaped storage (table, document, Redis hash, search index) Readers Query the view only; accept its staleness

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// Dashboard: full scan on every refresh by every manager
jdbc.queryForObject("SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount_paise) FROM order_line WHERE store = ? AND sales_day = ?", ...);

// Tracking page: three synchronous calls and an in-memory join per view
var s = shipmentClient.get(awb); var d = driverClient.get(s.driverId()); var e = etaClient.get(awb);
  • Repeating expensive work for identical answers.
  • Page latency = sum of three services' latencies; any one down breaks the page.
  • Heavy analytical queries slow down the transactional database.

docs.title: Example 1: Store Sales Summary with Full Refresh (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: 400 dark-store managers refresh a sales dashboard all evening. The raw order_line table gets 2 million rows a day. A summary table, refreshed every 5 minutes in one transaction, answers each dashboard request with a single primary-key lookup. A few minutes of staleness is acceptable for a dashboard.

Design:

flowchart LR L[(order_line: 21k+ rows)] -->|"every 5 min: GROUP BY store, day"| MV[(mv_store_daily_sales)] M[400 managers] -->|"SELECT ... WHERE store = ? AND day = ?"| MV

Full Code:

StoreSalesView.javaSalesViewDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.sales;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.Date;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;

/** A summary table rebuilt on a schedule: the dashboard reads one row instead of scanning every order line. */
public final class StoreSalesView {

    private final DataSource ds = Db.inMemory("mv_sales",
            "CREATE TABLE order_line (store VARCHAR, sales_day DATE, amount_paise BIGINT)",
            "CREATE TABLE mv_store_daily_sales (store VARCHAR, sales_day DATE, orders BIGINT, revenue_paise BIGINT,"
                    + " PRIMARY KEY (store, sales_day))");

    public void insertLines(String store, String day, int count, long paiseEach) {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO order_line VALUES (?, ?, ?)")) {
            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
                ps.setString(1, store);
                ps.setDate(2, Date.valueOf(day));
                ps.setLong(3, paiseEach);
                ps.addBatch();
            }
            ps.executeBatch();
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    /** Equivalent of PostgreSQL REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW: recompute in one transaction. */
    public void refresh() { // (1)!
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            s.execute("DELETE FROM mv_store_daily_sales");
            s.execute("INSERT INTO mv_store_daily_sales SELECT store, sales_day, COUNT(*), SUM(amount_paise)"
                    + " FROM order_line GROUP BY store, sales_day");
            c.commit(); // (2)!
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    public String dashboard(String store, String day) {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                "SELECT orders, revenue_paise FROM mv_store_daily_sales WHERE store = ? AND sales_day = ?")) {
            ps.setString(1, store);
            ps.setDate(2, Date.valueOf(day));
            ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
            return rs.next() ? rs.getLong(1) + " orders, INR " + rs.getLong(2) / 100 : "no data yet";
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    public long rawLines() {
        return Db.count(ds, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_line");
    }
}
  1. A full refresh: rebuild the summary from the source of truth. PostgreSQL has this built in (CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ...; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY ...).
  2. In one transaction, so readers see either the old or the new summary, never a half-built one.
package com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.sales;

public class SalesViewDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Store Sales Dashboard on a Refreshed Summary Table ===");
        StoreSalesView view = new StoreSalesView();
        view.insertLines("BLR-HSR", "2026-07-01", 12_000, 41_500);
        view.insertLines("BLR-KORA", "2026-07-01", 9_000, 38_000);
        view.refresh(); // nightly / every 5 minutes
        System.out.println("Raw order lines: " + view.rawLines() + "; dashboard reads 1 precomputed row:");
        System.out.println("  BLR-HSR  2026-07-01 -> " + view.dashboard("BLR-HSR", "2026-07-01"));

        view.insertLines("BLR-HSR", "2026-07-01", 500, 41_500); // evening orders after the last refresh
        System.out.println("Before next refresh -> " + view.dashboard("BLR-HSR", "2026-07-01") + " (stale by design)");
        view.refresh();
        System.out.println("After refresh       -> " + view.dashboard("BLR-HSR", "2026-07-01"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Store Sales Dashboard on a Refreshed Summary Table ===
Raw order lines: 21000; dashboard reads 1 precomputed row:
  BLR-HSR  2026-07-01 -> 12000 orders, INR 4980000
Before next refresh -> 12000 orders, INR 4980000 (stale by design)
After refresh       -> 12500 orders, INR 5187500

Why a materialized view here:

  • Read load is hundreds of times the write rate for this question.
  • Staleness is explicit and bounded by the refresh interval.
  • The transactional workload no longer runs aggregate scans.

docs.title: Example 2: Incremental Balance View (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A banking app shows the balance every time it opens (8 million opens a day). The source of truth is an append-only ledger. Summing the ledger per open is too expensive; a balance view is updated by each ledger event. The broker delivers at least once, so the view must ignore duplicates.

Design:

flowchart LR LG[(Ledger, append-only)] -->|"LedgerEntry events (at-least-once)"| C[View consumer] C -->|"dedupe by eventId, then balance += delta"| V[(balances)] App -->|"GET balance"| V

Full Code:

BalanceView.javaBalanceViewDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.balances;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** Incrementally maintained view: each ledger event updates the running balance once. */
public final class BalanceView {

    public record LedgerEntry(String eventId, String account, long deltaPaise) { }

    private final Map<String, Long> balances = new TreeMap<>();
    private final Set<String> applied = new HashSet<>(); // in production: a processed_events table

    public boolean apply(LedgerEntry e) {
        if (!applied.add(e.eventId())) { // (1)!
            return false;
        }
        balances.merge(e.account(), e.deltaPaise(), Long::sum); // (2)!
        return true;
    }

    public long balance(String account) {
        return balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L);
    }

    public Map<String, Long> all() {
        return Map.copyOf(balances);
    }
}
  1. Idempotency: a redelivered event is detected and ignored (Idempotent Consumer). In SQL, insert the event id and the balance update in the same transaction.
  2. Incremental update: the cost is proportional to the change, not to the history.
package com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.balances;

import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.balances.BalanceView.LedgerEntry;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class BalanceViewDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Account Balances Maintained Incrementally from Ledger Events ===");
        BalanceView view = new BalanceView();
        List<LedgerEntry> stream = List.of(
                new LedgerEntry("e1", "SB-1", 500_000),
                new LedgerEntry("e2", "SB-2", 120_000),
                new LedgerEntry("e3", "SB-1", -75_000),
                new LedgerEntry("e3", "SB-1", -75_000), // redelivered by the broker
                new LedgerEntry("e4", "SB-2", -20_000));
        int ignored = 0;
        for (LedgerEntry e : stream) {
            ignored += view.apply(e) ? 0 : 1;
        }
        System.out.println("Applied " + (stream.size() - ignored) + " events, ignored " + ignored + " duplicate");
        System.out.println("Balances: " + new TreeMap<>(view.all()));
        System.out.println("Balance lookup is O(1): no SUM over millions of ledger rows per app open.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Account Balances Maintained Incrementally from Ledger Events ===
Applied 4 events, ignored 1 duplicate
Balances: {SB-1=425000, SB-2=100000}
Balance lookup is O(1): no SUM over millions of ledger rows per app open.

Why an incremental view here:

  • Freshness in seconds without recomputing history.
  • The ledger stays the auditable source of truth; the view is a derived convenience.
  • Shown to customers, but payments still validate against the ledger, not the view.

docs.title: Example 3: Tracking Page from Three Services (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: A courier's tracking page needs the shipment's city (shipping service), the driver (fleet service) and the ETA (routing service). Instead of three calls per page view, a view builder consumes all three event streams into one denormalized document per AWB. Events from different services can arrive in any order, and the same source can deliver an older update late.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant F as Fleet participant S as Shipping participant R as Routing participant V as TrackingView F->>V: DriverAssigned v1 (before Shipped!) S->>V: Shipped v1 R->>V: EtaUpdated v2 (14:40) R->>V: EtaUpdated v1 (14:25, late) → ignored Note over V: page = {city, driver, eta 14:40}

Full Code:

TrackingView.javaTrackingViewDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** A denormalized view assembled from three services' events; tolerates out-of-order delivery per source. */
public final class TrackingView {

    public sealed interface Event permits Shipped, DriverAssigned, EtaUpdated {
        String awb();
        long version(); // per-source sequence number
    }

    public record Shipped(String awb, String city, long version) implements Event { }

    public record DriverAssigned(String awb, String driver, long version) implements Event { }

    public record EtaUpdated(String awb, String eta, long version) implements Event { }

    public record Page(String awb, String city, String driver, String eta) { }

    private final Map<String, Page> pages = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Long> lastVersion = new HashMap<>(); // key: awb + source

    public void on(Event e) {
        String source = e.getClass().getSimpleName();
        String key = e.awb() + "/" + source;
        if (e.version() <= lastVersion.getOrDefault(key, 0L)) { // (1)!
            return;
        }
        lastVersion.put(key, e.version());
        Page p = pages.getOrDefault(e.awb(), new Page(e.awb(), "?", "?", "?"));
        pages.put(e.awb(), switch (e) { // (2)!
            case Shipped s -> new Page(p.awb(), s.city(), p.driver(), p.eta());
            case DriverAssigned d -> new Page(p.awb(), p.city(), d.driver(), p.eta());
            case EtaUpdated t -> new Page(p.awb(), p.city(), p.driver(), t.eta());
        });
    }

    public Page page(String awb) {
        return pages.get(awb);
    }
}
  1. Keep the last applied version per source, so a late, older event can't overwrite newer data.
  2. Each event type updates only its fields: arrival order between sources doesn't matter.
package com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking;

import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking.TrackingView.DriverAssigned;
import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking.TrackingView.EtaUpdated;
import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking.TrackingView.Shipped;

public class TrackingViewDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: One Tracking Page Built from Three Services ===");
        TrackingView view = new TrackingView();
        view.on(new DriverAssigned("AWB-77", "Ravi (KA-01-AB-1234)", 1)); // arrives before Shipped
        System.out.println("After driver event : " + view.page("AWB-77"));
        view.on(new Shipped("AWB-77", "Bengaluru", 1));
        view.on(new EtaUpdated("AWB-77", "14:40", 2));
        view.on(new EtaUpdated("AWB-77", "14:25", 1)); // older ETA delivered late
        System.out.println("After all events   : " + view.page("AWB-77"));
        System.out.println("The late, older ETA (v1) was ignored; the page answers with one key lookup, no joins across services.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: One Tracking Page Built from Three Services ===
After driver event : Page[awb=AWB-77, city=?, driver=Ravi (KA-01-AB-1234), eta=?]
After all events   : Page[awb=AWB-77, city=Bengaluru, driver=Ravi (KA-01-AB-1234), eta=14:40]
The late, older ETA (v1) was ignored; the page answers with one key lookup, no joins across services.

Why a materialized view here:

  • The page works even if the routing service is down (it shows the last ETA).
  • One key lookup instead of three network calls.
  • The pattern behind CQRS read models and API composition replacements.
Unit Tests: MaterializedViewTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.balances.BalanceView;
import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.balances.BalanceView.LedgerEntry;
import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.sales.StoreSalesView;
import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking.TrackingView;
import com.handbook.microservices.materializedview.tracking.TrackingView.EtaUpdated;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class MaterializedViewTest {

    @Test
    void summaryReflectsDataOnlyAfterRefresh() {
        StoreSalesView v = new StoreSalesView();
        v.insertLines("S", "2026-01-01", 2, 100);
        assertThat(v.dashboard("S", "2026-01-01")).isEqualTo("no data yet");
        v.refresh();
        assertThat(v.dashboard("S", "2026-01-01")).isEqualTo("2 orders, INR 2");
    }

    @Test
    void duplicateEventsDoNotDoubleCount() {
        BalanceView v = new BalanceView();
        v.apply(new LedgerEntry("e1", "A", 100));
        v.apply(new LedgerEntry("e1", "A", 100));
        assertThat(v.balance("A")).isEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void olderEventsFromTheSameSourceAreIgnored() {
        TrackingView v = new TrackingView();
        v.on(new EtaUpdated("X", "10:00", 2));
        v.on(new EtaUpdated("X", "09:00", 1));
        assertThat(v.page("X").eta()).isEqualTo("10:00");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
PostgreSQL (reference) 
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_store_daily_sales AS
  SELECT store, sales_day, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount_paise) AS revenue_paise
  FROM order_line GROUP BY store, sales_day;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON mv_store_daily_sales (store, sales_day);  -- required for CONCURRENTLY
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_store_daily_sales;      -- readers aren't blocked
Variation Notes Database materialized views PostgreSQL, Oracle (with fast refresh), SQL Server indexed views Stream-processed views Kafka Streams KTable / state stores, Flink, Materialize, RisingWave: incremental SQL views over streams CDC-fed views Debezium → consumer → Elasticsearch/Redis/another DB Search index as a view OpenSearch documents built from several services for full-text and faceted queries Blue/green rebuild Build view_v2 alongside view_v1, verify, switch readers, drop old (coding challenge)

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Materialized views PostgreSQL CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY (schedule with pg_cron) Kafka Streams groupByKey().aggregate(...) → KTable with interactive queries Spring @Scheduled refresh jobs; Spring Kafka listeners building projections Axon Event-handling projections (@EventHandler updating query models) Cloud BigQuery / Snowflake materialized views; DynamoDB Streams → aggregates

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Expensive queries become cheap lookups Data is stale (by refresh interval or event lag) Combine data from several services/shards Extra storage and a builder to operate Reads keep working when sources are down Incremental logic must handle duplicates and ordering Offloads the transactional database Views drift if events are lost; need rebuild tooling

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Making decisions from a stale view

Approving a payment from a balance view that lags the ledger allows overdrafts. Use views for display; check the source of truth for decisions.

Non-idempotent incremental updates

At-least-once delivery + balance += delta without dedupe = double counting. Track applied event ids or versions.

Full refresh that blocks readers

PostgreSQL's plain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW takes an exclusive lock. Use CONCURRENTLY (needs a unique index) or swap tables.

No way to rebuild

If the view can't be recomputed from the source of truth (events retained, or source tables queryable), a single bug corrupts it permanently.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Treat views as disposable. Keep enough history (Kafka retention, event store, CDC from source tables) to rebuild any view from scratch. Build new versions side by side and switch readers atomically. This makes schema changes to views low-risk.

Lag is a product metric. Measure "event time → visible in view" and alert on it. Expose freshness to users where it matters ("updated 2 minutes ago").

Ordering. Per-key ordering (Kafka partition by aggregate id) handles most cases; across sources, apply per-source versions or "last-writer-wins by event time" carefully, and design fields so each source owns its own part of the document.

War story: the balance that was off by one payment

A wallet's balance view consumer crashed after updating the balance but before committing its Kafka offset. On restart it re-applied the event: thousands of users saw a refund twice. Some spent it, because the payment check used the same view. Fix: event id stored in a processed_events table in the same transaction as the balance update; payments validated against the ledger; nightly rebuild-and-compare job that alerts on drift. Lesson: incremental views need idempotency, decisions need the source of truth, and drift needs a detector.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Materialized View Cache-Aside CQRS Read Model Event Sourcing Built Ahead of time (scheduled/incremental) On demand (miss) From events Is the source of truth Shape Query-shaped, often aggregated Same as source Query-shaped Event log Staleness Refresh interval / lag TTL Event lag None (it's the truth) Rebuildable Yes, from sources Trivially Yes, by replay N/A

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Precomputed, query-shaped, disposable copy of data.
  • Full refresh (simple) vs incremental (fresh, idempotent).
  • Combine services/shards without runtime joins.
  • Stale by design: display, don't decide.
  • Keep history so you can rebuild and compare.
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_store_daily_sales;

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Make StoreSalesView refresh incrementally (only today's partition).
  • Add lastUpdatedAt to TrackingView.Page and show "updated N minutes ago".
  • Store BalanceView's applied ids and balances in H2 within one transaction.

Sharding Next: Competing Consumers

docs.title: Rate Limiter
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A rate limiter caps how many requests a client (user, API key, IP, tenant) can make in a period. Excess requests get 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After. Common algorithms are the token bucket (allows bursts), sliding-window log (exact), sliding-window counter (cheap and close to exact) and fixed window (simplest, but allows bursts at window boundaries). With many instances, counters must be shared (Redis).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English:

  • A buggy client loops and sends 5,000 requests per second to checkout.
  • Bots try to grab all concert seats in the first second of a sale.
  • Attackers trigger OTP SMS to a victim's phone 1,000 times. Every SMS costs money, and the victim is spammed.
  • A free-tier customer uses as much capacity as an enterprise customer.

Rate limiting protects availability (overload), cost (SMS, third-party APIs), fairness (one client can't starve others) and security (brute force, scraping).

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A ticket counter with tokens

A museum hands out entry tokens: a bowl holds up to 5, and one new token is added every minute. A group of 5 can walk in at once (burst), but after that, people enter at one per minute. If the bowl is empty, you wait. That's a token bucket.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     R[Request] --> K[Key: user / API key / IP / tenant]     K --> L{Limiter<br/>allowed?}     L -->|yes| S[Service]     L -->|no| E["429 + Retry-After<br/>+ X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0"]     L <--> ST[(Counter store<br/>local or Redis)] Algorithm Memory per key Bursts Accuracy Fixed window 1 counter Up to 2× limit at boundaries Low Sliding-window log 1 timestamp per request No Exact Sliding-window counter 2 counters Smoothed Close to exact Token bucket Tokens + timestamp Up to capacity (intended) Exact average rate Leaky bucket Queue Smoothed output Constant outflow

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
// "We'll just scale up"
@PostMapping("/otp") void sendOtp(String phone) { smsProvider.send(phone, code()); }
// Attacker: 10,000 requests/minute → 10,000 SMS billed → provider blocks your account,
// and real users can't log in.

docs.title: Example 1: Token Bucket per User (Grocery checkout)
docs.text:
Scenario: Each customer may burst up to 5 checkout API calls (the app makes a few calls when the screen opens), refilling at 1 token per second. A 7-request burst gets 5 × 200 and 2 × 429. Other customers have their own buckets. After waiting, tokens refill, but never above capacity.

Full Code:

TokenBucket.javaTokenBucketDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.tokenbucket;

import java.time.Clock;

/**
 * Token bucket: holds up to {@code capacity} tokens, refilled continuously at {@code refillPerSecond}.
 * Each request takes one token. Allows short bursts up to capacity, then a steady average rate.
 */
public final class TokenBucket {

    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerMilli;
    private final Clock clock;
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefill;

    public TokenBucket(long capacity, double refillPerSecond, Clock clock) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerMilli = refillPerSecond / 1000.0;
        this.clock = clock;
        this.tokens = capacity; // (1)!
        this.lastRefill = clock.millis();
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        refill();
        if (tokens >= 1) {
            tokens -= 1;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    public synchronized long tokensLeft() {
        refill();
        return (long) tokens;
    }

    private void refill() { // (2)!
        long now = clock.millis();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefill) * refillPerMilli);
        lastRefill = now;
    }
}
  1. Starts full, so the first burst is allowed.
  2. Lazy refill: no background timer; tokens are computed from elapsed time on each call (O(1) per request).
package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.tokenbucket;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class TokenBucketDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T09:00:00Z");
        Map<String, TokenBucket> perUser = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: checkout API, 5-request burst, refills 1 token/second per user ===");
        StringBuilder burst = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) {
            burst.append(allowed(perUser, clock, "CUST-42") ? "200 " : "429 ");
        }
        System.out.println("CUST-42 sends 7 requests at once : " + burst.toString().trim());
        System.out.println("CUST-77 is unaffected            : " + (allowed(perUser, clock, "CUST-77") ? "200" : "429"));

        clock.advanceMillis(2_500);
        System.out.println("2.5 s later, CUST-42 has " + bucket(perUser, clock, "CUST-42").tokensLeft() + " tokens");
        System.out.println("CUST-42 next 3 requests          : "
                + (allowed(perUser, clock, "CUST-42") ? "200 " : "429 ")
                + (allowed(perUser, clock, "CUST-42") ? "200 " : "429 ")
                + (allowed(perUser, clock, "CUST-42") ? "200" : "429"));

        clock.advanceMillis(60_000);
        System.out.println("After a quiet minute the bucket is full again (capped): "
                + bucket(perUser, clock, "CUST-42").tokensLeft() + " tokens");
    }

    private static TokenBucket bucket(Map<String, TokenBucket> perUser, FakeClock clock, String user) {
        return perUser.computeIfAbsent(user, u -> new TokenBucket(5, 1.0, clock));
    }

    private static boolean allowed(Map<String, TokenBucket> perUser, FakeClock clock, String user) {
        return bucket(perUser, clock, user).tryAcquire();
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: checkout API, 5-request burst, refills 1 token/second per user ===
CUST-42 sends 7 requests at once : 200 200 200 200 200 429 429
CUST-77 is unaffected            : 200
2.5 s later, CUST-42 has 2 tokens
CUST-42 next 3 requests          : 200 200 429
After a quiet minute the bucket is full again (capped): 5 tokens

Why a token bucket here:

  • Legitimate bursts are allowed, while the long-run rate stays capped.
  • Two numbers per user: cheap.
  • This is the algorithm behind Spring Cloud Gateway's Redis rate limiter, Bucket4j and most cloud gateways.

docs.title: Example 2: Sliding-Window Log for OTP (Fintech login)
docs.text:
Scenario: At most 3 OTP SMS per phone per 10 minutes. A fixed window would let an attacker send 3 at 10:09 and 3 more at 10:10. The sliding log stores each request's timestamp and counts those in the last 10 minutes, so it's exact and tells the user precisely how long to wait.

Full Code:

OtpRateLimiter.javaOtpDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.slidinglog;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

/**
 * Sliding-window log: remember the timestamp of each allowed request and count those inside the
 * last window. Exact (no boundary bursts), at the cost of storing one entry per request.
 * Used here to stop OTP SMS abuse (each SMS costs money and can be used to spam a victim).
 */
public final class OtpRateLimiter {

    private final int maxRequests;
    private final Duration window;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Map<String, Deque<Instant>> logs = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public OtpRateLimiter(int maxRequests, Duration window, Clock clock) {
        this.maxRequests = maxRequests;
        this.window = window;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    /** Returns 0 if allowed, otherwise the seconds to wait. */
    public long tryRequest(String phone) {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        Deque<Instant> log = logs.computeIfAbsent(phone, p -> new ArrayDeque<>());
        synchronized (log) {
            while (!log.isEmpty() && !log.peekFirst().isAfter(now.minus(window))) { // (1)!
                log.pollFirst();
            }
            if (log.size() < maxRequests) {
                log.addLast(now);
                return 0;
            }
            return Duration.between(now, log.peekFirst().plus(window)).toSeconds(); // (2)!
        }
    }
}
  1. Drop timestamps that have left the window.
  2. The exact wait time is when the oldest request leaves the window, which makes a good Retry-After.
package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.slidinglog;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class OtpDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T09:00:00Z");
        var limiter = new OtpRateLimiter(3, Duration.ofMinutes(10), clock);

        System.out.println("=== Fintech login: max 3 OTP SMS per phone per 10 minutes ===");
        int[] minutes = {0, 1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 11};
        int previous = 0;
        for (int minute : minutes) {
            clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(minute - previous));
            previous = minute;
            long wait = limiter.tryRequest("+91-98450-00000");
            System.out.printf("t=%2d min  send OTP -> %s%n", minute,
                    wait == 0 ? "SMS sent" : "429, try again in " + wait + " s");
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Fintech login: max 3 OTP SMS per phone per 10 minutes ===
t= 0 min  send OTP -> SMS sent
t= 1 min  send OTP -> SMS sent
t= 2 min  send OTP -> SMS sent
t= 3 min  send OTP -> 429, try again in 420 s
t= 9 min  send OTP -> 429, try again in 60 s
t=10 min  send OTP -> SMS sent
t=11 min  send OTP -> SMS sent

Why a sliding log here:

  • Low volumes per key (a few per phone), so storing timestamps is cheap.
  • Exactness matters: each SMS costs money and abuse must not slip through window boundaries.
  • In production, add limits per IP and per device too, plus CAPTCHA after failures.

docs.title: Example 3: Distributed Limit Across Gateway Nodes (Ticketing)
docs.text:
Scenario: During a concert sale, each fan may make 4 seat-hold requests per minute. Traffic is spread across 3 gateway nodes. With per-node counters, a fan gets 4 per node = 12 (3× the limit). With a shared counter (Redis INCR + EXPIRE, keyed by user and minute), the limit is global.

Full Code:

GatewayNode.javaSharedCounterStore.javaDistributedLimiterDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.distributed;

import java.time.Clock;

/**
 * One of several gateway instances behind a load balancer. A per-node counter would let a user get
 * N x the limit; a shared counter keyed by user and window enforces one global limit.
 */
public final class GatewayNode {

    private final String name;
    private final SharedCounterStore store;
    private final long limitPerMinute;
    private final Clock clock;
    private long localCount;

    public GatewayNode(String name, SharedCounterStore store, long limitPerMinute, Clock clock) {
        this.name = name;
        this.store = store;
        this.limitPerMinute = limitPerMinute;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public String handleShared(String user) {
        String key = "rl:" + user + ":" + clock.millis() / 60_000; // (1)!
        long count = store.incrementAndGet(key); // (2)!
        return name + (count <= limitPerMinute ? " 200" : " 429");
    }

    public String handleLocalOnly() {
        return name + (++localCount <= limitPerMinute ? " 200" : " 429"); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. The key includes the window number (minute), so old windows expire naturally.
  2. One atomic increment in the shared store. No read-then-write race between nodes.
  3. A local counter only sees this node's share of the traffic.
package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.distributed;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

/**
 * Stands in for Redis. {@code incrementAndGet} mirrors an atomic {@code INCR key} followed by
 * {@code EXPIRE key ttl} on first use; old windows simply expire.
 */
public final class SharedCounterStore {

    private final Map<String, AtomicLong> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public long incrementAndGet(String key) {
        return counters.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new AtomicLong()).incrementAndGet();
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.distributed;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.IntFunction;

public class DistributedLimiterDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z");
        System.out.println("=== Ticketing: concert sale, 4 seat-hold requests per user per minute ===");

        List<GatewayNode> local = List.of(
                new GatewayNode("gw-1", null, 4, clock), new GatewayNode("gw-2", null, 4, clock),
                new GatewayNode("gw-3", null, 4, clock));
        System.out.println("Per-node counters : " + send(12, i -> local.get(i % 3).handleLocalOnly()));

        SharedCounterStore redis = new SharedCounterStore();
        List<GatewayNode> shared = List.of(
                new GatewayNode("gw-1", redis, 4, clock), new GatewayNode("gw-2", redis, 4, clock),
                new GatewayNode("gw-3", redis, 4, clock));
        System.out.println("Shared counter    : " + send(12, i -> shared.get(i % 3).handleShared("FAN-9")));
        System.out.println("Allowed: per-node 12 of 12 (3x the limit!), shared 4 of 12");

        clock.advanceMillis(60_000);
        System.out.println("Next minute       : " + send(2, i -> shared.get(i % 3).handleShared("FAN-9")));
    }

    private static List<String> send(int n, IntFunction<String> request) {
        List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            results.add(request.apply(i));
        }
        return results;
    }
}

Output:

=== Ticketing: concert sale, 4 seat-hold requests per user per minute ===
Per-node counters : [gw-1 200, gw-2 200, gw-3 200, gw-1 200, gw-2 200, gw-3 200, gw-1 200, gw-2 200, gw-3 200, gw-1 200, gw-2 200, gw-3 200]
Shared counter    : [gw-1 200, gw-2 200, gw-3 200, gw-1 200, gw-2 429, gw-3 429, gw-1 429, gw-2 429, gw-3 429, gw-1 429, gw-2 429, gw-3 429]
Allowed: per-node 12 of 12 (3x the limit!), shared 4 of 12
Next minute       : [gw-1 200, gw-2 200]

Why a shared counter here:

  • The limit is per user, not per node: it must be enforced globally.
  • Atomic increments in Redis are fast (sub-millisecond) and race-free.
  • Trade-off: an extra network hop per request, and you must decide what happens if Redis is unavailable (fail open vs. closed).
Unit Tests: RateLimiterTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.slidinglog.OtpRateLimiter;
import com.handbook.microservices.ratelimit.tokenbucket.TokenBucket;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class RateLimiterTest {

    private final FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");

    @Test
    void tokenBucketAllowsBurstThenRefills() {
        TokenBucket bucket = new TokenBucket(2, 1.0, clock);
        assertThat(bucket.tryAcquire()).isTrue();
        assertThat(bucket.tryAcquire()).isTrue();
        assertThat(bucket.tryAcquire()).isFalse();
        clock.advanceMillis(1_000);
        assertThat(bucket.tryAcquire()).isTrue();
    }

    @Test
    void slidingLogHasNoBoundaryBurst() {
        OtpRateLimiter limiter = new OtpRateLimiter(2, Duration.ofMinutes(1), clock);
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(50));
        assertThat(limiter.tryRequest("p")).isZero();
        assertThat(limiter.tryRequest("p")).isZero();
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(15)); // a new calendar minute, but within 60 s of both requests
        assertThat(limiter.tryRequest("p")).isPositive();
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Redis token bucket in Spring Cloud Gateway (reference):

spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: checkout
    uri: lb://checkout-service
    predicates: [ "Path=/checkout/**" ]
    filters:
      - name: RequestRateLimiter
        args:
          redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 1     # tokens per second
          redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 5     # bucket size
          redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1
          key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"     # Bean: exchange -> user id from JWT

Atomic sliding window in Redis uses a sorted set per key inside a Lua script: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE old entries, ZCARD, then ZADD if under the limit, all atomically.

Option Notes Bucket4j Java token-bucket library; local or distributed (Redis, Hazelcast, JCache) Resilience4j RateLimiter Limits outgoing calls from your service (protect a partner API's quota) Gateway / mesh Envoy local + global rate limit service, Kong, NGINX limit_req (leaky bucket) Cloud AWS API Gateway usage plans, Azure APIM, Cloudflare

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Rate limiting Spring Cloud Gateway RequestRateLimiter + RedisRateLimiter (token bucket) Resilience4j @RateLimiter for client-side limits Guava RateLimiter (smooth token bucket, in-process) NGINX limit_req (leaky bucket) Envoy Local token bucket + global rate limit service

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Protects availability and cost Legitimate users can be blocked (false positives) Fairness between clients/tenants Distributed counters add latency and a dependency Blunts brute force and scraping Choosing keys is hard (NAT shares IPs; attackers rotate IPs) Enables pricing tiers Clients need to handle 429 correctly

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Per-instance limits for a global policy

Ten instances with a local limit of 100/min allow 1,000/min (Example 3). Use a shared store, or divide the limit by instance count as an approximation.

Rate limiting by IP only

Corporate NAT and mobile carriers put thousands of users behind one IP; attackers use many IPs. Combine keys: user ID, API key, device, IP.

No Retry-After

Clients without guidance retry immediately and make things worse. Send Retry-After and rate-limit headers.

Failing closed when Redis is down

If the limiter's store is unavailable and you reject everything, your limiter caused an outage. Usually fail open with a local fallback limit.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Layers of limiting. Edge (CDN/WAF: per IP, bot detection) → gateway (per user/API key/tenant, by plan) → service (concurrency limits, load shedding by priority) → outgoing (respect partner quotas with client-side limiters).

Rate limiting vs. load shedding. Rate limits enforce policy per client. Load shedding protects the server regardless of client: when CPU or queue depth is high, reject low-priority traffic first (e.g. prefetch before checkout). Adaptive concurrency limits (Netflix's concurrency-limits library) adjust based on observed latency.

Accuracy vs. cost. A Redis round trip per request at 100k rps is real load. Options: local token buckets synchronized periodically, or "approximately global" limits that allow small overshoot. Choose based on what overshoot costs (SMS money vs. a few extra API calls).

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Keys chosen per threat: user, API key, tenant, IP, device; limits per plan.
  • Shared counters (Redis, atomic Lua) for global limits; decide fail-open vs. fail-closed.
  • 429 + Retry-After + X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers.
  • Metrics: rejections by key and route; alerts on spikes (attack or client bug).
  • Allow-lists for internal/health traffic; documented limits for API customers.
  • Load shedding by priority for overload, separate from per-client policy.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"I'd rate limit at the gateway with a token bucket per user and per API key, stored in Redis with an atomic Lua script, so limits are global across gateway instances. Limits depend on the customer's plan. Rejected requests get 429 with Retry-After. Sensitive endpoints like OTP use stricter sliding-window limits per phone, IP and device. If Redis is down, gateways fall back to approximate local buckets (fail open). Separately, services shed low-priority load when overloaded."

War story: the SMS bill

A fintech startup's OTP endpoint had a limit of 5 per minute per IP. An attacker used a botnet to send OTPs to premium-rate numbers they controlled (SMS pumping fraud). In one weekend, the company paid for about 400,000 SMS messages. Fix: per-phone sliding limits (3 per 10 min, 10 per day), per-country caps and allow-lists, device fingerprints, CAPTCHA after the first resend, and alerts on SMS spend per hour. Lesson: pick rate-limit keys based on what the attacker can't easily change, and limit by cost, not only by traffic.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Rate Limiter Bulkhead Circuit Breaker Throttling (queue) Limits Requests per time per key Concurrent calls Calls to an unhealthy dependency Work processed per time Protects Server from clients Caller from one dependency Caller and dependency Downstream from bursts Rejection 429 Immediate error Fail fast / fallback Requests wait

See API Gateway (where limits usually live) and Retry / Timeout / Bulkhead.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • 429 + Retry-After. Key by user / API key / tenant / IP.
  • Token bucket: bursts to capacity, average refill rate.
  • Sliding log: exact. Sliding counter: two counters, near exact. Fixed window: boundary bursts.
  • Many instances → shared atomic counter (Redis + Lua). Fail open vs. closed.
  • Rate limit (policy) ≠ load shedding (server protection).

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a Retry-After value (seconds until the next token) to TokenBucket.
  • Implement per-plan limits (free 10/min, pro 100/min) using one TokenBucket per (plan, key).
  • Write the Redis Lua script for a sliding-window log using a sorted set.

docs.title: Retry, Timeout & Bulkhead
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Three small patterns that together keep remote calls safe: Timeout: never wait forever; give each call a deadline. Retry: repeat calls that failed for transient reasons, with exponential backoff and jitter, and only if the operation is idempotent. Bulkhead: cap concurrent calls per dependency so one slow dependency can't consume all threads.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English:

  • Without timeouts, one hung supplier blocks the search page forever (the default socket read timeout in many clients is infinite).
  • Without retries, a 50 ms network blip during a deploy becomes a customer-facing error.
  • With naive retries, 10,000 clients retry at the same instant and knock the recovering service over again (a retry storm).
  • Without bulkheads, slow statement PDFs use every thread, so payments, which share the pool, fail too.

The name bulkhead comes from ships: watertight compartments mean one breach doesn't sink the ship.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Calling a busy restaurant

Timeout: you hang up after 2 minutes on hold. Retry: you call back later, but not every 5 seconds, and you don't place the same order twice. Jitter: if everyone in town calls back at exactly 7:00, the line jams again, so you try at a random minute. Bulkhead: the restaurant has separate phone lines for deliveries and table bookings, so a flood of delivery calls doesn't block bookings.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     C[Caller] --> B{Bulkhead<br/>permit free?}     B -->|no| R1[Reject fast: 503]     B -->|yes| T[Call with timeout]     T -->|success| OK[Result]     T -->|transient failure| RT{Attempts left?<br/>idempotent?}     RT -->|yes| W[Backoff + jitter] --> T     RT -->|no| F[Fail / fallback] Pattern Key settings Timeout Connect timeout, read timeout, overall deadline (budget) Retry Max attempts, base delay, cap, jitter, which errors are retryable Bulkhead Max concurrent calls (semaphore) or a dedicated thread pool per dependency

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Patterns)
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {               // retries every error, including 400 Bad Request
    try {
        return http.get(url);                // no timeout: may block forever
    } catch (Exception e) {
        Thread.sleep(1000);                  // fixed delay: all clients retry in lockstep
    }
}
// and every dependency shares the same 200-thread Tomcat pool

docs.title: Example 1: Retry with Backoff and Jitter (Grocery inventory)
docs.text:
Scenario: Reserving stock gets two 503s during an inventory-service deploy, then succeeds. A 400 (invalid quantity) is never retried. A long outage gives up after 4 attempts. Waits are random between 0 and an exponentially growing ceiling ("full jitter"). The random source is seeded and sleeping is injected, so the output is reproducible.

Full Code:

Retry.javaHttpError.javaRetryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.retry;

import java.util.Random;
import java.util.function.LongConsumer;
import java.util.function.Predicate;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Retry with exponential backoff and "full jitter": wait a random time between 0 and
 * min(cap, base * 2^attempt). Only transient errors are retried.
 */
public final class Retry {

    private final int maxAttempts;
    private final long baseMillis;
    private final long capMillis;
    private final Predicate<RuntimeException> retryable;
    private final Random random;
    private final LongConsumer sleeper;

    public Retry(int maxAttempts, long baseMillis, long capMillis, Predicate<RuntimeException> retryable,
                 Random random, LongConsumer sleeper) {
        this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts;
        this.baseMillis = baseMillis;
        this.capMillis = capMillis;
        this.retryable = retryable;
        this.random = random;
        this.sleeper = sleeper; // (1)!
    }

    public <T> T call(Supplier<T> action) {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                return action.get();
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                if (!retryable.test(e) || attempt == maxAttempts) { // (2)!
                    throw e;
                }
                long ceiling = Math.min(capMillis, baseMillis * (1L << attempt));
                long wait = (long) (random.nextDouble() * ceiling); // (3)!
                System.out.printf("    attempt %d failed (%s), retrying in %d ms (max %d)%n",
                        attempt, e.getMessage(), wait, ceiling);
                sleeper.accept(wait);
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. The sleeper is injected, so tests don't actually sleep and the demo is deterministic.
  2. Only transient errors are retried, and never past maxAttempts.
  3. Full jitter: random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)). It spreads retries out and reduces load spikes on the recovering service.
package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.retry;

/** An HTTP failure with its status code, so retry policies can tell transient from permanent errors. */
public final class HttpError extends RuntimeException {

    private final int status;

    public HttpError(int status, String message) {
        super(status + " " + message);
        this.status = status;
    }

    public int status() {
        return status;
    }

    /** 429, 502, 503 and 504 are usually transient; 4xx client errors are not. */
    public static boolean isTransient(RuntimeException e) {
        return e instanceof HttpError h && (h.status == 429 || h.status == 502 || h.status == 503 || h.status == 504);
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.retry;

import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;

public class RetryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long[] slept = {0};
        Retry retry = new Retry(4, 100, 2_000, HttpError::isTransient, new Random(42), ms -> slept[0] += ms);

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: reserve stock in the inventory service ===");
        Iterator<Integer> statuses = List.of(503, 503, 200).iterator();
        String result = retry.call(() -> respond(statuses.next()));
        System.out.println("Result: " + result + " after sleeping " + slept[0] + " ms in total");

        System.out.println("-- a validation error is never retried --");
        Iterator<Integer> badRequest = List.of(400, 200).iterator();
        try {
            retry.call(() -> respond(badRequest.next()));
        } catch (HttpError e) {
            System.out.println("Gave up immediately: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        System.out.println("-- a long outage exhausts the attempts --");
        try {
            retry.call(() -> respond(503));
        } catch (HttpError e) {
            System.out.println("Gave up after 4 attempts: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    private static String respond(int status) {
        if (status != 200) {
            throw new HttpError(status, status == 400 ? "quantity must be positive" : "service unavailable");
        }
        return "reserved MANGO-1KG x2";
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: reserve stock in the inventory service ===
    attempt 1 failed (503 service unavailable), retrying in 145 ms (max 200)
    attempt 2 failed (503 service unavailable), retrying in 273 ms (max 400)
Result: reserved MANGO-1KG x2 after sleeping 418 ms in total
-- a validation error is never retried --
Gave up immediately: 400 quantity must be positive
-- a long outage exhausts the attempts --
    attempt 1 failed (503 service unavailable), retrying in 61 ms (max 200)
    attempt 2 failed (503 service unavailable), retrying in 110 ms (max 400)
    attempt 3 failed (503 service unavailable), retrying in 532 ms (max 800)
Gave up after 4 attempts: 503 service unavailable

Why this design:

  • Transient blips become invisible to customers.
  • Bounded attempts and jitter protect the dependency.
  • Reserving stock is safe to retry only because the inventory API uses an idempotency key (the order ID). Without one, a retry after a timeout could reserve twice.

docs.title: Example 2: Per-Supplier Timeouts (Travel flight search)
docs.text:
Scenario: A search page queries four airline suppliers in parallel. AirNova hangs; BlueWing returns 502. With a 300 ms deadline per supplier, the page shows fares from the two healthy suppliers on time and records which suppliers timed out or failed.

Full Code:

FlightSearch.javaFlightSearchDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.timeout;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * Searches several airline suppliers in parallel. Each call gets its own deadline, so one slow
 * supplier can't hold the whole search page hostage.
 */
public final class FlightSearch {

    public record Result(List<String> fares, List<String> timedOut, List<String> failed) {
    }

    private final ExecutorService pool;
    private final long timeoutMillis;

    public FlightSearch(ExecutorService pool, long timeoutMillis) {
        this.pool = pool;
        this.timeoutMillis = timeoutMillis;
    }

    public Result search(Map<String, Supplier<String>> suppliers) {
        List<String> fares = new ArrayList<>();
        List<String> timedOut = new ArrayList<>();
        List<String> failed = new ArrayList<>();
        Map<String, CompletableFuture<String>> calls = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        suppliers.forEach((name, call) -> calls.put(name, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(call, pool)
                .orTimeout(timeoutMillis, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))); // (1)!

        calls.forEach((name, future) -> {
            try {
                fares.add(future.join());
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException ? timedOut : failed).add(name); // (2)!
            }
        });
        return new Result(fares, timedOut, failed);
    }
}
  1. orTimeout completes the future exceptionally after the deadline. It does not stop the underlying task, so real code also sets HTTP client timeouts so sockets are released.
  2. Distinguish timeouts from errors: they mean different things for alerts and supplier SLAs.
package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.timeout;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class FlightSearchDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CountDownLatch never = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Map<String, Supplier<String>> suppliers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        suppliers.put("SkyHop", () -> "SkyHop BLR->DEL ₹4,820");
        suppliers.put("AirNova", () -> {
            await(never); // supplier hangs
            return "AirNova BLR->DEL ₹4,650";
        });
        suppliers.put("CloudJet", () -> "CloudJet BLR->DEL ₹5,110");
        suppliers.put("BlueWing", () -> {
            throw new IllegalStateException("502 from BlueWing");
        });

        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            System.out.println("=== Travel: flight search with a 300 ms deadline per supplier ===");
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            var result = new FlightSearch(pool, 300).search(suppliers);
            long tookMs = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
            System.out.println("Fares shown : " + result.fares());
            System.out.println("Timed out   : " + result.timedOut());
            System.out.println("Failed      : " + result.failed());
            System.out.println("Page returned within ~300 ms (not waiting for AirNova): " + (tookMs < 1_000));
            never.countDown();
        }
    }

    private static void await(CountDownLatch latch) {
        try {
            latch.await();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: flight search with a 300 ms deadline per supplier ===
Fares shown : [SkyHop BLR->DEL ₹4,820, CloudJet BLR->DEL ₹5,110]
Timed out   : [AirNova]
Failed      : [BlueWing]
Page returned within ~300 ms (not waiting for AirNova): true

Why timeouts here:

  • The page latency is bounded by the deadline, not by the slowest supplier.
  • Partial results are better than no results for search.

docs.title: Example 3: Semaphore Bulkhead (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: Generating PDF statements is slow today. Statements get a bulkhead of 3 concurrent calls; payments get their own bulkhead of 10. With 3 statement requests in flight, a 4th is rejected immediately (the client gets 503 and retries later), while payments continue normally. Latches make the timing deterministic.

Full Code:

Bulkhead.javaBulkheadDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.bulkhead;

import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/**
 * A semaphore bulkhead: at most N concurrent calls to one dependency. Extra calls are rejected
 * at once instead of piling up and starving threads that other features need.
 */
public final class Bulkhead {

    public static final class FullException extends RuntimeException {
        FullException(String name) {
            super(name + " bulkhead full");
        }
    }

    private final String name;
    private final Semaphore permits;

    public Bulkhead(String name, int maxConcurrentCalls) {
        this.name = name;
        this.permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrentCalls);
    }

    public <T> T call(Supplier<T> action) {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { // (1)!
            throw new FullException(name);
        }
        try {
            return action.get();
        } finally {
            permits.release(); // (2)!
        }
    }

    public int available() {
        return permits.availablePermits();
    }
}
  1. tryAcquire() without waiting means reject fast. Resilience4j's maxWaitDuration lets callers queue briefly instead.
  2. Release in finally, or permits leak and the bulkhead slowly closes.
package com.handbook.microservices.resilience.bulkhead;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class BulkheadDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Bulkhead statements = new Bulkhead("statements", 3); // slow PDF statement generator
        Bulkhead payments = new Bulkhead("payments", 10);    // UPI / card payments

        CountDownLatch reportsRunning = new CountDownLatch(3);
        CountDownLatch reportsMayFinish = new CountDownLatch(1);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: slow statements must not block payments ===");
        List<Thread> slow = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            String id = "STMT-" + i;
            slow.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> statements.call(() -> {
                reportsRunning.countDown();
                await(reportsMayFinish); // the statement service is very slow today
                return id;
            })));
        }
        reportsRunning.await();
        System.out.println("3 statement requests in flight; statements permits left: " + statements.available());

        try {
            statements.call(() -> "STMT-4");
        } catch (Bulkhead.FullException e) {
            System.out.println("STMT-4  -> rejected fast: " + e.getMessage() + " (client sees 503, retry later)");
        }
        System.out.println("PAY-101 -> " + payments.call(() -> "payment accepted") + " (separate bulkhead)");
        System.out.println("PAY-102 -> " + payments.call(() -> "payment accepted"));

        reportsMayFinish.countDown();
        for (Thread t : slow) {
            t.join();
        }
        System.out.println("Statements finished; permits left: " + statements.available());
    }

    private static void await(CountDownLatch latch) {
        try {
            latch.await();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: slow statements must not block payments ===
3 statement requests in flight; statements permits left: 0
STMT-4  -> rejected fast: statements bulkhead full (client sees 503, retry later)
PAY-101 -> payment accepted (separate bulkhead)
PAY-102 -> payment accepted
Statements finished; permits left: 3

Why a bulkhead here:

  • Failure isolation: one slow feature can't starve a critical one.
  • Rejection is immediate and visible (metrics), instead of a slow pile-up.
Unit Tests: ResilienceTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.resilience.bulkhead.Bulkhead;
import com.handbook.microservices.resilience.retry.HttpError;
import com.handbook.microservices.resilience.retry.Retry;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Random;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ResilienceTest {

    private final Retry retry = new Retry(3, 10, 100, HttpError::isTransient, new Random(1), ms -> { });

    @Test
    void retriesTransientErrorsUpToMaxAttempts() {
        AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> retry.call(() -> {
            calls.incrementAndGet();
            throw new HttpError(503, "down");
        })).isInstanceOf(HttpError.class);
        assertThat(calls).hasValue(3);
    }

    @Test
    void doesNotRetryClientErrors() {
        AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> retry.call(() -> {
            calls.incrementAndGet();
            throw new HttpError(400, "bad");
        })).isInstanceOf(HttpError.class);
        assertThat(calls).hasValue(1);
    }

    @Test
    void bulkheadRejectsWhenFullAndReleasesPermits() {
        Bulkhead bulkhead = new Bulkhead("b", 1);
        bulkhead.call(() -> {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> bulkhead.call(() -> "inner")).isInstanceOf(Bulkhead.FullException.class);
            return "outer";
        });
        assertThat(bulkhead.available()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Transient failures hidden from users (retry) Retries multiply load during outages Bounded latency and freed resources (timeout) Too-short timeouts cause false failures and duplicate work Failure isolation between features (bulkhead) Bulkhead sizing needs load testing Cheap to add with libraries Retrying non-idempotent operations causes duplicates

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Retries at every layer

Gateway retries 3×, BFF retries 3×, service retries 3× → 27 calls to the database for one user click. Retry at one layer (usually closest to the failure) and use retry budgets.

Retrying non-idempotent operations

A timeout doesn't mean the payment failed. Retry only idempotent operations, or make them idempotent with an idempotency key.

Timeouts longer than the caller's timeout

If the mobile app gives up after 5 s but the backend waits 30 s for a supplier, the work is wasted. Timeouts should shrink going downstream.

Fixed delays without jitter

Synchronized retries cause periodic load spikes (thundering herd). Always add jitter.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Timeout budgets. Start from the user-facing SLO (e.g. 1 s), subtract network and processing, and give each hop a share. Propagate the remaining deadline so downstream services stop when the caller is gone.

Retry amplification math. With 3 attempts at each of 3 layers, worst-case load is 3³ = 27×. During a partial outage, retries can turn a 10% failure rate into overload. Use retry budgets (Envoy, gRPC) or retry only at the edge.

Little's law for bulkheads. Concurrency ≈ throughput × latency. 100 req/s at 200 ms needs ~20 concurrent calls; a bulkhead of 25 gives headroom. When latency degrades to 2 s, the bulkhead caps concurrency at 25 instead of 200. That's the point.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Connect + read timeouts on every client (HTTP, JDBC, Redis, Kafka producer).
  • Timeouts shrink downstream; deadlines propagated.
  • Retries: transient errors only, exponential backoff + jitter, max 2–3 attempts, idempotency keys.
  • Retry at one layer; retry budgets in the mesh.
  • Bulkheads per dependency, sized from Little's law + load tests; rejections exported as metrics.
  • Combined with circuit breakers and fallbacks.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Every remote call has a timeout derived from the end-to-end budget, and deadlines are propagated. Idempotent calls get at most 2 retries with exponential backoff and full jitter, only for 5xx, 429 and connection errors, and only at one layer so retries don't multiply. Non-idempotent calls use idempotency keys before they can be retried. Each dependency has its own bulkhead sized by Little's law, so a slow dependency degrades one feature, not the whole service. Breakers sit on top to stop calling dependencies that are clearly down."

War story: 27 retries per click

A travel site's search went down for 40 minutes after a database replica briefly lagged. Investigation showed the gateway, the search BFF, and the search service each retried 3 times with fixed 100 ms delays. A small slowdown became 27× traffic to the database, arriving in synchronized waves every 100 ms, which kept it overloaded long after the original lag ended. Fix: retries removed from the gateway and BFF; the service retries at most twice with jittered backoff; Envoy retry budget of 20%; timeouts aligned to the page budget. Lesson: retries are load. Count them across the whole call chain.

13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Timeout every call; budgets shrink downstream.
  • Retry transient + idempotent only; backoff + jitter; max 2–3; one layer.
  • Bulkhead per dependency (semaphore or pool); size with Little's law.
  • Combine with circuit breakers and fallbacks.
  • Retries are load: watch for amplification.

docs.text:
• Add a retry budget to Retry: allow retries only while retries are under 10% of calls in the last minute.
  • Make FlightSearch take an overall deadline and give each supplier the remaining time.
  • Replace the semaphore bulkhead with a thread-pool bulkhead and compare behaviour.
