docs.title: Saga
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A saga keeps data consistent across services without a distributed transaction. It is a sequence of local transactions, one per service. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions that semantically undo the steps already completed. It can be coordinated by an orchestrator (a central "conductor") or by choreography (services reacting to each other's events).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: placing a grocery order touches inventory (reserve stock), payments (charge the card) and delivery (book a slot). Each service has its own database, so there's no single BEGIN ... COMMIT across them. Two-phase commit (2PC/XA) is slow, couples services' availability, and isn't supported by most brokers and NoSQL stores. Yet "charged but no delivery slot" is unacceptable.

Definition (Hector Garcia-Molina & Kenneth Salem, 1987; microservices.io):

A saga is a sequence of local transactions. Each local transaction updates the database and publishes a message or event to trigger the next local transaction. If a local transaction fails, the saga executes a series of compensating transactions that undo the changes made by the preceding local transactions.

Key vocabulary:

Term Meaning Compensating transaction Semantic undo: refund a charge, release a reservation (not a database rollback) Pivot transaction The go/no-go step; after it succeeds, the saga must complete Retriable transaction Steps after the pivot; retried until they succeed Orchestration A coordinator tells each participant what to do Choreography Participants subscribe to events and decide what to do next

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Planning a trip with separate bookings

You book a flight, then a hotel, then try to pay for a tour. The tour is sold out, so you cancel the hotel and cancel the flight, in reverse order, maybe paying a cancellation fee. Nobody "rolls back time"; you perform new actions that undo the effect. That's a saga.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph Orchestration       O[Order saga<br/>orchestrator] -->|1 reserve| I[Inventory]       O -->|2 charge| P[Payment]       O -->|3 schedule| D[Delivery]       O -.->|undo: refund| P       O -.->|undo: release| I     end flowchart LR     subgraph Choreography       A[Order: OrderCreated] --> B[Inventory: StockReserved]       B --> C[Payment: PaymentCompleted]       C --> E[Delivery: SlotBooked]       C -.->|PaymentFailed| B2[Inventory releases stock]     end Orchestration Choreography Flow visible in One class Spread across services Coupling Orchestrator knows participants Services know events Good for Complex flows, many steps Simple flows, 2–4 steps Risk Orchestrator becomes a "god service" Cyclic, hard-to-follow event chains

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@Transactional // only covers order-service's database!
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
    inventoryClient.reserve(o);   // remote call: committed in inventory's DB
    paymentClient.charge(o);      // remote call: committed in payment's DB
    deliveryClient.schedule(o);   // fails → local rollback only
}   // result: stock reserved and card charged for an order that doesn't exist

docs.title: 5. Three Real-World Examples
docs.text:
All orchestrated examples share one small orchestrator:

SagaOrchestrator.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.core;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * An orchestration-based saga: run local transactions in order; if one fails, run the
 * compensations of the completed steps in reverse order. Steps after the pivot step are
 * retried until they succeed instead of being compensated.
 */
public final class SagaOrchestrator {

    /** A step's action and compensation each call one service's local transaction. */
    public record Step(String name, Runnable action, Runnable compensation, Kind kind) {

        public enum Kind { COMPENSATABLE, PIVOT, RETRIABLE }

        public static Step compensatable(String name, Runnable action, Runnable compensation) {
            return new Step(name, action, compensation, Kind.COMPENSATABLE);
        }

        public static Step pivot(String name, Runnable action) {
            return new Step(name, action, () -> { }, Kind.PIVOT);
        }

        public static Step retriable(String name, Runnable action) {
            return new Step(name, action, () -> { }, Kind.RETRIABLE);
        }
    }

    public enum Outcome { COMPLETED, COMPENSATED }

    private final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
    private final int maxRetries;

    public SagaOrchestrator(int maxRetries) {
        this.maxRetries = maxRetries;
    }

    public Outcome run(String sagaId, List<Step> steps) {
        Deque<Step> done = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (Step step : steps) {
            if (step.kind() == Step.Kind.RETRIABLE) {
                runWithRetries(sagaId, step); // (1)!
                continue;
            }
            try {
                step.action().run();
                record(sagaId, step.name() + " ✔");
                done.push(step); // (2)!
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                record(sagaId, step.name() + " ✘ " + e.getMessage());
                compensate(sagaId, done);
                return Outcome.COMPENSATED;
            }
        }
        record(sagaId, "COMPLETED");
        return Outcome.COMPLETED;
    }

    private void compensate(String sagaId, Deque<Step> done) {
        while (!done.isEmpty()) { // (3)!
            Step step = done.pop();
            step.compensation().run();
            record(sagaId, "undo " + step.name() + " ✔");
        }
        record(sagaId, "COMPENSATED");
    }

    private void runWithRetries(String sagaId, Step step) {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                step.action().run();
                record(sagaId, step.name() + " ✔" + (attempt > 1 ? " (attempt " + attempt + ")" : ""));
                return;
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                record(sagaId, step.name() + " ✘ " + e.getMessage() + ", will retry");
                if (attempt == maxRetries) {
                    record(sagaId, step.name() + " needs manual attention"); // (4)!
                    return;
                }
            }
        }
    }

    private void record(String sagaId, String entry) {
        log.add(entry);
        System.out.println("  [" + sagaId + "] " + entry);
    }

    public List<String> log() {
        return List.copyOf(log);
    }
}
  1. Retriable steps (after the pivot) are never compensated; they are retried.
  2. Completed steps go on a stack, so compensations run in reverse order.
  3. Compensations themselves must be idempotent and retriable: in production, a failed compensation is retried, not abandoned.
  4. Retries are bounded; exhausted retries go to a human (a dead-letter queue plus an alert).

docs.title: Example 1: Place-Order Saga (Grocery, orchestration)
docs.text:
Scenario: Reserve stock → charge payment → schedule delivery. ORD-1 succeeds. ORD-2's pincode has no delivery slots, so the payment is refunded and stock released. ORD-3 fails at the first step, so there's nothing to undo.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant S as Order saga participant I as Inventory participant P as Payment participant D as Delivery S->>I: reserve ✔ S->>P: charge ✔ S->>D: schedule ✘ no slots S->>P: refund (compensate) S->>I: release (compensate)

Full Code:

PlaceOrderSaga.javaGroceryServices.javaPlaceOrderSagaDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator.Outcome;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator.Step;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.DeliveryService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.InventoryService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.PaymentService;

import java.util.List;

/** The order service owns this saga and tells each participant what to do. */
public final class PlaceOrderSaga {

    public record Order(String id, String sku, int qty, long paise, String pincode) {
    }

    private final InventoryService inventory;
    private final PaymentService payments;
    private final DeliveryService delivery;

    public PlaceOrderSaga(InventoryService inventory, PaymentService payments, DeliveryService delivery) {
        this.inventory = inventory;
        this.payments = payments;
        this.delivery = delivery;
    }

    public Outcome place(Order o) {
        return new SagaOrchestrator(3).run(o.id(), List.of(
                Step.compensatable("reserve stock",
                        () -> inventory.reserve(o.sku(), o.qty()),
                        () -> inventory.release(o.sku(), o.qty())), // (1)!
                Step.compensatable("charge payment",
                        () -> payments.charge(o.id(), o.paise()),
                        () -> payments.refund(o.id())),
                Step.compensatable("schedule delivery",
                        () -> delivery.schedule(o.id(), o.pincode()),
                        () -> { })));
    }
}
  1. Each action is paired with its compensation right where it's defined, so they can't drift apart.
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/** Three services, each with its own database and a local transaction per call. */
public final class GroceryServices {

    private GroceryServices() {
    }

    public static final class InventoryService {
        private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("MANGO-1KG", 10));

        public void reserve(String sku, int qty) {
            int available = stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
            if (available < qty) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock");
            }
            stock.put(sku, available - qty);
        }

        public void release(String sku, int qty) {
            stock.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum);
        }

        public int available(String sku) {
            return stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
        }
    }

    public static final class PaymentService {
        private final Set<String> charged = new HashSet<>();

        public void charge(String orderId, long paise) {
            charged.add(orderId);
        }

        public void refund(String orderId) {
            charged.remove(orderId);
        }

        public boolean isCharged(String orderId) {
            return charged.contains(orderId);
        }
    }

    public static final class DeliveryService {
        private final Set<String> pincodesServed = Set.of("560001", "560034");

        public void schedule(String orderId, String pincode) {
            if (!pincodesServed.contains(pincode)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("no delivery slots for " + pincode);
            }
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.DeliveryService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.InventoryService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.PaymentService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.PlaceOrderSaga.Order;

public class PlaceOrderSagaDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var inventory = new InventoryService();
        var payments = new PaymentService();
        var saga = new PlaceOrderSaga(inventory, payments, new DeliveryService());

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: place-order saga (orchestration) ===");
        System.out.println("Outcome: " + saga.place(new Order("ORD-1", "MANGO-1KG", 2, 79_800, "560034")));
        System.out.println("Stock left: " + inventory.available("MANGO-1KG") + ", ORD-1 charged: " + payments.isCharged("ORD-1"));

        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("Outcome: " + saga.place(new Order("ORD-2", "MANGO-1KG", 3, 119_700, "999999")));
        System.out.println("Stock left: " + inventory.available("MANGO-1KG") + ", ORD-2 charged: " + payments.isCharged("ORD-2"));

        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("Outcome: " + saga.place(new Order("ORD-3", "MANGO-1KG", 50, 1_995_000, "560001")));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: place-order saga (orchestration) ===
  [ORD-1] reserve stock ✔
  [ORD-1] charge payment ✔
  [ORD-1] schedule delivery ✔
  [ORD-1] COMPLETED
Outcome: COMPLETED
Stock left: 8, ORD-1 charged: true

  [ORD-2] reserve stock ✔
  [ORD-2] charge payment ✔
  [ORD-2] schedule delivery ✘ no delivery slots for 999999
  [ORD-2] undo charge payment ✔
  [ORD-2] undo reserve stock ✔
  [ORD-2] COMPENSATED
Outcome: COMPENSATED
Stock left: 8, ORD-2 charged: false

  [ORD-3] reserve stock ✘ out of stock
  [ORD-3] COMPENSATED
Outcome: COMPENSATED

Why a saga here:

  • Three databases, no distributed transaction, yet no orphaned charges or reservations.
  • The whole flow is readable in one place (orchestration).
  • Ordering tip: put steps that are most likely to fail, or cheapest to undo, first (validate delivery before charging in a real design).

docs.title: Example 2: Trip Booking with a Pivot (Travel)
docs.text:
Scenario: Hold a flight and a hotel (both cancellable), then charge the card: the pivot. After payment, the trip is sold; if the airport-cab partner is flaky, the saga retries forward instead of refunding the whole trip. If the hotel is sold out before payment, the flight hold is cancelled.

Full Code:

TripBookingSaga.javaTripBookingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.travel;

import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator.Outcome;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator.Step;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * Flight and hotel holds can be cancelled. Charging the card is the pivot: once it succeeds the
 * trip is sold, so the cab and confirmation e-mail are retried rather than undoing the whole trip.
 */
public final class TripBookingSaga {

    public interface Partners {
        void holdFlight(String trip);

        void cancelFlight(String trip);

        void holdHotel(String trip);

        void cancelHotel(String trip);

        void chargeCard(String trip);

        void bookAirportCab(String trip);

        void sendItinerary(String trip);
    }

    private final Partners p;

    public TripBookingSaga(Partners partners) {
        this.p = partners;
    }

    public Outcome book(String trip) {
        return new SagaOrchestrator(3).run(trip, List.of(
                Step.compensatable("hold flight", run(p::holdFlight, trip), run(p::cancelFlight, trip)),
                Step.compensatable("hold hotel", run(p::holdHotel, trip), run(p::cancelHotel, trip)),
                Step.pivot("charge card", run(p::chargeCard, trip)), // (1)!
                Step.retriable("book airport cab", run(p::bookAirportCab, trip)), // (2)!
                Step.retriable("send itinerary", run(p::sendItinerary, trip))));
    }

    private static Runnable run(Consumer<String> call, String trip) {
        return () -> call.accept(trip);
    }
}
  1. The pivot: the point of no return. Before it, compensate; after it, complete.
  2. Retriable steps must eventually succeed (idempotent calls, retries, a manual fallback).
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.travel;

import java.util.Set;

public class TripBookingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Travel: flight + hotel + cab, with a pivot step ===");
        new TripBookingSaga(new FakePartners(Set.of(), 0)).book("TRIP-1");

        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("-- hotel is sold out: cancel the flight hold --");
        new TripBookingSaga(new FakePartners(Set.of("hotel"), 0)).book("TRIP-2");

        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("-- after payment, the cab partner is flaky: retry forward, don't refund --");
        new TripBookingSaga(new FakePartners(Set.of(), 2)).book("TRIP-3");
    }

    /** Fake partner APIs: some always fail, and the cab API fails its first N calls. */
    private static final class FakePartners implements TripBookingSaga.Partners {
        private final Set<String> failing;
        private int cabFailuresLeft;

        FakePartners(Set<String> failing, int cabFailures) {
            this.failing = failing;
            this.cabFailuresLeft = cabFailures;
        }

        private void maybeFail(String partner, String reason) {
            if (failing.contains(partner)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException(reason);
            }
        }

        @Override public void holdFlight(String trip) { maybeFail("flight", "no seats"); }
        @Override public void cancelFlight(String trip) { }
        @Override public void holdHotel(String trip) { maybeFail("hotel", "sold out"); }
        @Override public void cancelHotel(String trip) { }
        @Override public void chargeCard(String trip) { maybeFail("card", "card declined"); }
        @Override public void sendItinerary(String trip) { }

        @Override
        public void bookAirportCab(String trip) {
            if (cabFailuresLeft-- > 0) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("cab API timeout");
            }
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Travel: flight + hotel + cab, with a pivot step ===
  [TRIP-1] hold flight ✔
  [TRIP-1] hold hotel ✔
  [TRIP-1] charge card ✔
  [TRIP-1] book airport cab ✔
  [TRIP-1] send itinerary ✔
  [TRIP-1] COMPLETED

-- hotel is sold out: cancel the flight hold --
  [TRIP-2] hold flight ✔
  [TRIP-2] hold hotel ✘ sold out
  [TRIP-2] undo hold flight ✔
  [TRIP-2] COMPENSATED

-- after payment, the cab partner is flaky: retry forward, don't refund --
  [TRIP-3] hold flight ✔
  [TRIP-3] hold hotel ✔
  [TRIP-3] charge card ✔
  [TRIP-3] book airport cab ✘ cab API timeout, will retry
  [TRIP-3] book airport cab ✘ cab API timeout, will retry
  [TRIP-3] book airport cab ✔ (attempt 3)
  [TRIP-3] send itinerary ✔
  [TRIP-3] COMPLETED

Why a pivot here:

  • Refunding a whole holiday because a cab API timed out is bad business.
  • Making the structure explicit (compensatable → pivot → retriable) forces the right conversation with the product owner.

docs.title: Example 3: Inter-Bank Transfer (Banking, choreography)
docs.text:
Scenario: No orchestrator. The debit service reacts to TransferRequested by debiting and publishing AccountDebited. The credit service reacts by crediting, or publishes CreditFailed if the target account is closed. The debit service listens for CreditFailed and refunds (the compensation), then publishes TransferFailed.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant Bus as Event bus participant A as Debit service (bank A) participant B as Credit service (bank B) Bus->>A: TransferRequested TX-2 A->>Bus: AccountDebited Bus->>B: AccountDebited B->>Bus: CreditFailed (account closed) Bus->>A: CreditFailed A->>Bus: TransferFailed (refunded)

Full Code:

TransferChoreography.javaTransferChoreographyDemo.javaEventBus.java (support) 
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.banking;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * A choreography-based saga: no orchestrator. Each service reacts to events and publishes its own.
 * The debit side listens for CreditFailed and refunds, which is the compensation.
 */
public final class TransferChoreography {

    public record TransferRequested(String id, String from, String to, long amount) {
    }

    public record AccountDebited(String id, String from, String to, long amount) {
    }

    public record AccountCredited(String id) {
    }

    public record CreditFailed(String id, String from, long amount, String reason) {
    }

    public record TransferFailed(String id, String reason) {
    }

    /** Owns source accounts (bank A). */
    public static final class DebitService {
        final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>();

        DebitService(EventBus bus) {
            bus.<TransferRequested>subscribe("transfers", e -> {
                long balance = balances.getOrDefault(e.from(), 0L);
                if (balance < e.amount()) {
                    bus.publish("transfers.failed", new TransferFailed(e.id(), "insufficient funds"));
                    return;
                }
                balances.put(e.from(), balance - e.amount());
                bus.publish("accounts.debited", new AccountDebited(e.id(), e.from(), e.to(), e.amount()));
            });
            bus.<CreditFailed>subscribe("credits.failed", e -> { // (1)!
                balances.merge(e.from(), e.amount(), Long::sum);
                bus.publish("transfers.failed", new TransferFailed(e.id(), e.reason() + ", refunded"));
            });
        }
    }

    /** Owns destination accounts (bank B). */
    public static final class CreditService {
        final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>();

        CreditService(EventBus bus, Set<String> closedAccounts) {
            bus.<AccountDebited>subscribe("accounts.debited", e -> {
                if (closedAccounts.contains(e.to())) {
                    bus.publish("credits.failed", new CreditFailed(e.id(), e.from(), e.amount(), "account closed"));
                    return;
                }
                balances.merge(e.to(), e.amount(), Long::sum);
                bus.publish("accounts.credited", new AccountCredited(e.id()));
            });
        }
    }

    public final DebitService debit;
    public final CreditService credit;

    public TransferChoreography(EventBus bus, Set<String> closedAccounts) {
        this.debit = new DebitService(bus);
        this.credit = new CreditService(bus, closedAccounts);
    }

    public long balanceA(String account) {
        return debit.balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L);
    }

    public void openA(String account, long balance) {
        debit.balances.put(account, balance);
    }
}
  1. The compensation is triggered by an event, not called by a coordinator.
package com.handbook.microservices.saga.banking;

import com.handbook.microservices.saga.banking.TransferChoreography.TransferRequested;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.EventBus;

import java.util.Set;

public class TransferChoreographyDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EventBus bus = new EventBus(true);
        var transfers = new TransferChoreography(bus, Set.of("B-CLOSED-9"));
        transfers.openA("A-100", 5_000);

        System.out.println("=== Banking: inter-bank transfer as a choreographed saga ===");
        bus.publish("transfers", new TransferRequested("TX-1", "A-100", "B-200", 1_500));
        System.out.println("A-100 balance: " + transfers.balanceA("A-100"));

        System.out.println();
        bus.publish("transfers", new TransferRequested("TX-2", "A-100", "B-CLOSED-9", 2_000));
        System.out.println("A-100 balance: " + transfers.balanceA("A-100") + " (debit compensated by refund)");

        System.out.println();
        bus.publish("transfers", new TransferRequested("TX-3", "A-100", "B-200", 9_999));
        System.out.println("A-100 balance: " + transfers.balanceA("A-100"));
    }
}

package com.handbook.microservices.support;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/**
 * A tiny, synchronous, in-memory stand-in for a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
 * Real brokers are asynchronous and at-least-once; the examples call that out where it matters.
 */
public final class EventBus {

    private final Map<String, List<Consumer<Object>>> subscribers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final boolean log;

    public EventBus(boolean log) {
        this.log = log;
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <T> void subscribe(String topic, Consumer<T> handler) {
        subscribers.computeIfAbsent(topic, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e -> handler.accept((T) e));
    }

    public void publish(String topic, Object event) {
        if (log) {
            System.out.println("  [bus] " + topic + " <- " + event);
        }
        for (Consumer<Object> s : subscribers.getOrDefault(topic, List.of())) {
            s.accept(event);
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: inter-bank transfer as a choreographed saga ===
  [bus] transfers <- TransferRequested[id=TX-1, from=A-100, to=B-200, amount=1500]
  [bus] accounts.debited <- AccountDebited[id=TX-1, from=A-100, to=B-200, amount=1500]
  [bus] accounts.credited <- AccountCredited[id=TX-1]
A-100 balance: 3500

  [bus] transfers <- TransferRequested[id=TX-2, from=A-100, to=B-CLOSED-9, amount=2000]
  [bus] accounts.debited <- AccountDebited[id=TX-2, from=A-100, to=B-CLOSED-9, amount=2000]
  [bus] credits.failed <- CreditFailed[id=TX-2, from=A-100, amount=2000, reason=account closed]
  [bus] transfers.failed <- TransferFailed[id=TX-2, reason=account closed, refunded]
A-100 balance: 3500 (debit compensated by refund)

  [bus] transfers <- TransferRequested[id=TX-3, from=A-100, to=B-200, amount=9999]
  [bus] transfers.failed <- TransferFailed[id=TX-3, reason=insufficient funds]
A-100 balance: 3500

Why choreography here:

  • Two participants and a short flow: no orchestrator needed.
  • The banks are separate organizations; neither should own a central coordinator.
  • The demo bus is synchronous for clarity; with Kafka, the same flow is asynchronous and at-least-once, so each handler must be idempotent (see Idempotent Consumer).
Unit Tests: SagaTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator.Outcome;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.core.SagaOrchestrator.Step;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.DeliveryService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.InventoryService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.GroceryServices.PaymentService;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.PlaceOrderSaga;
import com.handbook.microservices.saga.grocery.PlaceOrderSaga.Order;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SagaTest {

    @Test
    void failedStepCompensatesCompletedStepsInReverseOrder() {
        List<String> calls = new ArrayList<>();
        Outcome outcome = new SagaOrchestrator(1).run("S", List.of(
                Step.compensatable("a", () -> calls.add("a"), () -> calls.add("undo a")),
                Step.compensatable("b", () -> calls.add("b"), () -> calls.add("undo b")),
                Step.compensatable("c", () -> {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("x");
                }, () -> calls.add("undo c"))));
        assertThat(outcome).isEqualTo(Outcome.COMPENSATED);
        assertThat(calls).containsExactly("a", "b", "undo b", "undo a");
    }

    @Test
    void orderSagaLeavesNoChargeOrReservationWhenDeliveryFails() {
        var inventory = new InventoryService();
        var payments = new PaymentService();
        new PlaceOrderSaga(inventory, payments, new DeliveryService()).place(new Order("O", "MANGO-1KG", 4, 1, "000000"));
        assertThat(inventory.available("MANGO-1KG")).isEqualTo(10);
        assertThat(payments.isCharged("O")).isFalse();
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
A choreography participant with Spring Kafka (compiled in the spring-reference module):

package com.handbook.springref.saga;

import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

/**
 * A choreography participant: payment-service reacts to StockReserved by charging the customer,
 * and publishes PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed (which inventory-service uses to release stock).
 * Events are plain JSON strings here to keep the snippet short.
 */
@Component
public class PaymentSagaListener {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;
    private final PaymentRepository payments;

    public PaymentSagaListener(KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka, PaymentRepository payments) {
        this.kafka = kafka;
        this.payments = payments;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "inventory.stock-reserved", groupId = "payment-service")
    @Transactional
    public void onStockReserved(String orderId) {
        if (payments.alreadyProcessed(orderId)) {
            return; // Kafka is at-least-once: make the handler idempotent
        }
        boolean charged = payments.charge(orderId);
        // In production, write this event to an outbox table in the same transaction instead.
        kafka.send(charged ? "payment.completed" : "payment.failed", orderId, orderId);
    }

    /** The local database access this listener needs. */
    public interface PaymentRepository {
        boolean alreadyProcessed(String orderId);

        boolean charge(String orderId);
    }
}
Option Notes Hand-written orchestrator with a saga state table Full control; you build persistence, timeouts, retries Temporal / Cadence Durable workflows in Java code: retries, timers and state persisted for you Camunda / Zeebe BPMN workflows with compensation events Axon Framework @Saga with @SagaEventHandler, in an event-sourced style Eventuate Tram Sagas Orchestration sagas over the transactional outbox AWS Step Functions Managed state machines with catch/compensate branches

Countermeasures for missing isolation (sagas are ACD, without the I):

  • Semantic lock: mark records PENDING (order APPROVAL_PENDING) so other flows treat them carefully.
  • Commutative updates: design operations that can be applied in any order (debit/credit amounts, not "set balance").
  • Pessimistic view: order steps to minimize business risk (charge after cheap checks).
  • Reread value: check data hasn't changed before overwriting.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Saga Temporal (Java SDK) Saga helper with addCompensation() inside workflows Axon Framework @Saga, @StartSaga, @EndSaga Camunda BPMN compensation boundary events Eventuate Tram SagaDefinition with step().invokeParticipant().withCompensation()

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Consistency without 2PC across services Only eventual consistency; intermediate states are visible Each service keeps its own database and availability No isolation: concurrent sagas can interfere (anomalies) Works with brokers and NoSQL Compensations must be designed for every step Explicit business-level failure handling Debugging distributed flows is hard without tracing

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Non-idempotent steps and compensations

Messages are redelivered and orchestrators crash and retry. "Refund" executed twice refunds twice. Every step and compensation needs an idempotency key.

Losing saga state on crash

An in-memory orchestrator that crashes mid-saga leaves money charged and stock reserved forever. Persist saga state (see the coding challenge), or use a workflow engine.

Compensations that can't compensate

You can't "unsend" an email or "unship" a parcel. Move irreversible actions after the pivot, or compensate with a new business action (a correction email, a return label).

Choreography spaghetti

Ten services reacting to each other's events with nobody owning the flow. If you need a diagram to understand it, consider orchestration.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Orchestration vs. choreography in practice. Most mature teams use orchestration for core business flows (order, payment, onboarding) because the flow is versioned, testable and observable in one place, and use choreography for loose reactions (send email when an order ships). Workflow engines (Temporal) make orchestration durable without writing the state machine yourself.

Isolation anomalies. Lost updates (saga B overwrites saga A's change), dirty reads (reading a reservation that will be compensated), fuzzy reads. Use semantic locks (PENDING states), version checks and commutative operations. Discuss which anomalies are acceptable for the business.

Timeouts. A participant may never reply. Sagas need deadlines per step ("payment not confirmed in 15 min → cancel order"), implemented with durable timers (a scheduler table or a workflow engine).

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Saga state persisted (state table or workflow engine); recovery on restart.
  • Every step and compensation idempotent (idempotency keys, processed-message table).
  • Steps ordered: validations and reversible steps first, irreversible steps after the pivot.
  • Commands and events sent via the transactional outbox.
  • Per-step timeouts with durable timers; dead-letter handling and alerts for stuck sagas.
  • Semantic locks (PENDING states) visible in UIs and APIs.
  • Tracing across all steps (one trace or a correlation ID per saga).

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Order placement spans inventory, payment and delivery, each with its own database, so I'd use an orchestrated saga, owned by the order service or run in Temporal. The order starts as PENDING. Steps: reserve stock, charge payment (the pivot), book delivery (retried until it succeeds). If a step before the pivot fails, compensations run in reverse: refund, release. Saga state is persisted, commands go through the outbox, every handler is idempotent, and each step has a timeout. The customer sees 'processing' until the saga completes, then gets a push notification."

War story: the refund that ran three times

A marketplace's payment-failure compensation listened to DeliveryFailed events. During a broker rebalance, the same event was delivered three times, and the handler issued three refunds for one order. Finance found the loss two weeks later. Fix: compensations keyed by (sagaId, step) in a processed-messages table inside the same local transaction; the refund API called with an idempotency key. Lesson: "at-least-once delivery" means your code must make it "exactly-once in effect".

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Saga 2PC / XA Transactional Outbox Event Sourcing Consistency Eventual, with compensations Atomic Atomic DB write + event Events are the source of truth Availability High Lower (coordinator, locks) High High Typical use Cross-service business flows Single org, XA-capable resources Reliable event publishing for sagas Audit, temporal queries

See Transactional Outbox, Idempotent Consumer, and the in-process Command pattern (actions with undo).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Local transactions + compensations, no 2PC.
  • Orchestration (central coordinator) vs. choreography (events).
  • Compensatable → pivot → retriable.
  • Idempotent steps, persisted state, outbox, timeouts.
  • No isolation: semantic locks (PENDING).

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Reorder the grocery saga so delivery availability is checked before payment, and explain why that's better.
  • Add a timeout to the trip saga: if the hotel doesn't confirm within 5 minutes (FakeClock), compensate.
  • Rewrite the place-order flow as choreography with the EventBus and compare readability.

docs.title: Service Discovery
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Services find each other by name, not hard-coded addresses. Instances register with a registry and renew a lease with heartbeats; callers look up the healthy instances and pick one (client-side), or a load balancer or DNS does it for them (server-side). In cloud environments instances come and go constantly, so addresses must be discovered at runtime.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: order-service runs as 3 containers today, 7 during the evening rush, and each deploy replaces them with new IP addresses. A crashed instance should stop getting traffic within seconds. Hard-coding 10.0.1.11:8080 in configuration can't keep up.

Two halves of the pattern:

Part What happens Registration Instances register on startup (self-registration) or are registered by the platform (Kubernetes, ECS) and are removed on shutdown or when health checks or heartbeats fail Discovery Client-side: caller queries the registry and load-balances itself (Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer). Server-side: caller hits a stable name (Kubernetes Service DNS, AWS ALB) and the platform routes

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Taxi dispatch radio

Drivers radio in when they start a shift and check in every few minutes ("still available"). The dispatcher (registry) only sends rides to drivers who checked in recently. A driver who goes silent is taken off the board, even if they never said goodbye.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph Registry       R[(Service registry<br/>name → instances + leases)]     end     O1[order-1] -->|register + heartbeat| R     O2[order-2] -->|register + heartbeat| R     C[cart-service] -->|1. lookup order-service| R     C -->|2. call chosen instance| O1 Participant Responsibility Registry Stores instances and lease timestamps; evicts expired leases Service instance Registers, heartbeats, deregisters on graceful shutdown Client / load balancer Looks up instances, picks one (round-robin, zone-aware), retries the next on connection failure

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
# application.properties in cart-service
order.service.urls=http://10.0.1.11:8080,http://10.0.2.12:8080
  • Autoscaling adds instances nobody calls.
  • A crashed instance keeps receiving traffic until someone edits config.
  • Every deploy that changes IPs needs a config change in every caller.

docs.title: Example 1: Registry with Leases (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Three order-service instances register with a 30-second lease. order-2 crashes and stops heartbeating, so after 30 s it disappears from lookups and is evicted. During a deploy, order-3 deregisters gracefully (no 30 s of failed calls), and the autoscaler's new order-4 registers and immediately receives traffic.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant O2 as order-2 participant R as Registry participant C as Caller O2->>R: register (t=0) Note over O2: crashes at t=5 C->>R: lookup at t=20 → still listed (lease valid until t=30) C->>R: lookup at t=35 → gone (lease expired) R->>R: evictExpired() → [order-2]

Full Code:

ServiceRegistry.javaRegistryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

/**
 * A minimal service registry (think Eureka or Consul). Instances register, renew their lease with
 * heartbeats, and disappear when the lease expires, so a crashed instance stops receiving traffic.
 */
public class ServiceRegistry {

    public record Instance(String service, String id, String address, String zone, Instant lastHeartbeat) {
    }

    private final Map<String, Instance> instances = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration leaseTtl;

    public ServiceRegistry(Clock clock, Duration leaseTtl) {
        this.clock = clock;
        this.leaseTtl = leaseTtl;
    }

    public void register(String service, String id, String address, String zone) { // (1)!
        instances.put(id, new Instance(service, id, address, zone, clock.instant()));
    }

    public void heartbeat(String id) { // (2)!
        instances.computeIfPresent(id, (k, i) ->
                new Instance(i.service(), i.id(), i.address(), i.zone(), clock.instant()));
    }

    public void deregister(String id) { // (3)!
        instances.remove(id);
    }

    /** Healthy instances of a service: those whose lease has not expired. */
    public List<Instance> lookup(String service) {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        return instances.values().stream()
                .filter(i -> i.service().equals(service))
                .filter(i -> isLeaseValid(i, now)) // (4)!
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Instance::id))
                .toList();
    }

    /** Every registered instance of a service, including ones whose lease has expired. */
    protected List<Instance> lookupIncludingExpired(String service) {
        return instances.values().stream()
                .filter(i -> i.service().equals(service))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Instance::id))
                .toList();
    }

    /** Removes expired instances; registries run this periodically. Returns the evicted IDs. */
    public List<String> evictExpired() {
        List<String> expired = expiredIds();
        expired.forEach(instances::remove);
        return expired;
    }

    protected List<String> expiredIds() {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        return instances.values().stream()
                .filter(i -> !isLeaseValid(i, now))
                .map(Instance::id).sorted().toList();
    }

    protected int registeredCount() {
        return instances.size();
    }

    private boolean isLeaseValid(Instance i, Instant now) {
        return i.lastHeartbeat().plus(leaseTtl).isAfter(now);
    }
}
  1. Self-registration on startup (Spring Cloud does this automatically with @EnableDiscoveryClient).
  2. The heartbeat renews the lease. No heartbeat means the instance is assumed dead.
  3. Graceful deregistration on shutdown avoids a window of failed calls during deploys.
  4. Lookups filter expired leases, so callers stop seeing dead instances even before eviction runs.
package com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry;

import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry.Instance;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;

public class RegistryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z");
        ServiceRegistry registry = new ServiceRegistry(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(30));

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: order-service instances come and go ===");
        registry.register("order-service", "order-1", "10.0.1.11:8080", "zone-a");
        registry.register("order-service", "order-2", "10.0.2.12:8080", "zone-b");
        registry.register("order-service", "order-3", "10.0.1.13:8080", "zone-a");
        print("t=0s   3 instances registered", registry);

        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(20));
        registry.heartbeat("order-1");
        registry.heartbeat("order-3"); // order-2 has crashed and stops sending heartbeats
        print("t=20s  order-2 missed its heartbeat", registry);

        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(15));
        registry.heartbeat("order-1");
        registry.heartbeat("order-3");
        print("t=35s  order-2 lease (30s) expired", registry);
        System.out.println("       evicted: " + registry.evictExpired());

        registry.deregister("order-3"); // graceful shutdown during a deploy
        print("t=35s  order-3 deregistered on shutdown", registry);

        registry.register("order-service", "order-4", "10.0.2.14:8080", "zone-b");
        print("t=35s  autoscaler adds order-4", registry);
    }

    private static void print(String label, ServiceRegistry registry) {
        System.out.println(label + " -> " + registry.lookup("order-service").stream()
                .map(Instance::address).toList());
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: order-service instances come and go ===
t=0s   3 instances registered -> [10.0.1.11:8080, 10.0.2.12:8080, 10.0.1.13:8080]
t=20s  order-2 missed its heartbeat -> [10.0.1.11:8080, 10.0.2.12:8080, 10.0.1.13:8080]
t=35s  order-2 lease (30s) expired -> [10.0.1.11:8080, 10.0.1.13:8080]
       evicted: [order-2]
t=35s  order-3 deregistered on shutdown -> [10.0.1.11:8080]
t=35s  autoscaler adds order-4 -> [10.0.1.11:8080, 10.0.2.14:8080]

Why this design:

  • Leases make failure detection automatic: silence means gone.
  • Note the gap: between t=5 (crash) and t=30 (lease expiry), callers may still pick order-2. That's why clients need retries on connection failure (Example 2).

docs.title: Example 2: Client-Side Load Balancing (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: The trip service calls eta-service, which has three instances. eta-2 crashed 5 seconds ago, so its lease is still valid and the registry still lists it. The client round-robins across instances and, on a connection failure, tries the next one, so riders never see an error.

Design:

flowchart LR T[trip-service<br/>LoadBalancedClient] -->|lookup| R[(Registry)] T -->|round-robin| E1[eta-1] T -.->|connection refused| E2[eta-2 💥] T -->|retry next| E3[eta-3]

Full Code:

LoadBalancedClient.javaClientSideDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.discovery.clientside;

import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry;
import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry.Instance;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.function.BiFunction;

/**
 * Client-side discovery (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer style): the caller looks up instances,
 * picks one round-robin, and on a connection failure tries the next one.
 */
public final class LoadBalancedClient {

    private final ServiceRegistry registry;
    private final AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger();

    public LoadBalancedClient(ServiceRegistry registry) {
        this.registry = registry;
    }

    /** {@code call} sends the request to an address; it throws if the instance is unreachable. */
    public String call(String service, String request, BiFunction<String, String, String> call) {
        List<Instance> candidates = registry.lookup(service); // (1)!
        if (candidates.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("no instances of " + service);
        }
        Set<String> tried = new HashSet<>();
        while (tried.size() < candidates.size()) {
            Instance pick = candidates.get(Math.floorMod(next.getAndIncrement(), candidates.size())); // (2)!
            if (!tried.add(pick.id())) {
                continue;
            }
            try {
                return call.apply(pick.address(), request);
            } catch (RuntimeException unreachable) { // (3)!
                System.out.println("    " + pick.address() + " unreachable, trying next instance");
            }
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("all instances of " + service + " failed");
    }
}
  1. Real clients cache the instance list and refresh it every few seconds instead of calling the registry per request.
  2. Round-robin; floorMod keeps the index valid even after the counter overflows.
  3. Retry another instance only on connection-level failures (safe: the request never reached the server). Retrying after a timeout could execute a non-idempotent request twice.
package com.handbook.microservices.discovery.clientside;

import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.function.BiFunction;

public class ClientSideDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z");
        ServiceRegistry registry = new ServiceRegistry(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(30));
        registry.register("eta-service", "eta-1", "10.0.1.21:9000", "zone-a");
        registry.register("eta-service", "eta-2", "10.0.1.22:9000", "zone-a");
        registry.register("eta-service", "eta-3", "10.0.2.23:9000", "zone-b");

        Set<String> crashed = Set.of("10.0.1.22:9000"); // crashed 5s ago; its lease hasn't expired yet
        BiFunction<String, String, String> network = (address, request) -> {
            if (crashed.contains(address)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("connection refused");
            }
            return address + " answered " + request;
        };

        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: trip service calls eta-service via client-side discovery ===");
        var client = new LoadBalancedClient(registry);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            System.out.println("ETA request " + i + ": " + client.call("eta-service", "eta(trip-" + i + ")", network));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: trip service calls eta-service via client-side discovery ===
ETA request 1: 10.0.1.21:9000 answered eta(trip-1)
    10.0.1.22:9000 unreachable, trying next instance
ETA request 2: 10.0.2.23:9000 answered eta(trip-2)
ETA request 3: 10.0.1.21:9000 answered eta(trip-3)
    10.0.1.22:9000 unreachable, trying next instance
ETA request 4: 10.0.2.23:9000 answered eta(trip-4)
ETA request 5: 10.0.1.21:9000 answered eta(trip-5)

Why client-side here:

  • No extra network hop through a central load balancer.
  • The client can apply smart policies (retry next, zone preference, weighted) per call.
  • Cost: every client language needs the library. That's why meshes and Kubernetes moved this into infrastructure.

docs.title: Example 3: Zone-Aware Routing (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: A payments caller in zone-a should call ledger-service instances in its own zone for lower latency and to avoid cross-zone data transfer charges. But if zone-a drops below 2 healthy instances, the remaining one would be overloaded, so the balancer spills over to all zones.

Design:

flowchart TB C[Caller in zone-a] --> Z{>= 2 healthy in zone-a?} Z -->|yes| A[ledger-a1, ledger-a2] Z -->|no| ALL[ledger-a1, ledger-b1, ledger-c1]

Full Code:

ZoneAwareBalancer.javaZoneAwareDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.discovery.zone;

import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry;
import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry.Instance;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/**
 * Prefer instances in the caller's availability zone (lower latency, no cross-zone data charges),
 * but spill over to all zones when the local zone has too few healthy instances.
 */
public final class ZoneAwareBalancer {

    private final ServiceRegistry registry;
    private final String myZone;
    private final int minLocalInstances;
    private final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();

    public ZoneAwareBalancer(ServiceRegistry registry, String myZone, int minLocalInstances) {
        this.registry = registry;
        this.myZone = myZone;
        this.minLocalInstances = minLocalInstances;
    }

    public Instance choose(String service) {
        List<Instance> all = registry.lookup(service);
        List<Instance> local = all.stream().filter(i -> i.zone().equals(myZone)).toList(); // (1)!
        List<Instance> pool = local.size() >= minLocalInstances ? local : all; // (2)!
        if (pool.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("no instances of " + service);
        }
        return pool.get(Math.floorMod(counter.getAndIncrement(), pool.size()));
    }
}
  1. Same-zone preference: lower latency and no cross-zone traffic cost.
  2. Spill-over threshold protects a shrunken zone from being overwhelmed.
package com.handbook.microservices.discovery.zone;

import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry;
import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry.Instance;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ZoneAwareDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z");
        ServiceRegistry registry = new ServiceRegistry(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(30));
        registry.register("ledger-service", "ledger-a1", "10.1.0.11", "zone-a");
        registry.register("ledger-service", "ledger-a2", "10.1.0.12", "zone-a");
        registry.register("ledger-service", "ledger-b1", "10.2.0.11", "zone-b");
        registry.register("ledger-service", "ledger-c1", "10.3.0.11", "zone-c");

        var balancer = new ZoneAwareBalancer(registry, "zone-a", 2);

        System.out.println("=== Payments: zone-aware routing from a caller in zone-a ===");
        System.out.println("Both zone-a instances healthy -> " + picks(balancer, 4));

        registry.deregister("ledger-a2"); // zone-a loses an instance
        System.out.println("Only 1 left in zone-a (min 2) -> " + picks(balancer, 4));
    }

    private static List<String> picks(ZoneAwareBalancer balancer, int n) {
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            Instance chosen = balancer.choose("ledger-service");
            ids.add(chosen.id());
        }
        return ids;
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: zone-aware routing from a caller in zone-a ===
Both zone-a instances healthy -> [ledger-a1, ledger-a2, ledger-a1, ledger-a2]
Only 1 left in zone-a (min 2) -> [ledger-b1, ledger-c1, ledger-a1, ledger-b1]

Why zone-aware here:

  • Payments are latency-sensitive; same-zone calls are faster.
  • Zone failures are a real event in the cloud; spill-over keeps capacity.
Unit Tests: ServiceDiscoveryTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.registry.ServiceRegistry;
import com.handbook.microservices.discovery.zone.ZoneAwareBalancer;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ServiceDiscoveryTest {

    @Test
    void instanceDisappearsWhenLeaseExpires() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        var registry = new ServiceRegistry(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(30));
        registry.register("s", "a", "10.0.0.1", "z1");
        registry.register("s", "b", "10.0.0.2", "z1");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(25));
        registry.heartbeat("a");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        assertThat(registry.lookup("s")).extracting(ServiceRegistry.Instance::id).containsExactly("a");
    }

    @Test
    void zoneAwareFallsBackWhenLocalZoneTooSmall() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        var registry = new ServiceRegistry(clock, Duration.ofSeconds(30));
        registry.register("s", "a1", "x", "a");
        registry.register("s", "b1", "y", "b");
        var balancer = new ZoneAwareBalancer(registry, "a", 1);
        assertThat(balancer.choose("s").id()).isEqualTo("a1");
        assertThat(new ZoneAwareBalancer(registry, "a", 2).choose("s").id()).isIn("a1", "b1");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Spring Cloud (client-side) reference configuration:

# order-service: registers itself with Eureka
spring.application.name: order-service
eureka:
  client.service-url.defaultZone: http://eureka:8761/eureka
  instance:
    lease-renewal-interval-in-seconds: 10     # heartbeat
    lease-expiration-duration-in-seconds: 30  # lease

// cart-service: "order-service" is resolved through discovery + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer
@Bean @LoadBalanced
RestClient.Builder restClientBuilder() { return RestClient.builder(); }

String order = restClientBuilder.build()
        .get().uri("http://order-service/orders/{id}", id)
        .retrieve().body(String.class);

Kubernetes (server-side): a Service gives a stable DNS name (order-service.shop.svc.cluster.local); kube-proxy or the mesh routes to ready pods. Readiness probes play the role of heartbeats. In Kubernetes you usually don't need Eureka at all.

Option Style Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer Client-side, AP (favors availability) Consul Client- or server-side, health checks, KV store Kubernetes Services + DNS Server-side, built in Service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) Sidecar does discovery and balancing AWS Cloud Map / ALB target groups Managed

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Discovery Netflix Eureka Registry with leases and self-preservation Spring Cloud DiscoveryClient, @LoadBalanced, lb:// URIs in Gateway Kubernetes Endpoints/EndpointSlices, CoreDNS, readiness probes gRPC Name resolvers + load-balancing policies (round_robin, xDS)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Elastic scaling and self-healing routing Registry is critical infrastructure (must be HA) No hard-coded addresses Staleness window between crash and lease expiry Client-side: no extra hop, smart policies Client-side: library needed per language Server-side: simple clients Server-side: an extra hop through the balancer

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Retrying non-idempotent calls after a timeout

"Try the next instance" is safe only when the request never reached the first one (connection refused). After a timeout, the first instance may have processed the payment. Use idempotency keys (see Idempotent Consumer).

No graceful shutdown

Killing instances without deregistering (or without failing readiness first) causes a burst of errors on every deploy. Deregister, drain in-flight requests, then stop.

Health check that checks nothing

A /health that always returns 200 keeps broken instances in rotation. Check what the instance needs to serve traffic, but not shared dependencies (or one database blip removes every instance).

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
CAP choices. Eureka is AP: during partitions it keeps serving possibly stale data (self-preservation, see the coding challenge), because stale-but-mostly-right beats empty. ZooKeeper/etcd-based registries are CP: a minority partition can't serve registrations. For discovery, AP is usually the right call; clients compensate with retries.

Liveness vs. readiness. In Kubernetes, readiness controls traffic (in or out of the Service); liveness restarts the container. Confusing them causes restart storms when a dependency is slow.

Discovery in a mesh. Envoy sidecars get endpoints from the control plane (xDS), apply outlier detection (eject instances returning 5xx), zone-aware routing and retries, all without application libraries.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Registry (or platform DNS) is HA; clients cache instance lists and survive registry outages.
  • Heartbeat/lease or readiness tuned: fast enough to drop dead instances, not so fast that GC pauses cause flapping.
  • Graceful shutdown: fail readiness or deregister → drain → stop.
  • Client retries the next instance on connection errors; idempotency for others.
  • Outlier detection: eject instances with high error rates.
  • Zone-aware routing with spill-over.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"On Kubernetes I'd use built-in discovery: each service gets a Service DNS name, readiness probes control which pods get traffic, and the mesh or kube-proxy load-balances. Outside Kubernetes I'd use Consul or Eureka with self-registration and heartbeats, and client-side load balancing via Spring Cloud LoadBalancer. Either way: clients cache endpoints, retry another instance on connection failures, instances drain gracefully on shutdown, and routing prefers the same zone with spill-over."

War story: the health check that removed everyone

A payments platform's /health endpoint checked the shared Postgres cluster. A 40-second database failover made every instance of every service report unhealthy. The registry removed them all, so even endpoints that didn't need the database (static config, cached reads) went down. Recovery took 6 minutes because instances rejoined slowly. Fix: readiness checks only what's local to the instance (process up, warm caches, thread pools not exhausted). Database failures are handled with circuit breakers per request, not by removing instances. Lesson: a health check that includes shared dependencies turns a partial outage into a total one.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Client-side discovery Server-side discovery DNS Who picks the instance Caller's library Load balancer / proxy Resolver (coarse) Extra hop No Yes No Language-agnostic No Yes Yes Smart policies Yes In the LB Limited (TTL caching issues)

Related: API Gateway (routes to discovered services), Sidecar / Service Mesh, Circuit Breaker.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Register → heartbeat (lease) → lookup → pick → deregister.
  • Client-side (Eureka + LoadBalancer) vs. server-side (K8s Service, ALB).
  • Staleness window → retry next instance on connection errors.
  • Graceful shutdown; local health checks; zone-aware routing.
  • Registries are usually AP (self-preservation).

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add weighted random selection (seeded Random) to LoadBalancedClient.
  • Add outlier detection: eject an instance from selection for 30 s after 3 consecutive failures.
  • Write the Kubernetes Deployment probes and preStop hook for graceful shutdown of order-service.
