docs.title: Sharding
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Sharding splits one large dataset across several databases (shards) by a shard key, so each shard holds only part of the data and takes only part of the load. Use it when a single database can't keep up with writes or storage even after indexing, caching, read replicas and vertical scaling. Choose the shard key from your main access path, because everything else becomes harder.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: a payments ledger grows by 20 million rows a day. One PostgreSQL primary handles reads with replicas, but writes all go to one machine; it's at 85% CPU, vacuum can't keep up, and the next bigger instance doesn't exist. You need more than one primary.

Definition (Azure Architecture Center, Sharding pattern):

Divide a data store into a set of horizontal partitions or shards. Each shard has the same schema but holds its own distinct subset of the data, and runs on its own server.

Three ways to pick a shard:

Strategy How Good at Bad at Hash hash(key) % N or consistent hashing Even spread of writes Range queries; resharding with % N moves most keys Range Key ranges (A–F, dates) per shard Range scans Hot spots on sequential keys Directory / lookup A table maps key (tenant, city) → shard Moving or splitting individual tenants Directory is a dependency to cache and protect

Sharding vs partitioning vs replication: partitioning splits a table within one database (PostgreSQL declarative partitions); sharding puts partitions on different servers; replication copies the same data for availability and read scaling. Real systems combine all three.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Exam halls by roll number

A university with 30,000 students doesn't seat everyone in one hall. Roll numbers 1–5,000 go to Hall A, 5,001–10,000 to Hall B (range sharding). To find a student you only check one hall. A question like "who scored highest across all halls" needs every hall's results combined (scatter-gather).

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     C[Service] --> R{"Shard router<br/>shard = f(shard key)"}     R --> S0[(Shard 0<br/>primary + replica)]     R --> S1[(Shard 1<br/>primary + replica)]     R --> S2[(Shard 2<br/>primary + replica)]     D[(Directory / config)] -.-> R Participant Responsibility Shard key The field that decides placement (account id, customer id, tenant id, city) Router Maps a key to a shard: in the app, a library (Vitess, Citus, ShardingSphere) or the database itself Shards Independent databases with the same schema, each usually replicated Directory (optional) Lookup table for directory-based schemes; cached aggressively Scatter-gather layer Runs queries without the shard key on all shards and merges results

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Bigger instance → bigger instance → largest instance (still 85% CPU)
Add read replicas → reads fine, writes still on one primary
Archive old rows → buys months, not years
  • Vertical scaling has a hard ceiling and a steep price curve.
  • Replicas don't help write throughput.
  • One huge database means huge backups, slow migrations and a single blast radius.

docs.title: Example 1: Hash-Sharded Ledger (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A neobank has 40 million accounts and peaks at 15,000 ledger writes per second. Accounts are hash-sharded across databases by account id. Transfers between accounts on the same shard are a normal local transaction. Transfers that cross shards can't use one ACID transaction, so they go through a saga (debit, then credit, with compensation).

Design:

flowchart LR T["transfer(ACC-1001 → ACC-1004)"] --> R{"same shard?"} R -- yes --> L["one local transaction on shard 1"] R -- no --> S["Transfer saga: debit on shard A,<br/>credit on shard B, compensate on failure"]

Full Code:

ShardedLedger.javaLedgerShardingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.sharding.banking;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Db;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Hash sharding: each account lives in exactly one of N databases, chosen from its id. */
public final class ShardedLedger {

    private final List<DataSource> shards = new ArrayList<>();

    public ShardedLedger(int shardCount) {
        for (int i = 0; i < shardCount; i++) {
            shards.add(Db.inMemory("ledger_shard" + i,
                    "CREATE TABLE account (id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, balance_paise BIGINT CHECK (balance_paise >= 0))"));
        }
    }

    public int shardOf(String accountId) { // (1)!
        return Math.floorMod(accountId.hashCode(), shards.size());
    }

    public void open(String accountId, long paise) {
        exec(shards.get(shardOf(accountId)), c -> update(c, "INSERT INTO account VALUES (?, ?)", accountId, paise));
    }

    public long balance(String accountId) {
        try (Connection c = shards.get(shardOf(accountId)).getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT balance_paise FROM account WHERE id = ?")) {
            ps.setString(1, accountId);
            ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
            rs.next();
            return rs.getLong(1);
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    /** Same shard: one local ACID transaction. Different shards: refuse, a saga is needed. */
    public String transfer(String from, String to, long paise) {
        if (shardOf(from) != shardOf(to)) { // (2)!
            return "cross-shard (" + shardOf(from) + "->" + shardOf(to) + "): start a transfer saga instead";
        }
        exec(shards.get(shardOf(from)), c -> {
            update(c, "UPDATE account SET balance_paise = balance_paise - ? WHERE id = ?", paise, from);
            update(c, "UPDATE account SET balance_paise = balance_paise + ? WHERE id = ?", paise, to);
        });
        return "local transaction on shard " + shardOf(from);
    }

    private interface Work { void run(Connection c) throws SQLException; }

    private static void exec(DataSource ds, Work work) {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            try {
                work.run(c);
                c.commit();
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                c.rollback();
                throw new IllegalStateException(e);
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    private static void update(Connection c, String sql, Object... args) throws SQLException {
        try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) {
                ps.setObject(i + 1, args[i]);
            }
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
}
  1. Routing is a pure function of the shard key. % N is simplest but moves most keys when N changes; production systems use consistent hashing or many fixed virtual shards (e.g. 1,024 logical shards mapped onto 8 servers).
  2. The router knows when an operation spans shards and refuses to pretend it's atomic.
package com.handbook.microservices.sharding.banking;

public class LedgerShardingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Accounts Hash-Sharded Across 3 Databases ===");
        ShardedLedger ledger = new ShardedLedger(3);
        String[] accounts = {"ACC-1001", "ACC-1002", "ACC-1003", "ACC-1004", "ACC-1007"};
        for (String a : accounts) {
            ledger.open(a, 100_000);
            System.out.println(a + " -> shard " + ledger.shardOf(a));
        }
        System.out.println("ACC-1001 -> ACC-1004: " + ledger.transfer("ACC-1001", "ACC-1004", 25_000));
        System.out.println("  balances now " + ledger.balance("ACC-1001") + " / " + ledger.balance("ACC-1004"));
        System.out.println("ACC-1001 -> ACC-1002: " + ledger.transfer("ACC-1001", "ACC-1002", 10_000));
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Accounts Hash-Sharded Across 3 Databases ===
ACC-1001 -> shard 1
ACC-1002 -> shard 2
ACC-1003 -> shard 0
ACC-1004 -> shard 1
ACC-1007 -> shard 1
ACC-1001 -> ACC-1004: local transaction on shard 1
  balances now 75000 / 125000
ACC-1001 -> ACC-1002: cross-shard (1->2): start a transfer saga instead

Why hash sharding here:

  • Writes spread evenly; each shard takes about 1/N of the load.
  • Each account's rows live together, so single-account operations stay simple.
  • Cross-shard operations are explicit and handled with sagas, not hidden distributed locks.

docs.title: Example 2: City Shards and a Hot-City Split (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: A ride-hailing platform keeps driver locations and trip state per city, because matching only ever looks within one city. Bengaluru on a Friday evening generates 6× the load of the next city. A directory maps each city to a shard, and a hot city can be split by zone range without touching anyone else.

Design:

flowchart LR D[(Directory)] -->|"bengaluru zones 0-99"| S1[shard-south-1] D -->|"bengaluru zones 100+"| S3[shard-south-3] D -->|chennai, mysuru| S2[shard-south-2] D -->|delhi| N1[shard-north-1]

Full Code:

GeoShardDirectory.javaGeoShardingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.sharding.geo;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.NavigableMap;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** Directory-based sharding: a lookup table maps city (and, for hot cities, a zone range) to a shard. */
public final class GeoShardDirectory {

    private final Map<String, NavigableMap<Integer, String>> directory = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // city -> (zoneFrom -> shard)

    public void assign(String city, String shard) {
        directory.put(city, new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0, shard)));
    }

    /** Split a hot city: zones >= fromZone move to a new shard. Only that city's mapping changes. */
    public void split(String city, int fromZone, String newShard) { // (1)!
        directory.get(city).put(fromZone, newShard);
    }

    public String route(String city, int zone) {
        NavigableMap<Integer, String> ranges = directory.get(city);
        if (ranges == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("no shard for " + city);
        }
        return ranges.floorEntry(zone).getValue(); // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Splitting changes one entry in the directory. With hash % N, adding a shard would move every city.
  2. floorEntry finds the range a zone falls into, like range sharding within a city.
package com.handbook.microservices.sharding.geo;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class GeoShardingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: City-Based Shards and Splitting a Hot City ===");
        GeoShardDirectory dir = new GeoShardDirectory();
        dir.assign("bengaluru", "shard-south-1");
        dir.assign("chennai", "shard-south-2");
        dir.assign("mysuru", "shard-south-2");
        dir.assign("delhi", "shard-north-1");

        System.out.println("Bengaluru zone 12 -> " + dir.route("bengaluru", 12) + ", zone 140 -> " + dir.route("bengaluru", 140));
        Map<String, Integer> load = new TreeMap<>();
        for (int zone = 0; zone < 200; zone++) {
            load.merge(dir.route("bengaluru", zone), 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        System.out.println("Before split, Bengaluru's 200 zones: " + load);

        dir.split("bengaluru", 100, "shard-south-3"); // Friday-evening surge: move zones 100+ to a new shard
        load.clear();
        for (int zone = 0; zone < 200; zone++) {
            load.merge(dir.route("bengaluru", zone), 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        System.out.println("After split,  Bengaluru's 200 zones: " + load);
        System.out.println("Chennai and Delhi routing unchanged: " + dir.route("chennai", 5) + ", " + dir.route("delhi", 5));
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: City-Based Shards and Splitting a Hot City ===
Bengaluru zone 12 -> shard-south-1, zone 140 -> shard-south-1
Before split, Bengaluru's 200 zones: {shard-south-1=200}
After split,  Bengaluru's 200 zones: {shard-south-1=100, shard-south-3=100}
Chennai and Delhi routing unchanged: shard-south-2, shard-north-1

Why directory sharding here:

  • The access pattern is naturally per city, so queries hit one shard.
  • Uneven tenants (Bengaluru vs Mysuru) need individual placement, not a uniform hash.
  • Data can be placed near users (data residency, latency).

docs.title: Example 3: Scatter-Gather for a Cross-Shard Report (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A grocery platform shards orders by customer id, so "my orders" hits one shard. But the merchandising dashboard asks "top-selling SKUs today", which has no shard key and must query every shard and merge. A common bug is merging each shard's local top-N, which can miss the real winner.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Dash as Dashboard participant G as Scatter-gather participant S0 as orders-0 participant S1 as orders-1 participant S2 as orders-2 Dash->>G: top 2 SKUs today par in parallel G->>S0: totals per SKU G->>S1: totals per SKU G->>S2: totals per SKU end G->>G: merge totals, then take top 2 G-->>Dash: EGGS 133, ATTA 112

Full Code:

ScatterGather.javaScatterGatherDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;

/** A query without the shard key must ask EVERY shard and merge the partial results. */
public final class ScatterGather {

    public record SkuSales(String sku, long units) { }

    /** One shard's local data: orders of the customers that hash to it. */
    public record Shard(String name, List<SkuSales> orderLines) {
        List<SkuSales> topN(int n) { // (1)!
            Map<String, Long> totals = new HashMap<>();
            orderLines.forEach(l -> totals.merge(l.sku(), l.units(), Long::sum));
            return totals.entrySet().stream().map(e -> new SkuSales(e.getKey(), e.getValue()))
                    .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(SkuSales::units).reversed().thenComparing(SkuSales::sku))
                    .limit(n).toList();
        }

        Map<String, Long> totals() {
            Map<String, Long> totals = new HashMap<>();
            orderLines.forEach(l -> totals.merge(l.sku(), l.units(), Long::sum));
            return totals;
        }
    }

    public static List<SkuSales> globalTopN(List<Shard> shards, int n, ExecutorService pool) {
        List<CompletableFuture<Map<String, Long>>> partials = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Shard s : shards) {
            partials.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(s::totals, pool)); // (2)!
        }
        Map<String, Long> merged = new HashMap<>();
        partials.forEach(f -> f.join().forEach((sku, units) -> merged.merge(sku, units, Long::sum))); // (3)!
        return merged.entrySet().stream().map(e -> new SkuSales(e.getKey(), e.getValue()))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(SkuSales::units).reversed().thenComparing(SkuSales::sku))
                .limit(n).toList();
    }

    /** Wrong shortcut: merging each shard's local top-N can miss the true global top-N. */
    public static List<SkuSales> mergeOfLocalTopN(List<Shard> shards, int n) {
        Map<String, Long> merged = new HashMap<>();
        shards.forEach(s -> s.topN(n).forEach(x -> merged.merge(x.sku(), x.units(), Long::sum)));
        return merged.entrySet().stream().map(e -> new SkuSales(e.getKey(), e.getValue()))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(SkuSales::units).reversed().thenComparing(SkuSales::sku))
                .limit(n).toList();
    }
}
  1. Each shard can compute a local aggregate cheaply...
  2. ...queried in parallel, so latency is the slowest shard, not the sum.
  3. Merge complete partial aggregates, then rank. Ranking before merging is the classic bug.
package com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter;

import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter.ScatterGather.Shard;
import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter.ScatterGather.SkuSales;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class ScatterGatherDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: 'Top 2 SKUs Today' Across Customer-Sharded Order Databases ===");
        List<Shard> shards = List.of(
                new Shard("orders-0", List.of(new SkuSales("MILK", 50), new SkuSales("BREAD", 40), new SkuSales("EGGS", 39))),
                new Shard("orders-1", List.of(new SkuSales("ATTA", 60), new SkuSales("MILK", 45), new SkuSales("EGGS", 44))),
                new Shard("orders-2", List.of(new SkuSales("BREAD", 55), new SkuSales("ATTA", 52), new SkuSales("EGGS", 50))));
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            System.out.println("Scatter-gather of full totals : " + ScatterGather.globalTopN(shards, 2, pool));
        }
        System.out.println("Merging each shard's top 2    : " + ScatterGather.mergeOfLocalTopN(shards, 2)
                + "  <- EGGS (133 units, the real #1) missed: never in a local top 2");
        System.out.println("A query with the shard key (one customer's orders) would touch exactly 1 of 3 shards.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: 'Top 2 SKUs Today' Across Customer-Sharded Order Databases ===
Scatter-gather of full totals : [SkuSales[sku=EGGS, units=133], SkuSales[sku=ATTA, units=112]]
Merging each shard's top 2    : [SkuSales[sku=ATTA, units=112], SkuSales[sku=BREAD, units=95]]  <- EGGS (133 units, the real #1) missed: never in a local top 2
A query with the shard key (one customer's orders) would touch exactly 1 of 3 shards.

Why scatter-gather here:

  • Some queries legitimately span all data; parallel fan-out keeps them possible.
  • It's expensive (N queries, tail latency of the slowest shard), so frequent ones should move to a materialized view or analytics store.
  • Correct merging requires mergeable aggregates (sums, counts), not ranks.
Unit Tests: ShardingTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.banking.ShardedLedger;
import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.geo.GeoShardDirectory;
import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter.ScatterGather;
import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter.ScatterGather.Shard;
import com.handbook.microservices.sharding.scatter.ScatterGather.SkuSales;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ShardingTest {

    @Test
    void routingIsStableAndLocalTransfersAreAtomic() {
        ShardedLedger l = new ShardedLedger(3);
        assertThat(l.shardOf("ACC-1")).isEqualTo(l.shardOf("ACC-1"));
        l.open("ACC-1001", 100);
        l.open("ACC-1004", 0);
        assertThat(l.shardOf("ACC-1001")).isEqualTo(l.shardOf("ACC-1004"));
        l.transfer("ACC-1001", "ACC-1004", 40);
        assertThat(l.balance("ACC-1001") + l.balance("ACC-1004")).isEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void splittingAHotCityMovesOnlyThatCity() {
        GeoShardDirectory d = new GeoShardDirectory();
        d.assign("a", "s1");
        d.assign("b", "s1");
        d.split("a", 50, "s2");
        assertThat(d.route("a", 49)).isEqualTo("s1");
        assertThat(d.route("a", 50)).isEqualTo("s2");
        assertThat(d.route("b", 99)).isEqualTo("s1");
    }

    @Test
    void scatterGatherFindsTheTrueGlobalTop() {
        List<Shard> shards = List.of(new Shard("0", List.of(new SkuSales("A", 10), new SkuSales("C", 9))),
                new Shard("1", List.of(new SkuSales("B", 10), new SkuSales("C", 9))));
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            assertThat(ScatterGather.globalTopN(shards, 1, pool)).containsExactly(new SkuSales("C", 18));
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text: Variation Notes Logical (virtual) shards 1,024 logical shards mapped to a few physical servers; rebalance by moving logical shards, never rehashing keys Consistent hashing Adding a node moves ~1/N of keys (LLD: consistent hashing) Distributed SQL CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, Google Spanner, TiDB: automatic range sharding and cross-shard transactions Sharded PostgreSQL Citus (distributed tables, co-location by tenant), Vitess for MySQL App-level routing in Spring AbstractRoutingDataSource picks a DataSource per request from a shard key in context NoSQL DynamoDB/Cassandra partition keys: sharding is built in, so the key design rules still apply

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Sharding Spring AbstractRoutingDataSource, Apache ShardingSphere-JDBC (driver-level sharding) PostgreSQL ecosystem Citus create_distributed_table('orders', 'customer_id'); native partitioning on each shard MySQL Vitess (YouTube, Slack), ProxySQL Kafka Topic partitions: hash(key) % partitions: same rules, same hot-partition problem Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Index shards; routing by _routing key DynamoDB / Cassandra Partition key = shard key; avoid hot partitions with high-cardinality keys

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Write throughput and storage scale horizontally Cross-shard queries need scatter-gather Smaller databases: faster backups, migrations, vacuum Cross-shard transactions need sagas or distributed SQL Failure of one shard affects only part of the users Resharding is hard and risky Data can live near users (residency, latency) Operational overhead: N databases to monitor, upgrade, back up

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Sharding too early

Most services never need it. Exhaust indexing, query fixes, caching, read replicas, partitioning and a bigger instance first. Sharding is a one-way door.

Monotonic shard keys

Range-sharding on timestamps or auto-increment ids sends every new write to the last shard (coding challenge). Hash them, or prefix with a high-cardinality component.

hash % N with no plan for N+1

Adding a shard moves ~(N)/(N+1) of keys. Use logical shards or consistent hashing from day one.

Shard key that doesn't match the main query

If 80% of queries filter by store_id but you shard by customer_id, 80% of queries become scatter-gather.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Choosing the key. High cardinality, even distribution, present in nearly every query, and stable (never changes for a row). Co-locate data that's queried or updated together under the same key (Citus "co-location": orders, order lines and payments all keyed by customer_id).

Resharding without downtime. Dual-write or CDC-copy a logical shard to its new home, verify, switch the directory entry, then drain and delete. Logical shards make each move small and reversible. Rehearse it before you need it.

Hot keys. A celebrity seller or a viral product can overload one shard regardless of strategy. Split the key (product#1..#8 for counters), cache reads, queue writes, or give that tenant a dedicated shard via the directory.

War story: the last shard that took every write

An e-commerce team range-sharded orders by created_at month, reasoning that old months could be archived easily. Every new order went to the current month's shard; at the Diwali sale it hit 100% CPU while the other 11 shards idled at 3%. Checkout errors peaked at 30% for two hours. Fix: re-shard by hashed customer_id into 256 logical shards on 8 servers; time-based archiving moved to PostgreSQL partitioning inside each shard. Lesson: shard keys must spread writes, and time is the worst key for that.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Sharding Read Replicas Partitioning (in one DB) Database per Service Splits Rows across servers Nothing (copies) Rows across tables in one server Data by business capability Scales Writes + storage Reads Maintenance, pruning Teams and models Cross-part queries Scatter-gather N/A Transparent API composition / CQRS

Related: Database per Service, CQRS, Saga for cross-shard writes, Materialized View for cross-shard reads.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Split rows across servers by a shard key; scales writes and storage.
  • Strategies: hash (even), range (scans, hotspots), directory (flexible).
  • Key: high cardinality, in most queries, stable; co-locate related data.
  • Cross-shard: scatter-gather reads, sagas for writes.
  • Use logical shards or consistent hashing; shard last, not first.
int shard = Math.floorMod(hash(customerId), LOGICAL_SHARDS);   // then logical → physical via directory

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Replace % N in ShardedLedger with 64 logical shards mapped onto 3 physical databases.
  • Add a time-ordered unique id generator (timestamp + shard + sequence).
  • Add a timeout to ScatterGather that returns partial results with a "partial" flag.

docs.title: Sidecar & Service Mesh
docs.text:
🔴 Advanced Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A sidecar is a helper process deployed next to each service instance (same pod), adding capabilities such as mTLS, retries, metrics and tracing without changing the service's code. A service mesh is a fleet of sidecar proxies (the data plane) configured centrally by a control plane. Network concerns move out of every application and library into shared infrastructure.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: 80 services in Java, Go, Node and one PHP legacy app. Each needs encryption between services (mTLS), "who may call whom" rules, retries, timeouts, canary routing, metrics and tracing. Implementing these in every language's libraries means 4× the work, inconsistent behaviour and painful upgrades across all services. And security teams want guarantees that don't depend on every team getting it right.

Definitions:

Sidecar (Azure Architecture Center): Deploy components of an application into a separate process or container to provide isolation and encapsulation.

Service mesh: A dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication, made of proxies deployed alongside services (data plane) and a control plane that configures them.

Plane What it does Examples Data plane Proxies intercept all traffic: mTLS, routing, retries, metrics Envoy, linkerd2-proxy, ztunnel Control plane Distributes config, certificates, service discovery Istiod, Linkerd control plane, Consul

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A motorcycle sidecar, or a diplomat's interpreter

The rider (your service) focuses on driving. The sidecar carries the extra equipment. A diplomat doesn't learn every language; an interpreter next to them handles communication, checks credentials at the door, and keeps a log, and every diplomat gets one from the same agency (the control plane) with the same rules.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph PodA["Pod: checkout"]       A[checkout app] <--> PA[Envoy sidecar]     end     subgraph PodB["Pod: payment"]       PB[Envoy sidecar] <--> B[payment app]     end     PA <-->|mTLS, retries, metrics| PB     CP[Control plane<br/>certs, routes, policies] -.-> PA     CP -.-> PB Participant Responsibility Application container Business logic only; talks plain HTTP to localhost Sidecar proxy Intercepts inbound/outbound traffic (iptables); enforces policy; emits telemetry Control plane Issues workload identities/certificates (SPIFFE), pushes routing and authorization config (xDS)

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Java services:    Resilience4j + Spring Security mTLS config + Micrometer + OpenTelemetry agent
Go services:      different retry library, hand-rolled TLS, Prometheus client
Node services:    yet another set; PHP legacy: nothing at all
→ inconsistent retries, some traffic unencrypted, metrics with different names,
  and upgrading the TLS library means 80 pull requests.

docs.title: Example 1: Zero-Trust mTLS + Authorization (Grocery payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: Only checkout may create charges on payment-service; reporting may read reports but not charge; a compromised pod without a mesh certificate is rejected. Each sidecar presents its workload's SPIFFE identity outbound and checks the caller's identity inbound. The payment app contains no security code.

Design:

sequenceDiagram participant C as checkout app participant CS as checkout sidecar participant PS as payment sidecar participant P as payment app C->>CS: POST /charges (plain HTTP to localhost) CS->>PS: mTLS, identity spiffe://.../sa/checkout PS->>PS: policy: /charges allows checkout ✔ PS->>P: POST /charges

Full Code:

SidecarProxy.javaZeroTrustDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.mtls;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Runs next to the app (same pod) and intercepts all its traffic. Inbound, it checks the caller's
 * workload identity (from the mTLS certificate, simulated here by a header the mesh sets) against an
 * authorization policy. The app itself contains no security code.
 */
public final class SidecarProxy {

    private final String myIdentity;
    private final Map<String, Set<String>> allowedCallersByPath; // path prefix → SPIFFE IDs
    private final Function<Request, Response> app;

    public SidecarProxy(String myIdentity, Map<String, Set<String>> allowedCallersByPath,
                        Function<Request, Response> app) {
        this.myIdentity = myIdentity;
        this.allowedCallersByPath = allowedCallersByPath;
        this.app = app;
    }

    public Response inbound(Request request) {
        String peer = request.header("x-peer-spiffe-id"); // (1)!
        if (peer == null) {
            return Response.of(403, "rejected: no mTLS client certificate"); // (2)!
        }
        boolean allowed = allowedCallersByPath.entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> request.path().startsWith(e.getKey()))
                .anyMatch(e -> e.getValue().contains(peer)); // (3)!
        if (!allowed) {
            return Response.of(403, "RBAC: " + shortName(peer) + " may not call " + request.path());
        }
        return app.apply(request);
    }

    /** Outbound: the sidecar presents this workload's identity to the next hop. */
    public Request outbound(Request request) {
        return request.withHeader("x-peer-spiffe-id", myIdentity);
    }

    private static String shortName(String spiffeId) {
        return spiffeId.substring(spiffeId.lastIndexOf('/') + 1);
    }
}
  1. In a real mesh, identity comes from the peer's mTLS certificate (issued and rotated by the control plane), not from a header; the header stands in for the TLS handshake here.
  2. No certificate means the caller is outside the mesh: reject.
  3. Authorization policy per path, like Istio's AuthorizationPolicy.
package com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.mtls;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

public class ZeroTrustDemo {

    static final String CHECKOUT = "spiffe://shop.local/ns/prod/sa/checkout";
    static final String REPORTING = "spiffe://shop.local/ns/prod/sa/reporting";
    static final String PAYMENT = "spiffe://shop.local/ns/prod/sa/payment";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // The payment app only knows business logic.
        var paymentSidecar = new SidecarProxy(PAYMENT, Map.of(
                "/charges", Set.of(CHECKOUT),
                "/reports", Set.of(REPORTING, CHECKOUT)),
                r -> Response.of(200, "payment-app handled " + r.method() + " " + r.path()));

        var checkoutSidecar = new SidecarProxy(CHECKOUT, Map.of(), r -> Response.of(200, "checkout"));
        var reportingSidecar = new SidecarProxy(REPORTING, Map.of(), r -> Response.of(200, "reporting"));

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: zero-trust calls to payment-service through sidecars ===");
        Request charge = new Request("POST", "/charges", Map.of(), "{order: ORD-1}");
        System.out.println("checkout  -> POST /charges : " + paymentSidecar.inbound(checkoutSidecar.outbound(charge)));
        System.out.println("reporting -> POST /charges : " + paymentSidecar.inbound(reportingSidecar.outbound(charge)));
        System.out.println("reporting -> GET /reports  : "
                + paymentSidecar.inbound(reportingSidecar.outbound(Request.get("/reports/daily", Map.of()))));
        System.out.println("attacker pod (no cert)     : " + paymentSidecar.inbound(charge));
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: zero-trust calls to payment-service through sidecars ===
checkout  -> POST /charges : 200 payment-app handled POST /charges
reporting -> POST /charges : 403 RBAC: reporting may not call /charges
reporting -> GET /reports  : 200 payment-app handled GET /reports/daily
attacker pod (no cert)     : 403 rejected: no mTLS client certificate

Why a sidecar here:

  • Zero trust: being inside the network isn't enough; every call is authenticated and authorized.
  • Security rules are enforced uniformly, in every language, and audited centrally.
  • Certificates rotate automatically (hours, not years).

docs.title: Example 2: Canary Traffic Split + Retries (Streaming)
docs.text:
Scenario: The recommendations team ships v2. The mesh routes 10% of calls to v2, then 50%. v2 fails about 5% of requests; the client sidecar retries once, and most failures disappear (partly by retrying on v1). The calling app just calls "recommendations"; weights and retries are configuration.

Full Code:

TrafficSplitSidecar.javaTrafficSplitDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.traffic;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * The client-side sidecar (Envoy) applies routing rules pushed by the mesh control plane:
 * weighted subsets for canaries, and retries for failed calls. The calling app just calls "recommendations".
 */
public final class TrafficSplitSidecar {

    private final TreeMap<Integer, String> cumulativeWeights = new TreeMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Function<String, String>> subsets;
    private final int retries;
    private final Random random;
    private int total;

    public TrafficSplitSidecar(Map<String, Integer> weights, Map<String, Function<String, String>> subsets,
                               int retries, Random random) {
        weights.forEach((subset, w) -> {
            total += w;
            cumulativeWeights.put(total, subset); // (1)!
        });
        this.subsets = subsets;
        this.retries = retries;
        this.random = random;
    }

    public String call(String request) {
        RuntimeException last = null;
        for (int attempt = 0; attempt <= retries; attempt++) { // (2)!
            String subset = cumulativeWeights.higherEntry(random.nextInt(total)).getValue();
            try {
                return subsets.get(subset).apply(request);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                last = e;
            }
        }
        throw last;
    }
}
  1. Weighted subsets, as in Istio VirtualService route weights. Seeded random keeps the demo reproducible.
  2. Retries in the proxy. Configure them for idempotent requests only, with a retry budget.
package com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.traffic;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class TrafficSplitDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Function<String, String>> subsets = Map.of(
                "v1", req -> "v1",
                "v2", req -> {
                    if (req.hashCode() % 20 == 0) {
                        throw new IllegalStateException("v2 503");
                    }
                    return "v2";
                });

        System.out.println("=== Streaming: canary of recommendations v2 via mesh routing rules ===");
        for (int v2Weight : new int[] {10, 50}) {
            Map<String, Integer> weights = new LinkedHashMap<>();
            weights.put("v1", 100 - v2Weight);
            weights.put("v2", v2Weight);
            var sidecar = new TrafficSplitSidecar(weights, subsets, 1, new Random(42));
            Map<String, Integer> served = new TreeMap<>();
            int failed = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                try {
                    served.merge(sidecar.call("profile-" + i), 1, Integer::sum);
                } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                    failed++;
                }
            }
            System.out.println("weights v1=" + (100 - v2Weight) + "/v2=" + v2Weight + " -> served " + served
                    + ", failed after retry: " + failed);
        }
        System.out.println("The app code never changed: weights and retries are mesh configuration.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: canary of recommendations v2 via mesh routing rules ===
weights v1=90/v2=10 -> served {v1=9035, v2=959}, failed after retry: 6
weights v1=50/v2=50 -> served {v1=5046, v2=4825}, failed after retry: 129
The app code never changed: weights and retries are mesh configuration.

Why the mesh here:

  • Progressive delivery without touching application code or the client.
  • Weights change in seconds; combined with metrics, tools like Flagger/Argo Rollouts automate promotion.

docs.title: Example 3: Golden Signals for a Legacy App (Ride-hailing)
docs.text:
Scenario: The fare service is an old app with no metrics and no tracing. Its sidecar records traffic, errors and latency per route (normalizing IDs so /fares/TRIP-11 and /fares/TRIP-12 are one route), and starts a trace for requests without one. Dashboards and alerts work on day one, with zero code changes.

Full Code:

TelemetrySidecar.javaTelemetryDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.telemetry;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Records golden-signal metrics (traffic, errors, latency) for every request, for any app in any
 * language, without changing the app. Also starts a trace if the request has none.
 */
public final class TelemetrySidecar {

    private record Stats(int count, int errors, long totalMillis, long maxMillis) {
    }

    private final Function<Request, Response> app;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Map<String, Stats> byRoute = new TreeMap<>();
    private int nextTrace = 1;

    public TelemetrySidecar(Function<Request, Response> app, Clock clock) {
        this.app = app;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public Response handle(Request request) {
        Request traced = request.header("traceparent") != null ? request // (1)!
                : request.withHeader("traceparent", String.format("00-%032x-%016x-01", nextTrace, nextTrace++));
        long start = clock.millis();
        Response response = app.apply(traced);
        long took = clock.millis() - start;
        String route = request.method() + " " + request.path().replaceAll("/[A-Z]+-\\d+", "/{id}"); // (2)!
        byRoute.merge(route, new Stats(1, response.status() >= 500 ? 1 : 0, took, took),
                (a, b) -> new Stats(a.count() + 1, a.errors() + b.errors(), a.totalMillis() + b.totalMillis(),
                        Math.max(a.maxMillis(), b.maxMillis())));
        return response;
    }

    public void printMetrics() {
        byRoute.forEach((route, s) -> System.out.printf("  %-22s requests=%d errors=%d avg=%dms max=%dms%n",
                route, s.count(), s.errors(), s.totalMillis() / s.count(), s.maxMillis()));
    }
}
  1. Start a trace if the caller didn't send one; otherwise continue it (see Distributed Tracing).
  2. Normalize IDs out of paths; otherwise each trip ID becomes its own metric series (cardinality explosion).
package com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.telemetry;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.Map;

public class TelemetryDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-10-13T08:00:00Z");
        // A legacy fare service (imagine it's written in PHP): no metrics, no tracing.
        var sidecar = new TelemetrySidecar(request -> {
            boolean surge = request.path().contains("surge");
            clock.advanceMillis(surge ? 180 : 40);
            if (request.path().endsWith("TRIP-13")) {
                return Response.of(500, "fare table missing");
            }
            return Response.of(200, "fare ok, trace-id ..." + request.header("traceparent").substring(27, 35));
        }, clock);

        System.out.println("=== Ride-hailing: golden signals from a sidecar, zero app changes ===");
        for (String trip : new String[] {"TRIP-11", "TRIP-12", "TRIP-13"}) {
            System.out.println("GET /fares/" + trip + " -> " + sidecar.handle(Request.get("/fares/" + trip, Map.of())));
        }
        System.out.println("GET /fares/surge/TRIP-14 -> " + sidecar.handle(Request.get("/fares/surge/TRIP-14", Map.of())));
        System.out.println("Metrics exported to Prometheus:");
        sidecar.printMetrics();
    }
}

Output:

=== Ride-hailing: golden signals from a sidecar, zero app changes ===
GET /fares/TRIP-11 -> 200 fare ok, trace-id ...00000001
GET /fares/TRIP-12 -> 200 fare ok, trace-id ...00000002
GET /fares/TRIP-13 -> 500 fare table missing
GET /fares/surge/TRIP-14 -> 200 fare ok, trace-id ...00000004
Metrics exported to Prometheus:
  GET /fares/surge/{id}  requests=1 errors=0 avg=180ms max=180ms
  GET /fares/{id}        requests=3 errors=1 avg=40ms max=40ms

Why a sidecar here:

  • Uniform observability across all languages, including apps nobody wants to modify.
  • Same metric names and labels everywhere, so dashboards and SLOs are standard.
Unit Tests: SidecarTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.mtls.SidecarProxy;
import com.handbook.microservices.sidecar.outlier.OutlierDetector;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.FakeClock;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SidecarTest {

    @Test
    void onlyAllowedIdentitiesReachTheApp() {
        var sidecar = new SidecarProxy("me", Map.of("/x", Set.of("good")), r -> Response.of(200, "ok"));
        assertThat(sidecar.inbound(Request.get("/x", Map.of("x-peer-spiffe-id", "good"))).status()).isEqualTo(200);
        assertThat(sidecar.inbound(Request.get("/x", Map.of("x-peer-spiffe-id", "evil"))).status()).isEqualTo(403);
        assertThat(sidecar.inbound(Request.get("/x", Map.of())).status()).isEqualTo(403);
    }

    @Test
    void outlierIsEjectedThenReturns() {
        FakeClock clock = FakeClock.at("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z");
        var detector = new OutlierDetector(List.of("a", "b"), 2, Duration.ofSeconds(10), 50, clock);
        detector.record("a", 500);
        detector.record("a", 500);
        assertThat(detector.healthyHosts()).containsExactly("b");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
        assertThat(detector.healthyHosts()).containsExactly("a", "b");
    }
}

---

    - route:
        - { destination: { host: recommendations, subset: v1 }, weight: 90 }
        - { destination: { host: recommendations, subset: v2 }, weight: 10 }
      retries: { attempts: 1, perTryTimeout: 300ms, retryOn: "5xx,reset,connect-failure" }
Variation Notes Sidecar mesh (Istio classic, Linkerd) One proxy per pod; most features; per-pod resource cost Sidecar-less / ambient (Istio ambient, Cilium) Per-node L4 proxy (ztunnel) + optional L7 waypoint proxies; lower overhead Library approach (Resilience4j, gRPC xDS, Spring Cloud) No extra hop; per-language Other sidecars Log shippers (Fluent Bit), secret fetchers (Vault Agent), Dapr runtime, config reloaders Ambassador A sidecar specialized for outbound calls of a legacy app (retries, routing)

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Sidecar / mesh Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect, Kuma Service meshes Envoy The most common data-plane proxy (xDS API) Dapr Sidecar runtime providing pub/sub, state, bindings via HTTP/gRPC Kubernetes Native sidecar containers (restartPolicy: Always init containers, stable since 1.33) SPIFFE/SPIRE Workload identity used by meshes

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Language-agnostic cross-cutting features Operational complexity: a distributed system to run the distributed system Uniform mTLS, policy, telemetry Extra latency (two proxy hops per call, often ~1 ms or less) and resources per pod Changes via config, not redeploys Debugging gets harder (is it the app or the proxy?) Gradual delivery and traffic control Version upgrades of the mesh are significant projects

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Retries in the app AND the mesh

Resilience4j retries 3×, the sidecar retries 3× → 9 attempts per call, and more across hops. Decide which layer owns retries.

Adopting a mesh for 5 services

The mesh's operational cost only pays off at scale or with strict security requirements. Libraries or the platform's built-ins may be enough.

Treating mTLS as full authorization

mTLS proves which workload is calling, not which user. User-level authorization (JWT claims) still belongs in the app.

Startup/shutdown ordering

The app starts before its sidecar is ready (calls fail), or the sidecar exits before the app drains. Use native sidecar containers or holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts, and graceful drain settings.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Mesh vs. libraries. A homogeneous Spring estate with good platform libraries may not need a mesh; a polyglot estate with zero-trust requirements usually benefits. Many orgs adopt mTLS + telemetry from the mesh and keep business-aware resilience (fallbacks) in the app.

North-south vs. east-west. The API gateway handles client traffic; the mesh handles service-to-service traffic. Meshes often provide an ingress gateway too.

Cost and performance. Sidecars consume CPU/memory per pod (sizable at thousands of pods). Ambient/sidecar-less modes reduce this; measure p99 latency overhead under real load.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Clear reason (zero trust, polyglot, traffic management) and an owning platform team.
  • STRICT mTLS with automatic certificate rotation; default-deny authorization policies.
  • One layer owns retries/timeouts; budgets configured.
  • Telemetry: standard metrics, tracing propagation (apps still forward headers!), access logs.
  • Sidecar lifecycle (startup/drain) handled; resource requests sized.
  • Mesh upgrade runbooks and canaries for mesh config changes.

docs.title: Explain it in 2 minutes (system design round)
docs.text:
"Service-to-service traffic goes through a mesh (Istio or Linkerd). Each pod's proxy gets a SPIFFE identity from the control plane, so all traffic is mutually authenticated and encrypted, and authorization policies say which services may call which endpoints, deny by default. The mesh also gives uniform metrics and tracing, timeouts, limited retries, outlier detection, and weighted routing for canaries. Business-aware fallbacks stay in the apps. If sidecar overhead becomes an issue, ambient mode moves L4 to per-node proxies."

War story: the retry storm in the mesh

An e-commerce company enabled mesh retries (3 attempts on 5xx) globally while several Java services still had Resilience4j retries (3 attempts). During a database slowdown, one user click produced up to 9 attempts at each of 3 hops. The database load multiplied, and a 2-minute slowdown became a 40-minute outage. Fix: retries removed from the apps; mesh retries limited to idempotent routes with a retry budget of 20%; per-try timeouts aligned to the request deadline. Lesson: a mesh adds behaviour between your services. Audit how it combines with what's already in your code.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text:
Sidecar / Mesh API Gateway Library (Resilience4j) Ambassador Traffic East-west North-south In-process Outbound of one app Language-agnostic ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ Business-aware fallback ❌ Limited ✅ ❌

See Circuit Breaker, Service Discovery and the in-process cousins Proxy and Decorator.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Sidecar = helper container next to the app; mesh = sidecars + control plane.
  • Gives mTLS identity, authorization, retries/timeouts, traffic splitting, telemetry.
  • East-west (mesh) vs. north-south (gateway).
  • Apps still forward trace headers and own business fallbacks.
  • Watch retry layering, overhead, lifecycle ordering.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a per-path methods check to SidecarProxy (reporting may GET but not POST reports).
  • Add header-based routing to TrafficSplitSidecar (x-canary: true always goes to v2).
  • Make OutlierDetector double the ejection time for a host ejected twice in 5 minutes.

docs.title: Strangler Fig
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Microservices Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Replace a legacy system gradually: put a routing facade in front of it, rebuild one capability at a time as a new service, and switch that capability's traffic over, until nothing is left of the old system. Every step is small, reversible and delivers value, instead of a risky "big-bang rewrite".

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between components, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern, or press a Break it button to make something fail while the pattern is in place. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the grocery business runs on a 12-year-old monolith. A full rewrite would take two years with no new features. Meanwhile the old system keeps changing, the rewrite chases a moving target, and launch day is a single enormous risk. Many big-bang rewrites are abandoned.

Definition (Martin Fowler, named after the strangler fig tree):

Gradually create a new system around the edges of the old, letting it grow slowly over several years until the old system is strangled.

The loop:

  1. Intercept: put a facade (gateway, proxy, router) in front of the legacy system.
  2. Extract: build one capability as a new service.
  3. Route: send that capability's traffic to the new service (gradually, reversibly).
  4. Retire: delete the legacy code for it. Repeat.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Renovating a restaurant that stays open

You can't close for a year. So you rebuild the kitchen one station at a time over weekends: first the grill, then the fryer. Each Monday, cooks use the new station while the rest stays as before. If the new fryer has a problem, they use the old one for a day. One day, the last old station is removed.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: flowchart LR     C[Clients] --> F[Strangler facade<br/>gateway / router]     F -->|/catalog, /cart| N1[New services]     F -->|everything else| L[Legacy monolith]     L -.->|data sync / events| N1 Participant Responsibility Facade Routes per capability; supports rollback; invisible to clients Legacy system Keeps serving everything not yet migrated New services Own migrated capabilities and (eventually) their data Sync mechanism CDC/events keep data consistent while both systems are live

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Big-bang rewrite:
  Month 0-24: build "v2" in parallel; legacy still gets new features (now built twice)
  Month 24:   cut-over weekend; data migration; everything switches at once
  Month 24+1: unknown behaviours of v1 discovered in production, no rollback path

docs.title: Example 1: Strangling a Grocery Monolith Route by Route
docs.text:
Scenario: A router sits in front of the monolith. Over nine months, catalog, cart, orders and invoices move to new services. When a bug appears in the new order service, /orders is rolled back to the monolith with one call, without a deploy, while the other migrated routes stay put.

Design:

gantt dateFormat YYYY-MM axisFormat %b section Routes catalog → catalog-svc :done, 2026-01, 2026-02 cart → cart-svc :done, 2026-03, 2026-05 orders → order-svc :active, 2026-04, 2026-08 invoices → billing-svc :2026-07, 2026-09

Full Code:

StranglerRouter.javaStranglerDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.strangler.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * The facade in front of a legacy monolith. Routes that have been rewritten go to new services;
 * everything else still goes to the monolith. Migration = moving one route at a time.
 */
public final class StranglerRouter {

    private final Function<Request, Response> legacy;
    private final Map<String, Function<Request, Response>> migrated = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    public StranglerRouter(Function<Request, Response> legacy) {
        this.legacy = legacy;
    }

    public void migrate(String pathPrefix, Function<Request, Response> newService) { // (1)!
        migrated.put(pathPrefix, newService);
    }

    public void rollback(String pathPrefix) { // (2)!
        migrated.remove(pathPrefix);
    }

    public Response handle(Request request) {
        return migrated.entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> request.path().startsWith(e.getKey()))
                .findFirst()
                .map(e -> e.getValue().apply(request))
                .orElseGet(() -> legacy.apply(request)); // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Migration is a routing change: in production, gateway configuration rather than code.
  2. Rollback is just as cheap, which is what makes each step safe.
  3. The default stays legacy, so unmigrated paths keep working.
package com.handbook.microservices.strangler.grocery;

import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class StranglerDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var router = new StranglerRouter(r -> Response.of(200, "monolith"));
        List<String> paths = List.of("/catalog/MANGO", "/cart", "/orders/9", "/invoices/9");

        System.out.println("=== Grocery: strangling the monolith one route at a time ===");
        print("Day 0   (all legacy)            ", router, paths);

        router.migrate("/catalog", r -> Response.of(200, "catalog-svc"));
        print("Month 2 (catalog extracted)     ", router, paths);

        router.migrate("/cart", r -> Response.of(200, "cart-svc"));
        router.migrate("/orders", r -> Response.of(200, "order-svc"));
        print("Month 5 (cart, orders)          ", router, paths);

        router.rollback("/orders"); // bug found in the new order service
        print("Month 5 (orders rolled back)    ", router, paths);

        router.migrate("/orders", r -> Response.of(200, "order-svc"));
        router.migrate("/invoices", r -> Response.of(200, "billing-svc"));
        print("Month 9 (monolith retired)      ", router, paths);
    }

    private static void print(String label, StranglerRouter router, List<String> paths) {
        System.out.println(label + paths.stream()
                .map(p -> p.split("/")[1] + "->" + router.handle(Request.get(p, Map.of())).body())
                .toList());
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: strangling the monolith one route at a time ===
Day 0   (all legacy)            [catalog->monolith, cart->monolith, orders->monolith, invoices->monolith]
Month 2 (catalog extracted)     [catalog->catalog-svc, cart->monolith, orders->monolith, invoices->monolith]
Month 5 (cart, orders)          [catalog->catalog-svc, cart->cart-svc, orders->order-svc, invoices->monolith]
Month 5 (orders rolled back)    [catalog->catalog-svc, cart->cart-svc, orders->monolith, invoices->monolith]
Month 9 (monolith retired)      [catalog->catalog-svc, cart->cart-svc, orders->order-svc, invoices->billing-svc]

Why a strangler here:

  • Value ships every few weeks, not after two years.
  • Each step can be rolled back in seconds.
  • The monolith shrinks steadily until retiring it is a non-event.

docs.title: Example 2: Percentage Rollout of Statements (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The new statement service goes live for staff first, then 5%, 25% and 100% of customers. Each customer's bucket comes from a hash of their ID, so they consistently see one system (no flip-flopping between old and new statements). A kill switch returns everyone to the legacy system instantly.

Full Code:

PercentageRollout.javaPercentageRolloutDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.strangler.banking;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Moves customers to the new statement service gradually. A customer's bucket comes from a hash of
 * their ID, so each customer consistently sees one system. Staff are always on the new system,
 * and a kill switch sends everyone back instantly.
 */
public final class PercentageRollout {

    private final Function<String, String> legacy;
    private final Function<String, String> modern;
    private final Set<String> internalStaff;
    private volatile int percent;
    private volatile boolean killSwitch;

    public PercentageRollout(Function<String, String> legacy, Function<String, String> modern, Set<String> internalStaff) {
        this.legacy = legacy;
        this.modern = modern;
        this.internalStaff = internalStaff;
    }

    public void setPercent(int percent) {
        this.percent = percent;
    }

    public void setKillSwitch(boolean on) {
        this.killSwitch = on;
    }

    public String statement(String customerId) {
        if (killSwitch) { // (1)!
            return legacy.apply(customerId);
        }
        boolean useModern = internalStaff.contains(customerId) // (2)!
                || Math.floorMod(customerId.hashCode(), 100) < percent; // (3)!
        return (useModern ? modern : legacy).apply(customerId);
    }
}
  1. The kill switch beats everything, for instant rollback during an incident.
  2. Dogfooding: staff always use the new path first.
  3. Sticky bucketing by customer ID; the same customer gets the same system every time.
package com.handbook.microservices.strangler.banking;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class PercentageRolloutDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var rollout = new PercentageRollout(id -> "legacy", id -> "modern", Set.of("EMP-1"));

        System.out.println("=== Banking: moving statements to the new service by percentage ===");
        for (int percent : new int[] {0, 5, 25, 100}) {
            rollout.setPercent(percent);
            System.out.printf("%3d%% -> %4d of 10,000 customers on the new service; EMP-1 -> %s; CUST-1001 -> %s%n",
                    percent, modernCount(rollout), rollout.statement("EMP-1"), rollout.statement("CUST-1001"));
        }
        rollout.setKillSwitch(true);
        System.out.printf("KILL -> %4d of 10,000 customers on the new service (instant rollback)%n", modernCount(rollout));
    }

    private static long modernCount(PercentageRollout rollout) {
        return IntStream.range(0, 10_000).mapToObj(i -> "CUST-" + i)
                .filter(id -> rollout.statement(id).equals("modern")).count();
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: moving statements to the new service by percentage ===
  0% ->    0 of 10,000 customers on the new service; EMP-1 -> modern; CUST-1001 -> legacy
  5% ->  494 of 10,000 customers on the new service; EMP-1 -> modern; CUST-1001 -> legacy
 25% -> 2523 of 10,000 customers on the new service; EMP-1 -> modern; CUST-1001 -> legacy
100% -> 10000 of 10,000 customers on the new service; EMP-1 -> modern; CUST-1001 -> modern
KILL ->    0 of 10,000 customers on the new service (instant rollback)

Why gradual here:

  • Banking customers notice everything; the blast radius of a bug is limited to a small percentage.
  • Real production traffic validates the new service before everyone depends on it.

docs.title: Example 3: Parallel Run of a Premium Engine (Insurance)
docs.text:
Scenario: The rewritten premium engine must give exactly the same quotes as the legacy one. During a parallel run, every quote is computed by both; customers get the legacy answer, and differences are logged. The log reveals a misread spec: the legacy system compounds the claims loading; the new one doesn't. That's fixed before any customer is affected.

Full Code:

ShadowComparator.javaShadowRunDemo.java 
package com.handbook.microservices.strangler.insurance;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Parallel run ("shadow traffic"): every quote is computed by both systems. The customer gets the
 * legacy answer; differences are logged for investigation. When mismatches reach zero, switch over.
 */
public final class ShadowComparator<Q> {

    private final Function<Q, Long> legacy;
    private final Function<Q, Long> modern;
    private final List<String> mismatches = new ArrayList<>();
    private int compared;

    public ShadowComparator(Function<Q, Long> legacy, Function<Q, Long> modern) {
        this.legacy = legacy;
        this.modern = modern;
    }

    public long quote(Q request) {
        long answer = legacy.apply(request); // (1)!
        try {
            long candidate = modern.apply(request); // (2)!
            compared++;
            if (candidate != answer) {
                mismatches.add(request + ": legacy=" + answer + " modern=" + candidate);
            }
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            mismatches.add(request + ": modern failed " + e.getMessage()); // (3)!
        }
        return answer;
    }

    public List<String> mismatches() {
        return List.copyOf(mismatches);
    }

    public int compared() {
        return compared;
    }
}
  1. The legacy answer is authoritative during the parallel run.
  2. The new engine runs on the same input. In production, run it asynchronously so it can't slow down or break the response.
  3. Failures of the new engine are recorded, never surfaced to customers.
package com.handbook.microservices.strangler.insurance;

import java.util.List;

public class ShadowRunDemo {

    record Driver(String name, int age, int claims) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Legacy COBOL-era rule: base 12,000; under 25 +40%; each past claim +15% (compounded).
        var shadow = new ShadowComparator<Driver>(d -> {
            double premium = 12_000 * (d.age() < 25 ? 1.4 : 1.0);
            for (int i = 0; i < d.claims(); i++) {
                premium *= 1.15;
            }
            return Math.round(premium);
        }, d -> {
            // Rewritten rule: someone read the spec as "+15% per claim" (simple, not compounded).
            double premium = 12_000 * (d.age() < 25 ? 1.4 : 1.0) * (1 + 0.15 * d.claims());
            return Math.round(premium);
        });

        System.out.println("=== Insurance: parallel run of the new premium engine ===");
        for (Driver d : List.of(new Driver("Asha", 34, 0), new Driver("Ravi", 22, 0),
                new Driver("Meera", 41, 1), new Driver("Kabir", 29, 2), new Driver("Zoya", 23, 3))) {
            System.out.println(d.name() + " quoted " + shadow.quote(d) + " (legacy answer returned)");
        }
        System.out.println("Compared " + shadow.compared() + ", mismatches " + shadow.mismatches().size() + ":");
        shadow.mismatches().forEach(m -> System.out.println("  " + m));
        System.out.println("Not ready to switch: compounding rule differs for 2+ claims.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Insurance: parallel run of the new premium engine ===
Asha quoted 12000 (legacy answer returned)
Ravi quoted 16800 (legacy answer returned)
Meera quoted 13800 (legacy answer returned)
Kabir quoted 15870 (legacy answer returned)
Zoya quoted 25551 (legacy answer returned)
Compared 5, mismatches 2:
  Driver[name=Kabir, age=29, claims=2]: legacy=15870 modern=15600
  Driver[name=Zoya, age=23, claims=3]: legacy=25551 modern=24360
Not ready to switch: compounding rule differs for 2+ claims.

Why a parallel run here:

  • Legacy logic is often the only accurate spec; comparing outputs finds undocumented rules.
  • Zero customer risk while gaining confidence on real data.
  • Only works for side-effect-free operations (quotes, calculations); never shadow "charge card".
Unit Tests: StranglerFigTest.java 
package com.handbook.microservices;

import com.handbook.microservices.strangler.banking.PercentageRollout;
import com.handbook.microservices.strangler.grocery.StranglerRouter;
import com.handbook.microservices.strangler.insurance.ShadowComparator;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Request;
import com.handbook.microservices.support.Http.Response;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class StranglerFigTest {

    @Test
    void migratedRoutesGoToNewServiceOthersToLegacy() {
        var router = new StranglerRouter(r -> Response.of(200, "legacy"));
        router.migrate("/cart", r -> Response.of(200, "new"));
        assertThat(router.handle(Request.get("/cart/1", Map.of())).body()).isEqualTo("new");
        assertThat(router.handle(Request.get("/orders/1", Map.of())).body()).isEqualTo("legacy");
    }

    @Test
    void rolloutIsStickyPerCustomer() {
        var rollout = new PercentageRollout(id -> "legacy", id -> "modern", Set.of());
        rollout.setPercent(50);
        String first = rollout.statement("CUST-1");
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            assertThat(rollout.statement("CUST-1")).isEqualTo(first);
        }
    }

    @Test
    void shadowAlwaysReturnsLegacyAnswer() {
        var shadow = new ShadowComparator<Integer>(x -> 1L, x -> 2L);
        assertThat(shadow.quote(5)).isEqualTo(1L);
        assertThat(shadow.mismatches()).hasSize(1);
    }
}

# Spring Cloud Gateway as the strangler facade (reference)
spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: catalog-new
    uri: lb://catalog-service
    predicates: [ "Path=/catalog/**" ]
  - id: orders-canary                   # 10% of order traffic to the new service
    uri: lb://order-service
    predicates: [ "Path=/orders/**", "Weight=orders, 10" ]
  - id: orders-legacy
