docs.title: Structural Patterns
docs.text:
Structural patterns answer: how do classes and objects fit together into larger structures while staying flexible? They're about composition: wrapping, adapting, combining and sharing objects so that each piece stays simple.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Adapter Make an incompatible interface fit the one you need ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Bridge Vary an abstraction and its implementation independently ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Composite Treat single objects and trees of objects the same way ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Decorator Add behavior to an object without subclassing ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Facade One simple entry point to a complex subsystem ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Flyweight Share immutable state across many objects to save memory ⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Proxy Control access to an object (lazy, remote, cached, secured) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ flowchart TD Q1{What do you need?} -->|Make an existing class fit an interface| A[Adapter] Q1 -->|Add responsibilities at runtime, stackable| D[Decorator] Q1 -->|Control access: lazy, cache, security, remote| P[Proxy] Q1 -->|Simplify a complex subsystem| F[Facade] Q1 -->|Part-whole trees| C[Composite] Q1 -->|Two dimensions that vary independently| B[Bridge] Q1 -->|Millions of similar objects| FW[Flyweight]

Adapter vs. Decorator vs. Proxy vs. Facade

All four wrap something. Ask what changes: Adapter changes the interface. Decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior. Proxy keeps the interface and controls access. Facade gives a new, simpler interface to many objects.

docs.title: Adapter
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Adapter converts the interface of an existing class into the interface your code expects, so classes that couldn't work together now can. Use it to plug in third-party SDKs, legacy systems or devices without letting their quirks leak into your codebase.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: your checkout is written against a clean PaymentGateway.charge(orderId, BigDecimal) interface. The bank gives you an SDK where amounts are strings in paise, currencies are numeric codes and results are magic numbers like 51. You can't change the SDK, and you don't want "356" and 51 scattered across your business code.

Formal definition (GoF):

Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A travel plug adapter

Your Indian laptop charger has a Type-D plug; the hotel in London has Type-G sockets. You don't rewire the hotel or your charger. You put a small adapter between them. The charger still "thinks" it's plugged into an Indian socket, and the wall still "sees" a British plug.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram class Client class Target { <<interface>> +request() } class Adapter { -Adaptee adaptee +request() } class Adaptee { +specificRequest() } Client --> Target Target <|.. Adapter Adapter --> Adaptee : delegates + translates Participant Responsibility Target The interface your code wants to use (PaymentGateway) Adaptee The existing class with an incompatible interface (vendor SDK, legacy system) Adapter Implements Target, holds the Adaptee, translates calls, data and errors Client Talks only to Target

Object adapter vs. class adapter: the version above (holding the adaptee in a field) is an object adapter, which is what you'll use in Java 99% of the time. A class adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target. It needs inheritance, so it only works if the adaptee isn't final, and it couples you to one concrete class.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public class CheckoutService {
    private final LegacyBankGateway bank = new LegacyBankGateway();

    public String pay(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        String paise = amount.movePointRight(2).toPlainString();   // vendor detail
        int code = bank.doTxn(orderId, paise, "356");               // magic currency code
        if (code == 0) return "ok " + bank.lastTxnRef(orderId);
        if (code == 51) return "limit";                              // magic result codes
        ...
    }
}
// The same conversions are copied into RefundService, SubscriptionService...

What goes wrong:

  • Vendor details everywhere. Paise conversion and code tables are duplicated, and drift.
  • Vendor lock-in. Switching banks means editing every service.
  • Hard to test. Business logic can't run without the vendor SDK.

docs.title: Example 1: Checkout on a Legacy Bank SDK (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: An e-commerce company signs with a bank whose payment SDK predates modern Java: amounts are strings in paise, the currency is the ISO numeric code "356", results are integer codes, and the transaction reference is fetched with a second call. Checkout, refunds and subscriptions are all written against the company's own PaymentGateway interface, which another bank also implements. The new bank must plug in without changing any business code.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as CheckoutService participant A as LegacyBankAdapter participant L as LegacyBankGateway (vendor SDK) C->>A: charge("ORD-1001", 499.00) A->>A: 499.00 INR -> "49900" paise A->>L: doTxn("ORD-1001", "49900", "356") L-->>A: 0 A->>L: lastTxnRef("ORD-1001") L-->>A: "LB68940" A-->>C: ChargeResult(approved, LB68940, "Approved")

Full Code:

LegacyBankAdapter.javaPaymentGateway.javaLegacyBankGateway.javaCheckoutService.javaPaymentsDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.Map;

/** Adapter: implements our interface, translates every call to the vendor SDK. */
public class LegacyBankAdapter implements PaymentGateway {

    private static final String INR_NUMERIC = "356";
    private static final Map<Integer, String> CODES = Map.of(
            0, "Approved", 51, "Declined: amount above limit", 91, "Declined: currency not supported");

    private final LegacyBankGateway legacy; // (1)!

    public LegacyBankAdapter(LegacyBankGateway legacy) {
        this.legacy = legacy;
    }

    @Override
    public ChargeResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amountInr) {
        String paise = amountInr.setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY) // (2)!
                .movePointRight(2).toPlainString();
        int code = legacy.doTxn(orderId, paise, INR_NUMERIC);
        String message = CODES.getOrDefault(code, "Declined: code " + code); // (3)!
        String txnId = code == 0 ? legacy.lastTxnRef(orderId) : null;
        return new ChargeResult(code == 0, txnId, message);
    }
}
  1. Object adapter: holds the adaptee and delegates to it. The SDK is passed in, so tests can pass a fake.
  2. RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY makes the adapter refuse amounts with fractions of a paisa rather than silently rounding money. The unit test checks this.
  3. Error translation is part of adapting: magic numbers become meaningful messages (or domain exceptions), and unknown codes are still handled.
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

/** Target: the interface our checkout code is written against. */
public interface PaymentGateway {

    record ChargeResult(boolean approved, String transactionId, String message) {
    }

    ChargeResult charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amountInr);
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments;

/**
 * Adaptee: a vendor SDK we cannot change. Amounts are strings in paise,
 * results are numeric codes, and the reference comes back in a separate call.
 */
public class LegacyBankGateway {

    public int doTxn(String merchantRef, String amountPaise, String currencyCode) {
        long paise = Long.parseLong(amountPaise);
        if (!"356".equals(currencyCode)) { // ISO 4217 numeric code for INR
            return 91; // unsupported currency
        }
        return paise > 5_000_000 ? 51 : 0; // 51 = insufficient funds / limit exceeded
    }

    public String lastTxnRef(String merchantRef) {
        return "LB" + Math.abs(merchantRef.hashCode() % 100_000);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

/** Client: knows only PaymentGateway. */
public class CheckoutService {

    private final PaymentGateway gateway;

    public CheckoutService(PaymentGateway gateway) {
        this.gateway = gateway;
    }

    public String pay(String orderId, String amountInr) {
        PaymentGateway.ChargeResult r = gateway.charge(orderId, new BigDecimal(amountInr));
        return "%s INR %10s -> %s%s".formatted(orderId, amountInr, r.message(),
                r.approved() ? " (txn " + r.transactionId() + ")" : "");
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments;

public class PaymentsDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Checkout on a Legacy Bank SDK ===");
        CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService(new LegacyBankAdapter(new LegacyBankGateway()));
        System.out.println(checkout.pay("ORD-1001", "499.00"));
        System.out.println(checkout.pay("ORD-1002", "12999.50"));
        System.out.println(checkout.pay("ORD-1003", "75000.00"));
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Checkout on a Legacy Bank SDK ===
ORD-1001 INR     499.00 -> Approved (txn LB68940)
ORD-1002 INR   12999.50 -> Approved (txn LB68941)
ORD-1003 INR   75000.00 -> Declined: amount above limit

Why Adapter here:

  • The SDK can't be changed, and the business code shouldn't change.
  • All vendor knowledge (units, codes, call order) lives in one class that's easy to test.
  • Switching or adding banks means a new adapter, not a rewrite.

docs.title: Example 2: One Tracking Page, Many Couriers (Logistics)
docs.text:
Scenario: An online store ships through several couriers. An international courier returns tracking as an XML-like string with event codes (OFD); a regional courier returns a map with numeric stages and expects a numeric consignment number. The customer's "Track my order" page must show one consistent status (PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED) no matter who's carrying the parcel. New couriers are added every quarter.

Design:

classDiagram class TrackingProvider { <<interface>> +track(trackingId) Tracking } class GlobalExpressAdapter class QuickShipAdapter class GlobalExpressClient { +getShipmentXml(awb) String } class QuickShipApi { +fetch(long) Map } TrackingProvider <|.. GlobalExpressAdapter TrackingProvider <|.. QuickShipAdapter GlobalExpressAdapter --> GlobalExpressClient QuickShipAdapter --> QuickShipApi

Full Code:

TrackingProvider.javaGlobalExpressAdapter.javaQuickShipAdapter.javaCourier clientsTrackingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics;

/** Target interface used by the order-tracking page. */
public interface TrackingProvider {

    enum Status { PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED }

    record Tracking(String carrier, String trackingId, Status status, String location) {
    }

    Tracking track(String trackingId);
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class GlobalExpressAdapter implements TrackingProvider {

    private static final Pattern EVENT = Pattern.compile("code='(\\w+)' city='([^']+)'");
    private static final Map<String, Status> CODES = Map.of(
            "PU", Status.PICKED_UP, "IT", Status.IN_TRANSIT,
            "OFD", Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, "DL", Status.DELIVERED);

    private final GlobalExpressClient client;

    public GlobalExpressAdapter(GlobalExpressClient client) {
        this.client = client;
    }

    @Override
    public Tracking track(String trackingId) {
        Matcher m = EVENT.matcher(client.getShipmentXml(trackingId));
        if (!m.find()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Unexpected GlobalExpress response for " + trackingId);
        }
        return new Tracking("GlobalExpress", trackingId, CODES.get(m.group(1)), m.group(2));
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics;

import java.util.Map;

public class QuickShipAdapter implements TrackingProvider {

    private final QuickShipApi api;

    public QuickShipAdapter(QuickShipApi api) {
        this.api = api;
    }

    @Override
    public Tracking track(String trackingId) {
        Map<String, Object> raw = api.fetch(Long.parseLong(trackingId.replace("QS-", ""))); // (1)!
        Status status = switch ((int) raw.get("stage")) {
            case 1 -> Status.PICKED_UP;
            case 2 -> Status.IN_TRANSIT;
            case 3 -> Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY;
            case 4 -> Status.DELIVERED;
            default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Unknown QuickShip stage " + raw.get("stage"));
        };
        return new Tracking("QuickShip", trackingId, status, (String) raw.get("hub"));
    }
}
  1. Adapting inputs too: our tracking IDs are strings like QS-554201, but this API wants a long.
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics;

/** Adaptee 1: an international courier that returns an XML-ish string. */
public class GlobalExpressClient {

    public String getShipmentXml(String awb) {
        return "<shipment awb='" + awb + "'><event code='OFD' city='Pune'/></shipment>";
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics;

import java.util.Map;

/** Adaptee 2: a local courier that returns a map with numeric stages. */
public class QuickShipApi {

    public Map<String, Object> fetch(long consignmentNo) {
        return Map.of("stage", 2, "hub", "Hyderabad Hub");
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics;

import java.util.Map;

public class TrackingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: One Tracking Page, Many Couriers ===");
        Map<String, TrackingProvider> byCarrier = Map.of(
                "GX", new GlobalExpressAdapter(new GlobalExpressClient()),
                "QS", new QuickShipAdapter(new QuickShipApi()));

        for (String id : new String[] {"GX-7781230", "QS-554201"}) {
            TrackingProvider provider = byCarrier.get(id.substring(0, 2));
            System.out.println(provider.track(id));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: One Tracking Page, Many Couriers ===
Tracking[carrier=GlobalExpress, trackingId=GX-7781230, status=OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, location=Pune]
Tracking[carrier=QuickShip, trackingId=QS-554201, status=IN_TRANSIT, location=Hyderabad Hub]

Why Adapter here:

  • Many adaptees, one target: the page doesn't know or care how each courier reports status.
  • Each adapter normalizes to a shared enum and fails loudly on unknown codes, rather than showing customers garbage.
  • This is the Anti-Corruption Layer idea from Domain-Driven Design at class level: external models never enter your domain.

docs.title: Example 3: ICU Devices from Different Vendors (Healthcare)
docs.text:
Scenario: An ICU dashboard shows each bed's vitals and raises alerts (fever ≥ 38.0 °C, SpO2 < 95%). The hospital buys devices from different vendors: a US thermometer that reports tenths of a degree Fahrenheit as an int, and an older pulse oximeter that emits a raw serial-protocol frame like $OX,ID=OX-7,SPO2=94,PR=88*. The alerting logic must work on clean, metric readings. A corrupt frame must be rejected, never shown as a number.

Design:

flowchart LR T[VendorThermometer<br/>1013 = 101.3 °F] --> TA[ThermometerAdapter] --> R1[Reading 38.5 °C] O["LegacyPulseOximeter<br/>$OX,ID=OX-7,SPO2=94,PR=88*"] --> OA[PulseOximeterAdapter] --> R2[Reading 94 %] R1 --> D[ICU dashboard + alert rules] R2 --> D

Full Code:

VitalsSensor.javaThermometerAdapter.javaPulseOximeterAdapter.javaDevicesIcuDashboardDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare;

/** Target: the ICU dashboard reads every device through this interface. */
public interface VitalsSensor {

    record Reading(String deviceId, String metric, double value, String unit) {
        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return "%-8s %-11s %6.1f %s".formatted(deviceId, metric, value, unit);
        }
    }

    Reading read();
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare;

public class ThermometerAdapter implements VitalsSensor {

    private final VendorThermometer device;

    public ThermometerAdapter(VendorThermometer device) {
        this.device = device;
    }

    @Override
    public Reading read() {
        double fahrenheit = device.getTempF10() / 10.0;
        double celsius = Math.round((fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9 * 10) / 10.0; // (1)!
        return new Reading(device.serial(), "temperature", celsius, "°C");
    }
}
  1. Unit conversion (°F to °C) plus rounding to one decimal. Adapters often convert units and scales, not just method names.
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class PulseOximeterAdapter implements VitalsSensor {

    private final LegacyPulseOximeter device;

    public PulseOximeterAdapter(LegacyPulseOximeter device) {
        this.device = device;
    }

    @Override
    public Reading read() {
        String frame = device.readFrame();
        if (!frame.startsWith("$OX,") || !frame.endsWith("*")) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Corrupt frame: " + frame); // (1)!
        }
        Map<String, String> fields = new HashMap<>();
        for (String part : frame.substring(4, frame.length() - 1).split(",")) {
            String[] kv = part.split("=");
            fields.put(kv[0], kv[1]);
        }
        return new Reading(fields.get("ID"), "SpO2", Double.parseDouble(fields.get("SPO2")), "%");
    }
}
  1. Validation belongs in the adapter: it's the last place that knows what a valid frame from this device looks like. In a clinical system, a wrong number is far worse than no number.
package com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare;

/** Adaptee: US vendor device, reports tenths of a degree Fahrenheit as an int. */
public class VendorThermometer {

    public int getTempF10() {
        return 1_013; // 101.3 °F
    }

    public String serial() {
        return "THM-22";
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare;

/** Adaptee: old device that emits a raw serial-protocol frame. */
public class LegacyPulseOximeter {

    public String readFrame() {
        return "$OX,ID=OX-7,SPO2=94,PR=88*";
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare;

import java.util.List;

public class IcuDashboardDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Hospital ICU: Bed 12 Vitals ===");
        List<VitalsSensor> bed12 = List.of(
                new ThermometerAdapter(new VendorThermometer()),
                new PulseOximeterAdapter(new LegacyPulseOximeter()));

        for (VitalsSensor sensor : bed12) {
            VitalsSensor.Reading r = sensor.read();
            boolean alert = (r.metric().equals("temperature") && r.value() >= 38.0)
                    || (r.metric().equals("SpO2") && r.value() < 95);
            System.out.println(r + (alert ? "   <-- ALERT" : ""));
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Hospital ICU: Bed 12 Vitals ===
THM-22   temperature   38.5 °C   <-- ALERT
OX-7     SpO2          94.0 %   <-- ALERT

Why Adapter here:

  • Devices are hardware with fixed protocols: you can only adapt them.
  • Alert rules are written once, in metric units, against one interface.
  • Each adapter can be certified and tested on its own, which matters in regulated software.
Unit Tests: AdapterTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.structural.adapter;

import com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare.PulseOximeterAdapter;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare.ThermometerAdapter;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare.VendorThermometer;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.legacy.EnumerationIterator;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics.QuickShipAdapter;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics.QuickShipApi;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.logistics.TrackingProvider.Status;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments.LegacyBankAdapter;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.payments.LegacyBankGateway;
import com.handbook.structural.adapter.healthcare.LegacyPulseOximeter;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class AdapterTest {

    @Test
    void bankAdapterConvertsRupeesToPaiseAndCodesToResults() {
        var captured = new String[1];
        LegacyBankGateway spy = new LegacyBankGateway() {
            @Override
            public int doTxn(String ref, String paise, String currency) {
                captured[0] = paise + "/" + currency;
                return super.doTxn(ref, paise, currency);
            }
        };
        var result = new LegacyBankAdapter(spy).charge("O1", new BigDecimal("12.5"));
        assertThat(captured[0]).isEqualTo("1250/356");
        assertThat(result.approved()).isTrue();
    }

    @Test
    void bankAdapterRejectsFractionsOfAPaisa() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> new LegacyBankAdapter(new LegacyBankGateway()).charge("O1", new BigDecimal("1.005")))
                .isInstanceOf(ArithmeticException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void quickShipStageIsMappedAndUnknownStageFailsLoudly() {
        assertThat(new QuickShipAdapter(new QuickShipApi()).track("QS-1").status()).isEqualTo(Status.IN_TRANSIT);
        QuickShipApi weird = new QuickShipApi() {
            @Override
            public Map<String, Object> fetch(long no) { return Map.of("stage", 9, "hub", "X"); }
        };
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> new QuickShipAdapter(weird).track("QS-1")).hasMessageContaining("stage 9");
    }

    @Test
    void sensorsAreNormalised() {
        assertThat(new ThermometerAdapter(new VendorThermometer()).read().value()).isEqualTo(38.5);
        VendorThermometer normal = new VendorThermometer() {
            @Override
            public int getTempF10() { return 986; }
        };
        assertThat(new ThermometerAdapter(normal).read().value()).isEqualTo(37.0);
        LegacyPulseOximeter corrupt = new LegacyPulseOximeter() {
            @Override
            public String readFrame() { return "$OX,ID=OX-7,SP"; }
        };
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> new PulseOximeterAdapter(corrupt).read()).hasMessageContaining("Corrupt");
    }

    @Test
    void enumerationAdapterIteratesAndRefusesRemove() {
        var it = new EnumerationIterator<>(Collections.enumeration(List.of("a", "b")));
        assertThat(it.next()).isEqualTo("a");
        assertThatThrownBy(it::remove).isInstanceOf(UnsupportedOperationException.class);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Variation Example Object adapter (composition) All examples here. Preferred. Class adapter (inheritance) class Adapter extends Adaptee implements Target. Only when you must override adaptee behavior Two-way adapter Implements both interfaces so old and new code can call it during a migration Lambda / method-reference adapter When Target is a functional interface: Supplier<Reading> s = () -> convert(device.getTempF10()); Bulk adapters Arrays.asList(array) adapts an array to List; Collections.enumeration(list) goes the other way

Records make adapter outputs safe: return immutable records (ChargeResult, Tracking, Reading) so callers can't depend on mutable vendor objects.

Spring and adapters. Name adapters after the vendor (StripePaymentAdapter, RazorpayPaymentAdapter), implement your port interface, and pick one with @ConditionalOnProperty or a map of beans. This is how Hexagonal Architecture names them: adapters plugged into ports.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Example JDK Arrays.asList(T...): array to List JDK InputStreamReader / OutputStreamWriter: byte streams to character streams JDK Collections.enumeration(collection), Collections.list(enumeration) JDK Executors.callable(Runnable): Runnable to Callable Spring MVC HandlerAdapter: lets DispatcherServlet call @Controller methods, HttpRequestHandlers and plain servlets the same way Spring MessageListenerAdapter (JMS), WebMvcConfigurer-style adapters, HttpMessageConverters SLF4J Bridges such as jul-to-slf4j and log4j-over-slf4j adapt other logging APIs to SLF4J JPA AttributeConverter<X, Y>: adapts a Java type to a column type

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Reuse existing classes you can't or shouldn't change One more layer of indirection Single Responsibility: conversion logic in one place Many adapters if you integrate many vendors (each needs tests) Open/Closed: new vendors mean new adapters Can hide performance costs (extra calls, parsing) Easy to test: fake the adaptee or the target A "leaky" adapter that exposes vendor types defeats the purpose

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Leaky adapters

Returning vendor objects (LegacyTxnResponse) or throwing vendor exceptions from the adapter spreads the vendor's model into your code. Translate data, errors and units, and return your own types.

Silent defaults on unknown values

Mapping unknown status codes to "OK", or an unknown courier stage to IN_TRANSIT, hides integration breakages. Fail loudly (Examples 2 and 3) and alert.

Business logic inside adapters

An adapter converts; it doesn't decide. "Apply a 2% fee for this bank" belongs in the domain, not in LegacyBankAdapter.

Adapting what you own

If you control both sides, change the interface instead of adding an adapter. Adapters are for boundaries you can't move.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Adapters are where integrations fail; treat them as production code. For each adapter:

  • Contract tests against recorded vendor responses (WireMock, Pact) so vendor changes break the build, not production.
  • Timeouts, retries and circuit breakers around the adaptee call (Resilience4j), configured per vendor.
  • Metrics tagged by vendor (latency, error codes) so you can see "bank X is declining 30% of charges" before customers do.
  • Mapping tables as data for codes that change often, with a default "unknown, alert" path.

Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD). At system level, a set of adapters plus translators that protects your domain model from a legacy or external system's model is an anti-corruption layer. When migrating off a legacy monolith, the ACL lets the new service speak its own language while still reading and writing the old system.

Versioned vendors. When a vendor ships API v2, write a new adapter alongside the old one and switch with a feature flag per merchant. Don't add if (v2) branches inside one adapter.

War story: the decimal that cost a lakh

A marketplace integrated a new payment provider whose API took amounts in paise while the old provider took rupees. The adapter was copied from the old one and nobody changed the conversion. In staging every test charge was INR 1 and "worked" (charged 1 paisa). In production, a INR 1,000 order was charged INR 10. Over a weekend the company under-collected roughly INR 1 lakh before reconciliation caught it. Fix: the adapter now converts with movePointRight(2) and RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY; contract tests assert the exact request body for known amounts; reconciliation runs hourly with an alert on mismatched totals. Lesson: unit conversion is the most important line in a payment adapter. Test the wire format, not just the happy path.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Adapter Facade Decorator Proxy Bridge Interface Changes it to what the client expects New, simpler one over many classes Same as the wrapped object Same as the real object Separates abstraction from implementation Wraps One adaptee (usually) A whole subsystem One component One subject Implementor Purpose Make incompatible things work together Simplify Add behavior Control access Let two dimensions vary When designed After the fact (integration) Any time Any time Any time Up front

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Converts an interface so incompatible classes work together. Think plug adapter.
  • Object adapter (composition) over class adapter (inheritance).
  • Translate calls, data, units and errors; return your types; fail loudly on unknowns.
  • JDK: Arrays.asList, InputStreamReader. Spring: HandlerAdapter.
  • At system scale, it's the Anti-Corruption Layer / Hexagonal adapter.
class LegacyBankAdapter implements PaymentGateway { private final LegacyBankGateway legacy; /* translate */ }

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Add a third courier that pushes updates through webhooks, and adapt it to TrackingProvider.
  • Make LegacyBankAdapter throw a domain exception (PaymentDeclinedException) instead of returning a message.
  • Write a WireMock contract test for a pretend REST version of QuickShipApi.
  • Replace EnumerationIterator with Enumeration.asIterator() and compare.

Structural overview Next: Bridge

docs.title: Bridge
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate Structural Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

Bridge splits a concept that varies in two independent directions into two hierarchies, connected by a reference ("the bridge"). Use it when you'd otherwise need a subclass for every combination (SalesCsvReport, SalesHtmlReport, InventoryCsvReport...).

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: an ERP has report types (sales, inventory, payroll...) and output formats (CSV, HTML, PDF...). With inheritance alone you write SalesCsvReport, SalesHtmlReport, SalesPdfReport, InventoryCsvReport... That's reports × formats classes. Add one format and you write one class per report. This is the "class explosion" problem.

Formal definition (GoF):

Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently.

"Abstraction" here means the high-level, client-facing hierarchy (what a report contains), and "implementation" the low-level hierarchy it delegates to (how it's written out). It doesn't mean Java's abstract keyword.

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Remote controls and devices

A TV remote, a voice remote and a phone app are different controls. A Smart TV, a set-top box and a soundbar are different devices. Any control can work with any device because they agree on a small protocol (power, volume, open content). Manufacturers develop remotes and devices independently, so you don't need a different remote model for every device model.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text:
classDiagram class Abstraction { #Implementor impl +operation() } class RefinedAbstraction { +extendedOperation() } class Implementor { <<interface>> +operationImpl() } class ConcreteImplementorA class ConcreteImplementorB Abstraction <|-- RefinedAbstraction Abstraction o--> Implementor : bridge Implementor <|.. ConcreteImplementorA Implementor <|.. ConcreteImplementorB Participant Responsibility Abstraction High-level logic; holds a reference to an Implementor Refined Abstraction Variants of the high-level logic (SalesReport, VoiceRemote) Implementor Low-level primitive operations (render, setVolume) Concrete Implementor Platform-specific versions (CsvRenderer, SmartTv)

With Bridge, the class count goes from M × N to M + N.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
class SalesCsvReport       { String generate() { /* sales data + CSV code  */ } }
class SalesHtmlReport      { String generate() { /* sales data + HTML code */ } }
class InventoryCsvReport   { String generate() { /* inventory + CSV code   */ } }
class InventoryHtmlReport  { String generate() { /* inventory + HTML code  */ } }
// Add PDF: 2 more classes. Add Payroll: 3 more classes. CSV escaping bug: fix it in N places.
  • Class explosion: M × N classes.
  • Duplication: CSV logic copied into every report.
  • Fixed at compile time: you can't switch format at runtime.

docs.title: Example 1: ERP Reports × Output Formats (SaaS / ERP)
docs.text:
Scenario: An ERP (SAP-style) offers dozens of reports, and customers download them as CSV for Excel or view them as HTML in the browser; PDF and XLSX are on the roadmap. Report authors (finance and supply-chain teams) shouldn't need to know anything about formats, and the platform team should be able to add a format once for all reports. A CSV escaping bug (commas in product names) must be fixed in one place.

Design:

classDiagram class Report { <<abstract>> #ReportRenderer renderer +generate() String #title()* String #columns()* List #rows()* List } class SalesReport class InventoryReport class ReportRenderer { <<interface>> +render(title, columns, rows) String } class CsvRenderer class HtmlRenderer Report <|-- SalesReport Report <|-- InventoryReport Report o--> ReportRenderer : bridge ReportRenderer <|.. CsvRenderer ReportRenderer <|.. HtmlRenderer

Full Code:

Report.javaSalesReport.javaInventoryReport.javaRenderersReportingDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

import java.util.List;

/** Abstraction: WHAT the report contains. Holds a reference to the implementor (the bridge). */
public abstract class Report {

    protected final ReportRenderer renderer; // (1)!

    protected Report(ReportRenderer renderer) {
        this.renderer = renderer;
    }

    public final String generate() {
        return renderer.render(title(), columns(), rows()); // (2)!
    }

    protected abstract String title();

    protected abstract List<String> columns();

    protected abstract List<List<String>> rows();
}
  1. The bridge: the abstraction holds the implementor through an interface, passed in at construction. Any report can be paired with any renderer at runtime.
  2. The abstraction provides what (title, columns, rows) and delegates how to the renderer.
package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

import java.util.List;

public class SalesReport extends Report {

    public SalesReport(ReportRenderer renderer) {
        super(renderer);
    }

    protected String title() { return "Q3 Sales by Region"; }

    protected List<String> columns() { return List.of("Region", "Revenue (INR lakh)"); }

    protected List<List<String>> rows() {
        return List.of(List.of("North", "182.4"), List.of("South", "211.9"));
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

import java.util.List;

public class InventoryReport extends Report {

    public InventoryReport(ReportRenderer renderer) {
        super(renderer);
    }

    protected String title() { return "Low Stock Items"; }

    protected List<String> columns() { return List.of("SKU", "Name", "On hand"); }

    protected List<List<String>> rows() {
        return List.of(List.of("RICE-5KG", "Basmati Rice, 5kg", "12"));
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

import java.util.List;

/** Implementor: HOW a report is written out. */
public interface ReportRenderer {

    String render(String title, List<String> columns, List<List<String>> rows);
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class CsvRenderer implements ReportRenderer {

    @Override
    public String render(String title, List<String> columns, List<List<String>> rows) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("# ").append(title).append('\n');
        sb.append(String.join(",", columns)).append('\n');
        rows.forEach(r -> sb.append(r.stream().map(CsvRenderer::escape).collect(Collectors.joining(","))).append('\n'));
        return sb.toString().stripTrailing();
    }

    private static String escape(String v) {
        return v.contains(",") ? '"' + v + '"' : v;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

import java.util.List;

public class HtmlRenderer implements ReportRenderer {

    @Override
    public String render(String title, List<String> columns, List<List<String>> rows) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("<h2>").append(title).append("</h2>\n<table>\n  <tr>");
        columns.forEach(c -> sb.append("<th>").append(c).append("</th>"));
        sb.append("</tr>\n");
        for (List<String> r : rows) {
            sb.append("  <tr>");
            r.forEach(v -> sb.append("<td>").append(v).append("</td>"));
            sb.append("</tr>\n");
        }
        return sb.append("</table>").toString();
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting;

public class ReportingDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== ERP Reporting: 2 reports x 2 formats = 4 outputs from 4 classes ===");
        ReportRenderer csv = new CsvRenderer();
        ReportRenderer html = new HtmlRenderer();

        System.out.println(new SalesReport(csv).generate());
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println(new SalesReport(html).generate());
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println(new InventoryReport(csv).generate());
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println(new InventoryReport(html).generate());
    }
}

Output:

=== ERP Reporting: 2 reports x 2 formats = 4 outputs from 4 classes ===
# Q3 Sales by Region
Region,Revenue (INR lakh)
North,182.4
South,211.9

<h2>Q3 Sales by Region</h2>
<table>
  <tr><th>Region</th><th>Revenue (INR lakh)</th></tr>
  <tr><td>North</td><td>182.4</td></tr>
  <tr><td>South</td><td>211.9</td></tr>
</table>

# Low Stock Items
SKU,Name,On hand
RICE-5KG,"Basmati Rice, 5kg",12

<h2>Low Stock Items</h2>
<table>
  <tr><th>SKU</th><th>Name</th><th>On hand</th></tr>
  <tr><td>RICE-5KG</td><td>Basmati Rice, 5kg</td><td>12</td></tr>
</table>

Note "Basmati Rice, 5kg": the CSV escaping is written once, in CsvRenderer, and every report benefits.

Why Bridge here:

  • Two dimensions (report type and format) that grow independently.
  • M + N classes instead of M × N; a JSON format is a one-class change (the unit test adds one as a lambda).
  • Each team owns its own hierarchy: report authors and the platform team don't step on each other.

docs.title: Example 2: Remotes × Devices (Streaming / Telecom)
docs.text:
Scenario: A telecom operator ships streaming to Smart TVs (its app) and its own set-top boxes. Customers control them with a basic remote or a voice remote. Devices differ in hardware (the set-top box's volume tops out at 30). Remote features (voice commands) are built by one team; device integrations by another. Every remote must work with every device.

Design:

classDiagram class RemoteControl { #Device device +togglePower() +volumeUp() } class VoiceRemote { +say(command) } class Device { <<interface>> +isOn() boolean +setPower(boolean) +volume() int +setVolume(int) +open(content) } class SmartTv class SetTopBox RemoteControl <|-- VoiceRemote RemoteControl o--> Device : bridge Device <|.. SmartTv Device <|.. SetTopBox

Full Code:

RemoteControl.javaVoiceRemote.javaDevice.javaDevicesRemoteDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming;

/** Abstraction: user-facing controls, built only from Device operations. */
public class RemoteControl {

    protected final Device device;

    public RemoteControl(Device device) {
        this.device = device;
    }

    public void togglePower() {
        device.setPower(!device.isOn());
        System.out.println("  " + device.name() + " power " + (device.isOn() ? "ON" : "OFF"));
    }

    public void volumeUp() {
        device.setVolume(device.volume() + 10);
        System.out.println("  " + device.name() + " volume " + device.volume());
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming;

/** Refined abstraction: adds voice commands, still works with ANY device. */
public class VoiceRemote extends RemoteControl {

    public VoiceRemote(Device device) {
        super(device);
    }

    public void say(String command) {
        System.out.println("  \"" + command + "\"");
        if (command.startsWith("play ")) {
            if (!device.isOn()) {
                togglePower();
            }
            device.open(command.substring(5));
        } else if (command.equals("louder")) {
            volumeUp();
            volumeUp();
        } else {
            System.out.println("  Sorry, I didn't understand that");
        }
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming;

/** Implementor: the low-level operations every device supports. */
public interface Device {

    String name();

    boolean isOn();

    void setPower(boolean on);

    int volume();

    void setVolume(int volume);

    void open(String content);
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming;

public class SmartTv implements Device {

    private boolean on;
    private int volume = 20;

    public String name() { return "SmartTV"; }
    public boolean isOn() { return on; }
    public void setPower(boolean on) { this.on = on; }
    public int volume() { return volume; }
    public void setVolume(int v) { this.volume = Math.clamp(v, 0, 100); }

    public void open(String content) {
        System.out.println("    [SmartTV] launching app and streaming '" + content + "' in 4K");
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming;

public class SetTopBox implements Device {

    private boolean on;
    private int volume = 8;

    public String name() { return "SetTopBox"; }
    public boolean isOn() { return on; }
    public void setPower(boolean on) { this.on = on; }
    public int volume() { return volume; }
    public void setVolume(int v) { this.volume = Math.clamp(v, 0, 30); } // hardware max 30

    public void open(String content) {
        System.out.println("    [SetTopBox] tuning to channel for '" + content + "'");
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming;

public class RemoteDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Remotes x Devices ===");
        System.out.println("Basic remote + SmartTV:");
        RemoteControl basic = new RemoteControl(new SmartTv());
        basic.togglePower();
        basic.volumeUp();

        System.out.println("Voice remote + SetTopBox:");
        VoiceRemote voice = new VoiceRemote(new SetTopBox());
        voice.say("play Cricket World Cup Final");
        voice.say("louder");
        voice.say("louder");
        voice.say("make me a sandwich");
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Remotes x Devices ===
Basic remote + SmartTV:
  SmartTV power ON
  SmartTV volume 30
Voice remote + SetTopBox:
  "play Cricket World Cup Final"
  SetTopBox power ON
    [SetTopBox] tuning to channel for 'Cricket World Cup Final'
  "louder"
  SetTopBox volume 18
  SetTopBox volume 28
  "louder"
  SetTopBox volume 30
  SetTopBox volume 30
  "make me a sandwich"
  Sorry, I didn't understand that

The voice remote's "louder" is built from the device's primitive setVolume, and the set-top box enforces its own limit of 30, so the remote doesn't need to know about it.

Why Bridge here:

  • Refined abstractions (voice remote) add features using only primitive device operations.
  • New devices (a soundbar) work with every existing remote immediately.
  • This is the GoF's own example, in its modern form.

docs.title: Example 3: Post Types × Social Platforms (Social Media)
docs.text:
Scenario: A social-media scheduling tool (Buffer/Hootsuite-style) lets marketing teams write announcements and image posts once and publish them to several platforms. Each platform has its own API and limits: a microblog allows short text, a professional network allows 3,000 characters. Post types are added by the product team; platform integrations by the integrations team. The text must be trimmed to each platform's limit automatically.

Design:

flowchart LR subgraph Abstraction["Post types (product team)"] A[AnnouncementPost] I[ImagePost] end subgraph Implementor["Platforms (integrations team)"] M["Microblog<br/>max 80 chars (demo)"] P["ProfessionalNetwork<br/>max 3000 chars"] end A -- share() --> M A -- share() --> P I -- share() --> M I -- share() --> P

Full Code:

Post.javaPost typesPlatformsSocialDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

import java.util.List;

/** Abstraction: what kind of post. Platform limits come through the bridge. */
public abstract class Post {

    protected final SocialPlatform platform;

    protected Post(SocialPlatform platform) {
        this.platform = platform;
    }

    protected abstract String text();

    protected List<String> media() {
        return List.of();
    }

    public final String share() {
        String text = text();
        if (text.length() > platform.maxLength()) {
            text = text.substring(0, platform.maxLength() - 1) + "…"; // adapt to the platform's limit
        }
        return platform.name() + ": " + platform.publish(text, media());
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

public class AnnouncementPost extends Post {

    private final String headline;
    private final String body;

    public AnnouncementPost(SocialPlatform platform, String headline, String body) {
        super(platform);
        this.headline = headline;
        this.body = body;
    }

    protected String text() {
        return headline.toUpperCase() + " - " + body + " #launch";
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

import java.util.List;

public class ImagePost extends Post {

    private final String caption;
    private final List<String> images;

    public ImagePost(SocialPlatform platform, String caption, List<String> images) {
        super(platform);
        this.caption = caption;
        this.images = List.copyOf(images);
    }

    protected String text() { return caption; }

    @Override
    protected List<String> media() { return images; }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

import java.util.List;

/** Implementor: each platform's API and limits. */
public interface SocialPlatform {

    String name();

    int maxLength();

    String publish(String text, List<String> mediaUrls);
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

import java.util.List;

public class Microblog implements SocialPlatform {

    public String name() { return "Microblog"; }

    public int maxLength() { return 80; } // short for the demo; real limit 280

    public String publish(String text, List<String> media) {
        return "POST /statuses text(" + text.length() + " chars) media=" + media.size();
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

import java.util.List;

public class ProfessionalNetwork implements SocialPlatform {

    public String name() { return "ProNet"; }

    public int maxLength() { return 3000; }

    public String publish(String text, List<String> media) {
        return "POST /ugcPosts visibility=PUBLIC text(" + text.length() + " chars) media=" + media;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.bridge.social;

import java.util.List;

public class SocialDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Social Media Scheduler: Post Types x Platforms ===");
        String body = "Our grocery app now delivers in 10 minutes across 40 new pin codes in Pune.";
        for (SocialPlatform p : List.of(new Microblog(), new ProfessionalNetwork())) {
            System.out.println(new AnnouncementPost(p, "Now in Pune", body).share());
            System.out.println(new ImagePost(p, "Team photo from launch day", List.of("team.jpg")).share());
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Social Media Scheduler: Post Types x Platforms ===
Microblog: POST /statuses text(80 chars) media=0
Microblog: POST /statuses text(26 chars) media=1
ProNet: POST /ugcPosts visibility=PUBLIC text(97 chars) media=[]
ProNet: POST /ugcPosts visibility=PUBLIC text(26 chars) media=[team.jpg]

The same announcement is 97 characters on the professional network and trimmed to 80 on the microblog, without the post classes knowing either limit.

Why Bridge here:

  • Post types and platforms change on different schedules and are owned by different teams.
  • The abstraction (Post.share()) adapts to each implementor's capabilities (maxLength()) through the bridge.
  • A new platform is one class; every post type works with it on day one.
Unit Tests: BridgeTest.java (all three examples) 
package com.handbook.structural.bridge;

import com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting.CsvRenderer;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting.InventoryReport;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting.ReportRenderer;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.reporting.SalesReport;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.social.AnnouncementPost;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.social.Microblog;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.social.SocialPlatform;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming.SetTopBox;
import com.handbook.structural.bridge.streaming.VoiceRemote;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class BridgeTest {

    @Test
    void anyReportWorksWithAnyRenderer() {
        ReportRenderer json = (title, cols, rows) -> "{\"title\":\"" + title + "\",\"rows\":" + rows.size() + "}";
        assertThat(new SalesReport(json).generate()).isEqualTo("{\"title\":\"Q3 Sales by Region\",\"rows\":2}");
        assertThat(new InventoryReport(new CsvRenderer()).generate()).contains("\"Basmati Rice, 5kg\"");
    }

    @Test
    void voiceRemoteRespectsDeviceLimits() {
        SetTopBox box = new SetTopBox();
        VoiceRemote remote = new VoiceRemote(box);
        remote.say("louder");
        remote.say("louder");
        assertThat(box.volume()).isEqualTo(30);
    }

    @Test
    void postsAreTrimmedToPlatformLimit() {
        String shared = new AnnouncementPost(new Microblog(), "x", "y".repeat(200)).share();
        assertThat(shared).contains("text(80 chars)");
        SocialPlatform fake = new SocialPlatform() {
            public String name() { return "Fake"; }
            public int maxLength() { return 1000; }
            public String publish(String text, List<String> media) { return text; }
        };
        assertThat(new AnnouncementPost(fake, "hi", "there").share()).isEqualTo("Fake: HI - there #launch");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
• Implementor as a functional interface. When the implementor has one method (ReportRenderer), a lambda is a full implementor, as the unit test's JSON renderer shows.
  • Choose the implementor with DI. In Spring, inject the implementor (@Qualifier("csv") ReportRenderer) or pick one per request (?format=csv) from a map of beans.
  • Composition over inheritance. Bridge is the GoF's clearest example of this principle: instead of growing one hierarchy in two directions, you compose two hierarchies.
  • Bridge + Abstract Factory. An abstract factory can create the right implementor for the platform (for example, the device driver family).

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Abstraction Implementor JDBC DriverManager, Connection, Statement API your code uses Vendor drivers (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle) SLF4J Logger API Logback, Log4j2, JUL back-ends JDK AWT java.awt.Component (Button, Window) Platform "peers" per OS JDK java.util.logging.Handler Formatter (SimpleFormatter, XMLFormatter), so any handler can use any format Spring JdbcTemplate, RestClient DataSource, ClientHttpRequestFactory (JDK, Apache, Jetty, Reactor clients) Spring Data Repository abstractions Store-specific modules (JPA, MongoDB, Redis)

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons M + N classes instead of M × N More up-front design; abstract when you only have one dimension Abstraction and implementation evolve independently Harder to understand for newcomers (two hierarchies, one indirection) Swap implementations at runtime The implementor interface must be stable and general enough for every abstraction, which is hard to get right Hides platform details from client code Over-engineering if the second dimension never appears

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
A leaky implementor interface

If Device grows setHdmiCecMode() because one TV needs it, every other device must fake it. Keep the implementor to primitives that all platforms support, and let refined abstractions build features from them.

Bridge for a single dimension

One report, three formats? That's just Strategy (inject a renderer). Bridge pays off when both sides have variants.

Mixing it up with Adapter

Adapter is applied after the fact to make two existing things fit. Bridge is designed up front so two hierarchies can grow apart.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Bridge at architecture scale. Driver models (JDBC, SLF4J, cloud provider SDK "core + provider"), plug-in back-ends (storage engines in databases, rendering back-ends in game engines) and multi-platform UIs are all Bridges. The key design work is the implementor interface: small, stable, versioned, and with a capabilities query (maxLength(), supportsTransactions()) so the abstraction can adapt instead of failing.

Capability negotiation. Example 3's maxLength() is a simple version of capability negotiation. In larger systems, implementors expose a capability set (Set<Feature>), and the abstraction degrades gracefully (no image support, so post a link).

Testing. Test the abstraction with a fake implementor (records calls) and test each implementor with a shared contract test (every renderer escapes special characters; every device clamps volume).

Bridge vs. Strategy, honestly. Structurally they're nearly identical (an object delegating to an interface). The difference is intent and scale: Strategy swaps an algorithm for one context; Bridge separates two whole hierarchies that both keep growing. In interviews, saying that clearly is worth more than a diagram.

War story: 54 notification classes

A fintech's notification module started with OtpSms and OtpEmail. Two years later it had 9 notification types × 6 channels = 54 classes, each with copied formatting and retry code. A WhatsApp channel meant 9 new classes; a retry bug had to be fixed 54 times (they found 51). Fix: split into Notification (abstraction: what to say, with refined types) and Channel (implementor: send, with capability flags like supportsRichText). 54 classes became 15; retries moved into a single channel decorator. Lesson: when class names are two nouns glued together (OtpSms, SalesCsv), look for a Bridge.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Bridge Strategy Adapter Abstract Factory Intent Let two hierarchies vary independently Swap one algorithm Make incompatible interfaces fit Create a family of matching objects When designed Up front Up front After the fact Up front Structure Abstraction has-a implementor; both sides subclassed Context has-a strategy Adapter has-a adaptee Factory creates products

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Two dimensions that vary independently become two hierarchies joined by a reference.
  • Fixes class explosion: M × N becomes M + N.
  • Abstraction = what (high level); implementor = how (primitives).
  • vs Strategy: two growing hierarchies vs. one swappable algorithm. vs Adapter: up front vs. after the fact.
  • Real life: JDBC, SLF4J, AWT peers, Handler + Formatter.
abstract class Report { protected final ReportRenderer renderer; String generate() { return renderer.render(title(), columns(), rows()); } }
