docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: sometimes you can't, or shouldn't, hand clients the real object directly. It may be expensive to create (an 8 MB image), sensitive (a bank account), or in another process (a remote service). You want clients to use it as if it were the real thing, while something in between decides when, whether, and how the real object is used.

Formal definition (GoF):

Provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.

The common kinds of proxy:

Kind Controls Example below Virtual proxy When the real object is created (lazily) Example 1 Protection proxy Whether the caller may use it Example 2 Remote proxy Where it lives (another process or machine) Example 3 Caching proxy Reusing results Decorator page's challenge, Spring @Cacheable Logging / monitoring proxy Recording calls Coding challenge (dynamic proxy) Smart reference Reference counting, locking, lazy init of associations Hibernate lazy collections

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A company's receptionist

You want to meet the CEO. The receptionist (proxy) looks like the way in: you talk to them as if they were the office. They check whether you have an appointment (protection), call the CEO only when it's your turn (virtual), or connect you by video if the CEO is in another city (remote). The CEO's job doesn't change at all.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: classDiagram     class Subject {         <<interface>>         +request()     }     class RealSubject {         +request()     }     class Proxy {         -RealSubject real         +request()     }     class Client     Client --> Subject     Subject <|.. RealSubject     Subject <|.. Proxy     Proxy --> RealSubject : controls access Participant Responsibility Subject The interface clients use Real subject Does the actual work; contains no access-control code Proxy Same interface; decides when and whether to forward, and may add work around the call Client Can't tell (and shouldn't care) whether it holds the proxy or the real subject

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
public String withdraw(User user, String acc, long amount) {
    if (amount > 50_000 && !user.roles().contains("MANAGER")) throw new SecurityException();
    if (!user.roles().contains("TELLER") && !user.roles().contains("MANAGER")) throw new SecurityException();
    // ...actual business logic, mixed with security checks...
}
// Every method repeats checks. Someone adds a new method and forgets them.
  • Cross-cutting code mixed with business logic (security, laziness, networking).
  • Easy to forget in one method, which becomes a security hole.
  • Business classes become hard to test in isolation.

docs.title: Example 1: Lazy Posters on the Home Screen (Streaming) — Virtual Proxy
docs.text:
Scenario: A streaming app's home screen has rows of 40 titles each. High-resolution posters are 8 MB each to download and decode. Users usually see the first few tiles and scroll a little. Creating all posters up front means 320 MB of downloads per row, a slow start-up and wasted mobile data. Search and analytics only need the title, never the image.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant UI as Home screen participant P as LazyPoster (proxy) participant R as HighResPoster (real) UI->>P: new LazyPoster("Title 1") Note over P: nothing downloaded UI->>P: title() P-->>UI: "Title 1" (no download) UI->>P: render() P->>R: new HighResPoster(...) [8 MB download] P->>R: render() R-->>UI: pixels UI->>P: render() again P->>R: render() (already loaded)

Full Code:

LazyPoster.javaHighResPoster.javaPoster.javaHomeScreenDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

/** Virtual proxy: same interface, creates the real poster only when it is actually shown. */
public class LazyPoster implements Poster {

    private final String title;
    private HighResPoster real; // (1)!

    public LazyPoster(String title) {
        this.title = title;
    }

    @Override
    public String title() {
        return title; // (2)!
    }

    @Override
    public String render() {
        if (real == null) {
            real = new HighResPoster(title); // (3)!
        }
        return real.render();
    }
}
  1. The real subject starts as null: nothing expensive has happened yet.
  2. Cheap requests are answered by the proxy itself, without creating the real object.
  3. The real object is created on first use and then reused. For multi-threaded access, use the holder idiom or a lock (see Singleton).
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

/** Real subject: expensive to create (downloads and decodes an 8 MB image). */
public class HighResPoster implements Poster {

    private final String title;
    private final byte[] pixels;

    public HighResPoster(String title) {
        this.title = title;
        System.out.println("  [download] 8 MB poster for '" + title + "'");
        this.pixels = new byte[8 * 1024]; // scaled down for the demo
    }

    public String title() { return title; }

    public String render() { return "[poster: " + title + ", " + pixels.length / 1024 + "K px]"; }
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

public interface Poster {

    String title();

    String render();
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HomeScreenDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Streaming: Home Screen with 40 Titles ===");
        List<Poster> row = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 40; i++) {
            row.add(new LazyPoster("Title " + i));
        }
        System.out.println("Home screen built with " + row.size() + " posters (nothing downloaded yet)");

        System.out.println("User sees the first 3 tiles:");
        row.subList(0, 3).forEach(p -> System.out.println("  " + p.render()));
        System.out.println("User scrolls back to tile 1:");
        System.out.println("  " + row.get(0).render() + "  <- no second download");
        System.out.println("Search index uses titles only: " + row.get(39).title());
    }
}

Output:

=== Streaming: Home Screen with 40 Titles ===
Home screen built with 40 posters (nothing downloaded yet)
User sees the first 3 tiles:
  [download] 8 MB poster for 'Title 1'
  [poster: Title 1, 8K px]
  [download] 8 MB poster for 'Title 2'
  [poster: Title 2, 8K px]
  [download] 8 MB poster for 'Title 3'
  [poster: Title 3, 8K px]
User scrolls back to tile 1:
  [poster: Title 1, 8K px]  <- no second download
Search index uses titles only: Title 40

40 posters on the screen, 3 downloads. Scrolling back doesn't download again.

Why a virtual proxy here:

  • The real object is expensive and often never needed.
  • Clients (the UI) keep using the Poster interface unchanged.
  • This is exactly how Hibernate lazy loading works: your entity's getOrders() returns a proxy collection that queries the database on first access.

docs.title: Example 2: Role-Based Access at the Branch Counter (Banking) — Protection Proxy
docs.text:
Scenario: Bank branch software lets tellers check balances and make withdrawals up to INR 50,000; bigger withdrawals need a manager. Interns can't access accounts at all. The core account service is shared with ATMs and internet banking, which have their own rules, so it must contain no branch-specific security code. Auditors want access rules in one reviewable place.

Design:

flowchart LR T[Teller anita] --> P1[SecuredAccountService<br/>user = anita, TELLER] M[Manager vikram] --> P2[SecuredAccountService<br/>user = vikram, MANAGER] I[Intern sam] --> P3[SecuredAccountService<br/>user = sam, INTERN] P1 --> C[CoreAccountService<br/>pure business logic] P2 --> C P3 -. denied .-x C

Full Code:

SecuredAccountService.javaCoreAccountService.javaAccountService.javaBranchDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

import java.util.Set;

/** Protection proxy: checks the caller's roles before forwarding to the real service. */
public class SecuredAccountService implements AccountService {

    public record User(String name, Set<String> roles) {
    }

    private static final long TELLER_LIMIT_INR = 50_000;

    private final AccountService target;
    private final User user;

    public SecuredAccountService(AccountService target, User user) {
        this.target = target;
        this.user = user;
    }

    @Override
    public long balance(String accountNo) {
        require("TELLER", "MANAGER");
        return target.balance(accountNo);
    }

    @Override
    public String withdraw(String accountNo, long amountInr) {
        if (amountInr > TELLER_LIMIT_INR) {
            require("MANAGER"); // (1)!
        } else {
            require("TELLER", "MANAGER");
        }
        return target.withdraw(accountNo, amountInr);
    }

    private void require(String... anyOf) {
        for (String role : anyOf) {
            if (user.roles().contains(role)) {
                return;
            }
        }
        throw new SecurityException(user.name() + " lacks role " + String.join("/", anyOf)); // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Rules can depend on arguments, not just on the method: large withdrawals need a stronger role.
  2. Denials throw before the real subject is touched, so a denied call has no side effects.
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Real subject: pure business logic, no security code. */
public class CoreAccountService implements AccountService {

    private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>(Map.of("SB-1001", 250_000L));

    public long balance(String accountNo) {
        return balances.get(accountNo);
    }

    public String withdraw(String accountNo, long amount) {
        balances.merge(accountNo, -amount, Long::sum);
        return "withdrew INR " + amount + ", new balance INR " + balances.get(accountNo);
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

public interface AccountService {

    long balance(String accountNo);

    String withdraw(String accountNo, long amountInr);
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking;

import com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.SecuredAccountService.User;

import java.util.Set;

public class BranchDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: Branch Counter ===");
        AccountService core = new CoreAccountService();
        AccountService asTeller = new SecuredAccountService(core, new User("anita", Set.of("TELLER")));
        AccountService asManager = new SecuredAccountService(core, new User("vikram", Set.of("MANAGER")));
        AccountService asIntern = new SecuredAccountService(core, new User("sam", Set.of("INTERN")));

        attempt("Teller checks balance  ", () -> "INR " + asTeller.balance("SB-1001"));
        attempt("Teller withdraws 20,000", () -> asTeller.withdraw("SB-1001", 20_000));
        attempt("Teller withdraws 80,000", () -> asTeller.withdraw("SB-1001", 80_000));
        attempt("Manager withdraws 80,000", () -> asManager.withdraw("SB-1001", 80_000));
        attempt("Intern checks balance  ", () -> "INR " + asIntern.balance("SB-1001"));
    }

    private static void attempt(String label, java.util.function.Supplier<String> action) {
        try {
            System.out.println(label + " -> " + action.get());
        } catch (SecurityException e) {
            System.out.println(label + " -> DENIED (" + e.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: Branch Counter ===
Teller checks balance   -> INR 250000
Teller withdraws 20,000 -> withdrew INR 20000, new balance INR 230000
Teller withdraws 80,000 -> DENIED (anita lacks role MANAGER)
Manager withdraws 80,000 -> withdrew INR 80000, new balance INR 150000
Intern checks balance   -> DENIED (sam lacks role TELLER/MANAGER)

Why a protection proxy here:

  • Security is separated from business logic: CoreAccountService is reused by ATM and online channels with different proxies.
  • Access rules live in one auditable class.
  • In Spring, @PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER')") generates this kind of proxy for you.

docs.title: Example 3: Calling the Inventory Service (Logistics) — Remote Proxy
docs.text:
Scenario: An order service checks stock in the inventory service, which runs in another cluster. Order-service developers want to write inventory.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG") as if it were a local call. Behind it, the call must be marshalled into a request, sent over the network, and the response unmarshalled. Network failures must surface as a clear domain error (InventoryUnavailableException), not a raw IOException deep in business code.

Design:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant O as Order service code participant P as InventoryClientProxy (stub) participant N as Network (Transport) participant S as Inventory server O->>P: availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG") P->>P: marshal: "availableUnits|BLR-1|RICE-5KG" P->>N: send(request) N->>S: handle(request) S-->>N: "OK|120" N-->>P: "OK|120" P->>P: unmarshal: 120 P-->>O: 120

Full Code:

InventoryClientProxy.javaInventoryServer.javaInventoryApi + TransportRemoteDemo.java 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

import java.io.IOException;

/**
 * Remote proxy (a "client stub"): looks like a local InventoryApi, but marshals each
 * call into a network request and turns network failures into a clear domain error.
 */
public class InventoryClientProxy implements InventoryApi {

    public static class InventoryUnavailableException extends RuntimeException {
        public InventoryUnavailableException(String message, Throwable cause) {
            super(message, cause);
        }
    }

    private final Transport transport;

    public InventoryClientProxy(Transport transport) {
        this.transport = transport;
    }

    @Override
    public int availableUnits(String warehouse, String sku) {
        String request = "availableUnits|" + warehouse + "|" + sku; // (1)!
        try {
            String response = transport.send(request);
            String[] parts = response.split("\\|");
            if (!parts[0].equals("OK")) {
                throw new InventoryUnavailableException("Server error: " + response, null);
            }
            return Integer.parseInt(parts[1]); // (2)!
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new InventoryUnavailableException("Inventory service unreachable: " + e.getMessage(), e); // (3)!
        }
    }
}
  1. Marshalling: the method call becomes a message. Real stubs use JSON over HTTP, or Protobuf over gRPC.
  2. Unmarshalling the response back into a Java value.
  3. Transport errors become a domain exception. The caller learns "inventory is unavailable", not "socket closed".
package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

import java.util.Map;

/** The real subject, running in another process. Here it parses the wire format directly. */
public class InventoryServer implements InventoryApi {

    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = Map.of("BLR-1:RICE-5KG", 120, "BLR-1:OIL-1L", 0);
    private int calls;

    public int availableUnits(String warehouse, String sku) {
        return stock.getOrDefault(warehouse + ":" + sku, 0);
    }

    /** What the HTTP endpoint would do: decode, call, encode. */
    public String handle(String request) {
        calls++;
        String[] parts = request.split("\\|"); // "availableUnits|BLR-1|RICE-5KG"
        return "OK|" + availableUnits(parts[1], parts[2]);
    }

    public int calls() {
        return calls;
    }
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

/** The interface both the client and the server agree on. */
public interface InventoryApi {

    int availableUnits(String warehouse, String sku);
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

/** Network abstraction: sends a request string, receives a response string (HTTP/gRPC in real life). */
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Transport {

    String send(String request) throws java.io.IOException;
}

package com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote;

import com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote.InventoryClientProxy.InventoryUnavailableException;

import java.io.IOException;

public class RemoteDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Logistics: Order Service Calling the Inventory Service ===");
        InventoryServer server = new InventoryServer();
        Transport network = request -> {
            System.out.println("  [wire] -> " + request);
            String response = server.handle(request);
            System.out.println("  [wire] <- " + response);
            return response;
        };
        InventoryApi inventory = new InventoryClientProxy(network); // the order service only sees InventoryApi

        System.out.println("Rice in BLR-1: " + inventory.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG"));
        System.out.println("Oil in BLR-1 : " + inventory.availableUnits("BLR-1", "OIL-1L"));

        InventoryApi duringOutage = new InventoryClientProxy(request -> {
            throw new IOException("connect timed out after 2000 ms");
        });
        try {
            duringOutage.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG");
        } catch (InventoryUnavailableException e) {
            System.out.println("During outage: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("Server handled " + server.calls() + " calls");
    }
}

Output:

=== Logistics: Order Service Calling the Inventory Service ===
  [wire] -> availableUnits|BLR-1|RICE-5KG
  [wire] <- OK|120
Rice in BLR-1: 120
  [wire] -> availableUnits|BLR-1|OIL-1L
  [wire] <- OK|0
Oil in BLR-1 : 0
During outage: Inventory service unreachable: connect timed out after 2000 ms
Server handled 2 calls

Why a remote proxy here:

  • Location transparency: business code uses an interface, not HTTP.
  • Marshalling and error translation live in one generated or hand-written class.
  • This is what gRPC stubs, Spring Cloud OpenFeign and Spring 6 HTTP interface clients (@HttpExchange) generate for you.

Remote calls are not local calls

A remote proxy makes a network call look local, but it can fail, time out and be slow (the "fallacies of distributed computing"). Always add timeouts, retries for idempotent calls, and circuit breakers. Never call a remote proxy in a tight loop without thinking.

Unit Tests: ProxyTest.java (all three examples + challenge) 
package com.handbook.structural.proxy;

import com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.CoreAccountService;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.SecuredAccountService;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.dynamic.LoggingProxy;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote.InventoryClientProxy;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.remote.InventoryServer;
import com.handbook.structural.proxy.streaming.LazyPoster;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

class ProxyTest {

    @Test
    void lazyPosterDoesNotLoadForTitleOnly() {
        LazyPoster p = new LazyPoster("X");
        assertThat(p.title()).isEqualTo("X");
        assertThat(p.render()).contains("X");
    }

    @Test
    void protectionProxyEnforcesLimits() {
        var teller = new SecuredAccountService(new CoreAccountService(), new SecuredAccountService.User("t", Set.of("TELLER")));
        assertThat(teller.withdraw("SB-1001", 50_000)).contains("withdrew");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> teller.withdraw("SB-1001", 50_001)).isInstanceOf(SecurityException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void remoteProxyMarshalsCalls() {
        InventoryServer server = new InventoryServer();
        var client = new InventoryClientProxy(server::handle);
        assertThat(client.availableUnits("BLR-1", "RICE-5KG")).isEqualTo(120);
        assertThat(server.calls()).isEqualTo(1);
        var broken = new InventoryClientProxy(r -> "ERR|db down");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> broken.availableUnits("a", "b")).hasMessageContaining("db down");
    }

    @Test
    void dynamicProxyLogsAndRethrowsOriginalException() {
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
        var secured = new SecuredAccountService(new CoreAccountService(), new SecuredAccountService.User("x", Set.of()));
        var proxied = LoggingProxy.wrap((com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.AccountService) secured,
                com.handbook.structural.proxy.banking.AccountService.class, log::add);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> proxied.balance("SB-1001")).isInstanceOf(SecurityException.class);
        assertThat(log).singleElement().asString().contains("threw java.lang.SecurityException");
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Variations & Modern Java Take
docs.text:
Three ways to build proxies in Java:

Mechanism How Limits Hand-written (Examples 1–3) Implement the interface, forward calls One class per interface JDK dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) One InvocationHandler for any interface, generated at runtime (coding challenge) Interfaces only Bytecode subclassing (CGLIB, ByteBuddy) Generates a subclass at runtime Can't proxy final classes or methods; needs a non-private constructor

Spring AOP uses JDK proxies when your bean implements an interface and CGLIB subclasses otherwise (Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB: proxyTargetClass = true).

The self-invocation trap (Spring)

@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async work because callers hold a proxy. If a method calls another @Transactional method on this, the call bypasses the proxy, and the annotation is silently ignored. Fix: move the method to another bean, or inject the bean's own proxy. Almost every Spring interview at 5+ years asks about this.

docs.title: 7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Kind of proxy Spring AOP: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @Retryable, @PreAuthorize Protection / caching / smart proxies around beans Spring @Configuration classes CGLIB proxy so @Bean methods return singletons Spring Data repositories The interface you declare is implemented by a generated proxy Hibernate / JPA Lazy entity proxies (getReference), lazy collections (PersistentBag) gRPC, OpenFeign, Spring @HttpExchange, Java RMI Remote proxies (client stubs) JDK java.lang.reflect.Proxy; Collections.unmodifiableList (protection) Mockito Mocks and spies are runtime-generated proxies HikariCP ProxyConnection: close() returns the connection to the pool

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Controls access without changing the real subject Extra indirection; possible latency (remote) or complexity Separates cross-cutting concerns (security, laziness, remoting) Behavior can be surprising (self-invocation, lazy-init exceptions) Clients unchanged: same interface Dynamic proxies only work with interfaces; CGLIB can't handle final Enables lazy loading, caching, auditing transparently Debugging generated proxies is harder (stack traces, $Proxy12)

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Spring self-invocation

Calling a proxied method from inside the same bean bypasses the proxy. Transactions, caching and security silently don't apply.

LazyInitializationException

A Hibernate lazy proxy accessed after the session or transaction closed throws. Fetch what you need inside the transaction (fetch joins, entity graphs, DTO projections), and don't rely on Open Session in View.

Hiding expensive remote calls

for (Order o : orders) inventory.availableUnits(...) looks innocent but makes N network calls. Offer batch methods on remote interfaces.

Identity and equals

proxy == real is false, getClass() returns the proxy class, and Hibernate proxies may not be initialized when equals is called. Use IDs and instanceof carefully.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Proxies at every level of the stack:

Level Proxy Object Spring AOP, Hibernate lazy loading Process Sidecars (Envoy in Istio/Linkerd) intercept all traffic for mTLS, retries, metrics Network Reverse proxies (Nginx), API gateways, forward proxies, CDNs (caching proxies) Database PgBouncer, ProxySQL, RDS Proxy (connection pooling and routing)

The same trade-offs apply at each level: transparency vs. surprise, added latency, and a new failure point.

Designing remote interfaces for proxies. Coarse-grained operations (reserveItems(List<Item>)) instead of chatty ones; idempotency keys on writes; explicit timeouts and deadlines propagated across calls; versioned schemas (Protobuf field numbers).

Lazy loading strategy in JPA. Default @ManyToOne is eager (a common performance trap); set fetch = LAZY and fetch explicitly per use case with entity graphs or join fetches. Watch for N+1 queries caused by proxies initializing one by one. Enable Hibernate statistics in tests to catch them.

War story: the @Transactional that wasn't

A wallet service had transfer() call this.debit() and this.credit(), each annotated @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) to "isolate" them. transfer() itself wasn't transactional. Because of self-invocation, neither inner annotation applied: there was no transaction at all. When credit() failed on a constraint, debit() had already committed. Money vanished from wallets for 3 days before reconciliation caught it. Fix: @Transactional on transfer() (one transaction for both legs), inner methods moved to a separate LedgerService bean, and an integration test asserting rollback when credit fails. Lesson: annotations are proxies. If the call doesn't go through the proxy, the annotation doesn't exist.

docs.title: 11. Related Patterns & Comparisons
docs.text: Proxy Decorator Adapter Facade Interface Same as subject Same as component Different (converted) New, simpler Intent Control access Add behavior Make it fit Simplify a subsystem Who creates it Usually the framework/factory, hidden from the client Usually the client composes stacks Integration code Application code May skip the real call? Yes (deny, cache hit, not loaded yet) Rarely No N/A Lifecycle of real object Often manages it (lazy creation) Receives it ready-made Receives it Uses many

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Same interface, controls access: virtual (lazy), protection (security), remote (stub), caching, logging.
  • The real subject stays free of cross-cutting code.
  • Java: hand-written, java.lang.reflect.Proxy (interfaces), CGLIB/ByteBuddy (subclasses).
  • Spring: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize are proxies; self-invocation bypasses them.
  • vs Decorator: control access vs. add behavior.
T proxy = (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[]{iface}, (p, m, a) -> m.invoke(target, a));

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
• Make LazyPoster thread-safe without locking on every render() call.
  • Add a batch method availableUnits(String warehouse, List<String> skus) and update the remote proxy.
  • Reproduce the Spring self-invocation bug in a small Spring Boot app and fix it two ways.
  • Extend LoggingProxy to time each call and report slow calls (over 100 ms).

docs.title: Testing Patterns
docs.text:
Every pattern in this handbook ships with unit tests. This section is about the patterns inside those tests: how to replace dependencies, how to keep services compatible without a shared end-to-end environment, and how to create test data that makes each test's intent obvious.

Pattern Problem it solves Interview frequency Status Test Doubles Replace real dependencies with dummies, stubs, spies, mocks and fakes ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Contract Testing Catch breaking API and event changes between services before deploy ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅ Test Data Builder & Object Mother Readable, robust test setup with defaults, personas and generated data ⭐⭐⭐ ✅

docs.title: Where each pattern sits in the test pyramid
docs.text: flowchart TB     E2E["End-to-end smoke tests (few)"]     CT["Contract tests between services"]     IT["Integration tests: adapters vs real infrastructure (Testcontainers)"]     UT["Unit tests: domain + application with test doubles (many)"]     E2E --- CT --- IT --- UT     TD[Test Data Builders] -.-> UT     TD -.-> IT     DBL[Test Doubles] -.-> UT     CON[Contract Testing] -.-> CT

docs.title: Suggested learning order
docs.text:
1. Test Doubles: the vocabulary every testing conversation uses.
  2. Test Data Builder & Object Mother: make those tests readable.
  3. Contract Testing: scale testing across teams and services.

The one-sentence interview answer

"I unit-test domain and application code with fakes and stubs built from test data builders, reserve mocks for outgoing side effects, test adapters against real infrastructure with Testcontainers, protect service boundaries with consumer-driven contracts and can-i-deploy, and keep only a handful of end-to-end smoke tests."

Domain Events Start: Test Doubles

docs.title: Contract Testing
docs.text:
🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced Testing Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A contract test checks that a provider's API (or event) still satisfies what each consumer actually relies on. Consumers write the expectations; the provider verifies them in its own CI; a broker answers "can I deploy this version?". Use it between services owned by different teams, instead of slow, flaky end-to-end test environments. Match on shape and type, not exact values.

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: the inventory team renames available to availableQty in a "harmless cleanup". Their unit tests pass. The order service's unit tests pass too (they use a stub with the old field). Both deploy, and order placement breaks in production. The usual fix, a shared end-to-end environment, is slow, flaky and always on the wrong versions.

Definition (Martin Fowler / Ian Robinson, Consumer-Driven Contracts):

Each consumer captures its expectations of a provider in a contract. The provider runs all consumers' contracts as part of its build, so it knows immediately when a change would break a consumer.

What a contract covers:

Kind Consumer expectation Provider verification HTTP "GET /stock/MILK-1L returns 200 with sku (string), available (integer)" Replay the request against the real provider app, check the response Messages "payment.captured has paymentId, amountPaise (long)" Check the producer's schema/sample against every consumer's needs Provider states "Given SKU MILK-1L has stock" Set up that data before replaying

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
A plug and a socket

An appliance maker (consumer) states, "my plug has three round pins, 5 A". The building's electrician (provider) checks every socket against the plugs actually in use before renovating. Nobody needs to plug in every appliance in the building to know the renovation is safe.

docs.title: 3. Structure
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     autonumber     participant C as Consumer CI (order-service)     participant B as Contract broker     participant P as Provider CI (inventory-service)     participant D as Deploy pipeline     C->>C: consumer tests against a mock built from the contract     C->>B: publish contract (order-service 3.4.0)     P->>B: fetch contracts for inventory-service     P->>P: verify each interaction against the real app     P->>B: publish results (inventory 1.9 vs order 3.4.0: FAIL)     D->>B: can-i-deploy inventory 1.9 to prod?     B-->>D: NO Participant Responsibility Consumer Writes interactions (request + expected response shape + provider state); tests itself against a generated stub Contract Versioned artefact (Pact JSON, Spring Cloud Contract DSL, AsyncAPI/Avro schema) Provider Verifies all consumers' contracts in its build, with provider-state setup Broker Stores contracts and verification results; answers can-i-deploy per environment

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
Shared "integration" environment with 40 services
→ deploy your branch, run 600 end-to-end tests (45 minutes)
→ 7 fail because another team's service is broken today
→ re-run; 3 different failures; merge anyway
  • Slow and flaky; failures are often someone else's.
  • Tests the versions that happen to be deployed, not the ones going to prod.
  • Stubs in consumer unit tests silently drift from the real provider.

docs.title: Example 1: Order Service ↔ Inventory Service (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: The order service calls GET /stock/{sku} before reserving stock. Its team writes a contract with two interactions: a known SKU (needs sku, available as an integer, updatedAt as an ISO timestamp) and an unknown SKU (404). The inventory team verifies the contract in CI. When v1.9 renames available, verification fails in their pipeline.

Design:

flowchart LR O["order-service team<br/>writes contract"] --> K[(Contract)] K --> V1["inventory v1.8 verification: PASS"] K --> V2["inventory v1.9 verification: FAIL<br/>missing field 'available'"]

Full Code:

Contract.javaInventoryContractDemo.java 
package com.handbook.testing.contract.core;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** A tiny Pact-like consumer-driven contract: interactions written by the consumer, verified against the provider. */
public final class Contract {

    /** Match by TYPE or pattern, not by exact value, so provider test data can differ. */
    public sealed interface Matcher permits AnyString, AnyInteger, Regex, Exactly {
        boolean matches(Object actual);
    }

    public record AnyString() implements Matcher {
        public boolean matches(Object a) { return a instanceof String; }
        public String toString() { return "a string"; }
    }

    public record AnyInteger() implements Matcher {
        public boolean matches(Object a) { return a instanceof Integer || a instanceof Long; }
        public String toString() { return "an integer"; }
    }

    public record Regex(String pattern) implements Matcher {
        public boolean matches(Object a) { return a instanceof String s && Pattern.matches(pattern, s); }
        public String toString() { return "matching /" + pattern + "/"; }
    }

    public record Exactly(Object value) implements Matcher {
        public boolean matches(Object a) { return value.equals(a); }
        public String toString() { return "exactly " + value; }
    }

    public record Interaction(String description, String providerState, String path, int status, Map<String, Matcher> body) { }

    private final String consumer;
    private final String provider;
    private final List<Interaction> interactions = new ArrayList<>();

    public Contract(String consumer, String provider) {
        this.consumer = consumer;
        this.provider = provider;
    }

    public Contract uponReceiving(Interaction i) {
        interactions.add(i);
        return this;
    }

    public record Response(int status, Map<String, Object> body) { }

    /** Provider-side verification: set up each provider state, replay the request, check the response. */
    public List<String> verify(Consumer<String> setUpState, Function<String, Response> providerApp) {
        List<String> report = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Interaction i : interactions) {
            setUpState.accept(i.providerState()); // (1)!
            Response r = providerApp.apply(i.path());
            List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
            if (r.status() != i.status()) {
                problems.add("status " + r.status() + " != " + i.status());
            }
            new java.util.TreeMap<>(i.body()).forEach((field, matcher) -> { // (2)!
                Object actual = r.body().get(field);
                if (actual == null) {
                    problems.add("missing field '" + field + "'");
                } else if (!matcher.matches(actual)) {
                    problems.add("'" + field + "' = " + actual + " is not " + matcher);
                }
            });
            report.add((problems.isEmpty() ? "PASS " : "FAIL ") + consumer + " -> " + provider + ": " + i.description()
                    + (problems.isEmpty() ? "" : " " + problems));
        }
        return report;
    }
}
  1. Provider states let each interaction set up the data it needs ("SKU MILK-1L has stock"), so contracts don't depend on whatever happens to be in a shared database.
  2. Each field is checked with a matcher: present, right type or pattern. Fields the consumer doesn't mention can change freely.
package com.handbook.testing.contract.grocery;

import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.AnyInteger;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.AnyString;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.Interaction;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.Regex;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.Response;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class InventoryContractDemo {

    static final Map<String, Integer> STOCK = new HashMap<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Order Service's Contract with the Inventory Service ===");
        Contract contract = new Contract("order-service", "inventory-service") // written by the ORDER team
                .uponReceiving(new Interaction("stock for a known SKU", "SKU MILK-1L has stock",
                        "/stock/MILK-1L", 200, Map.of("sku", new AnyString(), "available", new AnyInteger(),
                        "updatedAt", new Regex("\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}T.*Z"))))
                .uponReceiving(new Interaction("unknown SKU", "SKU NOPE does not exist", "/stock/NOPE", 404, Map.of()));

        System.out.println("Provider v1.8 (current):");
        contract.verify(InventoryContractDemo::state, provider("available")).forEach(l -> System.out.println("  " + l));
        System.out.println("Provider v1.9 (renames 'available' to 'availableQty' in a 'harmless cleanup'):");
        contract.verify(InventoryContractDemo::state, provider("availableQty")).forEach(l -> System.out.println("  " + l));
        System.out.println("v1.9 fails in the INVENTORY team's CI, before it can break order placement in production.");
    }

    static void state(String providerState) { // provider states set up the data each interaction needs
        STOCK.clear();
        if (providerState.equals("SKU MILK-1L has stock")) {
            STOCK.put("MILK-1L", 37);
        }
    }

    static Function<String, Response> provider(String quantityField) {
        return path -> {
            String sku = path.substring("/stock/".length());
            Integer qty = STOCK.get(sku);
            if (qty == null) {
                return new Response(404, Map.of("error", "unknown sku"));
            }
            Map<String, Object> body = new LinkedHashMap<>();
            body.put("sku", sku);
            body.put(quantityField, qty);
            body.put("updatedAt", "2026-10-02T09:15:00Z");
            return new Response(200, body);
        };
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Order Service's Contract with the Inventory Service ===
Provider v1.8 (current):
  PASS order-service -> inventory-service: stock for a known SKU
  PASS order-service -> inventory-service: unknown SKU
Provider v1.9 (renames 'available' to 'availableQty' in a 'harmless cleanup'):
  FAIL order-service -> inventory-service: stock for a known SKU [missing field 'available']
  PASS order-service -> inventory-service: unknown SKU
v1.9 fails in the INVENTORY team's CI, before it can break order placement in production.

Why contract testing here:

  • The breaking change is caught before merge, in the team that made it.
  • Only fields the consumer uses are protected; providers can add or change the rest.
  • Runs in seconds against the provider app, no shared environment.

docs.title: Example 2: Evolving a Payment Event (Payments)
docs.text:
Scenario: payments.payment.captured.v1 is consumed by the ledger, notifications and analytics. The payments team wants to add the payment method, and later someone proposes renaming amountPaise to amount (decimal). Each consumer declares the fields it reads; the producer's new schema is checked against all of them before release.

Design:

flowchart LR S2["v2: + method (optional)"] --> C{Check against consumers} S3["v3: amountPaise → amount (decimal)"] --> C C -->|v2| OK["compatible"] C -->|v3| BR["BREAKING: ledger, analytics"]

Full Code:

SchemaCompatibility.javaPaymentEventDemo.java 
package com.handbook.testing.contract.messages;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Message contracts: can every existing consumer still read what the new producer schema emits? */
public final class SchemaCompatibility {

    public record Field(String type, boolean required) { }

    /** What a consumer actually reads from the event (its contract). */
    public record ConsumerNeeds(String consumer, Map<String, String> fields) { }

    public static List<String> check(Map<String, Field> producerSchema, List<ConsumerNeeds> consumers) {
        List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ConsumerNeeds c : consumers) {
            new java.util.TreeMap<>(c.fields()).forEach((name, type) -> {
                Field f = producerSchema.get(name);
                if (f == null) {
                    problems.add(c.consumer() + " reads '" + name + "' which no longer exists"); // (1)!
                } else if (!f.type().equals(type)) {
                    problems.add(c.consumer() + " expects '" + name + "' as " + type + " but it is " + f.type()); // (2)!
                } else if (!f.required()) {
                    problems.add(c.consumer() + " relies on '" + name + "' which is now optional");
                }
            });
        }
        return problems;
    }
}
  1. A field a consumer reads has disappeared: breaking.
  2. A field changed type: breaking (even if the name is the same).
package com.handbook.testing.contract.messages;

import com.handbook.testing.contract.messages.SchemaCompatibility.ConsumerNeeds;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.messages.SchemaCompatibility.Field;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class PaymentEventDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Payments: Evolving the payments.payment.captured.v1 Event Safely ===");
        List<ConsumerNeeds> consumers = List.of(
                new ConsumerNeeds("ledger", Map.of("paymentId", "string", "amountPaise", "long", "currency", "string")),
                new ConsumerNeeds("notifications", Map.of("paymentId", "string", "customerId", "string")),
                new ConsumerNeeds("analytics", Map.of("paymentId", "string", "amountPaise", "long")));

        Map<String, Field> v1 = schema("amountPaise", new Field("long", true), null, null);
        Map<String, Field> v2AddOptional = schema("amountPaise", new Field("long", true), "method", new Field("string", false));
        Map<String, Field> v3Breaking = new LinkedHashMap<>(schema("amount", new Field("decimal", true), null, null));

        report("v1 (today)", v1, consumers);
        report("v2 adds optional 'method'", v2AddOptional, consumers);
        report("v3 'amountPaise' -> 'amount' as decimal", v3Breaking, consumers);
        System.out.println("Breaking changes go to a NEW topic/version (...captured.v2), published alongside v1 during migration.");
    }

    static Map<String, Field> schema(String amountName, Field amount, String extraName, Field extra) {
        Map<String, Field> s = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        s.put("paymentId", new Field("string", true));
        s.put("customerId", new Field("string", true));
        s.put(amountName, amount);
        s.put("currency", new Field("string", true));
        if (extraName != null) {
            s.put(extraName, extra);
        }
        return s;
    }

    static void report(String label, Map<String, Field> schema, List<ConsumerNeeds> consumers) {
        List<String> problems = SchemaCompatibility.check(schema, consumers);
        System.out.println(label + " -> " + (problems.isEmpty() ? "compatible with all 3 consumers" : "BREAKING: " + problems));
    }
}

Output:

=== Payments: Evolving the payments.payment.captured.v1 Event Safely ===
v1 (today) -> compatible with all 3 consumers
v2 adds optional 'method' -> compatible with all 3 consumers
v3 'amountPaise' -> 'amount' as decimal -> BREAKING: [ledger reads 'amountPaise' which no longer exists, analytics reads 'amountPaise' which no longer exists]
Breaking changes go to a NEW topic/version (...captured.v2), published alongside v1 during migration.

Why message contracts here:

  • Events have no request/response cycle, so breakages surface late (in a consumer's logs, hours later).
  • Schema registries (Avro/Protobuf with BACKWARD compatibility) enforce the generic rules; consumer contracts add "what each consumer actually reads".
  • Breaking changes become a planned new version, not an incident.

docs.title: Example 3: "Can I Deploy?" for the Accounts API (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: The accounts API is consumed by the mobile BFF, statements and loans. Version 9.0.0 removes branchCode. Loans 1.3.0 (in prod) still reads it; loans 1.4.0 (fixed) isn't in prod yet. The broker records which consumer versions each provider version was verified against, and the deploy pipeline asks whether 9.0.0 is safe for the versions actually in prod.

Design:

flowchart LR M["Verification matrix<br/>accounts 9.0.0 × mobile-bff 4.2.0 ✅<br/>× statements 2.7.1 ✅<br/>× loans 1.3.0 ❌<br/>× loans 1.4.0 ✅"] --> Q{"prod runs loans 1.3.0"} Q --> N["can-i-deploy: NO"] Q -. "after loans 1.4.0 ships" .-> Y["can-i-deploy: YES"]

Full Code:

ContractBroker.javaCanIDeployDemo.java 
package com.handbook.testing.contract.broker;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** The "can I deploy?" question: is this provider version verified against every consumer version in that environment? */
public final class ContractBroker {

    public record Verification(String consumer, String consumerVersion, String provider, String providerVersion, boolean passed) { }

    private final List<Verification> results = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Map<String, Map<String, String>> deployed = new HashMap<>(); // env -> app -> version

    public void record(Verification v) {
        results.add(v);
    }

    public void deployed(String env, String app, String version) {
        deployed.computeIfAbsent(env, e -> new HashMap<>()).put(app, version);
    }

    public String canIDeploy(String provider, String version, String env, List<String> consumers) {
        List<String> blockers = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String consumer : consumers) {
            String consumerVersion = deployed.getOrDefault(env, Map.of()).get(consumer); // (1)!
            boolean ok = results.stream().anyMatch(r -> r.consumer().equals(consumer) && r.consumerVersion().equals(consumerVersion)
                    && r.provider().equals(provider) && r.providerVersion().equals(version) && r.passed());
            if (!ok) {
                blockers.add(consumer + "@" + consumerVersion);
            }
        }
        return blockers.isEmpty() ? "YES" : "NO, not verified against " + blockers; // (2)!
    }
}
  1. The check uses the consumer versions deployed in the target environment, not the latest ones.
  2. The answer names the blockers, so the provider team knows who to coordinate with.
package com.handbook.testing.contract.broker;

import com.handbook.testing.contract.broker.ContractBroker.Verification;

import java.util.List;

public class CanIDeployDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: 'Can I Deploy?' for the Accounts API ===");
        ContractBroker broker = new ContractBroker();
        broker.deployed("prod", "mobile-bff", "4.2.0");
        broker.deployed("prod", "statements", "2.7.1");
        broker.deployed("prod", "loans", "1.3.0");

        broker.record(new Verification("mobile-bff", "4.2.0", "accounts-api", "9.0.0", true));
        broker.record(new Verification("statements", "2.7.1", "accounts-api", "9.0.0", true));
        broker.record(new Verification("loans", "1.3.0", "accounts-api", "9.0.0", false)); // loans still reads 'branchCode'
        broker.record(new Verification("loans", "1.4.0", "accounts-api", "9.0.0", true));  // fixed, but not in prod yet

        List<String> consumers = List.of("mobile-bff", "statements", "loans");
        System.out.println("accounts-api 9.0.0 -> prod? " + broker.canIDeploy("accounts-api", "9.0.0", "prod", consumers));
        broker.deployed("prod", "loans", "1.4.0");
        System.out.println("after loans 1.4.0 ships -> prod? " + broker.canIDeploy("accounts-api", "9.0.0", "prod", consumers));
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: 'Can I Deploy?' for the Accounts API ===
accounts-api 9.0.0 -> prod? NO, not verified against [loans@1.3.0]
after loans 1.4.0 ships -> prod? YES

Why a broker here:

  • Independent deploys need a precise answer for this environment's versions.
  • Coordination becomes explicit: ship the consumer fix first, then the provider.
  • Pact Broker / PactFlow provide exactly this matrix and the can-i-deploy CLI.
Unit Tests: ContractTestingTest.java 
package com.handbook.testing;

import com.handbook.testing.contract.broker.ContractBroker;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.broker.ContractBroker.Verification;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.AnyInteger;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.Interaction;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.core.Contract.Response;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.messages.SchemaCompatibility;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.messages.SchemaCompatibility.ConsumerNeeds;
import com.handbook.testing.contract.messages.SchemaCompatibility.Field;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class ContractTestingTest {

    @Test
    void missingFieldFailsVerification() {
        Contract c = new Contract("a", "b").uponReceiving(new Interaction("x", "s", "/x", 200, Map.of("n", new AnyInteger())));
        assertThat(c.verify(s -> { }, p -> new Response(200, Map.of("m", 1)))).singleElement().asString().startsWith("FAIL");
        assertThat(c.verify(s -> { }, p -> new Response(200, Map.of("n", 5)))).singleElement().asString().startsWith("PASS");
    }

    @Test
    void addingAnOptionalFieldIsCompatibleRemovingOneIsNot() {
        List<ConsumerNeeds> consumers = List.of(new ConsumerNeeds("c", Map.of("id", "string")));
        assertThat(SchemaCompatibility.check(Map.of("id", new Field("string", true), "extra", new Field("int", false)), consumers)).isEmpty();
        assertThat(SchemaCompatibility.check(Map.of("ident", new Field("string", true)), consumers)).hasSize(1);
    }

    @Test
    void cannotDeployWithoutVerificationAgainstDeployedConsumers() {
        ContractBroker b = new ContractBroker();
        b.deployed("prod", "c", "1");
        b.record(new Verification("c", "2", "p", "9", true));
        assertThat(b.canIDeploy("p", "9", "prod", List.of("c"))).startsWith("NO");
        b.deployed("prod", "c", "2");
        assertThat(b.canIDeploy("p", "9", "prod", List.of("c"))).isEqualTo("YES");
    }
}

docs.text: Where Contract testing Pact Pact JVM (JUnit 5), Pact Broker / PactFlow, pact-broker can-i-deploy Spring Spring Cloud Contract (contracts → provider tests + WireMock stubs for consumers) Schema registries Confluent / Apicurio compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) OpenAPI oasdiff / openapi-diff breaking-change checks in CI gRPC buf breaking for Protobuf changes

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Catches integration breaks in seconds, before merge Teams must adopt it on both sides Replaces most slow, flaky E2E tests Contracts cover the interface, not end-to-end business flows Providers know exactly which fields consumers use Provider-state setup takes effort Enables safe independent deploys (can-i-deploy) Another piece of infrastructure (broker) to run

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Exact-value contracts

Asserting pricePaise == 28500 fails whenever the provider's test data changes, which teaches teams to ignore failures (coding challenge). Contract the shape; test values in unit tests.

Using contracts as functional tests

"Order total is correct after a 10% coupon" is business behaviour; test it in the provider's own tests. Contracts check that the conversation is understood.

Consumers over-specifying

Listing every field "just in case" freezes the provider's API. Include only what the consumer reads.

Skipping can-i-deploy

Verifying contracts but deploying without checking the matrix for the target environment still lets incompatible versions meet in production.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Where it fits. Unit tests with doubles inside a service; integration tests with Testcontainers for adapters; contract tests between services; a handful of E2E smoke tests for critical journeys. Contracts are what keep the consumer's stubs honest.

Versioning and branches. Tag contracts and verifications with git SHA and branch; use "pending pacts" so a new consumer expectation doesn't break the provider's main build before the feature is implemented; use "WIP pacts" to verify feature branches.

Events at scale. Combine a schema registry (generic compatibility rules) with consumer contracts (actual field usage). Treat a breaking change as a new event version published in parallel during migration, then retire the old one when no consumer contracts reference it.

War story: the field nobody knew was used

A banking platform removed branchCode from the accounts API because "no one uses it any more". The loans service used it to route documents. Shared-environment E2E tests didn't cover that path. Loan document generation failed for three days before anyone noticed. Fix: consumer-driven contracts for all 14 consumers of the accounts API, verification in the provider's CI, and can-i-deploy as a required pipeline step. Lesson: only consumers know what they depend on. Let them write it down.

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Consumers write expectations; providers verify them in CI.
  • Match shape and type, not exact values.
  • Provider states set up data per interaction.
  • Broker + can-i-deploy for the target environment's versions.
  • Events: schema registry + consumer field contracts; breaking change = new version.
new PactDslJsonBody().stringType("sku").integerType("available")   // shape, not values

Test Doubles Next: Test Data Builder & Object Mother

docs.title: Test Data Builder & Object Mother
docs.text:
🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate Testing Interview frequency ⭐⭐⭐

TL;DR

A Test Data Builder creates test objects with sensible defaults, so each test sets only the fields that matter to it (anOrder().express().build()). An Object Mother adds named, realistic personas on top (aYoungDriverInMumbai()). Use them whenever test setup is longer than the test, or when adding a constructor parameter breaks dozens of tests.

docs.title: See It in Motion
docs.text: Press Play to watch the calls travel between objects, or step through with Next and Back. Switch to Without it to see what goes wrong without the pattern. Open the full explorer

docs.title: 1. Intent & Problem It Solves
docs.text:
The problem in plain English: Order has nine fields. A delivery-fee test only cares about the subtotal and "express", but has to write new Order("O1", "C1", "560034", "18:00", "UPI", true, false, List.of(...), null). A reader can't tell which values matter. When a tenth field is added, 140 tests stop compiling.

Definitions:

Test Data Builder (Nat Pryce; Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests): a builder with safe default values for every field, and methods to override just the ones a test cares about.

Object Mother (Peter Schuh & Stephanie Punke, ThoughtWorks): a factory of example objects, each representing a meaningful, named scenario.

Test Data Builder Object Mother Gives you Defaults + fluent overrides Named, ready-made personas Flexibility High: any combination Low on its own (fixed shapes) Readability "What's different in this test" "Which business scenario this is" Best together The mother returns builders, so tests can tweak a persona

docs.title: 2. Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Ordering a thali

The restaurant's standard thali (defaults) comes with dal, rice, two sabzis and a roti. You only say what's different: "extra roti, no sweet" (overrides). The menu also lists named thalis, "Gujarati", "Punjabi" (the Object Mother's personas), which you can still customise.

docs.title: 4. Naive Approach (Without the Pattern)
docs.text:
@Test void expressSmallOrderFee() {
    Order o = new Order("O1", "C1", "560034", "Today 18:00-19:00", "UPI", true, false,
                        List.of(new Line("BASKET", 1, 30_000)), null);      // which of these matter?
    assertThat(o.deliveryFeePaise()).isEqualTo(5_500);
}
  • Noise hides the one or two values the test is about.
  • Every constructor change breaks every test.
  • Copy-pasted setups drift and carry irrelevant, sometimes invalid, values.

docs.title: Example 1: Delivery-Fee Tests with a Builder (Grocery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Delivery fee rules: INR 25 below INR 499, free above it, +INR 30 for express, and always free for a customer's first order. Each test should state its case in one line. The builder supplies a valid customer, pincode, slot, payment method and basket by default.

Design:

flowchart LR D["defaults: CUST-1, 560034, UPI, MILK-1L…"] --> B[OrderBuilder] T1["withSubtotal(30_000)"] --> B T2["express()"] --> B T3["firstOrder()"] --> B B --> O[Order]

Full Code:

OrderBuilder.javaOrder.javaBuilderDemo.java 
package com.handbook.testing.testdata.grocery;

import com.handbook.testing.testdata.grocery.Order.Line;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Test Data Builder: every field has a sensible default; tests override only what matters to them. */
public final class OrderBuilder {

    private String id = "ORD-1";
    private String customerId = "CUST-1";
    private String pincode = "560034";
    private String slot = "Today 18:00-19:00";
    private String paymentMethod = "UPI";
    private boolean express = false;
    private boolean firstOrder = false;
    private final List<Line> lines = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Line("MILK-1L", 1, 6_800))); // (1)!
    private String coupon = null;

    public static OrderBuilder anOrder() { // (2)!
        return new OrderBuilder();
    }

    public OrderBuilder express() { this.express = true; return this; }

    public OrderBuilder firstOrder() { this.firstOrder = true; return this; }

    public OrderBuilder withSubtotal(long paise) { // (3)!
        lines.clear();
        lines.add(new Line("BASKET", 1, paise));
        return this;
    }

    public OrderBuilder withCoupon(String code) { this.coupon = code; return this; }

    public Order build() {
        return new Order(id, customerId, pincode, slot, paymentMethod, express, firstOrder, List.copyOf(lines), coupon);
    }
}
  1. Valid defaults for every field: an order built with no overrides is a realistic, valid order.
  2. A static entry point so tests read as sentences: anOrder().express().build().
  3. Domain-level overrides (withSubtotal) rather than raw setters for every field.
package com.handbook.testing.testdata.grocery;

import java.util.List;

/** Production type with many fields, most irrelevant to any single test. */
public record Order(String id, String customerId, String pincode, String slot, String paymentMethod,
                    boolean expressDelivery, boolean firstOrder, List<Line> lines, String couponCode) {

    public record Line(String sku, int qty, long unitPaise) { }

    public long subtotalPaise() {
        return lines.stream().mapToLong(l -> l.qty() * l.unitPaise()).sum();
    }

    /** The rule under test: delivery fee. */
    public long deliveryFeePaise() {
        if (firstOrder) {
            return 0;
        }
        long base = subtotalPaise() >= 49_900 ? 0 : 2_500;
        return base + (expressDelivery ? 3_000 : 0);
    }
}

package com.handbook.testing.testdata.grocery;

import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.grocery.OrderBuilder.anOrder;

public class BuilderDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Grocery: Delivery-Fee Tests That Say Only What Matters ===");
        print("small order           ", anOrder().withSubtotal(30_000).build());
        print("order above INR 499   ", anOrder().withSubtotal(50_000).build());
        print("small + express       ", anOrder().withSubtotal(30_000).express().build());
        print("first order + express ", anOrder().withSubtotal(30_000).express().firstOrder().build());
        System.out.println("Each case sets 1-3 fields; the other 6 fields of Order come from defaults.");
    }

    private static void print(String label, Order o) {
        System.out.println(label + "-> fee INR " + o.deliveryFeePaise() / 100);
    }
}

Output:

=== Grocery: Delivery-Fee Tests That Say Only What Matters ===
small order           -> fee INR 25
order above INR 499   -> fee INR 0
small + express       -> fee INR 55
first order + express -> fee INR 0
Each case sets 1-3 fields; the other 6 fields of Order come from defaults.

Why a builder here:

  • Each test shows only its difference from a normal order.
  • Adding a field to Order means changing one builder, not 140 tests.
  • Defaults are valid, so tests don't accidentally exercise validation paths.

docs.title: Example 2: Driver Personas with an Object Mother (Insurance)
docs.text:
Scenario: Underwriters talk about "young drivers in metro cities", "experienced safe drivers" and "high-risk drivers". Premium tests use those exact personas, so business people can read them. Because each persona returns a builder, a test can still tweak one detail ("young driver in Mumbai, with one claim").

Design:

flowchart LR M["Drivers (object mother)"] --> Y["aYoungDriverInMumbai()"] M --> S["anExperiencedSafeDriver()"] M --> H["aHighRiskDriver()"] Y -->|".claims(1)"| Y1["young driver, 1 claim"]

Full Code:

Drivers.javaPremiumCalculator.javaPersonasDemo.java 
package com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance;

import java.time.LocalDate;

/** Object Mother: named, realistic personas for the domain, built on top of a builder. */
public final class Drivers {

    public record Driver(String name, LocalDate born, String city, int claimsLast3Years, int yearsLicensed, String vehicle) { }

    public static final class DriverBuilder {
        private String name = "Test Driver";
        private LocalDate born = LocalDate.of(1990, 1, 1);
        private String city = "Pune";
        private int claims = 0;
        private int yearsLicensed = 10;
        private String vehicle = "hatchback";

        public DriverBuilder born(LocalDate d) { born = d; return this; }
        public DriverBuilder city(String c) { city = c; return this; }
        public DriverBuilder claims(int n) { claims = n; return this; }
        public DriverBuilder yearsLicensed(int y) { yearsLicensed = y; return this; }
        public DriverBuilder vehicle(String v) { vehicle = v; return this; }
        public DriverBuilder named(String n) { name = n; return this; }
        public Driver build() { return new Driver(name, born, city, claims, yearsLicensed, vehicle); }
    }

    // ---- The mother: personas the business team actually talks about ----

    public static DriverBuilder aYoungDriverInMumbai() { // (1)!
        return new DriverBuilder().named("Young driver").born(LocalDate.of(2005, 6, 1)).city("Mumbai").yearsLicensed(1);
    }

    public static DriverBuilder anExperiencedSafeDriver() {
        return new DriverBuilder().named("Safe driver").born(LocalDate.of(1978, 3, 9)).yearsLicensed(25);
    }

    public static DriverBuilder aHighRiskDriver() {
        return new DriverBuilder().named("High-risk driver").claims(3).vehicle("sports");
    }

    private Drivers() {
    }
}
  1. Personas return a builder, not a finished object, which avoids the classic Object Mother problem of dozens of near-duplicate factory methods.
package com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance;

import com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.Driver;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.Period;

public final class PremiumCalculator {

    public static long annualPremiumPaise(Driver d, LocalDate today) {
        long premium = 900_000; // INR 9,000 base
        int age = Period.between(d.born(), today).getYears();
        if (age < 25) premium += 450_000;
        if (d.yearsLicensed() >= 20) premium -= 150_000;
        premium += d.claimsLast3Years() * 300_000L;
        if (d.city().equals("Mumbai") || d.city().equals("Delhi")) premium += 120_000;
        if (d.vehicle().equals("sports")) premium += 500_000;
        return premium;
    }

    private PremiumCalculator() {
    }
}

package com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance;

import com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.Driver;

import java.time.LocalDate;

import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.aHighRiskDriver;
import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.aYoungDriverInMumbai;
import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.anExperiencedSafeDriver;

public class PersonasDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Insurance: Premium Tests Written with Personas ===");
        LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 1);
        for (Driver d : new Driver[] {
                aYoungDriverInMumbai().build(),
                anExperiencedSafeDriver().build(),
                aHighRiskDriver().build(),
                aYoungDriverInMumbai().claims(1).named("Young driver, 1 claim").build()}) { // persona + tweak
            System.out.printf("%-22s -> INR %,d%n", d.name(), PremiumCalculator.annualPremiumPaise(d, today) / 100);
        }
        System.out.println("Personas read like the underwriting guide; builders let a test tweak one detail.");
    }
}

Output:

=== Insurance: Premium Tests Written with Personas ===
Young driver           -> INR 14,700
Safe driver            -> INR 7,500
High-risk driver       -> INR 23,000
Young driver, 1 claim  -> INR 17,700
Personas read like the underwriting guide; builders let a test tweak one detail.

Why an object mother here:

  • Tests speak the business vocabulary, which makes them reviewable by domain experts.
  • Persona definitions live in one place; when underwriting redefines "young", one method changes.
  • Builders keep the mother small and flexible.

docs.title: Example 3: Generated, Reproducible Data (Banking)
docs.text:
Scenario: A ledger must satisfy one invariant: money is never created or destroyed, so all balances sum to zero. Hand-written examples miss edge cases, so the test generates 10,000 random valid transfers from a seed. A buggy version that rounds large credits down is caught, and the seed is printed so the exact failing data can be replayed.

Design:

flowchart LR S["seed 20261101"] --> G["RandomTransfers.generate(seed, 10_000)"] G --> L1["correct ledger: Σ = 0 ✅"] G --> L2["buggy ledger: Σ = −2532 ❌ → replay with the same seed"]

Full Code:

RandomTransfers.javaLedgerPropertyDemo.java 
package com.handbook.testing.testdata.ledger;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;

/** Generated test data: many random-but-valid transfers from a SEED, so any failure can be replayed exactly. */
public final class RandomTransfers {

    public record Transfer(String from, String to, long paise) { }

    public static List<Transfer> generate(long seed, int count, List<String> accounts) {
        Random r = new Random(seed); // (1)!
        List<Transfer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
            String from = accounts.get(r.nextInt(accounts.size()));
            String to;
            do {
                to = accounts.get(r.nextInt(accounts.size()));
            } while (to.equals(from)); // (2)!
            out.add(new Transfer(from, to, 100 + r.nextInt(1_000_000)));
        }
        return out;
    }

    private RandomTransfers() {
    }
}
  1. Seeded randomness: the same seed always produces the same data, so a failure is reproducible.
  2. Generated data must still be valid (no self-transfers), or failures are noise.
package com.handbook.testing.testdata.ledger;

import com.handbook.testing.testdata.ledger.RandomTransfers.Transfer;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class LedgerPropertyDemo {

    /** System under test, with a bug: credits above INR 5,000 are rounded down to an even paisa, leaking money. */
    static Map<String, Long> apply(List<Transfer> transfers, boolean buggy) {
        Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>();
        for (Transfer t : transfers) {
            long credited = buggy && t.paise() > 500_000 ? t.paise() - (t.paise() % 2) : t.paise();
            balances.merge(t.from(), -t.paise(), Long::sum);
            balances.merge(t.to(), credited, Long::sum);
        }
        return balances;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== Banking: A Ledger Invariant Checked on 10,000 Generated Transfers ===");
        List<String> accounts = List.of("A", "B", "C", "D", "E");
        long seed = 20261101L;
        List<Transfer> transfers = RandomTransfers.generate(seed, 10_000, accounts);
        for (boolean buggy : new boolean[] {false, true}) {
            long sum = apply(transfers, buggy).values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
            System.out.println((buggy ? "buggy ledger  " : "correct ledger") + ": sum of all balances = " + sum
                    + (sum == 0 ? " -> invariant holds" : " -> INVARIANT BROKEN, replay with seed " + seed));
        }
        System.out.println("Same seed, same 10,000 transfers: first transfer is always " + transfers.get(0));
    }
}

Output:

=== Banking: A Ledger Invariant Checked on 10,000 Generated Transfers ===
correct ledger: sum of all balances = 0 -> invariant holds
buggy ledger  : sum of all balances = -2532 -> INVARIANT BROKEN, replay with seed 20261101
Same seed, same 10,000 transfers: first transfer is always Transfer[from=E, to=C, paise=67735]

Why generated data here:

  • Invariants ("sum is zero", "balance never negative") are best tested across many inputs.
  • Edge cases (large amounts, repeated pairs) appear without anyone thinking of them.
  • This is the idea behind property-based testing tools like jqwik, which also shrink failures to minimal examples.
Unit Tests: TestDataBuilderTest.java 
package com.handbook.testing;

import com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.PremiumCalculator;
import com.handbook.testing.testdata.ledger.RandomTransfers;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;

import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.grocery.OrderBuilder.anOrder;
import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.aHighRiskDriver;
import static com.handbook.testing.testdata.insurance.Drivers.anExperiencedSafeDriver;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class TestDataBuilderTest {

    @Test
    void freeDeliveryAboveThreshold() {
        assertThat(anOrder().withSubtotal(49_900).build().deliveryFeePaise()).isZero();
    }

    @Test
    void expressAddsThirtyRupees() {
        assertThat(anOrder().withSubtotal(49_900).express().build().deliveryFeePaise()).isEqualTo(3_000);
    }

    @Test
    void firstOrderIsAlwaysFree() {
        assertThat(anOrder().express().firstOrder().build().deliveryFeePaise()).isZero();
    }

    @Test
    void highRiskPaysMoreThanSafe() {
        LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1);
        assertThat(PremiumCalculator.annualPremiumPaise(aHighRiskDriver().build(), today))
                .isGreaterThan(PremiumCalculator.annualPremiumPaise(anExperiencedSafeDriver().build(), today));
    }

    @Test
    void generatedDataIsReproducibleAndValid() {
        var a = RandomTransfers.generate(42, 500, List.of("X", "Y", "Z"));
        assertThat(a).isEqualTo(RandomTransfers.generate(42, 500, List.of("X", "Y", "Z")));
        assertThat(a).allSatisfy(t -> assertThat(t.from()).isNotEqualTo(t.to()));
    }
}

7. Where It Lives in Real Frameworks
docs.text: Where Test data JUnit 5 @ParameterizedTest with @MethodSource feeding builders jqwik @Property, Arbitraries, shrinking Instancio Instancio.of(Order.class).set(field(Order::express), true).create() Spring @Sql scripts, TestEntityManager; builders save through repositories Testcontainers Seed data per test with builders + repositories rather than shared dumps

docs.title: 8. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Tests show only what matters Another class per important type to maintain Constructor changes touch one place Hidden defaults can surprise ("why is the customer in Bengaluru?") Personas speak the business language Object Mothers grow into god classes if unmanaged Generated data finds edge cases Random data without seeds causes unreproducible failures

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Shared mutable builders

A builder stored in a static field and modified by one test leaks state into the next, making results depend on test order (coding challenge). Create a fresh builder per test, or make builders immutable.

Relying on a default in an assertion

If a test asserts the fee for pincode 560034 but never sets the pincode, a change to the default breaks it mysteriously. Set explicitly every value you assert on.

Object Mother explosion

aYoungDriverInMumbaiWithOneClaimAndASportsCar(): dozens of factory methods. Return builders and let tests compose.

Unseeded randomness

new Random() in test data makes failures impossible to reproduce. Always seed and print the seed.

docs.title: 10. Senior / Architect Deep Dive (10–15 yrs)
docs.text:
Builders as a design signal. If building a valid object for a test needs 15 lines even with a builder, the production type probably has too many responsibilities, or invariants aren't enforced in the constructor. Use the pain to drive design.

Shared test fixtures module. In a multi-module build, put builders and mothers in a test-fixtures artefact (Gradle's java-test-fixtures plugin) so other modules' tests reuse the same, maintained definitions instead of copying them.

Integration tests. Build with builders, persist through the real repository (Testcontainers database), and clean up per test (transaction rollback or truncation). Avoid large shared SQL dumps: nobody knows which rows a test depends on.

War story: tests that passed only alphabetically

A banking team's test class kept one AccountBuilder in a static field. testA_frozenAccount set frozen = true; every later test then built frozen accounts. Tests passed in IntelliJ (alphabetical order) but failed randomly on CI once JUnit 5 ran methods in a different order and later in parallel. The team lost a week to "flaky CI". Fix: immutable record-based builders and a fresh base per test; JUnit's random method order enabled to surface hidden coupling. Lesson: test data must be independent per test, and builders are data.

docs.text:
Test Data Builder Object Mother Builder (GoF) Fixtures (SQL/JSON) Purpose Readable test objects Named scenarios Construct complex objects in production Preloaded data Defaults Yes, all fields Persona-specific Usually none Whatever is in the file Flexibility High Low (high when returning builders) High Low

See Builder (the production pattern), Test Doubles and Value Object (builders produce valid values).

docs.title: 12. Interview Corner
13. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Builder: valid defaults, override only what matters.
  • Object Mother: named personas that return builders.
  • Set explicitly anything you assert on.
  • Fresh or immutable builders per test; never shared mutable ones.
  • Generated data: always seeded, always valid.
assertThat(anOrder().withSubtotal(30_000).express().build().deliveryFeePaise()).isEqualTo(5_500);
